en: Śrīḥ.
The *Nārāyaṇīya*, composed by Śrī Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa,
accompanied by the commentary titled *Bhaktapriyā* composed by Deśamaṅgalavārya.
I bow down to Gajānana, the Goddess of Speech, Vyāsa, the slayer of Kaṃsa, and my gurus; to Bhūteśa, Īśa, and those who grant the desired objects.
This hymn called the *Nārāyaṇīya*, consisting of a compendium of the meaning of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, is heart-pleasing, priceless, most brilliant, and the dawning dispeller of darkness;
it shines with unsurpassed excellence upon the throats of the virtuous as something ever-fresh.
This commentary upon it is now composed by me according to my understanding, for it is dear to those who possess devotion.
The glorification of the Lord’s glory in this work of mine is incidental;
I endeavor in this way not for the sake of establishing myself as a commentator.

In this regard, the venerable poet Nārāyaṇa—whose fame is honored by all connoisseurs due to his having realized the true essence of the meaning of the entire Veda, his mastery of the further shore of the ocean of verbal supreme Brahman, and his status as a supreme devotee (paramabhāgavata)—desiring, out of supreme compassion, to compose for the grace of his devotees a jewel of a hymn named *Nārāyaṇīya* following the meaning of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*, first [addresses] the very beginning of the hymn he intends to undertake with the first verse, for the sake of its completion without obstacle and its successful progress.

And for the sake of accomplishing all the desired goals of the audience, he performs an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) consisting of the recollection of the Supreme Reality— the source of the ten-fold divine play (*līlā*) such as the creation and withdrawal of the universe— which is the subject matter of the hymn:

"It is of the nature of intense bliss and consciousness, incomparable, free from the limitations of time and space, eternally liberated, and that which is being manifested by hundreds of thousands of Vedas."

When the reality of Brahman, which consists of the great goals of human life, is seen even slightly and indistinctly, it nevertheless shines forth directly; alas, such is the good fortune of the people in Gurupavanapura! || 1 ||

Regarding the word *sāndra*: the connection is that Brahman manifests directly in Gurupavanapura. Brahman is the pure consciousness that is the support of all and pervades all. In Gurupavanapura—that is, in the sacred field well-known by that name—it "manifests directly" for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees; that is to say, assuming a form composed of exceedingly pure *sattva* for the purpose of favoring devotees, it becomes an object of visual perception for all people under the guise of an image, while its own true nature of being, consciousness, and bliss remains concealed.

Now, in response to the doubt—"Is it said that the Brahman, whether with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*), manifests directly?"—the author says: "That very [Brahman]" (*tattāvat*). The word *tāvat* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). The meaning is: "that very [Brahman] which is characterized by the aforementioned attributes, namely, the partless (*niṣkala*) Brahman. Furthermore, the non-difference of the pure being (*śuddhasattva*) from the partless Brahman will be demonstrated in the section on "unwavering" (*niṣkampa*). Alternatively, the word *tāvat* signifies sequence (*kramārtha*).

The meaning is that Brahman manifests, in due order, as something directly visible, as something mental, and as the nature of self-luminous consciousness. This is the underlying intention: for those who, having directly perceived the Lord of Pavanapura (Ujjain), the venerable Guru, through their eyes and worship Him with devotion characterized by hearing, chanting, and so forth, all impurities are instantly destroyed by the arising of devotion characterized by love. Consequently, through the purity of their minds, they immediately become qualified by the attainment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).

By the power of Śrī Hari alone, the Teacher of all the worlds, the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) arises that "I am the undivided Brahman. Being directed toward Brahman, it sublates the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) consisting of the body and so forth—which is the effect of ignorance residing in Brahman—by means of subverting that very ignorance; it likewise sublates the mental modification itself, which possesses the form of the undivided [Brahman]. Then, like the unity of the original object and its reflection when a mirror or such is absent, Brahman—existent, conscious, and blissful, non-different from the inner self—abides as the nature of self-luminous consciousness.

Thus, he says—"Ah, the good fortune of people!"—to show that the attainment of the supreme human goal occurs without effort, having as its sole root the ripening of past merit (*sukṛta-paripāka*). The meaning is that the good fortune of people is inferred from the completeness of the means for attaining the human goal. By the general statement "of people" (*janānām*), it is illuminated that everyone possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the worship of the Blessed One. "Ah" (*hanta*) expresses joy.

The manifestation of joy when people possess good fortune demonstrates, like that of Śuka, Nārada, and other exalted servants of the Lord, His supreme compassion and His eagerness to accomplish the welfare of others. Now, one might ask: for what purpose is this said—“Brahman shines; oh, how great is the good fortune of people”? It cannot be for the sake of one’s own realization, because the employment of such a statement would otherwise be redundant. Nor is it to inform another, since no supplementary explanatory statement such as “Worship Him” is heard following it. To this, we reply: not so.

Just as when some non-expert says, "This ground contains a treasure; come now, you are fortunate," the listeners supply the remainder of the sentence by supplying the ellipsis: "By this [statement], it is said that those who desire it should take possession of the treasure"—in the same way, here too, the remainder of the sentence must be supplied.

And thus, you who have somehow obtained this human birth through the ripening of merit accumulated over many lifetimes, should realize that this is the very secret of instruction: that by serving the Lord of Śrī Guruvāyupura—the Supreme Brahman who has assumed a physical form out of compassion for His devotees—preceded by the yoga of devotion, you shall experience the supreme goal of human existence. Now, one might object: "But 'fortune' (bhāgya) is said to be the fruit of past actions (karma)."

If it is argued that if the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*) were produced by that [ritual action], it would follow that it is impermanent, we say no; for the fruits of ritual action are exhausted by the fulfillment of the qualification (*adhikāritva*) [for knowledge]. As it has been said: "The ultimate purpose of these [obligatory rites] such as the *nitya* and others is the purification of the intellect. He states the definition of the essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman: "Reality is of the nature of intense bliss and consciousness. Bliss (*ānanda*) is happiness; consciousness (*avabodha*) is knowledge. That whose essence (*ātmā*) or nature is intense—that is, dense—bliss and consciousness is described as such.

The density of bliss (*ānanda*) consists in its being unconditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as garlands or sandalwood paste; and the density of consciousness (*avabodha*) consists in its being unconditioned by objects such as pots and the like. As it has been stated by the learned: "When every object of cognition that exists in the world is disregarded, that which remains as pure consciousness (*bodhamātra*) is Brahman—such is the certainty of the Vedānta."

Thus [it is said]. Reality (*tattva*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-sat*), because it is well-known as the self (*ātman*) of everything; for no one has the realization that "I am not. And so, since Brahman is established as the innermost self (*pratyagātman*) through the very notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*), there is no disagreement regarding its existence—this is the intended meaning. By these two qualifiers, the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman as "Existence-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānanda*) is stated, just as [one says] "the moon is the most excellent light."

One might object: "Even though Brahman possesses such characteristics, it does not descend into the range of direct experience. Therefore, let it be demonstrated with an illustration as to what it is like. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is incomparable" (*anupamitam*). The sense is that because there exists nothing else—neither of the same class nor of a different class—it is impossible to provide any comparison for Brahman. By this, the non-duality (*advitīyatva*) of Brahman is also stated by implication.

If it be objected: "Since the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as between the individual souls and their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*), is manifest while one is awake, how can Brahman be non-dual?", we reply: "Not so. Because the manifold of difference is falsely imagined upon Brahman by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), it is unreal—like a snake [superimposed] on a rope. Therefore, Brahman does not possess a second reality. And this ignorance, like the art of a magician, is a certain power residing in Brahman that, without deluding its own substrate—the magician-like Brahman—creates the entire phenomenal world.

Since there is no difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitatva*) is established. If it is argued that there is an inference for difference—namely, that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are distinct because they possess contradictory attributes, like fire and ice—that is not so; for the subject matter of this inference is sublated by the scriptural texts and traditional authorities (*smṛti*) concerning oneness. If it is further argued that if the Lord were one with the individual soul, He would be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), and if the individual souls were the Lord, the consequence would be the absence of transmigratory existence for them—that too is not so, because both states are logically consistent due to the distinction between ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*).

For instance, what is called *vidyā* (knowledge) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord, characterized primarily by the power of manifestation (*vikṣepa-śakti*), by which the Lord performs creation and so forth. What is called *avidyā* (ignorance) is the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*), characterized primarily by the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*); it is because of this that the soul, though being the Lord, becomes a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) through the distinction of the adjuncts produced by it. Therefore, even though the individual soul and the Lord are one, the existence of transmigratory existence due to ignorance and its absence due to knowledge is not logically untenable.

Because the Lord is beginningless and devoid of qualities, the attributes of transmigratory existence such as old age and death do not belong to Him, just as agency, enjoyership, and so forth do not belong to one who has awakened from a dream. Enough of this digression. Now, raising the objection that agency, enjoyership, and the like might be the inherent nature of the Self—such that there could never be a separation from them—the author says: "free from the limits of time and space."

"From time" means that which is a limit in terms of time and space; "freed from" those two means devoid of them. Consequently, since Brahman—which is formless like space and immutable—cannot logically possess conjunction with action and so forth, it follows that it lacks the status of being an agent or an enjoyer. Furthermore, the eternality of Brahman consists in its existence both before and after the emergence of the phenomenal world of effects.

And "pervasion" (vibhutva) is like the persistence of clay or gold as the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) in jars, earrings, and so forth; likewise, because Brahman—the material cause of all—is also interwoven everywhere as the cause in bodies and the like, it possesses all-pervasiveness. Therefore, by this, it should be understood that the definition of Brahman as the cause of the world—which exists as long as the object to be defined does—is stated by implication as an extrinsic definition (tāṭasthya-lakṣaṇa). Thus, when there is a need for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the reality established by these two definitions, he says "nigama... [and so on].

The *nigamas* are the *upaniṣads*; "a hundred thousand of them" is intended to indicate their great number. The meaning is: by means of many sentences from the *upaniṣads*. "Being manifested in a manner that is unclear" means being presented through implication (*lakṣaṇā*) with a specific intent (*tātparya*), according to the marks such as the opening and concluding passages (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra*). Alternatively, the connection is: "it is unclear at the mere sight [of it]. Even when there is knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, contrary notions, misconceptions, and so forth, do not cease immediately, just like a magical illusion (*māyā*).

Therefore, the sense is that when those [impediments] are removed through hearing, reflection, and so forth, the knowledge of Brahman remains as it culminates in direct experience (*anubhava*). Now, one might ask: what is the fruit when such a vision of Brahman occurs? To this he says: "consisting of the great human goal" (*punaḥ uru-puruṣārthātmakam*). "Punaḥ" means after the knowledge of Brahman. "Uruḥ puruṣārthaḥ" refers to liberation (*mokṣa*).

Its state as *ur* (the supreme) consists in its being free from the attachment of suffering, and its perfection arises from its lack of limitation by time and space; for other human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are produced by karma, whereas that [state] is not. The phrase "consisting of the human goal" means that immediately upon the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman itself abides in the form of the human goal. With the intention that one who has thus become Brahman does not return again, he qualifies Brahman as "eternally liberated" (*nityamukta*). It is eternally liberated, meaning it is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of *māyā* and its effects.

The sense is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is impossible for that which is non-dual to have any connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) or the body and so forth imagined by it. And thus, because the state of liberation is unproduced (*ajanya*), there is no returning again; this is the sense. In this way, by the two words "the Reality consisting of dense bliss and consciousness," the definition of the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) as "Brahman is Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (*saccidānanda*) has been stated. By the word "incomparable" (*anupamita*), its non-duality (*advitīyatva*) is stated.

By stating that [Brahman] is "freed from the limits of time and space," it is declared that even though Brahman is one with the individual soul (*jīva*), qualities such as agency—which belong to the soul—cannot possibly exist in Brahman. By implication, its *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (circumstantial definition) is also stated. By saying it is "illuminated by hundreds of thousands of scriptures," the authority of the Upaniṣads is affirmed. By stating that such a Brahman "shines directly in Gurupavanapura," it is declared that the vision of Brahman—which is otherwise achievable only through extreme effort—is easily accomplished by all people.

"Ah, the good fortune of people!"—thus it is stated that the qualification for the vision of Brahman has merit (*sukṛta*) alone as its sole root. "It is indistinct when merely seen"—thus it is stated that the experience of the bliss of Brahman is to be accomplished through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means. Furthermore, by the phrase "consisting of the great human goals," the twofold fruit of the vision of Brahman is shown: the eradication of the suffering of *saṃsāra* and the attainment of the bliss of Brahman.

By the statement "eternally liberated," the non-return of one who has attained Brahman is indeed demonstrated by the principle, "There is no return, according to the scriptural word. Thus, because of the stated nature of Brahman as the object of worship, and because the purport of phrases such as "Brahman shines" and "we meditate upon the Supreme" is one and the same, the meaning of the first verse of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* is shown by this very verse. Furthermore, in this hymn, Brahman is indicated as the subject matter (*viṣaya*) by virtue of being that which is propounded; its attainment is the purpose (*prayojana*); and fortunate ones are indicated as the qualified seekers (*adhikārin*). || 1 ||

Thus, although the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) have already been established by implication through the first verse— which was devoted to the performance of auspicious rites— the author now sets them forth explicitly for the sake of easy understanding by the audience:

"When such a rare object has thus become as easily attained as if held in the palm of one's hand, that people nevertheless honors it with their body, speech, or mind— alas, this meanness is manifest!"

We, for our part, shall now take refuge in that very Lord of the City of the Preceptor’s Wind (Śrīnivāsa), with a most steadfast mind, for the sake of destroying all afflictions of the universe without exception. || 2 ||

"Thus" (*evam*): here, by the word *vastu* (entity) used without qualification, Brahman—which is real in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-sat*)—is denoted, because the qualified term is observed to be used only for false objects. That [Brahman] is difficult to attain, meaning it can be known or reached only with difficulty; for it can be understood only through hearing, reflection, and so forth, by means of approaching a teacher, provided one is endowed with the fourfold qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). "In this manner" (*evam*) refers to the mode described; it signifies ease and lack of effort. The two terms *hastalabdha* (obtained in hand) and *prāpya* (to be attained) illuminate this facility.

That people, even when such a rare object is thus easily obtained and held in the palm of their hand, still worship another deity, sense-objects, or the like—whether through body, speech, or mind—is indeed a tragedy! This is nothing but pettiness, worthlessness, and a lack of discrimination; it is, in short, manifest and universally acknowledged. He speaks of the distinction of the discerning one: "We... The plural "we" is used for the sake of humility regarding oneself. By saying "these [people]," he demonstrates his own intense zeal for the worship of the Lord.

Alternatively, the listeners are also included by the words "we here. We, for our part, do not act with such meanness; rather, with a mind firmly resolved that devotion to Him alone is the highest good, we take refuge in and serve the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of the City of the Wind (Kāñcī), the Guru. Here, He shows the fruit for those who possess desires—namely, "viśva... etc. It is for the sake of removing (*apahatyai*), that is, destroying, all afflictions (*viśvapīḍānām*), including those pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*) and so forth.

Alternatively, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the removal of all suffering, because it consists precisely in the cessation of every form of affliction. By this, the distinction among types of practitioners (*adhikārin*) is also demonstrated in the hymn: those who serve Him without desire for rewards are the highest practitioners; those who serve with a desire for fruits are the middling practitioners; and those who, possessing a sense of duality, worship other deities while desiring rewards are the lowest practitioners. Thus, "for the removal of all suffering" states the purpose (*prayojana*).

The object [of devotion] is indicated by the epithet of the Blessed One, "the Self of all without remainder" (*niśśeṣātmā*). He is the Self—that is, the cause—of all things moving and unmoving; or, he is the one whose Self—that is, whose essential nature—is the entire manifold of moving and unmoving beings, meaning he is the Self of all (*sarvātmā*); or, he is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of all; or, he is the Self—that is, the essential nature—of all [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, meaning he consists of all the gods. Here, devotional practice (*sādhanabhakti*) in the form of action is also indicated as an object—by means of "body, speech, or mind. As it has been said:
Devotion is indeed said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the categories of the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana). For the goal is causeless love, while the means consists of ritual action.
"Furthermore, that [sādhanā] is said to be ninefold in the Purāṇa, consisting of the nature of practice.

Here, *vācā* refers to glorification (*kīrtana*); *tanvā* refers to worship, salutation, and prostration (*arcana-vandana-namaskāra*); and *dhiyā* refers to hearing, remembering, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender (*śravaṇa-smaraṇa-dāsya-sakhya-ātmanivedana*). Alternatively, human birth is a rare object; thus, by being the locus of Brahminhood, knowledge, and the proficiency of the senses, it is as if "obtained in the palm of one's hand," which indicates the absence of [other forms of] service and so forth. Even this being so, people resort to other things—such as sense objects—which are easily obtained even in other bodies.

"Alas! But we," and so forth, is the same [as previously stated]. And thus, in this hymn (*stotra*), the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*) have been shown. Herein, [the following points are indicated]: "Dharma here is free from hypocrisy"; "one worships with body, speech, or mind"; "the real reality"; "regarding the difficult-to-attain object"; "what need is there for others?"; "alas, one worships otherwise with body, speech, or mind"; "the uprooting of the three-fold suffering"; "for the removal of all affliction"; "immediately it is seized within the heart"; "with a most steady mind"; "the Lord."

The meaning of this [verse] should also be seen as identical to the meaning of the second verse of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*, due to the similarity of the sense of words such as "the self entirely" (*niśśeṣātmānam*). Furthermore, another meaning delights the hearts of the sensitive: that which is difficult to obtain is the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* Purāṇa; yet, even when it has been placed in one's hand—having become easily accessible through the lineage of Brahmā, Nārada, and Vyāsa—if a person still resorts to other Purāṇas or to poetry and the like, that is clearly nothing but meanness.

We, for our part, take refuge in this very Lord of the City of the Preceptor’s Wind (Gurupavanapurādhīśa), who is the primary subject expounded in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, by means of speech that is limited in extent and consists of a summary of the meaning of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata; the sense is that we shall summarize the meaning of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata in the form of a hymn to the Lord of the City of the Preceptor’s Wind. Is it only a portion of the meaning of the Bhāgavata? No, he says: "the whole self" (*niśśeṣātmānam*). His "self" (*ātman*) consists of the entirety of the meaning of the twelve cantos, characterized by the tenfold marks and divine sports.

He states the intermediate purpose with the words "viśve" and so forth: for the removal of suffering and for the liberation of all people, including women, Śūdras, and others; for indeed, there is eligibility for the recitation of this hymn even for women, Śūdras, and the like. By the phrase "with a most steady mind," it is suggested that this hymn is a compendium of the essence, through the extraction of the core and the stabilization of the mind.

By the word *tanvā* ("with the body"), its nature as consisting of more than a thousand verses is indicated; by the word *dhiyā* ("with the intellect"), which denotes the remembrance of the Blessed One, its possession of qualities such as sweetness obtained through His grace is manifested. Furthermore, in this way, the formal declaration of the intention to compose (*cikīrṣitapratijñā*) such a hymn is also made.

In this context, one should observe that the meaning of the third verse of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata* is also alluded to by this [verse], through the perception of a similarity of meaning between the original and its reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*) in such phrases as: "the fruit of the Veda-tree, the *Bhāgavata*, which is a nectar difficult to obtain," versus "having become easily obtained, as if held in the hand"; "it has fallen upon the earth from the mouth of Śuka," versus "that people resort to something else is indeed meanness"; and "drink the *Bhāgavata*," versus "we here are connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor (*rasika*) and seekers of devotion (*bhāvuka*)."

The fact that the meaning of two verses is subsumed within one also indicates its nature as a summary (*saṅgraha*). Furthermore, it is implied by this very [verse] that this hymn should be recited with reverence by all, because it is precisely through this that the primacy of *bhakti-yoga* is being indicated. To explain: the object known as *bhakti-yoga* is difficult to attain; yet, even when that has been placed in the palm of one's hand, to pursue something else—whether knowledge or ritual action—is nothing but pettiness. The rest is to be inferred.

Thus, only a mere indication of the direction has been shown regarding the greatness of the words of the illustrious poet Nārāyaṇa, who has become a vessel for the Lord’s compassion and whose speech possesses a profound majesty of manifold meanings. Now, it was said that this [work] is to be honored by devotees because it is devoted to *bhaktiyoga*. What, then, is this so-called *bhakti*? It is said: *bhakti* is the stabilization of the mind upon the Lord through a specific means (*upāya*). Furthermore, that essence of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) is manifold, being divided according to whether it is mixed with enjoined or prohibited actions, with knowledge, and so forth. Moreover, Bopadeva states that it is ninefold according to the distinctions of the means, such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.

Others, however, asserting that this same [argument] should be stated regarding devotion (*bhakti*), declare that devotion is not a rasa. For it is said: "Devotion is not a rasa, because it lacks the defining characteristics of a rasa;

for 'a stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) brought to a state of relish by means of the determinants (*vibhāvas*), the consequents (*anubhāvas*), the involuntary states (*sāttvikas*), and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) is known as rasa.'"

Such is the definition of rasa (aesthetic flavor). For example, in the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other rasas, there is a permanent emotion (*sthāyī bhāva*) such as love (*rati*); the excitants (*vibhāvas*) are the heroine, the hero, the moon, gentle breezes, and so forth; the ensuants (*anubhāvas*) are side-long glances, gazes, and so forth; the involuntary states (*sāttvikas*) are paralysis, perspiration, and so forth; and the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāriṇas*) are despondency, languor, and so forth. [If it is argued that] devotion (*bhakti*) does not attain the status of rasa because of the absence of such a conjunction of excitants and the rest—this is not so, for here too the totality of the conditions for rasa (*rasasāmagrī*) exists.

The stable emotion (*sthāyī bhāva*) consists of fixing the mind upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa by whatever means possible, according to the statement in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*: "Therefore, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa by whatever means possible. In that regard, the means are ninefold.

Thus it was stated by Bopadeva: "Because the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*) itself is experienced in the forms of the comic, the erotic, the pathetic, the furious, the terrifying, the loathsome, the tranquil, the marvelous, and the heroic"; and also: "'Devotional rasa' is the wonder produced by hearing and so forth the life stories—consisting of the nine rasas—of Viṣṇu or of his devotees as described by poets such as Vyāsa. Therefore, when these [rasas] are applied to the Blessed Lord, they attain the status of devotional rasa. Govinda and the cowherd girls are the *ālambana-vibhāvas* (the foundational excitants).

The moon, the gentle breeze, hearing [the Lord’s] deeds, and so forth, are the *uddīpana-vibhāvas* (excitants). Glances, sidelong looks, paralysis, perspiration, and so forth, are the *anubhāvas* (consequents). Despair, exhaustion, apprehension, fortitude, and so forth, are the *vyabhicāribhāvas* (transitory states), as applicable. Thus, even when this totality of conditions is present, the exclusion of devotion (*bhakti*) [from the category of rasa] is based solely on its being an external factor for the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Nor should it be said that because devotion does not have everything as its object, it cannot ascend to the status of *rasa*.

And thus, since even the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments would result in being non-sentiments (*arasa*) by virtue of not having as their object a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), and so forth, it is established that devotion (*bhakti*) alone possesses the nature of a sentiment (*rasatva*). Due to the experience of such devotion, devotees (*bhakta*) are also of nine kinds:
"The Gopīs [love] from desire; Kaṃsa from fear; the kings headed by Caidya from hatred;
the Vṛṣṇis from kinship; you from affection; and we, O Lord, from devotion."

In the printed edition, the portion beginning with "nanu" and ending with "sugamam"—which constitutes the explanation of the third verse—is misplaced within that section, extending from the start until the end of the phrase "uparistham upādīyate."

Thus it is stated in the *Bhāgavata*. The form of Viṣṇu to be worshipped by such devotees is also fivefold, according to the division into Puruṣa, Brahma, Giriśa, Viṣṇu, and Nirguṇa. Among these, Boppadeva maintains that the form of Viṣṇu alone, consisting of pure *sattva*, is the most worthy of worship. We shall explain the sequence of worship later on. All of this, indicated in the second verse, will be easily understood by those who follow it further below. || 2 ||
Having thus directed the listeners by demonstrating the subject matter and the purpose, he praises the Blessed One while describing His form for the sake of their accomplishment in worship:

"That which is *sattva*, stainless because it is not delimited by anything else—by means of that, Your body is composed of the elements and the sense-faculties; such is the statement of Vyāsa heard many times."
Because of its transparency, it possesses a form that is the manifestation of the inner essence of consciousness and the bliss of others;
in that body, which is sweet to the ear and the mind and easy to grasp, the fortunate ones take delight.

"Sattva" refers to that which is well-known. "By the absence of calculation" (*aparikalana*) means by the absence of that "calculation" (*parikalana*), which is the mutual mixing of the other two, *rajas* and *tamas*. By that [absence], [it is] stainless and pure *sattva*. "By that much" (*tāvat*) means by that very material cause. "By the elements" (*bhūtaiḥ*) means by those produced in the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*). "By the elements and senses" (*bhūtendriyaiḥ*) means by the five elements and the eleven senses; this also implies the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. "O Bhūman!"—this is taken from the subsequent position according to the maxim of the lion's glance (*siṃhāvalokita*).

"By these [means], Your body—the *līlā-śarīra*—was chosen by Your own will. Regarding this point, there is the statement of Vyāsa, who is regarded as Your very self in the words "I am Vyāsa among the sages," serving as authoritative evidence; this is heard many times, repeatedly, in the Purāṇas.

And there are scriptural statements such as: "He assumed a human form," "A pure and exalted *sattva*," "Pure *sattva* for the sake of security," "Consisting of a portion of Nārāyaṇa," and "In that body composed of *sattva*, indeed, the highest blessings shall accrue to men. Thus, that form has been heard of many times. Because of its transparency, like a crystal, it is exceedingly stainless.

That Brahman which is the supreme bliss-consciousness, whose sole essence is the one flavor of *cidānanda*, is "uncovered" (*acchādita*) and "unconditioned" (*anupahita*). That [body] into whose womb this has entered by way of reflection is "one whose womb is the uncovered supreme bliss-consciousness. For this very reason, it is "of a radiant nature" (*nirbhāsarūpa*). This is a qualification of the body. The intended meaning is as follows: because the dullness (*jāḍya*)—which is the aspect to be manifested—is suppressed by the supreme bliss-consciousness that has entered that body composed of pure *sattva* due to its extreme transparency, the body attains oneness with that supreme bliss-consciousness.

As it has been stated in the *Amṛtataraṅgiṇī*: "Because of the extreme transparency of Your body, that which reflects within it—the Brahman whose sole essence is consciousness and bliss—has its own inertia eclipsed and becomes itself of the sole essence of consciousness and bliss. The connection [of the words] is as follows: "That body of Yours is of the nature of a radiance whose interior consists of the supreme bliss and consciousness, which are not obscured because of its transparency."

"In that" means: in the form (vapuḥ) which has been established as non-different from the Supreme Consciousness through such passages as "This indeed is the Great Brahman to be sought," and "Kṛṣṇa, however, is the Lord himself. "Blessed ones" means those who, by having accepted the path of devotion, are free from the labor of the many practices prescribed in other paths. "They delight" means they practice devotion characterized by love (prema). He states the reason for this: "sweet to the ear and the mind."

The meaning is that, because it is endowed with sweetness, it gladdens all the senses through hearing, remembering, and so forth; for this very reason, his *vigraha*—his physical form—is *sugraha*, meaning easily grasped. || 3 ||
Having thus established the form of the Blessed One as consisting of pure being, he establishes its non-difference from the partless Brahman:

[He is] in the stainless ocean of Brahman, which is unwavering, eternally full, consisting of the nectar of boundless supreme bliss, and most beautiful with the many garlands of liberated souls merged within it.
They say that the most stainless *sattva* is indeed like the shimmering of a great wave;
yet, O Infinite One, how is it that You, who are partless (*niṣkala*), are called "possessing parts" (*sakala*)? This statement applies only to Your own creative energies (*kalās*). || 4 ||

Regarding the word "unwavering" (*niṣkampa*): therein, he establishes the similarity of Brahman to the ocean through four qualifiers. "Unwavering" means changeless; elsewhere, it means unshakeable and profound. "Eternally full" means undivided; elsewhere, it means that while during the rainy season there is a flood of water from many great rivers, in summer it remains uniform even when that [flood] is absent. "Boundless" means unlimited by time, space, or limiting conditions. It is "ambrosia" (*pīyūṣa*) because it is to be tasted by the liberated; it is "of that nature" (*tadrūpe*).

"Elsewhere" refers to that from which there is boundless supreme bliss—a bliss surpassing the pleasures derived from women, sandalwood, and the like—and from which proceeds the form, the manifestation, and the origin of that nectar; thus he is so described. "By the multitude" means by the assembly or collection of many liberated souls who have attained union with Brahman (*brahmasāyujya*) and reached the state of non-return after merging. [The phrase] "most auspicious" means most captivating to the mind; the sense is that it generates the desire for liberation even in others.

"Except for pearl necklaces—that is, clusters of pearl gems—[it is] most beautiful and adorned; [it is] the stainless ocean of Brahman. The stainlessness of Brahman consists in its freedom from the taint of *māyā* and its effects. In the case of the ocean, it refers to its lack of turbidity. In such an ocean of Brahman, that which is like the surging of waves—the rising of *kallolas*, or waves—is the exceedingly pure and stainless *sattva*. This is the intended meaning: [The following verse: "In the stainless ocean of Brahman... [is explained as follows: The stainlessness of Brahman is its being devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of *māyā* and its products. In the case of the ocean, it is its lack of turbidity. In such an ocean of Brahman, there is the manifestation of waves (*kallola-ullāsa*), that is, the rising of waves (*taraṅgas*); with that it is comparable. It means the *sattva* that is more stainless and pure. This is the underlying intention:

Just as there is no difference between the ocean and its waves apart from their being designated by terms such as "billow" and so forth, likewise there is no difference between Brahman and the pure *sattva*. Regarding this, he states the authority: "They say," with the word "the teachers" (*ācāryāḥ*) understood as the ellipsis.

For they say: "Alternatively, existence (*sattva*) is indeed a single, ever-new wave of the ocean of consciousness-bliss," and so forth. Now, if pure existence (*śuddhasattva*) is non-different from Brahman, what follows for the form of the Lord? To this he says: "That is His Self" (*tadātmā*). That is to say, He whose very Self is that existence is the venerable Form (*śrīmūrti*). The statement "Why are You not partless (*niṣkala*)?"—meaning "You are indeed the partless Brahman"—is thus logically consistent.

Now, one might object: "In that case, the term *sakala* (the manifest), having no other possible application, would be without a referent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "*sakala*. The implication is that the word *sakala* is applied only to those partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*) of Your powers (*kalā*). O Infinite One! O Perfect One! You, however, are indeed the partless Brahman (*niṣkalabrahman*)—this is the meaning. || 4 ||

Thus, O Lord, having reflected upon the emergence of the essential nature of the Form (mūrti), he now reflects upon its manifestation: "O Unborn One! Although You are devoid of activity and without cause, because You engage in the action called 'Beholding,' by that very act the latent primordial nature (prakṛti)—though nearly non-existent—arises at the beginning of a kalpa."

O Vaikuṇṭha, whose majesty and power are unimpeded! You, being that very essence, assume and maintain a certain perfectly pure portion of her—which is of the nature of *sattva* and non-obstructive—as Your own form. || 5 ||

Regarding the term *nirvyāpāra*: O Unborn Viṣṇu! although you are inactive (*nirvyāpāra*) and devoid of action (*niṣkriya*), you nevertheless undertake and accept the activity called "inspecting" (*īkṣaṇa*), which consists of impelling *māyā*. The meaning is that it is just as a magnet, though itself inactive, attracts iron merely by its presence. The word *niṣkāraṇam* is an adverb meaning "without cause," where "cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to a motive or purpose. The implication is that the motive for your impelling of *māyā* is not to be known by beings such as ourselves.

As for the statement, "In this way, you perform the activity called 'beholding' (īkṣaṇa)," for that very reason, at the end of two *parārdhas*, when the *prakṛti*—which is *māyā*—having been dissolved, attains dissolution within You, it "rises," meaning it manifests. Here, the words "dissolved" (*līnā*) and "rises" (*udeti*) indicate the absence of production and destruction in *prakṛti*; thus, there is no loss of its beginninglessness (*anāditva*). To the question "When does it rise?", he says: "at the time of the beginning of the *kalpas*. This means at the time of the commencement of the first day of the *kalpas*—the days of Brahmā—at the conclusion of the dissolution of Brahmā.

But not at the beginning of a *kalpa*, for at that time there is no emergence from dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛti*). He qualifies *māyā*—as "the unreal-like" (*asatikalpā*). The meaning is that it is generally unreal, being indefinable in terms of existence or non-existence. O Vaikuṇṭha! O dweller in Vaikuṇṭha! You, the impeller of that *māyā*, having taken up—that is, having extracted—a certain portion of that *māyā* in the form of *sattva*, you assume a form, a body for divine play (*līlāvigraha*), for the sake of showing grace to your devotees.

Now, anticipating the objection that "if He possesses a body, there would be the consequence of transmigratory existence," he says: "it is non-obscuring. He states the reason for this: "because it is perfectly pure. The underlying meaning is as follows: [He is not obscured] by *māyā*, which consists of pure *sattva*— ...[the rest of the sentence continues in the source text].

Because the body, due to its extreme transparency, lacks the capacity to delimit consciousness, the notions of "I" and "mine" cannot arise with respect to the Lord’s playful form (*līlā-vigraha*) which is identical with that consciousness; consequently, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which is rooted in those notions, is likewise impossible for the Blessed One. Now, one might object: "Even though the connection with a body is equal [in both cases], why is there this disparity such that one undergoes transmigratory existence while the other causes it? Dispelling this doubt, he addresses the Blessed One as "one whose power of His own majesty is unimpeded" (*svamahimavibhavākuṇṭha*).

His own greatness consists in yogic sovereignty (*yogaiśvarya*); that itself is his manifestation (*vibhava*) or power (*śakti*). By this, he is "unimpeded," meaning his power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is unobstructed. This is the intended meaning: the individual soul (*jīva*) transmigrates while dependent on *māyā*, whereas the Lord (*īśvara*), possessing a playful body (*līlā-vigraha*) assumed through *māyā* under his own control, performs the play of creation and so forth; thus, there is this great disparity. || 5 ||
Now he describes the beauty of the Lord’s form with two verses: "That [form] of yours, which performs the sport of a playful row of fresh rain-clouds,
which is the singular essence of loveliness, and the descent of full merit for the eyes of virtuous people..."

O Lord of the House of Wind! May you, who are the fearless abode for the playful sport of Lakṣmī and a mass of flowing nectar that sprinkles the bodies of those who contemplate you from within, grant me your grace. 6.

Regarding the word "tat" (that): O Lord of the Marutāgāra! I contemplate—that is, I remember—your body composed of pure *sattva*. "Pratyagra... means exceedingly beautiful, like a water-laden cloud or like a fresh jasmine flower; that is to say, it is dark-complexioned (*śyāmala*). "Lāvaṇyasyaikasāram" means fashioned from the very essence of the substance of beauty alone. "Sukṛtijanadṛśāṃ pūrṇapuṇyāvatāram" means it is the full descent of merit for the eyes of those who have performed virtuous deeds.

In this context, "well-performed deeds" (*sukṛta*) refers to all prescribed actions performed without attachment to their fruits; "people of well-performed deeds" (*sukṛtijana*) are those who perform them. The meaning is that the descent of the full and complete merit of their glances—that very mass of merit perceivable by the eyes of people of well-performed deeds—has transformed into the form of the Lord’s body. Furthermore, it is the fearless abode of His divine play (*līlā*), being the sole object of Lakṣmī’s love, confidence, trust, and so forth.

Furthermore, it sprinkles within the hearts of the contemplative devotees a flood of flowing nectar, a gushing stream of the liquid nectar of Brahman-bliss; the meaning is that by bathing the hearts of the devotees with the liquid nectar of Brahman-bliss, it pacifies all suffering. || 6 ||
"O Unconquered One! Previously, I perceived your creative activity as painful, bringing excessive weariness to existence for those possessing life; yet today I do not perceive it so.

Otherwise, how could living beings, having drunk with their eyes and ears this most sweet form of yours—moistened by the essence of aesthetic flavor—delight in the flood of the supreme nectar-ocean of rasa? (7)

"Alas! [O Ajita! O you who are free from dependence on *māyā*, your creative activity is "painful. Why is this? To this he says: "because it brings about the excessive suffering of worldly existence for those who possess a *jīva*. Here, by the word *jīva*, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is meant; those who "possess" (*bhājin*) that are the *jīvas* themselves. "Suffering of worldly existence" (*bhavakheda*) refers to the pains of birth and death; that which brings these about is so described. Thus was it previously reflected upon and contemplated by me, whose mind was deluded.

He says that this is not so: "I do not recognize it as such. The meaning is: "Now, since my mind is occupied with the savoring of your form, I am certain that this is indeed a great benefit for me. He states this certainty: "If not..."

If you do not create the individual souls (*jīvas*) residing within you, nor the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is their object of experience, then how—and by what means—could the souls drink with their eyes and ears Your body, which is moistened by the essence of consciousness and pervaded internally and externally by the liquid nectar of conscious bliss? Having taken it into their hearts through seeing You, worshipping You, and hearing Your stories, how could they delight in the flood of the ocean of supreme nectar—the ocean of the nectar of ultimate bliss—performing such actions as emerging, submerging, being sprinkled, and tasting [it]?
This is the meaning. || 7 ||

Having thus described the transcendental nature of the Blessed One’s quality of beauty, he now extols the transcendental nature of his capacity to bestow fruits: "O Hari! You stand ever before those who bow to you, even without being requested; you incessantly grant them their desired objects, and you bestow the state dense with supreme bliss. Thus, you are the Pārijāta tree, obtainable by all and yielding limitless fruit. This host of supplicants, however, vainly desires that insignificant tree belonging to Indra’s grove. (8)

Regarding the phrase "of those who bow": in the world, the *pārijāta* tree is known as the bestower of desired fruits; thus, the author describes the Lord’s qualities as surpassing even that. O Hari! You are the *pārijāta*, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) whose very essence is you; for those who worship you, even by a mere salutation, you constantly manifest before them, appearing out of a desire to grant boons.

However, another [type of] wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) does not manifest of its own accord, nor merely through prostration, nor constantly; rather, in his own manuscript, the ninth verse beginning with "out of compassion" (*kāruṇyāt*) is explained as the eighth, and the eighth verse beginning with "to those who bow down" (*namrāṇām*) as the ninth.

It manifests only before those who have gone to heaven after propitiating the gods through their own deeds. Furthermore, it bestows desired objects—the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*)—which are unrequested by those devotees both here and in the hereafter, and which are granted incessantly.

He gives; whereas the other does not give when unasked, nor all desired objects, nor constantly, but rather gives only certain things when requested for them in the hereafter. Moreover, he grants liberation—the goal dense with supreme bliss—to those who serve him without desire; the other, however, does not grant liberation to those who serve either with desire or without desire.

Thus, this Pārijāta tree—which is to be obtained in its entirety by all multitudes of living beings, which is of Your own nature, which yields boundless fruit, and which bestows the fruit known as liberation that is unlimited—is present; yet this host of supplicants, this multitude of seekers, vainly and in vain desires that other, inferior, and unsubstantial tree called Pārijāta belonging to Indra’s grove, meaning they wish to obtain it through great hardship. (8)

Now, one might object: "Since Brahmā, Rudra, and others are also givers of the desired fruits of their devotees due to their equality in lordship (*īśvaratva*), they too should be served. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the distinction of the Blessed Lord from them: "Indeed, other supreme beings grant various desires out of compassion; you, however, are the giver of your own self (*svātmada*) by virtue of your preeminent sovereignty. Others rule over the world and over others; you are the Lord even of yourself. Beings of abundant fortune find great delight in you, who are sweet at every step; yet you, O Śauri, are one who delights only in the Self (*ātmārāma*). O support of an incomparable multitude of virtues, salutations to you! (9)

"Out of compassion" means: other [deities] such as Brahmā and the rest, out of compassion—that is, by virtue of their affection for devotees—grant another desire or boon distinct from liberation. You, however, because of your particular or distinguished compassion, which surpasses that of Brahmā and the others, are the "giver of your own self," meaning you grant even your own self, your true nature, which is liberation.

Furthermore, other beings such as Brahmā and the rest exercise sovereignty over this phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—that is, they are capable of either punishing or favoring other beings, the "supreme people" distinct from themselves, among both the stationary and the moving; but you, however, are the Lord even of Brahman, the very nature of your own Self. The meaning is that you alone are capable of casting your very Self in the form of a living being (*jīva*) into the ocean of worldly existence to punish it, and at that very same moment, establishing it in the state of experiencing your own bliss to favor it.

Anticipating the objection, "What is the fruit for servants in surrendering their own selves?", he demonstrates that the Blessed One himself is the very form of the fruit—by the words "in you" (*tvayi*). "In you" means in Brahman. "Those of abundant fortune" refers to sentient beings (*cetana*), i.e., individual souls (*jīva*), who have attained the paths of devotion and knowledge through the accumulation of merit earned over many successive births.

"They rejoice on high" means they delight exceedingly; "and [you] are one who delights in the Self alone"—the word *ca* here has the sense of *tu* (but)—whereas you, however, delight in yourself alone, and for both yourself and others, you alone are the ground of unsurpassed bliss; this is the meaning. For this reason, O Śauri! O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! you who are the support, the substratum, of incomparable, world-transcending qualities—to you, I offer my salutation (*namaḥ*). || 9 ||
He also states the uniqueness of being the locus of the six qualities:
sovereignty that governs even Śaṅkara and other lords; valor that withdraws the splendor of those who steal the world's luster; and stainless fame sung by those free from desire.

Prosperity is ever attached to your limbs, yet there is no talk of your attachment to anything else, for you know all things; O dweller in the wind-temple, O slayer of Mura, you are the primary refuge of the word "Bhagavat. 10.

Regarding the word *aiśvaryam*: O dweller of the wind-palace, O slayer of Mura! Your sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists in the subduing of Śaṅkara and other lords, acting as the impeller of their respective offices. Furthermore, those who "seize the splendor" (*tejas*)—that is, the prowess—of all beings in the universe are the venerable Śaṅkara and others; you are one whose nature it is to withdraw (*saṃhartum*) the splendor and power of such individuals. And the author will say later: "Again and again [he struck] Indra," and so forth. Your fame, moreover, is stainless and purifying of sins.

The meaning is that this has been sung even by those who are free from desire and liberated; it has been described by them because their minds have been drawn away by Your deeds. And Śrī always remains clinging to Your limbs, having taken refuge in Your chest alone. "You are the knower of all" (akhilavit) means that You know everything—Your own self, Your Māyā, and its effects; the sense is that others do not know You in reality. Regarding any object whatsoever, there is not even heard a report, let alone a conversation, concerning Your association with them.

Therefore, from that—meaning, because the qualities denoted by the word *bhagavat*, namely sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), fame (*yaśas*), glory (*śrī*), valor (*vīrya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and non-attachment (*asaṅga*), reside in you to an exceeding degree; therefore, you are the primary substratum and the literal meaning of the word *bhagavat*, whereas in others the application of the word *bhagavat* is merely figurative. || 10 ||
Thus ends the first decade, which is a description of the majesty of the Blessed One.

In this way, through the introduction of the Lord’s qualities, the poet’s heart becomes moistened by the essence of the supreme consciousness that has suddenly arisen within his chest; with his body covered in horripilation, his hands joined in reverence upon his head, and the flow of his speech choked by tears, certain words emerge from his mouth in a faltering voice:
"His forehead is radiant between the brows, where the tilaka on his high crown vies with the sun..."

I worship Your form, with eyes agitated by compassion, radiant with the play of a tender smile, and beautiful nostrils; with a pair of shark-shaped earrings shimmering upon Your cheeks, the Kaustubha gem blazing on Your neck, and shining with a forest garland, a string of pearls, and the Śrīvatsa mark. (1)

"Rivaling the Sun" means possessing a golden crown that is exceedingly brilliant, like many solar orbs merged into one. "With an upward tilaka" means the forehead is radiant with a saffron tilaka-mark applied at its upper tip. "Eyes agitated by compassion" means the pair of lotus-eyes is occupied with repeatedly opening and closing due to being moistened by the essence of compassion directed toward devotees. "Radiant with moist laughter" means endowed with a gentle smile that shines intensely because it is moist with love.

I worship your form—meaning, I now meditate upon it—which possesses nostrils with beautiful nostril-pits, endowed with the exquisite beauty of a nose like a golden *tilaka* flower; which has a pair of shark-shaped earrings rising from the cheeks and hanging down upon the orb of the cheeks, marked by shark-designs; which has the Kaustubha gem shining upon the neck, the precious Kaustubha jewel resplendent on the region of the neck; and which is radiant with the splendor of a forest garland (*vanamālā*), a pearl necklace (*muktāhāra*), and the Śrīvatsa mark, being naturally luminous through these.

I take refuge in that form of yours which destroys all suffering—a form whose four glorious arms are adorned with armlets, bracelets, excellent bangles, and great jeweled rings, and which holds a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus; a form draped in shimmering yellow garments marked by golden borders, and possessing feet with the luster of stainless lotuses.

Regarding the word *keyūra*: the intention of the commentator is that there is no prohibition based on the rule "not [for] selection" (*na nirdhāraṇa*), because the three factors required for such a selection—namely, that in which something is selected (*yasminn ardhyate*), that which is selected (*yaś ca nirdhāryate*), and the cause of the selection (*yaś ca nirdhāraṇahetuḥ*)—are not present here. This refers to a large ornament set with the finest, most excellent *keyūras* (a specific type of armlet hanging from the shoulder), *aṅgadas* (armlets worn below them), *kaṅkaṇas* (bracelets on the forearms), and jingling *valayas* (rings). In this case, it is that in which the ornament is placed, and it is that which is being determined; since the cause of selection is absent, the prohibition does not apply.

She is one who holds—clinging to—the mace, conch, discus, and lotus, which are grasped by her four stout arms that reach down to her knees, are joined together, adorned with rings marked by those [weapons], and are glorious and resplendent; she is thus described. She is "marked by a golden girdle": she is one whose habit is to take up and wear the yellow garment itself, which has attained its supreme beauty (*parabhāga*) by being marked—that is, set above—by a golden girdle. Thus she is so described.

I take refuge in—that is, I resort to—Your form, whose feet possess the luster of stainless lotuses, whose pair of feet shines like a fresh red lotus, and which, being seated within the hearts of devotees, cuts away their suffering and affliction such as that of the internal self; thus, it is the "Destroyer of Suffering" (Ārticchedinī). It is a certain form whose beauty is impossible even for Brahmā and others to describe. The meaning is: having placed [the mind] upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, which has been turned upward and blossomed, I worship [You]. || 2 ||

Now he describes the good fortune of the Blessed One’s form: that which is more honored than even the greatness of the three worlds; more enchanting than the Enchanter himself; more lovely than the very treasury of loveliness; and sweeter than even the preeminent bearer of sweetness.
O Viṣṇu, O All-pervading Lord! Your form is more beautiful than the most beautiful and more wondrous than the most wondrous; in this world, whose curiosity does it not nourish? || 3 ||

Regarding the word "yat" (that which): in this world of the three realms, whatever object is most magnificent—that is, exceedingly great, honored, and excellent—even more honored than that; and whatever object is enchanting within the three realms, even more enchanting and delightful than that; and whatever object is beautiful—exceedingly splendid and a perfected elixir for captivating all the senses—even more beautiful than that which serves as a vessel of splendor by being a repository of luster.

That which is sweeter than even a thing that is preeminent in sweetness, capable of producing the effect of sweetness, and which brings peace to affliction; that which is more beautiful than even a thing that is superior in beauty, most excellent, and exceedingly lovely; and that which is more wonderful than even a thing that serves as the objective basis for the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*).

O All-pervading One! O Viṣṇu, capable of delivering one across the ocean of saṃsāra! In this world, whose curiosity would such a form of Yours not nourish? The meaning is that it indeed bestows an extraordinary eagerness for hearing, remembering, and so forth, even upon those who are bound, those already liberated, and those seeking liberation. || 3 ||
Having attained Your body, which is of such a sweet nature, that Goddess—who is composed of pure bliss—does not remain for long even among Her own devotees due to Her supreme longing;

alas, O Acyuta! O All-pervading Lord! because of the power of the steadiness of Her love for the beauty of Your form, and by the force of Her lack of fickleness, the very report of her fickleness has arisen as a source of distress for Her.

Regarding the word "tat": that which is "tādṛk" is similar to that; thus "tattādṛg" means incomparable. Having attained—that is, having obtained its dwelling upon the chest—your body, whose nature (ātman) is endowed with such sweetness, that goddess Mahālakṣmī, even among her own devotees, does not remain for a very long time (cirataram), having become composed of prosperity (sampanmayī) in the form of wealth, grain, and so forth, but remains indeed fickle.

He states the reason for this: "paramotsukā" (extremely eager). The meaning is that because her heart has been captivated by the excellence of the beauty of your form, she is unable to go elsewhere. Therefore, since this is so, O Acyuta! O All-pervading Lord! because of this—namely, being composed of the stability of love for the exquisite beauty of your form (*mānojñaka*)—and by the very power of this lack of fickleness (*acāpalya*), the report of her fickleness (*cāpalya*) is merely a rumor, as in "she is fickle."

"Bad reputation has arisen"—the word "alas" (*kaṣṭam*) expresses grief; the grief arises from the fact that even a virtue has become a cause for fault. Furthermore, the sense is: "I am grieved because the ill repute of your beloved, arising from the excellence of your own good fortune, now touches you as well."
One might object: "Has her fickleness not arisen from her serving you, her servant, only occasionally? What should I do about this? To dispel such doubt, [the author] says:
"O Lord of Lakṣmī! 'Lakṣmī is unstable toward others because she is struck down by your own loveliness'—now I shall state another proof for this:

those devotees who are deeply attached to the joy of chanting the virtues of meditating upon You, in them she dwells with perfect stability, bestowing her favor during conversations concerning her beloved. (5)

Regarding the word "Lakṣmī": this Lakṣmī, having had her heart captivated by your own loveliness and charm, has become unsteady and fickle even toward other devotees besides you; in this matter, mere tradition is not the only proof, but I shall now state another proof, namely inference.

Previously, based on the report of Lakṣmī’s fickleness arising from her having been stolen away by your good fortune, it was inferred that she is unstable toward others; and in that regard, you suspected the condition (*upādhi*) of her serving you only occasionally as a servant. Therefore, the meaning is that I shall state another inference.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Lakṣmī is unstable among others because her heart has been captivated by Your good fortune; for she dwells permanently among Your devotees—who are attached to the flavor of meditating upon You and chanting Your virtues—due to their devotion to the accounts of Your deeds currently being narrated. Whatever is thus [is] so; just as the Gopīs, whose hearts were captivated by Your good fortune, were unstable even toward their own husbands (who were "others"), because they dwelt permanently among Your devotees who were attached to the flavor of meditating upon You and chanting Your virtues due to their devotion to the accounts of Your beloved. And the verse is almost entirely explained. || 5 ||

Thus, with these thirteen verses, the form of the Blessed Lord to be meditated upon, as described in the three preceding chapters, has been depicted. Now, he demonstrates the arising of devotion to the Lord, which is the means for service: "Your form—consisting of the elixir of supreme consciousness, which distills the essence of the earth of ever-increasing loveliness, and which captivates the hearts of those who hear it..."
It instantly impels the mind, intoxicates it, makes the limbs bristle with horripilation, and drenches them with showers of cold tears born from the swoon of bliss.

"Thus": such is the aforementioned charm and loveliness; that very thing is a flow of fresh nectar, a fresh distillation of honey. Your form—which is the milking vessel for that [nectar], consisting of the elixir of supreme consciousness, consisting of the Supreme Brahman, captivating to the heart, and a constant reminder for those who remember it—is for those who hear it.

This is the intended meaning: when a man, having developed faith in Your story by chance, finds himself engaged in the discourse, Your form enters the region of his heart through the gateway of the ears and pacifies all his distress. He describes the manner of this: "Immediately" (*sadyaḥ*). It "impels the mind" (*matiṃ prerayate*), meaning it draws the mind away from sense objects and forcibly brings it into its own presence. It "intoxicates" (*madayate*), bringing about a state of being overwhelmed with bliss. Furthermore, it causes "every limb" (*aṅgakam*) to bristle with horripilation.

Moreover, with those cool streams of tears—which arise from a swoon born of the bliss of experiencing Your form—he sprinkles [the Lord]. By this, it is also stated that through the causeless intensity of love for the Lord, there arises devotion (*bhakti*) characterized by the functioning of all the senses toward Him; and that such devotion is produced by *sādhana-bhakti*, which consists of hearing Your stories, chanting Your names, and so forth. (6)

Immediately thereafter, he describes the excellence of devotion with four verses: "For this yoga, which is designated as devotion because it is of such a nature, is proclaimed by the lords of yogis to be far more excellent than the two other types of yoga consisting of action and knowledge."

O Beloved of Ramā! Since you consist solely of the essence of beauty, devotion toward you—which consists of the highest intensity of love—is indeed attainable by all men in the world without any exertion. || 7 ||

"Thus" means: that yoga, which is called *bhakti* (devotion) and is accepted even by Prahlāda and others as the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*), is "of such a nature," that is, of the manner described. This means it is of such a character that it arises effortlessly through hearing the sacred narratives and so forth, and once arisen, it gladdens the heart. [It is superior] to the yoga consisting of action and knowledge—that is, to the yoga consisting of ritual action and the yoga consisting of theoretical knowledge.

"Far superior," meaning most excellent and preeminent, to both [the other two]. He states the authority for this: "by the lords of yogis," meaning it is sung of and described in the Purāṇas by Vyāsa, Nārada, and others. Furthermore, O Beloved of Ramā! devotion whose very nature is the excellence and intensity of love for You is indeed attainable without effort—that is, effortlessly—by all people; there is no doubt in this matter.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "consisting of the single essence of beauty. This means that He is one in whom beauty alone is the aesthetic flavor (rasa), the self, and the very nature (svarūpa); it refers to Him as such. || 7 ||
That which is called *karmayoga*— the performance of one’s own duty with self-restraint and free from desire—
is far inferior; whereas that which is to be attained through the knowledge of the Upaniṣads is even more difficult for the mind to grasp due to its unmanifest nature, O All-pervading Lord!
Devotion consisting of love for You alone is eternally more delicious and more conducive to the highest good. || 8 ||

"Niṣkāmaṃ" means that which has "karmayoga" as its designation; thus, it is called "karmayoga. That from which desire—the expectation of results—is gone is "niṣkāma," and such is it. The performance—that is, the practice—of one's own duty (svadharma), which is prescribed and fixed as obligatory or occasional, is that whose fruit is "dūretya," meaning the fruit is distant, occurring at a later time.

The "Aupaniṣada" is Brahman, which is propounded by the Upaniṣads; its fruit, known as liberation (mokṣa), is to be attained through knowledge of that [Brahman]. Furthermore, because it is unmanifest and beyond the range of the senses, it is extremely difficult for the mind to grasp and is impossible to attain in any way whatsoever, since only those who have cast off all desires and renounced all ritual actions possess the qualification for it.

O All-pervading Lord! O You who are capable of bestowing the desired fruit even upon those established in the paths of action, knowledge, and devotion! Therefore, the meaning is that devotion consisting of love alone is always—both in its arising and once it has arisen—in the attainment of the fruit, more delicious (svādīyasī), exceedingly worthy of being savored, more auspicious, and more highly praised even by Brahmā and the other gods. || 8 ||
Having performed ritual acts that cause great exhaustion, those purified of impurities eventually attain fitness on the path of devotion or toward enlightenment; what does it matter?

Others, however, having exhausted themselves on the path of logic regarding Your supreme form known as Brahman, achieve success only after many future births, provided they lack the softening of their hearts through contemplation.

"Atīti" means: having performed—that is, having carried out—the various groups of rituals (*karma-paṭala*), consisting of manifold actions such as obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), expiatory (*prāyaścitta*), and meditative (*upāsana*) rites, which cause great exertion and must be practiced preceded by much effort and labor;
those whose mental impurities—namely, the stains of the mind in the form of passion, hatred, delusion, pride, and envy—have departed, that is, have gone away, are [the *atīta*].

Likewise, certain such individuals attain fitness—that is, they obtain the qualification—for either the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*) or the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*). If they are completely detached, then they are qualified for the yoga of knowledge; if they are somewhat detached, then they become qualified for the path of devotion. As it has been said: "Neither despondent nor overly attached, the yoga of devotion grants him success."

For us who have set out upon the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*), what purpose is served by such action as that? The meaning is: none at all. On the other hand, others—devoid of the softness of heart and free from passion and the like, yet considering themselves detached—having exerted themselves excessively on the path of logic within the Vedānta scriptures and become mere vessels for affliction, O All-pervading Lord! having contemplated Your form, which is the very essence known as Brahman, and having investigated it through various reasonings (*nyāya*) that serve as the means for deliberating upon the meaning of the Vedānta; [they remain thus].
Having worshipped through many methods of adoration over many successive births, they attain perfection and accomplish the fruit. || 9 ||
In that case, do the aforementioned defects also exist in the yoga of devotion? No; he says:
"But devotion to You, by immersing itself in the flowing stream of the nectar of the rasa of Your stories, becomes perfected of its own accord, effortlessly extending the path of pure awakening."

Victorious is that very maturity of love for Your feet, O Lord! May it be moistened by the essence of devotion to Your feet, bringing immediate success; may it come to me most swiftly, O Sovereign of the Wind-god’s abode! 10.

"Tvaditi": the meaning is that devotion to you (*tvad-bhakti*) is not like that [other devotion]. Rather, it "conquers," meaning it becomes superior to the two types of yoga consisting of action (*karma*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). He explains this very superiority with the words "the essence of your story" (*kathā-rasa*): the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in your story—whether in the form of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and so forth, or else faith in the story—is itself a stream of nectar (*amṛta-jharī*), a flow of honey; by immersing oneself completely in that, one attains perfection spontaneously. This is the meaning: for those who listen to your stories, a desire to hear them again and again arises.

Consequently, thirst for various sense objects departs; thereafter, through the purification of the mind, devotion (bhakti) arises spontaneously. Now, one might object: "Even if devotion has arisen, it does not remove the bondage caused by ignorance, because only knowledge (jñāna) destroys ignorance. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Vimalā" (the Stainless).

"Vimalaprabodha" (pure awakening) refers to that awakening through which the impurity—the ignorance consisting of the egoistic conceits of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth—is removed or destroyed without affliction (*akleśataḥ*), that is, without any effort. That very pure awakening is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*); it alone is the "path" (*padavī*), the way, the means for attaining Brahman. [The text says] "extending" (*tanvatī*) it, meaning she who effects or brings about that path. The underlying intention is this: since the knowledge of your own nature as Brahman is merely an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) in the production of the fruits called bondage and liberation by devotion, that devotion itself [accomplishes the goal] for the Goddess without any affliction.

Having produced the knowledge of Brahman, it bestows even liberation by means of the cessation of ignorance. Furthermore, it brings about accomplishment—the fruit—immediately in this very life, and not at some later time as is the case with the path of knowledge.

O Lord! O Sovereign of the Abode of Air! For me, whose sole refuge is You, let there be that very same melting of the heart—consisting of the intense maturity of love for Your lotus feet, which is exceedingly auspicious due to its freedom from affliction; for that maturity of love is itself the "rasa" (flavor), because it is worthy of being tasted. Let such devotion, characterized by this moisture, arise most swiftly. The meaning is: even if my service is sluggish, please favor me with such devotion alone, with the thought, "He has me as his sole refuge.
Thus ends the second decade, which contains the description of the Lord’s form and the description of the arising of devotion to the Lord and so forth.
Now, he describes the true nature of the devotees:

O Giver of Boons! Those devotees who, reciting Your names while fallen into an ocean of intense joy, remembering Your form, speaking of Your qualities, and moving about [in Your service], truly delight in You—I consider them most blessed, having attained all their desires. (1)

"Reciting," he says. Those devotees who indeed delight in You alone, O Lord, and not even occasionally in sense objects—I consider them alone to be supremely blessed and fortunate. He describes the manner of their delight: "reciting," and so forth.

Reciting those names and proclaiming them aloud—O Giver of Boons, O Bestower of the Desires of Devotees!—they remember Your form which has entered their hearts through such chanting; thus, they have fallen into an ocean of the abundance of joy, an ocean consisting of supreme bliss, and are characterized by the manifestations of that experience, such as tears of joy and horripilation. Reciting among themselves stories of Your qualities, such as Your affection for devotees, and Your most wonderful deeds, they wander about without regard for home or possessions.

For those who have become thus, even the highest station of Brahmā (pārameṣṭhya) and other such states are incapable of moving their minds away from Your lotus feet; thus he says: "samadhigata... etc. Those by whom all desired and cherished objects have been fully attained are "tathā. Since Your lotus feet constitute the fulfillment of every human goal (puruṣārtha), the meaning is that having attained them, they do not desire anything else. || 1 ||

Now, one might ask: "For what purpose do you praise the devotees? You too, by reciting their names, narrating their virtues, and remembering Your own form, should become one of them. In response to this doubt, He says that He is unable to emulate those devotees: "O Viṣṇu! Alas, my mind remains unattached even to the abundance of the nectar of serving Your feet, which is difficult to attain due to the affliction of disease; therefore, have mercy!
Delighting in the nectar of remembering Your lotus feet, I shall dwell somewhere in solitude, singing again and again the multitude of Your names. (2)

He laments: "My mind, afflicted by external diseases such as wind (vāta) and others, and by internal maladies such as passion (rāga) and the like—thus tormented and filled with distress—is unable to be composed even toward the abundance of the essence of serving Your feet, that supreme bliss consisting of worshiping Your lotus-feet; alas, what misery! I am weary. O Viṣṇu! Have compassion for me, who has no other refuge."

But I, being a connoisseur of the aesthetic delight in remembering the lotus feet of Your Honor, thinking with longing, "If I were free from disease, then I would remember [You]," shall dwell—that is, I shall make my special residence—in some secluded place, repeatedly singing and chanting the multitude of Your names. || 2 ||
If compassion has arisen in you, what indeed is not obtainable for embodied beings?
How insignificant is this state called the "allaying of the flood of my afflictions"? Who in this world is not constantly tormented by the fire of grief?
Those devoted to you are liberated; being unattached, they attain a state of happiness. || 3 ||

Regarding "compassion": O Viṣṇu! If Your compassion were to arise, what indeed would not be obtainable for embodied beings—be they women, Śūdras, and so forth, or even those possessing the bodies of elephants, deer, and the like? Let other human goals stand aside; even liberation, which is oneness with You, would be easily attained by them.

This being the case, how extremely insignificant indeed is the state of pacification—the condition consisting of the total uprooting—of the flood or multitude of my various afflictions (*kleśas*), mental anxieties (*ādhayas*), and physical ailments (*vyādhayas*)? The sense is that it is like the state of pacification of a heap of cotton consumed by a mass of flames. If one objects, "But such recipients of compassion are rare," he says, "Not so; for who are they not? (i.e., everyone is).

Who are those people who, being forever and always free from sorrow, are liberated from the egoism of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and other such things, and are thus devoid of the afflictions of mental anguish (*ādhi*), physical disease (*vyādhi*), and distress (*kleśa*) rooted therein; who, as devotees of You, having attained love for You, the Lord, chant Your names and sing of Your deeds; who, becoming liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), remain unattached to this world and are solely intent on the welfare of others, yet do not desire a happy state or a desired destination?

They perform [these acts], or rather, they do not provide that "easy path," which is the attainment of the bliss of Brahman. Indeed, in this world, many people are heard of who, having become Your devotees through Your very grace, move about [freely]. O Viṣṇu!
the sense is: "Grant such grace to me as well. || 3 ||
To the question "Who are those people?", he says:
