They are indeed the mature sages who are firmly established in the world, whose inner courses are hidden,
who are free from the pain [of worldly existence] through the remembrance of Your lotus feet, and who have Nārada as their foremost.

O Lord of the Moving! What more can be said of those who, having completely immersed themselves in the non-duality of the eternal bliss of the supreme consciousness that is perpetually radiant, wander at their own will? 4.

Regarding the word *muni*: those for whom the venerable Nārada is the foremost are the "exalted sages" (*muniprauḍhāḥ*), the best of sages, who are indeed well-known and established in the world. However, they are "those whose self and movement are hidden" (*gūḍhātmagatayaḥ*); that is, their selves (*ātman*) and movements (*gati*) are hidden and impossible to perceive by people such as ourselves. Alternatively, "movement of the self" (*ātmagati*) refers to the movement of the mind (*manogati*), meaning their specific intentions regarding restraint, favor, and so forth are unknown even to the gods. Or else, it means the knowledge of the self (*ātmano gatiḥ*).

By the remembrance of Your lotus feet, they are free from disease—that is, devoid of all suffering—and indeed they wander at will in this world. To the question "How so?", he says: "Constantly," etc. Constantly—meaning at all times—they are immersed in the expansion, that is, the overflowing, of that Supreme Brahman which is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), the Supreme Bliss of Consciousness which is ever-shining and has ascended to the path of direct experience; and because of the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that very Brahman is non-dual (*advaita*). Being one with That, they move about.
O Lord! Beyond this, what remains for them to pray for? The sense is: "In that same way, please show grace upon me as well."

One might object: "Since Śrī Nārada and others, by my grace, have become established in knowledge, shaken off all afflictions, and wander at will, one should simply pray for knowledge. What is the use of this uncertain devotion for the purpose of dispelling the afflictions born of ignorance? Dispelling this doubt, he prays for devotion:
"May my devotion to you flourish; that alone shall pacify the entire flood of my afflictions. Indeed, there is not even a grain of doubt in my heart.
Otherwise, the words of Vyāsa, your own words, and the words of the Vedas would all be false—mere like the talk of a man in the street. (5)

"Devotion to You": "May my devotion to You flourish; may that very devotion pacify the entire flood of my afflictions. Regarding this, he states the authoritative evidence: "If not," and so forth. The words of Vyāsa refer to the Purāṇic statements establishing the majesty of devotion to the Lord; "Your word" refers to what You have spoken to Arjuna and Uddhava; "the words of the Naigamas" refers to Vedic sentences, or alternatively, to the speech of the Naigamas—those who know the Vedas. If devotion does not [pacify] the entire flood of afflictions...

"It pacifies [the objection]; for then all this would generally be false and unauthoritative, like the speech of a man on the street"—this is the reductio ad absurdum (*vipakṣe bādhakaḥ tarkaḥ*) against the opposing view. However, those outside the Vedic tradition (*avaidika*) prattle thus: "The statements of the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas are not authoritative, because they are sentences, like the speech of a man on the street. He states that this inference does not establish the lack of authority of the statements of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas: "Certainly not," and so forth.

The intended meaning is as follows: "Whatever is a sentence, that is non-authoritative"—this very inference, being itself a sentence, is therefore non-authoritative; thus, the arrow released by them strikes those very targets themselves. Furthermore, the teachers have extensively demonstrated the authority of the Veda and, by virtue of being rooted in it, the authority of the statements in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas as well. Therefore, the status of devotion as a means to liberation is established through the words of Śruti, the Purāṇas, and the speech of the Lord. || 5 ||

And thus, in order to state that devotion alone is to be prayed for according to the aforementioned path, he speaks of its superiority over knowledge: "Devotion to you is first sweet with the flavor of your qualities;
if it has ascended even slightly further, it becomes the pacifier of all distress."
Furthermore, at the end, within one's own heart, it bestows the non-duality of great bliss arising from the dawn of stainless awakening; what else remains to be prayed for beyond this?

Regarding the word *bhavat*: the term *tāvat* signifies sequence. Devotion to you (*bhavadbhakti*) is sweet (*madhurā*), meaning of the nature of bliss, at the outset—that is, in the beginning, at the first encounter. Why is this so? To this he says: "Because of the flavor of your qualities" (*tvadguṇarasāt*). This is because of the joy arising from faith produced by hearing, remembering, and so forth, regarding your qualities. However, it is not thus on the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*), according to the Lord’s own words: "That which is at first like poison... and so on.

If that [faith], through its very devotion to hearing Your stories—which is rooted in the absence of [worldly] qualities and tastes—should somehow ascend and increase, then, because the realization of reality and detachment from sense objects are possible according to one's devotion, it becomes the pacifier of all distress; that is, it brings about the complete and radical cessation of all suffering, whether internal (ādhyātmika) or otherwise. Furthermore, at the end, in the final stage, when it has been brought to full maturity within one’s own heart, it is called "pure expansion" (vimalaprabodha).

The "stainless awakening" (*vimalaparibodha*) is that realization from which the impurity—the ignorance consisting of the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth—has departed and been destroyed. Through the arising of that knowledge—"All this is indeed Brahman"—it bestows the non-dual Great Bliss (*mahānandādvaita*), which is the Great Brahman itself, whose nature is bliss and which is non-dual because all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been cast away. The meaning is that devotion alone, by granting the knowledge of Brahman culminating in direct experience, grants even liberation (*mokṣa*) in the form of the scriptural statements concerning the non-duality of consciousness and bliss. Therefore, there is nothing other than this liberation for living beings.

"What is to be prayed for? Nothing at all"—this is the meaning. Alternatively, since this devotion is of the nature of bliss throughout its beginning, middle, and end, what else—such as knowledge and so forth—is to be prayed for? The meaning is that nothing else whatsoever is to be prayed for. || 6 ||

Having thus praised devotion characterized by love, while reflecting upon his own lack of qualification for it, he prays for devotion in the form of ritual action as its means: "Wash away my afflictions and make Your pair of feet full of relish; grant me also a hand for the purpose of worshipping You in Your sacred field."
May my eye be fixed upon the sight of your form, my sense of smell upon the fragrance of the tulasī at your feet, and my ear upon your beautiful deeds.

"Shake off"—having shaken off the afflictions (*kleśas*), whether they be diseases external or internal; make my pair of feet possess *rasa* (devotional flavor) upon reaching your field, and be filled with curiosity [to behold them], for otherwise, even if curiosity exists, it would be impossible to go to your field, perform circumambulations, and so forth. Furthermore, make your pair of hands (*kara*)—the very instrument of worship—possess *rasa* in that ritual act. And make your two eyes possess *rasa* in beholding (*āloka*) the aforementioned form of mine.

Now, let your sense of smell (ghrāṇa) take delight in inhaling the fragrance of the Tulasī worshipped at Your glorious feet; and let your sense of hearing (śravaṇa) also find its pleasure in Your beautiful and captivating deeds and praises.
Immediately thereafter, he prays for remembrance:
"In my heart, which is agitated by the onset of many mental and physical afflictions, may your form— whose nature is the supreme consciousness— arise therein."
With my hair standing on end and my multitude of heavy sorrows dissolved, may I forget the insults and sufferings that are so difficult to endure. || 8 ||

"Prabhūta" means: when my heart—my own heart—is violently and forcibly shaken by abundant internal mental afflictions (*ādhibhiḥ*) and external physical diseases (*vyādhibhiḥ*), and is entirely occupied with the acquisition and preservation of the body and so forth, may that form of yours which consists of supreme essence and consciousness arise; namely, that form described in the thirteen verses beginning with "That *sattva* which..."—wherein "supreme essence" (*paramarasa*) is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and "consciousness" (*cit*) is knowledge (*jñāna*), and [the form] is composed of that.

Just as the orb of the sun rises while simultaneously driving away the mass of rising darkness, so too may Your form arise in my heart while uprooting, along with its very foundation, the web of mental anguish and physical disease brought forth by the expansion of my ignorance; such is the intended meaning.

And thus, at that time, having attained such an excess of love that my body was adorned with rising horripilation, and being overwhelmed by a flood of joy so that my entire frame was drenched with tears, may I—so that I might properly forget those afflictions, whether internal or otherwise, which are difficult to subdue and impossible to pacify, as well as the insults and calamities caused by them—or rather, may Your form arise within my heart in such a way that I forget them. This is the connection [of the verse]. || 8 ||
Moreover—O Lord of Maruddeha! Even those who are hostile toward you are indeed happy; yet I, who am devoted to you, suffer greatly—what is this?
O Giver of Boons! May there be no infamy for you; O Subduer of Kaṃsa, quickly make me one who has cast off the burden of worldly existence and am uplifted by devotion to you. || 9 ||

"O Marut! O Lord of Veṅkaṭādri! O Sovereign of Śrī Guruvāyupura! Indeed, even those who are turned away from You, the Lord—those who are averse and even atheists—are seen to be happy; what then need be said of other devotees? I am one who possesses affection for You, the Lord—a 'bhavatsnehī' (one with love for You)—yet, while that affection exists, because I am overwhelmed by suffering, I am incapable of remembrance and other such acts of devotion. Such as I am, I experience intense and excessive torment (*paritavye*). Is this not like a form of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) even toward the Lord?"

Furthermore, it cannot be suspected that even they did not serve you in previous births—which would explain why they are now happy—while for some reason they have now become hostile toward you; for such a suspicion would undermine the established doctrine that your own servants never fall away from grace. Moreover, I include myself among the suffering, so there is no cause for grief on my part; however, it would result in ill repute for you, as the Lord, if it were true, would be seen to exhibit partiality toward living beings.

And so, my sorrow is that there might even be a slackening of the service of living beings; thus he says, "infamy" (akīrtiḥ). By these two vocatives, "O Giver of Boons! and "O Subduer of Kaṃsa!", the fact that the Lord assumes a body solely for the purpose of suppressing the wicked and granting the desires of the virtuous is revealed as his glorious fame. While that fame exists, let there be no infamy—nor even ill-repute—for you from any source. He states the remedy for this: "the burden of the donkey."

The mace is indeed a burden because it is impossible to bear; therefore, by quelling it, make me instantly—before I am overwhelmed by infamy—the foremost ornament and crest-jewel of Your devotees. In this way, both you and I shall have fulfilled our purpose. Thus is the meaning. || 9 ||

Thus, describing the nature of both the devotee and the object of devotion through praise and supplication, he concludes the section: "O Lord! What is the use of further words? For as long as your compassion has not yet arisen, I shall spend my days before you, O Giver of Boons, uttering various cries of distress, with your feet placed before me."
Performing prostrations, praises, and service as clearly as possible according to one's ability. || 10 ||

"What is the use?"—meaning, what fruit is there in these many repeated outpourings of lamentation? In the absence of Your compassion, there is nothing at all. O Lord, shining within the hearts of Your devotees! For as long as Your very own compassion, Your grace, does not arise—that is, manifest—itself, for that long I have uttered various kinds of useless words, consisting of the manifold lamentations of the distressed as described above. He by whom [this was done]... [is he].

Having uttered various cries of distress, being in such a state, I shall pass my days performing—before Your glorious feet, which are established (*klṛpta*) or intended (*saṅkalpita*) in the presence (*puraḥ-purobhāge*), or even associated with Your image—prostrations (*nati*), which are salutations; praises (*nuti*), which are hymns of praise; and service (*niṣevā*), which is worship, doing so especially with the activity of devotion and faith, as long as I am able and until my health is restored, as I clearly determine. My mere lamentation alone does not cause Your grace to arise.

Furthermore, there would be a vain waste of time; therefore, the meaning is that I spend my days performing service to You according to my ability and awaiting Your grace. Thus, through these fifteen verses, the nature of devotion and of devotees, as established by the narrative of Parīkṣit, has been described. || 10 ||
Thus ends the third decade, consisting of the description of the nature of the devotee and the prayer for devotion,
in the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The first chapter of the book:

The form of Hari described in the second [chapter] as consisting of three qualities, two qualities, one quality of pure *sattva*, and being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)— that very form is now described as the object of worship.

Now, intending to elaborate upon the various forms of the Lord, their worship, and the fruits thereof by relying on the second *skandha*, [the author] first prays for health so as to qualify himself for that [task]: "Grant me such soundness of health as will enable me to perform Your worship;
through the nourishment of the eightfold yoga-practice, may I swiftly attain Your satisfaction. (1)

"Be well. Grant me such health and well-being as will enable me to perform your worship; this is clear and certain. If I were free from illness, then I would attain your satisfaction and grace through the practice and fulfillment of the eightfold yoga consisting of the eight limbs, beginning with *yama* and *niyama*. The sense is that my current ill-health alone is the cause of the deficiency in the limbs of yoga. May I obtain your pleasure and favor. || 1 ||
Now, saying "I shall act according to my ability," he says:

"Purified by the restraints (yamas) such as firmness in celibacy, and by the observances (niyamas) such as ritual bathing, we, being devoted to you, shall firmly prepare a comfortable seat, whether it be one made of lotuses or otherwise. (2)

Regarding the term *brahmacarya*: the firmness of *brahmacarya* consists in the avoidance of seeing, touching, and so forth, women. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and the like are included. *Āplava* means bathing; here, by the word "and so forth," mental purification, recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and the like are included.

Purified and cleansed by these restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), we—being "bhavat-parāḥ," those for whom You are the supreme and primary goal—shall assume a firm posture, such as the lotus-seat (padmāsana), the svastika-seat, or any other comfortable seat, according to our ease, with the primordial lotus (the source of all) as its foundation. || 2 ||

Since stability of posture has been achieved, we shall perform breath control; thus he says: "Having meditated incessantly on the *tāra* (the syllable Om) within, having restrained the vital breath, and having withdrawn our senses from their objects so that they become stainless, we remain intent upon the worship of You. (3)

Regarding the word *tāram*: having meditated upon the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) within the heart as continuous—like a stream of oil or the sound of a bell—thereby creating a flow of homogeneous mental states uninterrupted by heterogeneous ones, and having mastered the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) through inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), one becomes "pure" (*nirmala*), meaning those from whom impurities such as passion (*rāga*) and the like have departed. As it has been said: "One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and sins by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*)."

Immediately following this, withdrawal (pratyāhāra) was described as the turning back of the senses from their objects. Now, being intent on ascending to the higher stages beginning with concentration (dhāraṇā) within Your worship, we remain here as those desiring to climb; the meaning is that while practicing the preceding stage itself, we await Your grace. || 3 ||
He speaks of the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) that follows in sequence:
"While Your form is not yet clearly manifest, let us repeatedly apply our intellect with effort;
through that, may we, contemplating Your feet, overflow with the inner moisture of the sentiment of devotion. (4)

"Unmanifested" (*asphuṭa*) means not clearly manifest, perceived only superficially. Regarding that body of yours, we would have to apply our intellect (*dhiṣaṇā*) with effort again and again. Here, "effort" (*prayatna*) refers to the exertion required to awaken the intellect when it is afflicted by the defect of sleep; likewise, it refers to the task of pacifying it when it is occupied with other objects—this is why it is said "again and again."

Thinking, "In this way we shall cultivate *dhāraṇā*," by that cultivation of *dhāraṇā*, may we carry—that is, attain—that very *rasa* which is devotion, as well as its attendant experience and inner moistening; thereby, may we become contemplators of Your feet and supreme devotees (*paramabhāgavatas*). || 4 ||

He speaks of meditation (dhyāna): "Devoted to the yoga of meditation and taking refuge in You, we contemplate Your body—beautiful with its clearly distinct limbs—in our minds effortlessly, by virtue of long-term cultivation. (5)

Regarding the word *visphuṭa*: that in which the various limbs, from the glorious feet to the tips of the hair, are *visphuṭa*—meaning exceptionally clear—that is "one whose distinct limbs are manifest. Such a beautiful body, its loveliness clearly perceived, we contemplate in our minds without effort (*aśrama*)—that is, effortlessly—by virtue of long-term cultivation, meaning the practice of *dhāraṇā* and *dhyāna*. The sense is: "Just as it was said by the venerable Nārada, 'As if summoned, it quickly comes to my sight within the mind,' so too [do we contemplate it]. And thus, we are engaged in the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*).

The remainder [of the thought] is: "May we be devoted to you, intent upon you, taking refuge in you, and possessing devotion to you, being engaged in the form of meditation which is the means for attaining you. || 5 ||
Then he prays for meditative absorption:

"O Mother! For those who meditate upon Your entire form in this way, their hearts captivated by the unfolding sweetness [of Your beauty], the internal Brahman—which is of the same nature as the intense bliss within—shines forth. (6)

"Let them meditate. O Blessed One! For those whose very selves—their minds—have been captivated by the blossoming sweetness and the physical splendor of Your entire form, Your form—which is of the nature of intense bliss and the essence of the single flavor of profound joy—is the Brahman that constitutes Your true nature. This internal reality, perceivable by the inner senses, manifests both as a distinction and as non-distinction in the forms of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

By this, conceptual meditative absorption (*savikalpaka-samādhi*) has been described; and therein, the manner of manifestation is exactly as follows. As it was stated by the Teacher: "Just as when an earthen elephant or the like is manifested, the earth itself is manifested, so too when duality is manifested, the non-dual reality is manifested. (6)
Now, he shows the nature of non-conceptual samādhi:
"O Leader of the Universe, we have taken refuge in that state consisting of Your samādhi, which has the form of its own savoring;
therefore, should there be a lapse from it, we shall once again undertake *dhāraṇā* and the other [limbs of yoga]. (7)

The word "tat" refers to that [Brahman]. The "tasting" (*samāsvadana*) of such Brahman is its perfect experience; the state consisting of that form is the abiding of both the knower and the known in the form of knowledge. This is your *samādhi*, meaning a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) *samādhi* having you as its object. And this very mode of manifestation is intended here. As it has been said: "Then, just as when salt has taken on the form of water, by the non-appearance of the salt there is the appearance of water alone, so too only the non-dual reality appears."

O Viśvanāyaka! O Jagannātha! Having resorted to such a state of *samādhi* as yours, we pray that should we ever fall away from this place or suffer a lapse, we may once again commence the practice of *dhāraṇā* and the rest. This is the intention: four obstacles can arise for the *nirvikalpaka-samādhi*, namely: *laya* (dissolution), *vikṣepa* (distraction), *kaṣāya* (turbidity), and *rasāsvāda* (relishing). Among these, *laya* is sleep; *vikṣepa* is taking hold of another object; *kaṣāya* is a state of rigidity caused by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) toward sense-objects;
and *rasāsvāda* is the relishing of the bliss associated with conceptual thought (*savikalpa*).

When one has fallen away due to these defects, one must begin again with concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and the other stages. However, when the mind, being free from these defects, remains motionless as nothing but Brahman, it is called "non-conceptual samādhi" (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), according to the words of the Blessed One: "As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker—this is the simile remembered. (7)

Now, he speaks of attaining liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) through victory in meditative absorption (*samādhi*): "Thus, with our hearts overflowing with the intensity of practice, having fashioned a festival for the face of the Supreme Self, and having attained the status of being crowns upon the heads of the multitude of liberated devotees, may we move about like Śuka, Nārada, and others. (8)

"Thus" means: in this manner, through the intense and preeminent practice of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*, we—having become such that our festivals are fashioned and perfected by the bliss of Your supreme Self which has shone forth and manifested, born from the experience of Your own nature as the Supreme Brahman—have attained the status of being the crest-jewels, that is, the preeminence, among the multitudes and assemblies of liberated devotees.

The meaning is this: although, when Brahman is directly realized, one becomes established in Brahman and free from all bondage because ignorance, its effects, previously accumulated karma, doubt, error, and so forth, have been sublated; nevertheless, as long as the *prārabdha* karma (karma that has begun to bear fruit) is not exhausted, actions continue to be performed through prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and [the fruits of] those actions are experienced.

Just as those who know "this is a magical illusion" do not perceive that illusion in the ultimate sense even while seeing it, so too these [sages], perceiving worldly transactions as non-ultimate because they have been sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, continue to move about for a certain time. This is what is called here the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*); such is the condition of Śuka, Nārada, and others.
"O Blessed One! If we too were to become recipients of Your grace, then we would move about as such [liberated beings]"—this is the meaning. || 8 ||

[Objection: "It has been stated that liberation occurs after the knowledge of Brahman, upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma. That is untenable, because it is heard in scripture that even for Śrī Nārada and others, despite the destruction of their *prārabdha* karma, there was the attainment of another body when their current bodies fell. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] describes, in seven verses, the voluntary departure (*yatheṣṭā gati*) of such persons who have mastered *samādhi*:

"But he who, desiring liberation quickly or gradually, once his *samādhi* is victorious over You, slowly raises the breath—which is brought under control by yoga—through the six supports via the *suṣumṇā*, O Unborn One! (9)

"Tvaditi": O Unborn One! "Tvatsamādhi" is the concentration (*samādhi*)—the one-pointedness of mind—upon You, the Lord. Its "victory" (*vijaya*) is its remaining for a long duration without effort, like a lamp placed in a windless spot. When that [concentration] exists, he who is again a relisher of liberation (*mokṣa-rasika*) becomes one who seeks immediate liberation (*sadyo-mukti*). Or, as for the phrase "or gradually," the meaning is that he may be one who seeks gradual liberation (*krama-mukti*).
That [yogin], having mastered the wind—the vital breath (prāṇa)—through yoga, raises it by means of the six supports;

that is to say, by means of the suṣumṇā channel, he gradually and sequentially causes it to ascend through the six supports or locations, namely: the secret place, the root foundation (mūlādhāra), the navel, the heart, the root of the palate, and the middle of the eyebrows. (9)
Up to this point, the description for both is the same; now he states the distinction regarding the one who is free from worldly attachment (*nirāgraha*):
"Then, casting off even the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), the one free from attachment merges into You, the Supreme.
But the one who is curious about the higher worlds departs through the crown of the head together with the sense organs. (10)

Regarding the word *liṅga*: one who is free from attachment and a grasper of immediate liberation, having fixed the breath (*anila*) between the eyebrows and remained there for a long moment, thereafter abandons even the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*). Having completely abandoned both the gross body and the subtle body so as never to return, he merges into You, the Supreme Brahman, by piercing the crown of the head. The meaning is that just as light merges into light, he attains union with You (*tvatsāyujya*).

He states the distinction for another case: if one is "curious about the upper worlds," meaning if one possesses a longing to experience the worlds of Brahmā and others, then [the soul] exits through the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*), having pierced it; by that opening, it departs together with the *karaṇas* (the senses), along with the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) which consists of the aggregate of the five vital breaths, mind, intellect, and the ten senses. The underlying intention is this: there is a constant connection between the solar rays and the *suṣumṇā* channel situated within the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).

Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), having reached as far as the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of that [channel], exits outward together with the rays of the sun as they emerge. || 10 ||
Immediately following this, he describes the manner of passing beyond the presiding deities of fire and the rest:

"Led by the deities who dwell in the fires, days, lunar mansions, fortnights, and [the divisions of] the northern solstice, and having reached the station of the Sun, one becomes supreme and, filled with joy, proceeds as far as the station of Dhruva. (11)
*Nirīyate* [is derived from] *īṅ gatau*, belonging to the *divādi* class.

*Agnivāsara-valarkṣapakṣaḥ*: the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is the "vala-constellation-fortnight. They go to—that is, they attain by way of presiding over—the fire, the day, and the vala-constellation-fortnight; thus, they are "those who enjoy the six months of the northern course" (*uttarāyaṇajuṣāḥ*), meaning they enjoy the six months of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).

"He presides over" means [presiding] by means of the deities who identify themselves with fire and so forth. By these deities, the individual soul (jīva) is led to the station of the sun, the wheel of light; "having the Lord as his supreme goal" means one for whom Bhavānī’s consort, the Lord (Īśvara), alone is the supreme object of service. Having become full of joy through the experience of enjoyments equal to those of each respective deity, he proceeds until the station of Dhruva, reaching as far as the world of Dhruva.

And here is the process: for the deities, beginning with Agni, lead this individual soul (jīva) step by step to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), like a puppet held in the hollow of one's hands. First, the deity Agni, having voluntarily cast off his own body, leads the soul—which is departing through the gateway of the sun’s rays—along the path to the world of Agni and delivers it into the hand of the deity presiding over the day. That deity delivers it into the hand of the deity presiding over the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). And that [deity] delivers it into the hand of the deity presiding over the six months of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*).

She delivers him into the hand of the deity presiding over the year (*saṃvatsara*). She, in turn, having led him by way of the world of the gods (*devaloka*), delivers him into the hand of the deity Wind (*vāyu*). And she leads him by way of her own world into the hand of the deity Sun (*āditya*). And she, leading the soul (*jīva*) as it proceeds through the gateway of her own orb, leads him by way of her own world into the hand of the deity Moon (*candra*). She causes him to proceed by way of her own world to the world of lightning (*vidyut*). From there, he goes as far as the world of the Pole Star (*dhruva*). Thus ends the section. || 11 ||
When he has taken refuge in the great abode and is tormented by the heat of the fire at the end of the aeon,
he then goes to your shelter, or rather, even before that, he goes to the station of Brahmā.

"Established": then, immediately after attaining the fixed station (*dhruvapada*), while dwelling happily established in Maharloka—the abode of Bhṛgu and others whose lifespan lasts for a kalpa—he, at a certain time, when the heat from the mouth of Śeṣa-vaktra, the fire that has issued forth from the mouth of Ananta to burn the three worlds, increases with its upward-pointing flames, and beholding the three worlds being consumed by it and being afflicted by its heat, he then takes refuge in You alone, the Lord, seeking Your protection.

One goes to, that is, reaches, the station of the Creator known as Satyaloka; the meaning is that, having transcended Janaloka and Tapoloka along with Bhṛgu and the others, one enters the assembly hall of Brahmā. Therefore, he knows it even beforehand.

Or rather, it is possible to go there at will even before reaching the heat of the fire that burns like the remaining [fuel]. This is the intended meaning here: if this person desires to go quickly to your abode, then someone of immeasurable form, having come from the world of Brahmā by the command of Brahmā, leads him along the path of the world of Vighna and the path of the worlds of Śakra and Prajāpati, causes him to cross the Virajā river, and brings him to the world of Brahmā;
at that time, he becomes possessed of a divine body. || 12 ||
Now he describes the two-fold destiny of those who have reached the world of Brahmā:
"Dwelling there, or rather in your own station, one attains liberation at the time of the dissolution of material nature (prākṛta-pralaya);
indeed, by his own will, he may even be liberated earlier, having forcibly split open the cosmic egg (jagadaṇḍa). (13)

Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): this means that having thus reached Satyaloka, he dwells either there in the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), or else in your own station, the world of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇuloka*). The underlying intention here is as follows: within the very domain of Satyaloka, there exist three worlds belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Giriśa (Śiva). Having attained those respective worlds, the worshippers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva experience enjoyments equal to those [deities] themselves.

When the elemental dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*) occurs, one attains liberation. For the "elemental dissolution" is the pre-eminent dissolution (*prakṛṣṭo layaḥ*) of the elemental effects—namely, the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and so forth—into their respective causes. When that dissolution occurs, one, liberated along with Brahmā, remains as nothing but Brahman. Alternatively, [one may attain it] by one's own will.

The following is intended here: if he attains detachment amidst these very enjoyments of Brahmā and the others currently being experienced, then he is liberated—that is, he becomes free—even before the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). To the question "How so?", he says: "Having shattered the cosmic egg," that is, the egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), by his own power of yoga, meaning by piercing through the shell of the cosmic egg. || 13 ||
He describes the manner of piercing the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa):

"O All-pervasive Lord! Entering the seven coverings consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the Great Principle (mahat), and primordial nature (prakṛti)—each of which is composed of its respective essence—one who is at ease goes to Your unconditioned state. (14)

Regarding the phrase "and of that": there are seven coverings of that cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). He states them as follows—beginning with "earth" (*kṣiti*): earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the five elements; *mahat* is the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*); and *prakṛti* is *māyā*. Of these...

The sevenfold [set] refers to the *āvṛtis*, the coverings. Here, the word "great" (*mahaḥ*) is also indicative of the principle of ego (*ahaṃ-tattva*). Thus, the five elements and both the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ego constitute the seven coverings. The eighth covering is Nature (*prakṛti*), which is all-pervasive. Regarding the phrase "entering by becoming identical with each": one whose self and form (*mūrti*) are precisely those respective coverings due to being of their nature is "identical with each"; the meaning is that he enters into those respective coverings by means of his subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) as their very self.

Experiencing unsurpassed bliss in each successive stage, O All-pervading Lord! he goes to Your unobstructed state, the state of Brahman. Thus, having transcended the veils and finally dissolved the vital breaths and the senses into their respective causes, then, through the dissolution of even that veil, he becomes nothing but the unobstructed Brahman alone; this is the meaning. || 14 ||
Thus, he says that one who is liberated does not return to the cycle of existence:

"O Lord of the World! O Essence of Being and Consciousness! O Lord of the Wind! As I travel by such a path as the one beginning with light (arcirādi), may I not suffer a fall; protect me as I ascend, singing of the emergence of Your qualities. (15)

"Acirādīti": The individual soul (jīva), proceeding by such a path beginning with *arciḥ* (light) and so forth, does not undergo falling away or rebirth. Here, there is an address containing a reason: "O Saccidātman! O Lord of Anila! O Sovereign of Śrī Guruvāyupura! O Lord of the World! Protect me—who am uttering [your praises] and praising you according to my ability through the arising of your qualities and the excellence of your attributes—from the perils of mental anguish and physical disease. || 15 ||

Thus ends the description of the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) and the description of the perfections of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), comprising the fourth decad along with the fifth. Having thus established the worship of the Sun, who consists of pure being (*śuddhasattvamaya*), up to its fruit, [the author], intending to show the worship of the Lord of the Universal Form (*viśvamūrtīśa*) for those who lack qualification for that [former practice], first demonstrates the prior non-existence of the Lord’s gross body in order to establish the origin of that body— [The text continues: "Thus... and so forth. This concludes the description of the eightfold yoga and the description of the perfections of yoga; this constitutes the fourth decad together with the fifth. Having thus set forth the worship of the Sun, who is composed of pure essence, up to its final result, [the author], wishing to demonstrate the worship of the Lord of the Universal Form for those who are not qualified for that [worship of the Sun], first shows the prior absence of the Lord's gross body in order to justify its subsequent production—
Before the dissolution of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), this world of the manifest and the unmanifest was nothing at all;

having entered into dissolution within you, whose transformations were restrained by the equilibrium of the *guṇas* in *māyā*, there was neither death nor immortality, neither day nor night. At that time, you alone remained, indeed, as the self-luminous essence of supreme bliss.

Regarding the word "manifest" (*vyaktā*): previously, at the time of the dissolution of the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), that is, during the dissolution of Brahman, this world consisting of bodies and so forth—whether manifest or unmanifest, or characterized by the gross and the subtle, or as effect and cause—did not exist at all. He states the reason for this: "when Māyā had gone to dissolution in You. He states the reason for the dissolution of Māyā: "when its transformations were restrained by the equilibrium of the *guṇas*."

The *guṇas* are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; in that state in which their transformations—meaning their effects—were obstructed and stilled by their condition of equilibrium, there was not even the slightest effect of *māyā*, because *māyā* had dissolved into Brahman. *Mṛtyu* is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); *amṛta* is liberation (*mokṣa*). At that time, neither bondage nor liberation existed. There was no abiding of day or night; that is, there was no demarcation of boundaries. In that period, you alone remained as Brahman itself.

He says that even for you [the Lord], there was no assumption of a body for sport at that time: "by means of the self whose nature is supreme bliss and light, which is the very essence of being, consciousness, and bliss. Here, the word *kila* indicates that this state is known solely through the final portion of the Veda, which consists of speech (*vāgrūpa*). || 1 ||
He elaborates on this very point:

"O All-pervading Lord! Time, action, the qualities, the multitudes of individual souls, and the entire universe as an effect—these all attained dissolution when You took delight in the play of consciousness."

O friend! they do not say that those [entities] lack existence; for if they were not present in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), how could they ever come into being again, being like flowers in the sky? (2)

Regarding the term *kāla*: *guṇa* refers to the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth; *kāla* is that which agitates them; *karma* is the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of individual souls; and there are the multitudes or groups of souls. To say more: O All-pervading One! O Source of creation, maintenance, and dissolution! O Thou whose essence is Consciousness! all things whatsoever—the entire universe, which is an effect of *māyā*—have attained a longing, a desire, for *cillīlā*, which is the play consisting of the contemplation of one's own true nature within You. The meaning is: when You are about to enter into *yoganidrā*.

Then these [factors] reached a state of dissolution and became invisible; yet, they did not become absolutely non-existent. To this he says: "Of them" (*teṣām*). He does not say that time, karma, and the rest are absolutely non-existent like the horn of a hare—this is either the meaning of the words themselves, or the remainder of the sentence is "the Śrutis and their seers. He states the reasoning for this: "In the form of power" (*śaktyātmanā*). O, Blessed One! This means: while You remain as the causal essence in the form of power.

Now, one might object: "If they are dissolved, then they must be non-existent. Anticipating this doubt, he states the refutation for the opposing view with the words "no cet" (if not). If these [elements] were non-existent, then, being like flowers in the sky, their re-emergence at the end of a dissolution would be impossible. And that is undesirable. Therefore, the meaning is that their existence in the form of a cause must be admitted. || 2 ||
Now, with these eight verses beginning with "evam," he demonstrates the manner in which the Lord’s Virāṭ form originated:
"And thus, when you had passed through a period of two parārdhas and were bearing the desire to create (sisṛkṣā), Māyā herself was agitated for the sake of bringing the three worlds into being."

Indeed, from Māyā emerged the power of Time (kāla-śakti), all unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), and inherent nature (svabhāva) as well; having manifested, they performed the function of assisting her by unfolding the qualities (guṇas). || 3 ||

"Thus" means: when the period of two *parārdhas* has passed—that is, at its conclusion—with nothing remaining but Brahman alone in the manner described. Here, the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the supreme lifespan of Brahmā is precisely measured by those two *parārdhas*. This is the intended meaning: one year for those like us is a day and night for the gods; as it is said, "A month shall be a day and night for the ancestors (*pitr*), and a year [for them] is for the gods (*daivata*)," all of which is to be understood accordingly.

It may be inferred that even the elemental dissolution (*prākṛtapralaya*) possesses a duration equal to two *parārdhas*, which is the measure of Brahmā’s lifespan. When such a period has elapsed, while You, O Brahman, were maintaining the creative vision (*īkṣā*) characterized by the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*), Māyā—while You were thus accepting, as it were, the activity consisting of the impelling of Māyā, which is denoted by terms such as "vision," "desire to emit," and "contemplation"—became agitated; she moved and remained as if having attained a manifestation separate from Brahman.

"For what purpose? means for the sake of becoming the three worlds—that is, so that [the Self], though previously not of such a nature, may again evolve in the form of the triple world. "From Māyā" means from Māyā thus agitated. The word "khalu" is used for emphasis. "Kāla-śakti" refers to the power of the Lord known as Time (Kāla).

For the sake of all previous living beings—this being the implied meaning—the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of merit and demerit, as well as inherent nature (*svabhāva*), having manifested, expanded her qualities known as *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*, and having cast off the state of equilibrium so that they were oriented toward activity, performed the preparatory service for that Māyā to effect the manifestation of the three worlds. || 3 ||

Having thus described the creation of Māyā, in order to declare the creation of the Great Principle (Mahat), which is its effect, he states the nature of the Puruṣa: "You, O Lord, are celebrated as the Witness when in proximity with Māyā without having entered her body; and when you have entered her through reflection via the various distinctions, you are the Jīva, and not anyone else."
Then, awakened by Time and other factors and impelled by you yourself,
that Māyā indeed created the principle of intellect (buddhitattva), which is called the Great One (mahat).

"Mayā" (by Māyā): [The Lord] is characterized by being proximate to Māyā, having Māyā as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and being indicated by His own nature (*vapuḥ*)—which is unconditioned, situated externally, and not entered [by Māyā] as its substratum. The meaning is that He remains supporting Māyā with one part [of Himself]. Here, by the word "proximate" (*sannihita*), the unreality of the connection between the Supreme Self, whose nature is ultimate reality, and the limiting adjunct, which is non-ultimate, is illuminated.

Being thus constituted, you are celebrated as the Witness (*sākṣin*) by the Upanishads and by those who know them—this is the ellipsis—because you are the illuminator of all. By means of "divisions" (*bhedaiḥ*), that is, having divided yourself according to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), you have entered—that is, you have entered in the form of a reflection (*pratibimba*)—that *māyā*, namely the adjuncts produced by it; thus, being one who identifies with the body and so forth as "I," you alone are the individual soul (*jīva*), and no other, for there is no individual soul distinct from you.

Having thus described the twofold nature of the person (*puruṣa*) through the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he shows the emergence of the Great Principle (*mahat*) in relation to that [person]—beginning with the words "from time" (*kālāt*). That *māyā*, indeed, having been awakened by time, karma, and inherent nature; having its qualities such as *rajas* and so forth agitated and made oriented toward the effect; and having been impelled by You and infused with potency, created—that is, brought forth—the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), which is called the "Great One" (*mahān*) or the "Great Principle" (*mahat-tattva*). The masculine designation is used for the sake of grammatical coordination with the word "Great" (*mahat*).
Its connection with the preceding is: "that [is] the principle of intellect. (4)

If it is asked, "Is this 'Great One' (mahat) not indeed what is denoted by the word 'Great,' namely the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva)?"—and if one wonders what that is and what its essential nature is—the author says:

"In that regard, although this Great One consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), it is primarily characterized by sattva; indeed, within this individual soul (jīva), it produces the emergence of the non-conceptual 'I'-consciousness."

O Viṣṇu! By Your impulsion, the principle of Mahat—the great one which is indeed fully nourished by the three qualities and abounds in tamas—is the source of conceptual cognition within this wheel. || 2 ||

Regarding the word "therein": therein, among the effects of Māyā, this Great One—though himself composed of the three *guṇas*—is predominantly *sattva*. Due to his abundance of luminosity (*prakāśa*), he is the single Great Individual Soul (*mahājīva*), the aggregate of all individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*). Just as a forest is the aggregate of trees, so it is here.

In this individual soul (*jīva*), which is of the nature of a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), that which brings about the realization of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*)—which exists in a state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) free from specific attributes such as "humanity"—is indeed the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*). O Viṣṇu! By Your impulsion, that Great Principle acted as the agent; for You, having presided over the Great Principle, indeed impelled it, and thus it produced the principle of ego (*ahaṃ-tattva*).

And that [intellect] in this living being is the producer of conceptual cognition, such as "I am a human," which brings about determinate knowledge; it is nourished by the three *guṇas* and consists of the three *guṇas*. Nevertheless, it is "overwhelmed by *tamas*," meaning that *tamas* is its predominant constituent. || 5 ||
Then I spoke of the threefold nature:

"I, having attained a threefold state through the sequence of the three qualities (guṇas), become— by means of that first [quality], which is essentially sattva— the Vaikārika, and furthermore the Taijasa and the Tāmasa."
He created the gods—those who pride themselves on their senses: the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Aśvins, Vahnis, Indra, Acyuta, Mitra, Kāma, Vidhu, Vidhi, Śrī, and the Śārīrakas. || 6 ||

Regarding the word "sa" (he): he, having become the Great Principle (mahat), and having arisen as both the "I" and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), again—furthermore—by means of the sequence of the three qualities (*triguṇakrama*), namely through the order of the three qualities, Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, and by means of the sequence of Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Tāmasa, having attained a threefold state or threefold nature, he created by means of the first, the Vaikārika ego-sense, which is of the nature of Sattva, the gods who preside over the senses (*indriyamāninaḥ*), that is, the presiding deities of the senses.

To the question "Who are they?", he says: "The directions," and so forth. The directions (Dik), Wind (Vāta), Sun (Arka), Varuṇa (Pracetas), and the two Aśvins are, respectively, the presiding deities of the organs of knowledge—the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. In this regard, this individual soul (jīva), impelled by the respective presiding deities of the sense organs such as the ear which reside in the openings of the ears and so on, experiences objects such as sound through the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) that emerge via the doors of the sense organs like the ear.

In this manner, the deities known as Vahni (Agni), Indra, Upendra (Viṣṇu), Mitra, and Prajāpati are, respectively, the presiding deities of the five organs of action called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Impelled by them, this individual soul (jīva) performs actions consisting of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure. Similarly, Candra (the Moon), Caturmukha (Brahmā), Śrī Rudra, and Kṣetrajña are the deities of the fourfold internal organs known as mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta). Through these, the soul attains volition, determination, self-identification with the body, and retention.

By Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Prajāpati; again, he describes the creation of the vaikārika [sattvic] type: "O All-pervading One! O Lord! That internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), accompanied by the functions known as mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness, was created from the very portion of *sattva* through Your power."

O Lord of the City of Maruts! From the Taijasa [ego] the group of ten sense organs was born; furthermore, from the Tamasa [ego], the subtle element of space arose, and by Your power, sound was born from that space.

"O Bhūman! O All-pervading One! By Your power—that is, through Your impulsion—the *sattva*-portion, namely the *sāttvika-ahaṅkāra* itself, brought forth that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is dominated by *sattva* and endowed with the mental function (*vṛtti*) called *citta*, accompanied by the *manas*, *buddhi*, and *ahaṅkāra*. From the *taijasa* (the *rājasa-ahaṅkāra*), the group of the ten organs—the five organs of knowledge and the five organs of action—was born."

From the tamasic portion of that ego (ahaṅkāra), O Lord of the City of Maruts! O Lord of the Abode of Wind! by Your power—that is, through Your impulsion—the subtle element of sound, being unquintuplicated (apañcīkṛta) and thus a subtle part of the ether (nabhas), was born. || 7 ||
Furthermore, he elaborates upon the creation from the *tāmasa* ego:
"From sound you created space; from that, touch and the wind;
from that, form and light; then taste and water; and smell and the earth."
Thus, O Mādhava! O Blessed One, you alone have revealed this multitude of beings, which has been burdened by the sins accumulated through successive kalpas, from out of the darkness.

"From sound": O All-pervading One! From sound You created the sky, that is, space (*vyoman*). From that space, You created touch, which is the quality of air; from that touch, air; from that wind, form, which is the quality of fire; from this form, the great fire; and immediately thereafter, from fire, taste, which is the quality of water; from taste, water; from water, smell, which is the quality of earth; and from smell, the great earth. You have thus created them all.

Thus, through the successive calculation and merging of each preceding element with its successor, each subsequent one is endowed with the qualities of each preceding one. The meaning here is as follows: space has sound as its quality; air has the qualities of sound and touch; fire has the qualities of sound, touch, and form; water has the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste; and earth possesses the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

O Blessed One! O You whose qualities are worthy of adoration! O Mādhava! O Lord of Śrī! You alone have manifested this collection of beings—the five great elements endowed with qualities—from the *tāmasa* *ahaṃkāra*. Now, he describes the manner in which the Blessed One fashioned the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) by means of these principles:

"These groups of elements, as well as the groups of sense organs and the gods, having been born separately, were not able at that time to perform the construction of the cosmic egg by means of these deities."

Your virtues have been praised with various hymns; having entered the principles (tattvas) as the Supreme Being, you manifested those excellent powers and fashioned the golden egg (hairaṇyamaṇḍa). || 9 ||

"Etāni" (these): these aforementioned groups of elements (*bhūtagaṇāḥ*)—namely, the ten groups consisting of the subtle elements such as sound and the gross elements such as space—as well as the groups of sense organs (*indriyagaṇāḥ*), which are fourteen including the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the four functions of the internal organ, along with the fourteen deities who preside over them. The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction, or alternatively, in the sense of "also."

Although these [gods] were born for the purpose of fashioning the cosmic egg (*bhuvanāṇḍa*), they were individually unable—indeed, powerless—to perform the task of creating the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*). When they were unable, you, whose qualities are praised, were extolled by these fourteen gods with various hymns (*sūkti*) and praises. The underlying meaning is this: immediately after the creation of Māyā, these gods praised you with hymns, you who had assumed a playful form (*līlāvigraha*) through a portion of your pure essence (*śuddhasattva*).

And by means of that purpose, entering into and penetrating these principles (*tattvas*), you manifested their power of motion, generated their capacity for action, and joined them together—uniting them through the relationship of subordinate and predominant qualities. You fashioned your own body, the cosmic egg known as the *brahmāṇḍa*, which, due to its abundance of light, was as intensely radiant as a mass of gold; this is the meaning. ||9||
That egg indeed remained for a thousand years in the waters created previously; then, piercing it, you fashioned this Virāṭ, known as the Puruṣa, whose form consists of the fourteen worlds.
With thousands of hands, feet, heads, and eyes, he is the essence of all individual souls.
O Lord of the City of the Maruts, you have been manifested; therefore, protect me from all disease! || 10 ||

"An egg"—that indeed was that insentient egg which remained for a thousand years (*sahasraṃ samāḥ*)—the accusative case here denotes duration—in the waters of the previous creation, the enveloping waters. Then, having entered it by means of your own portion and piercing it, you divided it manifold; thus you fashioned the body known as *Virāṭ*, which shines diversely in the form of the fourteen worlds.

Then, you who consist of the totality of all individual souls (niḥśeṣajīvātmaka)—your very nature being the collective self (samaṣṭy-ātmaka) of the life-principle of all moving and non-moving beings through thousands upon thousands of multitudes of limbs such as hands, feet, and heads—such as you, O Lord of Marutpura, have manifested. Therefore, protect me from all maladies (sarvāmaya), that is, from every external and internal disease. || 10 ||
Thus ends the fifth decade, which describes the manner of the origin of the Virāṭ Puruṣa.
Having thus demonstrated the origin of the gross body of the Lord known as Virāṭ, he now explains the method of conceiving the distinctions of its limbs for the purpose of meditation:
O Lord! For one who has thus become identical with the fourteen worlds, they say that Pātāla is the sole surface of Your feet; and even the region above Your feet, O God, they call Rasātala.
Indeed, O you whose nature is the great and wondrous foundation, [there are] two ankles. || 1 ||

"Thus," [it is said]. O Lord! In this manner, as described, those who know the methods of worship—the sages—declare that the soles of Your feet are the netherworld (pātāla), for You have attained identity with them, meaning You have assumed bodies composed of them. "The region above the feet" refers to the pair of forefeet. He whose self—that is, His body—is wonderful is called "adbhutātmā. || 1 ||
O Ambaramaṅga! Your calves are Sutala and Talātala; your knees are Vitala and Atala; your pair of thighs is Kṣoṇītala;
your hips are the celestial Gaṅgā; and your navel and chest, O wielder of the discus, are the abode of Śakra. || 2 ||

"Janghe" (the shanks) refers to the pair of thigh-sections; the lower part of the thighs is *vitala* and the upper part is *atala*. "Kṣoṇītala" (the surface of the earth) refers to the hip-region (*jaghana*). The use of the word *jaghana* for the Blessed One’s hip is intended to express its beauty, for it is said: "The buttocks (*nitamba*) are behind the woman's waist, while *jaghana* is the front. "O Aṅga! O Blessed One! "Śakranilaya" (the abode of Indra) is heaven, and "vakṣas" (chest) is yours, O Cakrapāṇi! || 2 ||
Your neck is Mahas, Your face Janas, Your forehead Tapas, and Your head is Satya, the essence of all;
O Blessed One, whose body consists of the entire universe, salutations to You, whose form is bound by others who themselves depend upon the world. || 3 ||

Regarding the word "grīvā": Your neck—the region of the throat—is Maharloka; Janas is Janaloka; Tapaḥ is Tapoloka; the forehead (phālam) is Satyaloka, belonging to the Universal Self (viśvātman). O You whose body consists of the world (jaganmayatanu)! O Viśvamūrti! To You, whose body is thus composed—constructed with limbs made complete by other [worlds] already mentioned and those yet to be described—O Blessed One, let there be obeisance to You. || 3 ||

It has been stated that [the world] is bound in body by others as well who depend upon the world. He elaborates on that very point: "O Keśava, the hollows of the cavities of Your nostrils are the dwelling place of the universe; O Lord, Your locks of hair are the meters of the cosmic root-stalk;
the pair of Your shimmering eyes is the abode of Brahmā."
The eyelashes are night and day, and the sun is his eyes.

"Tvaditi": O Lord! O Viśvakanda! O Cause of the Universe! Your *brahmarandhra*—the limit of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*)—is that very station; the *chandāṃsi* are the Vedas themselves. The clouds are the mass of your hair. The pair of your shimmering, beautiful eyebrows is the abode of Druhiṇa (Brahmā). The eyelashes—the hairs of the eyes above and below—are respectively night and day. The two eyes, the pair of visual organs, are the Sun (*savitṛ*).

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, one should seek [the following correspondences]: Sāṅkhya and Yoga are the two shark-shaped earrings, and the umbrella is the abode of Viṣṇu (Vikuṇṭha), and so forth. || 4 ||
O Blessed One, the creation of the entire universe without exception is the casting of Your side-glance;
the quarters of space are Your two ears; Your two nostrils are greed and shame; and Your lower lip is the organ of generation.
The clusters of stars are her teeth, and Śamana is her fangs.

"Without remainder": O Lord, the creation of the entire universe—the fashioning of the fourteen worlds—is the casting of Your sidelong glance. The quarters are Your ears; the two Aśvins are Your two nostrils. Greed is Your lower lip; shame is Your upper lip. O Blessed One! The hosts of stars, the lords of the constellations, are Your teeth; Śamana (Yama) is Your fang. 5.
O Lord! Your playful smile is illusion (māyā), your breath is the wind, your tongue is water, and your speech is a flight of birds;
the hosts of Siddhas and others are the vowels, the fire is the cavity of your mouth, the gods are your arms, and the god of dharma (Yama) is your pair of breasts. 6.

"Maya" refers to Your playful smile, that graceful laugh. "Samīra" is the wind; "śvasita" is the breath. Your tongue is the water. O Lord! O Īśvara! Your speech is a flock of birds, a multitude of winged creatures. Siddhas and others—Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and so forth—are the groups of musical notes (svaragaṇas), the sets of pitches (śrutibhedabhinnāḥ) such as Ṣaḍja and the rest. The cavity of the mouth is fire. The gods, Indra and others, are Your arms.
Dharma, the deity who is the embodiment of righteousness, is Your pair of breasts. || 6 ||
O Lord! Your back is Adharma; O Lotus-eyed One, Your mind is the moon, and Your heart-lotus is the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
Your belly is the multitude of oceans, while Your two twilights are Your garment; Prajāpati is Your penis, and Mitra is Your testicles.

Regarding the word "back": the back is non-dharma (the absence of unrighteousness). O Lord, O radiant one! In this form, the moon is your mind; your heart-lotus is the unmanifest *pradhāna* itself, the equilibrium of the three qualities such as *sattva*. O lotus-eyed one! The multitude of oceans is your belly. The morning and evening twilights are your pair of garments. Prajāpati, Brahmā, is your penis. And that Mitra is your two testicles.

O Ocean of Compassion! Your hips are the abode of herds of deer, your toenails are elephants, camels, and horses, and your gait is Time itself; your face is the lotus-born Brahmā, your arms are the Kṣatriyas, your two thighs are the Vaiśyas, and your feet are the Śūdras. 8.

"Thighs"—the hosts of deer are your two thighs. "Those" refers to the nails on your feet; they are like the faces of elephants, camels, and *saindhava* horses (where *saindhava* means a horse). "Your gait, however, is Time. O Ocean of Compassion! the sense is that you should show me grace because I am devoted to the worship of such a form. "Face-lotus," "arms," "beautiful and lovely pair of thighs," and "feet"—this is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). Because these are parts of a living being, the singular number is used.

Your lotus-face and other limbs are the abode—the dwelling place—of the social orders beginning with the Brahmins. The meaning is: your mouth is the station of the Brahmins, your arms are the station of the Kṣatriyas, your pair of thighs is the station of the Vaiśyas, and your feet are the station of the Śūdras. || 8 ||
O Wielder of the Wheel, the wheel of saṃsāra is your wheel; your activity is the spokes, your vigor is the multitude of great asuras, the bones are the mountains,
the collection of channels are the rivers, and the body hairs are the trees.
May this [world], which was previously inexplicable, be conquered by You, O Lord! || 9 ||

Regarding the word *saṃsāra*: O Cakradhara! O Lord! O Controller of all! *Saṃsāra* is the suffering of birth, death, and so forth; that very cycle, due to its revolving nature, is the *cakra*. Your *kriyās* (actions) consist of the forms of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), speech, grasping (*upādāna*), and purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*). The host or multitude of great *asuras* is the collection of your heroic prowess (*vīrya-parākrama*). Your bones or, according to another reading, "the collections of bones," are the mountains (*śaila*). Your veins (*nāḍī*) or channels (*sirā*) are the successions of rivers (*sarit-samudaya*). Your body hair (*roma*, *tanūruha*) is the trees (*taru*, *vṛkṣa*).

The particle *ca* is used here as a collective conjunction (*samuccaya*). The meaning is: "May this body, which is thus indescribable and immeasurable, prevail—that is, may it manifest with supreme excellence. (9)

Thus, having contemplated the form of the Blessed One for the sake of accomplishing the worship of the Universal Form (viśvamūrti), he speaks of those qualified for this worship: "They say that such a body of Yours, consisting of the universe, should be remembered by those who partake in karma at the time of the conclusion of their karma."
O Lord of the Abode of Vāta! Salutations to you, whose inner self is pure; may you ward off all diseases for me. || 10 ||

"Such as this": they say that such a form of yours—the cosmic body (*virāḍ-rūpa*) of the aforementioned kind—is to be remembered at the time of the conclusion of one's ritual duties by those who partake in such duties. "Those who partake in duties" (*karmabhājaḥ*) are those qualified for the practice of devotion (*sādhana-bhakti*), as they engage in duties that are limbs of devotion, such as hearing, remembering, and glorifying. For them, it is "to be remembered" (*smaraṇīyam*), meaning it is possible to remember it at the conclusion of their ritual service consisting of the sixteen offerings. The meaning is that other forms of worship, such as the formless meditation (*niṣkala-upāsanā*), are impossible for those who still possess identification with the physical body.

This was stated to Arjuna after the Lord had revealed His universal form (viśvarūpa): "Fix your mind on Me alone," and "For the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by those who possess bodies. Thus, demonstrating that the worshiper of the cosmic form consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) is gradually qualified for the worship of the form composed of pure goodness (śuddhasattva), he prays to the Blessed One with the words beginning with "tasya" (of him).

Salutations to You, that pure Self (vimalātman) of such a Virāj, whose body is the inner self (antarātmavapuṣ), who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin), and whose form consists of pure being (śuddhasattvamaya). O Lord of Vātālaya! Thus, for the sake of the power of my gradual worship, restrain—that is, destroy—my diseases. ||10||

Thus ends the sixth decade, which is a description of the Virāṭ body as being the self of the universe. Now, for one whose mind is thus fixed upon the Lord’s form consisting of the three guṇas, [the text] reveals the Lord’s form known as Hiraṇyagarbha, which consists of two guṇas: [The verse continues: "The worlds are His feet; the earth is His foundation. The atmosphere is His navel, and heaven is His head. (10.6.2) The meaning is as follows: the worlds—the fourteen worlds beginning with Bhūr—are His feet; the earth is His foundation—that is, the ground upon which He stands. The atmosphere is His navel; heaven is His head. By this, the Lord’s form as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is described. Furthermore, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are His lower part, while the seven worlds beginning with Mahar are His upper part. The worlds situated between them are His middle part. Thus, the entire universe is the body of the Lord. (10.6.3) By this, the Lord’s form as the *hiraṇyagarbha*—which consists of the two guṇas of sattva and rajas—is revealed. This is because the *hiraṇyagarbha* is the presiding deity of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the fourteen worlds, which consist of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), are His body. (10.6.4) Furthermore, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are His lower part, while the seven worlds beginning with Mahar are His upper part. The worlds situated between them are His middle part. Thus, the entire universe is the body of the Lord. (10.6.5) By this, the Lord’s form as the *hiraṇyagarbha*—which consists of the two guṇas of sattva and rajas—is revealed. This is because the *hiraṇyagarbha* is the presiding deity of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the fourteen worlds, which consist of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), are His body. (10.6.6) Moreover, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are His lower part, while the seven worlds beginning with Mahar are His upper part. The worlds situated between them are His middle part. Thus, the entire universe is the body of the Lord. (10.6.7) By this, the Lord’s form as the *hiraṇyagarbha*—which consists of the two guṇas of sattva and rajas—is revealed. This is because the *hiraṇyagarbha* is the presiding deity of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the fourteen worlds, which consist of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), are His body. (10.6.8) Furthermore, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are His lower part, while the seven worlds beginning with Mahar are His upper part. The worlds situated between them are His middle part. Thus, the entire universe is the body of the Lord. (10.6.9) By this, the Lord’s form as the *hiraṇyagarbha*—which consists of the two guṇas of sattva and rajas—is revealed. This is because the *hiraṇyagarbha* is the presiding deity of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the fourteen worlds, which consist of the gross elements (*mahābhūta*), are His body. (10.6.10) In this way, the seventh decade describes the Lord’s form as the *sūtrātman*, which consists of the single guṇa of sattva. (10.7.1) Furthermore, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr are His lower part, while the seven worlds beginning with Mahar are His upper part. The worlds situated between them are His middle part. Thus, the entire universe is the body of the Lord. (10.7.2) By this, the Lord’s form as the *sūtrātman*—which consists of the single guṇa of
Thus it is, O Lord! Having first come into being in the form of the fourteen-fold universe, you yourself were then born as the Creator (Dhātṛ) in the abode of Satyaloka above that.

Him they praise as Hiraṇyagarbha, the life-soul of the entire triple world, who became possessed of the essence of the desire to create various beings, blossoming through the transformation of abundant *rajas*. || 1 ||

"Thus" means this is the intended sense here: since cognitions penetrate an object through a sequence of gross and subtle stages, one first fixes the mind upon the form of the Lord consisting of the three *guṇas*; once it is steady there, one enters that which consists of two *guṇas*, then that which consists of the single *guṇa* of *sattva*, and finally, having entered the subtle Brahman which is beyond all *guṇas*, one attains the fulfillment of all duties through the attainment of unsurpassed bliss.

O Lord! Having yourself indeed arisen in this manner as the fourteen-fold world-form, you subsequently became the Creator (Dhātṛ) in the abode of Satyaloka above that very world—whom those learned in the scriptures call Hiraṇyagarbha. For you are the life-force (jīva) of the Virāj consisting of the three worlds, the presiding deity over the aggregate of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) composed of the five vital breaths, mind, intellect, and the ten senses; such is your nature.

He whose "flourishing interest in the desire to create manifold forms" (*vikasannānāsisṛkṣārasaḥ*)— meaning he whose eagerness (*rasa* = *āgraha*) for the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) various bodies such as those of gods, humans, and animals, along with their objects of enjoyment, manifests and expands through the "thick and increased transformations of *rajas*" (*rajovikāraiḥ*), which are the effects of the quality of *rajas* (wherein the cognition of duality, the cognition of utility, passion, and so forth are the effects of *rajas*)— is here shown in the form of Brahmā, the architect of the universe (*viśvakarmā*),
as follows: "Mounted upon a swan, four-faced, resembling molten gold,
clad in white garments, with long ears and a gentle beard, and four-armed."
Pot-bellied, wearing an upper garment and a sacred thread, seated in the yogic posture, enriched by the beauty of a crown of matted hair, with tawny eyes, she is the bestower of boons.
"Holding a water-pot, a rosary, a drum, a shield, and a book, the serene form of Brahmā should be meditated upon even by the gods. (1)
This very person, having surrendered his heart to the creation of the universe, remained agitated by anxiety, for he himself had not attained true awakening regarding the nature of the world;
at that moment, O Lord of the worlds! you indeed spoke these words from the sky: "Perform austerity! and so it was.
We have heard this speech of his, which is pleasant to the ear and provides an impetus toward asceticism.

"He" refers to him. Having set his heart upon the manifold creation—the emanation of all moving and unmoving beings—due to the imbalance of the *guṇas*, he remained there, filled with anxiety, as he himself observed, sought to know, and reflected, not knowing what support or what nature the consciousness regarding the universe has, nor how he himself should create. He stood there, agitated by thought.

O Lord of the worlds! O you who are skilled in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe! At that very moment, you caused this Brahmā to hear such a voice—one that was aerial, meaning it was manifested in the sky without a visible body—and which was pleasant to the ear, bestowing joy upon the listener. Thus, by making him hear these words, you performed the injunction that impels him toward austerity, saying, "Perform penance! || 2 ||
Immediately after those words, he describes the activity of the Creator:

"Who was that man who spoke to me?"— thus, while the entire circle of the world was filled with water, he looked toward the quarters, and seeing nothing at all, he contemplated the meaning of the sentence.
"For a thousand divine years you propitiated Him through intense austerity; He revealed to him His own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which is uniquely wondrous.

(1.3) "Who was he? [The meaning is: When the entire circle of the world was filled with water, who was that Person who spoke to me? When the universe consisted of nothing but water, someone hidden within it indeed spoke these words to me. Who was that Person? It cannot be said that no one existed at all. "He" (asau)—from hearing this distinct speech, it is inferred that there is certainly a speaker.

"Therefore, he must be seen"—thinking thus, he looked toward the four directions; desiring to see his speaker, he rose from his place and, walking about, raised his face and looked, yet saw nothing at all—not only the man who spoke, but not even water or any other object. Then, reflecting upon the meaning of those words, perceiving and understanding them—meaning that he was certain this was the impulse of the Lord directed toward him, saying, "Perform penance, and then you shall possess the power of creation"—thereafter... [and so on].

"Remaining in your own abode for a thousand divine years"—the accusative case here denotes duration (atyantasaṃyoga). By that Brahmā, who had undertaken—that is, accepted and performed—austerity, you were propitiated and served; and to that Brahmā, you showed your own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, the realm of Vaikuṇṭha. Of what nature was it? "Uniquely wonderful" (*ekādbhutam*): it is a single, preeminent wonder.
The meaning is that it is such that there is no other wonder beyond it; thus it is "uniquely wonderful. || 3 ||

He establishes its singular wonder through three verses beginning with "māyā": "Where Māyā never manifests her transformations, the world shines forth externally; states such as sorrow, anger, delusion, and fear have gone far away."

O All-pervading Lord! That abode of Yours, which consists of the radiance of the supreme light and wherein flows a torrent of intense bliss—that Vaikuṇṭha-form has been manifested and reigns supreme. || 4 ||

Regarding the word *māyā*: in that abode of Vaikuṇṭha, *māyā* never undergoes transformation even at the creation or dissolution of Brahmā; the meaning is that she does not perform her function of manifesting herself as distinct from the Lord, who is the source of her own body and so forth. This being the case, what need is there to mention the absence of the possibility of desire, anger, and the like? Thus he says: "States such as sorrow, anger, delusion, and fear have gone far away."

Grief is affliction; anger is resentment; delusion is the egoistic conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth; and trepidation is the fear of death and the like—all such states and objects have gone far away, as is understood from the ellipsis "because [they have]. And where there is a stream, a flow, of intense, condensed bliss—this being the implied meaning—there, for those who abide, there is only the constant experience of the bliss of Brahman. Now, one might object: even in Satyaloka, there is grief in some slight measure.

If Vaikuṇṭhaloka is but a single part of that [universe], one might wonder how it can be entirely free from even a trace of affliction; in response to this doubt, he says: "It shines outside the world. The meaning is that it shines, being external to the fourteen worlds.

Therefore, in that which consists of the manifestation of the supreme light—wherein there is no illumination from the lights of the sun, moon, and so forth, but rather the supreme light is the illuminator even of those; wherein Brahman is the light that bestows the power of illumination upon the sun and others—that is the "manifestation of the supreme light. In that essence, in such a nature: O All-pervading One! O Pervader of the Universe! That abode of Yours named Vaikuṇṭha, which was manifested and shown by You to Brahmā, thus shines forth, meaning it exists as the most excellent of all. || 4 ||

May that abode in the form of Vaikuṇṭha— where divine beings sport, their four-armed forms bathed in the pure luster of sapphire-blue Hari, illuminating the quarters with various jeweled ornaments and residing in shining celestial palaces; where such exalted stations are attained through devotion, and which has cast out all impurities— be ever victorious!
