Regarding the phrase "in which": in that world, divine devotees whose forms consist of pure *sattva* and who have attained a form similar to yours (*bhavatsārūpya*) sport—that is, they shine brilliantly. Now, one might ask: what doing will they go to Vaikuṇṭha? To this he says: "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*).

Those who have attained—that is, obtained—such a lofty station or state through devotion characterized by love and devoid of desire for fruits; being such as these, they "shine. This is intended to demonstrate that the attainment of similarity in form with the Lord does not occur through ritual action. He describes this very similarity in form with the Lord, beginning with the words "four-armed" and so forth: those whose luster and splendor are dark like a *harimaṇi* (sapphire) and yet bright and clear.

Furthermore, they sport as those whose dwellings are celestial vehicles (*vimāna*) shining with networks of jewels, tinkling bells, garlands, canopies, and so forth, which illuminate the quarters of the sky—meaning the spaces between the directions are lit up by the gems inlaid within various ornaments such as crowns, crocodile-shaped earrings, and anklets—and thus they shine brilliantly.

Where this is so, may that abode of Vaikuṇṭha—by which all your impurities, consisting of ignorance and its effects, have been cast out and dispelled—triumph, meaning may it shine forth as the most excellent of all. || 5 ||
Surrounded by various celestial women, and illuminated by the intermediate quarters with her vine-like limbs— charming and intoxicating to the entire world— which resemble flickering creepers,
Lakṣmī herself is seen, her sole curiosity fixed upon the fragrance of your lotus feet.
Grant me that state of yours, which possesses such wondrous and divine majesty.

"Nānā" (various): In that fragrance (*saurabha*) of Your two lotus feet, the Goddess Mahālakṣmī—the Mother of the Universe—out of a singular curiosity, for the very reason of her unswerving wonder, has herself, by her own self, [become manifold].

It is perceived; it becomes an object of sight for those dwelling there. Of what kind? It is surrounded and encompassed by thousands of various divine women. It is like a flash of lightning, resembling a streak of lightning smeared with nectar. This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: "the vine-like body which is heart-stealing and intoxicating to the entire world. Thus, by means of that [body], she illuminates the quarters, making the intervals between the directions radiant.

Furthermore, she is perceived as one whose divine, sattvic manifestations and instruments are wondrous, never before seen or heard of elsewhere. Now, if the reading is *vismayanīyadivyavibhavam*, then the connection is with the phrase "that state" (*tat padam*). "Grant me that; lead me, who am intensely eager, to that state of Vaikuṇṭha—what loss is there for you? is the implied sense. || 6 ||

Having described the realm of Vaikuṇṭha with three verses in this context and having also revealed his own longing for its attainment, he now descends to the subject at hand: "There, in his own abode thus displayed, [he beholds the Lord] seated upon a jeweled throne, adorned with a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments as radiant as ten million suns."
O All-pervading Lord! May that form of Yours—the cause of all worlds, marked with the Śrīvatsa and reddened by the luster of the Kaustubha gem—be revealed to me; may it shine before my eyes. 7.

Regarding the word *tatra*: "there," in that [place] thus indicated and revealed by grace—[the word] "by you" being understood as the ellipsis—*vidhiḥ*, Brahmā, beheld (*aikṣata*) your form in your own station (*nijapade*), that is, in your own world (*ātmaloke*). To the question of what kind of form it was, he says: "seated upon a jeweled throne," meaning seated upon a lion-throne of gems; "radiant" (*bhāsvat*).

That form which is the cause of all things, both moving and unmoving—that is, the material cause—is resplendent with ornaments such as crowns and bracelets that shine with the power of the gathered images of ten million suns; it is marked by the Śrīvatsa and the footprint of Bhṛgu; and it is reddish-pink, having attained a supreme luster through the all-pervading beauty of the shadow of the accepted Kaustubha gem, the jewel known as Kaustubha.

Brahmā beheld [the Lord] and said: "O All-pervading One! O Sovereign! Let that form of Yours shine before me; let it become manifest to my direct perception. The underlying intention here is this: You, who were pleased with Brahmā as he remained in his own abode, revealed Your own wondrous Vaikuṇṭha world and Your own essential nature seated upon a jeweled throne within a gem-studded palace there, radiant with the mass of light from exquisite divine ornaments—may that very same form appear before me in this manner.
There is no effort at all; therefore, I pray most earnestly that it may shine forth for me. || 7 ||
"Even though I do not possess such merit as this, nevertheless, pray for this," he said:

[May I behold] Him whose luster is as soft as a blue lotus in the rainy season, who covers the circle of the directions with His discus, whose noble face is brightened by the flow of a broad, gentle smile,
and whose beautiful circle of arms holds a shining conch, mace, sword, and lotus.
O All-pervading Lord! May this form of Yours, which brings satisfaction to the Creator, dispel my disease.

Regarding "kāla": it refers to that [face] wherein the countenance is serene due to the continuous flow (*syanda*) of a noble and most enchanting gentle smile, which covers the circle of the directions with a mass (*cakra*) of lovely splendors as tender as a dark rain cloud or a *kalāya* flower; and wherein the glorious (*śrīmat*), ever-resplendent circle of arms bears the shining conch, mace, discus, and lotus—O you who bring satisfaction to the Creator, Brahmā!

O All-pervading Lord! If Your form were to manifest within my mind, it would dispel my disease and drive away my illness; my maladies, which have their cause in sin, would surely flee. "When Govinda is remembered in the mind, sins depart to a great distance, just as darkness vanishes when the Lord of Day has ascended the Eastern Mountain."
The meaning is that even that [objection], on account of such a statement, was pacified. || 8 ||

Having thus expressed his aspiration out of eagerness due to the force of the context, he says— without forgetting the subject at hand: "Beholding [you], the lotus-born Brahmā, filled with agitation and overcome by a surge of joy, fell at the pair of your lotus-feet, becoming fulfilled through love."

O Lord, you surely know my desire; that knowledge which is rich in the realization of your own nature as both dual and non-dual—worshiping you who have declared such [knowledge], I take refuge in you. || 9 ||

"Having seen"—Brahmā, the lotus-born, having seen that form of yours, was seized by such agitation that he was rendered momentarily incapable of performing even the slightest action due to the confusion arising from his bewilderment regarding what ought to be done, such as the rites of service, worship, prostration, and praise; remaining thus for a time, being subject to and overwhelmed by the joy born of your presence, he fell at your lotus-feet, prostrating himself like a staff with all eight limbs touching the ground.

Rising again and feeling fulfilled with joy, he spoke thus: "O All-pervading Lord! You surely know the desire within my heart, for you are the witness to the intellects of all beings. Nevertheless, with the intention of saying it anyway, he says—[using the feminine suffix] *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*—"I worship You, whom he addressed, saying: 'Bestow upon me, through Your grace, that supreme knowledge which has as its object that reality—the nature of Yours which is both dual and non-dual, the higher and lower Brahman. || 9 ||
Then, touching his copper-hued feet with his own hand as he bowed low, [the Lord] spoke these words:
"Your awakening shall come; even bondage does not arise through the processes of worldly creation.
Having thus addressed him and greatly gladdened his heart, [the Lord], remaining hidden within his mind, himself—
O Blessed One, you raised him up at the time of creation; may he, in turn, cause our well-being to flourish.

"O you with copper-hued [feet]!"—then that Blessed One, touching hand to hand like a friend his friend Brahmā—who was bowing down with devotion, trust, and great respect toward his feet, which were slightly copper-colored like red lotuses—spoke these words: "The awakening you have requested shall soon be yours; moreover, through the processes of creation, even the bondage of the physical body shall no longer arise. Having thus addressed him, he spoke.

Having followed [his purpose], having gratified him exceedingly and made him fully satisfied, you yourself remained hidden within his mind; being thus concealed within the mind of that Brahmā, you raised him up for creation, meaning that you, remaining in the heart of Brahmā as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), properly impelled him toward creation—O Blessed One, you who are such, "ullāsayā" means "bring about my health," i.e., perfectly accomplish my well-being. || 10 || 45 ||

The form endowed with three qualities, that with two qualities, that with the single quality of pure sattva, and the qualityless (nirguṇa) form— these have been described as the objects of worship, bearing fruit in the second [chapter].

Thus ends the seventh decade, which describes the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, his performance of austerities, the true nature of Vaikuṇṭha, the direct realization of the Lord’s own nature, and the grace of the Lord.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra.
In the work titled *Bhaktapriyā*,
this is the second chapter-section.
It is for the purpose of removing the web of obstacles to the worship of the Lord in the manner previously described.
The pastimes of Viṣṇu are to be contemplated; therein, the creation is described.

Thus, the collection of conditions for *samādhi* that is capable of bringing about the success of the meditation (*upāsanā*) of those seeking liberation has been shown. In this regard, the obstacles to yoga (*yogāntarāya*) are: illness, languor, doubt, negligence, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability; as well as pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and irregular breathing, along with their concomitants. Among these, illness is unfitness for meditation. Lack of renunciation is desire for sense objects. Failure to attain a stage is the non-attainment of the plane of *samādhi*.

In the state of rising from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one should contemplate the divine play (*līlā*) of the Lord’s incarnations for the purpose of pacifying these [distractions] and for the attainment of the desired goal. As it has been said: “O Arjuna! He who thus knows in truth my divine birth and action, upon casting off the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me.”
Thus it is said. In that regard, the divine play (*līlā*) is tenfold:

"In this [system], there are creation (*sarga*), emission (*visarga*), maintenance (*sthāna*), nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), the secondary creations (*ūtayaḥ*), the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantara*), the accounts of the Lords (*īśānukathā*), dissolution (*nirodha*), liberation (*mukti*), and the refuge (*āśraya*)."

Because of this statement, there too [the author] begins first by showing the Lord’s sport of creation (*sṛṣṭilīlā*), as well as the incarnations relevant and incidental thereto—such as Varāha, Kapila, the four Sāṃkhyas, Śrī Rudra, Nārada, Manu, and others:

"Thus, at the end of the dissolution of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), having indeed taken birth in the first Brahma-kalpa, Brahmā, having again received the Vedas from you alone, performed the creation of beings similar to those of the previous kalpa. (1)

"Thus": the dissolution of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). When its end—the conclusion—has arrived, at the beginning of the first Brahmā-kalpa, at the start of the first day of the present Brahmā known as Śabdabrahman, having received birth from you, Viṣṇu, he became Brahmā. Having again obtained the Vedas, the *Ṛg* and so forth, from you alone, he performed a creation similar to that of the previous kalpa; for just as the seasonal signs are uniform throughout the seasons, so too is there a similarity of creation in every kalpa.
The meaning is that, according to the Mahābhārata, he has repeatedly performed creations in successive kalpas that were identical to those of the preceding kalpas. || 1 ||
He has thus passed many times through days measured by a thousand cycles of the four yugas, as well as nights of equal duration;
yet he now sleeps, having dissolved into you along with all that he created— therefore, they call this night of his the "occasional dissolution" (naimittika-pralaya).

"He" refers to this very Brahmā; he has passed many times—that is, numerous times—days known as *kalpas*, measured and delimited by a number of thousands of four-age cycles (*caturyuga*), as well as nights of equal duration. He has brought them to an end many times over.

"He sleeps, having dissolved together with all the moving and non-moving beings created by himself into You, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa. For at the end of the day, Brahmā, withdrawing the moving and non-moving world he himself created, becomes one with Śrī Nārāyaṇa—who lies upon the couch of the lord of serpents in the single ocean—and goes to sleep. Therefore, because this dissolution of Brahmā is caused by his own sleep, they call his night the "occasional dissolution" (naimittika-pralaya). || 2 ||
Moreover, by your grace, he daily creates for those like us a creation equal to the duties of the dawn;
and likewise for those born in the previous Brahma-kalpa, who possess supreme longevity.
Then that emission is like waking from sleep. || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "of those like us": furthermore, that Brahmā, by your grace, performs daily a creation equal to those duties—such as purification, ritual rinsing, breath-control, twilight worship, recitation, and fire-offerings—which are to be performed day after day at the break of dawn by those like us.

And here, those whose birth was previously in the former Brāhma-kalpa are "tathā" (such); for even those such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others, who possess an exceedingly long lifespan, their [experience] at the conclusion of that occasional dissolution is equal to falling asleep and waking up—that is, comparable to sleep and awakening. Now, one might object: "Should it not simply be said that they too, like Brahmā, undergo sleep and awakening? Why is it stated that there is a creation at the beginning of the kalpa? Do not say so; for they have merged into Brahmā and are created once again by Brahmā himself.

For Brahman, however, because there is no creation by means of a mental impression (*brahmamṛṣṭi*), there are only sleep and awakening. Now, one might object: "In that case, let it be simply a creation, just as it is for people like us; why is it said to be 'like waking from sleep'? Do not say so. Because the recollection of the objects of the previous *kalpa* does not cease, it is similar to waking from sleep. For those like us, however, because that [recollection] is absent, it is merely a creation; thus the distinction is established, and what was said is correct. || 3 ||
O Infinite One! Now, having exceeded fifty years—which constitute one half of Your own lifespan—He remains;
therein, O Lord, I shall first describe the events produced during the final night, and afterwards, Your divine sports upon the arrival of the day.

"Five thousand" means this Brahmā now exists having passed beyond one *parārdha*—which is half of his own lifespan characterized by two *parārdhas*, specifically the first half consisting of fifty years, where each "year" is a measure of five thousand [human] years. The word "hi" indicates well-known fact; the meaning is that this Vārāha Kalpa is well known as the beginning of the second *parārdha*. Among those Kalpas, the first, the Brāhma, has been described.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "born at the end of the final night": the immediately preceding Padma Kalpa has just passed; the night following that is the final night of the first *parārdha*. Those [deeds] born during that night—and subsequently, at the descent of the day and at the commencement of the [Vārāha] Kalpa—O Bhūman, O You who are unbounded by time and space! those *vilāsas* of Yours, Your playful sports (*līlā*) related to creation and dissolution—I shall describe them; the meaning is that I begin to praise them.
Then, at the close of day, the Lotus-born One, desiring deep sleep, dissolved into you;
and the worlds entered your belly, so that this entire universe became a single ocean.

"At the close of day": then, at the end of the day—that is, at the conclusion of the previous kalpa—the lotus-born Brahmā, desiring deep sleep, became absorbed in You, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa; having merged into You, he fell asleep. At that time, the worlds and all living beings also entered Your belly, reaching the region of Your abdomen along with Brahmā. Then, during that dissolution (pralaya), this universe became a single ocean, with nothing remaining but water. || 5 ||
While the serpent-king Śeṣa was your very garment, and while the world remained as water alone, you lay reclining;
your true nature being the experience of intense bliss, your self was sealed by the sleep of your own yoga.

"Thine": thus, when the world remained as water alone—that is, when only water remained—you lay (śeṣe), meaning you rested, upon Śeṣa, the king of serpents known as Ananta, who is indeed your own form in a particular state of manifestation. He is of the nature of that very experience which is both blissful and dense; that is to say, he is of the nature of perfect knowledge. Here, "density" means the absence of any form other than the experience of bliss; the sense is that his essential nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).

Yoga is the investigation into one's own true nature; that itself is like sleep, hence it is called "yoga-sleep. He whose self—his very nature—is thus properly sealed or marked by his own yoga-sleep is described as such. (6)

"It shone forth. The root *as* is used in the senses of "going," "shining," and "taking" (Dhātupāṭha 1.504); it belongs to the *bhvādi* class. Alternatively, *āsa* is an indeclinable, a substitute for a finite verb (*tiṅ-pratirūpaka*), having the sense of "being.
At the beginning [of creation], You indeed commanded: "Awaken the power known as Time at the conclusion of the dissolution," and so forth;
by You, the abode of all living beings, who were then fast asleep while the multitude of powers lay dormant. (7)

Regarding the word *kāla*: first, at the commencement of dissolution (*pralaya*), by You—who, as the abode of all living beings (*akhilajīvadhāman*) in which the multitude (*vraja*) of powers (*śakti*), namely the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, are fast asleep and dissolved; and who, being such, serve as the place of rest for a very long time for those souls exhausted by the sufferings of transmigratory existence—and by You, commanding and ordaining: "At the end of dissolution, when the night characterized by a thousand cycles of four ages has concluded, awaken me," [He said].

Likewise, [the Self] remains in a state of deep sleep together with the power called Time (kālākhyā-śakti), relying on the non-difference between the power and the possessor of power (śakti-śaktimatoḥ). The sense is as follows: just as a certain man with many wives, while the others are asleep, dwells for some time with his beloved wife; and having instructed her at dawn, "Wake me up," he then embraces her very tightly and goes to a blissful sleep—so it is here. || 7 ||
O Lord of the Universe! While you, the peerless one, were thus asleep for a thousand cycles of the four ages, the power known as Time first awakened and indeed roused you.

Regarding the phrase "of the four ages": while you alone, without a second, were thus asleep until the end of the dissolution for as long as a thousand cycles of four ages, O Lord of the Universe! the power known as Time (Kālākhyā-śakti), having first awakened, indeed roused you. Here, the word *kila* indicates that this is well-known solely from the Purāṇas. || 8 ||

And having awakened, O You who recline within the womb of the waters! beholding all the worlds dissolved, You cast Your gaze upon those very universes which, existing within Yourself, abide there in their subtle form.

"Vibudhya" (having awakened): O You who recline within the waters of the cosmic egg! Having awakened and beheld all the worlds dissolved within You—[an objection may be raised: how is it possible to behold those that are dissolved? To this He says: "In them. This means that because they abide within His own interior in a subtle form as the causal state, He cast His gaze upon and beheld all those very worlds. || 9 ||
He describes the manner of the creation of the phenomenal world through the gateway of the navel-lotus:

"Then, O Beloved! from the cavity of Your navel, there arose a certain divine lotus, which was the condensed form of the entire series of objects that had been dissolved within it, appearing like a closing bud. (10)
The reading "tayādau" would likely be that of the commentators.

Regarding the word "tataḥ": O Blessed One! "From that"—that is, immediately after Your glance—there emerged from the aperture of Your navel a certain divine lotus, abounding in light and consisting of pure essence (*sattva*). It was the "condensation"—meaning its existence in a subtle form—of the "garland," or the entire collection, of all living beings and the objects they enjoy; thus, it means it was the seed-form of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). It remained in the state of a bud, as if closing itself into a bud. || 10 ||
This very bud of a lotus of yours, having sprouted from your body upon the path of the waters,
emerged outside and utterly severed the impurity of darkness with its rays flashing in every direction.

Regarding the phrase "tadetad" (this very thing): this very bud, the unopened flower of the lotus, has sprouted—that is, it has taken root—in the watery path surrounding Your body, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa, because that region is enveloped by water. Gradually, having transcended the water, it has emerged outside. And then, with its own radiance—its innate effulgence—shining forth on all sides, it has utterly cut through the impurity of darkness, which is of the nature of gloom; or rather, it has completely, excessively, and utterly uprooted the darkness. || 11 ||
Upon that lotus, held by your power, which was exceedingly variegated with fully blossomed petals,
the lotus-born Brahmā appeared, having himself awakened to the entire mass of the Vedas.

Regarding the phrase "samphullapatra" (with fully blossomed petals): it refers to that lotus in which the petals—meaning the leaves—are perfectly *samphullāni*, or fully blossomed and expanded. Upon that lotus, which was exceedingly and pre-eminently variegated and extraordinary, and which was sustained and established by the power of your Lordship’s vigor—that is, the force of yoga—you yourself, O Creator, appeared; the meaning is that you entered it having assumed the form of Brahmā. For this very reason, your name became "Padmajanman" (Lotus-born).

Furthermore, the meaning is that he himself, independent of instruction, became one who had awakened to the entire mass of the Vedas—having mastered the collection of scriptures until their full comprehension—and was thus inherently omniscient. || 12 ||
O Supreme Self! Indeed, in this Pādma-kalpa, you were thus born from the lotus as the Lotus-born One;
O Viṣṇu, whose abode is the ocean and whose majesty is infinite, restrain the mass of my diseases! 13.

"In this... [The commentary explains: "O Supreme Self! O Paramātman! O Cause of the Universe! In this very Padma-kalpa, You—by whom the Lotus-born (Brahmā) was thus raised up or created—are indeed one whose abundance is infinite, whose greatness is unlimited; therefore, restrain my mass of diseases. The meaning is: ward off the multitude of ailments that would otherwise come upon me hereafter due to my past misdeeds. || 13 ||
Thus ends the eighth decad, consisting of thirteen verses, which describes the manner of the creation of the world after its dissolution.
Now, he describes the activity of Brahmā once he has thus come into being:
"That lotus-born one remains indeed within the lotus of your navel..."

"From where indeed has this arisen in the ocean?"—not looking [within], out of curiosity to see it, he turned his faces in every direction and thus attained the state of having four faces, each with eight expanding lotus-eyes. || 1 ||

"Standing"—for that lotus-born one, while standing upon the pericarp of your navel-lotus, did not perceive from what basis or from where this lotus had arisen. "Svid" expresses a conjecture. Not seeing that it had emerged—that is, been produced—from the ocean during the single expanse of the universal waters (ekārṇava), he turned his face in every direction—in the four quarters—out of curiosity and eagerness to see its place of origin. Thus, he came to possess four faces.

The meaning is that when there arose the desire to gaze simultaneously in the four directions, she came to possess four faces. The connection is that she attained the state of having four faces, she whose eight lotus-eyes—the lotuses of her vision—were blossoming, that is, opened wide. || 1 ||
Beholding only that lotus tossed about in the great ocean and taking refuge in it, yet not seeing your body,
who indeed am I here in the vast interior of the lotus, utterly helpless?
"From where indeed has this lotus arisen?"—such was the thought that occurred to him. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "mahārṇave" (in the great ocean): having seen only that lotus alone tossed about and shaken in the great ocean—its support and its foundation—but not seeing his body there, he fell into such reflection. He states the manner of his reflection: "Who is this? [Verse 2] "In the vast interior of the lotus, who indeed is this person here all alone? Moreover, from where has this lotus arisen?"—thus he reflected.
Furthermore, having thus reached a conclusion, he spoke as follows:

"Indeed, there must be some cause for this lotus," so thinking, that man of mature intellect entered through the path of the hollow stalk by means of the science of yoga-power; yet he did not see your body, which deludes the mind. (3)

Regarding the word *amuṣya*: "beneath this lotus (*saroruha*), that is, beneath the water-lily presided over by me, there might exist some cause or basis. The potential mood (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility. Having thus formed this conviction, Brahmā indeed descended through the path of the lotus-stalk's cavity—the cavity itself being the path—by way of that opening. To the question of how he understood this means, the author replies: "of mature intellect" (*prauḍhadhīḥ*).

"One whose intellect (*dhī*) is mature and skilled in reasoning and counter-reasoning (*ūhāpoha*) is thus described. Now, one might ask: "Even if there is such capacity of the intellect, how could entry through an extremely subtle aperture be possible? To this he says: "by means of knowledge (*vidyā*) together with the power of yoga (*yoga*). The power of yoga is the power of austerity (*tapas*), and knowledge is self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*). The meaning is: having become possessed of a body so subtle as to have attained sovereignty through austerity and knowledge, he entered that aperture in the lotus stalk.

Yet he did not see, nor indeed ever beheld, that body of yours—which so utterly deludes the mind and is endowed with transcendent beauty—due to his outward-turned activities, which make it difficult to attain. || 3 ||
Then, searching through the path of all the openings of the tubes for a hundred years with great effort, he saw nothing at all;
turning back and sitting comfortably within the heart of a lotus, his mind became one-pointed.
I shall summon the power of concentration, focused solely on your grace.

Regarding the word *tataḥ*: immediately after that, "going through all the openings of the stalks"—the openings of the stalks themselves being the paths—he goes through them; thus, he is "going through all the openings of the stalks," meaning he is searching, conducting an investigation. The meaning is this: because the lotus stalk has many holes, having descended through one hole and searched but not seen [the snake], he then searched again through another, and yet again through another, investigating untiringly in this manner.

Thus, having exerted himself for a hundred years—that is, for a hundred divine years—he did not perceive any object whatsoever as a support for the lotus. "Having desisted" means that, having determined that nothing can be known or accomplished without the grace of the Lord, he withdrew from outward-directed effort and ceased; thus, "seated comfortably within the interior of the lotus" is an indication of the eightfold posture. "One-pointed intellect" refers to *dhāraṇā* (concentration).

He established—that is, he exercised—the power of concentration (*samādhi*), which is the power of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*) characterized by immobility. He was one whose sole focus was upon your favor; thus, he was "one whose exclusive devotion is to your grace" (*bhavadanugrahaikāgrahī*). || 4 ||
Having thus conducted an internal investigation, he says that he has indeed seen you:

"Indeed, after a hundred years, that lotus-born one—his mind purified by the clarity of awakening shining forth through the firm bond of meditative absorption—beheld with his inner vision your wondrous form, never before seen, resting upon the coils of the serpent's body, his intellect being thoroughly satisfied. (5)

"By a hundred"—that is, by a hundred divine years (*parivatsara*). Indeed, that Brahmā, born from the lotus, was made clear—that is, rendered pure—by means of a hundred [years] through a firm and unwavering "binding" (*bandha*) of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), characterized by the one-pointedness of the mind; a binding consisting of the unification of the mind and its object, and a "clear awakening" (*prabodha*) shining forth through the absence of the perception of distinctions between the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditation—a knowledge directed toward the single Self which, being stainless through the subsiding of the impurity of ignorance, has been made manifest.

Indeed, he beheld—that is, saw—your very form, the manifest essential nature of Viṣṇu himself, with his divine eye granted by the Blessed One through his inner vision. Of what sort was it? It was unprecedented, never seen before even with great effort; it was a wondrous and most marvelous form resting upon a portion of the body of the serpent. "Bhujaga" refers to the serpent named Ananta; "bhoga" is its body; "bhāga" is a portion of that, namely the place fashioned as its couch; that which has this as its support is described thus.
The meaning is that, upon seeing that form of yours, his intellect became fully satisfied, and he fell under the sway of an excess of joy. || 5 ||
He describes that very form:
adorned with a crown and tiara, shining with bracelets, necklaces, and a pair of armlets, sparkling with jewels, with a girdle, and well-enveloped in yellow garments.
O Mother! I meditate upon that body of yours, which possesses the luster of a kalāya flower, with the kaustubha gem shining upon your neck, as it was shown to the Lotus-born Brahmā.

"Kirīṭa" means shining or resplendent with two crowns and diadems that adorn the head from the front and the back. "Kaṭakahārakeyūrayuk" means joined with bracelets (kaṭaka) which are bangles on the forearms, with pearl necklaces (hāra), and with armlets (keyūra) adorning the regions of the shoulders. That [form]. "Maṇisphuritamekhalam" means that upon which there is a girdle (mekhalā) shimmering and radiant with heaps of various most precious jewels (maṇi).

"Suparivītam" means that which is "parivītam"—surrounded or clothed—in yellow garments (*pītāmbara*) distinguished by an exceedingly enchanting appearance. O Blessed One! That body which was shown to the lotus-born Brahmā—that is, brought within the range of his vision—I now contemplate; the meaning is that I merely remember it. || 6 ||

Thus, describing the commencement of his ritual action immediately after beholding the form of the Blessed One, he prays to the Lord: "O Lord of abundant majesty revealed by the multitude of scriptures! O Consort of Śrī!
O Hare! Victory, victory, O Lord! By good fortune, You have come within the range of my sight."
"Quickly apply your intellect to the task of creating the universe"—O You whose own greatness of qualities was thus described by Brahmā, protect me! || 7 ||

"Śruti... etc. He whose abundant majesty (*pracuravaibhava*)—that is, His supreme greatness—is revealed (*darśita*), meaning established through implication (*lakṣaṇā*), by the various branches of the Vedas (*śrutiprakara*), that is, by the multitude of Upaniṣadic passages; or alternatively, "majesty" refers to the capacity for the creation of the universe and so forth, which has been established by the Vedas as His being the cause of the world. O Lord of Śrī! O Gracious One of the World! O Hara! O Destroyer of the World! May You be victorious; manifest Your excellence. The repetition [of the vocatives] arises from the agitation caused by an outburst of joy.

"O All-pervading Lord! You have come within the range of my vision; you have arrived by good fortune—oh, happiness has arisen for me! Quickly grant me an intellect capable (*karmaṭhā*) in the creation of the world—that is, favor me with the knowledge regarding the procedure for the construction of the universe."

Thus, you whose greatness—the abundance—of your own qualities such as sovereignty has been described and praised by Druhiṇa, the Creator; protect him who is thus describing your very qualities. The meaning is: "Having placed yourself before him just as you did for Druhiṇa, make him one who has attained his purpose. || 7 ||
Now, he describes the manner in which the Blessed One favored him as he was offering praise:
"O Creator! Obtain unimpaired skill in fashioning the three worlds;
accept my favor and perform further austerities."
"Let there be devotion toward me that accomplishes all goals and is exceedingly intense"—having uttered these words, he made the Creator’s heart rejoice.

"May you obtain [it]! O Creator! May you obtain—may you attain—that unimpaired and unfailing skill in fashioning the three worlds, that capacity for the construction of the triple universe. Accept my favor; the meaning is: "Whatever I grant you in the process of creating the world, accept all of that. Perform further austerities.

Furthermore, having uttered these words—"May you possess a most intense devotion characterized by supreme love, which effortlessly accomplishes for you whatever you desire that is entirely achievable through me"—you caused the Creator, Brahmā, to have a joyful heart and a satisfied mind. || 8 ||
Having thus favored him, when the Blessed One had vanished, the poet describes the activity of the Creator:
"Then, having performed a hundred divine years of penance, and having attained a power of asceticism and an intellectual strength even greater than before,
he indeed beheld a lotus trembling in the water due to the wind."
Manifesting his power, he drank up both the wind and the water.

Regarding the word "śatam" (a hundred): that very Brahmā, having performed penance for a hundred divine years—thus being one who has completed his austerity (*kṛtatapāḥ*)—and having thereby attained a power of austerity, intellect, and discernment even greater than before, beheld once more his own lotus-abode shaken by the wind upon the single ocean of milk, by that most violent wind of that time. [He did so] by means of "Bhavabala"—that is, by your very power—as Prahlāda’s statement says: "He indeed is the strength of the strong and of others."
Having yawned and grown large, he indeed swallowed the wind and the water, having drunk both air and fluid. || 9 ||
Once again, by your very grace, he fashioned the three worlds with that same lotus and proceeded to the creation of living beings;
O Lord of the City of the Winds (Indra), such is the weight of your compassion!
Protect me quickly with glances drenched in great compassion. || 10 ||

"Thine indeed. Furthermore, by that very same exceedingly vast lotus, through Thine grace alone, [He] fashioned the three worlds—*bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*, meaning the three realms. Regarding the phrase "having fashioned": here, because the seven netherworlds (*atala*, *vitala*, *sutala*, *talātala*, *mahātala*, *rasātala*, and *pātāla*) are included within *bhūrloka*, and because *mahar*, *jana*, *tapaḥ*, and *satya* are included within *svarloka*, the position of the three worlds is stated.

And then, having divided that lotus into fourteen parts, he fashioned the fourteen worlds; such is the meaning. Immediately thereafter, according to the varying degrees of the auspicious and inauspicious unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings, he set about—the word "pravavṛte" meaning he proceeded—in the creation of souls suitable for those respective worlds and in the construction of their bodies.

O Lord of Gurumaramarapura! You, whose burden of compassion and excellence of mercy extend to all people—such as you, who are sprinkled with heavy, dense, and moist glances (kaṭākṣas) born of profound compassion, protect me quickly and most swiftly! || 10 ||
Thus ends the ninth decade, which is a description of the manner of the world's creation.
Now, with ten verses beginning with "Vaikuṇṭha," he describes the various types of creation:
"O Vaikuṇṭha! Then, his strength increased by Your grace, the lotus-born Brahmā indeed created the bodies of living beings."
Likewise, he created stationary objects consisting of trees,
as well as the various species of animals, the multitudes of human beings, and the different classes of gods.

"O Vaikuṇṭha!"—O Viṣṇu! By Your grace, having increased in strength and attained sovereignty through knowledge and action, the lotus-born Brahmā then, immediately thereafter, indeed created the bodies of living beings. In that regard, bodies are of two kinds, distinguished as stationary and moving. He states this with the words "sthāsnūni": "consisting of trees" means primarily composed of trees; "herbs, creepers, and shrubs" means the stationary [beings].

The meaning is that he created the species of animals such as cattle; therein, cattle and the like are cloven-hoofed, horses and the like are single-hoofed, dogs and the like have five claws, as do crows, herons, vultures, and so forth—these, as well as gods and humans, he created. || 1 ||
Now, he describes the creation of darkness (*tāmasa-sarga*) produced by the Creator’s lack of discernment:
Having created this fivefold activity of ignorance— consisting of false attachment, the notion of "I," passion, agitation, and fear— he,
distressed by the production of such unrestrained objects of darkness, performed the remembrance of Your feet for the sake of purification.

"False" (mithyā): the perception of the existence of the phenomenal world as something other than the Self is false grasping (*mithyāgraha*); the conceit of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth is the notion of "I-am-ness" (*asmimati*); desire for wealth and such things through the thought that they are objects of enjoyment is attachment (*rāga*); anger toward one who takes away wealth and such is resentment (*vikopa*); and fear produced by the anticipation of the expenditure, destruction, or theft of objects of enjoyment is dread (*bhīti*). Thus, having created these fivefold—meaning five types of—functions of ignorance, which are the effects of ignorance of the Self, namely the five effects of ignorance such as false grasping and the rest; this is the meaning.

Immediately thereafter, distressed by the creation—that is, the production—of numerous fetters consisting of tamasic objects, which are effects solely of the quality of darkness, his mind became exhausted; thus, for the sake of purification and the cessation of ignorance, he performed the remembrance of your feet. || 2 ||
Then he created from his mind Sanaka, Sananda,
and furthermore the sage Sanātana and Sanatkumāra.
When they were appointed by him to the task of creation, being devoted to the nectar of devotion at your feet, they did not accept his command.

Thus it is said: "In the meantime"—that is, while he had become pure-minded through the remembrance of your feet—at that time he mentally created Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra. However, those [sages] beginning with Sanaka, being appointed and impelled by that Brahmā to the task of creation, did not accept his word—that is, they did not acknowledge his command. The reason for this is: "because they were connoisseurs of the rasa of devotion to your feet."

The meaning is that those who possess a longing for that devotion characterized by love for Your lotus feet did not desire the act of creation, which bestows bondage to the body and other such things. || 3 ||
While he was thus restraining his rising fury,
a portion of Bhava became deluded from the center of his brow and cried out:
"O Viriñca, give me names and steps!"— alas!
At that time, it is said, he wept, and for that reason he was named Rudra.

"Then" (tāvat) means: at the very moment when his own instruction was thus rejected by his sons. Although this Brahmā restrained and suppressed with his intellect the "arisen" (udita)—that is, the produced—intense anger (prakopa), Śrī Śaṅkara descended there, having taken that very anger as his body, from the middle of the eyebrows (bhrūmadhyataḥ) of that Brahmā; such is the meaning.

And he was a portion of Bhava, a partial incarnation of Viṣṇu himself, according to the scriptural statement: "The Supreme Person alone here assumes the names Hari, Viriñca, and Hara for the sake of its maintenance and so forth. It is said that as soon as he was born, he wept, crying out, "Alas, Viriñca! Give me names, words, and places! By virtue of that weeping, he obtained the name Rudra. || 4 ||
Having fashioned Rudra in eleven distinct forms and bestowed upon him beloved wives and consorts, he, impelled by you,
granted him as many steps.
And he spoke respectfully to him for the purpose of creating progeny.
Regarding the phrase "by having eleven names":
"Manu, Manyu, Mahādeva, Mahat, Śiva, Ṛtadhvaja,
Ururetās, Bhava, Kāla, Vāmadeva, and Dhṛtavrata."

Thus, having established Rudra as distinct—being the object of the notion of difference due to the elevenfold division of names, the particle *ca*, and the difference of locations—and having bestowed upon him beloved wives (*vanitāḥ*), namely the women mentioned as "Dhī, Dhīr, Vṛtti, Aśanī, Mā, Niyut, Sarpi, Iḍā, Ambikā, Irāvatī, Sudhā, and Dīkṣā," he gave him exactly those eleven *padāni* (steps) and locations (*sthānāni*). And these are: "The heart, the senses, earth, sky, wind, fire, water, and earth."

He gave [these] places that have been mentioned, such as "Sūrya, Candramas, and Tapas. Impelled by you—that is, urged by the Lord residing in his heart—the Creator (Vidhi), although Rudra appears as manifold through differences of name and so forth, addressed and appointed him—who is in reality of a single form—for the sake of creating progeny, so that he might produce sons through his wives, with due respect and honor. || 5 ||

His mind terrified by the three worlds being filled with throngs of Rudras of fearsome appearance unleashed by Rudra, the Lotus-born Brahmā, his soul addressed by you, said to him: "Do not create progeny; perform austerities for the sake of auspiciousness."

Regarding the word *rudra*: "Rudra-sṛṣṭa" means created by Rudra from his own wife. [The army] was filled with a multitude of Rudras whose forms were terrifying, mounted on bulls, with ashes on their limbs and bodies, holding skull-topped staffs (*khaṭvāṅga*), axes, deer, and skull-cups as garments, adorned with lordly serpents, and possessing eyes of fire. With his mind terrified by that triple world being thus filled, the lotus-born Brahmā—his soul (mind) impelled at that moment by Bhava (Śiva)—addressed that Rudra.
He said: "Do not create such offspring for me; rather, perform austerities for the sake of auspiciousness and for the happiness of all the worlds. || 6 ||
Then, from him who was fond of creation, Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Kratu, the sage Pulaha, Pulastya,
Bhṛgu born from his limbs, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, and the venerable Śrī Nārada, the servant of Your feet, were born. (7)

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): Then, having obtained permission from his own father to practice austerities, after Rudra had entered the forest of penance, ten sons—Marīci and the others—were born from the limbs of him who was contemplating, "How shall I create? while he was still relishing the creative impulse (*sarga-rasika*). Among them, Marīci was born from the mind of Brahmā; Atri from the eye; Aṅgiras from the mouth; the sage Ṛtu from the hand; Pulaha from the navel; Pulastya from the ear; Bhṛgu from the skin; Vasiṣṭha from the vital breath (*prāṇa*); Dakṣa from the thumb; and Nārada was born from the lap.
"Your servant at the feet" means one who considers himself a servant of Your glorious lotus feet. || 7 ||
Then, having created Dharma and the others, as well as Kardama and Vāṇī, the Creator, accompanied by his offspring, became engrossed in progeny; yet,
awakened by your sons headed by Sanaka and Dakṣa, he desisted from further creation, casting off the darkness [of ignorance].

Regarding the phrase "Dharma and the others": from the right breast of the Creator (Vidhi), Dharma and Śrī-Nārāyaṇa were born; from his back, Adharma and Mṛtyu; from his heart, Kāma; from his eyebrows, Krodha; and from his lower lip, Lobha—these and others are to be sought out in this manner. Then, while emitting Kardama, the meaning is that Kardama was born from his shadow. Then Vidhi, having brought forth Vāṇī-Sarasvatī, became overwhelmed by his own offspring, falling under the sway of desire.

Then, having been awakened by his own sons—Sanaka and others, as well as Dakṣa and the rest—who were themselves enlightened by you, the witness to the intellects of all people, he cast off the darkness of ignorance and desisted from worldly activity. || 8 ||

Having produced the Vedas, the collections of Purāṇas, and all branches of knowledge from his own multitude of faces, that four-faced one (Brahmā) entrusted them to those sons; then, failing to achieve further increase in creation, he took refuge at your lotus feet.

Regarding the phrase "the Vedas": that four-faced Brahmā, from his own collection of faces—the four mouths—[produced] the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*). These consist of the four Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*; the collections of Purāṇas in their condensed form; all the sciences (*sarvavidyāḥ*), which include the six auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) such as phonetics (*śikṣā*); the four secondary auxiliaries (*upāṅga*) such as Mīmāṃsā; and the four sub-Vedas (*upaveda*) such as Āyurveda. In this context, although the term "all sciences" (*sarvavidyāḥ*) already includes the Purāṇas, their separate mention as "collections of Purāṇas" is for the purpose of proclaiming their preeminence. As it has been said:
"If a Brahmin who knows the four Vedas does not know the Purāṇa according to its meaning..."

"Seeing him, he became afraid, thinking: 'The Veda will outstrip me. Furthermore, because it is the fifth Veda and was created from all his mouths, it possesses preeminence. Having deposited those sciences (vidyās) among his sons, Marīci and the others, and having transmitted them, that Brahmā—though eternally pervasive—failed to achieve the expansion of creation for the sake of multiplying progeny throughout the three worlds. Failing to obtain that [expansion], and suspecting an adverse fate therein, he took refuge at your lotus feet to avert it; the meaning is that he began to meditate. || 9 ||
Then, though unborn, knowing the means, you divided your body and assumed the state of male and female with Manu and his wife;
and through them, you caused the human races to multiply.
O Govinda! O Lord of the City of Marut! Repel all diseases! || 10 ||

Regarding the word "knowing" (*jānan*): by the power of meditating upon your lotus feet, the unborn Brahmā, who knows the means for the increase of creation, divided his own body into two parts; he created Manu Svāyambhuva with one half of his body and Śatarūpā, his wife, with the other half—meaning he assumed the state of both male and female through those two portions.

O Govinda! O Lord of the City of Marut! Since those two, Manu and Śatarūpā, having been directed by Brahmā, engaged in the procreation of offspring through the practice of sexual union and thereby increased the human lineages upon the earth, may you restrain—that is, ward off—the diseases of mine. || 10 ||
Thus ends the tenth decade, the description of the various types of creation.

As the process of creation gradually increased, at one point those divine beings, Sanaka and the others, departed for the world of Vaikuṇṭha from this world to behold Bhava, O Lord of the Mansion of the Wind! (1)

Regarding the word "krameṇa" (gradually): the meaning is that they were divine, non-material, and characterized by goodness (*sattva*). "Prapedire" means they attained or reached [these states]. || 1 ||

The lords of sages, having passed through successive courtyards, reached Your incomparable abode, Vikuṇṭha, which is described by those seeking the highest good as possessing charming forests and the like, along with many ponds and jeweled palaces. || 2 ||

"Manojñā" means: with various enchanting things such as the splendors of all seasons that are exceedingly captivating, and with the "naiḥśreyasa" groves and so forth—where "naiḥśreyasa" refers to the grove or garden named after liberation (*kaivalya*) itself, which stands as if personified—the lords of sages, Sanaka and others, who have transcended all worldly boundaries, [dwell] in Your incomparable abode, *Vikuṇṭha*, which is worshipped by all the worlds and possesses many ponds, oblong lakes, and jewel-palaces made of gems.
The meaning is that, having passed through six courtyards divided by moats, walls, and other such features, they reached the seventh courtyard situated near the palace. || 2 ||
O Infinite One! Jaya and Vijaya, the two gatekeepers, blocked those who desired to see you and wished to enter your abode;
yet it was anger that took hold of their hearts, all of which occurred solely through your own instigation.

Regarding the word *bhavat*: Jaya and Vijaya, the two gatekeepers who had attained a form similar to yours (*bhavatsārūpya*), barred with their staffs Sanaka and the others—who, desiring to see you and wishing to bring you, who are accessible through meditative absorption, within the range of their vision, were about to enter your abode (*bhavana*), that is, your palace of jewels (*bhavanmaṇimandira*)—for that purpose; consequently, anger found a foothold, an opening, in their hearts.

The attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by all of Sanaka and the others, the conduct opposed to that [attainment] by Jaya and Vijaya, and the anger of the sages—all this, O Infinite One, is solely by the impulsion of You, the Lord, who sport through Your incarnations as Varāha, Narasiṃha, Śrī Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth. || 3 ||
When the audience with the Blessed One was thus interrupted, the sages, feeling a slight anger arise within them, cursed the two gatekeepers; this he relates:
"O you two, whose conduct is unbecoming of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, you miserable ones, go the way of the Daityas!
Thus cursed, those two, who took refuge in Bhava and were mindful of Hari, bowed to the sages, saying, "May it not be so."

Regarding the phrase *vaikuṇṭhaloke*: "May Jayavijaya—who were cursed by the sages, saying, 'In the world of Vaikuṇṭha, which is free from the agitation of *rajas* and *tamas*, you two have performed improper actions never before committed by anyone; you two wicked and most cruel ones must take birth in the state of a Daitya, that is, an Asura womb'—and who are now our refuge and servants, may there be remembrance of Hari for us in whatever womb we enter as a result of transgressing against you."

Thinking, "May there be remembrance of the Blessed One even in that place," they bowed down, falling upon the ground; the meaning is that, grasping their feet while thus entreating, they paid homage. || 4 ||
Having understood this, O lotus-eyed one, you have arrived here together with Lakṣmī;
with your beautiful arms resting upon the shoulders of the lords of birds, you delight them with your enchanting form.

Regarding the phrase "tadetad" (this very thing): at that moment, O lotus-eyed one! having perceived and understood this transgression of your own [servants] and so forth, you emerged together with Lakṣmī onto the outer courtyard of the jeweled palace; you were placed and seated upon the shoulder of Śrī Garuḍa, the lord of birds—[you] whose beautiful arms hang down to his knees, meaning your thick, long arm was placed such that your body leaned slightly toward the left side, with your lotus-hand resting on the region of Śrī Garuḍa’s left shoulder.

Delighting those lords of sages with his exceedingly beautiful and charming form—meaning, he produced an agitation of body and mind even in those who were already fully satisfied by the bliss of Brahman. || 5 ||
Then, having propitiated with words those lords of sages who were praising you, you spoke to those two attendants— who had no other protector—
taking pity on me as I approached Bhava accompanied by the three states of agitation.

"Having propitiated," and so forth. And then, having propitiated with honeyed words the lords of sages who were praising You—having bowed their heads immediately after seeing You—You thereafter spoke thus, showing compassion toward Your two attendants, Jaya and Vijaya, who were in a state of distress, having no other protector and taking refuge in You alone; "āttakṛpam" is an adverb meaning that in which compassion (kṛpā) was assumed (āttā) or undertaken (aṅgīkṛtā). Thus indeed You spoke.

He asks, "How so? and replies: "By means of three births—namely those in the forms of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Rāvaṇa, and Śiśupāla—and through the application of intense passion (*saṃrambha*) directed toward Me in each of those instances, by means of uninterrupted meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused on Me as the agent of that passion, you two have approached Me; that is to say, you have come into My presence. (6)
Indeed, those two enemies of the gods, born of Diti from Kaśyapa, were your servants;
they were twins who exerted themselves in the arduous task of creating the twilight, like another pair of Yamas to the world.

Regarding the word "tvadīya": those two, your servants and attendants, namely the two heroic enemies of the gods named Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa—the foremost of the asuras—were indeed born from the sage Kāśyapa and his wife Diti.

Regarding the "painful exertion for the production of Sandhyā": it is said that Diti, her heart tormented by the abundance of sons belonging to her co-wives, being overcome by passion, requested her husband Kaśyapa—who was seated in the fire-sanctuary having worshipped the fire at twilight—to "beget a son upon me. Although he told her, "Wait for this moment," she was driven mad by love; thus, the reading "unmattānām" (of those who are crazed) is found everywhere.

With a steady mind, she took hold of the sage’s garment by force, and he entered into private union with her. Therefore, because they were produced during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), the twins—whose efforts were difficult and whose deeds were cruel—were held simultaneously in a single womb; the meaning is that these twins became like two other Yamas for the people of the world, being as cruel in their actions as Vaivasvata Yama himself. || 7 ||
One was indeed known as Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the other as the famous Hiraṇyākṣa;
both, blinded by their own latent impressions, obstructed the entire world along with its Lord out of anger.

Regarding the phrase "Hiraṇyapūrva": of those two, the elder was Hiraṇyapūrva Kaśipu, known as Hiraṇyakaśipu; the other, the younger, was known as Hiraṇyākṣa. Both of them—those whose protector (nātha) was you, thus "Bhavannātha"—oppressed (nyarundhām) the entire world, that is, all the people dwelling in it, out of wrath. By their own latent impressions (vāsanā), that is, by their demonic nature (āsura-svabhāva), they were blinded, meaning their knowledge of the supreme truth had been destroyed. || 8 ||
Of those two, Hiraṇyākṣa, the great lord of the Asuras, having failed to find his enemy while rushing to battle,
submerged the earth— which is dear to you— in the waters and roamed about, maddened with pride and roaring, armed with his mace.

Regarding the phrase "of those two": between them, the great lord of asuras, Hiraṇyākṣa—rushing through the three worlds for battle, finding no enemy, and encountering even the gods as his adversaries—submerged the earth, your beloved, into the waters of the dissolution-ocean; and having made the earth his ear-ornament, he moved about submerged in the water, mace in hand, with a great mace resting upon his shoulder, roaring out of pride. || 9 ||
Then, having heard from the Lord of Waters that you were his equal, he wandered about searching for you;
O Treasure of Compassion, you are visible only to your devotees! O Lord of the Abode of the Wind, restrain my diseases! 10.

"Then," it says: Then, desiring to sport in the ocean whose waters reached his knees, he went to Vibhāvarī, the city of Varuṇa, and challenged him to battle. Thereupon, having heard from the Lord of Waters, Varuṇa himself, that you were his equal, and having learned that on the paths of war there was only one who was your peer—the Ancient Being, Śrī Nārāyaṇa—he wandered about searching for and seeking you. You, therefore, are visible only to your devotees.

He is visible—that is, capable of being seen—only by devotees such as Prahlāda, Nārada, and others. If it is objected that since the Lord is visible only to devotees, the statement above, "he attained you," is inconsistent, do not say so; for Hiraṇyākṣa was indeed a devotee because he fixed his mind upon the Lord through the means of the *raudra-rasa* (the sentiment of wrath). This is according to the saying: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa. Thus, his vision of the Lord is possible;
moreover, it is indicated that this occurs specifically at the moment of death. || 10 ||
Thus ends the eleventh decade, describing the entry of Sanaka and others into Vaikuṇṭha, the curse of Jaya and Vijaya, and the birth of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa.
Now, he describes the activity of Manu in order to bring about the incarnation of the Boar and the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa:

Then Svāyambhuva Manu, whose nature is to create living beings, seeing the earth submerged in water at an improper time, went for refuge with the sages to the Creator in Satyaloka, whose heart was pleased by service to Your feet. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *svāyambhuva*: "Then," immediately after the command of Brahmā regarding the creation of progeny, he whose nature is the creation of beings—that is, the procreation of offspring—approached his own progenitor, the Creator Brahmā, who was situated in Satyaloka together with the assembly of sages. Even though it was not the appointed time—that is, even when the period of dissolution had not yet arrived—he approached him because Brahmā’s disposition was satisfied by the service of his feet, that is, by the worship of his lotus-feet. Or, the phrase may be understood as: "He sought refuge together with the assembly of sages. (1)
"Alas! The earth is sinking while I am creating living beings;
O Lotus-born One, provide a place for those creatures!"—when Manu had spoken thus, O lotus-eyed one, the Self-born Brahmā meditated upon your pair of feet.

"Alas! [He said: "O Lotus-born One! While I was creating the subjects, the earth became submerged in the waters of dissolution—alas! Because of my lack of support, I am not able to carry out your command. Therefore, please provide a place for the subjects and for me. Thus addressed and petitioned by Manu, this Self-existent One (Svayambhū), O lotus-eyed one, meditated upon the pair of your feet. || 2 ||
While reflecting thus, you appeared instantly before his heart; and with a distressed mind, he spoke as follows:
"Alas, alas, O Lord! Previously I drank water, yet even now the earth remains submerged; what shall I do?
Therefore, I take refuge in this pair of your feet."
From his nostril, you were born in the form of a young crocodile.

"Alas! O All-pervading Lord! Alas, alas! A calamity has occurred. Even before the creation of living beings, I drank up the waters for the purpose of establishing the earth; yet even now, while the water has been rendered insignificant, the earth sinks down. Though I have been appointed by you to this creation, what can I do? In this matter, you alone are our refuge."

Thus, for this Brahmā who has obtained refuge in your pair of feet, you appeared from his nostrils—that is, from the interior of his nose—assuming the form of a young boar; the meaning is that you descended [as an incarnation]. || 3 ||
At first you leapt forth as small as a thumb,
and then you yawned until you were like a large jar;
seeing you thus towering in the sky, Brahmā, along with his own sons, was filled with great amazement.

Regarding the word *aṅguṣṭha*: previously, at first, you emerged from the nostril with a body the size of a thumb—having a form measuring only a thumb—and then immediately thereafter, once more, you yawned, that is, you grew as large as an elephant, resembling a water-jar (*kumbhin*). Seeing you thus growing so rapidly in an instant, rising high in the sky along the path of the clouds, Brahmā, the Creator, raised his face and looked upon you, and he attained a state of wonder, reaching a condition of amazement.
"Along with his own sons"—the meaning is that his sons, Marīci and the others, were also filled with wonder.
"Who is this being of inconceivable majesty that has arisen from the cavity of my nostril? Could it be the Māyā of the Unconquered (Viṣṇu)?"—
while the Creator was thus reflecting, [the creature] grew as large as a mountain.
Having come into being instantly, you indeed roared most terribly.

"Who is this? [He thought: "Is it a *kiṭi*—a boar—of inconceivable majesty, whose bodily magnitude is immeasurable and whose power is unfathomable, who has arisen from the cavity of my nostril? Could it be the *māyā* (illusory power) of the unconquered Viṣṇu; could he himself have descended in the form of a boar through his *māyā*? While the Creator was reflecting thus, you, becoming as large as a mountain—indeed, possessing a body equal to two mountains—roared most fiercely, becoming exceedingly terrifying. || 5 ||
Hearing that roar of yours, the sages dwelling in Janasthāna and Tapasthāna, who abide in truth, offered hymns of praise to you;
with a mind delighted by those praises, you, assuming a vast form, descended again into the great reservoir of water after resounding through it.

"Tam iti": "That roar of yours, O Janārdana, even those residing in Janaloka and Tapoloka—meaning those situated in Janaloka and Tapoloka—as well as those established in Satyaloka, praised. With a joyful mind and a serene heart due to that hymn of praise, you, assuming a vast form with a body far more expanded than before, descended once again into the reservoir of waters—the ocean of dissolution—to roar for their propitiation."
With his body bristling with hair as he reared up and shook himself,
his tail raised aloft and his terrible snout turned downward,
he swiftly split open the clouds while rolling his eyes.
O Sage, cooling those who offer praise, you have descended. || 7 ||

"Ūrdhva... means: he whose body hairs (*roma*) are prone to bristling upward, smoke-colored, blackish-red, tossed about, and trembling; he is thus described. With his tail raised and his muzzle—whose nostrils were formidable and terrifying in appearance—turned downward; by whom the clouds were swiftly and very lightly rent asunder;
with rolling eyes—a pair of trembling, reddish-brown, swollen eyes that manifested compassion—he descended, gladdening and cooling the sages who were his worshippers. || 7 ||
Thereafter, having entered the water— which was crowded with circles of crocodiles, filled with schools of revolving *timiṅgila* fish, and garlanded with turbid waves—
you searched for [the horse], shaking the earth and its inhabitants in the subterranean realm with a terrifying roar.

"Into the water": after that, following the entry into the water, you [shall see] a place where there is a multitude of crocodiles (*nakra*), a swarm of revolving sharks (*grāha*), and a host of revolving *timiṅgila* fish; "revolving" means moving here and there, and *timiṅgila* refers to great fish many *yojana*s in length and breadth, whose "host" is their collective assembly. It is turbid because the water is agitated.

Having entered the interior waters—that water in which there were turbid successions of waves—you searched for your beloved, the earth, shaking her, the earth, on all sides with a terrifying roar, causing the people dwelling in the subterranean realm (rasātala) to tremble; the meaning is that you made a search. || 8 ||
O Lord! Having seen you suddenly placed within the depths of the netherworld by that wretched Daitya, you,
like a deceptive parrot, disregarded the attacking mounts of the enemies of the gods.
With the tip of your fang, you playfully supported the earth.

"Having seen [this]"—that is, immediately thereafter, O Lord! you, who possess the illusory body of a boar (*māyā-varāha*), disregarded—that is, treated as mere straw—the approaching enemies of the gods, those vilest of asuras led by Hiraṇyākṣa, that wretched demon; and having done so, you playfully lifted up with the tip of your tusk—that is, the point of your tooth—the earth (*vasudhā*) which had been cast down and settled at the depths of the netherworld (*rasātala*) by that same vile asura. 9.
O Lord, who lifted the earth with Your body made even more massive as if marked by the sprouts of a musta-grass blade caught on the tips of Your tusks,
and who emerged from the ocean of terrible waters in the form of the Playful Boar— protect me from disease! 10.

"Rescuing... Thus, while lifting up the earth, you appeared as if marked by sprouts of *mustā* grass caught on the tips of your tusks—just like another boar that, while foraging for *mustā* roots in a pond, becomes marked by such sprouts on the tips of its tusks. Being thus beautiful to behold, with a body exceedingly stout and massive, you were emerging from—that is, rising up out of—the ocean whose waters were surging, agitated, and terrible, inspiring fear. O Lord who assumed the form of a play-boar! O Lord who took on the body of a boar for the sake of sport!
Protect me from disease. 10.
Thus ends the twelfth decade, describing the lifting of the earth during the Varāha incarnation.
Immediately following this, he shows Nārada providing assistance to Hiraṇyākṣa:
"O Giver of Boons! First, [regard] Hiraṇyākṣa, who is intent on searching for you..."
While You were moving about in the boundless waters of the cosmic egg,
the sage Nārada, whose intellect was clever in deceit, approached Your devotee and spoke softly, praising Your power while disparaging even the demon Nanda.

Regarding the verse beginning with *hiraṇyākṣam*: At that very moment, coinciding with your lifting of the earth, there occurred the *saṃvarta* dissolution; in the waters associated with that [dissolution], he whose intellect was clever in deceit—his cunning mind being intent upon showing favor to the world—praising the demon Hiraṇyākṣa while censuring even your own strength, spoke slowly and persuasively. || 1 ||
He demonstrates the very words spoken by Śrī Nārada: "O Lord! That illusory Viṣṇu is seizing your earth! Alas, alas! What is this?"—thus was he addressed by him.
Saying, "O, what a roar! O, what a roar! he, shown the path by the sage, reached you as you were emerging from the water onto the mountain.

"He" refers to Viṣṇu, the wielder of *māyā*. Out of fear of you, he concealed himself under the pretext of a boar and, having taken away from Brahmā your Earth—whom you had deposited in the netherworld (*rasātala*)—he [recovered her]. By this, he demonstrates the impropriety of your indifference.

"O Lord, O you capable of warding that off! Alas, alas! What is this? Oh, even the dull-witted revile their masters, yet the masters remain indifferent; what kind of precedent is this? Thus addressed and encouraged by him, he roared a lion's roar and, asking with great persistence, "Where is he? Where is he?", was shown the way by the sage who replied, "This way, this way. Following that path, he reached you, the Upholder of the Earth (Dharaṇīdhara), as you were emerging from the water. || 2 ||
Immediately upon seeing him, he insulted the Blessed One, as it is said:

"O Blessed One! Disregarding the son of Diti—who was laughing, saying 'Oh, what a wild forest deer this is!', and piercing him with many harsh words—[the Lord], having seen the earth trembling on his head out of fear, [calmed her] by his own splendor."
Having placed it in the ocean, you forcefully employed it for the act of subduing adversaries. || 3 ||

"Alas! Alas, what a pity! This forest-dwelling boar has been presented by this sage as a means to awaken me"—saying such things, he mocked him with laughter and further insults, crying out: "O lowest of gods! O you whose power is mere illusion! With this mace, I shall shatter your head!"

O Blessed One! While the son of Diti—the beloved child of Diti, but not of Kaśyapa—was piercing and striking you with the arrows of his wicked words such as "I shall slay you," you, disregarding him and rebuking him, saw the earth trembling and distressed upon the tips of your fangs; and perceiving her to be terrified, thinking, "If I engage in combat with this one, my beloved will sink," you placed her upon the waters of the unfathomable ocean by means of your own extraordinary splendor and yogic sovereignty.

Having established Your own prowess within her so that she might not sink into the earth and so that the lineage of all things moving and stationary might continue—this is the meaning—You forcibly, by means of compulsion, engaged in the rites of battle, that is, You donned Your armor for the acts of war. || 3 ||
While the Daitya held a mace in his hand and He himself, grasping a raised mace, sported with him in wrestling— resounding the sky with the clanging "ghaṭ-ghaṭ" sounds—
the assembly of gods, eager to witness the battle, quickly gathered around Him.
"You should restrain [your senses] first from the morning twilight," thus was it commanded by the Creator.

Regarding the phrase *gadāpāṇau*: when the Daitya, mace-in-hand, was desirous of fighting—*hi* being used as a causal particle meaning "because"—for that very reason, you too, having taken up the great and lofty mace Kaumodakī which reached your lotus-like hand at the mere thought of it, were sporting in a wrestling match (*niyuddha*), that is, a duel, slowly and gradually.

Of what kind of wrestling? It was one in which the hollow of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakaṭāha*) and the sky (*viyat*) resounded loudly with the noise of *ghaṭ-ghaṭ*, arising from the mutual blows of the two maces; thus, it was a wrestling match in which the sky was made to echo with the sound of *ghaṭ-ghaṭ*.

When the assembly of the gods had gathered together in a great crush, out of an intense curiosity to witness the prowess of the Blessed Lord Śrī Varāhamūrti and their eagerness for the sight of the battle, Brahmā (the Creator) addressed you, saying: "Before this demon can reach the twilight hour and grow in strength, restrain him more swiftly than even the first part of the evening; seize him! This is the meaning of what was said by the Creator. || 4 ||
O crusher of the hosts of demons! When that mace of yours suddenly fell to the ground from the blow of Diti’s son’s mace— alas, O Lord!—
you, whose face was softly smiling, [remained unmoved].
Remembering the Great Wheel and placing it upon the palm of his hand, he desired to shine forth.

Regarding the phrase *gadonmarda*: in that *gadonmarda*, that is, in that club-fight (*gadāyuddha*), while your club was still held in your hand, the club of Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, suddenly fell to the ground due to the blow of your club—the impact of your striking it. "Aha! expresses either grief or wonder. The sense is: "While I was engaged in continuous meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the application of intense fury, the Blessed One himself dropped his own club, thinking, 'I shall accomplish even a single desired aim for my servant. Oh, how great is your affection for your devotees!"

O All-pervading Lord! For this very reason, Your face is softly smiling; You did not become weary from the blow of the mace, but rather, with the lotus of Your face blossoming through a gentle, slow smile, You shone forth while holding the great discus known as Sudarśana—which had arrived at Your hand the very moment it was remembered—having recalled it for the total eradication of the hosts of Danujas (the asura multitudes). Targeting the throat of the enemy, You held the Sudarśana with Your raised right hand and shone resplendent.

The meaning is that your form, having attained excellence through the blazing splendor of the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*) and the splendor of Viṣṇu, came within the range of the visual faculty of all people. || 5 ||
Then, as the Daitya, enraged like Time itself, was hurling his trident at you, he cut it down with a discus held in his hand; thereupon,
filled with fury and strength, he indeed struck you in return.
O Galanmāyā, indeed all the illusions that delude the world reside within you.

"From that" (tataḥ) means: because of the fact that even when the mace fell upon you, your heart remained unperturbed and the splendor of Viṣṇu’s power was revealed; for that reason. While the Daitya—who possessed a wrath resembling Kālarudra, the fire of universal destruction—was about to discharge his trident, that is, as he was preparing to hurl it, while you were still there, he [the Daitya] cut that very trident in two by striking with the Sudarśana discus held in his hand; indeed, that Daitya was utterly enraged.

Even more enraged than before, striking you with his fists and dealing a firm blow to your chest with both hands clenched as fists, he unleashed—meaning he employed—*māyās*, those illusions that cause the delusion of the world and produce bewilderment in people other than yourself. "In whom *māyā* flows away" (*galanmāye*) means one from whom such *māyās* are flowing away and becoming distant; or else, it refers to you in whom [the *māyā*]—which is the very nature of the Lord, which manifests itself as if separate, and which performs the creation of the universe and so forth—is dissolving away. || 6 ||

He demonstrates the very nature of its illusoriness: "Then, when the wheel of Māyā has been shaken by the falling of even a tiny fragment of a spark from the light of the Wheel of Existence, [the yogi perceives] the mind blinded by the dense darkness of attachment."
As the Asura struck you with his most formidable and massive fists, you,
with the tip of your own hand, struck him without restraint at the base of his ear.

"Bhavat" means: when the host of asuras called Māyā was shaken—that is, driven away—by the falling, or the spreading, of a minute particle, a spark, a tiny fragment of the light, the splendor, of the discus of Viṣṇu known as Sudarśana; the meaning is that it vanished from sight, just as nocturnal darkness does upon the falling of even a small portion of the sun's radiance.

Then, after the futility of his own efforts, he whose mind was blinded by a vast, pervasive, and dense rage—having seen both the Sudarśana discus held in [Viṣṇu’s] hand and its extraordinary power, yet failing to recognize his own master due to the influence of a curse from a previous birth; such is the sense.

Striking with the heaviest and most forceful blows of his fists, and repeatedly employing them out of a desire for victory—[the reading] "with the tip of his own hand at the base of the ear-hole" (*śravaṇapadamūla*) is the correct one, as evidenced by the *Bhāgavata* statements: "he struck him at the root of the ear with his hand" (*kareṇa karṇamūle’han*) and "he was struck by the hand" (*nihataḥ kareṇa*). Furthermore, in the subsequent verse, it says: "crushed by the lotus-hand of you" (*tava karasarojapramathita*). || 7 ||

This very one of massive body, crushed by your lotus-hand, fell with blood streaming from his mouth; his death was praised by the seers. At that time, your heart shone with an abundance of unrestrained joy.
The lords of sages praised the body of the sacrifice with dense hymns of praise.

Regarding "Mahākāya": while the Blessed One was striking him on the junction of his ear and cheek with the tip of his own hand, he cast off his body even as he gazed at his face; "Oh, what fortune! Who indeed could attain such a state?"—thus praised by the sages, he whose slaughter (hatih) or restraint was lauded with a nod of the head is so described.

Those lords of sages (munīndrāḥ), whose hearts possessed a radiant and virtuous nature through an excess of contentment that was difficult to sustain due to its unrestrained abundance, praised the glorious Varāha-form—the very body of the sacrifice—by means of hymns that deafened the ten directions because they were performed collectively with such intensity; these sages dwell in Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka. || 8 ||
He praises [the sacrifice] precisely by way of its being the performance of the *adhvara*:

the *chandas* are in the skin, the tufts of *kuśa* grass in the body hair, the eyes in the pupils, the clarified butter in the eye, the four *hotṛ*s in the arms, the *sruk* ladle in the mouth, and the *iḍā* in the belly.

O Supreme Person! May the planetary deities be upon your tongue; O All-pervading Lord! May the sacrificial cups be upon your ears; O Giver of Boons! May Soma be in your vigor, and Upasada in the region of your throat. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "on the skin": *chandaḥ* refers to the *gāyatrī* and other meters; the meaning is that the *gāyatrī* and other meters are indeed your skin. The four officiating priests—the *adhvaryu*, *brahmā*, *hotṛ*, and *udgātṛ*—along with the sacrificer, are the "four *hotṛ*s" (*caturhotṛ*) located in the feet. The *sruk* (ladle) is in the mouth, while the *tuṇḍa* (snout) is the face. The *iḍā*—a specific vessel for placing the sacrificial materials such as the *puroḍāśa* cake—is in the belly.
