The *grahas*—specific vessels for collecting the *soma*—are in the tongue.

The *camasa*s are specific types of vessels used for holding the substances to be consumed; "in the ears" means in the two ear-cavities. *Soma* is the juice of the *soma* creeper; "vigor" (*vīrya*) refers to semen. The *upasads* are the sacrifices performed immediately following the *pravargya* rite; these [offerings] are in your throat. 9.
O Madhuripu! With a mind gladdened by the praises of the lords of sages who were vocal with hymns such as these, and shining with a most exalted form and exceedingly pure fame,
you have returned to your own abode, sporting in the essence of bliss.
O Lord of the Abode of Vāyu! May you suppress every single disease of mine. || 10 ||

Regarding the word "munīn" (sages): by the phrase "by the lords of sages" (*munīndraiḥ*) and so forth, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* sacrifices, as well as [the verses] beginning with "those two tusks are the two offerings" (*te daṃṣṭre*). He whose mind was gladdened—that is, made gracious—by those who were vocal in praise, being talkative with words of eulogy;

he who was shining and resplendent with a most exalted (*mahīyasī*) and highly worshipful form, that is, his own body, and with a most stainless fame that purifies the world; he who sports in the essence of bliss, playing at will, has reached his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha. || 10 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth decade, which describes the battle with Hiraṇyākṣa, his slaying, and the praise of the Sacrificial Boar (Yajñavarāha).
Having thus established the earth through the Varāha incarnation, he now describes the manner in which Svāyaṃbhuva Manu protected the subjects by taking refuge therein:
Constantly recollecting the pair of your feet, that Manu— born from the body of the one who sprang from the lotus—
spent his time in happiness, recounting your deeds within his own heart, which was free from all obstacles.

"By whom your pair of lotus feet was recollected"—that is, by whom your two lotus feet were properly recollected, meaning meditated upon with right application of the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth, being free from such states as mental dissolution (*laya*) or distraction (*vikṣepa*). He is the son born from the body of the one who sprang from the lotus (*paṅkajasambhava*).

The renowned Svāyambhuva Manu spent his own *antara*—a period of time measuring seventy-one and a quarter cycles of four ages—free from obstacles, which consist of physical, mental, divine, and elemental afflictions (*kleśas*) that hinder the protection of his subjects; this was achieved through the power of remembering Your feet and recounting Your deeds. Thus, he passed that time happily and at his own ease. || 1 ||
Now, by way of introducing the doctrine of Kapila, the story of Kardama is set forth:
At that time, indeed, there was one named Kardama, born from the shadow of Dhaṭiṇa;
through his word, having taken up the essence of creation, he served you, O Blessed One, for ten thousand years in your naturally beautiful form.

Regarding the word *samaye*: at that time (*samaye*), in that period, the one named Kardama was a Prajāpati, born from the shadow of Druhiṇa (Brahmā), as it is said, "From the shadow, Kardama was born. By his word—that is, by the command of Brahmā to "Create progeny"—he, having taken up the essence of creation and desiring to produce offspring, practiced asceticism for ten thousand years (*ayutam samāḥ*)—a period of ten thousand years—which was naturally delightful and pleasing to the heart of even a contemplative. || 2 ||
O Goddess! You manifested that form for Kardama—one beautiful as a dark cloud atop Garuḍa, with lotus-hands sporting a playful lotus, and a face radiant with a smile. || 3 ||
"O Garuḍa! [He said: "To him, you manifested your form with your lotus-feet placed upon the shoulder-region of Garuḍa; you showed it to him. (3)

To him who praised you with hairs standing on end, you granted your beloved daughter Manu’s daughter, as well as nine other daughters, and later your own son Kapila; having thus bestowed your grace, you departed for your own abode.

"Thus he praised. And so, having fallen upon the ground and bowed, you rose and, out of affection for that Kardama Prajāpati—who was covered in horripilation by the weight of his joy as he offered praise—granted him your beloved wife Devahūti as his spouse; and to her, you granted nine daughters as well as your own son Kapila, who is a portion of yourself. Finally, at the end, having bestowed upon him your own state, which is liberation (*mokṣa*), you departed and set forth. Svāyaṃbhuva Manu dwells in the region named Brahmāvarta; he has come here from there with his chariot and his queen Śatarūpā.

The meaning is that, having blessed him by saying, "Tomorrow, desiring to see you, he will come and give his own daughter to you; you shall give birth to nine daughters by her, and I too shall descend as your son through my own portion," the Lord departed. ||4||
That Manu, accompanied by his queen Śatarūpā and their virtuous daughter Devahūtī,
having been instructed by Nārada as you had described, went to Kardama, who was awaiting their arrival.

"He" refers to the one instructed by Nārada as spoken of by you—that is, instructed by Nārada who was himself impelled by you. For Manu had been told by Nārada to give his own daughter to Kardama, after first describing Kardama’s age, character, beauty, and virtues. "Waiting for his arrival" means that he kept his gaze fixed on the path, thinking, "Perhaps Manu is now coming, bringing his beloved daughter. (5)
Having obtained Devahūti, that jewel among young women, who had been offered by Manu, Kardama— though already fulfilled by the bliss of worshipping You—
bestowed his grace upon her through his steadfast service.

"Manuneti": Having honored her when she was presented with her dowry, he bestowed his favor upon her through steadfast, unwavering, and guileless service—even though he was already satisfied by the worship of the Lord and devoted to the path of renunciation. (6)

Furthermore, by the power of his worship of you, that new self, having fashioned a celestial chariot for the sake of his beloved’s desire, traveled through the paths of the gods amidst throngs of women at the call of the deities.

"He" refers to him who, at the request of his beloved for the sake of her desire, and for the purpose of complying with her wish, fashioned by the power of his own yoga a new self—a body sixteen years of age, radiant in a charming attire—surrounded by a multitude of women and encircled by thousands of female Vidyādhara attendants.

Or rather, he whose "new selves" were nine bodies; having divided himself ninefold to delight his beloved who was eager for amorous play, he sported upon the celestial paths in the divine gardens such as Nandana, Puṣpabhadraka, and Caitraratha. || 7 ||

Then, after a hundred years had passed, having obtained nine maidens of auspicious form, he— though intent on departing for the forest— remained there, devoted to the welfare of his beloved and eager for the birth of your father.

"Regarding 'a hundred years': although he was prepared to depart for the forest and desiring to go to the woods for asceticism, he remained intent on performing acts beneficial to his beloved wife—such as granting a boon to his daughter and the birth of a son—and even therein, he was eager for your birth. (8)
Then, O Lord, while Devahūtī was devoted to your service at the word of her own husband,
you were born as Kapila, intending to propagate among people the knowledge of the reality of the Supreme Self.

"His own," etc. Being intent on spreading the knowledge—that is, the wisdom—of the Supreme Self and the twenty-four principles among people, he prepares to reveal it through the tradition of the lineage of teachers in the form of scripture. || 9 ||
When Kardama had gone to the forest and my mother’s entire being was filled with clarity, you taught her the essence of all knowledge;
O Kapila-natured one! O Lord of the abode of Vāyu! Protect me swiftly from the flood of diseases.

"Regarding 'to the forest': when [the sage] had gone to the forest after giving his daughters, Marīcī and the others, to the sons of Brahmā, he taught—that is, caused [his mother] to grasp—his own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*), which comprised all that he possessed and was endowed with all his own limbs; he did so swiftly and very rapidly. (10)
Thus ends the fourteenth decade, the narrative of Kapila.
Here, the intellect attached to the *guṇas* causes bondage; when unattached to them, it brings about immortality. But the yoga of devotion wards off that very attachment.
"In this matter, devotion alone—attainable through great grace—is the goal to be accomplished;
thus you declared to Devahūti, 'I am Kapila in bodily form.'"

Regarding the word "intellect" (*mati*): here, in these three worlds, the intellect of a person that is attached to those qualities consisting of objects such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and nectar causes bondage; it effects the bondage of the body. However, when unattached to those qualities, it does not lead to such bondage; moreover, it brings about immortality, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). If so, by what means is attachment to the qualities (*guṇasaṅga*) to be abandoned? To this he says: "it obstructs. But the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*) obstructs—that is, it blocks—attachment.

Now, as to by what means devotion is accomplished, he says: "By [serving] the great. Devotion is to be attained through following and serving the virtuous. That very devotion is what must be accomplished here in this world by those seeking liberation. Thus you, who possess the body of Kapila—having descended as the Vāsudeva Kapila—taught and instructed your own mother, Devahūtī. || 1 ||
"Nature, the Great Principle (mahat), egoism, the eleven senses, the five subtle elements, the gross elements, and the heart—these constitute the twenty-four; the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
Having thus explained the distinction between them, you, O one whose body is Kapila, spoke these words to Devahūti: "By this knowledge of Prakṛti, one is liberated. || 2 ||

Regarding "the primordial nature" (*prakṛti*): *prakṛti* is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), so called because it is the cause of all; it is designated by such terms as *pradhāna*, *avyakta*, *avidyā*, and *māyā*. *Mahat* is the principle of the Great (*mahattattva*), which is the effect of the root-nature. From *mahat* arise the *ahaṅkāras* (ego-senses), which are divided into the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types. The *mātrās* are the effects of the *tāmasa-ahaṅkāra*, consisting of the five unevolved subtle elements (*apañcīkṛta-pañcabhūtāni*) in the forms of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. The *bhūtāni* are the five gross elements (*mahābhūtāni*) in the forms of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. *Hṛt* refers to the mind (*manas*).

The "Ten-Eyed One" (*daśākṣī*) is so called because she possesses the collection of the ten organs (*akṣa*), namely the sense-faculties (*indriya*) of smell, taste, sight, hearing, touch, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Thus, there are twenty-four principles (*tattva*). He by whom the distinction—that the *puruṣa* (the Person) is twofold due to the division between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—is known, is such [a person]. This one is the *jīva*. [He is bound] by *prakṛti*, that is, by *māyā*, or by the bonds of the body and so forth which are its effects. || 2 ||

Now, raising the objection that if bondage were real, there could be no liberation for the individual soul (jīva) from it, [the author] states that it is removable by knowledge because it is a manifestation of ignorance: "If this Puruṣa is not colored by the multitude of qualities residing in Prakṛti, yet he becomes attached to her, then those qualities would affect him."
"You declared to Devahūti that even she would cast off her Kapila body through the contemplation of the truth of devotion to me."

Regarding the word "prakṛti": by "prakṛti" are meant the four types of bodies—viviparous, oviparous, sweat-born, and soil-born—which consist of the twenty-four principles that are the effects of primordial nature (prakṛti). The "multitude of qualities" refers to agency, enjoyership, and so forth, which reside within those bodies. [The Self] is not smeared or stained by them. The meaning is that although this individual soul (jīva) resides in the body, in the ultimate sense it is not tainted by the bodily attributes such as agency, enjoyership, birth, death, and the like.

If this person becomes attached to that *prakṛti*—the body and so forth—and identifies with it as "I" and "mine," then its qualities, the qualities of *prakṛti*, would affect him, meaning they would cause him to experience the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, such as birth and death. Here, the word "if" (*yadi*) indicates that the connection with *prakṛti* is not ultimately real. By "my worship" is meant devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*), and by "contemplation of reality" is meant the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-jñāna*); [liberation comes] through these.

In this context, the plural number is used due to the distinction between the various methods consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). That *prakṛti* would depart; as it has been said: "By means of intense concentration on the Self, *prakṛti*, being burned here day and night by the person (*puruṣa*), shall become invisible. (3)

He describes the eight-limbed nature of the worship of the Lord: "With a pure mind, having prepared the seat and other requisites, [one should meditate on] my own form as divine, mounted upon Garuḍa, and marked by celestial ornaments and weapons."
"You should repeatedly practice the discipline of wearing matted hair, which is as dark as a glossy tāla tree," thus you spoke to Devahūtī regarding your tawny-hued body.

"Vimala" means one whose mind is purified by the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama). "Upātta" means accepted or mastered; that is, by means of the postures (āsana) and so forth—namely, breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). "Mameśvarasyāṅgam" refers to my form as the Lord; "divyānyaprākṛtāni" means divine and non-material; "bhūṣāyudhānyevāṅko lāñchanam" means that which has ornaments and weapons as its very marks or insignia. One should practice or cultivate this at all times, without interruption. || 4 ||
Now he declares the ease of the path of devotion compared to the yoga of knowledge:
"Through hearing of the multitude of my qualities and divine sports, and through chanting and other such acts, there arises in me a flow of the mind resembling the torrent of the celestial river;
that indeed is supreme devotion, for it is the conqueror of death."
"You declared to Devahūtī that you would take on a Kapila body. || 5 ||

Regarding the word "mama" (mine): therein, devotion (*bhakti*) is twofold, distinguished by the categories of the means (*sādhana*) and the goal (*sādhya*). My qualities (*guṇagaṇa*), such as affection for devotees (*bhaktavātsalya*) and the rest; my pastimes (*līlā*), which are my deeds; and through the hearing of those [pastimes]—by means of those [acts] beginning with chanting (*kīrtana*), and including remembrance (*smaraṇa*), salutation (*namaskāra*), worship (*arcana*), praise (*vandana*), servitude (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and self-surrender (*ātmanivedana*)—that is the meaning: by means of the ninefold devotional practice (*navalakṣaṇā sādhana-bhakti*). It has been stated that supreme devotion is the devotion that is the goal. He describes its essential nature (*svarūpa*) with the words beginning "mathī."

The "following of the mind" (cittānuvṛtti), which consists of love and is like the current of the celestial river Gaṅgā—that is, devotion (bhakti) as the goal—is the conqueror of death, that is, of saṃsāra; the meaning is that it utterly uproots saṃsāra with ease. || 5 ||
Now, for the sake of demonstrating the depth of devotion, he describes the manner of falling into hell for one who performs only evil deeds:
"Alas! One who, with wealth accumulated through excessive violence, nourishes his family day after day, is conquered by women and dotes upon children."
"For one who is attached to home and is not devoted to me enters into torment"—
thus you spoke to Devahūtī regarding the one in the body of Kapila.

"Aha-ha" means "alas," expressing distress. Due to excessive and abundant violence, through affliction, and out of a longing for the welfare of others—by means of wealth, grain, and so forth, accumulated and acquired here and there through theft and other such acts—one enters into suffering, such as hell and the like, along with one's family, including sons, wife, and others.

The manner in which those who have committed exclusively evil deeds enter hell has been described: "Having been taken by the messengers of Yama to a body of torment and bound by nooses around the neck, he is dragged for three *muhūrtas* to the abode of Yama, located ninety-nine thousand *yojanas* away. After experiencing twenty-eight *koṭis* of distinct hells according to the gradations of his sins, he subsequently undergoes two million births among grass and other such things; nine hundred thousand among aquatic creatures; eleven hundred thousand among the species of worms; one million among the species of birds; and one million among the species of quadrupeds."

"After obtaining seven crores of births among the human species, and then four hundred thousand births among the Brahmin caste—ranging from low, middling, and high—one obtains another hundred births; yet if one commits evil there again, one falls into the hells. || 6 ||
Now, he describes the repeated attainment of the mortal world through equal measures of merit and demerit:
"Though weary from the womb of a young woman and having attained awakening, one's awakening slips away prematurely at birth; thus, having overcome childhood with great pain,"
Furthermore, you declared to Devahūti that even at the time of youth, one whose body is like Kapila is indeed deluded. || 7 ||

Regarding the word "yuvati" (young woman): distressed within the mother’s womb—a pit of feces and urine—harassed by the bitter, sour, alkaline, and hot food and drink consumed by the mother, and tormented by worms, the fetus, at the seventh month, may by chance regain its memory at a time when it is impossible to counteract suffering unexpectedly. Even so, what indeed can the living being do? At birth, through the pressure of the birth-wind and the constriction of the vaginal canal, its consciousness—which had previously been directed toward the karma accumulated over hundreds of births—is dissolved and departs.

Furthermore, having overcome childhood along with the suffering born from the inability to obtain the desired and avoid the undesired, he nevertheless becomes deluded again during the period of youth. Being under the sway of desire and anger, while performing actions that are either prompted by desire or forbidden, he enters into darkness; this is the meaning. || 7 ||
He shows that through merit alone one attains states such as heaven:
"The righteous householder who performs sacrifices for the hosts of ancestors and gods falls in due time, proceeding along the southern path."
"You declared to Devahūtī that your body as Kapila was assumed through illusion (māyā) for the sake of the waterway, though you were free from desire. || 8 ||

"Pitṛ" means one whose nature it is to sacrifice to the ancestors and the hosts of gods because of his aversion to the dharma of the Blessed One, and out of a desire for all desired fruits and the like. "Dhārmika" means one who performs only those actions prescribed by law, having abandoned prohibited deeds. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "also. He too, when his merit is exhausted in time, falls and returns again; he is one who goes by the southern path, characterized by traveling along the way of smoke and the rest.

The manner of traveling along and returning from the path beginning with smoke is as follows: at the conclusion of its *prārabdha* (projected karma), the soul that has performed only "black" (*kevalakṛṣṇa*) actions exits through the gates of the senses, such as the eyes, by means of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). The deity presiding over smoke then places it into the hand of the deity presiding over the night; the deity presiding over the time of night places it into the hand of the deity presiding over the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*); and she, in turn, places it into the hand of the deity presiding over the six months of the sun's southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*). She then brings it into proximity with the moon in the sky via the path of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).

In that regard, having experienced the bliss of heaven until the exhaustion of his good deeds, as he is about to fall back to earth, he first falls through the path of space, and then descends through wind, smoke, clouds, and rain in succession, finally falling upon plants. From the plants, becoming food, and from food, becoming semen, he enters the womb of a woman and becomes embodied. If there is a remainder of merit, he is born in the womb of a Brāhmaṇa or similar caste; if there is a remainder of sin, he is born in the womb of a Caṇḍāla or similar low caste. To the question, "Then, performing what does one travel by the path of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa)? he says: "In Me" (mayi).

"Deposited in Me, the Lord," means surrendered; "desireless" (akāma) refers to action other than that which is prompted by desire or prohibited—namely, the forms of obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), expiatory (prāyaścitta), and meditative (upāsana) rites. The particle "tu" has the sense of "indeed. This means it results in the attainment of the path of light (arcir-ādi-mārga) for the sake of reaching the northern route (udakpatha). || 8 ||
Now, he describes the departure of the Blessed One and the attainment of liberation by Devahūtī in a single verse:
"O Lord, having thus favored Devahūtī, who had well understood what is to be known and offered her salutations, you departed with the company of yogis."
Now, that Vimalamati has been liberated through the yoga of devotion;
you too, for the sake of the welfare of people, abide in the north-eastern direction.

"Thus" (iti): she by whom the object to be known—Brahman—and the means for attaining it have been well understood and correctly grasped. Now, after your departure, that Devahūti remains. You, Kapila, also abide in the north-eastern direction for the welfare of people and for the protection of the three worlds. || 9 ||
Now, concluding the Kāpila doctrine, he prays for devotion:
"O Supreme One! What is the use of much speaking? [Grant] devotion to Your lotus feet, which removes all fear and bestows all desires."
O Lord of the City of the Great Wind, you have indeed spoken firmly; therefore, shaking off my ailments, bestow upon me devotion toward you. 10.

"Supreme" (paramā): she who leads away (vinetrī) all fears, including the suffering of saṃsāra—that is, she who effects its subduing, its pacification, and its eradication from the very root—this is the meaning. She who brings about (upanayati), that is, causes one to attain, all desires (sarvakāmān), which are desired objects, is "the bringer of all desires" (sarvakāmopanetrī); her [I salute].

"Firmly" means with certainty. "Therefore" (tat): because you have stated without doubt that devotion to you alone is to be prayed for for the cessation of fear and the attainment of the desired goal; therefore is the meaning. "Bestow upon me" (upādhatsva) means transfer it to me. [Bestow] devotion characterized by love. || 10 || 83 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth decade, the narrative of Kapila.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The third section:
The origin of Mahat and the others, of the lords of creatures, and of the cosmic egg;
now, the emission (visarga) of Viṣṇu, arising from his sport of creation, is described.
Now, for the introduction to the account of the incarnation of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, which serves as the means for [explaining] the emission (visarga), he speaks of Dakṣa’s marriage and so forth:
"Then Dakṣa, the son of Viriñca, having obtained Prasūti, the daughter of Manu, begot here sixteen daughters."
To Dharma she gave thirteen daughters; to the Pitṛs, Svadhā; and to Giriśa, who partakes of the sacrificial oblation, she gave Satī, who was a portion of yourself.

Regarding the word "Dakṣa": the word *atha* (now/then) serves to introduce a new narrative. From Manu Svāyambhuva, in this [wife] named Prasūti, his own wife, he begot thirteen daughters—Mainyā and the others—for Dharma, that is, for Dharmadeva. To the Pitṛs, that is, to the joined Pitṛs, he gave Svadhā. In your portion, that is, in your very form. || 1 ||
For Mūrti, the wife of Dharma, gave birth to you, Nārāyaṇa, who is a friend to mankind and possessed of exalted majesty;
at whose birth the gods, filled with joy, sounded the drums of celebration.
The hosts of gods showered heaps of flowers and sang praises.

Regarding the word *mūrtiḥ*: Mūrti, the youngest among the wives of Dharma, gave birth to you, Nārāyaṇa—the friend of men—as well as Nara; thus she brought forth Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who are portions (*aṃśa*) of Viṣṇu. || 2 ||

The Daitya Sahasrakavaca was surrounded by thousands of armors obtained through austerities and battles lasting for a thousand years; you two, however, have achieved your austerities and battles through successive cycles of time.
They effortlessly struck down this [demon], who had only a single breastplate remaining. || 3 ||

"Regarding the word *daityam*: 'surrounded by armor' means his body was equipped with a natural thousandfold coat of mail. Regarding *sāhasra-*: it means they cut [each other's armor] through a battle performed for as long as a thousand years of asceticism (*tapas*) practiced over that same period. The phrase *paryāya-nirmitau* means those two by whom asceticism and battle were performed in alternation; that is to say, while one was performing penance, the other fought, and likewise while the other was performing penance, the first fought.
*Śiṣṭaikakaṅkaṭam* means having only a single remaining coat of mail; *nyahnutām* means they struck down [the opponent]. || 3 ||
Even while practicing and teaching the dharma of liberation,
you lived in the midst of Badarikāśrama together with your brothers; then Śakra, his soul rendered powerless by your tranquility and the power of your asceticism, approached you.
He dispatched Māra, who was surrounded by celestial women.

"Anvācaran" means practicing [the path] himself for the sake of setting an example for the world, while teaching it to those seeking it, such as Nārada and others—this is the implied sense. "Mokṣadharma" refers to the dharma characterized by renunciation (*nivṛtti*). You, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa, were accompanied by your brother Nara (*bhrātṛmān*). With your mind (*ātmā*) overcome by envy due to his tranquility (*śama*), which consists of the restraint of the senses, and the power of his austerity (*tapas*), you sent him away (*prajighāya*).
The meaning is that, suspecting he wished to seize heaven through his austerity, you dispatched Kāma along with his retinue in order to destroy his asceticism. || 4 ||
Now, he describes the activity of Kāma, who was dispatched by Śakra:
Kāma, appearing like a kinsman of the spring and the Malaya breeze, [acts] with the playful arrows of his beloved’s sidelong glances.
And seeing you gazing at him unflinchingly again and again, he was terrified; then, by you, who were possessed of a gentle smile, he was addressed.

"Kāma" refers to [the god of love]. His arrows are the side-long glances of lovely celestial women; those arrows, in which the blossoming or manifesting charms—such as the movement of the eyebrows and so forth—stand in the place of feathers, pierce you again and again. Seeing you, whose mind is unshakable due to your meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he looks upon you from afar with his face upturned in fear. Then, you spoke to him with a gentle smile, accompanied by a soft laugh. || 5 ||
"O women of the celestial realm! Enough of this fear; enjoy the springtime of amorous passion within your hearts!"—speaking thus, he [Viṣṇu] was then praised on all sides by them with wonder.
You revealed those women whose eyes were timid with fear as they served you.
Regarding the word "bhītyā": O Aṅgaja, Vasanta, and celestial nymphs! Enough of your fear; have no more dread.

"Do not do so! Come here into my presence and favor my mind—that is, follow my will. Or rather, favor with pleasure and accept without fear the hospitality conceived by my mind; or else, accept and take that certain object called 'the jewel,' difficult even for heaven to obtain, which is being created for you by my mind. In the reading *manmānanam*, the meaning is "the honor performed by me."

To you who were speaking thus, they approached from all sides, drew near, and surrounded you while offering praise; then, immediately after their words, you displayed your own female attendants—beautiful women with timid eyes—who were performing service for you, having created them through the power of yoga and manifested them before you. || 6 ||
Madana and the other gods assembled for the purpose of deluding you were themselves rendered bewildered by the fragrances of your handmaidens;
and they accepted from you that very Urvaśī— who humbles the pride of all the inhabitants of heaven— with nothing but shame.
"To delude you": Madana and the others—namely Madana, Malaya-breeze, Vasanta, and the celestial nymphs—have come together in a group to bewilder you; [and] Urvaśī, one of those created by you. (7)
Having seen Urvaśī and having heard your story, Śakra became agitated from the realization of your greatness;
thus, O Giver of Boons, this most peaceful and beautiful incarnation is even superior to you— you yourself are indeed the one in the form of Kṛṣṇa.

"Having seen [him]," it is said. "Tranquil" means gentle. He is superior to you—the incarnation of Śrī Nārāyaṇa—in terms of his tranquility, his performance of diverse deeds, and his extreme loveliness; thus he is preeminent. "Kṛṣṇatanuḥ" means one whose very self is Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 8 ||
Having thus related the story of Mūrti, the lawful wife among the daughters of Dakṣa, he tells the story of Satī, the wife of Bhava:
"But Dakṣa, blinded by passion through excessive indulgence,
was not very respectful toward you, and alas, there was great distress and unrest."
By him, Śarva, who obstructed that very body of yours at the sacrifice intended for the destruction of Vīra, his own daughter was carried away.

He insulted him. This is a form derived from the root *māna* (in the sense of "worship") belonging to the *ādhṛṣīya* group, used in the *luṅ* tense in the active voice (*parasmaipada*). Regarding the word *dakṣa*: because of Brahmā’s excessive fondling, Dakṣa was established in the sovereignty over the Prajāpatis through rites such as consecration; yet, blinded by passion (*rajas*)—that is, by its effects such as lust, anger, and greed—he was devoid of discrimination. For this very reason, he was not highly regarded even by Brahmā, but was neglected. He was *aśānti*, meaning one for whom peace or forbearance (*kṣamā*) did not exist; thus, he was intolerant.

Because of that lack of peace, Dakṣa obstructed Śarva—who was indeed a portion of you—and harbored hatred toward him; at the sacrifice known as Dakṣādhvara, which signaled the enmity between Dakṣa and Śarva, he insulted his own daughter Satī, the wife of Śarva. || 9 ||
He, whose sacrifice had been crushed by the enraged Śiva and whose head was severed,
was restored to life by Hara when propitiated by the gods;
having completed his excellent sacrifice through you, he then attained peace once more.
Therefore, O Bringer of Peace! O Lord of the City of the Maruts! protect me. || 10 ||

Regarding the phrase "by the enraged Lord": his sacrifice—meaning the sacrificial vessels, the sacrificial post, the hall, and other implements—was crushed and pulverized by the Lord (Iśa) who was incensed by the insult to His beloved; and Dakṣa himself had his head cut off. Then, having received back his life from Hara after being propitiated by the gods, he became goat-faced (Ajamukha). Subsequently, when that most excellent of sacrifices (Ṛtuvare) was completed and properly concluded by you, Dakṣa regained his peace and returned to his own natural state. O Bringer of Peace! You who possess such power, protect us.
Thus ends the sixteenth decade, containing the description of the lives of Nara and Nārāyaṇa and the description of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Having thus described the lineage of Manu’s daughters, and intending now to describe the lineage of their sons, he first relates the life of Uttānapāda for the sake of the story of Dhruva.
Suruci was the wife of King Uttānapāda, the delight of Manu, and she was exceedingly beloved;
the other, named Sunīti, was disregarded by her husband.
Being without any other resort, she has eternally come to you alone for refuge. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *uttāna*: he was the son of King Uttānapāda, who was the grandson of Svāyambhuva Manu and the younger brother of Priyavrata. He had two wives, Suruci and Sunīti. Of these two, the wife named Suruci was exceedingly beloved. The other wife, Sunīti, being disregarded by her husband, was not very dear to him; therefore, having no other resort (*agati*), she went for refuge to You, the Lord alone. The meaning is that she performed worship of the Lord in order to pacify the sins that were the cause of her own misfortune. || 1 ||
Seeing that excellent son of Suruci on his father’s lap, Dhruva— the son of Sunīti— was indeed about to climb up;
at which the infant was reportedly addressed quite harshly by Suruci.
Indeed, envy is born from those who are averse to existence. II.2.

Regarding the word "aṅka" (lap): Once, Dhruva, the son of Sunīti, seeing his father seated upon the throne with Uttamā’s son—who was being excessively pampered as the son of Suruci—on his lap, began to climb up to ascend it himself. Although he was still a very young child, he was rebuked and insulted by Suruci with harsh words. Indeed, malice toward those who have turned away from the Lord is difficult to abandon; it is truly impossible to cast it off. By this, it is suggested that through Suruci’s aversion to the Lord, there was the loss of her son and so forth, whereas through Sunīti’s grace toward the Lord, she attained the state of Dhruva along with her son. || 2 ||
While your father, deluded by you, looked on as a slave to his wife,
he was struck down by harsh words and went far away to his own mother;
she too, for the sake of crossing over the course of her own karma for men—
He pointed out your very feet as the refuge for the child. || 3 ||

"By you"—that is, one whose mind was deluded by the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*) and by destiny (*bhavitavyatā*). By the phrase "under your control," it is implied that although he saw his own son wishing to climb onto his lap, he did not let him do so out of fear of Suruci. Utterly struck—that is, pierced—by harsh words and evil speech, Dhruva went to, or reached, his own mother, Sunīti. She too [acted] for the sake of crossing over—that is, for the cessation of her own course of karma, the fruit of evil deeds, and her misfortune.

Or rather, she praised her own feet alone as the refuge—and nothing else—for the effortless crossing, that is, the transcending, of the ocean of saṃsāra which all embodied beings must traverse according to their own karma. By the word "children," it is suggested that she spoke while placing her son on her lap, preceded by such conciliatory words as "do not cry. (3)
Having heard this, that proud youth, having resolved his mind upon your worship, departed from the city at the age of five;
and having beheld the path of mantras revealed by Nārada, he propitiated you with austerity in the Madhuka forest.

"Having heard"—the remainder of the sentence being "having heard his mother's words. He, Dhruva, was one whose mind and heart were resolved upon performing penance for the worship of Bhava (Śiva); he was proud. Regarding the phrase "five years old": even though he was only five, seeing his own mother despondent as she wished to go [with him], and having somehow obtained her permission, he went out from the city alone by himself, without looking back at others. This is the meaning.

On the road, he was informed and instructed in the path of mantra by Nārada whom he had seen; thus, he propitiated you—that is, he sought your grace—in the region known as Madhuvana at the edge of the Madhu forest. || 4 ||
When his father had gone to the city with a dejected heart, he was comforted by the venerable Nārada; meanwhile,
the boy’s mind remained fixed upon you, as he grew up in due course.
He indeed spent five months in rigorous asceticism.

"O Father!"—when his father, King Uttānapāda, was thus situated, his mental state having its surge of grief assuaged by Śrī Nārada—who had gone to the city immediately after instructing Dhruva on the procedure for performing austerities, and who had consoled him with assurances of his future welfare—the boy, hearing through his own fault that the child had departed from the city, was filled with anxiety due to the fear of his son's misfortune; yet, his heart being full of longing, he was comforted by Nārada upon seeing his father. While things were in this state, the boy...

With his mind fixed upon you and his heart composed in you, Dhruva spent five months in austerities that were harsh and intense, characterized by a gradual increase in severity through a slow reduction of food—consisting of fruits, leaves, water, and so forth—in a sequence of progressive refinement. || 5 ||
Then, when the gods were filled with apprehension, Śrī Hari appeared before him; thus it is said:
"At that moment, while the quarters of the sky were rendered breathless by the power of his asceticism, you, whose heart was moistened by compassion, arose at the request of the gods."
O All-pervading Lord! You appeared before me, whose mind was absorbed in the nectar of the consciousness of Your form, as You were mounted upon Garuḍa.

"Then indeed" (*tāvāditi*): the meaning is that his mind was dissolved—that is, transformed into that very form—within the *cidrasa* (the essence of consciousness) in Your form, which, having become solidified as characterized by four arms and so forth, is the Supreme Brahman. Alternatively, it means that You appeared before him with such a mind. By this, it is suggested that his own form suddenly vanished from his heart, and upon opening his eyes, he beheld the external form of the Blessed Lord remaining in that very state. || 6 ||

Perceiving him— whose heart was rippling with the intense joy of beholding you, who seemed submerged in the aesthetic relish of your form through his two eyes, and who was offering praise— [she touched] the region of his cheek.
You have touched it with such fear and with such reverence. || 7 ||

"O You, [the Lord] touched the region of his cheeks with the conch named Pāñcajanya—which is the Śabdabrahman—with great reverence, in order to bestow upon him the capacity he lacked to praise You whom he desired to extol. [The conch] was rippled by the weight of the joy of beholding You; it was somewhat agitated by his bewilderment regarding what ought to be done; and then, having plunged its two eyes into the nectar of Your form—the essence of beauty—it remained as if its pair of eyes were submerged within that ocean of beauty.
[The Lord acted] with reverence, preceded by a tender caress. (7)
At that moment, having perceived his state of mind, you should address him who is praising [the Buddha] with a heart purified by awakening:
"O Dhruva! After enjoying sovereignty for a long time, you shall again attain the supreme, eternal state that is free from rebirth. (8)

"Then" (*tāvat*): as soon as [the Lord's] cheek was touched by fear, he became "pure" (*vimalaḥ*), meaning one from whom the impurity of ignorance has been removed through awakening—that is, through both knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*). Alternatively, "pure" (*vimalam*) may be taken as an adverbial qualifier of the act of praising, meaning "in such a way that it becomes pure. By this, it is suggested that the praise is grounded in the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*). Having understood his state—his intention—pertaining to that [Lord], you addressed him; that is, you spoke.
O Dhruva! That supreme station, situated even above the world of the seven ṛṣis, is a state free from cessation—that is, devoid of returning again. || 8 ||

He said: "When you had spoken thus and departed, that son of the king returned to the city, bringing joy to all the people; and with his desires fulfilled by your grace, he took up the burden of the kingdom after his father had gone to the forest and enjoyed himself for a long time. (9)
Furthermore, he describes his supreme conduct: "O Lord! When this supreme being was slain by the Yakṣa, he, though intent on battle with the Yakṣas, desisted at the word of Manu."
From the Great-Souled One, who had approached Śānti with a gracious heart as the Giver of Wealth, he chose only very firm devotion to you.

Regarding the phrase "by a yakṣa": while Dhruva was engaged in hunting, he was killed by a certain yakṣa in battle. Subsequently, out of indignation at his brother’s death, Dhruva became intent on fighting the yakṣas and slew them. However, at the word of Manu, his grandfather, he desisted. Because of this peace—that is, his withdrawal from battle—Dhruva was told by Dhanada (Kubera), the King of Kings, who had approached him: "Choose a boon. Dhruva chose nothing other than devotion to You; the reason for this is that he was a "great-souled one" (mahātman). || 10 ||
Now he describes Dhruva’s attainment of his own desired state:
"At last, having traveled in the celestial chariot brought by your servant, he remains joyful in the station of Dhruva together with his mother."
Thus, O Lord of the Wind! with a mind eager to protect your own servants, restrain the floods of my maladies. || 11 ||

"At the end": having experienced a reign of twenty-six thousand years at the end [of the Dvāpara-yuga], and having departed—having gone—by means of a celestial chariot brought by your two attendants, Sunanda and Nanda, he now remains here, joyful and satisfied together with his mother Sunīti. By this, it is indicated that he exists even now and is visible in the form of a constellation. || 11 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth decad, containing the description of Dhruva’s life, along with its supplement.
Now, in order to relate the life of Pṛthu, he introduces the story of Vena:
To Aṅga, whose fame was lofty and who was born in the very lineage of Dhruva, a son named Vena was born.
Because his mind was afflicted by that fault, that best of kings, having fixed his heart upon your feet, departed for the forest. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "of one who was born": to King Aṅga, who was born in the very lineage of Dhruva, a son named Vena was born by his wife Sunīthā. Distressed and despondent because of the fault—that is, the unrighteousness—of that Vena, that excellent king Aṅga went to the forest. It should be understood that he departed at midnight, unobserved by people. || 1 ||
He elaborates upon Vena’s unrighteousness:
"Though sinful and of fierce prowess, Vena was installed by the citizens and others for the protection of the earth."
Praising only his own strength against all, he has obstructed your sacrifices upon this circle of the earth. || 2 ||
"O Pāpa! Having been brought forward, he was seated upon the lion-throne and consecrated. || 2 ||
Then he says that, by censuring virtuous people and censuring the Lord, he was consumed by the fire of the sage’s curse:
"When the multitude of ascetics arrived to speak what is beneficial,
[he thought] 'There is no lord of the world other than me.'"
Vena, who was intent on speaking words of censure against you, was reduced to the state of a moth in the fire of their curses by those lords of sages. || 3 ||
Now he describes the incarnation as Pṛthu:

"When that [body] had been cast off after being churned from the thigh-staff—its parts having been long protected by the lords of sages who were afraid of wicked people because of its destruction—you, O Lord, manifested yourself when the arm-staff was finally churned. (4)

"Because of his destruction" means: because of the destruction of that Vena, while the kingdom was without a king, those who were fearful of wicked people and bandits were protected by his mother Sunīthā through the power of yoga; thus, from the thigh-staff of that body of Vena, which had been churned, [Pṛthu] was born, "having abandoned all evil. This is the meaning: from the thigh churned by the sages, a certain man named Niṣāda was born. And because he was a portion of Vena’s impurity, he was black in color. Those belonging to his lineage became the Naiṣādas, who wander through the mountains and forests.
Then, when that staff-like arm was crushed, you, possessing a massive body, manifested yourself—you descended. || 4 ||
Renowned as Pṛthu, with your future vast prowess praised by your sons and others as instructed by the ascetics, you made the earth—
which had been swallowed up by its wealth due to the oppression of Vena— level once again with your bow.

Regarding the word *vikhyāta*: You are renowned as Pṛthu; that is, you are one whose future manifold heroic deeds—such as the milking of the earth and the ninety-nine horse-sacrifices—have been celebrated and praised by Sūtas, Māgadhas, and bards who, through the instructions of ascetics such as "This is a direct portion of Hari," were made aware of His power.

By the pain caused by Vena—that affliction which devoured and swallowed the medicinal herbs of prosperity—you, with your bow drawn and rushing forward in anger, made that land even, having leveled it with the tip of your own bow as you traversed it, making it high and low; thus, while pulverizing the mountain peaks, you have for the most part made it level according to the divisions of cities and villages—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||

Then he describes how the subjects, by the command of Pṛthu, milked the Earth—who had assumed the form of a cow—of the milk consisting of the food desired by each individual: "Furthermore, by the gods and others, joined with their own family-chiefs as calves, [the milk was drawn] into appropriate and beautiful vessels;
whatever desired foods and so forth there were, those very things [were obtained]."
At your will, you have milked the fragrant body [of the earth].

"Furthermore," it says: "that earth, joined with the calves who were the leaders of their own families. This is the meaning: Pṛthu, having made Manu—the leader of his own family—his calf, milked the medicinal herbs into the vessel of his hands. The sages, having made Bṛhaspati their calf, milked the earth—which consists of the Vedic meters—as milk into the vessels of their senses. The gods, having made Indra their calf, milked Soma into a golden vessel. For the Asuras, Prahlāda was the calf, iron was the vessel, and wine was the milk; for the Gandharvas, honey [was the milk].

The ancestors [partake of] the *kavya*. It should be viewed thus: they milked her whose body was fragrant, that is, who had the form of a cow; the intended meaning is that they milked her by your command. || 6 ||
While you, O possessor of the threefold path, were performing sacrifices for yourself and had commenced the hundredth horse-sacrifice, Indra,
the performer of a hundred sacrifices, arrived in humble guise,
stole your horse, and was defeated by your son.

Regarding the word "ātmānam" (himself): O Viṣṇu, O you whose abode is threefold! while you, being Pṛthu, were sacrificing yourself—who is Viṣṇu composed of all the gods—with horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), when the hundredth sacrifice, the final one among a hundred in number, had commenced, Indra—the performer of a hundred sacrifices (*śatamakhah*)—who possessed the conceit that he alone in this world was the performer of a hundred sacrifices (*śatakratuḥ*), approached in the guise of a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*) with a lowly appearance, stole the horse, and [did so] from your son, the son of Pṛthu, who by this very deed was named Vijitāśva. || 7 ||

When the Lord of the Gods repeatedly urged the horse away as it was being offered into the fire by that circle of eminent sages, and when the Lotus-born Brahmā attempted to obstruct the sacrifice at its conclusion, you yourself beheld Madhuripu (Viṣṇu) directly as your own self.

"Regarding the phrase *devendram iti*: In this manner, when that Devendra—who was repeatedly and constantly stealing (harantam) and plundering (muṣṇantam) a horse (*vājinam*) while disguised in the garb of a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*) such as a naked ascetic, a red-robed monk, one with matted hair, or one smeared with ashes—was about to offer him into the fire, specifically the *dakṣiṇāgni* within the assembly (*maṇḍala*) of the best of sages, desiring to kill him through the performance of a malevolent rite (*ābhicāra-vidhāna*), and while Brahmā (*kamalabhava*) was restraining him, saying, 'Enough of your ninety-nine sacrifices; let Indra (*śatakratu*) be pleased,' [the sage said], 'O Pṛthu, for you..."

When [the sage] arrived and uttered the prohibition, "Enough with sacrifices," once the sacrifice had reached its conclusion, you, Pṛthu, beheld Madhuripu Viṣṇu directly through the faculty of sight (*sākṣāccakṣuṣatayā*). By the words "himself" and "his own," Pṛthu’s status as an incarnation is stated. (8)

O Lord! Having obtained that boon granted by You and having established Your feet upon the banks of the Gaṅgā, You once beheld the assembly of sages headed by Sanaka standing there, as they were proclaiming blessings for their welfare. || 9 ||
"Given by Him": having obtained from Viṣṇu the boon of unswerving devotion, he thereafter established his station (pada) at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, that is, between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;

while dwelling there, on one occasion, as he was instructing—that is, teaching—the two-fold dharma characterized by engagement and withdrawal to the assembly (nivaha)—the multitude—of sages, namely the celestial seers (devarṣis), brahminical seers (brahmarṣis), and royal seers (rājarṣis), who had arrived for a sacrificial session (satra), he beheld Sanaka and the others—Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, and Sanatkumāra—at the conclusion of that assembly. || 9 ||
Bearing within himself that consciousness which was uttered from the mouths of the ancient sages, he, the dweller of the forest, attained his own true Self;
O Lord of such a vast form! [grant] that very same state to me quickly.
O dweller in the abode of Vāta, pacify the flood of diseases! || 10 ||

Regarding the word *vijñānam*: You, who possess the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*)—the wisdom uttered from the mouth of Sanaka—and having correctly realized it, assumed a body of pure being (*sattvavigraha*) for the sake of favoring the world; you, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, experienced your own self as your true form, thinking "I am Brahman. Subsequently, dwelling in the depths of the forest and having entrusted the kingdom to your son, you went to the woods and, while performing austerities, you yourself attained your own Self. The sense is that you remained established as nothing other than the Supreme Brahman. || 10 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth decade, the description of Pṛthu’s deeds. Now begins the account of Prācīnabarhis:
"The great-grandson of Pṛthu, Prācīnabarhis, who was proficient in vast religious rites, begot two daughters upon his two young wives."
Sucetas gave birth to sons named Pracetas, who were like sprouts of your compassion. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *pṛthoḥ*: a *naptṛ* is the son of a grandson. *Pṛthu’s* son was Vijitāśva; his son was Havirdhāna; his son is this one who is called Barhiṣmat. He is called *Pṛthudharmā* because his dharma (righteousness) is broad (*pṛthu*), or rather, because his dharma is like that of Pṛthu; he is thus a master of action (*karmaṭha*), a hero in ritual work (*karmaśūra*), meaning he is proficient in the *Karmakāṇḍa*. For this very reason, he received the name *Prācīnabarhis*, because this circle of the earth was strewn with *prācīnāgni* *kuśa* grass by him. And he...

In his wife Śatadruti, Pracetas begot sons named Pracetas who shared that same name; and they were all of noble mind (sucetasaḥ). Therefore, they are like the sprouts of your compassion directed toward Prācīnabarhis. || 1 ||
By the command of their father, who was intent on the desire to create, all ten of them became devoted to asceticism;
having gone to the western ocean, they beheld a charming lake upon its shore.

Regarding the word "of the father": at the command of their father—who was intent on creation and desirous of producing progeny, saying "Procreate offspring"—all ten of those Pracetasas became devoted to asceticism. || 2 ||

Then the Blessed Lord Rudra, having arrived there, taught them a hymn of praise to the Blessed One, as it is said: "At that time, Bhava, having come to this sacred ford (tīrtha) and honored by the sight of his own devotees, appeared before the Pracetasas and taught them that hymn of praise, the most excellent of all. (3)
Chanting your hymn of praise within the waters, these beings have served you for ten thousand years;
because of their relish for the taste of the joy of your presence, such a vast time has passed for them as if it were but a moment, like the constancy of the Pole Star.
Regarding the word "stava" (praise): *bhavatsukham* means the bliss of your being, which is the bliss of Brahman; *tadāsvādarasaḥ* refers to the relish or intense attachment to its tasting.
By their ascetic practices, which increased beyond measure, even he who was devoted to the violence of sacrifice was purified;
and their father as well, having his true self revealed by Nārada, attained the state of being one with you.

Regarding the phrase "by austerities": that Vena, who was intent on the injury of sacrifices and was the progenitor of Pṛthu, was purified—that is, raised up from hell by means of the cessation of his evil deeds. His father, Prācīnabarhis, also had the Self—namely Śrī Hari—as his [teacher], having been shown and instructed by Nārada who had come to his house; for it is said, "Because He is the most authoritative and the knower of all, Hari is indeed the Supreme Self. [Vena attained] "the state of being Your Self," which is *sāyujya* (union). || 5 ||
Then he says that you appeared before them solely out of affection for your devotees:
"Thereupon, by the power of your compassion alone, you, whose vehicle is the king of birds, appeared before the Pracetasas;
with eight arms, your splendor rising upward, you shone with the rays of your excellent weapons, such as the resplendent discus. (6)
To the sons of Pracetas, even as they were merely entreating you, you yourself granted boons out of an abundance of compassion;
may this reflection upon you also lead to the welfare of embodied beings, and may this hymn of praise to Rudra grant all desires.

Regarding the phrase "of the Pracetasas": it was stated that they were "givers of boons," and that very point he now expresses with the words "your reflection. The reflection—meaning the remembrance—of you, the Pracetasas, leads to *śiva*, which is auspiciousness; likewise, the praise of Rudra and my own hymn of praise were sung by Rudra himself. || 7 ||
"Having obtained my beloved daughter of the trees, enjoy her for ten hundred thousand years;
let there be a capable son, and indeed, at that very moment, you shall depart from me"—thus did the Auspicious One speak to them.

"Having obtained," and so forth. Furthermore, "the daughter of the trees" (mahīruhām) means the daughter of the *vṛkṣas*; she was the daughter of the Apsaras named Pramlocā, who had been abandoned by her [mother] and adopted as a daughter by the trees—this is how it should be understood. Having obtained that lovely woman, you ten shall marry her together and enjoy pleasures for a period consisting of ten hundred-thousand years (*daśalakṣavatsarī*)—that is, for that length of time. And let there be a son named Dakṣa born of her.
"You shall depart from me at that very moment, after ten hundred thousand years, and you will be liberated"—thus you spoke to them out of sheer joy, even without their making such a request. || 8 ||
Then, as they were burning with rage the trees that obstructed the surface of the earth, they were restrained by Brahmā;
having obtained that daughter given by the trees, they lived happily for the duration of time you specified.

"Then," and so on. After the Lord had departed, they rose from the water; those who have the habit of obstructing the surface of the earth are called "earth-obstructors. While burning those trees with wind and fire arising from their wrath, they were restrained by Druhiṇa (Brahmā). Then, the trees, having been instructed by the terrified Brahmā, gave her—that lotus-eyed woman.

Having obtained Dakṣa as their son and performed the sacrifice, the Pracetasas attained the state of bliss through the wisdom received from Nārada; O Lord, O Master of Vātālaya, may you, who are likewise, protect me! 10.

"Having attained" means: by means of the intellect (*dhi*) obtained from Nārada—that is, through knowledge—they attained the state (*pada*) whose nature is bliss; for it is "attained" (*padyate*), thus it is called a "state," namely Brahman. Such [a Lord] is one endowed with such affection (*vātsalya*) for His devotees. 10. 41.
Thus ends the nineteenth decade, containing the description of the occasion of Dakṣa’s birth and the description of Dakṣa’s birth itself.
Thus [concludes] the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra known as Bhaktapriyā.
The Fourth Section: Now begins the description of Hari’s pastimes known as "Maintenance," which consist of the preservation of the boundaries of the worlds He previously created.

Now, describing the Lord’s pastime consisting of the maintenance of the bounds of propriety by resorting to the fifth *skandha*, he first states the lineage preceding the descent of Ṛṣabhadeva in order to relate that incarnation:
"Indeed, Nābhi was born from King Āgnīdhra, who was the beloved son of Priyavrata. Having seen You in the midst of a sacrifice, he performed the sacrificial rites solely for Your satisfaction. (1)

Regarding the phrase "of Priyavrata": Priyavrata was the eldest son of Svāyambhuva Manu. Ten sons were born to him by Barhiṣmatī; among them, the eldest was a king named Āgnīdhra, who was dear to his father because of their identical character. From him, a king named Nābhi was born to the Apsaras Pūrvacitti in the midst of a sacrifice, that is, during the performance of a ritual. || 1 ||
O Viśvamūrti! Having been praised there by the lords of sages while the king was requesting a son equal to yourself, you said, "I myself shall be born," and vanished from the sacrificial altar.
"Abhiṣṭuta" means equal to oneself, equal to Aśvin. "Tirodhāḥ" means [hidden] in the sacrificial grass (barhis) and in the fire (agni). || 2 ||

Then, you were born by a portion of your essence from Merudevī, the beloved of Nābhi, under the name Ṛṣabha, causing the joy of all people through the manifestation of your extraordinary qualities and power. (3)

"From Nābhi"—that is, from Merudevī, the daughter of Meru. He was "manifested," meaning produced, by means of extraordinary, superhuman qualities and powers, by which the joy of all people was generated without exception. || 3 ||

Having entrusted the burden of sovereignty to you, the sustainer of the three worlds, Nābhi, together with Merudevī, reached the forest of asceticism; serving you, he indeed departed for that state of yours which is the abode of bliss.
"In you" means: your abode is the station of bliss, the place of unsurpassed happiness; that abode is Vaikuṇṭha. || 4 ||
When Indra, out of indignation caused by your superior excellence, did not send rain upon this land during that drought,
you then, through the power of your own yoga, made this, your own domain, a land of abundant rain.
Then, although his heart was devoted to the Self, he married the lovely Jayantī, who had been bestowed by Indra after he was conquered;
and from her, he begot a hundred sons, among whom the lord of the earth Bharata was the eldest.

"Jita" means given by Indra, who was conquered through the power of yoga. "Ātmarataḥ" refers to one whose inner faculty (āśaya), that is, the heart, is intent solely upon the worship of the Self, which is Lord Hari. || 6 ||
Nine became the best of yogis, while nine others protected the regions of Bhāratavarṣa;
those eighty-one remaining sons of yours attained the state of brahmins through the power of their asceticism.

"Nine" refers to the regions of Bhāratavarṣa, such as Kuśāvarta, Elāvarta, Brahmāvarta, Malayaketu, Bhadrasena, Vidarbha, Kīkaṭa, and so forth. "Eighty-one" means eighty plus one. "The state of a *bhūsura*" means the status of a Brāhmaṇa. || 7 ||
Having thus taught his sons, in the midst of the lords of sages, the path to liberation characterized by detachment and devotion,
he himself adopted the conduct of a paramahaṃsa and subsequently assumed the behavior of one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost.

Having spoken thus, Ṛṣabhadeva himself, having adopted the way of life of the paramahaṃsas, wandered like one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost, and he practiced [the conduct] of a mendicant. || 8 ||

Though you have become the Supreme Self, you moved throughout the entire earth free from all modification, remaining absorbed in the essence of the Self, even while giving instruction to others and being disregarded by everyone.

[The verse] says: "He is the Supreme. You are the Supreme Self, having become Brahman; nevertheless, while giving instruction to others, you give instruction in Brahman. He states that the instruction to others is through his own mode of life as a Paramahaṃsa and not merely by word of mouth—by saying "all": "being rejected by all, he is an Avadhūta. Being free from modification due to the cessation of identification with the body, he is devoid of agency, enjoyership, pleasure, pain, and so forth.

The reason for this is: "merged in the essence of the Self," meaning absorbed in the experience of supreme bliss (paramānanda), having attained oneness with That—that is to say, he is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 9 ||

O Lord of the Wind! Having long practiced the conduct of a dog, a cow, a deer, and a crow, you have finally attained your supreme true nature; with your body scorched by fire on Mount Kuṭaka, please dispel my sufferings.

"Śayu"—meaning one who practices the "śayuvrata," the vow of a python, and for a long time conducts himself like a cow, a deer, or a crow; that is to say, being devoid of effort like a python, he abstains from the rules and prohibitions regarding purity and impurity, like a cow, a deer, or a crow, merely moving about according to the nature of his body. Having attained the supreme state, his body struck by the falling [thunderbolt] on Mount Kuṭaka—his frame consumed by the forest fire—he fell down. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twentieth decade, the description of the life of Ṛṣabha, the Yogin.
Now, he praises the Blessed One who, for the protection of the world, manifests in various forms in various regions of the earth:
"In the central part of the earth, in the region named Ilāvṛta..."
O Sovereign, I take refuge in You, who consist of Saṅkarṣaṇa, who are attended by Śarva with prayers and hymns of praise, and who are served solely by women headed by Gaurī. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "born in the middle" (*madhyodbhava*): the middle of the earth is Jambūdvīpa; it refers to the region or sub-division (*khaṇḍa*) situated in its center. Due to Gaurī’s curse, this place is inaccessible to men, and thus Śarva alone is the male inhabitant here. Consequently, he frequents only women, with Gaurī as their chief; hence he is so described. [He was worshipped] by Śarva with mantras and hymns of praise. || 1 ||
In the eastern region of Ilāvṛta, known as Bhadrāśva,
he was being celebrated by the sages of auspicious renown;
he is expert in recovering the Vedas that were hidden at the end of the kalpa.
O Lord! I meditate upon you, whose body has the head of a horse. || 2 ||
I bow to You, O Blessed One, as Narahari, who exerts Yourself in the southern region of Harivarṣa, being served by the foremost men led by Prahlāda;
You whose form is lofty, peaceful, and white, and who bestows the singular, pure knowledge. 3.
"I meditate. It is so called because it bestows a single, pure, and unconditioned knowledge. || 3 ||
In the western continent of Ketumāla,
which is delightful in nature, he whose limbs are beautified by a smile made exquisite through his playful grace was being attended upon by Lakṣmī and the sons of Prajāpati.
I worship you, who have assumed a body of desire for the sake of that beloved one. || 4 ||
"Varṣa" means one who has assumed a body of fulfilled desire—that is, one who has taken on the very form of the god Kāmadeva. || 4 ||
Indeed, in the delightful region named Uttarakuru to the north, he was being served by the best of men while honoring the lord of that region;
the word *saparyamāṇa* is derived from the root *sapara* (meaning "to worship") belonging to the *kaṇḍvādigaṇa*, used here in the passive sense (*śānac*).
O Lord of the World! I worship You in the form of a fish, shining within those whose hearts are free from envy and who cherish their devotees as their only child.
"Ramya" means being worshipped—that is, being propitiated—by the lord of the Ramyaka-varṣa, the eminent Manu Vaivasvata. || 5 ||
In the year known as Hiraṇmayasamāhṛya,
during the month of Uttara, Aryaman— the foremost of the host of ancestors— frequents this mountain-dwelling, which is the very limb of the tortoise and is skilled in supporting the earth.
I worship you, O Blessed One! O Supreme Consciousness-Self! || 6 ||

"Varṣam" means the northern region, situated in the north. "Abridhṛtikarmaṭham" refers to that which was capable of supporting Mount Mandara during the churning for nectar; "Kāmaṭham" refers to the Tortoise-form (Kūrma) limb of Him whose body is that Tortoise. O Thou whose self consists of supreme consciousness! O Thou whose nature is pure knowledge! || 6 ||
Moreover, in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, he was served by the beloved Earth with various forms of worshipful mantras and praises;
his most massive body rubbed against the surface of the earth by the tips of his fangs.
Protect us, O You who possess the form of the wise and noble sacrifice-sow! || 7 ||

"Kiñca" (furthermore): he whose body (*varṣma*)—his very form—is most heavy (*gariṣṭha*) and exceedingly lofty (*atyunnata*), with the surface of his back rubbed by the tip of his tusk; he whose form in the shape of the Sacrificial Boar (*yajñavarāha*) is praised (*nutā*) and extolled (*stutā*) by the wise (*vijñaiḥ*), those possessed of knowledge. || 7 ||
In the southern direction, in the region known as Kiṃpuruṣa,
he dwells, attended by Hanumān who possesses firm devotion;
he is endowed with a most wonderful form that is delightful to Sītā.
O Viṣṇu, shining forth as the very soul of Rāma, protect us completely! || 8 ||
"In the southern direction" means it occupies the southern quarter, situated in the region immediately adjacent to Ilāvṛta.

O Infinite One! Being worshipped here by Śrī Nārada along with the foremost leaders of Bhārata-khaṇḍa through the praises of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and as the protector of virtuous people until the end of the kalpa, do you, Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, protect us! 9.
"Śrī" refers to Sāṅkhya, which is the knowledge of the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and Yoga, which consists of eight limbs, as well as by praises from those two. || 9 ||

Surrounding this Jambūdvīpa, there are six continents in sequence named Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara. It is said that the inhabitants of those places worship the Blessed Lord there in the form of the Sun, Moon, Fire, Water, Wind, and Brahmā respectively:
"In Plakṣa they worship Him in the form of the Sun; in the continent of Śālmali, in the form of the Moon; and in the continent named Kuśa, in the form of Fire."
In Krauñca they behold you as water, and in Śāka as wind; but in the world named Puṣkara, O Mother, they behold you as Brahman.
Now, he describes the method of worship for the Blessed One, whose nature consists of the array of lights:
"By all the clusters of stars beginning with Dhruva, and by the planets, being superimposed upon the parts beginning with the tail..."
O You who recline upon the ocean! Assuming the form of a porpoise, you are worshipped by the great ones during the twilights; grant me freedom from hell. || 11 ||

"By all" means: You are characterized by the clusters of stars such as Aśvinī and so forth, and by the planets such as the Sun and so forth, which are respectively meditated upon by worshippers upon the parts of the body beginning with the tail; you possess a body like that of a *śiṃśumāra*—one whose head is turned downwards and whose body is coiled—and thus, in that form, you are to be worshipped at the three times of day during the twilight rituals by the great ones. || 11 ||
Now he praises Śeṣa, the deliverer from worldly proliferation (prapañca):

O Hara, O Lord of the Teacher’s House! I worship You in the form of Śeṣa upon the ground at the root of the netherworld (pātāla), with a thousand heads resplendent with a single swinging earring, clad in blue garments, holding a plow, and attended by the wives of serpents; [save me] from calamities. 12.22.
Thus ends the twenty-first decad, consisting of twenty-six verses, which describes the modes of worshiping the Blessed One in Jambūdvīpa and other lands.
Thus concludes [this section] in the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The Fifth Chapter:
Even when sin has been committed, there is no hellish torment for devotees;
thus, the grace of Viṣṇu, as described in the sixth [chapter], is now being praised.
Now begins the narrative of Ajāmila in eleven verses:
"O Lord! In former times, a Brahmin named Ajāmila, living as a householder, was walking along the path of dharma.
At his guru’s word, he went to the forest and beheld a woman of loose character, arrogant in nature and agitated by passion. (1)

Regarding the word "Ajāmila": Long ago, there was a certain Brahmin named Ajāmila, so called because he took (lāti) a woman of low birth (ajāmi-kulīnām). Living as a householder in the stage of life of a forest-dweller (*gṛhāśramī*), he followed and practiced the paths of dharma appropriate for his own stage—the ways of engagement and withdrawal. One day, by the command of his guru—that is, at his father's instruction—to fetch fruits, flowers, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass, he went to the forest. There, with a very bold mind, he saw a certain unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*) whose character was capable of supreme deception through false charms and the like; she was intoxicated with passion and her gait was unsteady from the intoxication of wine. ||1||
Although he was by nature tranquil, his mind was drawn away by her; abandoning his own duty, he engaged in worldly activity with her.
Committing unrighteous acts and reaching the tenth stage of life, he again placed his affection upon his son, who was joined with worldly existence.

"By himself" (svataḥ). And thus, although he was naturally tranquil, his disposition was drawn away by her; having abandoned his own duty and his lawful wife, he engaged in union with her and became an unrighteous doer for the sake of maintaining her household. Furthermore, having reached his tenth decade and being aged, he felt great affection and intense attachment toward his son named Nārāyaṇa, who was his tenth child and still a young boy. || 2 ||

At the time of death, perceiving the three terrifying messengers of King Yama and trembling with fear, he previously invoked by the power of the latent impression of your remembrance the son named Nārāyaṇa. (3)

Regarding the word "he": at the time of death, at the moment of dying, by the power of the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—that is, the mental residue (*saṃskāra*)—of even a slight recollection of himself or of the worship of the Lord, he offered his son named Nārāyaṇa as a libation; that is, he called out, "O Nārāyaṇa! || 3 ||

Even for one of evil intent, by the mere power of even a single syllable of Your name uttered at that moment, Your enchanting four-armed attendants, clad in yellow garments, rushed forward from before him. (4)

Regarding the phrase "of one with evil intent": although his mind was attached to his family, at that very moment—the state of death—as even a single syllable of your name issued forth from him, this indicates the absence of devotion, faith, mental activity, or clear articulation of the letters; nevertheless, by the power of those four syllables, "Nārāyaṇa," your own attendants, the messengers of Viṣṇu, rushed forward and appeared before him. || 4 ||
And as the soldiers were dragging him away after binding him, these powerful men rushed forward, crying, "Release him!
They were then restrained by the attendants of Bhava, who reported his entire transgression to them.

"Amum iti"—having seized that Ajāmila by the neck with a noose and dragging him away, the messengers of Yama were forcibly stopped by these messengers of Viṣṇu with these very words: "Release him! Those messengers of Yama then reported all of this sin of his, Ajāmila's, to him.
"O wise ones! How can there be punishment even when an expiation has been performed?
Is expiation not known to those such as you?"—thus did Your men speak, O Lord! (6)

"Let them be so! Immediately thereafter, the messengers of Viṣṇu spoke this reply to the soldiers of Yama: "O learned ones! Let the sins spoken of by you truly belong to him; however, even when atonement and expiation have been performed, how can there be punishment? For he has indeed performed the expiation consisting of the chanting of Hari’s name. Is it not known to those like you—the servants of Dharmarāja—what kind of atonement this is? || 6 ||

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to say that even for great sins, the mere utterance of [the Lord's] name is the expiation? For if so, there would follow the absurdity of the futility of the expiations prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, which consist of extreme hardships. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Vows and other rites ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti purify sin but do not sever latent impressions (vāsanā).
But service to the Infinite One severs both. Thus, O Lord! Your servants have declared. (7)

Regarding the word "śruti": vows such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others—by the word "others," bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth are included—are expiations that merely purify or cleanse one of sin; they do not, however, cut away the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which are the subtle tendencies (*saṃskāra*) that produce actions of a similar nature. Consequently, one commits sin once again. Thus, because practices like the *cāndrāyaṇa* lack the power to bring about the absolute cessation of sin, they do not constitute primary expiation.
But service to the infinite Hari—such as remembering, chanting, and glorifying Him—cuts through both sin and its latent impressions, uprooting them entirely. (7)
And because this man, being agitated by the fear of death, has uttered the name of Hari, he said: "Therefore, from now on, he does not deserve your punishment"—"O Lord!
By him, even for sins committed over billions of births, atonement has been made;
since, overcome by fear, he took the name of Hari," so spoke Your Majesty’s men. (8)

One might object: "Did he not utter the name of Hari while dying? Rather, he merely called his son by that name. Therefore, there can be no destruction of sin. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Even if men chant the praises of Mukunda without conscious intent, it burns away the flood of their sins; such is its majesty.
O Lord! Your own servants have declared that it is like fire to wood, or like medicine to diseases. (9)

Regarding the phrase "of men": this name of the Blessed One should be uttered with the thought that it always removes the entire multitude of sins. Even if recited with a different intention, the glorification of Mukunda burns away the multitudes of sins; it uproots them just as a spark of fire destroys a heap of cotton balls. One should not question how such power belongs to it, for the greatness of the Name is both heard of and witnessed. Thus he says: "Greatness. Such an immeasurable greatness exists in this Name.

To dispel their doubt, he speaks with an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as): just as fire cast by a child or the like out of ignorance, and medicine consumed out of ignorance [do not produce the intended effect]. || 9 ||
When the messengers of Yama had departed after speaking thus, and the host of your own soldiers had vanished,
that man— practicing the remembrance of you for some time— reached your abode by means of your soldiers.

Thus: When the messengers of Yama had departed after being made to withdraw by those [messengers] who were awakened by these words, and when the host of your own soldiers had vanished and disappeared, that Ajāmila, having stayed for some time at Gaṅgādvāra in a certain temple while practicing remembrance of you, attained a form identical to yours through those very attendants of yours who appeared upon his mastery of meditative absorption (samādhi), and was led to your abode, Vaikuṇṭha, by means of a celestial chariot. || 10 ||

O Lord, Master of Vātālaya, protect me! Fearing that his own servants might report [his negligence], Yama repeatedly instructed his subordinates, saying, "Do not go among those who are devoted to your feet."

"O Lord," [the devotee said]. Then all the servants of Yama reported [the matter] to their master. But Yama, alarmed by the report of his own servants and fearing that the offense of his subordinates might extend to himself, strictly instructed his servants with great insistence, saying: "You must not go among those who are devoted to Your feet; the devotees of the Blessed One must be avoided by you. May You, who possess such affection for Your devotees, protect us. || 11 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first decade (the Ajāmila episode).
Having thus described the grace shown to men by means of the example of Ajāmila, [the author] begins the story of Dakṣa in order to demonstrate the grace of the Lord toward the inhabitants of heaven:
"O Blessed One, even another Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, performed service to You, desiring the expansion of creation."
Then you appeared with eight resplendent arms and granted him a boon, as well as that bride Asiknī.
