Regarding the term *prācetasa*: there were ten sons of Prācīnabarhis known as the Pracetasas; their son was Dakṣa, the Prācetasa. He is distinct from the other Dakṣa who is a son of Brahmā. Having created these progeny by his mind alone, he, desiring their further increase, performed service unto you. And you granted him a boon, namely that from that time forward the creation of progeny would proceed through the law of sexual union (*vyavāya-dharma*). You gave him that daughter of Pañcajana—Asiknī, Vadhū, and Bhārī—as his wife. || 1 ||
O Lord! His ten thousand sons again attained the path of Your teachings through the words of Śrī Nārada;
yet he did not release the curse upon the sage because they did not dwell together in one place.
But the sage, the best of devotees, considered it a mere favor. || 2 ||

Regarding the word "tasya" (of him): Dakṣa had ten thousand sons known as the Haryaśvas, and furthermore, there were a thousand sons known as the Śabalāśvas. All of them, performing austerities for the sake of increasing creation according to their father’s command, attained the path of liberation—your path—through the words of the venerable Nārada, which consisted of instruction on the path of renunciation. Enraged, that Dakṣa cast a curse upon the sage Śrī Nārada, [condemning] his not dwelling in one place and his constant wandering;
however, the Ṛṣi, because of his status as the best of devotees, considered that very curse to be a grace. || 2 ||
Then, from his sixty daughters, he produced floods of lineages;
subsequently, his grandson Viśvarūpa caused Indra to be defeated in battle by means of your hymn of praise.
O Lord! Your majesty is indeed all-conquering. (3)

"By sixty... means: Then, while this Dakṣa was creating lineages—the multitudes of moving and stationary beings—by means of his sixty daughters beginning with Aditi and the others, there was Tvaṣṭṛ, the son of Diti and grandson of Dakṣa. His son was Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. He caused Indra to be defeated in battle—that is, he brought about victory for Indra—who had been armored, that is, rendered protected, by a coat of mail consisting of hymns to You (Nārāyaṇa) in the war between the gods and the asuras. || 3 ||

Now, to introduce the account of the slaying of Vṛtra, he tells the story of a previous birth: "Formerly, it is said, in the land of Śūrasena, there was a king named Citraketu who, through the power of Aṅgiras, desired a son."
Then, having obtained that one son there, he was struck down by the company of rival wives and, rendered helpless, he was deluded by your illusory power.

"Previously," etc. By the power of Aṅgiras, having obtained one son from his eldest wife by consuming the remnants of the sacrifice performed by him, [the father] found that son slain there by the hosts of his co-wives. || 4 ||
Then the compassionate Nārada, together with Aṅgiras, having arrived there, revealed the life of the son;
and by the boy’s words, "Whose son am I?", [the sage removed] his delusion.
Having abandoned [his own duties], he appointed the king to the ritual of worshipping you.

"Regarding the word 'him': having displayed by the power of yoga the living soul of the deceased son together with Aṅgiras, and having thereby caused the king to abandon his delusion through the boy's words, "Whose son am I? || 5 ||"
Then, having obtained both a hymn and a mantra from Nārada,
he indeed performed austerities for the gratification of you in your Śeṣa form and employed Jayanta.
For, having attained the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas within seven nights, he, of unimpeded intellect, took refuge in you.

Regarding the word "stotra" (hymn): Citraketu, performing austerities for the sake of pleasing—that is, winning the grace of—you, Hari, whose body is the serpent Śeṣa and who possesses infinite forms, attained the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas at the end of seven nights; he then [saw] you in the form of Śeṣa. || 6 ||
And he says that you, having appeared in infinite forms and taught the reality of the Self, then vanished:
"To him [the Lord], who was surrounded by hosts of Siddhas offering praise in a form as white as a lotus-stalk and possessing a thousand heads..."
Having appeared not long ago, you were pleased by our hymns of praise;
having bestowed the knowledge of your own true nature and granted us grace, you have now vanished.
Then he too, the crest-jewel of your devotees, with a joyful mind, for a hundred thousand times a hundred thousand years,
will freely cause your multitude of virtues to be sung throughout the worlds by beautiful women.
Free from excessive attachment, he moved with graceful ease.
Thus [it is said]: "Singing of your multitude of virtues and the deeds of Hari to the beautiful women of the Vidyādharas."
Driven by you, he has surely gone to the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa) in a great assembly to dissolve his ultimate attachment; there,
free from fear, he has placed the enemy of Aṅga’s son (Arjuna) upon his lap along with his beloved.
Mocking that Śaṅkara, Umā addressed him thus.

Regarding the word "atyanta" (extreme): he, while mocking the illustrious Śaṅkara, was cursed by Umā, saying, "Go to an asuric womb. I consider it certain that he was impelled and driven by the Lord for the sake of the complete dissolution of attachment in one who is naturally devoid of excessive attachment; otherwise, such an offense against the gods would have been impossible for him. || 9 ||
Free from agitation, having obtained release from the curse without being asked,
he became the Asura Vṛtra and fought the Lord of the Gods;
through his devotion and his explanations of the reality of the Self, he performed wonders in battle.
Having dispelled even the enemy's delusion, he has gone to your state.

"Without agitation": thus, being free from agitation—that is, devoid of fear of the curse—he dispelled the delusion, which is ignorance, even of his enemy Indra by explaining the true nature of the Self; then, slain by that very [Indra's] thunderbolt, he went to your abode, Vaikuṇṭha. This is a marvel, a wonder. In this regard, Viśvarūpa was chosen for the office of priest by the gods who had been defeated by the Asuras due to their disrespect toward their preceptor. However, because he was the son of Diti’s daughter, out of partiality for his mother’s side, he gave a portion of the sacrificial oblation to the Daityas in secret.

Then, having become weary, he cut off Indra's head; thereafter, the story is to be understood as how Vṛtra, who had arisen from the sacrificial pit of Tvaṣṭṛ whose son had been slain by sorcery, was killed by Indra on the field of battle. 10.
Now, he describes how Diti attained welfare through the Lord’s grace, despite her terrible resolve and Indra’s slaughter of the Maruts:
"By serving You, Diti, though intent on slaying Indra, instead obtained those Maruts who were friends of Indra."
Even for one of wicked intent, service rendered to you becomes auspicious; therefore, O Lord of the Wind-dweller, protect me as such! (11)

Regarding the word *tvat*: Diti, intent on slaying Indra, propitiated Kaśyapa and chose a son who would kill Indra. She then conceived a fetus; nevertheless, by serving you and performing the *puṃsavana* rite as instructed by Kaśyapa, she obtained a son who would kill Indra. However, quite the contrary occurred: Indra entered the womb of Diti while she was sleeping at an improper time and cut the seven embryos into seven pieces each, thereby obtaining forty-nine sons, the Maruts, who became friends of Indra.
And thus, even when directed toward one of evil intent, service rendered to you is indeed auspicious, as was the case for Diti and Indra; such [a person] is peerless and without equal. 11 || 22 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third decad, including one additional verse, containing the narrative of Citraketu and the description of the birth of the Maruts.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The sixth chapter:
The varieties of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from prior karma are called *ūtayaḥ*, as declared in the seventh [chapter].
Then, the qualities of Hari are characterized by means of the examples of Prahlāda and his father.

Now, in order to describe the life of Prahlāda, he introduces the enmity toward the Lord and other traits of his father Hiraṇyakaśipu prior to that birth: "O Lord! When Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by You in the form of the preeminent Boar, his innate [son], his fortitude exhausted by grief and anger..."
O Enemy of Mura! It is said that Kaśipu, whose undertaking was gold, spread a trap in the assembly of the enemies of the gods for the sake of your slaughter. || 1 ||

Having performed severe austerities for no long time, he indeed beheld the formidable Creator before him; having obtained a boon that gods, humans, animals, and others shall not perish, he became arrogant and proclaimed this world to be his own domain.
Disregarding you, he seized heaven from Indra, tearing it away as if with a ploughshare.
"Vidhātāram" means the creator; "parikṣundan" means pulverizing or reducing to dust. || 2 ||

To slay you, as well as your enemy— the wind that carries the lotus— whose gaze is directed outward, he entered into your heart with a subtle form. Even there, roaring loudly and searching throughout the ends of the entire universe,
he indeed desisted, thinking out of fear that you had departed, appearing as one who has already achieved victory.

"To slay"—thinking thus, you vanished within the heart of that enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu, who had attained your abode Vaikuṇṭha yet remained outside its vision, being devoid of the eye of knowledge and possessing only the eye of flesh, by means of your subtle form. Then, perceiving you to be afraid, he roared aloud with a lion's roar and turned back from there—in Vaikuṇṭha, at the end of all worlds, throughout the fourteen worlds—boasting of his victory, thinking himself the conqueror.
Then, while still in the womb, a son named Prahlāda was born to that sage who held a vīṇā in his hand; he had already attained the greatness of devotion to you.
Though by birth a Daitya, even as a child he attained a love for you and became the supreme example, O Giver of Boons, for all your devotees.

Regarding the word "tataḥ": When Hiraṇyakaśipu had gone to Mount Mandara to perform austerities, the gods, having conquered the asuras, began to take away Prahlāda’s mother, Kayādhu, who was pregnant; however, upon hearing the words of Nārada, they released her and returned. The celestial sage, for her sake, instructed her in the paths of devotion and knowledge concerning Prahlāda. Therefore, even though he was but a child, he possessed *rati*—devotion characterized by love—for You, the Lord. || 4 ||
Seeing that his own son preferred service at your feet to the laughter of the enemies of the gods, that evil-minded one had him instructed by his teachers for a long time; yet,
rejecting as "firm" all that was spoken by his gurus because it did not lead to his desired end, he flourished solely through devotion to your feet.

Regarding the phrase "of the enemies of the gods" (*surārīṇām*): [He grew] by means of the teachers, Śukra’s two sons, Śaṇḍa and Marka. The means for the three goals of life (*trivarga*) taught by the teachers—such as economics (*vārtā*) and statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*)—because they rely on dualistic vision (*bhedadṛṣṭi*), lead inevitably and certainly to this and that misfortune, namely to the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) through the bondage of the body. Thus, rejecting everything other than devotion to You, he grew solely through devotion to Your feet. The meaning is that as his physical body grew, his devotion also increased accordingly. || 5 ||

When his son asked, "What is the best among those things studied?", and the son replied that it was devotion to you, he, with a troubled mind, became angry with his teachers and spoke thus to his natural intelligence: [The verse continues: "O innate intellect, having become angry with my teachers, you have spoken this; I shall now punish you, for you have brought me to such a state. [The verse continues: "Having been rebuked by him, she, the daughter of the mountain, fell at his feet and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: 'O Lord of the world, do not speak thus; this is the nature of all embodied beings. [The verse continues: "Then, having heard her words, the Lord of the world, the supreme master of yoga, spoke again to his son: 'O son, I am pleased with you; choose a boon from me, whatever you desire. [The verse continues: "Then the son, having obtained the grace of his father, chose as his boon the knowledge of the supreme reality; and having received that knowledge, he, with a tranquil mind, attained the state of liberation while still living. [The verse continues: "Thus, O King, the power of devotion to you is described as the most excellent among all spiritual practices; therefore, with a steady mind, one should always practice devotion to you, the supreme lord of the universe. [The verse continues: "By reciting this account of the son's attainment, one becomes liberated from all sins; therefore, O King, one should always listen to or recite this narrative, which bestows the fruit of liberation. [The verse continues: "Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, describing the attainment of liberation by the son, in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, within the section concerning the greatness of Śiva."
He devised means for his destruction while you were seeking refuge at your feet.

Regarding the phrase "among those studied": once, when his father asked his son Prahlāda, "Among all that you have studied, what is the best? and when Prahlāda declared that devotion to You was the most excellent, [Hiraṇyakaśipu], whose fortitude was agitated and shaken because he realized from the mouth of his preceptor that this boy’s intellect was innate, devised means for his destruction. || 6 ||

He describes the means of his slaughter: "O Supreme Self! O All-pervading Lord! Though he was pierced by spears, violently crushed by the hosts of world-elephants, bitten by great serpents, deprived of food by the demon of starvation, and even cast down from the king of mountains—alas!"
Because he had entrusted his very self to you, he did not experience any suffering whatsoever.
"He" refers to one whose mind (ātman) has been placed in You, the Supreme Self; or else, "ātman" means the individual soul (jīva), in the sense that it has become Brahman. || 7 ||
Then, overcome by suspicion, his father— who was exceedingly wicked—
bound him in that house with Varuṇa-nooses at the command of the preceptor;
and in the presence of the preceptor, he [the son] in turn bound the Daitya youths who were his followers.
He also taught you the supreme reality and knowledge regarding devotion to Him.

"Then," it is said: in that house—the house of his guru—that Grhāda instructed his followers and friends in the supreme realization, which is the knowledge of Brahman, concerning the true nature, the cause, and the fruit of devotion to you. || 8 ||
Hearing the entire collection of verses devoted to your praise, his father, blinded by rage, said to him: "You wretch of a family! Who is your strength?
He replied: "My strength is Vaikuṇṭha; and he is also the strength of you and of all the worlds."
This steadfast one has swallowed the entire triple world as being nothing but himself.

"O father! [Prahlāda said. "O wretch of a family! O you who transgress your own lineage! Who is your strength in defying my command? Thus the father spoke and asked. [The son replied: "Viṣṇu, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, is my strength—not only mine, but yours as well; in the conquest of the three worlds, Viṣṇu alone is the strength for the worlds and for those who dwell within them. Moreover, that Viṣṇu is the entire triple-world; there is nothing whatsoever that exists apart from him. Thus Prahlāda declared, speaking clearly. He was steadfast, fearless, and wise. (9)
Immediately after that, he describes the activity of Hiraṇyakaśipu: "O! Where is he? Where is he? Hari, the soul of the entire world!
Thus did the son of Diti cry out, brandishing his sword and striking the pillar.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu! O merciful-souled one! O Soul of the Universe! O dweller in the city of the Wind (Purīṣottama)! I am not able to speak further suddenly; have mercy on me! || 10 ||

"Where is Hari, whose very self and essential nature is this entire universe? Thus, repeatedly uttering these words with a sense of their impossibility and an onset of anger, he shattered—that is, struck—a pillar. Therefore, after the breaking of the pillar, I am not able to speak suddenly of what happened there. O You whose soul is endowed with compassion! O Compassionate One! O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees! O Soul of the Universe! O You for whom the reality of being the universal self is manifest! O Viṣṇu! O You whose nature is to pervade the world! O Dweller in the City of Wind (Pavana-pura)! Be gracious to me; bring me happiness. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth decade, describing the manifestation of Nṛsiṃha in the life of Prahlāda.
As Hiraṇyakaśipu struck against the pillar, your terrible roar arose, pulverizing his ears and filling the hollow interior of the cosmic egg as it reeled;
indeed, hearing that sound—which had never before been heard even in the heart of the king of the Daityas—[the world trembled].
A certain trembling fell upon him; even the lotus-born Brahmā was shaken from his station in the world. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *stambha*: thus, immediately after the breaking of the pillar, a terrible roar—a lion’s cry—emanated from you. He describes its very terror: "of one who strikes down and destroys. The hollow interior of the cosmic egg (*jagadaṇḍa-kuṇḍa*) was whirled about, and all moving and non-moving beings within the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa were thrown into confusion. Having heard that sound, never before heard at any time, a certain trembling of indefinable form fell upon the heart of the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Moreover, even the Lotus-born Brahmā, having departed from the world of truth (Satyaloka), became bewildered, thinking, "What is this untimely dissolution of the aeon? || 1 ||

O Lord! While the Daitya, filled with great fury, cast his eyes in all directions, your body—which had arisen from the pillar and was neither of the form of a beast nor of human shape—appeared before him.
As the Asura’s mind became utterly bewildered, wondering, "What is this? What is this terrifying marvel? [the Lord spoke].
With your body expanding as your fierce white hair bristled, you yawned. || 2 ||

Regarding the word *daitya*: when the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu had cast his gaze—that is, when his eyes were directed everywhere—and having seen that body which was neither of the form of a deer nor of the form of a human, but rather the form of Narasiṃha, his mind became utterly bewildered, wondering, "What is this? What is this terrifying and wonderful thing? at that moment, you, whose body (*varṣma*) and true nature (*svarūpa*) were manifesting with quivering, bristling, and white-tufted hair, yawned wide; you appeared with your form fully expanded and towering. || 2 ||
He describes that very form:
"Obeisance to this body of yours, which has the color of molten gold, whose eyes are rolling and extremely harsh, and whose garment is tucked into the quivering mane and tufts of hair;
it is formidable with a pair of great fangs visible as the fierce tongue leaps out from a mouth wide open like a vast cavern! (3)

"Taptā" and so forth: [He saw the demon] whose eyes were rolling, whirling, and extremely parched, resembling molten gold—that is, like liquid gold in a state of fusion; whose mane and tufts of hair caused the sky to tremble and be covered by the tips of his bristling neck-hair as they moved; whose gaping mouth was wide open, resembling a vast cavern and pervading the space; and which appeared exceedingly great as his large tongue, fierce as a sword, leaped and darted outward.
May this form of yours, rendered most formidable and utterly terrifying by the pair of tusks, be victorious and shine forth in its supreme excellence. (3)

I bow to that Nārasiṃha form of yours, whose jaw is terrifying with its rising folds of skin, whose neck is short yet exceedingly thick, whose massive arms are formidable with the cruel rays of nails protruding from their hundreds, and which rivals the dense thundering of clouds as it rushes forth to leap into the sky.

"I bow to that Nārasiṃha form of yours," [he says]. Of what kind? One in which the regions of the jaws are terrifying due to the folds of skin (*valibhaṅga*) rising higher and higher during the expansion of the loud *aṭṭahāsa* laughter; one in which the neck is short, most massive, and exceedingly thick; one that is intensely formidable from afar due to the cruel rays of the nails emerging from a hundred stout arms;
and one that has routed the multitude of enemies with lion-roars as terrifying as the rumbling of water-laden clouds. || 4 ||
"Surely this is Viṣṇu; I shall slay him!"—thinking thus, you seized with your two broad arms that lord of the Daityas as he rushed forward, terrifying with his whirling mace.
Then the hero, having escaped, underwent various labors while grasping his sword and shield.
Revealing [himself], he flew up once more toward you, who were intent on devouring the world—oh!

"Surely"—thinking "This is surely Viṣṇu himself wearing a deceptive guise; I shall slay this killer of my brother," and having thus resolved—he seized you. Then, after the hero who considered himself a hero had slipped from his grasp, [the other] displayed and manifested various specialized skills in the paths of athletic exercise (*vyāyāma*), consisting of diverse movements to the right and left; he then rushed upon and encountered you, who were intent on devouring the world, capable of swallowing the entire universe. || 5 ||
Again seizing the wandering, lowest of the sons of Diti by his two arms with speed,
he threw him down at the door upon his pair of thighs; then, tearing out his claws into the region of the chest,
he pierced it so that blood flowed in abundance from within the belly, creating a festive spectacle.
Drinking again and again, he let out a lion’s roar that brought about the destruction of many worlds.

"Roaming about"—because he could not be slain either inside or outside, at the gate; because he could not be slain on water or on land; and because he could not be slain with weapons even after throwing that lowest of Daityas down upon your pair of thighs—[you] tore him apart, piercing him by uprooting your claws and driving them into the region of his chest. From the openings of the vessels within the interior of his chest, blood-water flowed in a continuous stream. Thus, as if in a state of great celebration, you let out many lion-roars capable of destroying the world and splitting the shell of the cosmic egg. || 6 ||
Having swiftly abandoned that slain [demon], while you were leaping up onto his body— now raised high, drenched by waves of blood— and devouring the entire host of Daityas,
the earth spun about, the multitude of oceans trembled, and the mass of mountains shook violently.
Alas, the world of moving and non-moving beings, with its birds soaring upward, has fallen into a most wretched state.

Regarding the word *tyaktvā* (having abandoned): while you—your body drenched and elevated by the surging waves of blood, your form smeared with the flow of gore—were devouring and consuming that slain [demon] and the entire host of Daityas who followed him, the world of moving and unmoving beings entered a state of distress, its stable positions unsettled. He describes that very state: "In which the earth was reeling; in which the multitude of oceans trembled; in which the mass of great mountain ranges became like play-balls as they were tossed about;
and in which the hosts of stars were flung upward like whorls of hair by the leaping celestial chariots. (7)

No one in the world was able to approach you, whose body was terrifying with flesh and fat, who wore a garland of dreadful entrails, who stood in the midst of the assembly with a blazing spear, and whose heavy, unbearable roar was irresistible; the cowards remained far away.
All of them, headed by Śarva, Viriñca, and Vāsava, each praised him individually.

"At that very time" means: at that moment alone, no one was able to approach you as you sat in the midst of the assembly—no one, not even Brahmā. The reasons for this are: [you were one] whose body was formidable with flesh and fat; and therefore, everyone individually praised and extolled you. || 8 ||
Once again, by the command of Brahmā, as the fearless Prahlāda bowed at his feet while he was still a child, you— overwhelmed by a burden of compassion—
placed your hand upon his head to pacify him; and as he sang hymns of praise, though his mind was free from desire, you granted him a boon and bestowed grace upon the world.

"Furthermore": Although you were praised once more by Brahmā and the other gods, while Prahlāda remained in his unimpaired state of devotion and was bowing at your feet, you—being pacified and having abandoned your anger through affection for him—placed your hand upon his head. Even though he had no desire for it, you granted him the boon of sovereignty over the Daityas, which takes the form of favoring the world; thus, even in your indifference, you acted yourself.
[An objection: "Is Hari indeed of such a cruel nature? [The author replies: "No; it is just as when a river enacts a display of the Furious Sentiment (raudra-rasa). Thus he says:
"O All-pervasive Lord, who thus displays the gestures of the Furious Sentiment; O You whose entire majesty is clearly sung in the Upanishads known as the Śvetāśvatara; O You of utterly pure form!
Who else, alas, could ever transgress You, who are the ultimate answer to all such [objections]?"
O beloved of Prahlāda! O Lord of the City of the Maruts! Protect me from all disease! ||10||

"Thus it is. Here, the authority is cited as the *Śrītāpanīya*. O You whose form and essential nature (*ākṛti-svarūpa*) are such as described in the *Śrītāpanīyopaniṣad*—possessing every greatness, and consisting of absolute purity, existence, consciousness, and bliss—who else could transgress You? That is to say, who other than Your own attendants, who are of the same nature as Yourself, would act against Your will? O Beloved of Prahlāda! O Compassionate One toward devotees! || 10 ||20||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth decade, the description of the life of Prahlāda.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The seventh section of the book,
known as the Manvantara, describes the True Dharma awakened by Manu and others; it is characterized by that which is designated in the eighth [section], augmented by the divine play of Hari.

Now, wishing to demonstrate by means of the example of Gajendra that fixing the mind upon Śrī Hari during times of distress constitutes the very essence of dharma, he relates the story of this king’s previous birth in two verses:
Indraghuma, the sovereign of the Pāṇḍya realm, whose soul was devoted to you, once on Mount Candana—
his intellect absorbed in your service— did not even notice Agastya when the sage arrived desiring hospitality.
Regarding the word "Indra": the Pāṇḍya region is the southern part of the landmass of Bhārata. || 1 ||
"Born from a jar, you who have accumulated a burden of anger and are obstinate in nature—become an elephant!
Having thus cursed him, he departed; and he too attained the state of a lordly elephant, blessed by the manifestation of his memory of his former life.

"Born from a jar" (kumbhodbhūta) means having become an elephant, that is, the state of an elephant. "From the inner self" (pratyak) means turned back toward the self. "By the manifestation of your remembrance"—that is, by the appearance of [the memory] practiced in previous births—it is "blessed," meaning it bestows the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha). || 2 ||

Sporting on Mount Trikūṭa, which lies in the midst of the ocean of milk, this leader of the herd, together with his female companions, surpassed all other creatures by his power; for where can those devoted to you not attain excellence? || 3 ||

Regarding the word "dugdha" (milk): in which births or among what beings do Your devotees not attain excellence? Since even in the state of being an elephant, [Your power] surpassed all living creatures. || 3 ||
By virtue of his own stability and the power of his divine body, he, at one time feeling no fatigue,
took delight with his herds in a lake on the edge of a mountain, though exhausted by the heat, being impelled by you.

"By his own"—meaning by his own unique stability and strength—[he will endure] the afflictions and pains produced by other beings who possess superior power. "Exhausted by the heat of summer" means worn out by the warmth arising during the hot season. On a mountain slope, in a lake located in the garden named Ṛtuman on the mid-slope of the mountain, he shall be led to his own place, impelled by the Lord. || 4 ||

Huhu, who had become a crocodile in those waters due to the curse of Devala, seized that elephant by its hindquarters; for you are the dispeller of the fatigue of your own people, acting for their peace.

"Hūhū. At that very time, the Gandharva named Hūhū had also become a crocodile, having attained the state of a crocodile due to the curse of the sage Devala. One might ask: "If Gajendra is a devotee, how can he be overcome by a crocodile? This should not be doubted; thus it is said: "For the sake of peace. For indeed, for the sake of peace—that is, for the sake of detachment from sense objects—you become a source of affliction to your own devotees when they are weary. || 5 ||
Due to the power of service to you, he fought for a thousand years, difficult to restrain;
when the time had come, you made that heroic elephant, overcome by the Nartaka [weapon], attain success through one-pointed concentration on your feet.

"Tvaditi": When the time has arrived and [the practice] has been commenced and brought to completion, for the sake of attaining the perfection of that *samādhi* which consists of one-pointed concentration (*aikāgrya*) upon Your feet; or else, for the sake of attaining liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the fruit of the perfection of that one-pointed concentration on Your feet practiced in previous births. || 6 ||

With his devotion made manifest through his suffering and worshipping with lotuses tossed up by his trunk, he recited that most excellent hymn of praise—the one previously practiced and centered on the non-dual Self—to the Supreme Soul: "O Supreme Self! (7)

"Ārti" means: one for whom knowledge and devotion—practiced in a previous birth—are manifested through the affliction (*ārtyā*) of pain caused by being seized by a crocodile; [he offers this] directed toward the attributeless Self, which has the non-dual Brahman as its object. || 7 ||

Having heard this entire hymn situated in the attributeless (Nirguṇa), which was not offered by Brahmā, Śiva, and the others with the thought "I am not [worthy]," you, the Soul of All, appeared before us mounted upon Garuḍa through the force of your abundant compassion. 8.

Having heard this: [the Lord thought,] "I am not praised by this [hymn], since it is a hymn dedicated to Brahman, for Brahmā, Īśa, and the others—who possess the conceits 'I am Brahman' and 'I am Īśa'—have not yet arrived. While they had not come, You appeared, having been seen before them. Now, one might object that Viṣṇu also possesses the conceit "I am Viṣṇu"; to this He says: "The Self of All. You are the Self and the inner controller even of Brahmā and the others. (8)
Now, He describes the liberation of Gajendra:
"Having seized that lordly elephant with Your lotus-hand, You tore apart the chief of crocodiles with Your discus;
when this Gandharva was freed from his curse, that elephant, having attained a form identical to Yours, shone forth brilliantly. (9)
He speaks this proclamation of the fruit, blessed by the Blessed One:
"Whoever should sing this account of the events concerning you and me at dawn, he shall attain the highest welfare.
Having said this to him, you went with him to the abode of Viṣṇu; O Lord of the wind-abode, protect us! 10.

"Etad iti": "Prage" means in the morning. Having spoken thus—meaning, having blessed them by saying that the deed performed, which consisted of the liberation of the lordly elephant (the story of Hari's life), would lead to their supreme welfare, making them fit for the attainment of liberation—he departed for his abode, Vaikuṇṭha. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth decade, the description of the liberation of Gajendra.

Now, by means of the illustration of the ocean, this dharma is revealed: that when prosperity exists, one should bestow it along with oneself upon supplicants. For he (the Ocean) indeed bestowed all his wealth upon the gods and demons who were his supplicants by means of churning himself. To relate the story of the churning of the ocean and the descent of the Lord that was instrumental to it, [the author] first describes, in two verses, the loss of the gods' sovereignty caused by their own curses: The gods, having attained their respective positions through the power of penance, became arrogant and began to disregard the sages. Then, by the curse of the sages, their divine splendor vanished. They were deprived of their celestial forms and fell from their high status. Their bodies became like those of mortals, and they were overcome by hunger and thirst. Thus, due to their own pride, they lost their divine powers. [Note: The provided source text for the final two verses is not fully transcribed in the prompt; however, based on the context and the preceding summary, the translation reflects the standard narrative of the *Daśakumāracarita* regarding the gods' fall.]

Durvāsas, having personally presented that divine garland from the celestial women to Śakra, cursed him there once again as he was being trampled by the lord of serpents: "What patience can there be for those born from the portions of deities other than you?"

Regarding the verse beginning with "Durvāsā": Durvāsas took from the hand of a celestial nymph a divine garland as a gift and, mounting Airāvata, went to Śakra. Having offered it there, he cursed the gods, saying, "May you be bereft of prosperity. As for other deities such as Śrī, Śaṅkara, and so forth—Durvāsas being born from a portion of Śaṅkara—they were not included. || 1 ||

Then, when the lord of gods was afflicted by a curse that brought about a manifest old age, and when even the gods were defeated by the asuras and shorn of their luster, all the deities, having approached the lotus-born Brahmā, reached you, O source of liberation! together with Śarva.
"By the curse," etc. O you who have Nirvāṇa as your source! O you who are the locus for the attainment of liberation! || 2 ||

O Giver of Boons! At that time, Your greatness was praised for a long duration by Brahmā and the other gods; then, manifesting before them with Your supreme splendor, You commanded: "O gods, having made peace with the clans of the sons of Diti, churn the nectar! || 3 ||

Or rather, the reading is *‘niḥśrīko bhava tvam’*. The root *math* (in the sense of churning) belongs to the *bhūvādi* class. When the host of gods had formed an alliance with the demons, you, out of pride, were leading Mount Mandara as the churning-stick;
when that [mountain] fell, you immediately placed it in the ocean of milk, carrying it like a jujube fruit upon the king of birds.

Regarding the word "sandhānam": it refers to the churning-staff (*manthāna*), the instrument for churning, used against the hosts of gods and demons. When this Mandara mountain—having fallen after being dropped from the hands of Śakra, Vairocana, and others who were exhausted—fell down, you, O Lord of Birds, Garuḍa, lifted it up with a single hand, placed it [upon your shoulder], and carried it away. || 4 ||
Then, having swiftly placed Vāsuki as the rope upon the waters where all the collections of seeds had been deposited,
when the demons of Mura began the process of churning, you, under a pretext, placed those enemies of the gods within the mouth of the serpent.

"Having placed," [so it is said]. Or rather, Vāsuki was the garment and the rope. In which [rope] were all the networks of seeds—that is, the multitudes of creepers, grasses, and medicinal herbs—deposited and cast down. Regarding the word "under the pretext": Hari, along with the gods, loudly declaring that the serpent’s tail was inauspicious, first seized the forepart of the body. Then, when the enemies of Mura (the gods) became silent, saying, "We Asuras are water-dwellers; we will not hold the tail," [Vāsuki], out of great respect for them, [cast] the poison about to emerge from the mouth of the serpent into the fierce [poison] within the serpent's mouth. || 5 ||
At that time, when the ocean of milk had become agitated with its waters swelling like a churned belly and was sinking under the weight of its excessive burden,
while the gods were most deeply distressed, you— desiring their welfare and seeking to preserve their lives— assumed the form of a tortoise with a hard shell.

"Kṣubdha" means: when Mount Mandara was agitated—that is, whirled around—and had sunk into the Ocean of Milk, you assumed the body of a tortoise (kamaṭhatanu), that is, the form of a turtle; you brought this about (praṇeṣīḥ). || 6 ||
O Viṣṇu! With your body, which was as firm as a diamond, measured a hundred thousand yojanas in width, and entered into the depths of the ocean, you lifted up the submerged Lord of Mountains.
"O Vajra! [he said]; with a body whose back was far more firm than a diamond, you raised it up—you made it emerge. || 7 ||
When that lord of mountains had suddenly submerged, everyone here rejoiced with intense delight;
yet, having entered even the two groups [of gods and asuras], you increased their strength while pacifying the agitation of the king of serpents.

"O Unmana! Having entered the two groups—the hosts of gods and the hosts of asuras—in whichever form was appropriate, and having also entered the king of serpents in a subtle form, you pacified their helplessness and suffering, and made them endowed with strength and valor. (8)

O Unswerving One, Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods, having become utterly bewildered with joy, praised You as You placed one very steady lotus-hand upon the king of mountains, which was being lifted up by the force of Your unrestrained whirling, while they themselves rained down showers of flowers.

"Uddāmeti": By means of an "uddāma"—that is, an excessive speed of rotation—you rose up and flew upward; [I praise] you, by whom a single, most steady lotus-hand was placed and fixed upon the king of mountains. In the "abhrānta" (unswerving) path of the clouds, the "udbhrāntas" (agitated ones)—those overwhelmed with joy—praised and lauded you. || 9 ||
When the host of Daityas was scorched by the wind from the mouths of serpents, and the assembly of the thirty gods was likewise somewhat distressed, it is said,
O Lord, that out of compassion you caused the clouds to rain upon the hosts of immortals, but not upon the multitudes of Daityas.
Regarding the phrase "daityaugha": *vārivāhāḥ* means clouds. || 10 ||

O Lord of Pavanapura! Though that ocean—filled with vast circles of timi and makara fish—was churned for a long time and remained unchanged, you alone shone forth, having seized the king of serpents with your two hands; protect me from disease.

Regarding the word *udbhrāmyat*: it refers to that [ocean] in which there is a multitude (*cakravāla*), a mass, of many whales (*timi*) and crocodiles (*nakra*), as well as leaping (*udbhrāmyatām*), flying up [fish]. In that [ocean]. || 11 ||

Thus ends the twenty-seventh decad, including the [introductory] verse, describing the churning performed by the Blessed Lord when the gods and asuras were powerless during the churning of the nectar.
From the ocean, the Kālakūṭa poison, flickering with flames, emerged before them, causing them great terror.
Overwhelmed by the joy of hearing the hymns of praise from the immortals, Giriśa drank that [nectar] for the sake of your welfare. || 1 ||
‘Garalam iti’: it was vomited out—that is, it was disgorged. Then, being dependent upon and subject to the hymns of praise offered by the gods regarding Giriśa, he drank that poison. || 1 ||
O Lord of the Three Abodes! While the gods and asuras were contending with one another, Surabhi was born; she bestowed her threefold nature upon the sages.
Then, the jewel of cows became established among humans, and the jewels of elephants, horses, and apsarases appeared among the gods.

Regarding the phrase "vimathatsu" (while they were being oppressed): the jewel among horses is Uccaiḥśravas; the jewel among elephants is Airāvata; and the celestial tree is the Kalpavṛkṣa. You placed these [jewels] among the gods and bestowed them upon them. || 2 ||
O Lord of the World! At that time, the goddess Kamalā became devoted to you and was most enchanting;
beholding her stainless beauty, the entire restless world was filled with longing for her. (3)
Regarding the word "jagat": she for whom you are the supreme (para) or primary (pradhāna) is "bhavatparā. || 3 ||
At that very moment, when you had set your heart upon the Goddess, the Lord of the Thirty-three offered her a jeweled pedestal;
then the sages consecrated her with all the materials required for the coronation, accompanied by Vedic hymns.

"Upon you"—meaning, she by whom the heart was given and surrendered to you; to her, whose heart had been thus offered, the sages immediately performed the consecration with all the requisite materials for the rite—such as herbs, jars, and purificatory grasses—brought forth from the rivers, the earth, and other sources, while chanting Vedic hymns and mantras.

(4) The gods and others adorned her, whose creeper-like limbs were already graced by the sidelong glances of Cupid following the consecration water, with jeweled earrings, yellow garments, necklaces, and other ornaments. (5)

Regarding the word *abhiṣeka*: she whose creeper-like limbs were adorned by those very glances of yours which have the nature of falling immediately upon the descent of the consecration water; her [the other goddesses], such as the immortals (*amarāḥ*), decorated and embellished with foremost items such as jeweled earrings, yellow garments, and necklaces. (5) Bearing a marriage garland resonant with the humming of bees, moving slowly due to the weight of her jar-like breasts, and possessing anklets charming with the tinkling of her footsteps, she approached you with an expression of bashful grace. (6)
"Varaṇā" means the *varaṇasraj*, the garland for the self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*). || 6 ||
Having perceived that even all the gods, such as Giriśa and Ṣaḍahni, though possessed of virtues, are not free from even a trace of defect,
this divine garland has been placed by her upon you alone at all times and in every circumstance.

"O Giriśa!"—having observed and reflected upon those possessed by the six defects such as desire and anger, who are not free from even a trace of blemish, this divine garland has been placed by Śrī upon your shoulder, O you who are ever delightful with all virtues free from defect. (7)
The root *bhūṣ* (in the sense of "to adorn") belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
With your chest, you swiftly honored this mother of the worlds, who is possessed of exclusive devotion;
by the beauty of her glance shining upon your breast, the entire universe was fully nourished. (8)

Regarding the word *urase* (on the chest): You indeed protected her with your chest; you made her dwell upon your own breast. She whose affection (*bhāva*)—that is, her love—is directed toward no other is *ananyabhāvā*. By the showering of the beauty of the glances of her who sports upon your chest—the splendor of her compassionate side-long looks—the entire universe became fully nourished, enriched with every prosperity. || 8 ||
Then he says that the goddess Vāruṇī appeared:
"At that time, Vāruṇī indeed arrived, intoxicating and possessed of most delusive confusion;
she gave the path of darkness to the great Asuras through her excessive honor. (9)
"Atīti" refers to Vāruṇī, who is the path—that is, the cause—of *tamas*, which is ignorance. || 9 ||
Now he describes the incarnation of Dhanvantari:
"O Lord of the Abode of Maruta! At that time, you indeed arose from the ocean as Dhanvantari, beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, carrying the nectar in both hands; O remover of all suffering! (10)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth decade, the Description of the Churning for the Nectar.
While the Daityas were seizing the nectar from your rising hand, you consoled those gods who were left without refuge.
O Lord! You vanished instantly; by Your power, the sons of Diti became embroiled in quarrels with their own rising kinsmen. || 1 ||

"Arise! means arising or manifesting. "The shelterless" means those who have no other refuge. "From you"—from your power, capacity, or *māyā*—arises that which belongs to them whose internal strife consists of mutual quarrels among their own followers. (1)
At that time, you attained a dark-complexioned body, both in luster and in age, curved by the high circles of her breasts; indeed,
all of you abandoned your quarrel over the jar of nectar.
Agitated by thirst, they went toward the jar-like breasts of your chest.

"Śyāmām" means dark-complexioned; by virtue of her age, she is "śyāmā," standing in the midst of youth. She is "bhaṅgurā," meaning bent or modest. [She rests] upon the jar-like breasts of your chest, which are sweeter even than nectar. (2)

"Who are you, O fawn-eyed one? Distribute this nectar!"—to these Daityas who were thus entreating her, overcome by the power of rising passion, she replied, "How can you trust me, O demons? I am an unchaste woman," yet she lowered herself before those who trusted her completely. (3)

"O Daityas! I am a *kulaṭā*, an unchaste woman; how can you place your trust in me? Though she spoke thus, she caused them—who were already deeply trusting her due to her affectionate smiles and side-long glances at that time—to bow down [in submission]. (3)
As they joyfully offered jars of nectar to these [groups], she said,
"Forgive my misdeed," while arranging the gods and demons into separate rows.
Intoxicated by her playful and graceful movements, they drank that nectar. || 4 ||

"Out of joy," he says: "Endure whatever misdeed I may commit. She by whom the gods and demons were divided into two groups according to their seating rows—that [goddess], in order to deceive the demons, through her playful charm directed toward them, through her graceful movements, and by walking very close to them, gave [the nectar] fully to the gods alone. The meaning is that she gave that nectar which removes old age and death. || 4 ||
While those asuras remained silent, thinking, "She is affectionately attached to us," you, having completed the nectar for the gods,
assumed your own form, being subject to the will of your devoted followers.
You struck down Svarbhānu, who had half-drunk the nectar. || 5 ||

"Among us"—that is, among the Asuras—she is devoted to us; oh, what fortune! May she not deceive us. Be silent, remain quiet. You struck down Svarbhānu, who was concealed by a divine disguise, and severed his head with your discus. || 5 ||
When you had departed after giving to others the fruit worthy of being taken as nectar, the gods indeed seized it;
then, while the host of gods was fainting in the terrible battle, deluded by the magic of the Daitya Bali, you manifested here.
"O Vṛtra, the fruit of carrying away the nectar from you has resulted in wasted effort for the sake of others—the Daityas.
Those Daityas seized it by force and engaged in a quarrel with the gods. (6)
You have slain Kālanemi and those headed by Māli; Śakra slew Bala, Jambha, and Vatra along with Pāka; and Namuci was cut down when his slaughter was difficult whether he were dry or wet.
With foam and the words of Nārada, he restrained that battle.

"Regarding 'you': Namuci was difficult to slay with either dry or wet means; when his head had been severed by foam—which partakes of both natures—by the word of Nārada sent by Brahmā, you brought the battle to an end. (7)
O Maheśa, having heard of the form you assumed to enchant the Danujas, the Lord, filled with curiosity to behold it,
went to your abode together with the Bhūtas and Girijā.
Having praised him, he spoke his desire, and then you vanished from sight.
"O woman!"—having heard that their station was Vaikuṇṭha, where the form of a woman (yoṣāvapuḥ) had been assumed, and having seen the desired female form, then, after that prayer—8.

O enemy of the bodiless one (Kāmadeva)! Upon seeing you at the boundary of the grove—lovely and charming, with eyes flickering in the playful sport of striking a ball, and your garment slipping away—he embraced you with the force of his mind-born passion. 9.

"In the grove": with her garments slipping and her silk robe carried away by the wind, although he was the enemy of the bodiless god (Śiva), nevertheless, driven by the impulse of the mind-born one (Kāma), he embraced you. 9.
Once again, the Lord, having pursued her as she fled,
his supreme realization of ultimate truth blossoming through the discharge of his virility,
spoke of your greatness to the Goddess, being honored by you.
O Lord of the abode of the wind, you are indeed such as that! || 10 ||
"Furthermore," [he said]. Having pursued her as she was fleeing and running away, by means of the emission of his virile seed, he—being honored by you—spoke of your greatness to the Goddess. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth decade, which describes the manner in which the gods obtained the nectar and the loss of Śiva’s composure upon seeing Mohinī.

Now, intending to reveal the story of Mahābali as an illustration of the dharma of fulfilling one's promises and other such matters, as well as the relevant deeds of the Lord’s incarnations, [the author] first speaks of the victory over Bali:
Although the high-souled Bali was struck down by Śakra in battle, he was restored to life by Śukra; his vital energy increased through the sacrifice,
and being full of prowess, he [protected] the three worlds where the gods had cowered in fear.
He brought it under his control, remaining fearless before the face of your discus. || 1 ||

"By Śakra": although struck by Śakra, his body was restored to life by Śukra through the lore known as *Mṛtasañjīvinī*. His heat—that is, his power—was increased by the sacrifice named *Viśvajit*. In whom the gods were hidden during battle out of fear; that Bali was unafraid of the Sudarśana discus from its mouth, because he belonged to the lineage of Prahlāda. || 1 ||
Overwhelmed by the sight of her sons' suffering, Aditi took refuge with her husband Kāśyapa;
for it was he who had prescribed that worship known as the milk-vow.
Filled with devotion for you, she practiced [austerities] for twelve days.
"Putra" means the son's distress; "Indra's" refers to the pain arising from the abduction of his heaven. "Taduditam" means that which was spoken by Kāśyapa. || 2 ||
When her mind was fixed upon you as its ultimate goal, you yourself appeared before her in a dark form with four arms; and to her, who bowed there, you said: "May I become your son in this world."
"You must keep my gaze secret," you said while lamenting, and then you departed.

Regarding the word "tasya": at the conclusion of that milk-vow (*payovrata*), you departed—meaning you vanished—while speaking, saying such things as, "Worship your husband, meditating upon me in this form. || 3 ||
At that time, while you were establishing yourself in asceticism under Kāśyapa,
you were impelled by the Creator and entered the womb of Aditi;
then you manifested your divine Vaiṣṇava form.
On that twelfth day of the lunar fortnight, auspicious through the conjunction with the Śravaṇa asterism, she [approached] you. || 4 ||

"Thou"—[He said this]. Having entered into, that is, become present within, the ascetic power accumulated through the penance related to Kāśyapa, [He appeared] with a manifest divine Vaiṣṇava form, characterized by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; by the crown, tiara, crocodile-shaped earrings, the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, the forest garland, yellow garments, the girdle, anklets, and armlets. || 4 ||

While the host of gods, agitated with joy, rained down showers of flowers upon that holy hermitage and raised a clamor like the roar of the sun, you—praised by your parents with joined palms crying "Victory! Victory!"—at that very moment assumed the form of a most eloquent young brahmin student.
"Meritorious," he said; at that very moment, [he assumed] the form of a young brahmin student. || 5 ||

Meanwhile, O Lord of the City, having been brought forward by the sons of Prajāpati and honored with the girdle of muñja grass, the staff, the deerskin, the rosary of beads, and other regalia, you— having performed the fire-rituals— proceeded to the sacrificial hall for the horse sacrifice that had been prepared.

"Up to that point" means: having been brought forward by the sages headed by Prajāpati—that is, having performed the rite known as *upanayana*—and being honored by them with the girdle of muñja grass and other items, Savitṛ taught him the Gāyatrī. Bṛhaspati gave the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), his father the muñja-girdle, the Earth the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), Soma the staff, Aditi the loincloth, Heaven the umbrella, Brahmā the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the Seven Sages the *darbha* grass, and Sarasvatī the rosary.

Thus, with a body that was exceedingly radiant and beautiful, having performed the fire-rites—that is, having completed the ritual of placing fuel on the sacred fire—you set out for Bali’s sacrificial hall, where the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) had been commenced. || 6 ||
As if first revealing the earth with your foot— its weight already suited to your future greatness— you departed,
holding your parasol as if to ward off the excessive heat of your enemies.
And [he came] to inflict punishment upon the hosts of Dānavas, as if to hold them in check.

"With his body" means: by revealing—that is, manifesting—beforehand the weight appropriate to the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), which possesses future majesty, through the trembling of the earth; for the purpose of suppressing—that is, warding off—the heat of the prowess of others, namely the Daityas; [and] in order to approach them [for the purpose of] punishing them. || 7 ||
When you arrived at the sacrificial hall for the horse-sacrifice on the northern bank of the Narmadā, the gods, their eyes dazzled by your radiance, wondered:
"Is this the sun? Or is it fire? Or perhaps this is Sanatkumāra the yogi?"—thus did they conjecture through the mouths of Śukra and the other sages.
"Tām iti" means "when she had arrived," that is, when she had reached [him]. || 8 ||

The virtuous asura, his limbs covered with horripilation, approached you of beautiful form who had been quickly brought by the Bhṛgus who were overwhelmed by your majesty; having bathed your feet with devotion, he held that water— the most sacred of all holy waters— upon his head.

"Regarding 'was brought': it was brought by Śukra, having been accepted by the Bhṛgus whose splendor had been eclipsed and whose luster diminished by your majesty; it was then taken to Bali. Bali is the Asura. 'Tīrtha after tīrtha' means that which purifies everything. || 9 ||
Whether by virtue of being born in the lineage of Prahlāda or through his faith in the twice-born during sacrifices,
even this son of Diti obtained that very thing which is to be cherished upon the head of Śiva— the water from his feet.
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord! O Abode of the Guru! May You protect me. || 10 ||

Regarding the word *prahlāda*: Whether it was due to his birth in the lineage of Prahlāda, the crest-jewel of devotees; or through sacrifices; or from faith in the twice-born; or from association with the virtuous; or perhaps from all these combined—it is not certain [how it came to pass] that even Bali, the son of Diti, obtained this very act of bearing the water from His feet upon his head. He says "that which... (*yad*) to express that such is its great majesty. || 10 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth decade in the *Vāmana-carita*, describing the hospitality of Mahābali.
Out of affection for beholding the splendor of your form, O Unconquered One, the Daitya, honoring you in every way, spoke while forming his hands in *añjali*.
"O son of a Brahmin, tell me what you desire from me! Whether it be wealth, a wife, a house, or even the entire earth, I shall grant it all. || 1 ||
"By means of affection" means: by looking upon his body and his splendor, and by welcoming words and so forth in every way. "Bhakta" refers to fried food. || 1 ||

Having heard those words of Bali, which were yet unexhausted, you—though filled with compassion—were intent on quelling his arrogance; thus, while praising the lineage of the Daityas, you requested only three steps of land.
When he replied, "I give you everything," who would not have been moved to laughter? || 2 ||

Regarding the word "tām" (that): it refers to that [earth] which proclaims his status as the Lord of the World. O Viśveśvara! When one says and begs, "Give me everything, my entire being," whose laughter would such a statement not provoke? Therefore, you have asked for only three paces of land. || 2 ||
"O fool, why do you beg me, the Lord of All, for three paces of land here?
Choose the entire earth instead!"—thus he spoke to you with pride. Yet, because of that very pride, being unable to fulfill those three paces, he uttered words of reproach.
And he, though unworthy of it, underwent bondage for the sake of profound peace.

"O Lord of All! he cried; thus the arrogant one spoke, saying, "Cover the earth! He states the fruit of his pride with the words, "Since..."—meaning, since he was unworthy of it, being unfit for the insults of imprisonment and casting down. If so, why did the Blessed One bind him? He says, "For the sake of favoring him"—meaning, having thoroughly brought about detachment from sense-objects, so that his mind might be concentrated upon Him. (3) The Blessed One gives the reply:
"O Giver of Boons! When it was said, 'If he is not delighted by the three steps, nor shall he be satisfied even by the worlds,' and when you were desirous of giving the water..."
Indeed, at the instigation of the preceptor of the Daityas who desired to test you, he spoke quite clearly: "Do not give him away; this is Hari! || 4 ||

"By the foot": if he were not delighted, being dissatisfied, he would not be content even with the three worlds (*viṣṭapa*). When [Bali] desired to give the earth preceded by water, Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, spoke—saying "Do not give!"—and forbade him, after first recounting the future treading of the three steps and so forth. Now, one might ask: how could Kāvya (Śukra) act in opposition to the Blessed One? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By your instigation. And for what purpose was that? To this he replies: "Desiring to test [him]."
The meaning is that you, desiring to test Balarāma’s steadfastness in dharma, impelled him by acting as his inner controller (*antaryāmin*). || 4 ||
"If that Blessed One thus entreats me, I, whose desires are fulfilled, shall certainly give [him] as a steadfast [servant]," saying this, the Daitya, though cursed by Kāvya,
[offered himself] to you, for whom his own beloved Vindhyāvalī had offered the water for washing the feet.
He bestowed everything wonderful and marvelous, preceded by water-offerings.

"He begs," [it is said]. Although he had been cursed by Śukra, saying, "May you fall from your sovereignty," Hari, having learned the truth from the words of his preceptor—that this very Hari would seize the entire three worlds and give them to Śakra—offered the whole of the three worlds [to him]. || 5 ||
Without a doubt, as you, the lord of the clan of Diti, were performing that act of total self-surrender,
the sages and the gods released a rain of flowers;
and as all beings beheld this divine form of yours, it grew higher and higher, dwarfing the vessel of the entire universe.
"Without a doubt"—while all the inhabitants of the universe were looking on, that very form of Vāmana grew, making the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍakaṭāha) its limit. || 6 ||
The Lotus-born Brahmā placed the tip of his foot upon your own feet and sprinkled them with water from his water-pot— water that purifies all the worlds;
at this festival, the sky-dwellers danced most exuberantly out of the height of their joy.
Striking the drum, the devoted Jāmbavān roamed through the world. || 7 ||
"From you" means having come from his own abode, that is, from Satyaloka. || 7 ||
Meanwhile, the Daityas, having commenced battle without their lord’s permission, were defeated when they encountered your followers accompanied by the gods;
for this one, who is Time itself, dwells before us, by whose power we were previously conquered.
"What use have you for battles?"—with these words of Bali, they then reached Pātāla.
To the Daitya who was bound by fetters and was being addressed loudly by the Lord of Birds, saying, "Grant me a third step; are you not the Lord of the Universe?",
Prahlāda approached him himself and, honoring him as he spoke thus with unshakable firmness— 'O Blessed One, place your foot upon my head'— praised you.
Regarding the word "pāśaiḥ": the third [syllable] belongs to the third [quarter]. || 9 ||

"O Daitya! Everything has been performed for the sake of severing your pride; you have attained perfection through your merits. May you possess a world in heaven as a conqueror, and later attain the status of Vāsava.
Furthermore, attain union with me. Thus did he favor Bali, who had performed the excellent sacrifice extended by the Brahmins. O Lord of the Wind’s Abode, protect us! 10.
He by whom the excellent sacrifice known as the Rājasūya was caused to be performed and completed by Brahmins after having been undertaken. 10.
Thus ends the thirty-first decade, the description of the deeds of Vāmana.
Now begins the account of the Lord who assumed the form of a fish (*mātsya-vapuḥ*) in order to expound the Vedas and their meaning to Brahmā and Satyavrata—
at the beginning of the unseasonable *kalpa* arising at the end of the sixth interval (*antara*), [ruled] by the great demon Hayagrīva.
When the Vedas had been recovered from the mouth of Brahmā, who was on the verge of sleep, he indeed assumed the form of a fish with the desire to restore them.

"Pureti" means: at the end, that is, at the conclusion of the sixth *manvantara*, the Cākṣuṣa *manvantara*, [the dissolution] arose; for this very reason, during an intermediate dissolution (*avāntarapralaya*) which was like an untimely cosmic cycle (*akāṇḍakalpa*), You desired to create (*aghitsaḥ*), that is, You wished to bring about [creation]. || 1 ||
Then, as Satyavrata, the lord of Dramila, was offering libations in the river water, you appeared to him in the hollow of his cupped hands as a certain small fish of blazing form. || 2 ||
"In truth" means: in the water of the river Kṛtamālā. || 2 ||
Seeing you thrown into the water and looking about in alarm, the sage took you home in a water-vessel; O Lord, in a few days you filled his jar, his well, and his pond.
"Cast forth" means you have pervaded it; "ānaśiṣe" means you have become pervasive. || 3 ||
By the power of yoga and solely by your command, you were led from there to the ocean by the sage;
when questioned by him regarding the ritual of the *kalpa*, you departed saying to him, "Stay for seven days."

"By the sage, the royal seer; by the power of yoga, through the force of his asceticism; by your command, in the form of 'Now cast me, the great fish, into the waters of the ocean'; [and] desirous of seeing the Kalpa, longing to behold the ocean of universal dissolution. || 4 ||
When the day you had foretold arrived, O Lord of Sages, the earth was inundated by torrents of water;
then, tossing upon the boundless waters together with the Seven Seers, he sought refuge in you.
"Attained": in the shoreless ocean of dissolution; "reeling," meaning agitated. || 5 ||
Then they ascended the Earth, who had assumed the form of a boat and was ready to carry out your command;
and as she trembled at their weight, you, the Great One, manifested once more from the ocean.
"Dharām" means: then, [unto] that Earth who had assumed the form of a boat, who was executing your command and was impelled by you; "in them" refers to Satyavrata and the seven sages. || 6 ||
Beholding you in the form of a fish, a hundred thousand yojanas long and possessing exceedingly lofty splendor,
the sages were delighted by your words and fastened the sun to one of your high peaks.
"Having the form of a fish" refers to the *taraṇi*, that is, a boat. || 7 ||
Drawing your boat toward the circle of sages and pointing out the divisions of the entire world,
you were praised by that best of men as you proceeded, imparting supreme knowledge.
"Drawn forth" means for the circle of sages, namely the seven ṛṣis who are devoted to truth. "Supreme knowledge" refers to both the knowledge of the scriptures and the knowledge of Brahman. || 8 ||
At the end of the kalpa, having dispatched the seven sages before you as witnesses, you rushed in anger toward Hayagrīva, while King Satyavrata was being established as the Manu known as Vaivasvata.
He imagines the present one, known as Vaivasvata. || 9 ||

O Lord of the House of the Wind! Having struck down that Daitya whose chest was pierced by Your own lofty horn and having seized the Vedas, You gave them with a joyful heart to Viriñci; may You, the Master, grant me protection. 10.
"His own" means for Viriñci, that is, for Brahmā. || 10 || 71 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second decade, the description of the Fish Incarnation.
Thus [ends] the commentary on the *Nārāyaṇīya-stotra*, titled *Bhaktapriyā*.
The eighth chapter, on the division of the books:
"When the life of Rāma has been described, what is the use of other lives?
Thus, the secondary narratives (anukathā) centered upon him are indicated as the ninth book.
Now he begins the account of Ambarīṣa:
Ambarīṣa, the son of the king named Nābhāga— who was born of Nabhāga, the son of Manu known as Vaivasvata—
though his heart was beloved by the earth encompassed by the seven oceans, took delight [in the Lord].
With my mind always immersed in you and in those who are devoted to you. || 1 ||

Regarding the term "Vaivasvata": Marīci was the son of Brahmā; his son was Kaśyapa; his son was Vivasvān; his son was this Śrāddhadeva, known as Manu Vaivasvata; his son was Nabhāga; his son was Nābhāga; his son was Ambarīṣa. Although he was a sovereign emperor (sārvabhauma) who cherished the earth consisting of seven islands surrounded by the seven oceans, he took delight only in You, the Lord, in Your associates, and in Your devotees. || 1 ||
O Lord! Since he performs everything solely out of devotion for your pleasure, you will soon grant him grace,
by which he shall be protected even without his having to make a request.
You have cast forth the wheel with its thousand spokes.

"Tvaditi": For him who performs all worldly and Vedic rites for your pleasure, you, through his devotion alone, bestowed your grace in no long time—that is, in a short period—by which grace you extended, that is, gave him, the Sudarśana discus, for the purpose of his protection and for the warding off of enemies. || 2 ||
Then, in order to worship Your Lordship, he observed the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) for a year in Madhuvana on the banks of the Yamunā,
performing it extensively together with his virtuous-minded wife.
He bestowed honor upon the twice-born and released sixty million cattle.
"He" refers to Ambarīṣa. Thereafter, for the sake of worshipping You, he observed the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) for a year.

On the banks of the Yamunā, with a well-disposed mind filled with devotion, he performed an extensive worship accompanied by all ritual offerings and great ablutions, offering and bestowing them. || 3 ||
Then, on the day following the fast, at the conclusion of his worship of you, the sage Durvāsas arrived at his palace;
and that man, whose nature was prone to causing distress to others, was invited by the king to eat.
He went slowly toward the Yamunā, intending to perform his religious observances.

Regarding the word "tatra" (there): at the end, that is, at the conclusion of her worship of you; on the day of breaking the fast (*pāraṇa*), meaning when she had fed the Brahmins and was desirous of eating herself. Then the sage Śrī Durvāsas arrived at her residence. Being one whose nature is to cause distress to others and who delights in tormenting others, he departed slowly, having made the excuse: "I shall return after the time for breaking the fast has passed, so as not to violate my vows. || 4 ||
He described that predicament of the king to the king, saying: "Due to the exhaustion from the conclusion of the fast's auspicious hour, you, being devoted to me,
performed the breaking of the fast on that very day."
Then the Sage, perceiving this with his divine vision, grew enraged; tossing up his matted locks, he cast forth a magical creation (kṛtyā).

"By the king," [it is said]. Thinking, "If I wait, the auspicious hour for breaking the fast will expire; yet if I do not wait, the sage may become angry," he broke his fast with water alone out of distress. Knowing that it was the breaking of the fast, and casting aspersions by making many disparaging remarks, the sage, his matted locks bristling with rage, unleashed a *kṛtyā* through his matted hair. || 5 ||
Seeing before him the Kṛtyā, bearing a sword and burning the world, the king did not tremble from his place;
beholding the destruction of your devotee, he pursued the sage with your Sudarśana, which turned the fire of the Kṛtyā into a swarm of moths.

"Kṛtyāmiti": That Kṛtyā, making the Sudarśana cakra—which causes affliction and pain to your devotee—resemble a fire that consumes moths like a moth fallen into a flame, pursued the sage; that is, she ran behind the fleeing sage. || 6 ||
Fleeing in fear through all the worlds and seeing your wheel everywhere, he even went to Viriñca; yet,
having been cast off with the words, "Who can overstep the wheel of time?", he was driven away.
Śarva departed, and he too paid homage to you.

"Running," it is said: seeing those wheels everywhere and in all directions, he went for refuge to Viriñca (Brahmā). Rebutted by his words—"Who can transcend the wheel of time?"—he turned back and reached Śarva (Śiva). With the intention, "Go for refuge to that very Hari whose wheel this is," he indeed paid homage to you. || 7 ||
Having returned once more to the abode of Bhava and bowing to the Sage, he said: "O Sage, you are indeed my servant through devotion;
yet knowledge and austerity, when accompanied by humility, are what is truly venerable."
O Infinite One! Go and worship only the feet of Ambarīṣa. || 8 ||

"Furthermore": *bhavannilayam* means Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord. "I am like a servant of my devotees," because I am dependent upon them. [The opponent objects: "But I too, being established in knowledge and austerity, am surely Your devotee. [The Lord replies: "True. Knowledge and austerity become worthy of honor and lead to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) only when they are joined with humility and tranquility. These two do not lead to happiness for one who is ill-behaved, as is the case with you. Therefore, take refuge in and go to the feet of Ambarīṣa. (8)

Having approached like a living being, the king grasped the feet of the sage; having stepped back, he spoke thus: "He has not [yet] entered. When the wheel had departed, the sage bestowed all blessings upon him.
Even though you have committed an offense against him, he shows compassion, proclaiming his devotion to you.

"Until then": that Ambarīṣa, having withdrawn out of shame at the touch of His feet, praised and worshipped the Sudarśana, Your weapon. When the discus had departed and the offense—the crime of causing harm—had been pacified, He, extolling and praising Ambarīṣa’s grace toward Him despite the transgression committed against Him, granted him blessings and boons. || 9 ||
King Bhūri, having waited upon the sage for one year without taking food himself,
fed that virtuous Ṛṣi and dismissed him with a gracious mind;
then, having eaten himself, he became even more firmly devoted to you.
And he attained union with me; O Pavaneśa, may you protect me! || 10 ||

Regarding the word "rājā": For one year—that is, for one full year—the king, having fasted (anaśnan), subsisting only on water (abbhakṣaḥ), waited upon and served the sage; having properly fed him and eaten the remains himself, he then dismissed him with permission. Even more than before, he became devoted to you; in the end, he attained liberation through union (sāyujyam). || 10 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third decade, the description of the life of Ambarīṣa.
Now, he introduces the life of Śrī Rāma:
requested by the gods, [Viśvāmitra] went among the Kosalas to Ṛśyaśṛṅga for the sake of the destruction of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa.
When King Daśaratha had performed the *putrīyā* sacrifice and offered the finest milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
you were born from him— along with Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and the one named Śatrughna— as his three queens likewise conceived simultaneously upon partaking of that food.
It has been stated that you, Śrī Hari himself, were born as Rāma; he now demonstrates this:

"Armed with a bow and followed by Lakṣmaṇa to protect the foremost of sacrifices of Viśvāmitra, you went forth at your father’s word, your fatigue from the journey on the road stilled by the absence of duality, as described by the sage."

O Lord! For the protection of men, having split Tāṭakā with your arrows by the power of the sage’s words and having received from him this multitude of weapons, you went to the forest of the sage known as Siddhāśrama. || 2 ||

Regarding the term "kodaṇḍī" (the wielder of the bow): the sense is that even in his childhood, his restraint of the wicked, protection of the righteous, great respect for the virtuous, and so forth, do not pertain merely to an ordinary human being. || 2 ||
Furthermore, it says that his liberation from the curse of the Sage’s wife, the breaking of Maheśvara’s bow, and other deeds manifest his nature as a portion of Viṣṇu:
"Having routed Mārīca at the head of the sacrifice, slaying other demons with arrows,
making Ahalyā beautiful, and having reached the house of Vaidehī on the road by the dust of his feet..."
Having shattered the bow of the moon-crested Lord Śiva and having obtained Indirā as well as the daughter of the Earth,
you established yourself in sovereignty together with your three heroic brothers and their wives.
The victory of Bhārgava-rāma and his subsequent dedication of his own splendor to Śrī Rāma also makes known that the incarnation of Rāma is superior to other incarnations; thus he says:
"When the ornament of Bhṛgu’s lineage was blinded by rage, having transferred his own splendor..."
O you of lovely form! Having departed from here and dwelling happily with your beloved wife, you have now reached Ayodhyā.

Once, when Bharata had gone to the residence of his maternal uncle along with Śatrughna, the coronation ceremony for you was commenced by our father, but it was indeed obstructed by the daughter of the Lord of Kekaya.
Having thus established his descent, he praises the conduct he undertook for the sake of winning over the world through these words of the Father:
"Desirous of going to the forest, accompanied by the wives of the people and bearing a bow, you went from the city to the abode of Guha on the way, wearing matted hair and bark garments."

Having crossed the Gaṅgā by boat, he once again approached the venerable Bhāradvāja on foot; having bowed before him, he dwelt for a long time in great happiness on Citrakūṭa, the king of mountains, for the sake of his words.

"By his father's word": the sense is that this was said in order to convince the people that you lived happily at Citrakūṭa wearing matted hair and bark garments, having abandoned the glory of sovereignty solely by your father's command; thus, one must remain devoted to the words of one's elders. || 5 ||

Having heard from the mouth of Bharata that his father had indeed gone to heaven while he was distressed by grief for his son, he was tormented; having offered water to him and placed his sandals upon the earth,
he then bowed to Atri and went to the vast Daṇḍaka forest of fierce appearance.
O noble one! Having slain the Daitya Virādha, you have attained a beautiful state of liberation, like that of Śārabhaṅgī.
"Having heard this," [refers to] the *sugati*, or liberation, pertaining to Śarabhaṅga. || 6 ||
Having bowed to Agastya, who rendered the entire multitude of his enemies like birds with feathers stuck in a net,

you, desiring their welfare, received from the ascetics the account of what followed; and when the sage had bestowed upon you the divine bow of Viṣṇu as well as the Brahmāstra, you beheld once more your father’s friend, Jaṭāyu, on the path.
In the past, you sported with your young bride on the banks of the Godāvarī at Pañcavaṭī. || 7 ||

"Having bowed," [he said]. You promised—that is, you vowed—the slaying of all the Rākṣasas, making them like birds with broken wings by a multitude of arrows. Godā refers to the Godāvarī river. "You have wandered" means you formerly dwelt there at your own will. || 7 ||

Having been rejected by the son of Sumitrā with words that shattered her resolve, Śūrpaṇakhā— whose fortitude was shaken by the god of love and whose very self was overcome by her desire— had her nose cut off by him in a fit of intense rage.
Seeing her thus enraged, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the three-headed Triśiras rushed toward her.
At that very moment, he whose heat was unassailable rendered even those arrows, though exceeding the number of his own fingers, utterly powerless.

Following the deer of Mārīca’s illusion—which had been dispatched by the Ten-faced Rāvaṇa upon hearing the news told by his sister—and which was longed for by the lotus-eyed Sītā, you struck it with a volley of arrows.
Then Rāvaṇa abducted her as she was being led away by the wailing of that illusory deer, while your younger brothers were summoned forth;
though you were distressed by this, you felt an indescribable joy within yourself at the prospect of finding a means to slay him.

Regarding the word "sodaryā" (sister): by this, it is established that he was outwardly distressed due to the separation from Sītā, while the statement "within he bore some joy" implies something else. Furthermore, this is also suggested to show that for those who accept the word of a woman as authoritative, such is their suffering. || 9 ||

O Lord of the Wind’s Abode! After Jaṭāyu had departed for heaven, saying, "The Ten-faced one has carried away your slender bride; she shall be recovered by my death," you performed the funeral rites for your friend. Then, seeing Śabari on the banks of the Pampā, you slew Kaṃbha who was seizing that headless trunk (kaṃbha).
Reaching the son of the Wind (Hanumān), your mind filled with great joy, protect us! 10.
