Thus ends the thirty-fourth decade in the *Śrīrāmacarita*, describing the meeting with Hanumān at Lake Pampā.
Thereafter, Hanumān led [Rāma] to the friendship with Sugrīva by means of the massive carcass of Dundubhi.
Having struck with your toe, you simultaneously crushed seven *sāla* trees with a single arrow;

then, having slain Vālī— who possessed incomparable strength and was intent on killing Sugrīva— under the pretext of hunting, you spent the rainy season at the edge of Mataṅga’s hermitage, agitated by separation.

Then, seeing that army of bears drawn up in battle array by Sugrīva—who had approached with apprehension at his younger brother’s command—and seeing them bowing low in every direction to search swiftly for his beloved, he, filled with joy, placed a message and a ring in the hand of the Wind-god’s son;
meanwhile, on every path along my route, your beloved was being sought with great effort even by other monkeys. (2)
"By Sugrīva": by the speech of his younger brother Lakṣmaṇa, [he was told] that he had set out together with Sugrīva and searched for the army of bears along my path. || 2 ||
Having heard news of you, Hanumān leaped with great speed and force; having crossed the ocean by means of the words of Sampāti, he beheld Janakī within the city and gave her his ring.

Having crushed the garden and engaged in a fierce battle that exhausted even Akṣa, and having endured his bonds, he saw the Ten-faced one, searched Laṅkā, and quickly presented the crest-jewel to you.

"Tvaditi": by the words of Sampāti, who had grown wings through hearing the *Rāmāyaṇa* and, flying upward with great speed, beheld Sītā; "prakṣudya" means having crushed or reduced to powder; "akṣakṣapaṇena" refers to one whose battle is famous for the destruction of Akṣa, that is, the slaying of Akṣakumāra; "soḍhabandhaḥ" refers to one by whom his bonds were endured—that is, forgiven—due to the recollection of a curse. || 3 ||

You, having traversed the circle of the earth with the prowess of a vast host of monkeys and bears led by Sugrīva and Aṅgada, and having reached the shore beyond the ocean while being honored by the younger brother of the lord of night-stalkers (Hanumān), listened in secret to the news of the enemy as reported by him; then, through the words of the ocean—which was drying up under the heat of the Agneya weapon discharged out of anger at the failure of your entreaties—you regained the middle path.
"Tvamiti": "Pārejaladhim" means on the far shore of the ocean. "Āpārthyam" refers to the futility or fruitlessness of the prayer. "Prāstas" means cast away or discarded. || 4 ||
Having constructed a bridge by means of hosts of monkeys who carried heaps of mountains from other regions,

you— along with your younger brother— proceeded against the demons with your own armies, whose mountain-like peaks of tusks and claws served as formidable weapons of wood. On the battlefield, you displayed supreme valor against the conqueror of Indra.
Bound by the force of the serpents, you were liberated by the wind-like wings of the Lord of Birds. || 5 ||
"By monkeys"—thus explaining, that is, making clear. || 5 ||

But here, the son of Sumitrā, perceiving through the scent of the mountain that his life-breaths were departing due to the discharge of the Śakti weapon, restored his own life and destroyed the evil path of Meghanāda, who sought to seize the waters.

When Kumbhakarṇa arrived— shaking the surface of the earth and devouring the entire army— you, your paralysis removed by the words of Vibhīṣaṇa during the disturbances caused by his illusions, destroyed him.
Seizing the chariot and armor sent by Janabhari, engaging in combat with Ravana, shattering his neck-throat with the Brahma-weapon, and taking up the invincible sword purified by fire—O Lord!
you returned to your own city with your beloved, accompanied by the hosts of bears who were unharmed and revived in battle by the power of Shrenimat, and together with the lord of Lanka. || 7 ||

"Taking up" means: those hosts of bears (*ṛkṣasaṅgha*) who had died in battle were restored to life by the best of the ranks of the *śreṇīs*, such as Hanumat and others; or, they were restored to life by the best of the ranks of the gods (*devaśreṇī*). || 7 ||
Delighted by divine consecrations, you sported with Maithilī for more than ten thousand years; yet, alas, alas! at the word of a wicked man, you mocked her when she was pregnant.
After Śatrughna had struck down the night-stalker Lavaṇa, you destroyed the Śūdra Pāśa;
meanwhile, Sītā, having taken up residence in the house of Vālmīki, gave birth to your two sons.
"Delighted," [he said]; having tormented and caused [him] to be killed, he himself utterly crushed that loathsome Śūdra-ascetic, Śūdrapāśa. || 8 ||
At the command of Vālmīki, whose sweet compositions were sung by your son at the sacrificial enclosure,
Sītā entered the earth while you were desirous of regaining her; and you yourself, impelled by Time,
became the slayer of Saumitri for that very reason, along with all your remaining servants who had previously drowned in the Sarayū.
O Lord! Having ascended to the celestial realm together with her, he went to his own primordial abode, Vaikuṇṭha. || 9 ||

Regarding the words "of Vālmīki": he is one by whom the sweet composition, the *Rāmāyaṇa* poem, was caused to be sung aloud by your two sons, Kuśa and Lava. You were "implored by Time," meaning you were requested by Yama, the King of Dharma, to ascend to heaven. As for the reason given—"the slayer of Saumitri"—the meaning is this: having made a vow before the King of Dharma that "I shall kill anyone who witnesses our secret conversation," Rāma abandoned Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa), who arrived in the interim, out of fear of breaking his promise.

Then, together with all the remaining portions of the gods and the citizens, he ascended from that place to Nāka (heaven), and from there to his own abode, Vaikuṇṭha—the primordial realm existing even before the creation of the universe.

This is because the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) characterized by the indicatory vowel *i* in the root *yudh* (as in *yudhyann*) is not mandatory. If it is argued that if even the Lord possesses a bodily bond, then the consequence of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) would follow, he says "no":

"This incarnation of yours as a mortal is surely for the sake of instructing mortals; thus, through excessive attachment to the nature of desire, there may arise the pain of separation even from innocent people."
If there is no transformation of your mind due to the experience of your own self, O wielder of the discus!
Then you, who are the singular embodiment of pure being, O Lord of the City of Wind—dispel the torments of disease! 10.

Regarding the word "sa" (he): for you, whose *māyā* is under your own control, this manifested incarnation as a mortal—whose glory is unknown even to Brahmā and the other gods—is indeed merely the assumption of a body for divine play (*līlā*), and not, like others, a cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) due to dependence on *māyā*; this is the sense. Furthermore, it was for the sake of instructing mortals. But what exactly is taught by this? To that he says: "In this way... (*evam*).

Through excessive attachment to desire, there arises the pain of separation and the suffering of being apart from one's beloved; through excessive attachment to dharma, even innocent people become objects of abandonment, as was the case with Sītā. Therefore, let there be no excessive attachment to desire and the like. He establishes this by saying "no cet" (if not): for you, whose very self is the experience—that is, the light—of your own true nature, the Supreme Brahman whose form is self-luminous consciousness, where indeed could there be modifications of the mind such as passion, hatred, or delusion? The meaning is that they simply do not exist.

Time has no power over him who holds the wheel of time in his hand by virtue of his own sovereignty; rather, O embodiment of pure being (*sattva*)! The sense is that this incarnation is precisely the assumption of a form composed of pure *sattva* for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees. [O Lord,] shake off [and] dispel [this suffering]. 10.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth decade, the description of the life of Śrī Rāma.
Now, he describes the incarnation of Dattātreya:
"In former times, you were indeed born as the son of Atri by Anasūyā under the name Datta."

Born with a mind weary of binding disciples, you were seen by the most devoted king of the Haihayas as you wandered at ease with your beloved; having granted him boons such as the eightfold sovereign powers, you yourself finally bestowed upon him his own death.

Regarding the word "Atri's": because it was said by the Blessed One, "I have been given [by you]," you bear the name Datta; yet, due to the interruption of your continuous meditative absorption (*samādhi*), your mind became slackened by the attachment to disciples. To dispel that, you displayed a state of being overcome by the intoxication of wine together with your beloved, while remaining self-abiding and delighting in the Self (*ātmarāma*). [Thus you were addressed] by the lord of the Haihayas, Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna. Now, he describes the incarnation of Śrī Paraśurāma: "In order to make true the boon of Arjuna, and because he was bowed down by his mere power... (1) ...bowed down by his mere power—[the verse continues: "Having taken up the form of a sage, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (2) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (3) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (4) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (5) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (6) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (7) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (8) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (9) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (10) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (11) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (12) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (13) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (14) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (15) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (16) "Then, having performed the sacrifice of the head of the demon Arjuna, the Lord, who is the supreme reality, assumed the body of a son of Jamadagni, which was the very essence of the Supreme Brahman. (17) "Then,
O Hari! Then, in order to destroy that entire royal lineage hostile to the Brahmins and to remove the earth's burden, you were born in the family of Bhrigu as Rāma, the son of Jamadagni and Reṇukā;
and among his sons, you were the youngest, who bestowed prosperity upon your parents.
"It is true. [He granted] Arjuna a boon that his own hand would be the cause of his death. That power belongs to Arjuna; by that alone, the slight affliction caused by Brahmā was pacified. || 2 ||

Having acquired the collection of traditional lore while at the age of fourteen, you—by the command of your father who was agitated with anger toward your mother for being slightly infatuated with the King of the Gandharvas—cut her asunder along with your paternal kinsmen and brothers; then, from your pacified father, you obtained the boon of their restoration to life, and your mother also granted you a boon.

"Labdha" means that even at the age of fourteen, he had mastered the entire collection of the Vedas (*āmnāya*) up to the level of understanding their meaning. When his mother Reṇukā was slightly delayed in fetching water because she was somewhat attached to Citraratha, the king of the Gandharvas, those brothers—referring to themselves as such because they were transgressing their father Jamadagni’s command by saying "Kill her"—along with their elder siblings, having cut down and restrained their mother Reṇukā, [obtained] from their peaceful and gracious father... of them.
He obtained the excellent means of livelihood for his mother and brothers. || 3 ||
Then, having departed from his own hermitage for the sake of his mother’s joy, and at the word of Bhṛgu, having worshipped the Lord of Gaurī on the Snowy Mountain,
he obtained from Him that axe as well as great weapons and other gifts, whereby he became the slayer of the demons.
Then, having reached his friend Muni Akṛtavraṇa, he returned to his own hermitage.

"O father," [he said]. Then, immediately after, from that hermitage where the celestial cow Surabhi had been brought by his father Jamadagni for the pleasure of his mother Reṇukā, he departed at the word of his grandfather Bhṛgu. Having obtained the axe (paraśu) of that Lord of Gaurī, and having received from that very Lord of Gaurī great weapons and other gifts, and having found his friend Muni—who was protected by the lion-faced [guardian] and remained unscarred—he returned to his own hermitage. || 4 ||

Arjuna, having returned from the hunt, was honored by his father with a multitude of riches obtained from the celestial cow; yet, upon returning to the city, he was once again incited by the words of a wicked minister and dispatched his counselor to purchase a cow. That evil-minded man, obstructing the path, killed the calf with a poisoned arrow as it rushed toward the sage to offer him life-sustaining milk. || 5 ||

"Ākheṭeti" means that he went to the hermitage on account of hunting, having become addicted to the chase. He returned to the city of Māhiṣmatī with divine objects of enjoyment, a collection of riches obtained from Surabhi, the celestial cow. Again, at the word of his evil minister, he sought to purchase—that is, to take possession of—that cow, Surabhi. By that wicked-minded minister, the calf of Surabhi was stolen and taken to Māhiṣmatī by one who had caused the army-host to be struck down by the cow, which was filled with rage because the sage Jamadagni had been deprived of life—his slaughter—by the king while he was obstructing the taking of the cow. || 5 ||
Then, his anger stirred by the words of his father Śukra, who had been restored to life,
he ascended a chariot drawn by a bull and entered the arena, bearing a bow, an axe, and arrows that had been meditated upon and placed within Mahodara’s belly, and accompanied by his driver.
With words, you should praise the battle to the king who has not yet granted his son's request.

"Śukra" means: while Arjuna was the lord of the earth, he—bearing the fourfold set of items beginning with the bow, which had been brought and presented by Mahodara, a follower of Śiva who was meditated upon by his friend Akṛtavraṇa—and having mounted [the chariot], began [his journey]. || 6 ||
Now, it is said that when his army was destroyed, Arjuna himself fell before the venerable Paraśurāma:
"With seventeen *akṣauhiṇīs* of sons, accompanied by ten thousand great generals and multitudes of various allies, the battlefield expanded;
yet, with the mere stroke of your axe, the entire mass of that army was shattered and utterly annihilated."
The son of Hehaya, having fled in terror and lost his remaining followers, rushed toward you.
Obstructing him as he discharged many weapons and missiles from his thousand glorious arms— which had humbled the pride of the Lord of Laṅkā and sportively stemmed the waters of the Narmadā—

you rendered even that Vaiṣṇava power of yours fruitless; then, perceiving you to be Hari himself, meditating upon you with joy and free from all faults, he slew him, and he went to your supreme abode.

"Līlā" means: he who destroys the pride of the Lord of Laṅkā as he was whirling and leaping in the waters of the Narmadā when they were diverted by his thousand arms through mere sport; he by whom Rāvaṇa was cast into prison; with that glorious thousand-armed one, [he is] him by whom many weapons and missiles were released—[him] Kārtavīrya, while obstructing and warding him off. Furthermore, when even the Vaiṣṇava discus discharged by him became fruitless against you, [he] recognized you as Hari and meditated upon Śrī Hari; therefore, [he is so called].
Having cleansed him of all faults and destroyed his defects such as desire, anger, and the like, you cut off his thousand arms and slew him. || 8 ||
When your father was slain by the sons of the Hehaya clan, you— beholding their hearts as they struck Reṇukā and bearing a terrible vow made many times over—

brought forth your chariot and weapons through meditation; then, hacking at the kṣatriyas who had harmed brahmins with your axe and piercing them with your arrows in the four directions, you rid the earth of the kṣatriya caste.

"Furthermore," [he said]: "When your father Jamadagni was slain, the sons of the Hehaya king—indignant, unable to endure the murder of their own sire, and having destroyed all who remained virtuous—arrived at the hermitage which was now bereft of you. As she was lamenting with heart-rending cries and beating her breast, [Parashurama], as before, summoned his chariot and weapons through meditation; he struck down with his axe those Kshatriyas who were enemies of Brahmins throughout the quarters of the world, and he slew them with his arrows."
Then, having conquered the lineage of the protector of kings twenty-one times and thereby restored them to life,
he gratified his ancestors with a great flood of blood at Samantapañcaka; subsequently,
while bestowing the earth upon Kaśyapa and others during a sacrifice, he again fought with Śālva.
Thinking, "Kṛṣṇa will slay him," you were restrained from battle by the princes.

"O Father!"—having joined his father's head to his body, bringing his father back to life through sacrifices, and instructing and bestowing gifts upon the officiating priests such as Kāśyapa and others; then, while fighting with Śālva, he was pacified from battle by the princes Sanaka and others, who, knowing that Śrī Kṛṣṇa would slay him according to their word, spoke thus. || 10 ||

The suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule: "After a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), [the suffix] is frequently used in the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and it is treated like the suffix *iṣṭhan*. Thus, we have *viśikhayan*. Now, he describes how, while performing austerities on Mount Mahendra, being entreated by sages, he raised up the land of Kerala which had been submerged in the ocean: "Having laid down his weapons on Mount Mahendra and performing penance, he saw that the earth as far as Gokarṇa was again submerged in the ocean; then, being entreated by the ascetics..."

O Lord of Bhrigu! O Lord of the Wind! Having dispelled the ocean—which was terrified by the fire-weapons held in your bow—by the casting of your sacrificial ladle, and having rescued Kerala, protect me! 11.41.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth decad, including the one [additional verse], which contains the description of the incarnations of Dattātreya and Paraśurāma, as well as the narrative of Paraśurāma’s life.
Through reflections on the meaning of verses, the clearing of doubts, the answering of questions, explanations, and demonstrations—
activities inseparable from meditation upon Hari— we shall make this moment fruitful.
Thus ends the section on the ninth book in the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktapriyā.
The pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, known as the "Cessation" (Nirodha) and consisting of the removal of the earth's burden,
are praised here— not too concisely— in verses that are captivating to the ear and mind.

O Hari, whose body is dense bliss! Indeed, in the ancient war between the gods and the asuras, even those who were slain by you did not attain liberation because of the persistence of the remnants of their karma.
Now, [the earth] is severely oppressed by the weight of those very beings born on the surface of the earth who possess two worlds.
The earth was measured by Viriñca, whose feet were resorted to by the gods who had arrived there previously. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "sāndrānanda": having employed the word *ānanda* at the beginning for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), and intending to employ it again at the end in the expression "the splendor of the mass of supreme bliss" (*paramānandasandohalakṣmīm*), he uses the word *ānanda* once more in the middle for the sake of auspiciousness—namely, "sāndrānanda. O You whose very nature is supreme bliss! Regarding the conflict between gods and asuras (*daivāsure*): even those who have been struck down by You shall surely attain liberation either immediately or within two or three births.

In that regard, those well-known Daityas such as Kālanemi and others, although subdued by the Blessed One, did not go to—that is, did not attain—liberation (gati), because they were dependent on the remnants of their merit and demerit which brought about their human state due to the force of the residue of their past actions. For this very reason, the earth reached Viriñca together with the gods who had arrived even before she was previously afflicted by the excessive burden—the weight—of those whose births on the surface of the earth took place in the forms of Kaṃsa and others.

The term "āśritapada" means residing in Satyaloka; or, it refers to one whose lotus-feet have been worshipped; or, it means he whose lotus-feet are resorted to by the gods—thus he is so described. || 1 ||
"Alas, alas! Protect this earth, which is being crushed by the heavy burden of many wicked men and is now about to plunge into the ocean; indeed, ask these gods for help!
Seeing the Earth thus overwhelmed by such profuse lamentation, the Creator looked around at the faces of the gods and, O Hari, meditated upon you.

"Alas! Alas! What misery! Alas, alas, what a tragedy! [Thus she cried. She was being crushed by the heavy burden of wicked people; she was utterly distressed and, as if about to sink, was on the verge of falling into the ocean of obstructive waters. Having looked all around at their faces—faces filled with the words "What she says is indeed the truth"—[she spoke]. || 2 ||
And the Lotus-born One said: "O gods, the words of the Earth are indeed true;
for the Lord of Lakṣmī is truly skilled in the task of protecting both her and you.
Therefore, let all of us, led by Śarva, go from here to the ocean of milk."
Having bowed to him, they went together with speed to your abode, saying, "We shall praise him. || 3 ||

"‘It is so,’ [he replied]. The words of the Earth are true; I have seen this with my divine eye. ‘The Lord of Lakṣmī’—the sense is that if he does not protect the earth, he would be merely the Lord of Lakṣmī. Your abode is the Ocean of Milk. (3)

While those deluded ones had reached the shore of the milk-ocean stirred by gentle breezes and gathered together with their minds solely intent on meditating upon your feet, the Lotus-born Brahmā, having heard your voice within his heart, spoke while gladdening them all: "I have been personally commanded by the Supreme Self; let my words be heard. (4)

"Those [demons]," it is said. As soon as they had reached the shore, the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), having heard and understood the words of the Lord reclining upon Śeṣa—which were revealed in his heart and in the space of his heart—spoke thus: "I have been personally designated by the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, himself; let that speech of his be heard. || 4 ||
"I know the wretched state of the gods and the earth due to fearsome kings; therefore, with my entire self, I shall manifest in the Yadava clan to remove that [suffering].
Let the gods be born in the Vrishni clan by their portions, and let the celestial women also be born on earth for the sake of serving me"—thus spoke the Lotus-born One (Brahmā) regarding your words.

"Know this": by means of the formidable kings, Jarāsandha and others, who act as the cause, [I shall bring about] their miserable state—that is, their condition of being dependent on others—for the sake of their removal and subjugation. I, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), with my entire self and not merely in part—[let it be so]. Let the gods become cowherds in the Vṛṣṇi clan through a portion or part, and let the celestial nymphs become the cowherd-wives (gopīs). || 5 ||

O Lord! When all had departed with their hearts cooled by having heard Your words—which are like nectar to the ears—and their souls satiated by the ambrosia of Your grace, that king, the son of Śūra, married the blessed Devakī, daughter of Devaka, in the renowned city of Mathurā, which was preeminent in merit due to Your presence. || 6 ||

Having heard this—those whose hearts were extinguished [of passion] and made happy; by means of that merit which, through your presence, brings about both worldly prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*); in that most excellent [marriage]; he wedded; Śūra’s son, Vasudeva. || 6 ||

When the wedding was concluded, his brother Kaṃsa, honoring them both, set out on the road in his chariot as their driver; there, by your voice rising from the sky, he was incited, saying, "Her eighth son will kill you, O most wicked one!
Driven by terror, he drew his sword to slay the slender maiden who had come near him.

"Udvāha" means he marries, showing honor to these two, Devakī and Vasudeva, by acting as their charioteer. He goes with horses because of Kaṃsa’s words: "Even fate speaks untruth. "Hantā" means he will kill. "Hanta" is used in the sense of "oh," as it was said that the gods and the earth have achieved their purpose. "Tanvīm" refers to the slender Devakī. "Adhāt" means he took her [as his wife].
Seizing her by the hair, that man of wicked mind did not release her for a long time despite Śauri’s consolations; yet, pleased by her words of offering herself as his daughter, he then went home.
O Lord! He did not even kill your first-born, though she was offered by him out of affection;
for the steady compassion of even the wicked is indeed seen at times.

Regarding the word "gṛhṇāna" (accepting): by means of conciliatory words employed over a long period of time, and by the speech of offering his own sons—that is, by the promise, "I shall give her sons to you. || 8 ||
Then, by his very mind, the sage Nārada said to the Lord of the Bhojas:
"O Lord, you know well that you are indeed Asuras, while the Yādavas are Suras;
that Hari is a master of illusion who will become the destroyer of your progeny at the request of the gods. Having heard this, he (Kamsa) crushed the Yādavas and slew the two sons of Śūra.

"Until then" means: until Kaṃsa had gone home, [the child] was indeed impelled by your mind; otherwise, it would have been impossible for Śrī Nārada to manifest his duplicity toward Kaṃsa. You are the asuras such as Kālanemi and others. For the sake of slaying you—who have become kings—Hari shall be the eighth son of this woman for the purpose of killing you. He "shook" him, meaning he caused him to fall from his position. || 9 ||

O Mādhava! When the Lord of the Earth had attained the state of being the seventh embryo and was led away by Your illusory power at Your instigation, You too, O All-pervading Lord, whose singular essence is pure existence, consciousness, and bliss,
entered the womb of Devakī while being praised by the gods.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa! having shaken off this mass of diseases, grant me supreme devotion. || 10 ||

"Attained": when the Lord Ananta, the lord of serpents, had attained the state of being Devakī’s seventh embryo and was transferred to Rohiṇī by means of His illusory power (māyā); "Being-Consciousness"—meaning He whose singular essence is Being-Consciousness-Bliss; O Kṛṣṇa! He is the one residing within the womb of Devakī. || 10 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh decade, the description of the occasion of the descent of Kṛṣṇa.
O Lord whose form is bliss! O Friend! When Your incarnation arrived, those who were gazing upon Your radiant limbs—
Shrouding the light as if with circles of rain-clouds that were like processions of lovers, the time of the monsoon truly shone forth.
"Ānandeti" means: by those [rays] issuing forth, that is, emerging outwardly, from your body which is ablaze and radiant with light. || 1 ||
When the quarters were most cool with the waters of the clouds, when virtuous people were rendered helpless by their longing for the fulfillment of their hopes,
and during the rise of the moon at midnight— then you, the remover of the world's suffering, appeared here in this middle watch of the night.

Regarding the word *āśāsu*: when people are overwhelmed by the force of joy at the attainment—that is, the acquisition—of the desired object they had hoped for, and are thus unaware of what ought to be done; at midnight, that is, at the middle watch of the night. || 2 ||
Though his body was touched by childhood, he displayed divine splendors through the radiance of his towering crown, bracelets, armlets, and necklaces;
and though dark as a cloud, he shone in the birth-chamber, resplendent with his conch, discus, lotus, and mace.
Regarding the word *bālye*: "touching childhood" means that which is connected with it; thus, it is *bālyaspṛk*. The root *īṅ* (in *vibhūtīrīśva*) belongs to the *divādi* class, meaning "to go.

[The phrase] *dadhuṣā* means by one who has maintained (*dhṛtavatā*) those things which indicate joy. He states this very point with the word *udyat*: the body is qualified as that in which the rising splendors of the crown and other ornaments reside. *Parilesitha* means you shone. || 3 ||

O Vāsudeva! You shone forth as if eradicating the impure misfortune created by the wicked Kaṃsa, through the various glances cast from the bashfulness of Lakṣmī—who was marked by her delight at resting happily upon Your chest—as she released those side-long looks. || 4 ||

Regarding the phrase "the region of the chest": it refers to Lakṣmī, who, having been comfortably nestled upon the region of the chest of her own husband, assumes another form as a playful woman (*vilāsinī*) characterized by specific gestures that manifest the heightening of renewed love; she is marked by bashfulness, meaning she is characterized by eyes languid with shame, as if stained with red lac. || 4 ||

But Śauri, beholding with his own eyes your form standing at a distance—even though the minds of the assembly of steadfast sages were [already captivated]—was moistened by a voice faltering from the rising of tears of joy and horripilation, and praised you, who are the nectar-essence for the eyes. (5)

"Śauri" means: having become wet—due to tears of joy, the rising of horripilation, and a faltering voice—and having met [the Lord], even though he remained far from the mind of the assembly of wise sages who were endowed with the fourfold means and established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
"O Lord! Be gracious, O Supreme Person, O axe that cuts down the creeping vine of suffering, O One with the lotus-eye, O You who sport in the arts!
Remove our sorrows with Your glances, heavy with compassion"—thus were You praised for a long time by him, who was filled with joy. (6)

"O God! O Supreme Person! O Supreme Self! O you who are like a sickle for cutting the root of the creeping vine of suffering! O you who have become an exceedingly sharp weapon! O you with the eye [of wisdom]! O Ruler of all! O you whose nature is to sport in the creation and other activities of the world through *māyā*, which is a portion (*kalā*) of yourself; or rather, [you are so called] because you possess the play of the side-glance (*kaṭākṣa*) from the faculty of the eye, which is like a sickle for cutting the creeping vine of suffering. || 6 ||
With your body praised by the creeper-like limbs of your mother’s tears,
and your virtues extolled by hymns, you, the abode of compassion,
awakened those two from their former births.
By the word of his mother, he assumed the guise of a human child.

"Only this much": having awakened them by informing them that in a previous pair of births, he was born as the son of you two—Pṛśni and Tapaḥ—under the name Pṛśnigarbha, and again as Vāmana, the son of Aditi and Kaśyapa; || 7 ||
Then, impelled by you, that son of Śūra indeed set about exchanging [the roles] with the daughter of Nanda;
for he placed you— so beautiful as a young swan resting upon a lotus, and held in the hearts of the noble— within his hands.

"Thus [he said]: 'In order to create the illusion that it is Kaṃsa, place me on Yaśodā’s bed and place her son, my mother’s child, on yours'—thus urged by you, he was restrained in mind and meditated upon by the noble sages. (8)
Then, while you were born in the house of Paśupati, Yoganidrā caused the city-dwellers to be awakened from their sleep;
what wonder is there in this that even insentient things act here at your instigation?
The doors, though firmly bolted, opened of their own accord.

Regarding the word *jātā*: at that time, when your departure was about to begin, the Illustrious Goddess Māyā, who is the Yoga-sleep (*yoganidrā*), having been born—that is, descended—into Yaśodā in the house of Nandagopa, the cowherd of the Lord of Creatures (*paśupati*), rendered the city-folk—the people residing in Mathurā—sealed by sleep and motionless through your instigation. "What is there to wonder at? means that, because you are so skillful in accomplishing the impossible, it is no wonder that you performed such acts as opening the city gates through your instigation. || 9 ||
Then, with the remainder of the water shielded by his many hoods,
and with his path freely revealed by the light of his jewels,
he— truly the most blessed one— set forth while supporting you.
Therefore, O Lord, you who are he, destroy the force of my diseases! || 10 ||

Regarding the phrase "by Śeṣa": by that Śeṣa, who is Ananta, whose path was thus freely revealed—he by whom the raindrops of water were warded off by his many hoods, and who was illuminated by the jewels upon those hoods. || 10 ||

Thus ends the thirty-eighth decade, containing the description of the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa and the description of Kṛṣṇa’s leading Gokula away. Carrying you, this descendant of Yadu’s lineage departed.
He beheld the daughter of Kalinda, her mass of water rising toward the sky;
oh, that accumulation of water, like a flood produced by Indra’s magic, in that very instant became immeasurable at its base. || 1 ||

"Going forth toward you," means departing. [He saw] the river filled with a flood of water that leaped into the expanse of the sky with its network of waves, bearing a mass of water rising high into the heavens. || 1 ||

Entering the cattle-pen where the cowherd women were fast asleep, its gates unfastened, he stealthily ascended a young girl; presenting you to her as she lay upon the bed of new-born babes, he carried that [child] from her feet and, assuming the guise of a maiden, returned swiftly to his own city. || 2 ||

"Prasuptā" means: while the cowherd women were fast asleep, in that place where a young girl was crying very softly for the purpose of discreetly signaling Yaśodā’s birth-house, and where the small door-panels were opened and removed—Vasudeva, entering that cow-pen (paśupavāṭikā), which was the house of Nandagopa, placed you upon Yaśodā’s maternity bed and departed from that spot. || 2 ||

Then, his sleep dispelled by the sound of the clamor of soldiers rushing [to the news], the King of the Bhojas, distressed by the report of his sister’s plight, arrived in haste with his mass of hair disheveled;
and, as if dissatisfied, he beheld the maiden in the hand of his sister.

"Then," [it is said]: by the multitude of guards—the soldiers who had been awakened from the force of their sleep by the sound of weeping from your younger sister, the daughter of Yaśodā, and who were rushing and running forth—they announced the news of the birth: "The eighth son of Devakī has been born. At this very report of the delivery, he became distressed, filled with the fear of death; and as if not satisfied by the turmoil of various anxieties, such as "How could this be a girl? [he remained thus]. || 3 ||

"Surely this must be the illusion of that honey-thief who dwells in deceit"—thinking thus, this elephant, as if snatching a lotus stalk from within a cluster of lotuses, has ground your younger sister, who was embraced by her own sister, against the stone slab. (4)
"Certainly" means: of Madhusūdana, the stealer of honey; [he perceives] the unborn Māyā. || 4 ||
Then your devotee, suddenly released as if from the noose of death, immediately ascended to that intermediate state which had assumed a form;
having descended to the lower realm, she indeed soared through the sky with her eight expanding arms flashing great weapons, crying out "Aho! in wonder.

"Then" (tataḥ) means: having been released from Kaṃsa’s hand, she went through the sky—that is, by way of the path—and shone brightly; "in which [sky]" is an adverbial phrase describing her movement, referring to the eight blossoming great weapons flashing from her arms. || 5 ||
"O most cruel Kaṃsa! What has been gained by my being crushed? Consider whether your own end has come anywhere near you; think of what is for your benefit!
Having thus addressed that wicked one, O Lord, your younger sister departed.
Praised by the hosts of Maruts, she came to dwell upon the earth in temples.

"O cruel one! "O most cruel one! O performer of exceedingly wicked deeds! Having thus addressed that villain Kaṃsa, [the Gopīs] fled with speed, their sleep dispelled by the desert wind; this is indeed appropriate.
Praised—that is, extolled—by the Gaṇas, she went to the dwellings on earth, having arrived there to bestow grace upon men, remaining in those various places as their presiding deities. || 6 ||
At dawn, however, at the king's command,
the proud demons led by Pralamba, Baka, and Pūtanā,
desiring his death, wandered fearlessly through the world.
What indeed is difficult for those devoid of compassion, who cause the destruction of young children? || 7 ||

"At dawn" means: again on the following day, at dawn—the break of day—the sons of the mountain, headed by Pralamba, were addressed with the words spoken by the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, to King Kaṃsa. || 7 ||
Then, O Mukunda, while you lay upon the birth-couch of Nanda’s beloved in the temple of Paśupati, as you cried out slightly with your feet twitching,
the women woke up and joyfully proclaimed the birth of a son;
oh, how can I describe the entire state of agitation that pervaded Gokula?

"Then" means: then, while you were crying—that is, weeping—in that lying-in chamber of the house of Nanda, the temple of the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), at which your feet were slightly bent, with your tender sprout-like feet moving just a little; || 8 ||
Oh, how wonderful! Yaśodā first drank you in with her eyes— eyes that captivated the heart with your fresh black beans—
and then, with joy, she immediately made you drink from her own full breasts.
In this world, those possessing merit have been surpassed by her touch, which captivates the mind. || 9 ||
"Ah! By Yaśodā—through the sight of you, your touch, the giving of her breast-milk, and so forth—even the meritorious sages have indeed been conquered and cast down; oh, how wonderful! (9)
Out of a desire for your welfare, what indeed did that cowherd Nanda, overwhelmed by a weight of joy, not bestow upon the assembly of brahmins at that time?
And likewise, why did the cowherds not perform auspicious rites?
O auspiciousness of the three worlds! protect me here from disease. || 10 ||
"Bhavaditi" means: out of a desire for your welfare, that is, out of a wish for your prosperity. || 10 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth decade, describing the bringing of Yogamāyā and other events.

Following that, having observed that Nanda—the abode of abundant auspiciousness—had gone to the royal city to pay tribute, your father spoke, as he had learned of the efforts of Kaṃsa’s allies. 1. Thus ends the thirty-ninth decade, describing the bringing of Yogamāyā and other events. Following that, having observed that Nanda—the abode of abundant auspiciousness—had gone to the royal city to pay tribute, your father spoke, as he had learned of the efforts of Kaṃsa’s allies. 1.

Regarding the phrase "tadanu" (thereafter): Your father Vasudeva, residing in the city of Mathurā, learned that Nanda—the abode of abundant auspiciousness and a mine of superhuman virtues—had gone to King Yadu to pay tribute, specifically to offer his annual sixth share of the produce; he was one who had witnessed the efforts of Kaṃsa’s allies, such as Pūtanā, Tṛṇāvarta, and others, in their zeal to slaughter all the children. || 1 ||
"O friend! Today your son's birth gladdens me as much as the birth of my own son.
Having thus addressed him with affection, he assumed the role of his father toward the leader of the Vraja people. || 2 ||

"O! Vasudeva did not say to Nanda, "The child staying in your house is my son," but rather, having established the status of fatherhood in Nanda—the leader of the Vraja—he spoke of him with reverence. It should be understood that this was done so that he might be protected with the same care as his own son. || 2 ||
"And here at the border of your kingdom, there are hundreds of omens of ill omen; therefore, depart quickly.
By these words of his, the leader of the travelers, fearing misfortune for you, departed in haste.
"Here," [he said]; hundreds of omens were ill-omened in the cow-pen at Kaṭakasī. || 3 ||
Before Nanda’s arrival at the cow-pen, he describes the entry into the settlement of Pūtanā, who was dressed in charming attire:
"At that very moment, a certain woman of sweet appearance, whose hair was fondled by restless bees, approached you, O deceptive infant, in the vicinity of the cow-pen. (4)

At that very moment, Pūtanā, born of the lineage of night-stalkers, her heart's consciousness stolen away, took you up while the inhabitants of Vraja were reflecting for a moment, "Who is this who has come here to slaughter us? || 5 ||
"Sapadi" means one who has stolen away the consciousness of the child; that is to say, a child-killer. || 5 ||

Unable to be restrained by young women whose hearts were captivated by the charms of her graceful movements, she sat within the house and offered her breast to you, who were disguised in a deceptive form.
"Lalita" means: being unable to be resisted or surpassed by the young cowherd girls, she sat down at the edge of the house and gave [the gift]. He whose self, mind, or form was deceptive. || 6 ||
Then, having climbed upon her lap without hesitation, you— provoked by the theft of your childhood toy—
sucked at her orb of breasts as if it were a large mango fruit, though it was tainted by bitter poison.

"Having mounted [him]": enraged by the stealing and killing of children, you sought to suckle him; having placed him in your mouth from the sour fruit and pressed him between your lips, you spat him out many times. (7)
Sounding with a voice like thunder, she suckled at your breast along with the [other] foul-smelling ones;
then, stretching out both her arms, she cast off her own terrifying form and departed.
"With foul breaths" means that she who possesses a cry resembling thunder, like the sound of a cloud, and who sucks—that is, drinks—along with her foul vital breaths, is thus described. (8)
When the cowherds were bewildered by hearing and seeing Your terrifying form with its fearsome roar, did not the gopīs seize You as You played upon their chests in the pastures of Vraja? (9)
"Bhayada" means: where the cowherds and cow-keepers were bewildered by hearing of his terrifying proclamations and by seeing his formidable form. || 9 ||

O Auspicious One of the World! You, whose protection has been manifoldly secured by young maidens through Your very names—O Lord whose abode is the wind! Make me, who am free from disease, Your servant. 10.
"Bhuvana" means making free from disease, that is, rendering healthy. || 10 ||
Thus ends the fortieth decade, containing the description of Nanda’s entry into Mathurā for the purpose of paying the annual taxes, and the description of the liberation of Pūtanā.
Having heard the words of Śauri, the Lord of Vraja returned along the road with a heart filled with fear.
Having beheld some object that had crushed every tree without exception, he has come to you for refuge. || 1 ||

"Go away! he cried, while Śauri (Vasudeva) said, "And here there are hundreds of omens. As they were returning and approaching their own home, all the trees within a distance of two gavyūtis were completely crushed and pulverized by the force of his falling. Amidst such a calamity, the child—who was unable to discern what that certain object was because of its immense size and because it had never been seen before—wandered about; and being helpless, he sought refuge in you alone for your protection, taking you as his protector. || 1 ||
Having heard the news from the words of the cowherd women, all the cowherds, blinded by fear and wonder,
then beheld from afar that terrible body of the piśāca, severed by your axe.

Having heard this news—the account of Pūtanā—they were struck with fear at the sight of her terrible form, yet they were filled with wonder that she had been felled by you. Then, having cut her into pieces with many axes at a distance and carried her far away, they reduced her body to ashes. || 2 ||
Indeed, from your body, whose breasts have been sucked dry, a very thick smoke rises;
it has caused doubt among the Agaru trees as to whether this is [smoke] from them, or from sandalwood, or perhaps from guggulu resin. (3)

"From you" (tvaditi): The meaning is "from that body of Pūtanā which had become composed of pure *sattva* due to its being drunk by You; for when passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) dissolved, it became pure *sattva*, and thus her body—serving as the locus for Your breast and because the Lord ascended onto her lap—had attained the state of being composed of pure *sattva*. For this very reason, since smoke is an effect of *sattva*, there was no suspicion that it was from incense or the like. (3)
"The fruit of contact with my limbs will not be far off; it shall belong to you all in an instant.
Uttering these words to the cowherd maidens, you caused Pūtanā to emit a sweet fragrance.

"Maditi! For me, the fruit of that bodily contact which occurs during the placing of the *brahmamaya* mark, my caressing, and so forth, is liberation—not far off in another birth—just as it was for this *piśācī* who desired to kill me. For you, whose minds are solely intent on my welfare (*yoga-kṣema*), [it shall come] in a moment. Thus speaking to the most excellent of cowherds (*vallava-tallaja*), those preeminent cowherds by virtue of their good fortune, you made Pūtanā fragrant, solely for the purpose of providing them with perfect awakening. || 4 ||
"It is wonderful that the prince was not killed by the Piśācī! It is wonderful that Śauri had already told us this!
Thus praising, the cowherd folk indeed immersed themselves in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of beholding your face. (5)

Regarding the word "wonderful" (citram): previously, by means of the verse beginning with "And here there are hundreds of omens," this fear was told—that is, spoken—by Śauri Vasudeva. Thus, praising Śauri, [the king] sank—that is, became immersed—in that aesthetic flavor (rasa), which is bliss, upon beholding your face. || 5 ||
Day by day, O Vāsudeva, this Vraja— its prosperity ever-increasing and its hundreds of auspicious signs undiminished through your residence there— shone forth on all sides, dense with joy.
"Day by day... and so forth. By the phrase "the Vraja, the people of Vraja, were everywhere dense with joy," the excess of bliss experienced even by the moving and stationary beings is expressed. (6)
In their homes, who else could have so greatly rejoiced every day, filled with tender smiles, mutual laughter, and conversation,
while attending to their duties under your watchful gaze?

"In the houses" means: filled with the mutual conversation of tender forms and smiles, and thus occupied with activity; "when they have ceased" means when these activities have come to an end. || 7 ||
"Aha! The prince has cast his gaze upon me; Vatsaka has smiled toward me.
'Come, come to me!'—stretching out his hand, O Lord, what indeed have you not done for us, your brides? (8)

"Aho! O Lord Viṣṇu! While you were in the form of a cowherd boy, what did those young brides not do for you—placing you on their laps, embracing, kissing, caressing, and so forth? Aho! They have reached the pinnacle of fortune; such is the meaning. (8)
Out of curiosity to touch your body, the cowherd women passed you from hand to hand;
thus you were led until you reached the beauty of a trembling, hanging scale-beam adorned with a garland of slightly reddish lotuses.

"Bhavaditi" means that because the succession of hands of the womenfolk resembled a garland of red lotuses, and because you were like a restless bee (lolamba) greedy for fresh honey clinging to them, you attained equality with them; this is the meaning.
O Hari! Protect me, who am like a cow; for what state did Yaśodā not experience while she was feeding you at her breast, gazing upon your face as you smiled? 10.

"Feeding [him]" means: what state—of what kind—did Yaśodā not experience? That is, what condition consisting of wonder, eagerness, fear of misfortune, supplication to the gods, helplessness, and so forth, did she not attain? || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-first decade, describing the burning of Pūtanā’s body and the description of the unsurpassed joy of Yaśodā and others through the fondling of the Child.
Once, O Lord, on the day of Your birth-star, the invited kinsmen, their wives, and the Brahmins—
Having placed you nearby in the kitchen, that mistress of Vraja turned toward the front of the kitchen.

"Kadāpi" means: she by whom kinsmen, invited guests, their daughters-in-law, and Brahmins were summoned; for her, [the task] proceeded—that is, it was undertaken—in the great kitchen, the large cart, and so forth, such as the cooking house. || 1 ||
Then, from your presence, the crackling sound of splintering wood was heard mingled with the tumultuous cries of the boys appointed as your protectors, who were shouting in terror. || 2 ||

The word *alāsīt* is derived from the root *lā*, meaning "to take," in the *luṅ* (past) tense. Regarding the word *tataḥ*: due to the loud cries of many children who had been appointed by Yaśodā for the protection and guarding of Your infant, and because of their terror arising from the *caṭacaṭā* sound of the cart's collapse, there arose a tumultuous din. Mixed with these intensified clamors, the roar of the wooden parts of the cart whose joints had been shattered was heard—that is, it was heard by Yaśodā and the others. || 2 ||
Then, their breasts trembling with the agitation and exhaustion of hearing that news,
the women of Vajra beheld you from all sides, situated amidst the dreadful wood as it was being split apart.

"Then" means: upon hearing that, as before, they were trembling with the agitation of wondering "What is this? and with the exhaustion of running from their respective homes toward the house of Nanda; with the weight of their breasts shaking, they saw [the chariot] situated amidst the falling, harsh, and massive wooden parts of the vehicle—such as the axle, the pole, and other components—scattered everywhere within the interior of the house. || 3 ||
"Alas, what has happened to the child? crying out thus, Nanda, the cowherds, and the brahmins ran forward in haste;
beholding you held by Yaśodā, they took heart, their eyes moist with tears.
Regarding the word "of the infant": Nanda and the others, having rushed forward and arrived with speed, beheld Yaśodā holding the lifted [child] and were comforted—that is, they took heart. || 4 ||
"Who indeed is this person from nowhere, this great wonder, that this massive cart has been torn asunder?
There is no cause for this here," they stood saying, their hands placed over their noses, gazing at you.

"Who is this? "Who indeed? From where? Who, who? Of what sort? From whence? From what cause has he come? The repetition [of the question] is due to agitation. "Viśaṅkaṭam" means expanded; it has been split open by someone, its parts torn asunder. There is no reason for this here, since this child possesses such inconceivable power that he has placed his hand upon his own nose—this is the manifestation of the emotion of wonder. || 5 ||

"O Lord! We saw this child crying for his mother's breast; our lotus-like feet were struck by him as he wept, and because of that, our minds became agitated," so sang those boys who were his guardians.
"Of the young boy"—his mind was struck by the lotus-feet of the boy, and he became one whose limbs were overturned; "I have seen him! I too have seen him! thus the children cried out. (6)
Then, out of fear, this most difficult speech uttered by the boys—who were ignorant of your power—was suspected to some extent by those who had previously seen Pūtanā. (7)

"Out of fear!"—this statement is extremely difficult to reconcile and utterly untenable. The reason for this is: "by the children, the infants, especially at that time, who out of fear did not know anything at all. This was uttered by certain people who were ignorant of, or unacquainted with, your power and capacity; it was said by Nanda, Upananda, and others who had previously seen the Pūtanā incident, and who merely suspected that "this has happened in such a way because of your power," though only slightly. || 7 ||
"Is this foot wounded and copper-red like a coral sprout? Or have these hands, once as beautiful as lotuses, been torn?
Thus, with waves of compassion spreading forth, the women touched your limbs. (8)

Saying, "Is your foot wounded or bruised? Are your hands scarred or broken? the women—the cowherd girls—trembled with compassion as they proceeded to wipe away the continuous streams of tears caused by her [the heroine's] distress; thus, with their bodies quivering, they touched your limbs very gently. || 8 ||
"O child, grant me protection today from falling into the waves of the Lord of the World's compassion!
Thus saying, your father, his throat constricted by emotion, would repeatedly embrace your little body and press it to him. (9)

"Alas!"—this was uttered upon the certain realization of calamity, arising from seeing things as they truly were, when that which was unforeseen had arrived. "By the falling of a wave of grace from Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, through the attainment of a mere fragment of His compassion, my son has today reached his deliverance and is protected"; thus did the father Nanda lament. (9)
It is said that Aniruddha, the enemy of the gods, came here intending to kill you, yet he was destroyed by you in this manner;
not even a speck of his dust was seen—how then could he have surely dissolved into you, who are of pure essence?
"Anonilīna" means merged into that very form. Now, an objection might be raised: "It was said that he was destroyed;

how then is not even a particle (*rajas*) of this demon Śakaṭāsura seen? Anticipating this doubt, he says "He" (*sa*). "I am certain that that Daitya has indeed merged into You while still possessing his body. Since not even a particle is seen, what need is there to speak of his gross form? The meaning is that the statement that he merged into You upon the dissolution of both *rajas* and *tamas* is logically sound. || 10 ||

O Lord of the City of the Maruts! Having been specially honored there by the twice-born and having received their auspicious blessings, please destroy my afflictions while deluding Vraja with Your own childhood pastimes. 11.

Regarding the phrase "by those who have worshipped": you, whose auspicious blessings and favors have been especially bestowed and brought forth by them out of fear of future calamity—such as you, please destroy (jahīhi), that is, abandon, my disease (rujām). || 11 ||
Thus ends the forty-second decad, including the one [following], describing the slaying of the demon Śakaṭāsura.
O Lord of Gurumahatpura! Once, unable to bear you as you had assumed an exceedingly heavy weight, she—
Having laid [the child] upon the bed, the mother, wondering "What is this? and filled with apprehension, remained motionless within the house, lost in thought.

"Regarding the word *tvām*: Your mother Yaśodā, unable (*apārayantī*) to lift you—who had attained an exceedingly great weight (*gāḍhādhirūḍhagarimāṇam*)—from her lap onto the bed, placed you there and remained with the thought, 'Alas, what is this?'; thus, filled with apprehension, she stayed within the house meditating upon you. || 1 ||

At that very distance, that preeminent Daitya named Tṛṇāvarta—whose form was like a whirlwind, who had filled the quarters with masses of dust swelling from his terrible roar, and who had drawn near your ears—indeed carried you away, you who steal the hearts of all people. 2.

The suffix *ac* is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) by means of a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *ac*, according to the opinion of Padmanābha. Alternatively, the word *āśis* itself, ending in the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense, is incorporated into the compound because [the class] beginning with *prajñā* is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Regarding the word *tāvat*: it refers to you, who possess a whirlwind (*vātyā*)—a mass of wind known as *tṛṇāvarta*—which captivates the minds of people; that very whirlwind has carried you away. (2) You are one by whom the ten directions have been filled with a terrifying roar heard from afar and with a burgeoning mass of dust that has spread far and wide. You, O whirlwind, have indeed carried him away. (2)
In this world of herdsmen, whose vision is struck by the darkness of unrestrained dust and who are unskilled in seeing anything at all—
alas, why has she come to your side for the sake of a mere child?
Not seeing you, your mother wept bitterly. || 3 ||
"Uddāmeti": His range of vision was struck by two unrestrained [clouds] of dust and darkness; therefore, being unable and incompetent to see anything, he asks, "What has happened to the boy? || 3 ||

Then that foremost of Dānavas, his form wretched and his momentum shattered by the weight of the devotee’s embrace, fell into a crouch; immediately thereafter, amidst the sound of the dust raised by his retreat,
the cry of your mother spread throughout Ghoṣa.

"At that time" means: with a dejected form, his body exhausted; by bearing the weight—the heaviness—of yours (bhāvatka), his speed was cut off, his momentum for movement destroyed, and he fell into contraction, a state of motionlessness. Thereafter, immediately following that, he spread out and pervaded that cowherd settlement (ghoṣa), a place where the dust and noise had subsided. || 4 ||
Upon hearing the sound of the weeping from the families of cowherds headed by Nanda as they returned home in distress,
the wretched Dānava, desiring liberation, released you— who grant liberation to all— from the expanse of the sky and fell down.

He weeps; having approached Yaśodā’s house because of hearing her lamentation, he is distressed and his life is ebbing away, desiring to release you who are bound around the neck with his arms. || 5 ||

Thereafter, the groups of cowherds, crowded together, beheld his body—extremely massive—falling upon the surface of a stone slab outside; alas, they saw him laughing heartily, yet remaining unharmed upon his chest.

He cried out. Then they beheld Tṛṇāvarta’s exceedingly massive and even bulkier body falling down, and they beheld you also falling upon his chest; because he was laughing heartily, they beheld both with eyes that were not at all diminished [in their wonder]. || 6 ||
Approaching You— who were laughing boldly over the wicked Danuja fallen from his massive body crushed by the falling of the pressing-stones—
and who were striking him with Your lotus-hand, the cowherds took You up as if they had retrieved a sapphire from the peak of a great mountain.

"Grāva! [They cried. The cowherds lifted up the one who was laughing with a feigned smile, his lotus-hand moving as if striking the wicked demon—who had lost his life-breaths from that most massive body crushed and pulverized by the falling of the pressing-stones and the impact of their stone surfaces—in order to make the gods in heaven believe, "He has been killed by me," as he struck him with his lotus-hand. || 7 ||
We bow to you, who were embraced and kissed by the cowherds of Nanda’s village as they each quickly and joyfully seized you;
and who, when the lotus-hands of the cowherd women suspected you of wishing to take [their garments], fell down [in surrender]. 8.

"One by one" means: his limbs—each one such as the soft hands and feet—were grasped and simultaneously embraced and kissed by Nanda and the others, who were intensely and exceedingly rejoicing and delighted. He fell even before their hands could be extended, landing upon the lotus-like hands of the cowherd women who, fearing "she wishes to seize me," had been apprehensive; thus he threw them into a state of agitation. (8)
"Furthermore, what indeed shall we do?

May Govinda alone, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, protect our son"—this is the meaning of "we shall do. [The root] *kṛ* [is used here] in the sense of "to do" or "to act," as in the rule: *kṛvi hiṃsākaraṇayośca* ("the root *kṛ* is used in the senses of harming and doing").
Thus addressed at that time by his mother, father, and others, O Lord, you alone [resolved] for the sake of protecting the world. || 9 ||
"Furthermore": May Govinda, who is indeed Viṣṇu, protect our son once again in such perils as these. || 9 ||
O Lord of the abode of the wind, while thus shaking this demon who is of the nature of wind,
why do you not shake away my deep-seated ailments born of wind?
Or rather, what more can I do, O Lord of the wind’s dwelling?
I repeatedly entreat you for the complete pacification of all diseases. || 10 ||

"O Vāta! [He says: "O Lord of the abode of the wind (Anilālayeśa)! While you are indeed the wind-natured one who agitates and restrains Tṛṇāvarta, why do you not shake away my diseases born of the wind, even though you reside in the wind and possess the power to restrain it? If you say, 'Is it because of the fault of my own prārabdha-karma? then what can I do?

Or rather, I pray for and entreat even liberation—the complete pacification of all external diseases such as wind and so forth, as well as internal diseases such as passion and so forth—through the falling away of both the gross and subtle bodies at the conclusion of prārabdha. || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-third decade, the description of the slaying of Tṛṇāvarta.
Now, with a decade of verses, he shows the account of Garga’s naming ceremony and birth rites:
"In order to perform the sacraments for you, who are beyond ritual action, at the secret word of Vasudeva..."
O Lord! The sage Garga, who knows the true nature of the heart and the day-and-night cycle, has come to your house.

Regarding the word "secretly" (gūḍham): although [the child] is in reality devoid of action, one who has internalized the truth of the day and night and has correctly understood the true nature of the science of astrology should perform the purificatory rites, such as the naming ceremony, from the perspective of worldly convention. || 1 ||
Then Nanda, his soul delighted, honoring that foremost among self-restrained ascetics,
spoke with words moistened by a gentle smile, his mind eager to perform the purificatory rites for him.
"Nanda"—one whose soul is joyful and contented, honoring and worshipping according to the prescribed rites the most eminent among the self-restrained sages. || 2 ||

O Noble One! Speaking thus, "This task must be performed with great secrecy because you are the preceptor of the Yadu lineage," Garga, his hair standing on end with thrill, recited the names of you and your elder brother.

Regarding the phrase "yadviti": because I am the preceptor of the Yadu lineage, Kaṃsa might suspect that your son has been consecrated by me; therefore, to avoid this, this task must be performed with great secrecy and extreme concealment. [He is one] whose hair stands on end from the touch of you. || 3 ||
"How shall I give a name to this one who indeed possesses a thousand names or even infinite names?"—
certainly it was with these thoughts that the sage Garga bestowed a secret name upon you in private, O Lord! (4)
"How so? "How indeed shall I make names for one whose names are infinite? When asked how he made certain names, what could he say? Thus dejected, the sage made a name for you in secret. (4)
He explains the etymology of the name Kṛṣṇa:

"The Seer (Ṛṣi) fashioned the name 'Kṛṣṇa' for you by means of the verbal root *kṛṣ* and the letter *ṇa*, expressing either your existence, bliss, and essential nature (*sattā-ānanda-ātmatā*), or your state of having consumed the world. (Verse 5)

Regarding the word *kṛṣi*: the verbal root *kṛṣ* denotes existence (*sattā*), and the letter *ṇa* denotes bliss (*ānanda*). Through their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the name *Kṛṣṇa* expresses the nature of existence and bliss and thus denotes the Supreme Brahman. The particle *kila* here indicates its well-known status in the Purāṇas. As it has been said:
"The word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and *ṇa* denotes bliss (*nirvṛti*);
the unity of these two is the Supreme Brahman, designated as *Kṛṣṇa*."

Thus [it is said]. Alternatively, he provides the etymological derivation (nirvacana) that Kṛṣṇa is so called because he "draws away" (karṣati) the sin (agha) of the worlds—this is expressed by the word "jagat. The word "kathayat" is an adjective qualifying the name. || 5 ||
Explaining other distinctions of names, such as Rāma and others who were his elder brothers,
he described your superhuman majesty while concealing it from his father.

"Others" refers to Vāsudeva and others. While explaining [the name] by describing its etymological significance (*anvarthatayā*), he previously said: "Once this son of yours was unknown to Vasudeva; therefore, let his name be Vāsudeva. Furthermore, without revealing to his father Nanda that Viṣṇu possessed superhuman power (*atimānuṣānubhāva*)—existing beyond the reach of ordinary men—he spoke to him from the perspective of the birth-ritual (*jātaka*). || 6 ||
Regarding this, he said:
"He who feels affection for your son is not deluded by further sorrows born of illusion;
but he who bears him malice shall perish. Thus did that best of sages proclaim your greatness. (7)

"He feels affection" means this: he who feels affection for Your son—that is, he who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa—is not overwhelmed by "sorrows," which are illusory; he does not experience the suffering of birth, death, and so forth. But he who bears malice toward Your son—that is, he who is turned away from Kṛṣṇa—shall perish and remain a transmigrating soul. This is the meaning: the best of sages spoke of Your greatness in the form of a hidden significance. || 7 ||
"He shall conquer many Daityas and lead his own kinsmen to the stainless state;
you shall hear of his most pure glories"—thus did the Sage speak of your future glory.

"He shall conquer. He will lead—that is, cause you to attain—the stainless state of the partless Brahman. This world shall hear the exceedingly pure, sin-destroying glories of this son of yours, and [he shall attain] your own prosperity and sovereign power. || 8 ||
"By this very [means] you shall cross over all difficulties; remain here with confidence," thus did that sage describe you, saying "It is Hari alone," and so forth.

"By this very son, you shall cross over all difficulties and the multitude of calamities; you will cross them. Thus he spoke. "Remain with this son, showing him honor and respect as is fitting; do not be negligent toward him. Without explicitly saying, "This is Hari," the sage Garga described the entire purpose of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s incarnation, addressing [Nanda] in these words. || 9 ||
Now that Garga has departed, O Lord of Śrīmarutpura, you who gladden Nanda and others and whose compassion has been aroused by my affliction, please release me from my fetters.
"Garga": O you who are being celebrated and cherished by Nanda and the others who are delighted and joyful, drive away—that is, eliminate—my gad, my disease. || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth decade, describing the birth-rites and naming ceremony of Kṛṣṇa.
O Murāri, accompanied by Balarāma, with the movements of your hands and knees—
Adorning certain parts of the palace, you two, your lotus-like feet set in motion and filled with curiosity to hear the sweet tinkling of your anklets, moved about gracefully with great speed. (1)

"O! [she cried]. Moving from one part of the palace—such as the porticoes and other areas—by means of the movements of their hands and knees, that is, by crawling on both hands and both knees, they adorned those places for some time, as they did not remain long in any single spot. Since their lotus-feet were moving, and since they were filled with curiosity to hear the tinkling of their beautiful anklets, they therefore moved away with speed.
Gently smiling with their teeth slightly visible, their hair falling over their faces, and the regions of their lotus-feet visible;
with the marks of bracelets upon their wrists as they let go of the serpents clinging to their arms—
Behold the most exalted and great wisdom of all people in the universe. || 2 ||

"Softly," [it is said]. Looking at one another from time to time, they were smiling very gently; for that very reason, their budding teeth were visible, appearing as a few emerging tooth-buds. Their lotus-feet were beautiful to behold, marked with the signs of the banner and the thunderbolt (dhvaja-vajra) which became visible when they drew back their two feet. Because the bracelets on their wrists had slipped down from the upper part of their arms, they acquired a secondary beauty (parabhāga); you two have carried away—meaning you surpassed—the lofty minds of all men. (2)
They follow along with the throngs of people whose eyes are agitated by curiosity,
making some sound and laughing aloud as they run;
with their lotus-faces turned back, they cast glances behind them.
O Vāsudeva! What wonder do you two not perform? || 3 ||

"Anviti": While the multitude of people was following behind, you two, running with speed—that is, moving swiftly—cast your glances backward from that distance where the crowd remained, with your lotus-faces turned sideways (tiryak-kṛta-mukha-padma), as if creating an exceeding sense of curiosity, meaning you aroused great wonder as to what it could be. || 3 ||
As they fell and rose again with swift motion upon the muddy ground, being praised with smiles by the mud-free sages in the sky,
they were then quickly taken up with compassion by their two mothers.
Again and again you two were embraced and quickly kissed. || 4 ||

"Swiftly... [The commentary explains: While they were moving swiftly with great speed through the mud of Vraja, the sages who had come to the heavens to witness them said with smiles, "These two are capable of making even us free from mud; yet, fearing a fall themselves, they seek refuge in those very ones who are falling down. Thus they were being praised, [the sages exclaiming], "Oh, the dependence of the two Lords upon their devotees! || 4 ||

O Lord who feigns being a beast! How exceedingly blessed is Yaśodā, whose fickle mind now holds you—who bear the weight of full breasts—upon her lap as she gives you milk; for amidst you, there is the sprout of a charming smile.
Seeing her face, which was charming with its budding teeth, he rejoiced.

"She has milked," it is said. "In whom the pair of breasts has milked—that is, from which milk has flowed"—and "in whom the mind is tremulous and overwhelmed with compassion"—these are adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa). Thus, she who holds you on her lap and gives you milk, that Yaśodā is most blessed of the blessed. O you, the deceptive beast! She rejoiced—became satisfied—upon seeing your face, in which there was a charming sprout of a smile, a gentle laugh, lovely with its budding teeth even amidst the drinking of breast-milk. || 1 ||
Thereafter, moving about on foot and full of childish restlessness, you played with the boys in the rows of nearby houses;
chasing the domestic parrots, cats, and calves, you were somehow turned back by the cowherds who laughed at you.
Regarding the phrase "tadanu": he was wandering, moving about, through the rows of dwellings—the interior apartments—situated nearby. || 6 ||

He says that because the gopīs’ minds were focused solely on following you, they even forgot their household duties and so forth: "Wherever you went together with Haladhara, there the gopīs fell helplessly, their eyes fixed upon you."
O Slayer of Mura! With their household duties fallen away and their children and servants forgotten, they remained perpetually and utterly distressed.
He says that you even performed dances and other acts for the sake of being seen by them, desiring fresh butter and other offerings given by the gopīs:
"Desiring fresh butter offered by the gopīs at every turn, singing sweetly with soft words and dancing here and there..."
In some places you ate ghee offered by compassionate young women,
and in others you drank even freshly boiled milk.
"I had indeed intended to make my request here at the house of Bala; however, I shall not do so before these women.
Having resolved thus, O Lord, why did you abandon that request and take the curd and ghee by means of a beautiful theft? 9.

"‘Mine’—formerly, a request was made by me at the house of Bali. Let that matter rest; it was due to Bali’s very power that it did not result in our humiliation. But here, in the presence of those who are the opposite—those who are weak—I shall not do so. Thus resolved in mind and determined in heart, he proceeded with the act of theft through a charming, multiform stratagem of stealing. || 9 ||
O Lord of the Abode of Wind! When you stole the curd and ghee of the women of the cowherd settlement, anger found no place in their hearts, nor did grief;
having stolen even their very hearts, you placed them in an ocean of joy—please pacify my diseases.

"O you who plundered!"—in you, the plunderer of curds, clarified butter, cowherd hamlets, and cowherd women, anger and grief found no room or place upon the loss of their property. Why was this so? To this he says: "The heart. Having plundered—that is, having carried it away. [An objection: Surely, where the stolen heart is, there anger and grief would certainly find a place. To this he replies: "In the ocean of joy. Just as it is impossible for fire to enter wood situated in water, so too, in the heart situated within that ocean of joy, there is no room even for anger and grief, which are its opposites. This is the sense. || 10 ||
Then, seeing the moon at the tip of a branch and repeatedly entreating his mother and father that it was a fruit, you raised both your arms at their word;
O Lord, it is a marvel that the moon entered your hand! What can we say? As its entire body was filled by the falling orb of light, it first assumed the form of Virāṭ.

O Father, having for a moment immersed me—who was seized with the agitation of wondering "What is this? What indeed is this?"—in the ocean of Brahman, and then again spreading forth the illusion consisting of delusion regarding Your son, O You who are composed of bliss and consciousness, O You who are identical with the universe, protect me from disease! 12.
Thus ends the forty-fifth decade, consisting of fifty-six verses, describing Kṛṣṇa’s childhood sports.
O Lord! Long ago, while you were still a suckling infant lying on your back, a cowherd woman beheld the entire universe within your mouth as it opened wide during a yawn. (1)

"O, my Lord! O You who are devoted to play, when You were still in Your earliest childhood, while You—the manifest Lord Yourself—were lying on Your back with Your face turned upwards, Yaśodā, the cowherd woman, beheld the entire universe within Your mouth as it was opened wide during the state of yawning, while she herself was nursing at Your breast. (1)
Furthermore, O Lord of the World, while you were once engaged in play with the children, the boys, provoked by your deception regarding the collection of fruit, said, "You eat earth! (2)
"Punar" means: again, when some time has further elapsed, [I shall see you] together with the children.

"O All-pervading Lord! At the time of universal dissolution, when you devour the entire world including earth, water, and all else, will not pain arise from even a slight morsel of food? Thinking thus, his mother became afraid and grew angry. (3)

"O friend! 'Pralayāvadhi' means that which has the dissolution (pralaya) as its limit. He whose nature it is to devour the entire cosmic manifestation (prapañca), beginning with the earth, at every dissolution—just as he does every day—for him, pain or disease might arise from eating soft food, namely, by consuming even a mere morsel of earth. || 3 ||
"O you of ill-behaved nature! Alas, my child, have you indeed eaten clay?"—to these words of his mother, O Lord, you long replied with a laugh, "It is false! (4)
"O, you have made a false and meaningless vow. || 4 ||
