"O, if you have any doubt despite this being determined by all [of us], let your mouth be torn open! Thus rebuked by your mother, you tore open your face, which resembled a blooming lotus.

"O child! Since all your friends and your elder brother have unanimously decided upon this soft food, if you alone have a dissenting opinion or a dispute, then open your mouth—tear it wide—to dispel our doubt. Thus rebuked and reproached by your mother, you opened [your mouth] so that it resembled a blooming lotus. || 5 ||
As if greatly satisfying his mother, who was eager to see even a fragment of clay,
he beheld not only the entire earth, but all the worlds as well.
"O! [he said], and while greatly satisfying and gladdening [him], you showed yourself; you manifested yourself.
In one place a forest, in another the ocean, in another the clouds, and in another the netherworld;
in one place humans, in another demons, and in another the gods—what was not seen then within your face?
"Kuhacid" means somewhere or in some part within you. || 7 ||
How many times did she not behold you in her own mouth— lying in the ocean of the *kalaśa* vessel, then dwelling in the realm of the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, and again as her own child within her own city?

Regarding the word "kalaśa": how many times did she not behold You—who recline upon the ocean-jar (the milk-ocean), who lie upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk, and who, thereafter, dwell in the state of Para-Baikuntha—standing right before her in Your own form as her child, in the guise of Yaśodā’s son? || 8 ||
Now, it was said that Yaśodā saw her own son within the mouth of her own son; yet, one might wonder whether worlds exist within his mouth as well or not. To address this doubt, he says:

"Within the mouth’s interior where worlds were blossoming, you indeed appeared once more with a face of the same kind; clearly beheld by her, O Lord, you have brought about an infinite regress of worlds! (9)

Regarding the word *vikasat*: that in which the worlds blossom is "the blossoming world" (*vikasadbhuvana*), meaning the manifested universe; [He] whose mouth—that face of such a blossoming world—is thus [described], that Lord was clearly and distinctly beheld by her. [She beheld] the instability and endlessness of the worlds, of the cosmic manifestations. This is the meaning: Yaśodā saw the universe and her own son within the mouth of her son.

He saw the world and his own son within the mouth of that son as well; again, it was the same for that one, and again for that one too—just as there is an infinite regress of mirrors containing reflections of mirrors, you have thus established an infinite regress of worlds. || 9 ||

Then, momentarily deluding his mother—who possessed a mind fixed on the ultimate truth—with affection, he cried out, "O Mother, give me the breast! and approached her; "O Blessed One, O Lord of the wondrous hair-tuft, protect me! (10)

Regarding the word *dhṛta*: because one can see within its interior many Brahmāṇḍas as well as the Vaikuṇṭha-loka situated outside them, it is beyond even that external Prakṛti; it is Brahman alone, non-dual in existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). [The Lord] deludes [the world] by manifesting Himself through His yogic power in the form of "My son. Thus, for a moment, she held her realization of reality—that is, perfect knowledge—firmly. While she was clinging to Him, desiring to climb onto His lap, O wonderful Child, You were like a mirror reflecting many Brahmāṇḍas! 10.
Thus ends the forty-sixth decade, the description of the manifestation of the universal form.
Once, you approached your mother as she was churning curd; desiring her breast-milk, you climbed onto her lap and drank from her two breasts while she tried to ward you off.

"At one time" (*ekadā*): "one who performs the churning of curd"—that is, the act of agitating it—is so described. "Having approached" (*samupasedivān*) means having come near. "Having come to the lap" (*aṅkam etya*) means having climbed up; "preventing the churning of the curd"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 1 ||
O Lord! while you, whose face is sweet with a gentle smile and whose budding breasts are half-drunk, were thus, your mother went quickly to catch the milk flowing from the fire.

She says, "Half-drink": while your bud-like breast is half-sipped and you remain unsated, and while your lotus-face is sweet with a tender smile as you move your cheeks between your mother's fingers. || 2 ||
Alas, O Lord! With a mind overwhelmed by the weight of anger arising from the breaking of the vessel of half-cooked rice-pudding, you seized the churning-stick and shattered the pot of curd.
"Sāmī" means: he whose mind was overcome—that is, possessed—by the weight of anger incurred through the interruption and cessation of the flow of the milk that had been partially drunk. || 3 ||
Then, hearing that loud sound rising up, his mother ran toward it;
she immediately saw curd spread upon the ground, like the spreading radiance of your fame.

"Uccalatīti": Having heard the sound—a loud, resonant noise rising up intensely from the breaking of the full water-jars—she rushed forward with speed. "The expansion of fame" refers to its pervasiveness. By the statement that she saw [the butter] immediately upon rushing there, it is implied that you had gone elsewhere for the purpose of stealing the fresh butter. || 4 ||
Not seeing you, whom she had been searching for with anger while following the path of the Vedas,
that virtuous woman beheld you being given butter-milk to drink by a mortar.

She perceived: that Yaśodā, searching with anger—and not with devotion—for You, whom the sages had sought through the paths of the Vedas consisting of the three divisions (*kāṇḍas*) yet had not seen, beheld You clearly with her eyes. Therefore, she was a woman of merit, for she saw You standing on Your front paw upon the mortar placed beneath the vessel of butter, while butter was being given to a cat. || 5 ||
Seizing you, alas, with the lotus of her face radiant with the dawning of fear, she— her countenance flushed with anger— quickly took up her girdle before her friends for the purpose of binding you.

"Tvām iti": [The phrase] "you"—referring to you whose lotus-face is radiant with the manifestation of fear as if in a dramatic performance (*nāṭya*). She is one whose face is marked by various signs of anger, such as the knitting of the brows, the biting of the lips, and the redness of the eyes. In the presence of her friends, that is, before them, she [seized] the girdle, which is like a noose (*pāśa*). || 6 ||
Seeking a kinsman, that noble lady sought you as her kinsman; having fastened many cords of her girdle, she indeed looked [at you] until she saw that you were short by a finger-breadth.

"O Lord! Yaśodā, desiring to bind you—who are the very kinsman whom a virtuous person seeking liberation desires as a refuge—with a rope, has applied many strands of her waist-cord to your body; yet, because [your body] is ever so slightly less than eight finger-breadths [in height], she has repeatedly applied the cord, and indeed, she has seen that the entire length of the waist-cord remains eight finger-breadths short. (7)

Beholding her, whose body was perspiring and languid, watched by her friends who smiled in wonder, O Hari! though your own form is eternally liberated, you indeed consented to bondage out of compassion—how marvelous! (8)

"Vismitā" (astonished): She was gazed upon by her circle of friends, who were astonished—and for that very reason smiling—by the sight of her being lowered by two cubits; she whose body was perspiring, moist with sweat, and languid, exhausted. You, whose body is the eternally liberated Supreme Brahman, permitted even the binding—the very act of confinement—by means of the cords of her girdle. || 8 ||
When she came to the house saying, "O rogue, stay for a long time in the mortar," you then remained hidden within the cavity of the mortar with the ghee and the food offered to you.

"Stay! When she had bound you, saying, "O wicked one! You must stay in the mortar for a long time," and had returned to her home, then you remained—having stayed there—within the hollow of the previously placed mortar, eating ghee and fresh butter. || 9 ||
"O All-pervading Lord! If you are easily accessible even to those bound by fetters, how much more so to me who am already bound by this [worldly] snare!
Thus praised by the gods with such words, O Lord of the Wind, protect me from disease! 10.

"If"—meaning, for those who are *apāśāḥ*, having lost faith in sense objects, He is easily attainable (*sugamaḥ*), capable of being reached with ease. This being so, how indeed was He bound and fettered by this Yaśodā, who is *sapāśayā*, accompanied by a noose? || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh decade, the description of Kṛṣṇa’s binding to the mortar.
Having been joyfully addressed as "Dāmodara" by the sons of Mura, who were filled with noble delight, you—
whose belly was soft— laying yourself down at ease upon the mortar, gazed not far away toward the two Kakubha trees.

He was joyfully praised by the hosts of gods, who were already filled with great delight and overflowing with intense satisfaction; having addressed him as "Dāmodara" because he was bound within the belly of the serpent-demon [Dāma], they cried out that name. You, whose belly is soft and thus unfit for binding, having become attached to them at your own will and according to your pleasure, beheld two trees (kakubh) upon which you had clung. || 1 ||
The two sons of Kubera, known as Nalakuvara and the other as Maṇigrīva,
having attained prosperity through the service of Maheśa, sported for a long time, intoxicated by their wealth and indeed averse to you.

"Kubera," it is said; the other son became renowned as Maṇigrīva. Intoxicated by the prosperity obtained through service to Maheśa (Śiva), they both became arrogant and, turning away from you—turning away from Viṣṇu—they indeed roamed about. || 2 ||
It is said that on the banks of the celestial river, those two, intoxicated with passion and surrounded by many young women singing along the celestial river, were naked and intent on amorous play;
Nārada, whose mind was solely devoted to Your feet, beheld them.
"Yes," he said. On the celestial river Gaṅgā, surrounded by a vast multitude of young women singing, he beheld your feet—the sole object of his devotion, upon which his heart was fixed. || 3 ||

Although they had already beheld their beloved before them, appearing as if clothed in fear, the two of them—whose minds were blinded by passion—the Sage spoke this peace for the sake of achieving tranquility through devotion to you; for without peace, whence can there be happiness?

"Out of fear"—out of fear of a curse, he [Nārada] cursed the beloved group of women who had put on their respective garments; that is, the assembly of their wives. "Devotion to you" means devotion to Viṣṇu, and "tranquility" (upaśānti) means the restraint of the mind from such actions. For the sake of achieving these two, the sage Nārada sang—that is, he uttered the curse. Now, what is the fruit of tranquility? To this he says: "Tranquility," meaning that without it, there is no happiness, which is liberation (mokṣa). || 4 ||
"Having long beheld Hari, you two attained the state of *kakubha* trees and then reached your own abode"—
addressed thus, the two, filled with a longing for the sight of Bhava, became *kakubha* trees at the edge of Vraja.

"O you two! [referring to the two Arjuna trees]—having assumed the nature of *kakubha* trees and the form of a pair of *arjuna* trees; then, having beheld Hari Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you both attained your own place in the presence of Kubera. || 5 ||

The two trees, long worn out and shaken by the striking against the mortar, were brought to an end— trees such as those you once approached with an unwearied pair of Indradru horses, while moving with such sluggish gait.

Regarding the word *atandram*: in such a manner, the pair of *indradru* trees—the twin Arjuna trees—having met with the mortar that had become slow-moving and sluggish due to being dragged [by them], and which was thus *atandram*, meaning full of energy; by the obstruction of the mortar which had moved transversely (*tirāyita*), their roots were shaken loose and torn out; they became worn out over a long time, ancient, and were felled, having been brought down on all sides because their spreading branches and sub-branches had fallen. || 6 ||

O Govinda! When you split that very pair of trees by emerging from their interior, at that very moment you too were honored with hymns of praise by the two Yakṣas of great luster who had come forth from within them.

Regarding the word *abhāji*: when the pair of trees was *abhāji*—that is, broken by you—then you too were *abhāji*, meaning served with hymns of praise (*stavaiḥ*) by a pair of Yakṣas who emerged from within the interior of that pair of trees, possessing great splendor (*mahatī dyutiḥ*). Here, it is understood that the broken pair of trees assumed human form and paid their respects in return. (7)

Even though he is devoted to another here, he will gradually come to you; for these two are indeed servants of Rudra, who have arrived at your feet through the grace of the Sage, seeking supreme devotion.

"Here" means: in this world, even one who is a devotee—a servant—of others such as Brahmā, Giriśa, and so forth, whose forms consist of three or two *guṇas*, shall gradually, by way of the sequence of qualification, approach you, whose form is pure *sattva*; that is, he will certainly become qualified for worship. Why is this? To this he says: "These two," meaning they are praying for, or seeking, supreme devotion characterized by love. (8)
Then, while the circle of cowherds was fleeing in terror at the fierce sound of the uprooting of trees,
you, the bestower of liberation, were released by Nanda, who looked toward the face of his own mother with shame.

"Then," [it means]: when the uprooting and breaking of the two trees produced a harsh sound that caused the earth to tremble, and as your mother approached in agitation, wondering "What is this?", she was filled with shame due to her lingering attachment to her bondage; at that moment, Nanda—casting his eyes upon your face with the underlying thought, "O Yaśodā, what have you done? Oh, how thoughtless you are!"—released you from the bond of the rope. || 9 ||
"Alas, the child situated between the two trees is now unharmed by the power of Hari!"—speaking thus, you were sent home; O Lord of the City of the Wind (Garuḍa), protect me from Gaḍā! 10.

"Mahī" means a tree or a mountain. "Prabhāvaḥ" means power. "Aparikṣataḥ" means one whose limbs are unimpaired. The words "by Nanda and others" are to be understood as the ellipsis for "bruvāṇaiḥ" (speaking). || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth decade, the Description of the Breaking of the Yamalārjuna Trees.

Indeed, the cowherds, ignorant of Your power, became apprehensive regarding the fall of the trees and other such occurrences in this cow-pen; suspecting them to be a causeless multitude of portents, they set their minds on departing elsewhere. (1)

"O Lord," [he said]. "Those who do not know Your power—those who are ignorant of the majesty of Your true nature and possess only a mortal intellect—fear a multitude of portents such as the falling of trees and other calamities, taking them to be a flood of evil omens despite their lack of cause. (1)
There, the eminent cowherd named Upananda sang: "Surely by Your very inspiration, it has been revealed that to the west of here lies the enchanting forest known as Vṛndāvana. (2)
Regarding the word "therein": there, among those cowherds, the best of cowherds named Upananda spoke thus; I am certain that this was surely by your own instigation. || 2 ||
Having established that great forest as their primary pasture in an instant, the leaders of the herd,
following the most venerable vehicle occupied by your mother, moved about accompanied by you.

"Bṛhat" refers to the cowherds, Nanda and others, headed by Nanda. Having established—that is, having made—the place where the Lord had spent so much time playing into a "bṛhadvana," meaning a pasture (gauṣṭhīna) or a former site for cattle (bhūtapūrvagosthāna), that is to say, having left the former cow-pen known as Bṛhadvana; "accompanied by you" means that the cowherds followed the wagon, which was the most excellent and venerable vehicle because it contained Yaśodā and Rohiṇī along with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and they moved on. || 3 ||
Amidst the sounds from the hooves of the herds of cows with lovely voices, the young women drank in the syllables of your playful conversation; thus, they did not perceive the length of the road.

"Ana" means "of the cart. Between the charming sound of the cart and the noise of the hooves of the herd of cattle belonging to Dhenu-pālī, the nectar-like syllables heard within those sweet conversations of yours were drunk in by the cupped hands of the ears; thus, the length of the road was neither perceived nor known. || 4 ||

O Lord, beholding Bṛndāvana—with its multitude of trees headed by the Nandana, Punnāga, and Kunda, and with a beauty enhanced by emerald-paved courtyards and the lush splendor of its verdant meadows—you were filled with delight. || 5 ||

"Having observed": [He saw] a place where the multitudes of trees, headed by the *kunda*, were such that their blossoms were flourishing and blooming; and which, through the dense beauty of its meadows—the splendor of the ground thick with green grass—possessed a full and perfect beauty like a floor paved with emeralds or sapphire. You rejoiced; you became satisfied. || 5 ||
When all the cowherds have settled comfortably in their new dwellings built on the outskirts,
you, mingled with the young cowherd maidens, shall behold the splendor of the forest and gaze upon its beauty.

Regarding the word *navāka*: you have seen all around (*paryak*) the various types of dwellings—specific mansions that were newly constructed and brought forth from nine [architectural] sources. || 6 ||
You beheld the daughter of Kalinda, whose pure waters flow along winding paths, who delights with the playful warbling of swans,
and whose lotus-face is ever-blossoming.

She is *arālet*: she whose playful conversation is made with the warbling of swans (*marālaka*) and the cries of ruddy geese (*kalahaṃsa*), and who utters elegant words; she from whom pure waters have come by way of a winding (*arāla*) path. She whose face consists of lotuses (*saroja*) that are incessant (*nirantara*), dense (*nīrandhrita*), and smiling (*smera*). [He approached] the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), and for that very reason, one fit for enjoyment. (7)
And you beheld Mount Govardhana, variegated by the garlands of rays from its jewels, enchanting with hundreds of peacock cries,
touching the realm of Brahmā with its lofty peaks.
"Mayūra" means: it is enchanting and captivating due to the hundreds of *kekā* cries—the sweet, warbling sounds—of peacocks.
The word "anvaga" functions like a suffix; when combined with a subsequent word, it forms a compound meaning "all around.

It is variegated—that is, of diverse colors—due to the garlands of rays, the masses of luster, of jewels. It touches the world of Viriñca, namely Satyaloka, with its high and lofty peaks. Thus [it is described]. || 8 ||
Then, together with the cowherd boys, you went all around to the edge of the forest;
there, in every direction, you beheld that winding Yamunā, who was like a single woman full of passion.

"Along with [them]" means: then, together with the cowherd boys (*gopakumāraka*), wherever you went throughout the entire forest, there, in each place, you saw the daughter of Kalinda alone. How so? She was winding, having come here and there by a crooked path; therefore, because of your following her, she seemed as if full of passion (*rāgavatī*) for you. || 9 ||

O Lord of the House of the Wind! While you were wandering with the children in such a cattle-grazing forest, eager for the movement of the herd of calves, may you protect me from disease along with Sītā and the princes. 10.
"So be it. [The word] *paśavya* means beneficial for cattle (*paśu*). || 10 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth decade, the description of the journey to Vṛndāvana.
Then, in the enchanting Vṛndāvana filled with swarms of restless bees, [Kṛṣṇa], eager to tend the calves, was together with the children of the cowherds.
O Lord, friend of Haladhara! O Illustrious One! You wandered about, holding a dark-hued flute and a staff, Your bodily luster delighting the eyes. || 1 ||

*Taraleti*: Amidst a swarm of restless bees (*taralamadhukṛdvṛnde*), a multitude of moving bees; holding a *gavala* horn, a flute (*muralī*), a bamboo pipe (*veṇu*), and a staff (*vetra*), You wandered, having performed Your movement. || 1 ||

O Lord of Kamalā, while You—the sanctifier of Vṛndāvana, who have established the protection of the world and are caressed by the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī—were bestowing Your pair of feet, what did not shine forth as abundant wealth? Even the trees, creepers, waters, earth, mountains, fields, and so forth were filled with prosperity. || 2 ||

"Vihitā" means by whom the protection of the earth (jagatī) was provided. "Lālitaṃ" means cherished or massaged by the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī. What did not shine—that is, what did not appear magnificent—there, being filled with prosperity? The meaning is that the trees shone with the wealth of flowers and the like; the creepers, with water-lilies and the like; the water, with lotuses and the like; the earth, with crops and the like; the mountains (gotra), with jewels and the like; and the fields (kṣetra), with gold and the like—all were full of such riches and thus shone. || 2 ||
In the forest regions where the ulapa grass flourishes, cooled by gentle breezes,
upon the vast banks of the Yamunā and on the peaks of Mount Govardhana,
he indeed wanders with his herd of calves, his charming flute-song resounding.
On a certain day, you beheld a Daitya in the form of a calf.

"Vilasat" means: in the edge of the forest (*kāntārānte*), which is possessed of shimmering *ulapa* grass—a specific kind of beautiful grass—and on the broad bank of the Yamunā, which is cool due to the breeze touching the waves of the Yamunā and extensive because it consists of sandbanks; there you beheld (*udaikṣathā*) the herd of calves (*vātsakam*). || 3 ||
Beholding his tail waving impetuously and his body devoid of luster, looking about with his neck slightly turned as if waiting for an opening,
he then seized him by the foot and whirled him repeatedly high into the air.
Somewhere, you cast that wounded life into a great tree. || 4 ||

"Rabhasā" means: observing the gaze of this Vatsāsura—who was moving about with his tail wagging violently and darting here and there with speed—as he went along with his neck slightly turned and twisted, and who was watching for a vulnerability in the form of waiting for an opportunity; then, having ascertained, "This one desires to kill me," and seizing him by the foot, he whirled him around repeatedly with great force and speed, and by that very act of whirling—
In some place, at some time, you cast away that life which had been wounded. || 4 ||
As the great Daitya, wicked by nature, fell at that moment,
crushing the trees and mangling the forest with the force of his descent,
the gods in heaven, their throngs gathering together, rained down heaps of flowers.
O Hari! Then, indeed, they rain down upon your head out of joy. || 5 ||
"Descending": from birth—that is, from the very moment of his appearance—he was a wicked-souled one due to his demonic nature; thus he is "fallen.

By him, the forest was destroyed and ruined by trees (*kṣoṇīruha*) crushed and pulverized by the force of his descent. "The gods" (*bṛndāraka*)—those whose groups (*vṛnda*) have gathered together in throngs—[honored him] with heaps of flowers (*kusumotkara*), that is, with clusters of celestial tree blossoms. || 5 ||
When you were asked by the children with playful curiosity, "Why does this most fragrant garland of flowers fall from above upon your head?",
you suddenly rose up from the circle of trees by hurling the demons upward.
"This is surely that very mass of flowers returning slowly," he thought. || 6 ||

"O most fragrant one! [Thus addressed by the children: "Whence does this garland of flowers, exceedingly fragrant and endowed with sweetness, fall upon your head? Since there are no trees above, in the upper part, how can this be? Being thus questioned by the children, you replied with playful ease: "By the hurling of the Danuja—that is, by the throwing down of the corpse of the demon Vatsāsura—the mass of flowers arising from its momentum has gone upward from the circle of trees; that very mass is now slowly approaching and falling upon my head, I believe for certain. (6)
One day, when the harsh heat was at its peak,
you and others went to drink from the waters of the Yamunā;
there, you indeed beheld a crane with wings outspread, which you had forgotten [to kill].
In its destruction of the weight of mountains, it was like another Mount Kailāsa.

"At some time"—that is, again at another day, during the summer season when the harsh heat was most intense, you and the other cowherd boys went to drink water from the Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun (Tapanatanayā), and there they beheld Baka, the demon Baka. He had his wings flapping; he was like that second [bird], whose wings had not been clipped by Indra during his clipping of the wings of the mountains. || 7 ||
O Lord! While he was drinking water, having rushed toward you amidst the herd of cows, he reportedly swallowed you;
but then, spitting you out again quickly as you resembled a blazing fire, he went to strike you with the tip of his beak. At that moment, O All-pervading One! [You struck him down].
And his beak, ever intent on pecking at the wicked, seized him and tore him apart.

"He drinks"—that is, rushing toward you in the midst of the herd of cows, swallowing and devouring you who resemble fire, and thus vomiting you out immediately, he went forth to tear you apart with the tip of his beak (*troṭi*) after the act of vomiting. You, who are renowned for your skill in crushing the wicked by subduing the evil, seized him by the upper and lower parts of his beak and tore him apart; that is, you subdued him. || 8 ||

Immediately after that host of gods had departed for the abode of Death, you returned home from Vṛndāvana, scattering a multitude of flowers, as if to see Pūtanā— who had surely died along with her innate nature— or perhaps to wait for even the sinful Anujamaga who had gone before them. || 9 ||

"Sapadi" means: having gone ahead first to wait for and await Agha, the demon Aghāsura; when that Bakāsura—the elder brother of Aghapūtanā—had departed for the abode of Yama, the residence of Death, you went just as you did when a shower of *sumanas* flowers (or a multitude of well-disposed gods) was being scattered [upon you]. || 9 ||
Having heard from afar the charming sound of Your flute, the women approached quickly and gazed upon You with joy as You ascended nearby;
O Śauri, who brings blissful delight to Your mother and whose dwelling is celebrated as the abode of the Wind-god, dispel my maladies! 10.

"Lalita" means: Having heard from afar the charmingly beautiful sound of the flute (*muralīnāda*), he was gazed upon with his face upturned; then, having quickly approached—that is, having set out and gone near him—he was gazed upon with rising joy due to the sight of his limbs and minor members (*aṅga-pratyaṅga*) nearby, by which the joy of both his mother and father was produced. || 10 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth decade, containing the description of the slaying of the demon Vatsāsura and the description of the birth of the demon Bakāsura.
Once, you [were] together with the children of Vraja...
O Lord, having long ago set Your mind upon consuming the forest, You emerged surrounded by vast circles of calves who were eager for food and intent on eating.
"At some time," [it is said]; that is, when the dawn was near, with various side-dishes, savory foods, and boiled rice. || 1 ||

The dust raised from the two lotus-feet of yours as you emerged, which purifies the three worlds, was received by the great sages with their hair standing on end; they held it upon their bodies, experiencing the festival of beholding you.

"Viniryataḥ" means those who were emerging or coming forth. "Udañcitam" means that which was lifted up; "patitam" means fallen; it is the purifier of the three worlds and the cleanser of the sins of all beings. "Pulakadharaiḥ" refers to the physical manifestation of devotion (bhakti-anubhāva). "Udūhire" means they held [it] aloft. ||2||
O Lord! While you were grazing your cattle upon the ground covered with dense sādvala grass together with the young boys,
the demon Aghāsura blocked the path for the sake of evil.
Terrifying, he suddenly assumed the form of one lying down. || 3 ||

"He moves about" means: upon a ground covered with dense grass and abundant vegetation, he blocked the path—the way to commit a sin against you and your lords in the form of devouring; yet in the ultimate sense, it was to abandon the evil, the misfortune that brings the fear of worldly existence. He was in the form of a serpent (ajagara) lying down. || 3 ||

While you were at some distance in the forest, young boys, out of curiosity to enter your mouth, went into the interior of the mouth of you whose body was like a great mountain and whose wide-open mouth resembled a cave.

"O Great Mountain! [The children said: "The boys, devoid of discernment, while you were at some distance, far away in the forest, entered—out of curiosity to play—the mouth and interior of his face. How so? Because he possessed a mouth and face that was spread wide, covered, renowned, and vast, resembling a mountain cave; thus, it means that due to the delusion that the body of the python was a great mountain, and the delusion that his mouth was a mountain cave. (4)
Out of negligence, one enters the belly of a serpent;
even among beasts and birds that possess offspring, this happens.
Knowing this, O Lord, you too have entered [the womb].
To quickly protect his circle of friends who have come for refuge. || 5 ||
"Out of negligence" means: while your own body, along with that of Vatsaka and his entire retinue, was being consumed by fire; you too, knowing and perceiving this deed of the demon Aghāsura. || 5 ||
As you, with your expansive body, rolled upon the great serpent whose breath was obstructed within its belly,
you swiftly tore open the circle of its throat.
Liberating the animals and their keepers, he went forth.

Regarding the phrase *galodara*: by you, whose body (*varṣman*) had expanded—that is, whose physical frame had grown—the vital breath (*māruta*, *prāṇavāyu*) was obstructed. Precisely because of that obstruction of the breath, as [the body] rolled about and writhed here and there, your throat-circumference (*kaṇṭhamaṇḍala*) became split open and torn asunder; through that path of the exit of the breath, you, while releasing the cattle-herders and the cattle, yourself also went forth. || 6 ||
For a moment, a great and immense radiance, originating from the great Asuras, remained in heaven for the sake of your arrival;
but as soon as you had departed, it instantly vanished.
Then the gods danced and sang in the expanse of the sky.

"An instant": for the purpose of approaching you, or for the purpose of entering you—that is, to enter into you—a great and vast *mahaḥ* (splendor), originating from the great Asura, emerged from the body of the Asura Agha while he was stationed in the divine ether for a moment; it was a mass of intensely brilliant light, which, because even the subtle body had been abandoned, was free from all limitation, and became absorbed into you, the Light, like one light merging into another.

Oh! Even though Aghāsura was your enemy, he died having placed you within his heart; therefore, at that very moment, he attained before the eyes of all the world the fruit thereof—liberation known as *sāyujya*. Oh, how great is your affection for your devotees! Such is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
Then, pursued by the gods led by Brahmā who were filled with wonder, and followed by the young princes,
you, O Lord, when the day had reached its youthful stage [midday], performed a feast of food together with your own people.

"Filled with wonder," it is said: followed along the path of the sky in an unmanifest form, when the day had reached its youthful state and midday had arrived, [he witnessed] the festival of the meal—the curiosity of eating in the forest. || 8 ||
Placing his horn-flute upon his hip, holding a morsel of food in his lotus-hand,
he delighted the young boys with his sweet words.
You ate, being joyfully praised by the hosts of the thirty gods.
Regarding "viṣāṇikām": *viṣāṇikā* means a horn; *muralī* means a flute; and *nitambake* refers to the region of the hips, within the yellow garment. || 9 ||
"O Lord of the World! Your eating of cow products here in the circle of cowherds is as dear to you as the eating of sacrificial oblations is to the gods in the celestial realm.
Thus was he praised by the best of the thirty deities.
O dweller in the city of the Maruts! Protect me with your mace. || 10 ||

Regarding "Sukhāśana": He is praised as if dear to the best of the thirty gods, such as Brahmā and others, because he is the "consumer of happiness" (sukhāśana) in the circle of cowherds (gopamaṇḍala), and because he is the "consumer of the sacrifice" (makhāśana)—that is, the eater of the sacrificial portion—in the circle of the gods (devamaṇḍala). || 10 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first decade, describing the slaughter of the Asuras.
Having observed your excessive delusion, which has not been seen in other multitudes of incarnations, [you acted] then for the sake of their liberation from sin.
Then Brahmā, desiring to test him, employed his power of illusion and caused the groups of calves to disappear from sight.

"Others" refers to other manifestations such as Nṛsiṃha and others, in whom an excess of power—an excellence of sovereignty never before seen or observed—was present. Desiring to examine even this further excellence of power, wishing to see it, he expanded [his power] and applied it; "the state of being out of sight" means disappearance. || 1 ||

Seeing the herd of cattle helpless and longing for their calves, you, following the will of the Creator as if desiring to bring them back, went away at that moment with a mouthful of grass only half-chewed; meanwhile,
the lotus-born Brahmā vanished from the sight of the boys who had finished eating.

"Vatsān" (the calves). The word *dhātṛ* refers to the foster-mother; her "opinion" (*mata*) is the perception of an abundance of calves, and one who follows that is "one who acts according to that perception. [The Lord acted] as if he were desirous of bringing back the calves, having addressed the children who were eating—those who had already eaten some morsels or those whose hands still held food—saying, "I myself will bring the calves," though he was not actually desirous of bringing them. Rather, you went for the sake of complying with the foster-mother's opinion. At that time, while Śrī Kṛṣṇa was at a distance, Brahmā, the lotus-born, made those who had eaten and those who were eating disappear [from view]. || 2 ||

Thus, when Brahmā had dismissed the calves and the cowherd boys, the Blessed One reflected: "If I enter the cow-pen alone this evening without them, the cows and the gopīs will suffer the grief born of not seeing their own offspring; yet if I go after deceiving Brahmā by taking these [calves and boys] away, Brahmā himself will suffer. Thinking thus, in order to prevent both [kinds of suffering], He accomplished everything by His own power through His own Māyā; as it is said:
"Then You acted as a calf, and subsequently as a group of cowherds; You took the form of carrying-baskets, vessels, flutes, buffalo-horns, and other such things."
Having wandered for a long time in the forests as before, you then returned to Vraja in the evening by means of your manifold illusory power.

Regarding the phrase "acted as a calf": subsequently, when the assembly of calves and cowherds had been rendered invisible by Brahmā through his power, you, assuming all forms through your *māyā*, acted as a calf (*vatsāyita*) in many ways; you acted like the cowherd community (*gopagaṇāyita*) and took on forms such as carrying-baskets (*śikya*) and the like. Having sported for a long time in the forests as before, you then returned to Vraja at evening twilight by means of your *māyā*. || 3 ||
Bearing only you in the form of the rope, the calf, and so forth, and you yourself again appearing in the form of the animal, the cowherd boy,
and the tail-hair; you were approached with great joy by the cowherd women who had assumed the forms of cows, as if they were your own mothers.

"Tvām iti" (Regarding "you"): Furthermore, you, appearing in the form of a calf among the animals, were held by [the cows] consisting of carrying-ropes, yokes, and the like. Regarding "by those in the form of cows": by the mothers in the form of cows, you—who possessed the form of a calf among the animals—were approached with extreme joy and excessive affection; thinking each of them that you were their own calf, the cows suckled you with milk from their udders while uttering lowing sounds (*huṅkāra*).

Likewise, by the mothers consisting of cowherd women, you—who possessed the form of a cowherd boy—were approached; they too, thinking you were each their own son, performed acts such as placing you on their laps, embracing you, and giving you their breasts. This is the meaning. || 4 ||

Now, one might ask: what is the cause of such extreme joy among the cows and the cowherd girls toward their calves and calf-keepers? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the following resolution: everyone indeed feels affection for the self; others are dear only for the sake of that self. And since Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa is the Self, therefore love arose intensely for those sons who were His very form. Thus, while carrying a fullness of passion, thinking of some living being as "my own" by the power of ego-inflation and regarding him as "my son," [they feel this way].
But having obtained you, their very own self, as a son, they attained such joy that even the cows did not wander away with their eyes upturned.

Regarding the word *jīvam*: certain mothers, by virtue of their ego-identification (*abhimāna*) and the imposition of possessiveness (*mamatva*), consider some living being (*jīva*)—who is intent on experiencing the fruits of his own commenced karma—to be their very self; they regard that body, whether gross or subtle, as their own, thinking, "He is my son," and thus carry a weight of attachment. For since such attachment exists even in this state [of ignorance], what need is there to speak of it when [the truth] is known? Thus he says: "The Self... and so forth.

Having obtained you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who are of the nature of the "this" (idamaṃśa) within the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya)—as their very son, how much joy did the women, the gopīs, and the cows not attain? The meaning is that they attained exceedingly great joy. || 5 ||
Thus, even your elder brother perceived you— whose vast form was cherished by the entire host of cowherds who were overwhelmed by the weight of joy manifesting at every moment— at the end of a year;
yet, great indeed is the difference between you two, even from the perspective of Brahmā and the Self (Ātman).

Thus: At the end of the year—that is, at the conclusion of the year—the elder brother Śrī Balabhadra also recognized you, whose many forms were cherished by the entire host of cowherds whose burden of joy and excess of contentment blossomed and increased at every moment; for although both of you possess the nature of Brahman, there is a great distinction: you are the partless (*niṣkala*) Brahman, while the elder brother is the whole (*sakala*). || 6 ||
During the rainy season, seeing that the Creator and the Destroyer had become dull through their lack of discernment regarding new and old cowherds,
[the Lord] manifested [himself] with four arms, adorned with fresh crowns, armlets, and other ornaments, resembling water-laden clouds.

"At the end of the rainy season" means: at the conclusion of the year, having seen the calves and cowherds—who were composed of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who were ancient, and who had been concealed by Himself—while Druhiṇa (Brahmā) was utterly bewildered, lacking right knowledge, his discrimination dulled, and unable even to investigate whether "these are real or these others are illusory," You manifested the newly created illusory ones, distinguished by crowns, armlets, and other ornaments. || 7 ||

The lotus-born Brahmā beheld each of you individually— your limbs cherished by Kamalā, reclining on the coils of the lord of serpents, delightful to the eye, with eyes closed in playful repose, and attended by yogis such as Sanaka and others.
"Each one," he says; she beheld Viṣṇus who had closed their eyes in play, having accepted the yogic sleep. || 8 ||
Beholding that immeasurable form of Nārāyaṇa and seeing his own servant everywhere, the Creator,
his heart submerged in *māyā*, was utterly bewildered until you became one with half a mouthful in hand.

"Nārāyaṇa! [He addressed] his own servant, himself—the one whose heart was deluded and submerged in *māyā*. While he remained thus, almost unconscious due to his extreme bewilderment, you, having withdrawn your manifold forms, became alone, with a water-pot in hand, in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, intent on searching for the calves. || 9 ||
Desiring to reach that state, he repeatedly bowed and praised the Lord of All,
the Ordainer who has entered his own abode;
then, together with the joyful *pota* priests, he entered the sacrificial hall.
O Lord of the abode of wind! O All-pervading One! Protect me from disease! || 10 ||

"Naśyat" means as follows: when [the demon] had perished, and when [Brahmā], having been praised, had gone to his abode—Satyaloka—and was entering his own residence (niketa) together with the calves and the cowherd boys (vatsapāla). || 10 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second decade, containing the description of the theft of the calves by Brahmā and the description of Brahmā’s delusion through the Māyā of the Blessed One.
Having passed beyond childhood, O Lord of the worlds, you attained the charming age of Paugaṇḍa.
Having left the calf-pen with a festive spirit, you set out to tend the herd of cattle. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *atītya*: childhood lasts for five years; the second five-year period is the stage of *paugaṇḍa*, which is more charming than childhood and exceedingly enchanting. Having reached—that is, having attained—that stage, and having neglected the protection and guarding of the calves, you engaged yourself with festive curiosity in the tending of the herd of cows. || 1 ||
O Lord of the City of the Wind (Kubera)! This conduct of yours is indeed consistent with your previous undertaking;
for it was precisely for the sake of protecting the lineage that you descended [to earth], and that very thing you have now begun. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the undertaking": it is suitable and appropriate for the undertaking, that is, the commencement. For the sake of protecting the lineage—that is, for the purpose of guarding the earth—that very protection of the lineage is the protection of the cows. || 2 ||
Once, while wandering happily with Rāma at the edge of the forest, beholding the splendor of the woods,
you went out of joy to the Dhenuka forest at the word of your friend named Śrīdāman.
"Kadā? [means: "When? Dhenukakānana is the Tāla forest, the dwelling place of the demon Dhenuka. || 3 ||
Then, while the dense grove of palm trees was being held up by the strength of your arms as you spoke,
the gentle Dānava Dhenuka also fell before him like a heap of fruit, rendered harsh by his own fate.

He shook [the palm grove]. When that immense mass of *tālī* trees—that collection of *tāla* trees—was shaken and moved by force, by power, and by his two arms, first the soft, unripe, and then the harsh, ripe clusters of fruit fell down together. Immediately thereafter, the demon Dhenuka also rushed forward in the form of a donkey, provoked to anger by the sound produced by the falling palm fruits. || 4 ||
Thinking, "I am intent upon protecting the herd; how can I slaughter the herd today?", you surely caused the elder brother to destroy the obstructors of the hosts of gods.

Regarding the word *samudyata*: "eager" means one who is enthusiastic in the protection of a herd (*dhainuka*), that is, a multitude of cows; the literal meaning is the slaughter of the demon Dhenuka. Thinking, "How shall I do it? I will certainly not do it," you have surely—having so resolved—caused him to be slain by your elder brother. || 5 ||

O Blessed One! at that time, you who were free from worldly attachment played among the palm trees, and together with your elder brother, you disregarded even his servants who had taken the form of jackals, just as one ignores the rose-apples on the palms.

Regarding the word *tadīya*: having become jackals (*jambuka*), that is, having arrived as *kroṣṭṛ*s (howling jackals), those who had approached him—being free from attachment (*nirāsthaḥ*), meaning devoid of reliance—he cast them out (*nirāsthaḥ*), that is, he repelled and subdued them. || 6 ||
The suffix *trap* is applied according to the rule *initrakaṭyacaśca*.

When you were then striking down the host of jackals, I think that Varuṇa—because of his sharing the same name [with them]—was overwhelmed by fear and, as it were, altered his name to one well-known in the Vedas. (7)
"Striking down" [is said] because of having the same name, since he himself also has the name "jackal. || 7 ||

"O Murāri, the fruit of your incarnation has been realized today! Thus praised by the gods, you laughed and said, "The fruit has indeed been realized here," as you ate palm fruits together with a child.

"Thine! [He said. The fruit of the incarnation was the subduing of Dhenuka; that has now been accomplished. Thus you were celebrated by the gods. From hearing your praise, the gods—who speak truthfully according to reality—have truly obtained here the fruit born of the palmyra fruit. || 8 ||
Having eaten those large fruits, dripping with honey and heavy with fat,
you surely returned to the fruit-bearing mansion with your young sons, who were both satisfied and satiated as they carried the fruits.

"Madhudrava" means those from which honey-like juice flows; having eaten palm fruits that were heavy with fat and possessed of internal pulp, they were satisfied—and for that very reason, arrogant—carrying to their home a flood of fruit to be brought on their shoulders in order to give it to their kinsmen. || 9 ||
"Slain! Slain is Dhenuka!"—thus addressed by the people who approached and offered sweet fruits, and being praised with cries of "Victory!
and "Live long!", O Lord, Sovereign of the City of the Maruts, protect me from disease.
"He is slain!"—the repetition of "slain" is due to an excess of joy. || 10 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third decade, describing the slaying of the demon Dhenuka.
Now, with three decades, he praises [the Lord] by narrating the deeds of the Blessed One consisting of the subduing of Kāliya:
"In former times, one named Saubhari, eager for service to you, performed penance within the Kālindi river for twelve years."
Once, amidst a swarm of fish, he saw Tārkṣya himself standing before him, full of affection for those greedy for enjoyment. || 1 ||

"From you": the sage named Saubhari, eager for service to you, beheld [the couple] directly—that is, with his own eyes—as they were intent on worldly enjoyments and devoted to the pleasure of mutual affection. || 1 ||
Observing him devouring a certain fish—Tṛkṣa, the son of Manu, who was hungry—he cursed him whose heart was thus scorched: "If you eat living beings here, you shall also lose your life. (2)

"O you who eat excessively! Beholding Tārkṣya, the son of Tṛkṣa, who is your vehicle and who devours [serpents], you are tormented in your heart with grief. If you, O eater, should devour the creatures such as fish in this pool of the Kālindī, you will lose your life; you shall die. || 2 ||
At that time, Kāliya, consuming his allotted portion from the enemy of serpents out of pride in his venom,
went to that difficult-to-reach water, having had his wings clipped by Him who, out of anger, was occupied with Your lotus feet.

Regarding the phrase "in that": eating the monthly portion of the *bali* offering prepared by the serpents for their own protection out of the pride of his frolicking and the intoxication of the potency of his venom, he was one who worshipped Your lotus feet; thus [he is described]. Therefore, cast down by Your left side and rendered helpless, he went to the waters of the Kālindī lake, which are difficult even for the enemies of the serpents to attain. || 3 ||
On that terrible shore, the abode of the daughter of the Sun, trees were shattered by the force of the waves;
flocks of birds fell as if dropping from the sky, and because of this, your mind became moistened with compassion.

Regarding the word *ghore*: when that Kāliya, who performs cruel deeds, dwells in the abode of the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā) within the pool of the Kālindī, [all beings] were "wounded" (*vikṣatāḥ*), meaning they perished by being licked by the flames of his poisonous fire. "In the clouds" (*abhre*) means in the upper region. By this it is meant that not only was there an absence of enjoyment of its waters, but rather there was the destruction of the entire world. || 4 ||
Once, at that time, when you had gone to the edge of the forest on the Yamunā leaving the plow-wielder behind,
the cows and cowherds, scorched by the fierce heat of the unrestrained summer, drank the water of the [hot] breath.

Regarding the word *kāla*: when you had gone to the forest region (*kānanānta*) on the Yamunā—belonging to the Yamunā (*yāmuna*)—leaving behind Rāma, who holds the plow (*sīrapāṇi*), [the snakes] were tormented by the fierce heat arising from the advanced summer season; thus, being distressed, they drank the water of their venom (*kṣvelatoya*) at their ease. || 5 ||

O Acyuta! seeing all those living beings perishing and fallen upon the surface of the earth, you, moistened with compassion, reached their side and instantly restored them to life with your glorious sidelong glances raining down nectar-like waters.
"Naśyat" means perishing; "viśvān" means all—those living beings who are dying, falling away, or having fallen. || 6 ||
"What is this excessive rain of joy that has arisen over all our limbs?"—thus the hosts of cowherds stood up;
seeing you before them and recognizing that work of yours, they embraced you, having witnessed your manifold powers.

"What is this?"—thus the cowherd communities exclaimed. Then, [thinking], "What is this? Oh, how great is this excess of a rain of joy throughout all our limbs! A flood of the nectar of supreme bliss has arisen," they were as if awakened from a dream. Even though they had previously witnessed His various powers in such acts as the liberation of the sinful Pūtanā, they recognized that this protection from the poison-water was performed by Him; and embracing You, they performed an embrace of longing. || 7 ||
And thus the cows, having regained their lives and filled with abundant joy in an instant, beheld you before them;
they immediately surrounded you from all sides, shedding tears of delight and emitting low, rising sounds.

"O cows! Thus the cows, having suddenly arisen, quickly surrounded [him] and stood encircling him. (8) "This horripilation of ours has spread throughout our bodies, and within us there is a certain fainting fit of bliss. This is a wondrous surge of laughter, 'Mukunda!'—thus addressed by the cowherds, you were gladdened and honored. (9)

"Romāñca" (The Horripilation): O Mukunda! This "kṣvelavega"—this "viṣavega" (poisonous impulse)—is a marvel, never before seen among those bitten by serpents. Within our inner hearts, there is a certain fainting fit (*mūrchā*) of immeasurable bliss, an unsurpassed happiness that has become exceedingly dense. How is this known? Behold, my lord, this horripilation all over the body; such is the sense. || 9 ||
In this way, you dispel the diseases even of liberated souls who are your devotees with the glances from the corners of your charming eyes;
O Dweller in the Abode of Air, may you, such a vast reservoir of abundant compassion, protect me from disease! 10.
Thus it is said: "You restore even those liberated souls who have passed away, freeing them from disease and granting them life once more, while causing them to cast off all sorrow. (10)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth decade, describing the restoration to life of the cows and cowherds who were filled with the poisonous water during the subduing of Kāliya.
Now, O Blessed One, having resolved to ward off that most terrible serpent in the water—
You swiftly crushed the *nīpa* trees standing on the bank, whose clusters of leaves had been withered by the harsh wind. || 1 ||
Then, having resolved his mind—that is, having made a firm determination—to ward him off, he reached the *nīpa* tree, a *kadamba* tree. || 1 ||
And having ascended with his lotus-feet, which possessed a lovely luster like a fresh sprout,
they both fell far into the waters of the lake, amidst a mass of most terrible, swirling waves.

Regarding the phrase "having ascended": by the expression "possessing a charming luster equal to fresh sprouts," it is suggested to those standing below that the *nīpa* tree, through contact with the Blessed One, has abandoned its poisonous defect and has come to possess newly emerged sprouts. || 2 ||
The river, its waters surging as they trembled under your heavy burden— O bearer of the weight of the three worlds—
suddenly submerged your hundred bows with a loud, crashing roar.

Regarding the word *bhuvana*: she who bears the burden of the three worlds (*bhuvanatraya*) within her womb is so described; by the heavy weight of such a one as you, the river—whose waters were trembling (*vikampin*), prone to shaking, and surging (*vijṛmbhin*), prone to swelling—suddenly submerged, that is, flooded, a distance of a hundred bows. || 3 ||

Then, from the waters, the lord of serpents rose up, his mind blinded by unappeased rage, amidst the weight of the roar of the ocean's belly as it was violently agitated and whirled in every direction and intermediate quarter.

"Then," it is said: with his mind blinded by unappeased rage, caused by the weight of the roar of the waters—which were agitated, tossed, whirled, and filled with whirlpools within their depths in the eight cardinal and intermediate directions—he rose up from the water and reached your presence. || 4 ||
They beheld before them a serpent with many hoods, like a mountain of collyrium, appearing as a cloud of virulent poison fierce with sparks of blazing fire issuing from its thousands of hood-tips.

"Phaṇeti": They are so called because they bear (*dharanti*) the water of poison (*viṣāmbu*), that is, the liquid poison (*viṣadrava*), which is fierce (*ugra*) and cruel (*krūra*) precisely because it consists of flaming sparks of fire (*jvaladagnikaṇa*) that flow forth (*viniḥsṛmara*) and are prone to dripping (*kṣaraṇaśīla*) from their thousands of hoods (*phaṇaśṛṅga*). || 5 ||
That great serpent, bearing a mass of heat from his fierce breath that issued from his flaming eyes, bit you—
who possess infinite strength— and coiled around you, alas, while you were rendered motionless.

"Blazing," etc.: he whose mass of heat from the fierce venomous breath was flowing forth in such a way as to be blazing; having been seen, [the serpent] bit him in his vital parts and coiled around him, so that he became motionless and his activities were no longer visible.
Then, seeing that the herd of young cows going toward the bank was agitated upon not finding you,
and observing hundreds of ill omens even within the courtyard of the cowherd village, the cattle-herders went to the Yamunā.
"Having observed" means having seen a hundred omens and a flood of ill omens. "The keepers of the cattle" refers to Nanda and the others. || 7 ||
O All-pervading Lord! Seeing Your state and desiring to cast off their burden of life, all beings quickly released the binding of their hoods and rose up with speed, as You smiled in delight.

Regarding the word "akhileṣu" (in all): to those who, unable to bear the burden of life during separation from you, were desiring to abandon their lives—wishing to give them up—you, possessing a smile, arose and went forth for the purpose of making them know that you were well. 8.
Then, having ascended the hoods of the king of serpents, she danced before you with the lovely glow of her tender feet,
amidst the tumultuous jingling of her anklets and the beautiful clashing of her moving bracelets.

"Having ascended": then, having ascended the hoods of Kāliya, the king of serpents, you performed a dance (*nanṛte*). Your foot was soft and glossy because it was adorned with the jewels on the hoods. "Accompanied by the tinkling of anklets" (*kalaśiñjitanūpura*) refers to that [dance] in which the anklets produced a ringing sound; "charming" (*mañju*) means beautiful. Furthermore, it is an adjective for the act of dancing, describing the jingling of the bracelets on the hands as they met while occupied with keeping the rhythm (*tāla*). || 9 ||
The cattle-herders rejoiced, the sages were satisfied, and the hosts of the gods of heaven rained down flowers;
for you, O Lord of the House of Wind, are now dancing—protect me from the disease that remains unsubdued! 10.
"Jahapuḥ" means they rejoiced; "tutuṣuḥ" means they were satisfied. Protect us from the disease of the gadā (mace), which is insatiable and increases without ceasing. 10.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth decade, the description of the Lord’s dancing upon the head of Kāliya during the subduing of Kāliya.
O Lord! with your circle of earrings swaying beautifully, you danced for a long time upon the serpent.
In the sky, the celestial maidens sing beautifully to the sound of drums beaten by the immortals.

"Rucireti": While the host of celestial women (*daivata-yauvata*) sang in the sky among the aerial chariots (*vimāna*) with a sound as beautiful as the beating of the drums of the immortals, you danced for a long time upon the hoods of the serpent. || 1 ||
O Hari! Whichever head of his was the highest, you bowed down after bypassing each successive height;
then, crushing it with your lotus-like foot, you long uttered a sound as charming as the clapping of hands.

"Namati" means: whichever head of that serpent bowed down because it was crushed by the feet of the Blessed One, each of those heads, having been raised up again and again, you sported with by crushing them with your lotus-like feet. || 2 ||
O Mādhava! When the Lord of Serpents, his multitude of expanded hoods crushed by you, sank down in the water reddened by the blood flowing from them, his wives bowed down at your feet.

"By you"—[he] whose multitude of hoods (*phaṇāgaṇa*) has been broken, crushed, bent, curved, and turned downward; by whom the water (*pāthaḥ*) has been made red with blood (*śoṇita*) that flowed and was vomited; while he sinks with his limbs shattered, those weak women, the wives of the Nāgas, [suffer]. (3)

O Lord! Since their hearts have long been dissolved by the majesty of Your power, which has been celebrated from of old, they indeed praise You, who are free from all constraints, with hymns that even the sages cannot reach through their paths.

"O! Long ago, by your majesty—your greatness—which had been heard of for a long time, their hearts were dissolved, that is, their hearts became slackened; therefore, with hymns in which even sages could find no path—that is, a way consisting of the unification of the meanings of both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala) forms—they praised you unrestrainedly and without inhibition. || 4 ||

O Acyuta! With a heart overflowing with compassion, blossoming at the sight of the devotion of the multitude of serpent-slayers, the Lord of Serpents, having offered his very life to you, bowed down before you.

"The serpent!"—thus [thinking], he who had been restored to life and turned back from death, having surrendered his body to you, prostrated himself with a full eight-limbed salutation and bowed down. || 5 ||
"Go to Rāmaṇaka, situated in the midst of the ocean; the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) will not cause you opposition.
Greatly honoring these words of yours, the lord of serpents departed together with his snakes.

"Ramaṇaka": Ramaṇaka is the island known as Ramaṇaka, the dwelling place of the nāgas. Even though you have committed an offense, the enemy of the serpents, Garuḍa, does not harbor hostility toward you. (6)
Adorned with fine silken garments and blazing necklaces of jewels bestowed by the wives of the serpent-chiefs,
he met his kinsmen gathered on the riverbank at the end of the day, their eyes filled with tears mingled with joy.

"Phaṇīti": You met with your own kinsmen who were mingled with the tears of women—meaning they were joined by women, or else mingled with the tears of women, which may be either tears of grief or tears of joy. || 7 ||
Furthermore, at night, when the multitude of people was unable to go to the cowherd settlement because of the darkness,
the forest fire, having its source in your feet, surrounded them on all sides.
"At night"—furthermore, subsequently, at night during the darkness, being unable to go to the very abode of Vraja, she covered her husband right there on the bank of the Kālindī with a veil. || 8 ||
Then, as the herdsmen cried out in rising distress, "Protect us!
Protect us!", you quickly descended into the great fire to save them; what wonder is this indeed, for your face is truly full of compassion?

"Prabudhitān" means: then, in order to protect (*avituṃ*) those who had been awakened by the heat of the fire (*kṛśānu*), you drank (*papātha*) them; that is, you swallowed them. What is surprising here about the drinking of the great fire? For this fire was your very mouth. (9)
"O Lord! In the peacock, yellowness already shines forth by its very color; now it shines even through its action.
Thus praised by the joyful Paśupatis, O Hara, O Hara, take away my miseries along with my sins! 10.

Regarding the word *śikhinī*: in the context of fire (*śikhin*), yellowness (*pītatā*) exists by way of its specific color or form; now, by way of action (*kriyā*), this yellowness also exists as the object of the act of drinking. O Hari! Along with the evils (*durita*)—the fruits of wicked deeds that serve as the causes of disease—take away (*hara*), that is, destroy, the diseases (*gada*) which are their effects. 10.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth decade, describing the Lord’s grace toward Kāliya during the subduing of Kāliya, and the description of the Lord drinking the forest fire.
O Friend of Rāma! O Bestower of Desires! One day, O Blessed One, you went to the forest.
Surrounded by the sons of the cowherds as well as by their cows, he shone with radiant garments. || 1 ||
"O Rāma! [He says: "Your Honor, whose friend is Rāma, possesses a radiant dress—that is, a beautiful and distinguished ornamentation. (1)
Displaying the pure splendor of Vṛndāvana at his own will to Bala,
he went with the boys armed with reeds to the Bhāṇḍīraka banyan tree while playing.
"Displaying" means with [clubs] having prongs, with staffs, and with raised poles; that is the meaning. He arrived at the banyan tree named Bhāṇḍīraka. || 2 ||
Meanwhile, a merciless demon named Pralamba, who desired your destruction and had assumed the form of a cowherd, approached you, whose arms were long. || 3 ||

"Tāvat" means: the demon named Pralamba—desiring your end (tāvakanidhanaspṛhayālu), meaning wishing to seize you; appearing in the form of a cowherd (gopamūrti), meaning wearing the dress of a cowherd; and merciless (adayālu), meaning pitiless—attained (āpede) Pralambabāhu, who was endowed with such a pair of arms.
Though knowing [the truth], as if not knowing, he formed a bond of friendship with him;
and near the banyan tree, they began a duel between two skillful wrestlers.

"Jānan" means: although he knew that his friendly disposition (*sauhārda*)—the state of being a friend—had been bound [by others] for the purpose of inciting enmity, he nevertheless began a duel (*dvandvayuddha*) that was "interconnected" (*vyābaddha*), meaning mutually engaged, with the cowherds such as Śrīdāmā and others who were "skilled" (*paṭu*), that is, experts in the sport of wrestling, near the banyan tree. || 4 ||
A friend of Rāma; however, according to the method of commentary, the reading should be *rāmasakhaḥ*.

O Blessed One! Having divided the cowherds and established an association with them, You likewise became the beloved of Balabhadra; thus, You considered the Daitya, who was afraid of Your strength, as having come under Your own power.

"Regarding the cowherds": having divided the cowherds according to the distinction between those who are allies of the yogin and those who are his adversaries, he forms the *saṅgha* of Balabhadra and the *saṅgha* of Bhavatrata. "O you who are timid toward your strength": Pralamba thought, "In this duel, it is the rule that those defeated shall carry the victor. By good fortune, though defeated falsely, I shall go carrying one of these two."

In that regard, thinking, "While carrying Kṛṣṇa while situated within the Rāma-group, I might at some point meet with disaster like Tṛṇāvarta," you, out of fear of his strength, permitted him—him who was dependent on your strength, situated within your group, and devoted to you—to go [to Vraja]. || 5 ||

In battle, having mounted an imagined victorious chariot, You defeated Śrīdāmā—who was dearer to You than Your own life—as he approached with his troop; thus, being conquered, You proclaimed His status as the servant of Your devotees.

"Kalpitā" means that in which the vehicle of the conquerors was fashioned. Manifesting and proclaiming His state as a servant to His devotees—showing that even His own head can be stepped upon by them—He bore Śrīdāmā, having carried him. || 6 ||
Thus, O Vibhūman! while many calves were running about and being driven, Pralamba, defeated by Rāma, carried him off from afar out of fear of you.
"Thus" means out of fear of you, he [took] Rāma. "From afar" means having gone slowly as far as the place for disembarking, he then quickly seized him—that is, he carried him away. || 7 ||
Seeing him carrying away [the earth] far from you, while Balarāma had assumed a weighty burden,
the Daitya resumed his own form— that form by which even Bala himself was struck with awe.

"From you"—seeing that Daitya leading him away from you, to a distant place, and perceiving him to be full of apprehension, Balarāma (Halī) assumed a weightiness of being, generating a sense of his own majesty; then, due to his inability to carry [the burden], the Daitya assumed an exceedingly terrifying form. Upon seeing that form, even Bala—though he was indeed the very embodiment of Śeṣa—was startled, becoming slightly terrified by the manifestation of a human state. (8)

The meaning is "having Balabhadra as its leader. Similarly, [the suffix] *kani* is applied in the sense of "belonging to such a one" (*bhavatkam*). In both cases, the suffix *kan* is used according to the rule: "He is their leader" (*sa eṣāṃ grāmaṇīḥ*).
Beholding the body of the Daitya from afar due to its great height, Rāma—his fear dispelled—immediately crushed this utterly wicked being with a firm grip of his hand.

Regarding the word "by height" (*uccatayā*): because of his great height and loftiness, Rāma, standing upon that shoulder, beheld your face even from afar; he then instantly and suddenly crushed—that is, seized it—with an exceedingly fierce and firm fist. || 9 ||
Having slain the heroic Dānava, you embraced Bala with affection upon his arrival;
meanwhile, a rain of flowers was showered by the hosts of immortals upon the heads of you two as you met.
"Having struck" means having become one with each other upon the dissolution of their respective natures, like the unification of the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (partless). || 10 ||

O Lord whose garment is like a restless bee! By arranging the support of the worlds as their very foundation and their ultimate dissolution, you instantly dispel the sufferings of Hari, setting aside all constraints of time. 11.

"Ālamba" means the support or refuge of the worlds; "prālamba" refers to this destruction or subjugation of Pralamba. Arranging it in the manner thus described, abandon—that is, cast aside—any delay of time and destroy Hari.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh decad, the description of the slaying of the demon Pralamba.

While you were lingering in your playful dalliance, the cows, wandering at their own will, were delayed by the thickets of your hair as you engaged in the destruction of Pralamba; they grazed further and further away, intent upon their curiosity for the grass.
They came upon a certain forest named Aiṣīka. || 1 ||
Regarding the word "tvayi": when you were delayed by the slaying of Pralamba, these [demons] went to the forest named Aiṣīka, because it abounded in *iṣīkā* grass. || 1 ||
Those cows, who had come out from the interior of Vṛndāvana before the cruelty of the summer heat was yet fully felt, have reached this forest;
dejected by separation from you and distressed by the spreading waters of the intense summer heat, they have become motionless.

"Unattained": they have gone from the edge of that Vṛndāvana to this forest called Aiṣīka, located outside, where the "heat of summer"—the intensity of the summer season—is unattained and unreached; and being dejected by separation from you, they have reached a state of rigidity or motionlessness due to thirst, which is agitated by water that is "dissipating"—that is, whose moisture has vanished—through the spreading heat of the scorching summer. Or else, they have reached a state of rigidity because they are overwhelmed by thirst, which spreads and pervades through the water [evaporated] by the expansion of the heat of the scorching summer. || 2 ||
Thereafter, O Śauri! having searched far and wide with your companions,
and seeing the herd of cattle exhausted from wandering in the dense forest and having lost their track, you quickly approached them from nearby to lead them back.
Alas, alas! When you had departed, fire burst forth on all sides. || 3 ||

"Following that... [means: when you had approached nearby—in a forest where the paths were lost, where the way was gone, and which was dominated by grass called *muñja*—alas, alas, what misery! O cowherd, a forest fire blazed up and spread on all sides around the cows. || 3 ||
When the fire blazes with a full halo, terrifying with its fierce crackling, and their paths are obstructed, all beings, distressed as if half-burnt, cry out:
"Alas, O Friend of the World! Protect us! Protect us!"
They have come to you for refuge, to you, the sole remover of suffering.
"Entirely" means in all eight directions. With their paths obstructed and unable to go outside, they have come to you for refuge. || 4 ||
"Enough, enough! Out of extreme fear, close your eyes on all sides!"—
at these words of yours, when they had closed their eyes,
where indeed was that forest fire, and where was that thicket of muñja grass?
Alas, they immediately took refuge in the region of Bhāṇḍīra. || 5 ||
"Enough," he said. Then, immediately after opening their eyes once more, they all stood there at the place of the Bhāṇḍīra tree.
It should be understood that they had been led back to their former location by the Blessed One through his power of yoga. || 5 ||
"Victory, victory! What is this illusion of yours, O Lord?"—with these words of praise from them, his smile arose and he assumed various playful gestures;
once more he moved within the forest, where the power of his nature could be perceived only through the clusters of blossoms of the *pāṭala* and other trees.

"Victory! O Lord, victory, victory! May you become transcendent to the world. What is this illusion of yours, by which we, who were standing at the base of the Bhāṇḍīra fig tree with our eyes closed, have now found ourselves at the point of an awl? Regarding the verse beginning with "pāṭala": you performed your wandering (*prācaraḥ*) in that place where the intensity of the summer heat (*gharmānubhāva-ūṣmā*) could be perceived merely by the flowers of trees such as the *pāṭala* and *śirīṣa*. || 6 ||
Like your own face, it bears a great burden of heat;
like your lotus-feet, it dries up the internal mire;
and like your eyebrows, it radiates a vast stream of splendor.
He brought them to the state of asceticism in those forest regions.

Regarding the phrase "tvayi" (in you): while sporting on the banks of the Yamunā, in the regions along the Yamunā, you passed the summer season characterized by heat (*tapasamaya*). He describes this period of heat: "tvayi"—[meaning] as if carrying a burden of heat that was turned away from you, the Lord, and devoid of service. In the case of one who is not a servant, it means bearing or maintaining a burden of heat, that is, mental anguish. [He also carries] the mud or the filth of the internal river and so forth within his mind, as if it were your worship. In the context of the heat-season, *tejas* refers to the scorching sun; elsewhere, it refers to valor. || 7 ||

Thereafter, dwelling at will within the caves of the mountains, you spent the rainy season— which brings joy to all inhabitants of the world— with masses of clouds whose luster equals your own body, and with the splendor of blossoming, pure lightning and yellow garments.

"Following that... [The commentary explains: Those whose dark radiance is a luster equal to Your body; those whose garments are the very blossoming, beautiful, and stainless lightning-flashes, and whose splendor consists of their playful movements—Your body too is clad in yellow garments and possessed of such grace. Bestowing joy through the alleviation of distress or through the abundance of crops, You spent Your time sporting at will in the mountain caves, the caverns of Govardhana. 8.
The Lord of Mountains, offering hymns of praise through the fresh, melodious cries of flocks of peacocks, honors you as he rests within his deep caverns,
presenting a handful of flowers from the blossoming clusters of *kuṭaja* and *kadamba* trees.
O Lord! That Govardhana mountain, providing [these offerings], attended upon him. || 9 ||

"Kuhareti. The mountain Govardhana, the lord of mountains, seated upon the hollows of its own caves—reclining within its own caverns—worshipped you, the most venerable and majestic Lord, by offering a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) consisting of clusters of blooming *kuṭaja* (mountain jasmine) and *kadamba* blossoms; he did so while performing a hymn of praise through the "crows"—the fresh *kekā* cries of flocks of peacocks arising at the start of the rains—which were like special utterances born of the excess of his devotion. 9.

O Lord of the City of Wind! Honoring that autumn which has arrived— with its flood of pure water in the form of the hearts of those devoted to you— and while gracefully grazing the cows upon the pure grass at the edge of the forests, grant me the well-being of my body.

Now, regarding the word "atha": honoring the autumn season—which has approached like a heroine who has come to meet him, her pure flood of water being bound by the hearts of those devoted to you—he grazes [or consumes] the grass; that is, he eats it. [The result is] my health, known as the well-being of the body, or else the bliss of the body, which is the liberation of the disembodied (videhakaivalya). 10.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth decade, describing the liberation of the cows and cowherds from the forest fire and the description of the season.
Your body is as tender as a fresh kalāya pea, yielding the milk of love and enchanting all without exception.
Beholding the Brahman-tattva, which consists of the bliss of supreme consciousness, the women became utterly bewildered by the ego-sense. || 1 ||

"O You! [He said. Your form is Brahman, and that is composed of the joy of the accumulation of reality, consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). Therefore, it yields love and increases passion. The women—the cowherd girls—became utterly infatuated. || 1 ||
O Hari! With minds agitated by the god of love, the cowherd girls, gradually intent upon beholding you here and there, could not endure even your arrival at the forest at the break of day.

"O Manmatha! Thus, the cowherd girls, from here and there, could no longer endure—nor tolerate—the gradual increase in his excellence as he approached them one after another; nor could they bear it at the break of day rather than all the time, nor his arrival in the forest rather than traveling further away. || 2 ||
When you had departed, those fawn-eyed women cast their gaze upon you with minds fixed on you;
having heard the sound of your flute from afar, they passed the time delighting in mutual conversations about your playful charms.

Regarding the verse beginning with "nirgate": when you, O Lord, had gone forth—that is, had set out—those women directed their glances toward you. Consequently, with their minds absorbed in you, they abandoned their household duties; and even from a distance, having heard the sound of your flute, they delighted in the conversation concerning your amorous pastimes, spending their time in mutual discourse.
Having reached the edge of the forest, you too, standing upon the delightful ground beneath the lush trees with your feet positioned in reverse,
filled the flute's pipe.
"Kānanāntamiti": He stood with his feet placed in a reversed or inverted position, and thus situated, he filled the hollow of a bamboo flute. || 4 ||

O Lord! Your flute-playing was manifested as a means of dissolving the host of sky-faring beings tormented by Māra’s arrows, the assembly of beasts and birds rendered free from agitation, and even stones themselves. || 5 ||

He causes death; by him, the host of sky-faring beings (khecarī-kula) has been shaken, giving rise to trembling, perspiration, and so forth. Even for stones and rocks, a melting—meaning a means of liquefaction—has manifested. || 5 ||
With fingers like petals trembling over the holes of his flute and feet like sprouts moving to the rhythm of the beat—
oh, even though he was out of their sight, the women of Vraja fainted as they contemplated him thus standing!

"O flute-player! Thus did the cowherd women, the gopīs, become bewildered as they contemplated that position of yours standing with feet reversed, even though it was beyond their sight and not directly perceived. (6)
Beholding your limbs without any apprehension, those sky-dwellers, birds, deer, and even beasts, as well as the forest that cherished your footprints, truly celebrated themselves as most blessed. (7)
