"Free from doubt": those cowherd women of Vraja honored that forest as exceedingly fortunate—most blessed—because it was free from doubt; because they could behold Your form without hesitation; because, by virtue of being so close to You, they were habitually seeing every limb and member of Your body; and because, being devoid of blinking, they gazed eternally upon You. Furthermore, they honored it because it was directed toward Your feet and was in contact with Your lotus-feet. || 7 ||
"When shall I drink the nectar of her lower lip? When, indeed, the remnants of the essence tasted by the flute?
"Alas, it has been cast far away by one of evil intent! Thus, agitated, these women repeatedly lamented to one another. (8)

"May I drink it! [He thought. That nectar of the lower lip, in which a special essence had been tasted by the flute—that is not possible for us from afar. Enough with such vain hope! They fainted; they swooned. (8)
And day after day, O Lord, these women— rendered helpless by the passion bound to you through the grace born of their hearts— constantly fall here into a state of bewilderment regarding their duties.

"Daily" means through grace, and not through affliction. Why? Because, being rendered helpless by their intense passion for you—helpless through devotion characterized by love known as *śṛṅgāra*—they have fallen into a state of confusion regarding their duties, devoid of the certainty that "this must be done by me alone. || 9 ||
Passion indeed arises from one's own nature; the means to liberation may or may not be achieved through effort.
Of those two, she has obtained both; O Māruteśa, protect me, whose fortune is such! ||10||

Regarding "passion" (*rāga*): passion arises between women and men from their very nature. However, love for the Lord as a means to liberation occurs through effort only for some, and may or may not arise. For those women of Vraja, both of these were obtained: love for their beloved that grants the pleasure of desire, and love for the Lord that grants the bliss of liberation; this was because Kṛṣṇa alone was both their beloved and the Lord. Oh, what fortune! What fortune! (10)
Thus ends the fifty-ninth decade, the description of the flute-song.
Day after day, with hearts afflicted by love and desiring service to Your two feet,
those tremulous-eyed maidens worshipped Girijā on the sandy banks of the Yamunā.
"Madaneti": They worshipped—that is, they honored—a sand image made of *sikatā*. || 1 ||

O Mother, those of beautiful vision, delighting in the story of your name, came together to the river and worshipped with hundreds of offerings, saying, "May the beloved son of Nanda become [our own]."

"Of you": devoted to your name and to stories about you—meaning, chanting your names and narrating tales concerning you—they have gathered together and, with hundreds of offerings such as water, perfumes, flowers, and incense, they pray, "May the son of Nanda become our beloved"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
Thus, having observed those tremulous-eyed women who had undertaken their vows for a month, you, tender with compassion, approached the riverbank with the desire to favor them. (3)
"Thus" means: those who have undertaken vows, that is, those who have maintained their vows. || 3 ||
Having concluded their ritual observances, they then cast off their garments at the edge of the bank;
distracted by their play in the waters of the Yamunā, they were filled with shame upon seeing you before them. || 4 ||

She restrains them. Having concluded their observances and finished their vows, they cast off their own garments; naked and agitated by water-sports, musical instruments in the water, and the like, they have set out to play in the Yamunā. || 4 ||
Then, as the women bowed their faces with modesty, he seized the web of cloth held nearby and swiftly climbed up the branch of that tree.
"Out of bashfulness": out of shame (*trapā*) born from being unclothed in the presence of her beloved. "Of the tree" (*bhūruhaḥ*): of the tree (*vṛkṣasya*). || 5 ||
"Come here first, O fair-eyed ones, and take your garments as is fitting!"—
as you spoke thus with a playful, gentle smile, the young wives were utterly bewildered.

"Here! [He said. "O fair-eyed ones! Come here and take back each your own garment as it belongs. While you were speaking thus with a gentle smile born of jesting, the young women became utterly bewildered; the meaning is that they were unable even to say, "Do not do so. || 6 ||
"O young soul! Live long! Why do you not bring us, your maidservants, under your control?
Grant us a glance, O lotus-eyed one!"—when addressed thus, you gave nothing but a smile. (7)

"O, young prince! May you live long! Why do you bring us—your maidservants who carry out your every command—under your subjugation and render us dependent? When we said, 'Give us a garment,' and entreated you, you gave nothing but a smile, not even a cloth."

"O youth! O you who have not yet married! Why do you disregard your maidservants who are worthy of your love? Subdue them, accept them, and bestow your garment upon us; for you are our husband, O lotus-eyed one! Without the glance of your side-long look, our lives are dependent on others"—because she spoke thus with such deep meaning, you gave her a gentle smile as a form of consent. || 7 ||

Having ascended the bank, those pure women, with palms joined in reverence, beheld their own auspicious destinies; then, with joy, they offered all their garments and spoke these words once more as a favor: || 8 ||

"Having ascended," [it means]: having become purified—having turned away from the fault of breaking their vows by stripping off their clothes through the penance consisting of bowing down to you—they, whose own paths were their refuge, spoke these words of grace, which will be described below. || 8 ||
Surely your desire is known; as speakers, you ought to give the fitting reply.
Thus those women spoke: "May the nights on the banks of the Yamunā be filled with moonlight. (9)

"Understood. "Manīṣita" means intention or resolve. Regarding this intention of yours, I do not say now that a suitable reply shall be "so be it"; rather, on the sandy banks of the Yamunā, the nights graced by moonlight will speak the appropriate reply to you through action alone. || 9 ||
Having overheard the honey-dripping words falling from your mouth, O beloved,
those fawn-eyed women looked again and again at your lotus-face out of affection and slowly returned home.
"Having heard" means having drunk with the cupped hands of their ears. || 10 ||
Thus, O Hara, cool with compassion! Having favored me by wandering as before at the edge of the forest grove, quickly remove for me the entire multitude of my maladies. 11.
Thus [it is said]: "by compassion" means having a heart that is cool and moist with affection for his devotees. || 11 ||
Thus ends the sixty-first decade, titled "The Description of the Stealing of the Gopīs' Garments.
And thereafter, having gone to a forest very far from Vṛndāvana along with the cowherds and their herds of cattle,
you indeed carried within your heart a firm resolve to bestow grace upon the multitude of the wives of the most devoted brahmins.
"Tataḥ" means from Vṛndāvana; "atidūrato" means at a very great distance from Vṛndāvana. || 1 ||
Then, beholding the young calves in the shelterless forest interior, hungry and distressed by thirst,
he sent them from nearby toward the twice-born who were intent on sacrifice, to beg for food.

"Then," it is said: in that shelterless place devoid of houses, the world of calves—the young ones—was distressed by thirst and hunger. Not far from that spot, in its vicinity, you dispatched those cowherds—who were intent on sacrifice, being preoccupied with ritual action and thus averse to devotion and knowledge—to beg for food, that is, to beg for alms. || 2 ||
Then, when they had departed after announcing their names and requested food from the boys,
those best of Brahmins— though firm in their learning— concealed their lack of learning and said nothing at all, O Lord.

Regarding the word "gateṣu" (having gone): they addressed him by name, saying, "O Kṛṣṇa, ask for rice-porridge. Although their intellects were firm and certain in their learning (*śruti*), they acted as if they had not heard it—that is, they feigned a lack of hearing. Thinking themselves the best of Brahmins, those excellent householders did not say even "I will give you something," nor did they say "no. || 3 ||
Indeed, children whose minds are distressed by neglect approach; this is indeed appropriate among sacrificers.
For those gods on earth have long been without devotion; how indeed could they offer what is devoted to you? (4)

"Because of disregard. This dismissal of one who seeks something is appropriate toward those who perform sacrifices and those who are constantly engaged in sacrificing. *Bhaktam* means cooked food. || 4 ||
"Announce me to the householders; let these women, overwhelmed with compassion, give us food.
With these words, smiling gently, those boys went and made their request to the wives of the householders.
"Announce it! Thus addressed, those young boys—the sons—requested the householders' wives, the wives of the sacrificers, saying, "May they give food; may they provide it. || 5 ||

When your name was uttered, they became agitated with excitement; taking up the four kinds of flavorful foods and having long maintained their intense longing to behold you, they arrived swiftly even though restrained by their own attendants.

Regarding the word "gṛhītā" (taken): as soon as their names were mentioned—[the messenger] saying, "Kṛṣṇa requests alms from you through our mouths"—those women, upon merely hearing your names, quickly [came], even though they were restrained by their own husbands and others; [they brought] the fourfold variety of food—edible, chewable, drinkable, and lickable—and delicious, flavorful nourishment. || 6 ||

Beholding you standing there with your arm resting upon the shoulder of a friend— your hair adorned with trembling peacock feathers, earrings shimmering on your cheeks, and your gaze moist with emotion— they gazed upon you.
She causes it to tremble; when gazed upon with a sidelong glance, it is moistened, drenched by the tears of joy born from an excess of maternal affection. || 7 ||

And at that time, a certain woman, having her hand taken by her beloved sacrificer—her arrival at you having been rendered futile—reflected upon you at that very moment and immediately entered into absolute liberation; oh, how fortunate she was!

"At that time" means: while the others had set out, a certain wife of a sacrificer, having raised her hand toward you, was seized by the hand by her husband. Though restrained with the words, "O sinful woman! Why this perverse conduct?", she meditated upon you; through the experience of the unsurpassed bliss of her resolve for you and the experience of the suffering born from the torment of separation from you, her merit and demerit were exhausted, and she effortlessly—without exertion—entered into *kaivalya*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). She was fortunate (*kṛtinī*). || 8 ||

Having taken food and shown them favor, you then dismissed those women who were casting their eyes upon your limbs as they departed for home; and by sending these away for the sake of sacrifice, you made even their husbands free from reproach.

"Having taken [them]," [it means]: seeing them abandoning their homes along with their dependents out of a longing for contact with your limbs—that is, out of a desire to sport with you—you favored them by making them free from reproach and endowed with great honor. || 9 ||

O Lord of Marutpura! Having examined their own faults among women and observed their devotion, those twice-born ones who investigate further and have awakened to the truth have praised you; please ward off my diseases.
"Having observed," etc.: Having observed their own fault regarding women and having observed their devotion, he was praised by those twice-born ones who had awakened to the truth. (10)

Thus ends the sixty-first decade, the description of the rescue of the sacrificer’s wife. Once, O Śauri, beholding the cowherds who had prepared the wealth of materials for a sacrifice, you were intent on uprooting Indra’s pride.
Although he already knew these things, being gentle in his discipline, he questioned Nanda and the other cowherds: "O Janaka! Who is this person, and what is this undertaking of yours? || 1 ||

Regarding the word "kadācit" (once): you questioned those cowherds, Nanda and the others, who had respectfully prepared and gathered the wealth of sacrificial requisites—the materials required for the Indra-sacrifice—in a manner that was gentle and free from arrogance. || 1 ||
Nanda said to him: "O son! Surely the sacrifice of Indra must be performed by you year after year;
for that sacrifice refreshes the earth with rain, and everything that is to be lived upon on the surface of the earth depends on the rains for men."
Especially for us, animals indeed subsist on grass and water. || 2 ||
He spoke thus: "The means of subsistence, such as crops and the like, are especially [beneficial] for us who live by our herds; for cattle subsist on grass and water. (2)
Having heard these words of his father, you replied with this poignant speech: "Fie on us!
That which is called 'the rain produced by Indra' is not true, for it is the unseen [karma] that indeed creates the appropriate vision for living beings."
In the great forest, do trees offer any tribute whatsoever to Indra? || 3 ||

"Thus," [he says]. "Fie! Alas, what a blind tradition—even the minds of the great are touched by it! For the claim that 'rain is produced by Indra' is not true for us. Since it is indeed the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings—the fruit of their actions—that produces rain, and not Indra; and he too attained his station as Indra solely through unseen merit. He states the reason for this: "In the great forest. The meaning is that even for trees which have not performed sacrifices to Indra, one observes the attainment of well-being (*yogakṣema*) brought about by rain. || 3 ||
This much is certain: since cattle are our family wealth here, it is fitting that this offering for sustenance should be made to the Lord of the Mountains;
for on the surface of the earth, the gods of the soil are surely superior even to the celestial gods.
Therefore, you have declared to your own people that they too are worthy of being propitiated.

"This," he said, "that which was stated here—that cattle are our wealth—is indeed true. Therefore, for their sustenance and for the abundance of grass and water, this offering has been commenced for Govardhana, the lord of mountains; since the mountain provides us with grass and water, it is appropriate. Furthermore, the Brahmins are the gods of the earth, and thus they too must be propitiated and honored. Thus you have declared. (4)
Having heard your words, those cowherds, filled with great respect, worshipped the best of the twice-born and offered abundant oblations to the mountain-king.
With profound reverence, they performed circumambulations and bowed down deeply; then, O Mountain-Daughter, you yourself accepted all the offerings in the presence of the Ābhīras.

"Bhavat" means: they offered a great sacrifice (*bali*) and worship (*pūjā*), highly distinguished from the previous one and augmented by many ritual implements; they performed (*vyadhuḥ*) or accomplished it. You, O Soul of the Mountain, having assumed a body as vast as a mountain, spoke before the Ābhīras—the cowherds—saying, "I am the mountain; I am pleased," and you ate the sacrificial offering. || 5 ||
And you said this to them: "What falsehood have I spoken here?
Indeed, this Lord of Mountains enjoys his own offering with his own body;
and this Gotra is capable of protecting [us] when the enemy of the Gotra is enraged."
Thus addressed, all those inhabitants of Gokula abandoned their bodies entirely.

He said: "In another form, while standing among the multitude of cowherds, you spoke to those very cowherds in the manner about to be described: 'Is this which I have declared here anything other than the truth? This mountain named Govardhana, appearing here in embodied form, is capable and able to protect [us] even if Indra, the enemy of the mountains, should become enraged. (6)
The inhabitants of Vraja, having departed filled with joy upon meeting you, had indeed returned to their village;
meanwhile, hearing of the collapse of his own sacrifice,
and though he knew of your presence, his heart was overwhelmed by excessive passion.
Even Śakra, the lord of the gods, does not equal you, whose self-elevation is fashioned by your own [virtues]. || 7 ||

"Pariprītāḥ" (fully delighted): although he knew you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to be Viṣṇu himself, as he heard and listened to the account of the interruption of his own sacrifice, he could not endure that interruption because his heart was overwhelmed by excessive passion (*rajas*) and attachment to its [worldly] affairs. He whose self-elevation—the attainment of Indra’s station—was brought about by you. || 7 ||

"Even though he has attained human form, if the slayer of Madhu (Viṣṇu) displays such lack of discipline toward the gods, then some great majesty of the assembly of the thirty deities must have perished;
therefore, I shall destroy the fortune of this wretched beast."
That Maghavan, a treasury of insolence, has indeed set out to conquer you.

"Humanity"—[this is the thought: even Viṣṇu, the slayer of Madhu, has attained human status and become base. If this slayer of Madhu does not display insolence toward the gods, then [it is fine]; but if he does display it, then he is no longer the slayer of Madhu. If this were so, then the indescribable majesty of the assemblies of the thirty gods would surely be destroyed by Kṛṣṇa, that wretched cowherd, the lowest of herdsmen. || 8 ||
Setting forth to destroy your abode, he who traverses the sky like a cloud at the time of universal dissolution and wields a thunderbolt-like gait set out,
mocked by others such as Antardāhana, Marut, and the rest.
O Lord of the three worlds! Whom indeed does your māyā not delude?

"Tvaditi": Sending forth—that is, releasing—Atri, he mounted Airāvata; meanwhile, he was laughed at—that is, derided—by others such as Dahana (Fire), Marut (Wind), and so forth, within his own heart. Whom indeed does your Māyā not delude? || 9 ||

O Lord of the Maruts! O Enemy of Mura! Having reassured the cowherds by saying, "Surely Indra will not be angry, for by compassion for the twice-born and pity for the mountain, he will surely remain free from wrath toward us," and then dwelling there while reflecting, "Aha! Why has the Mountain-Cleaver not arrived?", please dispel my anxieties.

Regarding the word *surendra*: "Anātaṅka" means happiness that is distinct from illness (*ātaṅka*) or distress (*saṅkaṭa*); it is constant and certain. While dwelling there, one reflects, "Has Indra, the shatterer of mountains, not arrived in his anger?"—[therefore,] drive away [fear], abandon it! 10.
Thus ends the sixty-second decade, describing the obstruction of Indra’s sacrifice.

At that very moment, indeed, the clouds above the cowherd settlement—whose edges were made to tremble by the expansion of your unassailable thundering and which had attained a likeness to your own limbs through their beauty—were beheld by you. (1)

"They were seen" means: by you, the clouds—which caused the horizons to tremble through their unceasing thunder, their yawning, and their pervading expansion, and which, through their beauty, attained a likeness or comparison with the splendor of your own limbs—were seen above Vraja-pada, your home. || 1 ||

O Ajita! While the herds of cattle were being punished in every direction by showers of water mixed with vast quantities of mud, you heard their cries—"Protect us! Protect us from the wrath of Hari!"—and you said to them, "Do not be afraid. || 2 ||

"Vipuleti" means: [you said], "Do not fear"—that is, do not entertain any dread—of the rain caused by the enraged lord of deer (the lion), which was mixed with large fragments of water-stones (or hailstones). Thus you spoke. || 2 ||
"What indeed is one's lineage here? Truly, the deity is the lineage; who could obstruct the destruction of the lineage-enemy here? What doubt do you have in this matter?
Thus he spoke with a laugh, O Lord! And quickly, with his two arms, he uprooted Mount Govardhana from its very base, O Child! (3)

Regarding the word *kula*: here, in this family (*kula*), the mountain is the lineage (*gotra*) and the deity. May that Govardhana destroy (*rundhyāt*) the hostility born from Indra, the enemy of the lineage (*gotra-śatru*). What doubt do you have concerning this which I have spoken? For his name is both *Gotrāṇa*—from the root *gṛ*, "to protect"—and *Govardhana*. You have uprooted him (*udamumūla*). 3.
Thereafter, while this best of mountains was being lifted up,

you placed it beneath [your arm] with your lotus-hand upon a sandy and soft spot far removed from the heat of the sun; meanwhile, you stationed the cows and cowherds, mingled with their attendants, below [the mountain].

Regarding the phrase "tadanu" and so forth: on a sandy, soft, and moist spot where water was excluded from the vicinity, beneath that great mountain, you placed and settled—by means of your attendants using ropes, baskets, and other implements—the items mixed together; that is, you held them there. || 4 ||
While the mountain was being held steady by young girls and even by their companions, who were engaged in playful sports with parrots and other birds,
and while he was scratching with one hand the cows gathered nearby, all the cowherds attained great satisfaction.

The phrase "bhavatīti" means: they sought satisfaction—that is, contentment—in playful chatter and the like, in sport and gentle conversation, and in the longing for curiosity. The meaning is that, through childish and innocent jesting, the scratching of a cow with one hand, and so forth, their fear of falling from the mountain vanished, and they attained satisfaction. || 5 ||
"This mountain is truly immense, yet he holds it for a long time upon his lotus-like left hand;
what is this marvelous power of the mountain?"—thus was it spoken by the cowherds who were gazing at you.

"Atīti" means: she holds or bears [the mountain] upon her lotus-like hand; thus was it said or described: "Is this the power of the mountain, or rather its capacity for flight, even though it is devoid of wings? || 6 ||
"Aha! The audacity of this boy; with his arms trembling, he might even topple the mountain!
Thus reviling you, Hari rained down fierce showers for seven days.
"Ahaha! [he cried]. With his arms distressed and his strength gone, Hari—Indra—filled with self-reproach, caused a fierce rain to fall for seven days. || 7 ||

O Lord! While you remained motionless, not moving even a step from your place, as the mass of clouds had shed all its water and was carried away by the wind, the Lord of the Maruts, his mind filled with apprehension regarding you, rushed forward.

"Moving away": while you were moving even a distance of one step from your own place, all the water having drained away and [the earth] being rendered substanceless, it was consequently carried off by the wind; thus, with a mind filled with apprehension—fearing [you]—or rather, Viṣṇu himself being suspicious that "this is he," his mind full of doubt, he rushed toward you. || 8 ||
O Lord! When the burden of the rains had then subsided and the herd of cattle had departed for their pastures, you were embraced by the joyful cowherds upon the earth, which was laden with mountains.

When [the mountain] had attained peace—that is, when it had come to rest—upon the earth, you, having placed the mountain Govardhana back in its proper place, embraced him; you were clasped by him. || 9 ||
"Long ago you indeed supported the earth; what effort could there be for you in lifting up the mountains?
Thus praised by the gods, O Lord of Kamalā, O Abode of the Guru! Protect me from disease. 10.
"Regarding 'Dharaṇī' (the Earth): formerly, during the Varāha incarnation. || 10 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third decade, the Description of the Lifting of Govardhana.
Having beheld Your supreme majesty in the form of lifting the mountain and other such feats, all the cowherd folk,
recognizing You as the Lord of the Universe, asked Nanda about the birth of Your son.
"Having beheld," etc.: Having beheld your exceedingly exalted power, all the cowherds, realizing you to be the Lord of the Universe, inquired of Nanda concerning your birth. || 1 ||
Your power has been proclaimed by your father to his own circle;
meanwhile, their affection for you has become even greater than before, and the weight of their great esteem has increased.

Regarding the phrase "declared by Garga": your power, in the form of the declaration made by your father Nanda—"He will conquer many more Daityas"—was proclaimed (*nirgadita*) and taught (*upadiṣṭa*) to your own group, the assembly of cowherds.
Then, his realization of the ultimate truth awakened by that humiliation, the king of the gods, accompanied by the celestial cow,
approached and— his pride destroyed— praised you after touching your lotus feet with his jeweled crown.

"Then" (*tataḥ*): then, through that humiliation and defeat, his realization of the truth arose: "He has descended for my sake; he is my master. *Divyagavī* is Surabhi; "with her" means together with her. (3)

Indra, filled with joy, also consecrated you with the waters of the divine Gaṅgā brought by Airāvata, while Surabhi sprinkled you with her own milk, which was scented with fragrant oils and marked with the name Govinda. || 4 ||

"Sneha" means: Indra also sprinkled [him] with the waters of the divine Gaṅgā, which were fragrant because they had been milked—that is, poured out—with affection; for this very reason, [the child] was marked with the name Govinda. || 4 ||
When you, the Lord of the three worlds, were consecrated as the Lord of Gokula, the cowherd settlement attained,
through your power, a splendor unattainable even in heaven or in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Regarding the word "jagat": when you were consecrated as the Lord of Gokula, the cow-pen (vraja) became the celestial realm (nāka), that is, heaven.
Once, while bathing at dawn in the Yamunā, your father was led away by Varuṇa in the form of a boar;
assuming a mortal form for that purpose, you went to that city of Varuṇa to bring him back.

"At one time" means: within the Yamunā, at Antaryamuna, by means of a Varuṇa-puruṣa—a messenger of Varuṇa—you, assuming a causal mortal form—that is, having taken on a human body for the purpose of removing the earth's burden—went to the city of Varuṇī. || 6 ||

Having been honored with great haste by that Lord of Waters and having accepted him as a father, you returned to your own home at that very moment; your father then related his deeds to his own people.

"With agitation" means: he was honored by Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who was filled with agitation upon seeing him. "The father" refers to Nanda; "his conduct" refers to the act of abducting Nanda. || 7 ||

Having ascertained that you were Hari, and seeing these [beings] whose thirst was fixed upon beholding your feet, O Viṣṇu, you revealed to them that supreme state which is difficult for others to attain. (8)

"Regarding the word 'Hari': having ascertained you to be Hari by such powers as these, and because of your thirst for the vision of your state—which is the Supreme Brahman—you have shown, that is, revealed, the Supreme Brahman, the highest state. (8)

O Infinite One! Those hosts of cowherds who were long submerged in the great ocean of liberation, filled with the surging flow of the essence of supreme bliss, have indeed been raised up by You alone once again. 9.
"Throbbling," etc.; [it occurs] in the great ocean called Kaivalya, which is filled with the flowing stream of the nectar of supreme bliss. || 9 ||
"You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, are the manifest Supreme Self (paramātman) yourself, because you reveal your own nature as Brahman to devotees like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. Thus he says:
"O Lord! In such a manner, in every incarnation, you have shown your own state—which is otherwise unattainable—to those possessed of devotion, just like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand."
Therefore, O Supreme Self, you who are manifest here in the form of a beast, dweller of the city of the wind (the body), protect me from all ailments! || 10 ||
Thus ends the sixty-fourth decade, containing the description of Govinda’s consecration and the description of Nanda’s arrival from the world of Varuṇa,
as told to the cowherd women at the conclusion of their religious observance.
Then, having set out to celebrate the festival of Māra,
you filled your flute at the edge of the Yamunā forest, cooling all directions with your dense moonlight. || 1 ||

"Gopī" means: at the conclusion of the observance, upon the completion of the vow of worshiping Girijā, you stood at the edge of the Yamunā forest and filled—meaning sounded—the flute (muralikā). You had promised—that is, vowed—to perform the festival of Māra, such as the rāsa-dance and other festivities.

O Lord! Hearing the sound of Your flute, which fills the entire expanse of the world with rising circles of notes through its resonances, the young women have attained an indescribable state of mental infatuation. || 2 ||

Regarding the term *sammūrchanābhiḥ*: those [melodies] in which the circles of notes (*svaramaṇḍala*) that have arisen are the varieties of musical application; by means of those *sammūrchanās*, which consist of the seven notes in the form of ascending and descending scales—as it is said, "The seven notes joined in sequence are proclaimed as the *mūrchanās*. It means that which causes one to faint or become bewildered. Such is that incomparable [sound]. (2)
Those lotus-eyed women, devoted to household duties, attached to their sons, and intent on serving their husbands—
having abandoned everything, they were enchanted by the sound of the flute.
O you of lovely form, we have come together to this forest region! || 3 ||
"Those women" refers to those devoted to serving their beloveds and dedicated to the service of their husbands. (3)
Some women, while in the midst of adorning their own limbs,
heard the sound of the flute and left their ornaments half-finished;
having come toward you, they shone even more beautifully for your eyes, adorned as they already were.

"Kāścit" (some): Some women, while putting on their own bodily ornaments—that is, adorning every limb—heard the sound of the flute and came to you; others, having heard the sound of the flute while their ornaments were only half-applied, arrived in that very state, with their adornment incomplete. Among those who were fully adorned—with all their limbs decorated and moving slowly due to the weight of their finery—these women, though only half-adorned, [shone forth] because they had forgotten the lack of complete decoration out of an excess of love for You. "Aho" (Oh! indeed, they became pleasing to Your eyes; the meaning is that they became objects of delight for Your vision. || 4 ||
O Lord! A certain woman has come before You, wearing a necklace upon her hips and a girdle around her neck;
O Mukunda, she has surrendered the beauty of her own loins to You.
The girl with the charming face spoke clearly, especially so.

Regarding the word *hāram*: that which possesses a necklace (*hāra*) is *hārī*; that essence, namely *hāritva*—the quality of being captivating—and specifically the captivating nature of her own hips, the charming-faced girl seemed to speak to you, O Lord. (5)
Another woman, whose bodice was clinging to her breasts, approached you— unobserved by the wives of others due to her confusion—
as if she were a water-jar-bearing vessel for the consecration ceremony of the kingdom of incomparable love.

"Kācit" (a certain woman) refers to one whose bodice is unfastened and whose lower garment is not tied. This is due to her own infatuation and that of other men's wives. "Nirupamā" (incomparable): she is like a jar bearing the weight of her breasts, consecrated for the coronation in the kingdom of supreme love. || 6 ||

O Lord! Surely those women who, unable indeed to emerge from their homes, have meditated upon You alone with firm resolve in their hearts, and having cast off the body, have entered into You—the one supreme form of the bliss of transcendental consciousness—are truly, truly blessed. (7)

"Some" refers to certain women who, being forbidden by their kinsmen, were unable—indeed powerless—to depart from or leave the house; yet, having firmly contemplated and concentrated upon You, they shook off and abandoned both the gross and subtle bodies. "Supreme Consciousness" (paracit) refers to the supreme Brahman, which is non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss; they entered that. "Blessed, most blessed" means exceedingly fortunate. || 7 ||
Women who remember [the Lord] as their lover rather than as the Supreme Self attain the state of the Paramahaṃsa in an instant;
therefore, bearing You—who are the very body of the luminous Supreme Self—in my heart somehow, may I enjoy the nectar of immortality without toil. 8.

Regarding the phrase "jārātmanā": by thinking of You as a lover—that is, with the notion of a lover and not as the Supreme Self, but merely with the thought of a human being—the women, the cowherd girls (gopīs), have attained the goal, which is liberation (mokṣa), the destination of the Paramahaṃsas who discriminate between the Self and the non-Self. Since this is so, may I somehow—whether through desire, hatred, or fear—bear You, whose body is the manifest Supreme Self, within my heart; contemplating You, may I attain immortality, that is, liberation. || 8 ||

O Supreme Lord, you whose face is moist with a charming smile, who look upon all with compassion, and who are an ocean of boundless splendor— being gazed upon by the beautiful women of Vraja gathered from all sides, O sole object of affection for the universe, remove my diseases! 9.

"By those who have approached from all sides": O sole heart of the universe! being gazed upon by those who have come together from every direction, standing surrounding you, you have become the object of their sidelong glances. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth decade, describing the approach of the gopīs to the Blessed One during the Rāsa-dance;
[now follows] those beautiful-eyed women who have arrived, rendered helpless by the falling arrows of the flower-weaponed god of love.
Although her mind was resolved to fulfill his desire, she nevertheless spoke to him as if it were something disagreeable. || 1 ||

"Of those who had approached" means: although his mind was resolved and determined to perform—that is, to carry out—the desired festival of love for those beautiful women (*sudṛśaḥ*) who had arrived at his side, he first spoke to those cowherd girls in a manner that was, as it were, perverse or contrary. || 1 ||
To cause the multitude of sages situated in the sky to hear it, you have proclaimed the dharma of a virtuous wife;
indeed, your words are righteous, yet your conduct is not trustworthy for one who is supposed to be stainless.

"Gagane" means he spoke. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for one who has not been initiated, a festival of desire with women of good family is unrighteous (*adharma*)? How then can there be confidence in the sages regarding the duty toward women of good family as proclaimed by the author [of that work]? To this doubt, he says: "Indeed, it is righteous. That word of the Lord is *dharmyam*, meaning not departing from *dharma*. But our own action is not to be trusted; for in some cases, it may even take the form of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Therefore, there is no fault on your part, because you are stainless; due to being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), you are not subject to the authority of ritual action (*karma*). || 2 ||
Hearing those contrary words, the fawn-eyed women became deeply distressed;
"Do not, do not [go], O ocean of compassion! they lamented for a very long time.

Having heard this, they—meaning those who were hostile toward you, saying such things as, "It is improper for you to come here to my presence at night after leaving your husbands"—were dejected with broken hearts and lamented, crying out, "Do not, do not abandon us! || 3 ||
O Murāri, your mind overwhelmed with compassion by their weeping and lamentation,
you proceeded with them to sport at will upon the banks of the Yamunā.
"Of them" means by their words and speech. Together with them, he began—that is, he set out—to sport and enjoy himself according to his desire. || 4 ||
On the paths along the banks of the Yamunā, beautiful with the moonbeams shimmering like water-pots,
you sat down upon a seat prepared by the upper garments of the cowherd women.

"Candra" refers to the moon. Upon the beautiful banks of the Yamunā, which shimmer with the flowing, liquid nectar of the moonbeams, you sat down—you who had prepared a seat (viṣṭara) using the upper garments of the cowherd women. || 5 ||
With exceedingly sweet jesting conversations, with the grasping of hands, with the delights of kissing,
and with the embrace of firm embraces, you have thrown the world of women into a state of agitation.

"Sumadhuraiḥ" means with very sweet, ear-pleasing playful conversations—jesting words—and with firm embraces that cause the limbs and members of the body to merge like milk and water; thus you were made agitated, that is, you were moved to melting passion. || 6 ||
O Lord! On the day their garments were taken away, You fulfilled that promise of returning the clothes for those fair-browed women whose hearts were overcome by passion for You.

"Vāsa" (garment): On the day of taking away their garments—the day the worship of Girijā was completed—you performed the "taking away of garments," which means you seized the clothing from the region of their hips, as had been promised or vowed. || 7 ||

O Son of Nanda! Having embraced you—who have blossomed with even a trace of dharma, whose lotus-face smiles softly like a jasmine flower, and who are the most beautiful in the three worlds—the young women were filled with joy. 8.

"Kandalita" means sprouted; that in which drops of sweat (gharmaleśāḥ) have sprouted. His lotus-face (vadanapadma), like a jasmine flower (kundakusuma), has a soft smile—a slight smile. "Nanditāḥ" means delighted. || 8 ||
In separation you consist of embers, yet even in union you consist of passion;
that you should become utterly composed of embers even in that union—this is a marvel!

Regarding the phrase "in separations": you, who consist of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment), meaning you possess the speech, dress, and activities appropriate to that sentiment, become "consisting of embers" (*aṅgāramaya*) for women during their separations, because you cause them torment. That you are "even more consisting of embers" (*nitarām aṅgāramaya*) even during union is a paradox. O dear one (*aṅga*), the actual meaning is simply that you are "consisting of ambrosia" (*amṛtamaya*). || 9 ||
Among them, because of the Lord’s extraordinary love for Rādhā, she prays to the Lord as He especially delights her:
"O Lord of the City of Wind! May I worship You, whose soul is eager for the beautiful embrace of Rādhā’s breasts; please pacify all my ailments. (10)

Thus ends the sixty-sixth decade, describing the instruction in dharma given by the Blessed One to the gopīs during the rāsa-dance, and the description of His pastimes with them on the banks of the Yamunā.

Having attained the play of enjoyment through you, whose essence is the surging nectar of supreme bliss, the lotus-eyed women reached a state of great intoxication, having entered into a boundless abundance of joy. (1)

Regarding the word *sphurat*: by you, whose form is the Self in which the essence of supreme bliss (*parānanda-rasa*) vibrates, the play of enjoyment (*bhoga-līlā*), that is, the sport of passion (*ratikrīḍā*), was attained. Having reached the boundless and limitless essence of bliss—the bliss of Brahman, which is synonymous with the pleasure of passion—the great ones attained intense intoxication. || 1 ||
He describes that manner [of disappearance]:

"He, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is delightful to the minds of all the world, has merged into me, into my very self"—thinking thus, O Govinda, you became invisible to all those women who were filled with pride upon seeing you. (2)

"He hides himself": that Kṛṣṇa hides himself—that is, becomes attached—to me without artifice or deceit; whereas toward others he acts as if affectionate through illusion for the sake of kindness and so forth. Having observed those women who held such a conceit—that "he hides himself in me"—you became invisible, having withdrawn within yourself. || 2 ||
O Murāri! Having taken that most beloved cowherd maiden named Rādhā—who was yet free from pride—and having engaged in unrestrained dalliance with her, you have gone far away. (3)
She wins over her exceedingly beloved wife by means of her lack of pride. || 3 ||
Then, O Blessed One, when you had vanished, those lotus-eyed women, overcome with grief, gathered together; searching for you in forest after forest, they fell into boundless despair.
"Disappeared"—meaning, having become equally distressed, sharing the same anguish, they gathered together and searched for you; yet they did not find you, but instead fell into despondency. || 4 ||
Out of despondency, they questioned even the insentient beings; thus he says:
"O mango tree! O campaka! O karṇikāra! O mallikā! O mālatī! O young creepers!
Was he not seen by you—the sole thief of our hearts? Thus did they lament, being entirely devoted to you. (5)
"Alas, O mango tree! O young creepers! Have you not seen our sole thief of the heart? We are devoted to you, with our minds fixed on you alone. || 5 ||
"O friend! This lotus-eyed one is before me"—speaking thus in agitation, a certain woman, seeing you with the eye of her imagination, doubled the distress of her companions. (6)

"Beheld": O friend! This lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa has been beheld—that is, directly perceived—before me. Having seen you as if before his very eyes through the eye of contemplation consisting of mental resolve, he has doubled the distress of his friends by generating hope. || 6 ||
Those [gopīs], who were essentially of your own nature, imitated your activities on the banks of the Yamunā;
yet, having searched for you again in that same manner, they saw Rādhā separated from you due to her pride.

"Tvaditi": Consisting of you, they attained identification with you through the power of their meditation and imitated your deeds, such as the slaying of Pūtanā and the breaking of Arjuna. Having searched for and sought you out once more, they saw Rādhā separated from you due to her pride—the conceit that "I am his most beloved," just as it was for the others. || 7 ||
Then, searching for them together throughout the forest until the descent of darkness, they were once again reunited at the edge of the Yamunā’s bank; they lamented intensely and sang of his virtues.

"Then," it says: then those gopīs, together with her, searching for Him throughout the forest on all sides from the time of the descent of darkness until the setting of the moon, lamented—being united and joined together, they wept with longing and in melodious voices. || 8 ||
O sole ocean of compassion! To the women of Vraja whose minds were overwhelmed by such agony, you—whose very self deludes even the deluder of the three worlds—manifested with a gentle smile. (9)

"So be it. Thus, you appeared with a gentle smile, your form being the deluder even of Kāma—the one who deludes the three worlds—while their minds were agitated and overwhelmed by such an indescribable anguish and pain. || 9 ||
O Lord of the Wind! Seeing you, whose own beauty was eclipsed by your appearance as a leper, those slender women were suddenly overwhelmed by an excess of joy;

what did they not do then? Protect me from disease! 10. O Lord of the Wind! Seeing you, whose own beauty was eclipsed by your appearance as a leper, those slender women were suddenly overwhelmed by an excess of joy; what did they not do then? Protect me from disease!

"Sandigdha" means one whose sight is uncertain—doubting whether he will see him again from this point forward or not. [This occurs] due to the excessive weight of joy, through an onset of rapture. || 10 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh decade, which describes the Lord's disappearance for the sake of dispelling the intoxication of the gopīs during the rāsa-dance, the description of their search for the Lord, and the description of the Lord’s manifestation.
O lotus-eyed one! Upon beholding you, the cowherd women, overwhelmed with joy, stood motionless before you as if drenched by a stream of nectar. || 1 ||
"Thine!"—thus [exclaimed], they were filled with splendor, overwhelmed with joy, and drenched; having been consecrated, they attained stillness, that is, immobility. || 1 ||
Thereafter, a certain woman, suddenly and without hesitation grasping your lotus-hand, placed it against her firm breast and stood for a long time covered in horripilation. (2)

Regarding the phrase "tadanu" (thereafter): immediately upon seeing her, while the others remained there, she stood for a long time, free from hesitation, covered by horripilation born of the intense experience of bliss produced by the touch of your lotus-hand upon her thick, dense breast. || 2 ||
O Lord! Overwhelmed with intense joy, she entwined your exceedingly tender arm around her own neck, as if obstructing the vital breath rising from her throat. || 3 ||
"Yours. Another, having grasped your arm, wound it around her own neck and bound it there, as if restraining the vital breath that was about to escape due to the agony of separation from you. (3)
A certain lovely woman, having departed from your lotus-face with a morsel of betel she had been chewing,
attained the fulfillment of her desire as she placed it back into your lotus-mouth.

"Having departed": having accepted and taken that betel-chewing paste, she placed it in her own lotus-like mouth and tasted it; thus she attained the fulfillment of all desires and reached the state where the fruit of life has truly ripened. || 4 ||
"O pitiless one, you have departed from the forest, abandoning me; who here could possibly touch you?"—thus were you gazed upon with tearful eyes by one woman full of wrath. (5)

"O merciless one! Having abandoned me in the forest, you have gone away and traveled far; therefore, why have you now come back, you who are so pitiless and cruel? Who here among us would touch you? Thus he was gazed upon with eyes full of tears. (5)
Thus, having arrived at the bank of the Yamunā with the cowherd women who were overwhelmed with joy,
you two shone as you sat upon a seat fashioned from their soft breasts and garments, radiant with the scent of musk.
"Thus" means: on a seat prepared with soft breast-cloths as upper garments (*uttarīya*), radiant with *ghusṛṇa* and beautified by saffron (*kuṅkuma*). || 6 ||
Then, as they sat together, they spoke to you; thus he says:
"How many kinds of compassion are there? Some possess the dawning of mercy toward all, while others toward their own dependents.
Yet some are such that they extend it even to those like me"—thus were you addressed by the cowherd women. (7)

"Of how many kinds is compassion in this world? [He asks: "Are there some compassionate ones who have aroused the dawn of mercy toward all people everywhere? Or are there some who have aroused the dawn of mercy only toward those who have taken refuge with them? And are there some others who, even toward those like me who have sought refuge, are as merciless as you? In that regard, please state the truth"—this is the implied sense of the verse. (7)
Your Honor spoke the supreme words:
"O young maiden! Let there be no suspicion of hardness in me, for I am tender with love.
Rather, I said, 'I have done this in order to comply with the wishes of your hearts. (8)

[The Lord said: "O young maidens! O frail ones! Since I am distressed by love and fearful of the loss of your affection, you should not suspect any hardness or cruelty in me. This disappearance was brought about by me solely for the sake of following your hearts and for the purpose of concentrating your minds upon me. (8)
"O Lord! Listen: my beloved is not such a person as this living husband;
therefore, please enjoy yourself here during these delightful nights without restraint. Thus she spoke.

"O! O beloveds of my life, lords of my breath! Listen to the truth: there is no one so dear to me as you are. Therefore, on these nights made beautiful by the moonlight upon the banks of the Yamunā, let us enjoy ourselves with me here without restraint and free from fear"—thus did you speak, thus did you address me. (9)

O Lord of the city of Gokula, having felt great curiosity, you took delight together with the women of Vraja, who were overflowing with joy at these words; protect me from disease through this play of the *rāsa* dance. 10.
Thus: "with [limbs] swollen—that is, pervaded—by joy; sporting with Himself; having conceived a longing—that is, having taken up an intense attachment—for the *rāsa*-sport, the *rāsa*-dance. || 10 ||

Thus ends the sixty-eighth decade, which describes the gopīs’ state of being overwhelmed by bliss due to their union with the Blessed Lord during the Rāsa dance, the description of their lover’s quarrels, and the description of the consolations offered by the Blessed Lord.
Now he describes the rāsa-dance:
with a mass of peacock feathers held in her locks of hair, with swaying crocodile-shaped earrings,
charming with clusters of necklaces and forest garlands, and possessing the intense fragrance of unguents;

O Lord! We indeed perceive Your form, adorned with yellow garments and a golden waist-cloth, graced by shimmering sun-crystal earrings and anklets, and beautifully embellished for the rāsa-dance pastime. || 1 ||

"Keśa" refers to one who possesses a mass of hair adorned with a profusion of peacock feathers—that is, a particular head ornament fashioned from peacock plumes displaying circular eye-patterns (*candraka*) visible all around. He has shark-shaped earrings (*makarakuṇḍala*) swaying upon the surface of his cheeks. He is lovely and beautiful with networks of necklaces and forest garlands (*vanamālikā*). His fragrance is dense and intense due to being thoroughly anointed with cosmetic unguents such as saffron and the like.

We contemplate and worship Your form, adorned for the Rāsa-sport with a girdle of jewels over a yellow garment, beautified by a waist-cloth of ghee and sour gruel, and wearing jeweled anklets from which radiant rays of light stream upward; thus we behold You, fully arrayed in Your festive attire. || 1 ||

Just then, O Beloved of Indirā! as you were moving between the two most beautiful women in that circular assembly of young women—who had completed their adornments, whose breasts were covered by bodices, and whose cheeks trembled with jeweled earrings— ... [you were seen].
O Lotus-navelled One! Following that, You performed the charming rāsa-sport. || 2 ||

"At that time" means: while the Blessed One was still in the attire suitable for playing at *dhṛtarāsaka*, he was already adorned with such ornaments. His breast-circles were covered by a bodice (*kañculī*) which he wore; thus he was "one whose breast-circles had a bodice placed upon them. Then, after being adorned, as he moved between every pair of all the beautiful women—standing in a circular formation on level ground marked by stakes—he proceeded gracefully, his two arms busily engaged in mimetic gestures (*abhinaya*) toward their breasts, necks, cheeks, and other parts. [He performed] the charming, heart-stealing dance. || 2 ||
O Vāsudeva! Having perceived from afar the fragrance of the rasa of the rāsa-sport emanating from you here, as described by Nārada,
she— agitated by curiosity and surrounded by hundreds of graceful women adorned with fine attire and ornaments— [approached].
Then, the host of gods arrived simultaneously from the sky with great speed.

Regarding the word *vāsudeva*: having perceived—that is, having heard—the fragrance, meaning the exquisite charm, of that very *rāsakelī* (the Rasa-dance) which is a "flavor" (*rasa*) because it delights all the senses, as described and reported by the venerable Nārada; [there arrived] a host of gods (*suramaṇḍalī*), a multitude of deities, who came simultaneously from heaven (*nāka*) through the sky in their celestial chariots (*vimāna*) with great speed, accompanied by hundreds of playful women—his own thousands of wives—who were clever and skillful in their dress, ornaments, and amorous gestures. || 3 ||

This [dance] would be characterized by its circularity, enchanting through the synchronization of rhythmic clapping with the soft falling of feet— charming due to the melodies, scales, and modulations produced by the sound of flutes— and accompanied by bracelets jingling against the palms and lotus-like hands repeatedly suspended from the shoulders.
Enjoy the grand display of the rasa-sport, wherein the garment on her rounded hips is swaying.

Regarding the word *veṇu*: by means of the flute-playing performed through the sounding of notes (*tāna*) which are the basis for melody (*svara*), and by means of the singing—which is sweet due to its resonance arising from the throat and which involves the application of the movements of musical modes (*rāga-gati-yojanā*) as well as the connection with the remaining paths of those modes—the footfall [of the dancers] becomes alluring; and by the resulting synchronization of rhythm (*tāla-melana*), there is a charming intensification of the splendor of the rasa of the rāsa-sport. || 4 ||
Then, amidst a dance performed with faith, accompanied by voices rising in sweet, high-pitched tones, and graced by graceful movements of the limbs and shimmering jeweled ornaments,
the host of gods appeared in the sky, manifesting and raining down flowers in great joy.
As he dissolved into you, who consist of consciousness, the fire became bewildered along with the assembly of his wives.

"With faith" means: when that dance was performed—wherein the pitch grew progressively higher and sweeter through faith, curiosity, enthusiasm, accompaniment, and emulation; wherein the jeweled ornaments on the body were displaced from their positions by graceful *aṅgahāras* (limb-movements); and wherein a rain of flowers was showered by him out of "exultation," that is, an onset of joy born from witnessing the extraordinary excellence of the performance.

The host of the gods, eager to behold [the event] and accompanied by their wives and families, was utterly bewildered by the intensity of the sight; they were as if hidden away, meaning that the distinction between the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing had vanished from view. || 5 ||
Thereafter, a certain cowherd woman, her slender vine-like body drenched with sweat, her eyes drooping with the weight of exhaustion, leaned upon the shoulder of her beloved;
while another, her hair disheveled, [inhaled] the fresh fragrance of the essence of new sandalwood paste.
Through deception, he kissed your arm, which was covered with sprouts of horripilation.

"Svinna" means one who is perspiring; she whose slender vine-like body was drenched with sweat and had reached a state of exhaustion was thus described. With her eyes closed due to the weight of fatigue and extreme weariness, she leaned upon your beautiful, lovely arm-pit (*asaṃ-bhuja-mūla*). Another woman, whose tresses were disheveled and the mass of her braided hair loosened, kissed your arm under a pretext—by means of a deceptive excuse—using a garland (*māleya*) possessing the essence of fresh sandalwood (*navapaṭīrasāra*), that is, a fragrance never experienced before; or rather, a fragrance as fresh as the essence of new sandalwood. [This was] produced by that [act].
In which there is the sprout of a vast thrill of joy.
A certain woman, pressing her own cheek against yours on the surface of your cheek— her earrings thereby jingling—
obtained from you, O treasure-trove of a mass of merit, the nectar-like juice of the betel nut she had chewed;
for you are the abode of Lakṣmī’s pastimes, the beauty of the world, and the stage for her dance.
Having obtained you, did women not indeed assume a state of intense intoxication? || 7 ||

"Kāpi" (a certain woman): Having placed her own cheek against the region of your cheek so that her earrings were set in motion, she experienced the nectar-like essence of the betel-roll, which was like the nectar of immortality itself, as it was being chewed. Through *sammada*—an excess of joy—an intermediate state of intoxication arose, characterized by a lack of connection between what precedes and what follows. || 7 ||
O Lord! The singing has indeed ceased in due course, and the ensemble of instruments has stopped; agitated by the essence of the bliss of Brahman, the women in the assembly danced alone.
They were not even aware of their bodices, nor their tresses, nor their bodices.
Even the cluster of luminaries suspended in the sky—what more shall I say? || 8 ||

Regarding the word "singing" (*gānam*): the women, overwhelmed by the essence of the joy of union with Brahman—the experience of the bliss of Brahman—became utterly helpless and danced solely within the assembly. He describes the exclusivity of their dancing with the word "singing. By the phrase "even the cluster of luminaries, such as the planets and stars, was suspended in the sky," the protracted duration of the night is indicated due to the delay in sunrise. What more need I say? The meaning is: why describe the helplessness of those staying on earth, such as the loosening of the waist-knot, the hair, and the limbs, and the failure to perceive these things, when there is already the grace [of the gods] regarding the singing and other matters? || 8 ||
O Lord! Having dissolved the universe at the end of the eon and having concluded Your cosmic play, You—

impelled by the merit of those whose very souls are made beautiful by the slightest trace of the dharma of women who delight in amorous sport, and whose minds cannot endure the God of Love— then assumed a manifest form and bestowed the supreme festivals of the heroic Māra upon the wives of the Paśus.

He rejoices. Having dissolved—that is, having immersed—the world, the realm of perceivers, within the limit of joy that is the bliss of Brahman, he assumes as many forms as there are gopīs, impelled by their own merit.

These forms possess limbs that are delicate and stainless due to being rubbed during amorous play; their bodies are made auspicious by fresh traces of the ritual marks [of love]; and their minds are impatient with passion, unable to endure any delay in the time of amorous dalliance. || 9 ||
O Lord! Indeed, you have performed a charming pastime on the banks of the Yamunā at your own will, accompanied by groups of women who are exceedingly fondled and agitated by various sports;
and even in the forest, which is enchanting with the spreading, cool, youthful breeze.
It sported in that place filled with the fragrance of the musk-deer, enchanting hundreds of playful women. || 10 ||

Thus he played. With various modes of play—consisting of the application of embraces, kisses, blows, tooth-marks, nail-scratches, sucking, whistling, hiccups, sighs, and so forth—he was agitated and overwhelmed by them. He performed aquatic sports (*vihṛti*) in the Yamunā waters, the milk of the Sun’s daughter, and also performed sports in the forest. By means of the cool, youthful breeze—which is pervasive, fanning, and pleasant—in that place made charming by the fragrance of flowers, you shone, captivating hundreds of playful women. || 10 ||
O treasure-house of all that is desirable! Indeed, during the nights, you— who manifest an indescribable ocean of the essence of perfect bliss—
inspire even Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and the other gods with great respect for the wives of the cowherds.
O Kṛṣṇa, whose form is beloved by the world of devotees, O desirable one, protect me! 11.

"O Kāminī! [The commentary explains: O treasure-trove of loveliness! O ocean of good fortune! You, who during the nights experience and savor the bliss of Brahman—an ocean of the essence of perfect joy that is accessible and attainable by yogis—and who cause even Brahmā and the other gods to hold in high esteem the wives of the cowherds, making them full of great respect; O you whose form is to be approached and attained by the world of devotees! O lovely one! O beloved! O Kṛṣṇa! Protect me completely. || 11 ||

Thus ends the sixty-ninth decad (along with the seventieth), which describes the playful dalliances of the cowherd women, such as dancing and singing, together with the Blessed One who assumes a most enchanting form during the Rāsa-līlā.
Thus, while you, the beloved, were absorbed in the aesthetic rasa of the sport, the cowherds—

Once again, on one occasion, in the forest of Ambikā, the serpent Kāliya, having approached you and partaken in a divine festival together with you at night, fell asleep happily; at that time, O Lord of Vraja, he was overcome by exhaustion. || 1 ||

Thus: In this manner, while you—who had caused your beloved to take delight in such a way that she was overwhelmed with passion and curiosity—were present, the cowherds (ballavāḥ) once again met with you at Ambikāvana, a sacred field of Śiva known as Ambikā’s grove; having enjoyed a divine festival together with you during the night, they slept happily. At that time, a fierce and cruel serpent, an ajagara, swallowed Nanda, the lord of Vraja. || 1 ||
Then, even as he was struck by firebrands held upward, he did not forcibly release your feet; rather, crying out "Save me! Save me!", he fell down.
At that moment, you indeed approached and touched him with your foot, and he, having regained his own Vidyādhara body, shone forth.

"Samunmukham" means facing upward, intent on devouring. "Ulmukaiḥ" means with firebrands. By those cowherds, [the weapon] fell upon your feet. Having approached—that is, having reached—the Vaidyādharī [weapon], which pertains to the Vidyādharas, it shone; that is, it gleamed. || 2 ||
"O Lord, bearer of the Sudarśana! Is it not true that I am named Sudarśana?
Once, I mocked the sages, and they made me a vehicle here;
but by surrendering myself at your feet, I have attained purity. Thus he spoke.
Praising his own feet, he departed for the land of Vraja, while the cowherds went with joy.

"Sudarśana," he said. "Once upon a time, I mocked the sages of the lineage of Aṅgiras. Those sages, in this very place, transformed me into a python (*ajagara*). Because I was arrogant due to my own handsome appearance and mocked them because of their deformity, they cursed me, saying, 'Therefore, you shall become a python. Now that you have attained purity, you are released from the curse. Having spoken thus, while praising him, [the sage] departed for his own abode, the realm of the Vidyādharas. || 3 ||
Because the rules for the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings are not always fixed:

once, while you were sporting with the women, that Śaṅkhacūḍa, the follower of Kubera, indeed carried off those helpless ladies; then, pursued by you who followed him with extreme speed, he abandoned the women.
You shattered his crest-jewel and gave it to the wielder of the plow.

"Once upon a time": while You were sporting and playing with Śrī, namely Balabhadra, the follower of Dhanada—a servant of Vaiśravaṇa—carried off the weak women, the gopīs. You pursued him very swiftly; You crushed Śaṅkhacūḍa, from whom the group of women had escaped out of fear, and You gave his crest-jewel to Your elder brother, the wielder of the plow (Balarāma). || 4 ||

And during those days, while you were intent on sporting in the forests with your friends, enchanting the mind with the god of love and offering the nectar of the sound of your flute-playing—you who bestow the attainment of the immortal state— [The verse continues: ...I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (12) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (13) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (14) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (15) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (16) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (17) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (18) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (19) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (20) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (21) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (22) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (23) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (24) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (25) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is strewn with golden sand, and where the deer gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder. (26) O Lord, I have seen you there, where the mountain slopes are adorned with blossoming *campaka* trees, where the earth is covered with the pollen of *mallikā* flowers, and where the sky is filled with the fragrance of blooming *kunda* blossoms. (27) I have seen you, O Lord, in that forest where the trees are like the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, where the ground is stre
Having reflected thus, why did he not speak to the gopīs who were tormented by separation? || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the days": thus, day by day, together with his friends—the cowherd boys—he whose flute-sound was like nectar itself, having tasted [the sweetness] which was more enchanting than even the god of love (*manobhava*), brought about for the celestial nymphs (*amarīdṛśām*)—those with the eyes of heavenly women—a feast of nectar, providing them with the drinking of the nectar of his own form. Tormented by even a moment's separation, their hearts burning with heat, did they not speak? The meaning is that, reflecting upon his various states, they lamented. || 5 ||

Then a certain servant of King Bhoja, an ill-omened man whose vision was fixed upon a wretched and evil path, stood before you in the form of a bull, possessing a cruel appearance and a harsh, discordant cry.

He was a servant—a hireling—of Kaṃsa, the King of the Bhojas. His vision was fixed upon a cruel path, full of violence and intent on harassing others. He possessed a harsh and cruel appearance; having the form of a bull and emitting a discordant, cruel-sounding roar, he stood before you, remaining within the range of your sight. || 6 ||
Then Śākara, the sustainer of the world, assuming the form of Bṛhatī,
quickly agitating Paṅkti, attained you, the treasury of the meters of cattle.

Regarding the word *śākara*: a *śākara* bull has the nature (*dhṛti*) of supporting (*dhartum*) the earth (*jagatyāḥ*, i.e., the ground). Likewise, having caused the herd of cattle (*paśūnām paṅktim*) to scatter and flee, he [the Bull] is the treasury of the meters (*chandasām nidhim*), containing the Vedas within his womb. This [Bull] is unharmed (*ariṣṭaḥ*), being liberated from the mere constraints of the meters—namely the *śakvarī*, *jagatī*, *dhṛti*, *bṛhatī*, and *paṅkti*. It is understood that there is a great distinction between you and the mere treasury of meters; you are the Great One. Thus ends verse 7.

Seizing with impetuosity that Daitya— who was rushing forward with his lofty horn-like face raised and who, though possessing a handsome form, was inauspicious— the Bull, free from pity, trampled him and roared, bringing joy to the world of the gods.

"Tuṅge" means: [the bull] whose face or the tip of its horns was lofty, or whose face possessed lofty horns; [you], having seized—that is, having captured—the one who was approaching, who was fearless (*abhīyam*), who had an auspicious form (*bhadrarūpam*) yet was actually inauspicious (*abhadram*) in his wicked nature as a bull, by crushing and subduing him, you gladdened us (*amadayaḥ*). || 8 ||
"How wonderful today, O Blessed One! Through the slaying of the bull, the stability of the Dharma (vṛṣasthiti) has become firmly established upon the earth;
and since great joy increases in the mind of the Dharma (vṛṣacetas), you are being extolled by the gods. (9)

"It is a marvel! [This is the meaning. Following the slaughter of the bull—the killing of Ariṣṭa—there arose a firm establishment of the bull, that is, Dharma, upon the earth. Furthermore, in the mind of Vṛṣṇi (Indra), or in the mind of the bull, that is, Dharma, or in the virtuous person whose intellect is fixed on Dharma; it is a marvel that from the slaughter of the bull there came both the stability of the bull and joy in the mind of the bull. || 9 ||
"O calves! Run far away and look out for this bull-slayer here!"—thus, along with the cowherds who were filled with laughter, you entered their homes; protect us, O Lord of Vātapura! 10.

"Aukṣakāṇi!"—O *aukṣakas*, O herds of bulls, O herds of oxen! Run far away! Here is this one who distinguishes between oxen, the slayer of bulls, or the slayer of the inviolable (*ariṣṭa*). Thus, with loud laughter and words spoken in jest. || 10 ||

Thus ends the seventieth decade, containing the description of the liberation from the curse of the Vidyādhara named Sudarśana, the description of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa, and the description of the slaying of Vṛṣabhāsura. In all his efforts, that Keśin—the beloved kinsman of the Lord of Bhoja—was not defeated;
thinking, "He has obtained [the horse] born of the ocean," he assumed the form of a horse born of the ocean and arrived [there]. || 1 ||

"Wherein [he is] *iṣu*... means: O Keśin, you who are not devoid of effort (*nāvakeśī*)—that is, not fruitless—in your endeavors; having obtained Lakṣmī from the ocean (*sindhujayā*), as if thinking, "If he has obtained her from the ocean, then I too shall become one born of the ocean (*sinduja*). || 1 ||

Although he had become a Gandharva and terrified all the world with his harsh cries, that wicked one, having ravaged the cowherd settlement until the moment of your glance, has now fallen upon you once again.

Regarding the phrase "gandharvatām": although he had attained the state of a *gandharva*—that is, the state of a horse—he did so with harsh neighs; for a *gandharva* (celestial musician) indeed possesses a gentle voice. || 2 ||
O you whose feet were once placed upon Tārkṣya, this very Tārkṣya has now cast his foot upon the surface of your chest;
as if out of delusion, thinking "since it was possible for him even by himself," he has heard the story of Bhṛgu’s kick and acted accordingly.

Regarding the word "tārkṣya": this Danuja is Tārkṣya. For Bhṛgu once struck Viṣṇu on the chest with his foot; having heard that story, [the demon] acted as if out of delusion, thinking, "That striking with the foot can be done by me as well. || 3 ||
Deceiving him by suddenly treading upon the tip of his hoof, you flung him far, far away;
for though he was already unconscious from being utterly overwhelmed, he rushed toward you in a rage, driven by the heat of his fury, intent on devouring you.

"Deceiving," it is said: deceiving—that is, evading—the horse's kick with its hoof, you suddenly and instantly seized him by the feet and cast him far, far away. He was rendered utterly unconscious; [you] rushed forward—that is, you fell upon him. || 4 ||
You, whose mind was fixed on the punishment of the steeds, then placed the goad upon his mouth;
with his breath obstructed by that growth, he became lifeless and attained identity even while becoming a horse.

"Thou art... [The commentary continues: *Vāhadaṇḍe* means in the killing of horses (*aśvavadhe*). *Bāhādaṇḍam* means the staff-like arm (*bhuja-daṇḍam*). By the increase of that—that is, by the increase of the staff-like arms—there is union (*aikyam*) or *sāyujya* with the Blessed One, even though one has become sevenfold through the breaking of the horses. Furthermore, there is a suggested paradox (*virodha*), as one whose mind is fixed on the "horse-staff" (*vāhadaṇḍa*) is also said to possess the "arm-staff" (*bāhādaṇḍa*). || 5 ||

O Keśava, by the mere act of seizing the sacrificial animal for the propitiation of the gods—just as if a horse-sacrifice had been performed—you have acted out of joy; therefore, the lords of the gods shall surely be pleased with you.

"He sacrificed" (ālambheti). For in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is only when an animal has been actually sacrificed and used for the offering that the favor of the gods is secured. But here, by the mere act of sacrificing—the mere killing of the horse—the favor of the gods was produced. Therefore, having performed this unprecedented (nūtne apūrve) Aśvamedha sacrifice or the slaughter of the horse, they praised you, whose name is Keśava. (6)
Having told Kaṃsa the truth regarding your being the son of Śūra, you restrained him with words;
then, at the conclusion of Keśin’s destruction, you were praised by the venerable Nārada who had arrived.

"To Kaṃsa": [The Lord] spoke thus, restraining with His words Kaṃsa—who was intent on killing Vasudeva and eager for the slaughter of Kṛṣṇa—after having told him that this Kṛṣṇa was not the son of Nanda, but rather the eighth child of Devakī, and after [the Lord] had reached the end of the subduing of Keśin. || 7 ||
Once, while you were eager for the game of hide-and-seek with the cowherds at the edge of the forest,
my son, named Vyoma— a practitioner of difficult illusions who obstructs those who move through the sky— overtook you.

"Kadāpi" (at some time) refers to the game of hide-and-seek, consisting of concealment, watching, and touching, performed with great devotion. The enemy of the gods was an obstructer of those who move through the sky. || 8 ||
Acting like a thief among the cowherds who had fled from the bandits, he seized the young cowherds and the cattle;
having placed them in caves, he covered them with rocks, but upon being recognized by you, he was utterly crushed.

Regarding the word "sa" (he): some cowherds acted like thieves, while others fled. But the son of Maya, wearing the guise of a cowherd, acted as a thief; having placed the cattle and the cowherd boys inside mountain caves, he closed and sealed them. He was crushed and captured by you. || 9 ||

O Lord of the Wind, whose form is the Supreme Self! May you protect us, ever renewing at every step our boundless state of incomparable bliss through such various and sudden manifestations of play. 10.
"By such [means]" means that there is an infinite and limitless increase of bliss at every step, at every moment; the reason for this is that he is the embodiment of the Supreme Self. || 10 ||
Thus ends the seventy-first decade, containing the description of the slaying of Keśin and the description of the slaying of Vyomāsura. Now, the slaying of Kaṃsa is described in four decades:
Then Kaṃsa, having heard from the words of Nārada that you were residing in Vraja, his heart rent with fear, summoned the son of Gāndinī and dispatched him,
under the pretext of a bow-sacrifice, O Lord who reclines upon the ocean, to bring you here.

Regarding the word "Kaṃsa": Having heard the words of Nārada that Viṣṇu had been born to Devakī for the purpose of slaying him and was now living in Nanda’s cowherd settlement, Kaṃsa’s heart was rent asunder and his mind became terrified; thus, under the pretext of a bow-sacrifice—a ruse for observing the archery festival—he dispatched Akrūra, the son of Gandinī, sending him forth with this excuse. || 1 ||
This Akrūra, long devoted to your feet, was unable to behold you for a long time due to fear of the king; yet,
by his very command, he has now prepared to see you again and has borne an exceedingly great burden of bliss.

Regarding the word "Akrūra": he is devoted to your feet, a devotee of yours; due to fear of the king—that is, out of dread of Kaṃsa—his mind was such that he felt incapable of seeing Kṛṣṇa, thus he was one whose mind was incapable of beholding you. || 2 ||

Thus this virtuous man, traveling by chariot to your dwelling, repeatedly relishes the multitude of desires cherished within you, yet [remains] mindful of fate through the fear of impending misfortune.
Praying thus on the path, he did not perceive anything at all.

"Saḥ" (He): While on the way, he tasted with his mind the multitude of desires for you—the three of you—consisting of seeing, touching, and so forth, which were being held in his thoughts; and fearing the danger of misfortune caused by his own service to Kaṃsa, and fearing the absence of the Lord's vision, he prayed to fate, "May there be a vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for me today. Thus, thinking only of you on the path, he was not aware of anything else at all. || 3 ||
He says that very thing:
"I shall see the Person whose gait is sung of by hundreds of Vedas;
shall I touch him, or even perhaps embrace him?"
