"What will he say? Where indeed might he have seen me?"—thinking thus, he led her along a path that was entirely composed of her own being.

"I shall see Him. What indeed shall I see—that Person (puruṣa) whose nature and state are proclaimed by hundreds of Vedas and Upaniṣads, as well as by the Gītā? Shall I touch Him, that I might experience the bliss of His touch? May this indeed come to pass! Will that Blessed Lord say to me, with palms joined in reverence, "O, you are not far away"? In which place, pray, shall He be beheld by me?
Thus, through the continuity of remembrance of You as his support, he led his path to consist entirely of You, having transcended all else. || 4 ||
Entering once again, in due order, Vrindavana— which is purified by Your feet and worshipped by Hara, Virincha, and the gods—
he was as if absorbed in bliss, as if clinging in a state of supreme delusion.
O lotus-eyed one! What change of state has he not undergone? || 5 ||
"Furthermore": while clinging to extreme delusion, because of the absence of outward manifestations of change, what other state did he not undergo as if he were utterly stupefied? (5)
Beholding them, he paid homage to the places where you had appeared; he rolled in the dust marked by your footprints.
What more can we say? For even then, many people were born.
But those who are thus made tremulous by devotion are rare, O Supreme Self! || 6 ||

"Beholding," he says: he paid homage to the places of your pastimes, the sites of your play; he rolled in the dust marked by your feet, applying the dust of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet to all his limbs. What more can we say? At that time, many people were born during your era; nevertheless, like Akrūra, those who are thus agitated by devotion and dependent on others are rare, few indeed. || 6 ||

In the evening, beholding the cowherds' dwellings— which served as an elixir for his ears through the nectar of songs concerning your deeds— he proceeded toward your abode, as if being carried away by a river of joy.

Regarding the word "sāyam": at the time of evening twilight, the song of Your deeds is itself the nectar; its flowing forth is the oozing of that nectar. Beholding those cowherd dwellings in which that very [song] is an elixir for the ears—providing bliss to the sense of hearing—he was as if being carried along by a river in the form of supreme joy. || 7 ||
At that moment, O Lord, he beheld you, the elder brother, whose eyes were restless with the desire to look upon the milking of the cattle, as if awaiting the arrival of the supreme devotee;
you who seemed to be pouring forth an ocean of the essence of the bliss of internal Brahman-realization.

"Until then" means: Akrūra beheld you, who were eager to gaze upon the milking of the cows and full of faith, as if waiting for the arrival of Akrūra, that best of devotees. "The experience of Brahman" is the knowledge of Brahman; the ocean of rasa produced by that is the sea of bliss, which is *ānanda*.

Because the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) had been transformed into the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa while on the road, and because it was situated within [him], immediately upon the vision of the Lord, that state emerged outward through the doors of the senses; thus the meaning is that he seemed to be vomiting out the internal bliss of seeing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 8 ||
Their bodies were purified by the special bath taken at the end of the day; they were enchanting in their beautiful garments of yellow and blue silk;
and they wore lovely attire with ornaments that were not excessively elaborate.
He beheld you two, with faces moistened by gentle smiles.

In this context, the term *udvami* (vomiting) refers merely to the externalization of that which was previously functioning as an internal process conducive to emerging; this is understood by resorting to the *nivṛttapreṣaṇa* (cessation of the causal impulsion) view. Thus, the epithet of the Blessed One—"standing like an ocean of the nectar of the experience of Brahman emerging from Akrūra’s heart"—is logically justified. To support this very interpretation, the statement "On the path, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa... was uttered [in the commentary]. [The word] *sāyantanā*... [etc. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "sāyantaneti". The translation reflects the available portion.)

They were at the time of evening twilight; they had performed an immersion bath reaching up to their necks, by which their bodies were especially purified and clear. They possessed a charming and captivating appearance, adorned with ornaments that were neither overly elaborate nor excessive. || 9 ||
Descending from his chariot from afar, he raised up the crest-jewel of the devotees as he bowed; then,
embracing him with words of measured joy, the Lord, together with his army, took his hand and inquired after his welfare before leading him to his palace.
"From afar... [means: Out of joy, you embraced him; with words of measured syllables, inquiring after his welfare, you led him home—that is, you caused him to enter. || 10 ||
Having honored that Yādava along with Nanda with boundless respect and having heard the news he had uttered,
[Nanda] announced the king’s command to the cowherds.
With various stories, you spent the night here with him.

"O Nanda," [he said], "having reported the king’s command and Kaṃsa’s orders, and having instructed him on the preparation of gifts, the arrangement of wagons, and so forth, you spent the night with that Akrūra, engaging in various conversations."
On that night, there arose among the gopīs a suspicion that Śrī Kṛṣṇa was attached to another; thus it is said:

"Is he in the house of Candrā? Or perhaps in the house of Candrabhāgā? Or is he in the house of Rādhā? Or is he in the abode of Maitravindā?"—thus was the rogue suspected aloud by the young women in the night. O Lord of Marutpura, may you protect us! (12)

Thus ends the seventy-second decade, consisting of seventy-two verses, describing Akrūra’s journey to Gokula, his arrival at Vṛndāvana, his meeting with the Lord, and the honors bestowed upon him by the Lord.
Then, having heard the news of your departure, those cowherd girls were deeply distressed;
gathered together, they uttered these lamentations: "What is this? What is this? How could this be? (1)

"Having heard this"—meaning they heard that Akrūra had arrived the next morning at the time for the departure of the vehicles to lead Śrī Kṛṣṇa away—they uttered these lamentations and wailings: "What is this? A most painful change of state has befallen us, like poison in the midst of tasting nectar! How can this be? Is it due to the fault of our own fortune, or because of the heartlessness of the Son of Nanda? || 1 ||
She spoke these very lamentations:
"How could this son of Nanda, a treasure-house of compassion, abandon us who have no other protector? Alas!
What fate has befallen us? Thus they lamented, their minds fixed upon you. (2)
"O Compassion! Our destiny, which bestowed such unsurpassed happiness, has suddenly perished; alas, why indeed should we not grieve? (2)
Setting out during the final watch of the night with your father and your circle of friends,
you left behind a single companion, intending to soothe the heavy burden of grief of the women of the city.
"Carama" means: at the final watch, the last period of the night, as he was setting out and departing, he dispatched one trusted friend as a messenger. || 3 ||
"I shall come into your presence before long; the glory of union with me alone shall soon be yours.
I will quickly immerse you in the ocean of nectar"—with these words, you gave comfort to the bride. 4.

"Before long"—the glory of union with you, the bliss of enjoyment, shall surely come to pass for you before long. Furthermore, in the ocean of nectar, that is, in the ocean of happiness; or rather, in the ocean whose nature is *amṛta*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). The meaning is: "In the end, I shall even bestow liberation upon you. (4)
Gazed upon from afar by women with eyes full of sorrow and longing, you cast tender side-glances toward them; accompanied by your army, you set forth in the chariot of Akrūra.

"Full of despondency" means: as you were being gazed upon by the women with eyes that were slightly closed like buds, casting side-long glances (kaṭākṣas) toward that direction, you departed—being looked upon in such a way that was both full of deep despondency because "our lives will depart if there is further delay in your arrival," and thus full of entreaty because "therefore, you must come quickly. || 5 ||
Then, followed by the abundant minds of the cowherds and by the hearts of those dear to you,
you passed beyond the forest filled with distressed deer and dejected trees, and reached the bank of the Yamunā.

"With wagons" means with the carts of the *ballavas*, the cowherds. "Followed in mind by the beloved cowherdesses. He had completely passed beyond—that is, he had traversed—that forest in which the deer were distressed and tormented, and in which the trees were despondent. || 6 ||

Having immersed himself in the water for his ritual observance, the son of Gāndinī beheld you even from his chariot and became helpless; O Lord, what indeed is this? For your vision is truly wondrous, reaching everywhere.

"For the sake of a religious observance"—that is, in order to perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and other rites, Akrūra, the son of Gāndinī, having submerged himself in the water of the Yamunā and beheld you there, and then, immediately after emerging, beheld you even in the chariot, became helpless. Indeed, what is so wonderful about your all-encompassing vision? The meaning is that it is not surprising at all, precisely because of your omnipresence and pervasiveness. || 7 ||
Then, having submerged again, that meritorious one beheld you, the supreme Person, upon the coils of the serpent,
shining with a discus, conch, mace, and lotus, and surrounded by hosts of gods and siddhas.
"Again"—this Akrūra is virtuous and meritorious; otherwise, he would not have seen you reclining upon Śeṣa. Having dived once more, he beheld—you, the Supreme Person, Viṣṇu. (8)
Then, having offered himself through various modes of praise into that ocean of the bliss of the Supreme Self,
and no longer perceiving anything else, he was once again enveloped by horripilation as he followed after that ocean of joy— [he who is] You.

"He"—referring to Brahmā—having praised and lauded You within the ocean of the Supreme Self’s bliss, the flood of Brahman, through various modes distinguished by qualities and the absence of qualities; and having perceived Your form as withdrawn from view, yet upon not seeing it again, because the experience of supreme bliss did not cease due to the persistence of the ocean of joy even in that state of non-perception, he approached You, covered in horripilation, having emerged from that ocean and come into Your presence. || 9 ||

When he was asked, "Is there such great coolness in the water that this shivering occurs?", O Lord of the Wind, protect me along with him who remained speechless from excessive joy while seated in his chariot. 10.

"But how so? [He replied: "Because, upon seeing the true form of the Blessed One, I was rendered speechless by extreme joy; my throat was choked with tears of bliss, and thus I did not offer an answer. (10)

Thus ends the seventy-third decade, containing the description of the Blessed One’s departure for Mathurā and the description of Akrūra’s direct perception of the Blessed One’s true form within the waters of the Yamunā.
Having reached Mathurā at the close of midday, he stayed there in a grove for that interval, taking his meal; then, accompanied by his friends, he went to behold the city.

He reached the royal highway, while men and women—who had long cherished the curiosity to gaze upon him—seemed as if they were being drawn forward by the countless fetters of their own accumulated merit.

"Arrived": at midday, when half the day had passed, while staying there in Mathurā within that garden (ārāma), the Kāñca grove, he reached the royal highway (rājapatha). Being drawn by the very chains of countless, immeasurable merits—which were like fetters—now ready to bear fruit, for those men and women whose curiosity to behold him had been sustained by long-standing reports; what indeed [is this]? || 1 ||
In this regard, he says that the women of Mathurā experienced the joy of seeing you through the merit inferable from your likeness:
"The women, lovely with passion like the dust of your feet, have arrived; they possess the luster of shimmering breasts like your form, and they are restless like your unseen glance."

O Lady, your side-glances are captivating like the surface of your chest; they possess the boldness of your gentle smile and shine with the purity of the luster of your mass of hair, resting upon your radiant tresses. || 2 ||

"O You whose feet... [The commentary explains: Your feet possess a luster that is passionate (*sarāga*), meaning red in color and beautiful to describe. Even the women of the city are passionate (*sarāga*) because of hearing of Your virtues; they have long held affection for You and are truly beautiful. They have arrived here for the purpose of beholding You. Your form possesses the splendor of shimmering clouds, as do those women, who—due to the agitation of their arrival—have breasts that quiver. Their hair is matted like a net, and they are adorned with garlands. Thus, they too possess the radiance of shining breasts.

Your gaze is restless and flickering because it is occupied with beholding women encountered here and there; likewise, they too are restless, filled with curiosity to see you. Her chest is "hāriṇī" (possessing necklaces), yet those women are truly "manohāriṇyaḥ" (captivating the mind). O Blessed One! The excellence of your gentle smile—that magnificence of your mild smile—is radiant with purity; they too are "nairmalyollasitāḥ," possessing clear bodies and pure minds.

She has beautiful skin and hair, possesses a radiant luster, and is adorned with peacock feathers resting upon her silver-colored [ornaments]. Elsewhere, "ornaments" refers to the arts; the meaning is that she is adorned with all types of ornaments. || 2 ||
Observing the joy of those women through the flickering of their sidelong glances amidst a crowd agitated by delight, wonder, and excitement, you asked a certain washerman there for a cloth.
When he replied, "Who will give you a royal garment? Go away!", you immediately struck his head with your hand; he, too, attained a meritorious state.

"Of them" (tāsām): perceiving and bringing joy to those [women] with the turning of their outer corners—their sidelong glances—he, out of great delight and impetuosity, caused the *parṭīs* to tremble. He [attained] the state of the *puṅgas*, which is liberation. || 3 ||
Furthermore, you led to your own station with joy that weaver who was single-mindedly devoted and dressed appropriately for his work; who knows what merit he gained through his living soul?
He was honored again by you with garlands and bouquets fashioned from your own hair.
O Lord of Lakṣmī! You have bestowed upon him supreme devotion and prosperity as well. || 4 ||

"Furthermore": You led a single weaver (*vāyaka*), a recipient of the Blessed One’s grace, who was of noble intellect and expansive mind, and who was suited to his station by providing him with garments such as variegated-colored silk cloths (*dukūla*)—you led him to your own abode, which is identical in form (*sārūpya*). Who knows what merit he had? The sense is that it can only be inferred from its fruit. He was honored—that is, worshipped—by one who makes garlands (*mālākṛt*), so called because he creates garlands with clusters of flowers (*stabaka*) and hymns of praise (*stava*).
You bestowed upon him supreme devotion characterized by love. || 4 ||
Seeing the hunchbacked woman with eyes like blue lotuses on the road again, and having been given body-unguent by her,
he indeed gave a great amount of body-unguent to her heart;
for he clearly wished to manifest the nectar residing in his mind even upon her body.
Then, with his beautiful hand, he took hold of that Jagatsundarī as she was being led away.

"Kubjām iti. [The meaning is: You made the hunchbacked woman—three-fold bent, lotus-eyed, and possessed of an excellence of beauty in her other limbs—as well as the cosmetic ointment applied by her, manifest in her heart; that is, you bestowed upon her body, which was the very form of yourself, a great passion (rāga), another name for intoxication (mada). Or, "aṅge" may be a separate word. To make manifest—that is, to bring into direct perception—the one residing in the mind who was previously beyond the senses, you surely, with your hand, grasped her gently so as not to cause pain, and straightened her out. || 5 ||
O Lord! At that time, people whose wealth was certain were not utterly wicked;
they would give whatever little they could, such as betel, garlands, and the like.
Alas, O Master! I stood before You with joined palms, yet I did not accept even a few flowers or such things; therefore, today I suffer great anguish. (6)

"Until then" means: while he was still favoring even Trivakrā by offering her body-unguents, during that time, by that same example, those people whose wealth and power of granting boons were certain, and who were not utterly sinful, gave you whatever little they possessed—such as betel leaves and the like—in accordance with their capacity; and they were fulfilled. At that time, I too, taking some flowers and such, stood on the path with my hands joined in reverence.
Alas, what misery! For because of not having performed that [virtue], I now undergo vast and great affliction—the pain produced by disease and other such ailments. (6)
Thinking, "I shall come," you entered the city gate, O Blessed One, while she— though already liberated and free from worldly attachment— watched your departure from afar with eyes full of longing;
and your fame, entering within her, was as if it were the water dripping from the breasts of Devakī, which surged up in great joy at the news of your arrival.

"I shall come. Though she was sent by you—who had been requested to "come to my house"—and who had already accomplished your purpose, saying "I shall come" and "I am coming," she was Trivakrā, the ointment-applier, timid and fearful of separation.

Having observed your gait from afar, you entered the city gate. Your fame—which had previously remained within [the city]—entered the city as well, under the guise of the milk-essence that flowed from Devakī’s breasts, which were leaping and agitated with great joy produced by that imagined excellence of yours inferred from the clamor raised by the citizens upon seeing you. || 7 ||
Having entered the city where a great festival was underway, he proceeded toward the armory;
whether by his sweetness or his splendor, he was given wide space by the men at a distance.
Ahead of him, a choice bow—adorned with garlands and honored—was being held up with the cry, "Do not touch me!"
Indeed, you first seized them, then placed them upon the battlefield, and you even attacked and shattered them.

Regarding the word *āviṣṭa*: Because of the sweetness of the Śrīmūrti’s form, or because of its splendor, or because it was impossible to resist due to its invincibility, you were granted an opening by the guards who kept their distance; thus, having had your path cleared, even before the words of the guards’ sons—"Do not touch the bow!"—you took up the bow first (*puraḥ*). Again, even before the words "Do not string it!", you strung it. Likewise, even before the words "Do not draw it!", you drew it.
And even before the words "Do not break it!", you indeed broke it. || 8 ||

O Lord! Before the festival of Kaṃsa’s destruction tomorrow, the great roar of the shattering of the bow—resembling the sound of the inaugural trumpets—will cause the hair of the gods to stand on end. And even Kaṃsa will experience a trembling, agitated by the cries of the guards and men struck violently by the two fierce fragments of that shattered bow, brought about by you.

"Tomorrow," he said, "the festival for the slaying of Kaṃsa—the destruction of Kaṃsa—is to take place. Prior to that, for the sake of auspiciousness, the sound of the inaugural trumpets must be sounded. Seeing this, the great roar of the destruction of your bow will cause the gods' hair to stand on end and will surely slay Kaṃsa as well"—thus he made their bodies bristle with horripilation.

In Kaṃsa as well, a trembling arose from hearing the great sound of the bow snapping; and by the cries of the guards—who were struck violently and fell with their two halves of the bow, crying out "Fie! Fie! Alas, we are slain!"—that trembling was further stirred up and increased by you. || 9 ||
Regarding the rule "janivadhyośca," the author of the Vṛtti states: "The root *vadh* exists as a distinct verbal base ending in a consonant.

Having observed the majesty [of the city] from both the virtuous and the wicked, and beholding the prosperity of the city with both affection and fear, he entered it at evening and went to the garden.

O Lord of the Wind! Protect me, who am speaking of the sorrow born of separation from Rādhikā while with Śrīdāman, and who am falling asleep due to the performance of the task of bringing about bliss. 10.

"By the cultured" (śiṣṭaiḥ): His greatness—His wondrous prowess—was seen with affection by the virtuous; yet His greatness was seen with fear by the wicked. Having gone to the garden, the site of the wagons, at evening twilight, accompanied by the cowherd Śrīdāman, he experienced joy through the fulfillment of the purpose of His incarnation, the sight of the successful removal of the earth's burden, and the contemplation that Kaṃsa having been slain, the humiliation of his father-in-law Māgadha, and the subsequent slaughter of him, his kinsmen, and others such as Śiśupāla were now certain to occur.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth decade, describing the Blessed One’s entry into the city of Mathurā, the subjugation of the king, the favor shown to the weaver, the florist, and the hunchback, the breaking of the bow, and other such events.

In the morning, at the command of King Bhoja who was filled with trepidation, the martial drums for the wrestling match were sounded; the kings ascended their platforms, and Nanda the cowherd also went to the palace.

When Kaṃsa had ascended to his palace, you too, accompanied by your army and followers and dressed in beautiful attire, went to the city gate, which was being licked by the enraged elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa. || 1 ||

"In the morning": On the following day, when the morning trumpet for the wrestling match had been sounded and its performance commenced—having been ordered by Kaṃsa, who was terrified that this [child] would kill him as his eighth son by Devakī through superhuman prowess—you went to the entrance of the wrestling arena, which had been blocked and your entry obstructed by the elephant named Kuvalayāpīḍa, enraged by the prodding of the mahout. You then ascended [the elephant].

O beloved, when you were seized by an elephant of exceeding speed— driven by the Ambaṣṭha chief whose mind was harsh with rage at your words, "Wicked one, leave this path quickly"— you struck its temple, which had long vied with the jar-like breasts of the cowherd girls, and having escaped the sport, you hid yourself at the base of his feet and laughed charmingly as you emerged again.

"O most wicked one!"—O you who are exceedingly evil! "Depart from the path more quickly, withdraw!"—by these words of his, the intellect of that Ambaṣṭha minister, which was already harsh, cruel, and enraged, was further impelled by his urging.

Released from play, having slipped from the trunk of the elephant, You then—after which [moment]—having struck his head (the "pitcher") with Your hand, You sportively lay down upon the ground at His feet, in the midst of His four legs, within the space between them. [This was] because He had been vying for a long time with the jar-like breasts of the gopīs; it was precisely through the merit that brought about such similarity that He obtained the touch of the Lord's hand. || 2 ||
Though within reach of his trunk, he was inaccessible; like a great elephant fleeing from a sage, he rushed forward, and while playing, he fell to the ground.
As he charged again, [the hero] uprooted his tusk—alive with its root—and from that root, he extracted for his own friend those great pearls which were as harmful as the roots themselves.
"You gave this necklace, beautifully fashioned by Lalita, to Rādhikā; please direct [it] to her. || 3 ||

"Hasta" means: having reached with his trunk (*śuṇḍā*)—so that he was being touched yet remained unapproachable—and while running swiftly and playing, he himself fell upon the ground like a staff; then, as the elephant charged back from behind and struck the ground with his tusks, you uprooted one of its tusks along with the living root, leaving it unbroken at the base, and gave those precious, most excellent, large, and thick pearls located at the root of the tusk to your dear friend Śrīdāman.
"Give, that is, bestow, upon Rādhikā—my beloved—the necklace (hāra) or garland (mālā) fashioned by Emirlāleta, which has been crafted with such charm," saying these words. || 3 ||

Then, seeing you entering the arena with the plow-wielder [Balarāma] grasping you by the flesh of your tusk, the people—whose minds and eyes were captivated by the intense speed of that auspicious sight—exclaimed:
"O, is it not Nanda who is blessed? No, no! It is not Yaśodā, the wife of the cowherd!"
"No, no, O fair-eyed ones! We alone are the ones who have remembered [this] in the three worlds," they all said to Śaraṇyu.

"Seizing," etc. O dear Śrī Kṛṣṇa! [I see You] entering the arena for the wrestling match accompanied by the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), who is seizing [Hastin] by his other shoulder; [and You] whose limbs have been forcibly carried away—snatched away with impetuosity—by that auspicious form of bodily movement.

"O people! Is this son, Nanda, truly the most blessed one in the three worlds? Or rather, no, no; those cowherd women who held him between their breasts and experienced the bliss of embracing him and so forth are even more blessed than Nanda. "No, no, O Gopīs; she who experienced the state of being his mother, Yaśodā, is the blessed one."
"No, no, Yaśodā! We alone are the truly fortunate ones; our very eyes are blessed, for they are immersed in the Supreme Brahman known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thus they praised and extolled them. || 4 ||
Now, in response to the doubt—"What is the cause of such affection and great respect for me in everyone?"—he says:
You yourself were the full Brahman, the direct manifestation of boundless and supreme bliss, dwelling among the cowherds; indeed, you were not revealed by the many people [in that form].
Having seen you at this very first arrival during the auspicious season, the throngs of people, filled with bliss and cleansed of sin, sang of your deeds as they were remembered with fresh emotion.

"Full" (*pūrṇam*): it means all-pervading. Therefore, because You alone abide in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) within all bodies, and because supreme affection, great respect, and so forth toward You are possible for everyone, this [state of yours] is appropriate; such is the sense. Now, as to how one can abide in many places simultaneously, he says: "Brahman. The meaning is: precisely because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*), like space (*ākāśa*). But how can Brahman be visible? To that he says: "Directly, You have sported among the cowherds."

The meaning is: because [He] has descended as the very self of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Now, one might object: "If there is the assumption of a body, then the predicament of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) would apply to me as well. To this he says: "It is the dense radiance of limitless supreme bliss. "Limitless" means eternal; "supreme bliss" is its nature; and "dense radiance" means a mass of pure consciousness (vijñāna). In that state, because of its eternity, birth and death are impossible; because its nature is supreme bliss, there is an absence of suffering; and because it is a mass of pure consciousness, there is an absence of ignorance. Thus, since the causes of transmigratory existence are absent, the aforementioned defect does not apply—this is the intended sense.

How is it then that Kaṃsa and others do not know me as Brahman? To this he says: "Certainly not. The meaning is that you were revealed as Brahman only by those who possessed the ripening of merit acquired through various births and previous lives. If it is asked, "In that case, how does the vision of you arise for the most sinful? the answer is true: when there is a predominance of merit over demerit, the happiness of seeing you is possible by virtue of the ripening of that merit.

With the intention that, by means of seeing you, remembering you, and describing your deeds, they too—having become cleansed of sin—are indeed gradually qualified for the knowledge of your true nature, he says: "Then, having seen you... (dṛṣṭvātha tvām).

The multitudes of people, both those with knowledge and those without, having seen you for the very first time at a "time of merit" (puṇyakāla)—that is, when the ripening of their merit has arrived—become cleansed of sin and filled with bliss; then, through the sight of you, they sang praises of your deeds as they were remembered, in a manner that was full of flavor and joy. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
Then, at the king's command, the wrestler-hero Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika, who was skilled in the fist,
challenged you and Rāma respectively with a harsh exchange of blows, clashing hand-to-hand with a *jhaṭajhaṭiti* sound;
various feats of leaping up, falling down, and dragging each other occurred there in a wondrous manner.
Even before death, this lord of wrestlers underwent numerous instances of bondage and liberation.

Regarding the word *cāṇūra*: with loud "jhaṭajhaṭi" sounds, they struck each other with fists in such a way as to be exceedingly harsh. Let alone those various kinds of combat—such as "utpāta," which is lifting up; "āpātana," which is throwing down to the ground; and the mutual dragging of one another by their hands and feet when they are locked together—it was even before death that he attained release from the bonds inflicted by each other's hands, feet, and so forth. The sense is: what need is there to say that he attained release from bondage after being dead? || 6 ||
"Alas! What a tragedy! Shall we not see the two princes, so delicately formed yet firm heroes among wrestlers?
Let us depart in haste!"—while the people were speaking thus at that moment, you dashed Cāṇūra to the ground, his life-breath escaping as he was whirled about by your hands.
Then Muṣṭika was also quickly ground to powder by the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), and he fled with the few who remained.

"Alas, what a tragedy! With that very hand by which you had raised him up, you dashed him to the earth while his life was still departing; he fled, pursued by those who remained after the slaughter, seeking to save their own lives. || 7 ||

Restraining the musical instruments, the wicked-minded Kaṃsa—failing to recognize his noble duties toward those venerable fathers and failing to perceive Your all-pervading form—commanded You to be driven far away so that he might slay them.

Enraged by their harsh words, like Garuḍa against a mountain, You leaped upon the platform; and though Ugrasena was difficult to seize as he struggled with his sword brandishing and lunging, You forcibly seized him.

Regarding "Kaṃsa": Kaṃsa, this being the state of affairs, did not know—that is, was unaware—of the duty that ought to be performed, which is falling at your feet; he intended to strike—that is, to suppress—the noble ones, the virtuous people, his own fathers, by the force of destiny.

He commanded the removal of Vasudeva, Nanda, Ugrasena, and the others; yet even though that was impossible because [the arena] was already filled, he gave the order. Enraged and provoked by the words of the wicked Kaṃsa, you, rising up and moving with a sidelong glance, forcibly seized by sheer power—even though it was difficult to grasp—the son of Ugrasena, Kaṃsa, as he brandished his raised sword. || 8 ||
Having instantly cast the king upon the ground with his joints crushed, and while you were falling right on top of him, a rain of flowers from the gods fell upon you.
What can we say then? Even though his soul was constantly devoted to you, he was seized by fear.
O Supreme One! This is the supreme latent desire (vāsanā) of Kālanemi: union [with You] arising from Your slaughter. || 9 ||

Regarding the word *sadyas*: having caused him to fall (*āpātya*), that is, having made him fall; while you were falling upon him, from above—that is, from above you—your falling upon Kaṃsa and the falling of a shower of flowers from the gods occurred simultaneously. What more can we say? We shall not state many reasons here for the claim that "remembrance of you grants union with you" (*tvatsāyujya*); for at that time, Kaṃsa, his mind constantly fixed on you out of fear, attained union with you.

Even that remembrance of Viṣṇu which arises out of fear is, in fact, merely the residual impression (*vāsanā*) born from the slaying of Kālanemi by you. Kaṃsa was formerly an asura named Kālanemi, and he was killed by Viṣṇu. (9)
Then, having quickly crushed his brothers and his parents,
he installed Ugrasena as king, greatly delighting the entire Yadu clan with the granting of their desires;
and he made Uddhava— the best among devotees and a friend of the preceptor of the gods who had mastered political science— his own companion.
Having obtained [this], O Lord of Pavanapura, may I be satisfied; ward off all my diseases! ||10||

"Regarding that": [He was] gladdening exceedingly his brothers—the younger brothers of Kaṃsa such as Kaṅka, Nyagrodhaka, and others—as well as his parents, Devakī and Vasudeva. Having obtained Uddhava as a friend—both as a minister for state affairs and as a companion in jest—who had acquired the science of polity (nīti-śāstra) from Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, he remained satisfied in the city, as if having accomplished all his purposes; this is the sense of the verse. || 10 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fifth decade, containing the description of the killing of Kuvalayāpīḍa, the description of the Lord’s entrance into the arena for wrestling, the description of the wrestling match, the description of the killing of the wrestlers, and the description of the killing of Kaṃsa and other events.
The word *āpātya* means "one who comes" (*āpatati*), derived with the suffix *ṇyat* in the sense of the agent according to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *bhavyageya*.

Then, having acquired knowledge preceded by the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), and having offered his deceased son as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), he is described as one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*). Thus it says:
"Then, having gone to Sāndīpani, in sixty-four days..."

Having acquired all knowledge together with the wielder of the mace (Balarama), you, the omniscient one, took your lost son—who had been brought from the abode of Yama—and gave him to him as a sacrificial fee; then, sounding the Pāñcajanya conch, you returned to your own city. || 1 ||

"Having gone... means: although You are by Your very nature omniscient, nevertheless, for the sake of gathering the world (lokasaṅgraha), You went to the sage named Sāndīpani and, having received initiation (upanayana), You mastered all branches of knowledge—including the Vedas with their limbs (aṅgas), sub-limbs (upāṅgas), and auxiliary sciences (upavedas). Then, having restored the deceased son of Your guru and given him to that guru as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), You [took] the conch Pāñcajanya, which originated from the body of the demon named Pañcajana who had assumed the guise of a conch. || 1 ||

He says that, remembering again and again how the cowherd women were overwhelmed by the weight of their love, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, residing in Mathurā, being himself rendered helpless by compassion, sent Uddhava—who is non-different from Himself—to pacify their distress at the time of His departure from Vṛndāvana for Mathurā, having promised them, "I shall soon come into your presence," in order to make that promise true.
Thus he says: "Remembering again and again how the cowherd women were overwhelmed by the weight of their love, you too, out of compassion, sent Uddhava, who was himself rendered helpless."
Moreover, he, wishing to demonstrate to that supreme friend and most excellent devotee the intensity of their devotion—which is rare to find in all the worlds—[acted thus]. || 2 ||

"Thinking thus": the cowherd girls, who are beautiful to behold, having remembered You again and again—through such repeated remembrance—were driven by the weight of their love, that is, by an excess of passion, and became helpless. You too, out of compassion and affection for Your devotees, were rendered helpless and overcome. "Furthermore" means there is another reason for sending Uddhava; he states that very point with the words "from him."

Intending to demonstrate to Uddhava—that is, for the purpose of showing—the intensity of their devotion, meaning the excellence of their bhakti; and [intending to show] that "your status as His supreme friend" is appropriate only when the pride of being the foremost among devotees has vanished from one who is the best of devotees—this is the intended meaning. || 2 ||
Having reached Gokula in the evening— a place that proclaims the vastness of your majesty— he greatly delighted Nanda and Yaśodā with news of you;
but in the morning, the lotus-eyed women were filled with apprehension upon seeing a chariot made of jewels.
Having heard that your follower had arrived, they abandoned their tasks and gathered together.

"Tvaditi": Having reached Gokula—the indicator (*piśuna*) of the vastness (*prathimā*) and expansion of your own majesty—and specifically the house of Nanda there at the time of evening twilight, [Kṛṣṇa] delighted only Nanda and Yaśodā exceedingly. This was because the cowherd women staying in their own homes were unaware of Uddhava's arrival; therefore, they suspected your arrival only in the morning. || 3 ||
Having seen him, who was charming with the ornaments of your spotless and playful anger, and repeatedly remembering those various manifestations of yours,
they somehow managed to speak words that were choked and faltering, their speech obstructed.
Through their goodness and other virtues, they completely forget even the distinction between self and others.

"Having seen" (dṛṣṭvā): [the women] were delightful because of their two garments and ornaments—clothing and decorations resembling yours—which were shining. Therefore, due to seeing these similar things, they intensely and excessively recalled those various playful sports; with their speech choked by tears, and because their minds were fixed on you, they even forgot the distinction between self and other. || 4 ||
"O Illustrious One! Have you been sent for the sake of my father by that merciless man?
Where is that lover of the city-birds? Alas, O Hari! O Lord!
May You protect me! O Beloved, whose body is like nectar to embraces, alas, who could ever forget Your kisses, Your intoxications, and Your deceptive words? (5)

"O Illustrious One! [They said: "Have you been sent by the merciless Kṛṣṇa for the sake of his father, for the purpose of pleasing Nanda and Yaśodā? He is now the beloved of the beautiful women of the city and the one who commands the wise—where is he? Overwhelmed by the remembrance of the Lord’s qualities evoked by these words of affection, they cried out, "Alas! "O Hari, the quencher of the suffering of your devotees! O Lord, the protector of our very lives! Rejuvenate us by drinking the nectar of your own form!"

O you whose body consists of nectar, alas, who could forget those various playful gestures and deceitful words of yours—performed as kisses that cause burning, yet done while completely forgetting one's own self? Or rather, O deceiver, O fraud, who indeed could forget your words of madness, in which the preceding and the following are not even considered? || 5 ||

O Ocean of Compassion! Show me Your enchanting body— graceful and agitated by the play of the rāsa dance, with its mass of hair loosened, and with drops of perspiration emerging from the slight exertion— so that I may embrace it even once.
O Madana of the world! Out of the madness of longing, your beloveds lamented for you.

"O Ocean of Compassion! O You who are affectionate toward Your devotees! O Delighter of the World! O Bestower of the intoxication of all desires upon everyone at all times! [I pray that] Your limb—which is both *lulita* (tossed about) and *mardita* (pressed) during the play of the *rāsa*, and which is *lalita* (graceful) and beautiful—may be embraced even once, for a single moment. (6)
Then, with such words of helpless lamentation, those cowherd girls were brought back to their natural state by his messages, which were filled with profound wisdom;
thereafter, for some days, he spent time in the company of those joyful-minded women who were absorbed in him, sharing various delightful conversations.

Thus it was said. Then Uddhava, by means of your messages which were pregnant with spiritual wisdom, brought them to the fulfillment of their natural purpose. Through those various accounts—which were permeated by you and through which they forgot themselves in meditation upon you—he spent several days in a manner that was full of aesthetic delight. || 7 ||
All household duties are performed incessantly accompanied by your songs;
news of you alone spreads among one another, as do idle chatter and jests;
most actions are imitations of you—thus, everything is composed of you.
Having seen that there, Uddhava was utterly bewildered by his astonishment.

"Tvaditi": Their uprooted chatter consists of words about dreams; their very news of you is that same [dream-talk]. Their activities and movements are for the most part in the form of imitations of you. Thus, seeing all of them as consisting of you in the manner described, Uddhava became utterly bewildered with astonishment; the meaning is that he was completely deluded and rendered incapable of discernment. || 8 ||

Thus, Uddhava, having observed that even among the women there was devotion characterized by extraordinary love for the Lord, abandoned his own conceit of being a devotee and consoled each of them individually. Regarding that, he describes the manner of consoling Rādhā, who was the foremost among them:
"This [Lord], who is most dear to me, speaks thus;
O friend, why do you maintain silence? Are you not like my beloved, who is full of indignation?"
"O friend! Your beloved spoke thus in a secluded place; with such words, he delighted me, his beloved, who has eyes like lotuses. (9)

Regarding the words "of Rādhā": O friend! O Rādhā! Your beloved Śrī Kṛṣṇa speaks only words concerning you in private, such as: "O friend Uddhava! This is most dear to my Rādhā; she, my beloved, says this to you. Why do you, like one who is offended by me, maintain silence as if you were displeased? However, in the assembly of people, because of his profound nature of mind, even though the pain of separation from you exists within him, it is impossible to perceive.
This Uddhava, by means of such words that indicated his love for you, has indeed delighted your beloved Rādhā. || 9 ||
He delivers the message:
"I shall come soon; let there be no grief, for even though we are separated by the weight of my duties, a firm state of remembrance remains possible."
"By your words, 'In the bliss of Brahman all meet before long; for you, union and separation shall be equal,' he rendered those [sorrows] free from pain. (10)

"I shall come. I will come quickly and immediately. My failure to approach you, my not coming into your presence, is due solely to the weight of my duties, and not out of a lack of affection. Furthermore, your separation from me leads to a great fruit, because it gives rise to a firmness of remembrance [of me]. Therefore, let there be no grief regarding this separation. He states the fruit of that firmness of remembrance—which is synonymous with *samādhi*—as follows: "The bliss of Brahman."

"When there is firm remembrance of me in my form as Brahman, and when you have soon merged into the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), then for you, union with me and separation from me shall be equal. Even in separation, there is no separation from me for you in every respect, because I myself abide within you in the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). This was the message of your speech; by it, Uddhava made them free from distress. || 10 ||
"Has such devotion ever been seen or even heard of anywhere in all the worlds? What is the use of floods of scriptures or what is the use of penance here? Salutations to the Gopīs!
Thus spoke Uddhava, who had returned from Gokula overwhelmed with bliss.
Having seen [this], I am delighted; O Lord of the City of the Guru, protect me from the flood of diseases! || 11 ||

"Thus" means: as in the case of the Gopīs. What is the fruit of a flood of scriptures or of austerity? Since devotion is seen even in those devoid of them, the meaning is that devotion is not the fruit of scriptures and the like. Therefore, "let there be obeisance to the Gopīs.

Thus, having repeatedly offered obeisance to him with the mantra beginning with "evam evaṃ-bhaktiḥ" and ending with "namo'stu," he saw Uddhava—who had come from Gokula overwhelmed with bliss, who had arrived in His presence, and whose pride regarding his status as a devotee had been cast off—and was delighted, satisfied thinking, "Now his qualification for friendship with Me has arisen. || 12 ||
Thus ends the seventy-sixth decade, including one additional verse, describing Uddhava’s mission as a messenger.
Thereafter, you departed with Uddhava in a graceful manner, while Sairandhrī remained for a long time afflicted by love.
Of her who always meditates upon her residence—the festival of the arrival of the Khadupa—and who is daily arrayed in her garments. || 1 ||

"By Sairandhrī"—meaning that because she waited daily in the bedchamber, having first prepared the appropriate dress, ornaments, and luxuries, thinking "my beloved will come today," you went with grace to the residence of Sairandhrī—the one who applies unguents—along with her charming attire, ornaments, and abundance of attendants; [you went] for the festival of your arrival, the joy of your union. || 1 ||
Upon your arrival, she— her desires fulfilled,
her breasts trembling with the agitation of joy,
and assuming various expressions of delight— [embraced you].
In secret, you took delight in her with pleasure. || 2 ||

"Approached" means: you took pleasure with her who was causing various honors—that is, showing respect—while her two breasts were trembling, prone to shaking, due to the agitation of intoxication and the haste of virtuous conduct born from excessive joy. || 2 ||
When asked for a boon once more, that wretched woman chose nothing other than sexual union with you during the intervals between nights; indeed,
only a wise man would say, "Let there be union [with the Absolute]."
Did he not even say, "May there be constant proximity"? || 3 ||

Regarding the word "pṛṣṭā" (asked): When you asked her for a boon once more upon setting out, saying, "Choose whatever you desire," that Sairandhrī chose sexual union (*surata*) again, and not liberation (*mokṣa*) in the form of *sāyujya* (union), *sāmīpya* (proximity), and so forth. In that regard, only a wise man who is conversant with the essence of liberation known as *sāyujya* would say or pray, "Let there be *sāyujya*. But this poor woman is ignorant of the essence of objectless liberation; let it be as it may. Why did she not even say, "Let there be *sāmīpya* incessantly"?
Indeed, she has already experienced the happiness of your proximity for some time; therefore, it should be understood that everything is dependent upon the will of the Lord. || 3 ||
Then, O Lord, while you were privately delighting that fawn-eyed woman during certain nights,
it was heard that he gave birth to a son named Upakṣloka;
and that son, a knower of the Sātvata system, shone forth through Nārada.

"Then," it is said: he gave birth to, that is, produced, a son who was "Upaśloka," meaning one renowned and famous. He was one who knew the *Sāttvata-tantra*, the *Pāñcarātra* and other scriptures, from Nārada; thus he is so described. (4)
Then, having been greatly honored and praised by the joyful Akrūra, you departed from Akrūra’s residence with Balarāma and Uddhava;
and after dismissing him, you learned of the conduct of the Pāṇḍavas who had returned to the forest, as well as the actions of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Akrūra": Having dismissed this Akrūra, you learned of the conduct of the Pāṇḍavas who had returned from the forest, as well as the actions of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. || 5 ||
Then, when Jarāsandha— blinded by boundless rage— besieged Mathurā, having imprisoned your supreme friend, King Bhoja, the husband of your daughter-in-law,
you, accompanied by Balarāma and possessing only a small force of chariots and other units, utterly crushed those twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs brought against you by him.

Regarding the phrase "due to the frustration": Kaṃsa was the son-in-law of Jarāsandha because he was the husband of his two daughters, Asti and Prāpti. When Jarāsandha, blinded by boundless rage following the killing of that King Bhoja, besieged Mathurā, you—accompanied by a limited force and provided with chariots and other equipment brought from heaven (Dyo) by Mātali—destroyed the twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs of troops brought by Jarāsandha. || 6 ||
Then, though he was bound by force and might, you, possessing supreme strength, released him once more through the savor of your exertion of power,
from the universal army gathered during your conquest of all directions.
For who else at that time possessed such strength and prowess?

Regarding the word "baddham" (bound): Now, having bound him with superior strength—that is, with a force more powerful than his own—and having defeated Jarāsandha through the vigor of further exertion of power, you released this Jarāsandha out of curiosity, thinking, "He will bring even greater forces once again. In response to the question of what kind of person Jarāsandha was, he says: Who else besides Jarāsandha could there be, from whom all the armies of every king in the entire conquest of the quarters have been gathered? || 7 ||
Though his heart was fixed on battle, he was broken by the kings who pressed him; thus did he wage war with you sixteen times.
O Viṣṇu, O Śiva! You have destroyed his Akṣauhiṇīs—how wonderful, how wonderful!
Then, having come together, they numbered three hundred and eighty-nine. || 8 ||
"Defeated": that Jarāsaṃdha has been defeated by you seventeen times. || 8 ||
When his eighteenth battle was at hand, you saw the Yavana before you with thirty million Yavanas; thereupon,
Tvaṣṭṛ quickly constructed a city in the midst of the ocean for you.
Then, by the power of yoga, you brought your own kinsmen there.

Regarding the word "eighteen": when this eighteenth battle was about to commence, seeing the Yavana at the forefront accompanied by thirty million Mleccha Yavanas, you had the city named Dvāravatī constructed in the midst of the ocean by Tvaṣṭṛ (Viśvakarman) and, through the power of yoga—that is, by yogic sovereignty—you led the people there. || 9 ||
Once, wearing a garland of lotuses, you fled from the city on foot as if in terror;
pursued by the Mleccha king who was devoid of merit earned through righteous deeds, you took refuge upon a mountain.
Then, when that mountain was reduced to ashes by the swift kick of the sleeping Mucukunda’s foot, [you were saved].
O you of most graceful form, you remained within the cave for this king who was devoted to you. ||10||

Regarding the phrase "by the feet": Your killing can only be achieved through [proper] means; it cannot be done by one devoid of them. While the Yavana was sleeping for a long time in a cave on that mountain due to the sleep granted by Devadatta, Mucukunda—mistaking him for Kṛṣṇa because he had not been struck [by the appropriate means]—reduced that Yavana to ashes. To that Mucukunda, You remained standing, having manifested Yourself. || 10 ||

Seeing that descendant of Ikṣvāku— who was dispassionate toward all royal pleasures, who desired only your grace, and who was crying out "O Lord! while praising you amidst the multitude of boons— free from longing and filled with joy,
[the Lord] granted him liberation, along with devotion equal to that of liberation itself, having shaken off all impurities.
For you spoke of austerity at that time for the sake of purifying violence in ritual action, merely to conform to worldly convention.

"O descendant of Ikṣvāku! [He replied: "O descendant of Ikṣvāku, born of the lineage of Ikṣvāku, you are dispassionate toward the pleasures of sovereignty and the enjoyment of kingship. Immediately after this present birth as a brāhmaṇa, at its conclusion, you shall attain liberation (*mokṣa*)—the cessation of saṃsāra constructed by ignorance—in which all impurities have been shaken off. Furthermore, having bestowed upon you devotion (*bhakti*) characterized by love, which is equal to liberation for that duration and consists of unsurpassed bliss, I then spoke thus: 'Since violence was committed according to the duty of a kṣatriya, you must perform penance (*tapas*) for its purification.'"

Although Mucukunda has already achieved his purpose merely by seeing you, nevertheless, for the sake of public conviction and to cause the world to understand the duty of a Kṣatriya, you have spoken thus—this is the meaning. || 11 ||
This is an explanation of the underlying meaning.
Thereafter, having gone to Mathurā and having destroyed the army summoned by the Yavana, he was again obstructed on the road by the forces of the Lord of Magadha, just as before.
O Lord of the Wind’s Abode! Having bestowed upon him his final victory and fled, he went to the city of the ocean; protect me! 12.

Regarding the phrase "tadanu" (thereafter): while traveling toward Dvārakā, he was stopped on the way by Jarāsandha, the lord of Magadha, just as he had been previously. Having been granted his final victory—the triumph in eighteen battles—to fuel his pride and arrogance, Kṛṣṇa fled; running away, he climbed a mountain named Pravarṣaṇa, leaped from it, fell to the ground, and, unnoticed by Jarāsandha, proceeded to Dvārakā, the city by the ocean. || 12 ||

Thus ends the seventy-sixth decade, comprising the seventy-seventh chapter, which contains the description of the origin of Sairandhrī as told by Upakṣepa, the description of the battles with Jarāsaṃdha and others, and the description of the grace bestowed upon Mucukunda.

With the splendor of your body, you adorned the new city situated in the midst of the ocean—a city whose craftsmanship was increased by Viśvakarman and which possessed all the riches bestowed by the gods. || 1 ||

"Tridiva" means: that city where all crafts were fashioned with every effort by Viśvakarman, the architect of the heavens; and which possesses all the splendors—such as the Sudharmā assembly hall and the Pārijāta tree—bestowed and returned by the Tridaśas, the guardians of the worlds. You adorned Navapura, Dvārakā, with the grace of your body’s luster. || 1 ||
When King Revata gave his daughter Revatī to the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) in accordance with the decree of fate, you,
together with the joyful Yādavas, augmented the celebrated sound of festivity.

Regarding the word "daduṣī" (the giver): A king named Revata took his own daughter, named Revatī, went to Satyaloka, and asked Brahmā, "To whom shall I give her? Brahmā replied, "The kings of your own time have now vanished from sight. However, when you have descended to earth, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa will appear as incarnations. Give her to Rāma among them," according to the command of the Creator. [This was said] by the combined ones, that is, together. || 2 ||

Then, O Lord, your brother, resorting to his own darkness and taking refuge in wickedness, sought to seize by force the daughter of Vidarbha, Rukmiṇī, who was truly devoted to you, from the king of Cedi.

The word "atha" (now) refers to his uterine brother Rukmi. It was he himself—not others such as his father—who desired to give [his sister] to Śiśupāla, the King of Cedi; thus, through his own darkness of ignorance, he took refuge with that wicked king of Cedi. || 3 ||
The young girl, who had long cherished affection for you, was suddenly overwhelmed by the fear of her desire being thwarted;
she dispatched a brahmin to inform you of her own distress, wrought by the god of love.
She laments: "The torment, the suffering created for herself by the bodiless one. (4)
And the son of the twice-born also quickly arrived at your city, which was difficult to approach for those of evil intent;
honored with respect by you, he personally attained joy, as you yourself removed his worldly suffering.

"O twice-born one! [The commentary explains: For it is difficult to approach and hard to attain because it is inaccessible to those of evil intent; it removes the heat of worldly existence—that is, the suffering of *saṃsāra*—and is thus called "the remover of the heat of worldly existence. (5)
And he said to you: "The princess Rukmiṇī indeed shines in Kuṇḍina;
for she, longing for you and deprived of her own composure, has sent me here."
"And he," [he said]. "In Kuṇḍina, the city of Vidarbha; I have been sent by her. (6)
He relates Rukmiṇī’s message in two verses:
"I was already captivated by your virtues long ago; yet now, it is said, the King of Cedi carries me away.
O Abode of Mercy! O Sole Lord of the World! Protect me!"—thus she spoke. (7)

"O You whose qualities, such as affection for Your devotees, act like bonds—long ago, even before the occasion of my *svayaṃvara*, [I was Yours]. Now, at this *svayaṃvara*, King Śiśupāla of Cedi is indeed attempting to carry me away while my mind is fixed upon You. O Abode of Mercy! O Compassionate One toward Your Devotees! Protect me; having taken even my body, unite it with Your mind. Thus she spoke. (7)
"If you disregard me, who am without refuge, I shall immediately give up my very life"—
by these words of your daughter, your compassionate heart was deeply pierced with anguish.

"Without refuge!"—by these words of the fair-limbed Rukmiṇī, "This is a twice-born one," your heart, O lover, became intensely distressed, fearing for the loss of the life-breath of your beloved. || 8 ||
Then you said to him: "O friend! My pain from love is even greater than that.
Therefore, O dear one, having approached the presence of the king, I shall carry off that beloved lady with her dark eyes."
He said: "Therefore, that [pride] was surpassed by Rukmiṇī; for that reason, O friend, I shall carry off that beloved in the presence of the king, while the other kings look on. (9)
Then, accompanied by him who was filled with joy, he quickly reached Kuṇḍina seated in a chariot;
O Guru, Lord of Amarāvatī, may you dispel the multitude of all my misfortunes. (10)

"By the delighted one": having become delighted by hearing your words, you went together with that twice-born man in the chariot; *laghu* means quickly, you arrived [there]. May he extend—that is, increase—the state of *tanu*, which is deficiency. ||10||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth decade, containing the description of the residence in Dvārakā and the description of the Lord’s arrival at the city of Kuṇḍina during his marriage to Rukmiṇī:
"Honored by Bhīṣmaka, you entered the city accompanied by Bala and followed by Balā."
But she, her passion aroused, quickly bowed down to the son of the twice-born who spoke of approaching you. || 1 ||

Accompanied by Śrī Balabhadra—who was accompanied by his army and feared a quarrel—and honored and worshipped by Bhīṣmaka, the father of Rukmiṇī, she entered. She, whose essence was joy, bowed down with speed to him who announced that her beloved had arrived, saying, "He has come to you"; she gave nothing else. Being a portion of Śrī herself, by that salutation she offered her entire self as the fullness of Fortune. || 1 ||
Beholding your body, which is the delight of the world, and hearing of the prince’s conduct,
the night passed away in the midst of weeping and wailing from the city-dwellers who were overcome with profound grief.

"O Lord of the World! Having observed the conduct of Prince Rukmin—his endeavor to secure the maiden for Śiśupāla—and having seen that your form was worthy of Rukmiṇī, they [lamented] with weeping cries and outbursts of wailing. (2)
Thereafter, the moon-faced Śivā, radiant with auspicious ornaments,
having offered her life to Bhava, went forth from before him, surrounded by excellent warriors.
Regarding the phrase *tadanu*: "from his own city" means from his own town; "in front" means in the space before him. || 3 ||
Having approached and reverently worshipped the Daughter of the Mountain, the young women fell at her feet and repeatedly entreated her, saying: "May she fall only for you. 4.

"O Kulā! Having approached together with the noble women—the auspicious ladies—she fell at his lotus-feet, which are like the lotus-feet of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), and prayed again and again: "May Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone become my husband. || 4 ||
Having observed the royal assembly crowded with curiosity and you standing there in silence,
the princess emerged from the temple of Girijā, most beautiful and illuminating the quarters of the sky with her splendor.
While you remained hidden, waiting for a vulnerability to seize her, she by whom the quarters of the sky were colored with delight. || 5 ||
Then, O Lord, you too were slightly intoxicated by that young woman, whose beauty was enchanting to the world and who had rendered the entire assembly of kings helpless with her sidelong glances.

"Bhuvana... etc. By that young woman, Rukmiṇī, by whom the entire host of kings was rendered helpless—that is, brought under her sway—you too were made to feel even a slight intoxication; you were made to experience a degree of passion. || 6 ||

"O moon-faced one, where will you go?"—saying this, you approached her with passion, seized her by the hand, and in an instant placed her upon your chariot; then, from the ground, a vast outcry arose from your enemies.
"Where indeed will you go? [He replied: "I have carried away; I have taken it away. || 7 ||

"Where has Paśupāla gone?"—with such cries, the kings were defeated by the Yadus in battle through their wrath; yet you, O Lord, were not moved by them, who were like sycophantic dogs before a lion. (8)

"Where have they gone?"—those kings who waged war and were conquered and defeated by the Yadus; you were not shaken by those malicious, wicked men, meaning that you did not take them into account, just as a lion is not disturbed by dogs. || 8 ||

Thereafter, having disregarded the slaughter of Rukmin who had arrived for battle, he bound him, disfigured him, and then—his pride humbled by Balarāma’s words—released him; and together with his beloved Ramā, he returned to the city.

Following that, making Rukmin deformed—rendering him ugly by shaving his hair and so forth—and having released him from his bonds by means of the words of Balarāma, that is, the words of his elder brother, he returned to the city together with his beloved Ramā. || 9 ||

O Lord, you indeed delighted her at your ease in private—she whose mind was abashed by this new union, whose passion blossomed through affection and curiosity, and whose face was radiant with flashes of laughter. (10)
In this new union, you delighted her in secret, as she shone with a face radiant with the rays of her smile. 10.
Thus, indulging in various jests day and night, you once again,
with a crooked word, provoked the extreme restlessness of that fair-limbed woman who was otherwise of straightforward mind.

"With various jests," means bringing about or producing delight and joy; with his "crooked speech"—that is, through his artful words—he extended the extreme restlessness and dependence of the straightforward-minded Rukmiṇī. || 11 ||
Then, delighting this beloved even more with superior skills of fondling, [the Lord said:
"O Mukunda! By recounting Your deeds to us, please dispel our final suffering. (12)
"By those who are superior to that": remove the affliction of disease from those who are praising [you] and speaking [of you] with devotion. 12.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth decade, consisting of sixty-two verses, describing the marriage of Rukmiṇī.
Now, O Blessed One, you requested from Satrājit the divine Syamantaka jewel, which he had obtained from the sun-god like a hunter.
That cause appears to me indeed to be manifold, surely intended to awaken her daughter, who is devoted to you, by means of a stratagem. || 1 ||

Regarding the name Satrājit: the reason for his request for the Syamantaka jewel appears to me, and indeed strikes my mind, as being manifold in form—consisting of Jāmbavān’s favor, the acquisition of his son, the giving and receiving of Satyabhāmā, and the instilling of affection in Akrūra through the slaying of Śatadhanvan. However, I am certain of this: it was for the sake of marrying by means of a pretext or artifice Satyabhāmā, the daughter of that Satrājit who was devoted to him, so that he might cause his own daughter to be given away even though she was unwilling, out of fear of his own offense. || 1 ||
That excellent jewel was taken from you by this small-minded man;
while carrying it around his neck, its brother Prasena went out hunting.
A lion killed him, mistaking the brilliance of the jewel for a piece of meat.
The lord of monkeys, having slain him, gave even the jewel to the boy.
"Adattam" refers to Jāmbavān, the lord of monkeys. || 2 ||
The people praised you, the stealer of the people's jewels, according to the words of Satrājit; for to the virtuous, nectar becomes a mere speck of poison.
Therefore, though you were omniscient, accompanied by your kinsmen, you remained intent on seeking [the truth].
Having seen that Prasena, you also went to the cave of the monkey Hari. || 3 ||

"They accused [you]," they said. Having heard Satrājit’s words—"Kṛṣṇa killed my brother and took the jewel"—the people, even before he had asked for the jewel, perceived your desire to seize it; thus they accused you of being the jewel-thief. For even a tiny speck of fault in those possessed of virtues becomes as sweet as nectar to people. Even upon seeing Hari—the lion—[they entered] the cave of Jāmbavat, the monkey. (3)
Thinking of you without hesitation, the aged Jāmbavān himself said, "Who indeed here can obstruct me who have taken refuge in Mukunda?

O All-pervading Lord! O Lord of the Raghus! O Hari! "Victory! Victory!"—thus crying out, that crest-jewel of devotees performed your worship by wandering about begging for alms with his fists. || 4 ||

"O Lord!"—thus [he spoke]. Being of advanced age, an elder, and therefore unable to discern or recognize you who have descended as the soul of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he cried out: "O All-pervading One! O Hari! O Lord of the Raghus! Victory! Victory! Manifest your own excellence! Speaking thus as if chanting a mantra again and again, moving along the path of the duel as if performing circumambulations, he struck with his fists as if with flowers upon you, his own master.
He performed a perfect worship—characterized by intense devotion—and propitiated [the deity], for this crest-jewel of devotees has performed every action for the sake of your pleasure. || 4 ||
Then, accepting the excellent jewel and the most beautiful woman given by him, you went forth favoring him;
and immediately thereafter, you took the jewel from Satrājit.

"Having understood," [he said]. Then, having understood and feeling pain from the blow of your fist, Jāmbavān recognized you as the Ancient Puruṣa; to atone for his offense, he offered you the youthful and beautiful Jāmbavatī as a prize, along with the excellent jewel Syamantaka. Accepting these and favoring that devotee, you stroked him limb by limb with your lotus-hand, thereby removing all his distress, and returned to Dvārakā.
Immediately upon your arrival, you gave the jewel to Satrājit, preceded by an account of how it had been obtained. || 5 ||
Thereupon, that wise king, overcome with shame, gave his daughter Bhāmā— whose eyes were tremulous— to you by word alone as a gift;
and you, having approached her, have now obtained her along with the jewel.
With a joyful mind, Gahanāśaya took that very jewel from him.

Regarding the phrase "tadanu" (thereafter): that Satrājit, indeed, having given the jewel as well as the jewel-like woman named Satyabhāmā to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, possessed a wise mind—wise because he thought, "I shall wipe away my offense"—and thus, by word alone and not by deed, he gave to you the jewel along with the eight loads of gold that were to be obtained from the jewel, according to the agreement that it was to be delivered to the other, Śatadhanvan; yet he gave that very jewel to Satrājit himself.
For what purpose does he, whose intention is profound—his aim and purpose unknown even to the gods—act again to bring about this calamity caused by the jewel, or perhaps something else? (6)
When you had departed for the Kurus with the story of the burning of Kuntī’s son, Satyabhāmā— overwhelmed with shame— was comforted by you; alas,
having been brought down by the words of Gāndinī’s son, Kṛtavarman!
Śatadhanu seized the jewel from Satrājit.

"Overwhelmed with shame," it is said: there was a public rumor that the sons of Kuntī had been burnt in the house of lac; when you had gone from the Kurus to Hastināpura, Śatadhanvan, having struck down Satrājit with the words "Kill him who does not give what was promised to Akrūra, the son of Gāndinī, and to Kṛtavarman," took away the jewel after killing him—how painful! || 7 ||
Seeing his beloved arrived among the Kurus out of grief,
they quickly killed Śatadhanu and brought her back; then,
as if apprehensive regarding the jewel, they went to the house of the King of Mithilā.
Rāma instructed Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in the art of the mace.

"Out of grief"—he comforted Satyabhāmā by promising the slaying of her father’s murderer. He searched for the jewel in her garment to make it known that he had slain Śatadhanvan, who was apprehensive regarding the gem; the meaning is that he sought the jewel for the sake of the gem itself. Having said to Kṛṣṇa, "Go to the city and search for the jewel," Rāma went to the house of the King of Mithilā and practiced with his mace against Suyodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. (8)

One might ask: "How could Akrūra, who is so devoted, have been appointed by Satyabhāmā to kill her father Śatadhanvan? Anticipating this doubt, the Lord says in two verses beginning with *akrūra* that it was his own evil intent that he himself instigated in him, in order to remove his pride in being considered a devotee:
"O Blessed One! It was indeed by Your will that this Akrūra was joined to the act of violence against the ill-behaved Satrājit."
They say that you did not take the jewel from Akrūra, but rather to bestow prosperity upon him once again.

Regarding the name "Akrūra": when Śatadhanvā fled out of fear of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he left behind a jewel; you did not take that jewel away. [The wise] say that it was for the purpose of bestowing—that is, producing—the prosperity and sovereignty of that Akrūra. The word "the wise" (abhijñāḥ) is to be understood as the subject. || 9 ||
O Lord! How could that son of Gāndinī, whose devotion to You was so exceedingly firm, have come to follow such a wrong path?
Surely this was done by You to quell his rising pride—the conceit that "I am possessed of wisdom and tranquility. 10.
"Devoted" means: on the evil path, that is, the contemptible path such as violence and the like; "arisen" means produced. || 10 ||

O Lord of the Wind! May You, who lie between the breasts of Bhāmā and rejoice, protect us—You who, having seen Kṛtavarmā depart in fear, called him back, revealed the jewel he had deposited, and placed it right there with Suvratadhara. 11.

"Yātam" (you have gone): Fearing that because of the killing of Satrājit, Kṛṣṇa would eventually kill both of us as well—the two of us who were the instigators—Akrūra had fled to a foreign land along with Kṛtavarman. Having summoned him back by means of a messenger and brought him here, [the Lord] revealed that the treasure deposited by Śatadhanu was indeed with Akrūra; having shown it to His elder brother and the others, He placed it back with Akrūra himself, and being satisfied and feeling His purpose accomplished, He remained there. || 11 ||
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, the Syamantaka episode.
Having constantly cherished the affectionate and charming Satyabhāmā,
he indeed went once more with her to the marriage of Yājñasenī.
O Lord! For the sake of pleasing Pārtha, you remained for a short while once more in Hastināpura, and having made arrangements even for the city of Śakraprastha, you have now arrived. || 1 ||
"Affectionate" (snigdhām): affectionate, loving, charming, and possessing a form that enchants. "Having arranged" means having caused Viśvakarman to fashion her. || 1 ||
When Bhadra— the younger sister of Bhava— was being sought by the Kaurava,
the son of Śakra, disguised as an ascetic, carried her away at your word.
Thereupon, pacifying the enraged Bala, he returned with him.
Accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he went to Śakraprastha, his dear friend, for the sake of joy. || 2 ||
"Bhadrām" means Subhadrā, your younger sister, the youngest. "Kuhanā maskarī" refers to a deceitful mendicant. In that matter, regarding the abduction of Subhadrā, you went with him, Arjuna. || 2 ||
There, while sporting, you took up that girl seen on the bank of the Yamunā and went to the city of Kālindī; O Lord, having gratified the fire at Khāṇḍava,
you brought her— the daughter of your father’s sister— who was terrified of her brother and overcome by love.
In the midst of kings, he forcibly took Mitravindā, the princess of Avanti.

Regarding the word "there" (*tatra*): there at Śakraprastha, while sporting and going out for a hunt with Arjuna, he carried off her—the daughter of the Sun, Kālindī—who had been terrified because her choice [of husband] was forbidden by his two brothers, Vinda and Anuvinda; he won her in a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) in the midst of kings, having at that very moment gratified and satisfied Agni through the Khāṇḍava forest. || 3 ||
O Lord, O Giver of Boons! Having gone to Satyā, you who possess seven forms seized that daughter of Nagnajit within a moment and bound even her seven excellent bulls.

O God, she whose chariot was difficult to overcome due to her pride—named Bhadrā—and her sisters, Santardana and the others, as well as she who is your father’s sister’s daughter (your paternal aunt’s granddaughter), were all won by you.

Regarding the word "Satyām": Having gone again to the capital city of King Nagnajit, he divided himself into seven parts, bound seven excellent bulls, and married Satyā, his daughter. His brothers—Santardana and the others—gave to you their sister Bhadrā, the daughter of Śrutakīrti; she was the paternal aunt's daughter (paitṛṣvaseyī), the sister of Vapu-deva. || 4 ||
Even by the sons of Pṛthā and others, the target—a mere expanse of water where no fish could be caught—was pierced;
yet they failed to win Madrakanyā, whose very name signifies "a fish.
Thus, among them, you alone became their beloved in eight ways.
You heard from the words of the Lord of the Gods about the wicked deeds of Bhaumadukṣa.
Regarding the combination of the letters *ha* and *ra*, there is an optional lightness (*laghutva*) for the short vowel according to the rule *prahe vā*.

"By the sons of Pṛthā and others" means by Arjuna, Bhīma, Duryodhana, Māgadha, and so forth. He chose (*avṛthāḥ*, from the root *vṛ*) as his target a hundred thousand fish (*śaphara*), which were impossible to cut (*akṛtalavana*)—meaning they could not be severed—with arrows other than those made of iron; they were visible only in the water (*toyamātre*), existing merely as reflections in the water. || 5 ||
Mounted upon that foremost of birds who had come at your call, you went, carrying your beloved on your lap, to the enemy’s city as if it were a pleasure grove;
shattering its fortresses with the blood of the shattered armies as if with liquid juices.
First, you made the city of Prāgjyotiṣa into Śoṇitapura.

"Smṛtāyātam" means reached merely by being remembered. It refers to the city of Arāti, the son of Bhūmi. Piercing through the fortresses composed of mountains, trees, water, fire, wind, and so forth, you made the city called Prāgjyotiṣa red—meaning crimson—with the liquid blood, the flow of gore, from the armies that were shattered and cut down by weapons. || 6 ||
Mura, however, sprang up from the midst of the ocean and the forest toward you; his head was swiftly split by your discus,
while he was engaged in battle with four-tusked lordly elephants.
Having cut through Naraka with his discus, he crossed over Naraka.

Regarding the word *mura*: there was a Daitya named Mura [who emerged] from the midst of the ocean's waters, from within the depths of the sea. That Mura had his head split asunder by Your discus (*cakra*). While the battle was raging and intensifying, You delivered Naraka, the son of the Earth (*bhauma*), who had already crossed over hell (*tīrṇanaraka*)—that is, one who has transcended the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). || 7 ||
Praised by the Earth, you immediately bestowed upon his son Bhagadatta both sovereignty and an elephant, and sent him back to his own city;
yet you again bound sixteen elephants whose minds were fixed on their own homes by that rogue.
And thousands of women, as well as a vast heap of wealth. || 8 ||
"O you who are praised! You dispatched sixteen thousand women bound by the wretched Bhauma, along with a vast heap of wealth and even four-tusked elephants, back to your own city. (8)
Having gone to heaven with your beloved to return the earrings taken from Aditi by Bhauma,
you were honored by Indra and the other gods;
yet, having seized the Kalpa tree in anger and fallen upon it after defeating Indra, you did so merely to explain that such was the fault of pride in prosperity.

"Regarding the phrase *bhaumāpāhṛtakuṇḍalam*: the earrings were taken from Indra by Bhauma (Naraka) in order to give them to Aditi, his mother. Together with his beloved wife—who had cast aside her pride (*hrī*) because of her superior beauty among the celestial women such as Śacī and Urvaśī—he was honored and worshipped. You acted [in this way] precisely to reveal and explain that such a fault of pride in prosperity belonged to Indra, namely, the production of Indra's humiliation through the seizure of the Pārijāta tree. || 9 ||
Creating a wish-fulfilling tree in the courtyard of Satyabhāmā’s palace, and having accepted eight thousand women, he assumed many forms in each house and delighted them with various amorous sports;
thus, even in every single home, his diverse movements were beheld by Nārada in wonder.
