Furthermore, O Lord of the Abode of the Wind, protect us by producing ten sons in each of all [our wives]! ||10||

Regarding the phrase "kalpadruma" (the wish-fulfilling tree): In the garden of Satyabhāmā’s residence, He who assumes many forms established Himself in every house; having simultaneously accepted and married eight thousand women by residing in each palace with a distinct form, His various modes of domestic life were observed by Nārada, who heard of those wonders in amazement. || 10 ||

Thus ends the eighty-first decade, containing the description of the abduction of Subhadrā, the description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s taking of another queen, and the description of the slaying of the demon Naraka and other deeds.
Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, was indeed a portion of yours; having been carried off by Śambara, he slew him and, together with Rati, reached his own city and married the blessed daughter of Rukmin.
Then his son, Aniruddha—a treasury of virtues—married Rocanā, the granddaughter of Rukmin.
There, having gone to the wedding, you were struck down by the wielder of the mace (Balarāma), while Rukmin was also slain because of his long-standing enmity.

Regarding the word *praghumna*: he is a portion (*kalā*) of yours and a part of Viṣṇu. Having slain Śambara, Praghumna returned to his own city with his wife Rati; there, he married Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Rukmin. Later, during the wedding of Aniruddha, Rukmin—having falsely attributed defeat to Balabhadra due to a grudge arising from a previous deception—was killed by the wielder of the mace (Kṛṣṇa) because of his insults. By the use of the word "also" (*api*), it is further implied that the teeth of the King of Kaliṅga were shattered. || 1 ||

O Blessed One! That celebrated daughter of Vāṇa, the son of Bali, the thousand-armed Mahiṣmān, and the devotee of Maheśvara—she, having experienced this grandson of yours, Aniruddha, never seen before in a dream, has become distressed by separation. || 2 ||
Regarding the word "bāṇasya": [it refers to] Bāṇa, a devotee of Maheśvara (Śiva). "Mahitā" means praiseworthy. || 2 ||
Citralekhā, the yoginī who is indeed exceedingly skilled, is painting all the young men as her friend;
there she will find Aniruddha at night and, by the power of yoga, bring him from your abode.

Regarding the word "yogī": the Yoginī possesses the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with *aṇiman*, and she is exceedingly skillful, possessing mastery in the arts such as painting. There, among the things depicted, it was known by her exactly as it had been seen in a dream; thus, she brought from your abode, Dvārakā, the unobstructed [image] and carried it here. || 3 ||
While he was enjoying himself happily with his beloved in the inner apartments of the princess,
even though Śiva’s son (Skanda) had somehow bound him,
you, along with the Yadus, besieged his city of Śoṇitapura due to the unbearable wrath provoked by the news of that event told by the venerable Nārada.

Regarding the phrase "in the harem": while he was sporting and playing together with his beloved Uṣā, you besieged Bāṇa’s city—known as Śoṇita-pura—along with the Yadus, who were possessed of boundless and inexhaustible wrath upon hearing from the venerable Nārada the news of Aniruddha’s capture, that is, the account of his being bound by Bāṇa, the kinsman of Śarva, with the serpent-noose. || 4 ||
The Lord of the city, the protector of mountains and beloved husband of the Daughter of the Mountain, together with the guardians of the elements, fearlessly checked the Yadu force;
meanwhile, the mighty Vāṇa suddenly engaged Yuyudhāna in combat.
Guha joined with Pradyumna, and you also sought to unite with the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva).

Regarding the term "Purīpāla": the Lord of this Bāṇa’s city-guardian is the Blessed One, the husband of Pārvatī, the beloved daughter of the Himavat mountain; he is possessed of great vital power and great strength. You, too, engaged in combat—that is, you fought—with Śrī Śaṅkara, the destroyer of cities. || 5 ||
When Giriśa had become bewildered by your weapon as all his own weapons were neutralized,
the spirits fled in terror and the heroic warriors of the Pramatha host were crushed;
then Skanda, along with his companion, the flower-arrowed god, leaped forward.
That Kumbhāṇḍa quickly shattered the vessel with force, as if it were new.

"Niruddha" means one by whom all weapons have been neutralized and pacified through counter-weapons. When you became bewildered—that is, when you fell into delusion—by your own weapon of infatuation, [the enemies] fled in haste; they were crushed and tormented. Skanda retreated, overpowered by the arrows of Kusumaśara (Pradyumna). Kumbhāṇḍa, the minister of Bāṇa, was shattered like a new earthen vessel filled with water. || 6 ||
When five hundred bows were forcibly brought forward, yet the arrows became useless as their strings were severed, the Lord of Fever approached; but at your fever, he was instantly cured.
Then that wise one, having offered praise and granted freedom from fever to those who take refuge in your deeds, departed.
For generally, even those who possess inner knowledge are fierce and engage in terrible deeds due to the abundance of darkness.

Regarding the word *cāpānām*: when the archer had become disarmed and departed, the Lord of Fever—the fever of Maheśvara—fought, joined by your own fever; yet, suddenly and instantly, he became feverless (*ajvari*), meaning he was relieved of his distress. Then the fever of Maheśvara, being wise, praised you and, having been favored by your grace, bestowed upon those who delight in your deeds a state free from fever (*vijvaram*)—that is, freedom from affliction—and having thus granted his blessing, that fever of Maheśvara departed. Alternatively, *sajvaraḥ* means "possessed of burning heat."

For even though they possess knowledge within their hearts, due to the abundance of the quality of darkness (tamas) and great gloom, they are fierce in their conduct and performers of cruel deeds; thus they are indeed "raudras," the attendants of Rudra.
As Bāṇa, fierce with various weapons, again rushed forward out of the fault of pride, Śaṅkara— desiring to instantly manifest him as one whose faults were entirely eradicated— sang this song;
by its words, Bāṇa’s two arms were severed on both sides, yet he remained fearless and dear to Him.
Having abandoned that pride bestowed [by him], you returned to your own city together with Aniruddha and Uṣā.

Regarding the word *bāṇam*: pride (*darpa*) alone was his sole defect; therefore, all his defects—both his arms and his vices such as arrogance—were completely severed. He had been praised and lauded by one who, desiring to know himself, had realized even Viṣṇu to be the One. By the word of that Śrī Śaṅkara, he was fearless toward both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, for he was dear to them and a devotee of Śiva. Having received the dowry (*pāribarha*) granted by him (Bāṇa), he returned to his own city, Dvārakā. || 8 ||

In the battle with Bāṇa here, he repeatedly conquered Indra while seizing the joy [of his city], Varuṇa while capturing Nanda, Yama while leading away the children, the friend of the Wind (Agni) while drinking forest fires, Brahmā while stealing the calf, and Śiva.
O All-pervading Lord! This incarnation of Yours, which excels the entire universe, is victorious. || 9 ||

Regarding the word *muhuḥ*: on many occasions—such as during the sacrifice of Indra, the abduction of the Pārijāta tree, and the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest—you achieved victory over Śakra. Therefore (*tat*), this incarnation of yours is *viśvadevotkṛṣṭa*, meaning it possesses superiority over all the gods. For this very reason, it *jayati*, that is, it becomes superior to all other incarnations. || 9 ||

O Lord of the Wind! Protect me—you who, out of anger toward a twice-born, sent King Nṛga to the abode of the gods while he was assuming the form of a chameleon, and who taught supreme devotion to the twice-born among your own kin.

"By the anger of the twice-born": by means of the curse—which was the effect of the anger born from the theft of what had been given to a brahmin—he caused King Nṛga, who was in the form of a chameleon and situated in a waterless well, to reach the abode of the three gods, namely heaven. [He did so] by teaching [the truth] preceded by an account told through the mouth of Nṛga, concerning that which is unsurpassed (*anuttamā*)—for there exists no one superior to it—regarding how Nṛga attained heaven through the greatness of that gift despite having become a chameleon due to the theft of a brahmin’s cow. || 10 ||
Thus ends the eightieth decade, containing the description of Uṣā’s marriage, the description of the battle with Bāṇāsura, and the description of Nṛga’s release from his curse.
Regarding the statement "four of these are Brāhmaṇas, the rest are Śiṣṭas," its connection is more appropriately made with the preceding [verse] rather than the subsequent one.
Then, while Rāma had gone to Gokula and was absorbed in amorous dalliance, and while [Kṛṣṇa], blinded by pride, had subdued the Yamunā when summoned but did not return, [Kaṃsa]—
deluded by the talk of his servants— began to act according to his own will.
Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva dispatched a messenger to you.

Regarding the word "Rāma": while Rāma was passionately attached to the women—the gopīs—and was thus fickle, Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva, deluded by the servant-like praises that you are the Lord of the Universe, dispatched a messenger to him. This Rāma was blinded by the intoxication of *vāruṇī* liquor; even when summoned, he did not approach or come, and thus [the messenger] sought to subdue Yamunā. || 1 ||
"I am Nārāyaṇa descended here upon this earth;
you indeed bear my very own marks.
Cast them aside and come to me for refuge"—thus [he spoke] to you.
The messenger spoke, while being laughed at by everyone in the assembly. || 2 ||
"Nārāyaṇa! he said; "you too indeed bear my own marks, such as the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha; therefore, casting them aside, come to me for refuge"—thus he spoke in the assembly. || 2 ||
Then, when the messenger had departed, you, O Yadava soldier,
went forth and beheld the form of Pauṇḍraka;
upon his chest was a great imprint made by the heat [of the discus], along with the priceless, glorious Kaustubha gem, and yellow garments adorned with crocodile-shaped earrings.

Regarding the word "dūta" (messenger): You, whose soldiers are Yādavas, having gone to Kāśī, beheld the body of Pauṇḍraka; his Śrīvatsa mark was fashioned by applying heated iron, and he wore upon his neck the Śrīkaustubha gem, which was of no small value, having been purchased for a great price and brought there. || 3 ||
As he discharged his own Sudarśana discus made of black iron,
you severed his head with that Sudarśana which scattered masses of the fire of cosmic destruction, and you crushed his army.
You also made even the head of that friend, Kāśīpa, [a part] in Kāśī.

"Kālāyasam" means: while this Pauṇḍraka was hurling—that is, employing—his own Sudarśana discus made of black iron (kālāyasa), [the Lord], with that [discus] which scattered heaps of the fire of cosmic destruction and rained down coals for the purpose of universal dissolution, cut it off; He caused the head of his friend, the King of Kāśī, to fall in Kāśī. || 4 ||
Due to his dullness, he had long held the firm conviction that even as a child’s speech, it was indeed I who am Śrī Vāsudeva;
thus, through the thought of identity with you, he attained union (sāyujya).
Who indeed could know whose good deed it was, and how? || 5 ||

"By dullness" means: one whose intellect is firmly rooted in the speech—that is, the words—of children or the dull-witted, due to dullness, which is characterized by dependence on others caused by delusion. || 5 ||
Then the son of the Lord of Kāśī, named Sudakṣiṇa,
having worshipped Śarva and performed a rite of exorcism (abhicāra),
discharged a certain magical fire-weapon (kṛtyānala) together with various spirits who had somehow been surrounded by those terrified of Bāṇa’s arrows in battle.
"Of the Lord of Kāśī": somehow, together with the *bhūtas* he had summoned, he released—that is, discharged—the *kṛtyānalas*, the fire arising from the sorcery-pit in embodied form. || 6 ||
O Lord! Though pointed out by the terrified citizens who beheld a Kṛtyā demoness with feet as large as palm trees, burning everything,
you did not move at all during the festival of the dead.
You swiftly dispatched the Wheel of Time that was standing at your side.

Regarding the phrase "of the height of a palm tree": although informed and entreated by the citizens during the festival of the liquor-vat, he did not move nor did he turn away from the spectacle of the pot-game; rather, he dismissed the wheel standing nearby with a gesture of his hand. ||7||
When your great weapon of immeasurable splendor fell upon her,
the Ghorakṛtyā indeed fled, crying "Alas! Alas!",
out of anger toward him whose actions were contrary to the right, though he was well-disposed toward the South.
He utterly consumed the wheel and burnt down the city of Kāśī.

Regarding the phrase "it rushed toward": when that great weapon of yours known as Sudarśana—which possesses immeasurable and unlimited splendor (*dhāman*), or which is indeed of immeasurable splendor because it bestows splendor even upon limited splendors such as those of Agni and others, according to the scriptural statement, "And that which is the supreme [splendor], the splendor of all splendors"—was rushing toward the magical creation (*kṛtyā*) and charging at her, she fled away, crying out "Alas! Alas! (*hā hā*).

Because the success of his malevolent spell against one who was not a Brahmin had been granted by Śarva, Sudakṣiṇa, through his improper conduct, burned with rage at having directed it toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the God who is the friend of the Brahmins—and he consumed even the city of Kāśī, the capital of Sudakṣiṇa. || 8 ||
Indeed, that Vīdūratha, having previously rendered assistance in the destruction of the Rākṣasa, then fell into wickedness in order to meet his death at your hand;
acting as a minister of Naraka, he is now causing affliction to the land near the city.
Fighting with Balarāma, he suddenly fell down, struck by the palm of the hand.

"He indeed" refers to him who, having rendered assistance in the destruction of the Rākṣasas—that is, in the slaying of Rāvaṇa—was a partisan of Śrī Rāma; nevertheless, he became wicked and hostile toward you because of your portion (kalā), namely Śrī Balabhadra, and thus met his death. Narakasaciva, the minister of Naraka (Bhauma) and your friend, while causing affliction and calamity to the lands near your city, was struck by the plowman with his palm—the very hand of his palm—and fell down dead immediately, truly, and without effort. ||9||

Seeking to pacify the Kurus, Rāma went to Sāmba— who had been imprisoned by the sons of Kauravya for abducting their daughter— and released him after he had uprooted the city of Karṇi by the force of his words;
yet you did not then release the army of the Yadus, saying they were to be slain by the Pāṇḍavas.
O Lord of the City of Wind! I serve you, whose play is difficult to comprehend, for the sake of quelling my suffering.
Regarding the word "Sāmbam": Sāmba abducted Lakṣaṇā, the daughter of Suyodhana and the granddaughter of Kuru, during her *svayaṃvara*.

Hearing that she had been bound and imprisoned by the Kurus, Rāma went there seeking to pacify them so that there would be no conflict with the Kurus. Upon hearing their insulting words, his anger was aroused, and he uprooted Hastināpura (the city of elephants); thus, Rāma liberated Sāmba. At that time, [Balabhadra] said: "Since you did not abandon the Yadu dynasty when it suffered humiliation from your elder brother, they shall be slain by the sons of Pāṇḍu. Thus, his pastimes are difficult to comprehend. 10.
Thus ends the eighty-third decade, containing the description of the slaying of Pauṇḍraka, the description of the burning of the city of Kāśī, and the description of the majesty of Balabhadra.
Then, at a certain time during a solar eclipse, [Kṛṣṇa] stationed Kṛtavarman and the son of Kāma (Pradyumna) in the city.
Surrounded by the ladies of the Yadu clan, you have arrived at the excellent sacred site known as Samantapañcaka.
"At one place" means: at the time of the solar eclipse (*tapanoparāga*), having stationed Kṛtavarman and Aniruddha in the city of Dvārakā for the purpose of protection. || 1 ||
For the greater welfare of the multitude of people, you yourself again immersed yourself there in the waters of that sacred ford;
having relinquished heaps of wealth to the throngs of brahmins, you were reunited with your friends, the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and others.

Regarding the word *bahutara*: there, at Samantapañcaka, while purifying the waters of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*)—thereby generating the power of those waters to cleanse sin—you, who had bestowed a vast heap of wealth upon the hosts of twice-born for the benefit of the great multitude and for the favor of those bathing in the ford, have now met and been reunited with your friends and kinsmen. ||2||
Indeed, the daughter of Drupada, together with her beloved women and burdened by a deep weight of devotion toward you,
rejoiced exceedingly at the various ways in which you brought about her rescue, as she spent the nights in your company.

"O yours!"—thus addressed by her beloved wives, Rukmiṇī and the others, the daughter of Drupada rejoiced exceedingly together with those other beautiful women, Subhadrā and the rest, as they recounted the ways in which you had carried her off yourself—the seven bulls being bound and so forth—as she herself had described them. || 3 ||

And thereafter, O Blessed One! having observed the cowherd women and approached them out of great curiosity, you honored them and affectionately followed after those wives of the herd-keepers, whose bodily forms were distressed by the pangs of long separation. || 4 ||
Regarding the phrase "tadanu" and so forth: those whose limbs were emaciated and distressed by a very long separation; you followed them, that is, you went after them. || 4 ||

And immediately, as the hearts of the broad-hipped women were stolen by the festival of beholding you, they cast off their bodices with excessive passion; you rested upon their breasts, which were even more delightful due to that intimacy. || 5 ||

"Sapadi" means: those whose hearts were such that pride had been stolen away from them; from whom the bodice (*kañculīkā* or *gātrikā*) had been somehow removed due to an excess—an intensification—of mutual passion; you sought [your embrace] upon their breasts, which were more heart-stealing through familiarity because they were recognized as having been experienced before, and which generated a special sense of wonder; you experienced the pleasure of the embrace known as "milk-and-water" (*kṣīranīra*). || 5 ||
"Because quarrels with my kinsmen have repeatedly approached me, this much delay has occurred"—
as you embraced her thus, Rādhikā, truly overcome by intense passion, suddenly hid herself within you.

"By the quarrels with my kinsmen"—saying this, as you embraced me after I had repeatedly encountered such disputes with my kin, resulting in this very great delay and waste of time, I suddenly became utterly helpless; instantly casting aside my pride, I dissolved into you as if experiencing oneness with you. (6)
Then, having placed them in a secluded place and freed them from the pain of separation, you bestowed upon them the awakening to reality, saying:
"May it clearly arise in your minds thus: 'I am the Self, whose nature is consciousness and supreme bliss. (7)

"Regarding the word 'gone away' (*apagata*): at that time, having dispelled the pain of separation for them through embraces and other means in private, I—being of the nature of the consciousness of supreme bliss, whose essence is the awakening of supreme joy, and the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the Self of all—bestowed upon you the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*), so that by my grace there may arise in your minds a clear, decisive conviction: "In the ultimate sense, neither my separation from you nor any occasion for sorrow exists at all. May this surely come to pass. (7)

In the past, their separation was somewhat mitigated by the instructions of Uddhava, being mixed with the essence of happiness; but thereafter, through the contemplation of You, it became for them a state consisting of supreme bliss and oneness.

Regarding the phrase "with the essence of happiness": previously, the separation—the sorrow of being apart—from those cowherd women had been mixed with only a very slight amount of the essence of happiness due to the instructions given by Uddhava through his own mouth. But now, as a result of your instruction, it has become something else entirely; for they have attained a state consisting of the singular essence of supreme bliss, which is identical with the highest joy born of meditating upon you. || 8 ||

Then, as the multitudes of excellent sages and your father asked for auspicious rites to pacify his misfortunes, he was made to desist by them with broad laughter, saying, "While you are present, what need is there for these other auspicious rites? || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "O best of sages": Then, when Vasudeva, your father, was questioning and inquiring of the hosts of excellent sages such as Vyāsa, Nārada, and others—asking what auspicious rites should be performed to pacify misfortune and turn back evil deeds—even though you, his son, were the abode of all auspiciousness, they laughed heartily, wondering why there was this prayer for the pacification of misfortune when he possessed other auspicious karmas and so forth; nevertheless, at that time, Vasudeva was made to sacrifice, that is, he was caused to perform a sacrificial rite. || 9 ||

While that great sacrifice was being performed and the circle of friends was filled with joy, the cowherds together enjoyed for three months the nectar of their association with you, honored by the people as they had been in the past.

"Sumahatīti": When a very great sacrifice was being performed according to the highest ritual manual (*uttamakalpaka*), the cowherds Nanda and the others—along with their friends and kinsmen who were exceedingly joyful—honored by the Yadus, experienced for three months the essence of attachment to you and the joy of your company, just as they had previously in Nandavraja. || 10 ||

At the time of their parting, having come together, firmly embraced Rādhā, and beheld her free from distress, He departed for His city with a joyful heart; O Lord of Pavanapura, protect me from calamities! 11.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of departure": at the time of departure, that is, at the moment of parting, having met Rādhā and embraced her firmly upon setting out, and having seen her free from distress—her anguish of separation dispelled by that very embrace which was a form of His grace—He departed for the city of Dvāravatī with a joyful heart. Therefore, You who are endowed with such affection for Your devotees, protect me from diseases. 11.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth decad, with its supplement, describing the pilgrimage to Samantapañcaka.
Then, O Lord, the King of Magadha [offered] two hundred and eighteen million mountains, which had been tormented by long confinement.
He sent some man to seek refuge with you, who are the protector of the helpless; he entreated you specifically for the Māgadha ascetic—what need is there for further words? || 1 ||

"Then," [meaning] immediately thereafter, the messenger requested from you—those two hundred and eight thousand kings (*bhūmībhṛt*) who had been tormented by long confinement in mountain caves by Jarāsandha, the lord of Magadha—nothing more than the destruction of the Magadhan king, that is, the slaying of Jarāsandha itself. What need is there for further entreaty? || 1 ||
Desirous of going to Magadha immediately after that, and being perplexed by the two tasks arising from Yudhiṣṭhira’s preparations for the sacrifice as described by Nārada,
[Uddhava] said to Uddhava: "Success in both [objectives] will come from a sacrifice that ensures victory over adversaries."
Having praised [him] together with his own [people], he went to the city of Yudhiṣṭhira. || 2 ||

"Desirous of going" (*yiyāsuḥ*): having turned his face toward Magadha, he was desirous of departing, wishing to go. "Regarding both" (*ubhayeti*): being preoccupied with the two tasks consisting of the punishment of the Magadha king and the favoring of Yudhiṣṭhira; when Uddhava had spoken—stating that from the sacrifice known as the *rājasūya*, which must be performed after first punishing the enemy who has achieved a contrary victory, both goals would be accomplished, namely the punishment of the Magadha king and the fulfillment of Yudhiṣṭhira’s desire—he went to Indraprastha, the city of Yudhiṣṭhira. || 2 ||
When you, accompanied by your entire retinue of consorts, arrived, Yudhiṣṭhira— having conquered the earth with his innate brothers who were nurtured by your sidelong glances—
bore incomparable prosperity, alas, acting as a servant to his devotees.
O noble lady! He has sent you to the King of Magadha, along with Bhīma and Arjuna.

Regarding the word "aśeṣa": O Lord! when You, accompanied by Your entire retinue of sixteen thousand wives, arrived, the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), having conquered the entire earth through the strength nurtured by Your side-glances (your kaṭākṣa), and carrying the incomparable wealth and hoards of riches obtained during his world-conquest—O Blessed One! Alas, what a marvel! He sent him against Jarāsandha of Magadha, who was acting like a servant to Your devotees, for the sake of defeating him. || 3 ||
O King! Thereafter, you three went to the city of Girivraja and, under the pretext of being Brahmins, challenged that Magadhan king to a festival of battle;
for his merit was not yet complete, you engaged him in combat with the son of the Wind-god.
Having observed this together with Jiṣṇu, you too, O King, stood ready for battle.

"To Girivraja" means they went to the city of Girivraja, the capital of Jarāsaṃdha, to witness the duel—a festive battle that arouses the curiosity of those who come to see it—and they requested [permission]. "One whose merit is incomplete" means that although at the time of death there might be an opportunity to behold you through one's merit, nevertheless, because he was killed by one who grants immediate liberation, he is devoid of the merit [that would otherwise arise from such a death].

Therefore, by causing King Bhīma and the King of Magadha to engage in combat with the son of Pavana (Bhīmasena), or by having the Pāṇḍavas, Duryodhana, and their respective allies fight one another, you are "rājayudhvā"—one who has caused kings to fight. || 4 ||
Having cast down the son of Jarā— who was arrogant due to his unceasing battles— with the signal of breaking off a branch, and having him torn apart by the wind-born [Hanumān],
he joyfully released the kings and favored them with supreme devotion.
And you dispatched [the Buddhas], though they were free from desire, for the protection of the Dharma on this earth. || 5 ||

"Unpacified" means: in an unpeaceful battle where neither victory nor defeat has been seen, there was a haughty and arrogant son of Old Age (*jaras*), born of the ogress named Jarā. As soon as he was born, she clearly joined together two fragments of a body; because consciousness had arisen [in him], she adopted him as her son. Thus, for him, death consists precisely in the splitting apart of these two body-fragments.

Knowing this, you—by means of the signal in the form of the tearing of the branches, through that indicator who had realized the truth, namely the son of the Wind (Hanumān)—had his body torn apart and mangled; having caused him to be struck down and killed, you released the kings who had been confined in a mountain cave during your world conquest. Having joyfully bestowed upon them supreme devotion characterized by love, you dispatched them to protect the earth according to Dharma, even though they were themselves free from desire for the enjoyment of their own kingdoms.
Alternatively, for the sake of protecting the self-dharma consisting of the protection of subjects, you assigned and gave the various regions of the earth to the kings. || 5 ||
Thereafter, when Yudhiṣṭhira had commenced the Rājasūya sacrifice—
which was bustling with all the kings acting as contented laborers—
you too, O Lord of the World, were nourished by the washing of the feet of the twice-born and other such rites.
What more can be said? The rise in the fortune of this best of kings is truly marvelous!

"Pracakruṣi" means when [the king] had begun. "Bhṛtakībhavadbhiḥ" refers to those who become laborers (bhṛtakāḥ), that is, hired servants (dāsāḥ). [The city was] crowded with all the royal attendants who were well-disposed, free from envy, and acting as laborers. || 6 ||
Then, having deliberated upon the procedure for the foremost worship during the sacrificial rite, that son of Dharma, following the words of Sahadeva,
joyfully performed the offering for the sake of the Soul of All Beings in the assembly.
Then the entire world, including gods and humans, attained complete satisfaction.

"Then," [it is said]: following Sahadeva's words that the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa is worthy of the foremost worship, he performed the rite of first worship for the one who is the Self of all beings (*viśvabhūtātmane*). Therefore, the entire world, including gods and humans, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, attained satisfaction. || 7 ||
Then, while the sages and kings stood by, the King of Cedi suddenly exclaimed, "Alas! What fool would honor such a wicked, low-born brat?
As he uttered this stream of insults, he sprang from his seat with weapons raised; the Pāṇḍavas then rushed forward to strike him down.

"Then," [it is said]. Śiśupāla, the King of Cedi, honors—meaning he pays homage to—the "beast-like wicked man," that is, the one who devours the cattle of the virtuous. Regarding you, in your presence, vomiting forth a vast expanse of foul speech—just as someone about to die vomits up everything they have eaten—he, speaking thus with weapons raised—that is, with his arms uplifted—leapt up from his seat and rushed forward. At that time, out of indignation at your humiliation, the Pāṇḍavas fell upon him, intent on killing him. || 8 ||

Having warded off those on your own side who were facing your enemy, you alone—possessing a pure intellect—were slain by that foe, the destroyer of demons, with his own weapon; for he, through constant meditation attained over three lifetimes, achieved with you that supreme unity which is difficult even for yogis to attain.

Regarding the combination of the letters *ha* and *ra*, there is an optional lightness (*laghutva*) of the short vowel according to the rule "prahe vā. "Having warded off" means: having warded off the Pāṇḍavas who were on your own side, you severed—meaning you cut off—the head of your enemy Śiśupāla with your own discus called Sudarśana, which is the destroyer of demons (the one whose nature is to pierce the bodies of asuras). This was achieved through [the power] obtained in three births, namely in the forms of Hiraṇyakaśipu, Rāvaṇa, and Śiśupāla. || 9 ||
Then, when that most excellent and highly auspicious sacrifice had been established by you, the people went about saying, "Victory to the son of Dharma! Victory to Kṛṣṇa!
But that wicked Suyodhana, his mind shaken by the prosperity of his rival, was distressed.
Offered at the entrance of the assembly hall by me, it caused confusion due to the delusion of [mistaking] land for water.

"Then" (*tataḥ*): After the slaying of Śiśupāla, when [the rite] was highly honored and completed by you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa "triumphs," meaning he is superior to all; and the "son of Dharma" (Yudhiṣṭhira), under whose control that Lord [Kṛṣṇa] stands, triumphs—thus speaking, the people, the great multitude, went each to their own home. But that Suyodhana, possessing only a small portion [of merit], his mind shaken by envy and other vices at the abundant prosperity of his rivals, the Pāṇḍavas, [remained behind].

During the burning of Khāṇḍava, because of the confusion regarding land and water concerning the assembly hall provided and given by Maya, he became bewildered and agitated—falling into the water thinking it was dry land, and grasping the hem of his garment on dry land thinking it was water. ||10||

Then, O Lord Janārdana, dwelling in the city of the Maruts, protect me from disease— You who, at that time, manifesting some indescribable smile with the playful glances of Drupada’s daughter and Abhimanyu, sowed the very seed for the immediate removal of the earth’s burden.

"At that time"—meaning, when Suyodhana was in a state of stupor—the smile arising on the faces of Drupada’s daughter and Abhimanyu, while manifesting and intensifying something indescribable through a mere fraction of a sidelong glance (*apāṅga-kalā*), was like sowing the very seed for the removal of the earth's burden, establishing it as the cause [of his downfall]. || 11 || Thus ends the eighty-fifth decad (plus one), containing the description of the slaying of Jarāsaṃdha and the description of Yudhiṣṭhira’s Rājasūya sacrifice. Sālva, having been defeated by the Yadu army at the wedding of Bhīṣma’s daughter, [obtained] a celestial chariot from the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva).
Having found Saubha, that master of illusion dwelt with you; meanwhile, he devastated the Kurus and your city.
While Pradyumna was besieging him along with all the Yadu warriors, he captured his minister Ghumanta, who possessed fierce valor;
and a battle ensued between them lasting for twenty-seven days.

Regarding Śālva: at the wedding of the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, the *svayaṃvara* of Rukmiṇī, he was defeated and vanquished by the Yadu force, the army of the Yadus. Having obtained the celestial chariot named Saubha from the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva), after propitiating him on the condition of the extermination of the Yādavas, while you were residing in the Kuru country, Śālva attacked and destroyed your city, Dvārakā. But Pradyumna, obstructing that Śālva, seized and slew Ghuṣmanta. || 1 ||
Just then, O Rāma, you arrived swiftly and hemmed in that lord of Saubha, whose army was nearly shattered; he, it is said, caused your Śārṅga bow to fall with his mace,
and even before your eyes, he struck down your illusory father for half a moment by you as well.
Some say that it was not known; Vyāsa himself prohibited this disparagement. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase *tāvād iti*: [He] caused the Sālva king, the lord of Saubha, to drop—that is, to abandon—his Śārṅga bow; he even killed your father Vasudeva, who had been created by magic before you. Vyāsa himself described this defeat of Sālva’s illusory delusion:
"Where are grief, delusion, affection, or fear, which arise only in the ignorant?
And where is Hari, the Lord of unimpeded wisdom, knowledge, and sovereignty?"
Thus he forbade him. || 2 ||
Having swiftly cast Saubha, crushed by his mace, into the ocean, and having cut down even Śālva with his discus, Dantavakra rushed forward and hurled a mace at you;
yet, struck by the Kaumodakī, he too—like the Caidya—attained the divine state.
Indeed, this incarnation was for the sake of liberating all those whose minds were previously fixed upon you.
"Having hurled," it means: he released the mace at you in order to kill you. "This incarnation is for the liberation of those whose minds are fixed upon you. ||3||
Then, when you had arrived at the assembly of the Kurus— having become, as it were, a mere owl—

the bound and weeping Yājñasenī offered an endless garland of piteous cries; thereafter, she was meditated upon by Draupadī, who was terrified by the son of Anānta, Mātali, and Śarva, and by the sages.
Having arrived at the edge of the forest, you caused the multitude of sages to be satisfied while eating only vegetables. || 4 ||

Regarding the word "tvayi" (in you): Now, when you had come from Indraprastha to Dvārakā, and while the deceitful game of dice was being played in the assembly of the Kurus, Draupadī—having been seized by Duḥśāsana and bound—was trembling with fear of a curse at the end of the meal, as she had been seized by her garment. Thinking of the sage Durvāsas who had arrived there, she offered him the vegetable food clinging to his vessel; thus, you caused the entire host of sages along with their circle of disciples to be satisfied.
Then, when the preparations for war were underway and the council had assembled, you alone were chosen by Phalguna;
having been granted an army, O Kauravya, you went to the city of the enemy as an envoy for the sake of the Pandavas.
When your words, which deserved respect from Bhishma, Drona, and the others, were indeed reviled by the Kaurava, [the battle commenced].
Revealing your universal form and having agitated the city, you arrived at the assembly of sages. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "yuddhodyoga" (the mobilization for war): Now, when the mobilization for war was gathering, you alone were chosen by Phalguna (Arjuna) for counsel and the determination of affairs; and at that same time, having been granted an army by the Kaurava, you gave the Yadu army to Duryodhana. Thus, you performed the work of an envoy for the sake of the Pandavas, so that they might obtain half the kingdom.

When the Kaurava Duryodhana—who was honored and worthy of respect by Bhishma, Drona, and others—reviled [Krishna] in the assembly of sages, you revealed and manifested your own universal form. || 5 ||

O Kṛṣṇa! You were indeed the charioteer for the victorious Arjuna at the front of the battle. Seeing that hero distressed and compassionate toward the slaughter of his kinsmen, you said: "Alas, friend! This self is eternal and one.
Who here is to be slain, and who is the slayer? Therefore, casting aside the fear of death, offer yourself to Me."
He engages in righteous battle, displaying his universal form by leading nature away from its ordinary course.

Regarding the word *jiṣṇoḥ*: You spoke to that Arjuna, who was distressed and turned away from the field of battle. By saying "He is eternal and one," [you meant] that because He is eternal He is indestructible, and because He is one there is no distinction between the slain and the slayer.

Therefore, since the Self is indestructible, you instructed him to cast off the fear of death—that fear of unrighteousness (*adharma*) regarding the slaughter of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others—and to engage in righteous battle, which does not deviate from the duty of a Kṣatriya. Then, in order to inspire confidence, you showed Him the Universal Form as the singular Self, and you led Him to the state of being free from delusion, having returned to His natural state. 6.

Then, while Bhīṣma—the crest-jewel of devotees—was constantly intent on the sole task of relieving the earth’s burden, and while Arjuna was perpetually weary from piercing tens of thousands of demons, you, seeing that best of enemies approaching with fury as he broke his vow of weaponlessness yet held him back, rushed forward; and beholding him with palms joined and head bowed, you departed with joy. (7)

Regarding the phrase "the crest-jewel of devotees" (*bhaktottaṃsa*): when Pārtha had become distressed and afflicted by Bhīṣma’s arrows, [Kṛṣṇa] abandoned his vow, "I shall not take up a weapon," and as if possessed by anger, he made Sudarśana—the best of enemies—take up a weapon. This was solely to make his own vow true, "I shall cause him to take up a weapon," and not because he was actually overcome by wrath. || 7 ||
He protected Arjuna from the Nārāyaṇa-weapon discharged by Bhagadatta, from the vow regarding the slaying of Jayadratha, and from the serpent-weapon of Karṇa; thus he says:

In battle, he placed upon his chest the Vaiṣṇava weapon hurled by Bhagadatta, whose elephant was a steady battlefield for Droṇa, while he, obscuring the sun with his discus, tormented the King of Sindhu.

When the Naga-missile was released by Karṇa, it caused the earth itself to bow down; yet even there, O Pārtha, you cut off his head—what indeed have you not accomplished for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas? || 8 ||

"In battle," [it is said]. He by whom the splendor of the sun was obscured and eclipsed by his discus—[he protected] Jayadratha, the King of Sindhu, whose crown and hair were severed. He protected him there. What service indeed did you not perform for the Pāṇḍavas? || 8 ||

At the beginning of the war, that wielder of the plow (Balarāma), who goes to sacred fords, having reached the Naimiṣa forest and caused the destruction of those who did not rise to greet him, appointed his son in their stead; then,

crushing the sacrifice-destroying Balvala on the day of the full moon, he bathed at the holy sites and, reaching the end of the battle, beheld the unceasing conflict between Bhīma and Duryodhana and departed for your city.

"In battle and so forth" means: while proceeding on his way, he performed the slaughter—the destroyer—of the Sūta Romaharṣaṇa, who did not rise to greet him; then, by the word of the sage, he placed his son (the Sūta's son) in that position, upon the Brahma-seat granted by the sage; and at every sacred festival (parvan), he utterly crushed—that is, killed—the Daitya Balvala, the destroyer of sacrifices. || 9 ||

Approaching the son of Droṇa, whose mind was clouded by the slaughter of the sleeping sons of Draupadī, Vijaya (Arjuna) neutralized that released Brahma-weapon with your words and seized his crest-jewel;
then, for the sake of exterminating the Pāṇḍavas, he entered once more into the womb of Uttara by means of that weapon.
O All-pervading Lord! While protecting [the world], Cakrapāṇi, it is said, entered the belly as one the size of a thumb. 10.

Regarding the word *saṃsupta*: having approached the son of Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, whose intellect was clouded by the slaughter of the five sons of Draupadī while they were fast asleep and who was thus unaware of what ought to be done, Arjuna (Vijaya) neutralized by your word the Brahmāstra discharged by that Aśvatthāman and seized his crest-jewel.

Furthermore, when that Brahmāstra was again employed for the destruction—that is, the total eradication—of the Pāṇḍavas, and it entered the womb of Uttarā, you, assuming a body the size of a thumb and bearing the discus in hand, indeed entered the belly of Uttarā. 10.
Then, having granted liberation to both Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīṣma, the Blessed One, his purpose fulfilled, spoke thus:

"Bhīṣma, who was the death of the Vedas, having proclaimed the entire flood of dharma to the son of Dharma, attained the state of the partless Brahman immediately upon beholding you with the fullness of devotion.
Then, having performed three most magnificent horse-sacrifices for the son of Dharma, whose desires were now fulfilled—"
O Lord of Pāvanapura! You have arrived at Dvārakā; protect me from all diseases. || 11 ||

Regarding the phrase "the flood of dharma": Bhīṣma, that supreme friend in the removal of the earth's burden, beholding you and through his own abundant and unfailing devotion to you, immediately attained *niṣkalabrahmabhūyam*—that is, the state of the partless Brahman, which is liberation. Then, having performed the horse-sacrifices as officiating priest (*saṃyājya*), [he attained this]. || 11 ||
Thus ends the eighty-sixth decad, consisting of one [chapter], which describes the slaying of Śālva and others, the commencement of the Bhārata war, and the description of the Bhārata war itself.
The brahmin named Kucela, who became your fellow student, resided in the house of Sāndīpani.
With his sole passion fixed upon you, the tranquil householder spent his days free from desire for wealth and other worldly things.

"Kucela by name; [he shared] the state of being a fellow student and a co-practitioner of the holy life. Through devotion characterized by love for you and through passion for you alone, he became tranquil and had conquered his senses. || 1 ||
Her beloved wife, though sharing the same disposition, likewise had not yet attained mastery over her mind;
she once said, "Alas! For the sake of obtaining a livelihood, why is the Lord of Ramā, our friend, not served? (2)

Regarding the phrase "of similar character": although she was of similar character, nevertheless, like Kucela, she had not attained mastery over her mind nor freedom from desire for wealth and the like. For the sake of obtaining a livelihood—a means of subsistence—the Lord of Ramā [Viṣṇu] acted with the propriety of a friend. (2)
Thus addressed by his beloved, who was tormented by hunger— even though he felt loathing for wealth that brings intoxication—
he then departed, carrying as a gift for her the pṛthuka grains tucked within the hem of his garment, out of curiosity to behold you.
Thus addressed, he went to Dvārakā, carrying a gift as an offering at the edge of his garment. || 3 ||
Having arrived at your wondrous city, he reached the palace of Śaibyā within the houses;
entering it, he found bliss as if in Vaikuṇṭha itself—how much more so, then, through your own great honor?

"Having gone"—this Kucela went to your city of Dvārakā, which is wondrous and fashioned with no small skill; there, among eight thousand houses, he reached the palace of Śaibyā. What more need be said than that, through your great hospitality and supreme honor, he attained bliss and happiness? (4)
Having taken in your hand that [lotus] which was honored by your beloved and fanned by her, you spoke of what had been done in the past:
how, at the command of your preceptor’s wife, you had endured the heat of the summer season in the forest for the sake of fuel.

"Regarding 'prapūjitam' (highly honored): that you endured—that is, tolerated—that very great rain during the non-season, that is, at a time other than the rainy season, was due to the work performed previously in the house of the guru; this is what you have related. || 5 ||

Then, having forcibly seized a piece of flattened rice from you who were caught in the snare, once it had been tasted by you in a single mouthful, she approached with agitation and, crying out "Enough! Enough! Surely this much is sufficient!", she grasped your hand.

Regarding the phrase "trapājuṣa" (possessing shame): When you had forcibly seized the flattened rice from the one possessing shame—whose face was cast downward out of embarrassment at having to offer a handful of *pṛthuka* to the Lord of Śrī—and had eaten it once from your fist, Ramā, the Goddess of Fortune, approached in agitation and held back your hand, saying, "Enough, enough! Enough indeed! By this much favor it has been done; truly, I am incapable of providing further wealth worthy of your grace. || 6 ||
Honored by you with devotion while dwelling in the city for a single night among your devotees, he—of wondrous form—departed indeed without any further wealth; such truly was your gracious favor.

"Among the devotees," it is said: among the devotees such as Uddhava and others, that Kucela was honored and worshipped by you, who were filled with love for the devotee; "batā" expresses grief, for on the following day, when tomorrow had dawned, he departed without wealth or riches. His form was wondrous, appearing in many ways through distinctions such as being visible or invisible to the eye. (7) "If indeed I had asked him, Acyuta would not have given [anything]; I say: 'What shall I do with my wife? As he was departing, he—devoid of worldly wisdom—again beheld in due order your abode, radiant with jewels, characterized by your speech, divine play, and smile. (8)

"If...": "If I had requested it, then Acyuta would have given it; I did not request it, and Acyuta did not give it"—this is the meaning. Thus, while walking along, thinking, "What shall I say to my wife?", his mind was fixed upon your playful words and smile. He gradually beheld his own residence, a palace radiant with jewels and gems that served as lamps. || 8 ||

Wandering for a moment, wondering if he had lost his way, he entered the house and beheld her of radiant splendor, surrounded by her companions and adorned with jewels and gold; and he recognized your most wonderful compassion.

"What is this?"—wondering for a moment whether he had lost his way and returned once more to Dvārakā, he entered the house; and seeing his beloved, so full of great wonder, he realized that her compassion was his own supreme wealth and the very cause of it. (9)
Though dwelling in palaces of jewels, he himself, filled with joy and the weight of his devotion, attained immortality;
O Great Lord of the City! you who thus fulfill the desires of your devotees, take away my sins. 10.

"He" refers to him; although he himself resided within the jeweled palaces amidst the excitants that kindle passion, his burden of devotion steadily rose, and with his excellence of devotion thus gradually increased, he attained immortality, which is liberation. || 10 ||
Thus ends the seventy-seventh decad, the narrative of Kucela.

Having previously received an offering on the ground for your son at the word of your mother— who, through her constant observation of the teacher’s son, had long desired a vision of her own six children— you were honored by him.

By the power of a curse, you brought these sons of Śauri—who were born as children in Kaśī endowed with gold—and having shown them to Dhātu, you led them to your own abode; they were the former sons of Marīci. || 1 ||

"Even before that," [he said]. Having heard the report that he had brought back his deceased son as the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), Devakī—the mother who had longed for a very long time to behold her own six sons killed by Kaṃsa—spoke to you. Having obtained great strength, you first showed her the sons of Marīci named Smara, Udgītha, Pariṣvaṅga, Pataṅga, Kṣudrabhuk, and Vṛṇī; and then, having shown her the sons of Śauri (Vasudeva) born of Hiraṇyakaśipu due to the curse of the Creator Brahmā, you led her to your own abode, heaven. || 1 ||
Desiring to bestow grace simultaneously upon the lord of brahmins named Śrutadeva and upon King Bahulāśva, who was filled with devotion, You arrived at Mithilā accompanied by ascetics.
Regarding "Śrutadeva": *śruta* means "renowned. ||2||

Moving with two forms simultaneously to the abodes of both, you were honored with abundant riches by one, and by the other with fruits, boiled rice, and other offerings gathered that very day; thus you were equally pleased and granted liberation to both.

"Going," [it means] having assumed two forms (*dvimūrtiḥ*), having accepted two bodies. By one [form], he for whom worship (*upacāraḥ*)—that is, honor (*pūjā*)—was performed (*vihitaḥ*) with many horses (*bahulāśva*), with abundant riches (*bhūribhiḥ vibhavaiḥ*), and with various implements (*upakaraṇaiḥ*). || 3 ||

Then, He describes the manner in which He instilled in Himself the realization of His true nature by first removing the pride of Arjuna through bringing back the dead son of a twice-born man: "Furthermore, in Dvāravatī, even though you are the bearer of the universe, you were unable to endure the death of a brahmin’s son and his lamentations, saying, 'Who indeed can obstruct destiny?'"

I believe that he has come here to humble the pride of Jiṣṇu and, by leading him toward the supreme state, to establish his intellect—which had been dulled by the notion that you were a mere human—upon the ultimate reality. || 4 ||

"Furthermore," [he said]. "Who could obstruct destiny—the fruit of one's own actions? Who is capable of making it otherwise? Speaking thus, even you, the sustainer of the universe and Lord of the world, did not tolerate—that is, you endured—even the lamentations of that twice-born man. I believe this was done in order to humble and remove the pride of this Jiṣṇu by showing him the supreme state, the realm of Vaikuṇṭha; and to establish in him a conviction grounded in reality, which had been stunted and rendered uncertain by his human intellect regarding You. || 4 ||
Your eight sons were lost, yet through your indifference, a harsh report clearly spread among the people; then, O Hero of Dvārakā, at that moment, Pārtha dwelt there out of friendship,
and upon the death of the ninth son, he heard the lamentation of the excellent brāhmaṇa.
Having heard this, he made a vow: "If my son is not restored, I shall enter the fire."

"Lost!"—the eight sons of this best of the twice-born have been lost. Then, due to your neglect—that indifference toward protecting the son of the brahmin—a painful report and public scandal arose among the people. At that juncture, Pārtha arrived at Dvārakā. He dwelt there out of friendship and camaraderie. "If I do not recover my son, I shall enter the fire, the consumer of oblations. (5)

That proud one, having gone to the abode of the twice-born without asking your permission, was suddenly seeing the infant son vanish again and again as he blocked the maternity chamber with nets of arrows— great celestial weapons.
Having quickly reached the southern, northern, and other cities of the foremost gods through his magic power,
his efforts rendered futile, he was on the verge of falling into the fire when he was stopped by you with a smile.

"Arrogant": that son of Pṛthā was arrogant, possessing the conceit, "I am peerless in protecting those who have sought refuge. For this very reason, without even asking you—his supreme kinsman—he blocked the maternity chamber with great weapons such as the Āgneya and others, creating a cage of arrows. When [the child] had vanished from sight while still visible, having become invisible in his physical body as soon as he was born, he reached and attained through his yogic power and knowledge the city of Yama (the southern city), the city of Indra (the eastern city), and other cities of the foremost gods such as Varuṇa and Kubera; and [he cast him] into the fire, the consumer of oblations.

"Having begun to drink, you have started drinking with a smile; what conclusion have you now reached regarding human effort being dependent on fate?"—this communication of Arjuna's inner thought is the cause of your smile. (6)
Together with him, he set out toward the western direction on that exceedingly swift chariot;
having passed beyond the Lokāloka mountain, he then dispelled the mass of darkness with the brilliance of his wheel.
Then, seeing Vijaya standing there with his vision obscured by the rays of the wheel, [the Lord] called out repeatedly, "Look! Look! to the people.
On the further shore, you beheld that which is indeed a station of austerities, far, far beyond reach.

"Together" means with one who is exceedingly swift, possessing an excess of speed. "On the far shore of the waters" means situated within the causal ocean. "Something indescribable" refers to that which cannot be specified. "Far, far from the darkness" means situated at an extreme distance. || 7 ||
There, seated upon the couch of the lord of serpents, adorned with divine ornaments and weapons, wearing yellow garments, and possessing a glorious body dark as a fresh rain-cloud—
you, the sole sovereign of the three forms and the single goal of the Vedas— O Supreme Self, you alone were worshipped by Nemi together with his dear friend in your aspect of Peace.

Regarding that: you alone have bowed down—that is, you have offered salutation—to You, the Lord and Controller of the three forms; therefore, the supreme cause of the universe, the sole object of the Vedas, the primary subject of their teaching, the embodiment of security, and the ultimate goal of human existence. || 8 ||
I myself had previously brought together two young Brahmin sons who were like two cows separated by excessive distance and hidden from one another; now,
thinking "Let him lead these two away quickly," I once again bestowed them [upon him].
The descendants of Pāṇḍu, whose greatness was celebrated by the twice-born, were without heirs. ||9||

"O you two!"—I have myself brought these sons of the twice-born here to see you two, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, who are none other than me, my own partial manifestations (*aṃśa*), yet appearing divided by being respectively more manifest and concealed. One is more manifest due to having pure goodness (*sattva*) as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), with his own sovereignty revealed; the other has his own sovereignty concealed by a different adjunct. Therefore, appearing divided in the forms of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), I have brought them here to see you face to face.

"Quickly, instantly, lead them; bring them into the presence of the best of the twice-born"—having taken these sons of the brahmin who were thus bestowed and given, he delivered them to the brahmin. His greatness was extolled and praised by Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu. || 9 ||
Thus, delighting the world with various pastimes, nourishing the clan of the Dṛṣṇis, performing diverse sacrifices with incomparable pleasures, and gratifying the deer-eyed women,

You— who are the full Brahman itself descended among the Yadus in the form of a human being for the sake of relieving the earth's burden and liberating those who take refuge at Your lotus feet— manifested Yourself. 10.
Thus: under the pretext of removing the burden of the earth, he was merely "human" in appearance, externally smeared [with the guise of humanity]. || 10 ||

At that time, Nārada, whose heart was moistened by the nectar of your love, generally remained unimpeded in Dvāravatī; therefore, your father—a treasure-house of merit—attained the awakening to reality. Furthermore, the wise Uddhava, the foremost among devotees, received the essence of realized knowledge from you alone; he now dwells at Badarī for the welfare of all people.

Regarding the word "prāyeṇa" (mostly): Śrī Nārada, because it was generally impossible for him to remain in one place for long due to the curse of Dakṣa, had previously been coming and going, and thus he was residing in Dvārakā. Then, from that Nārada [he heard this], for the benefit of the people—that is, for the purpose of instructing the devotees in knowledge. || 11 ||

Victorious is this incarnation as Kṛṣṇa of yours, O All-pervading Lord! Through various incomparable yogic means—such as friendship, fear, affection, hatred, and passion—all people everywhere have crossed over every affliction and attained the immortal state. May You, the Lord of the City of Wind (Pavana-pura), be present for the pacification of the world's suffering and for the fulfillment of devotion! 12.

"Thus [it is said]: 'So this'—referring to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by means of various types of yoga which are specific methods for fixing the mind upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa through friendship and other qualities. Among them, the Pāṇḍavas and others [attained Him] through friendship; Kaṃsa through fear; the Yadavas through affection; Śiśupāla and others through hatred; and the Gopīs through passionate love. 'From all sides' means everywhere. All people, having crossed over—that is, transcended—all forms of suffering (ārta), such as those pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika) and so forth, went to the immortal state, that is, liberation (mokṣa)."
May it be for the pacification of all afflictions, for the removal of every suffering, and for the fulfillment and further growth of devotion already undertaken. || 12 ||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth decade, along with its supplement, describing the excellence of Arjuna’s devotion.

O Mother of Ramā! I know that if Your power among Your devotees were not truly manifest here, then the state of being free from pride would not immediately arise in those who have severed their egoism.
Having first brought about peace, you then grant every desire;
indeed, among those who are at peace, there is never even a mention of death.

"O Consort of Ramā!"—thus [the Lord is addressed]. O Lord of Lakṣmī! I know that among Your devotees, the fruit of Your majesty does not manifest immediately upon the mere act of worship; rather, it does not reach full fruition until later. This is because that majesty is "madakṛt"—that is, it generates intoxication [of pride]. Therefore, You bestow every desired object only after first bringing about peace for those who are unpeaceful (aśaminām). But for those already peaceful, You bestow it instantly.
Consequently, in one who is Yours—a true devotee of Yours—there is indeed not even a mention, nor even the sound of the word, of "cyuti," which means fall or ruin. || 1 ||
But Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and others are not like that; thus he says:
"O Lord! Some, worshipping Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and others according to their own qualities, [attain results] immediately upon being pleased or angered by them."

That which is accomplished (*sampadyate*) is "accomplished" (*sampadya*). Its grammatical correctness is established by the rule *kṛbhvastiyoge sampadyakartari*, due to its being a formal derivation (*nipātana*) ending in the suffix *śa* (denoting the agent).
Alas, what a tragedy! Those of short-sighted vision clearly fall away; indeed, the demon Ṭaka serves as an illustration of this. (2)

Regarding the word *sadyaḥ*: "immediately" means by virtue of slight qualities or defects; [thus] Brahmā, Śiva, and others are immediately propitious and immediately wrathful. Some, worshipping them according to their own qualities—that is, in accordance with their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—fall away immediately thereafter due to a lack of peace, precisely because of His anger. "Alas, what a pity! expresses grief. The sense is that through a lack of long-sighted vision, one abandons the worship of Viṣṇu—which is exceedingly difficult to perform—and instead worships another. As it has been said:
"That man who is possessed of passion necessarily seeks a fruit from Śiva."
Then he obtains the fruit, and thereafter he will forget it.
Thus; in this matter, the demon Vṛka is a clear and appropriate illustration. (2)
For once, that son of Śakuni asked the Lord Nārada about one who was quickly satisfied;
and he directed him to worship the Lord of the Mountains (Śiva), but not you, who are a kinsman among the wicked.
Regarding the term *śakunija*: for that Vṛkāsura questioned the Lord, who was pleased by his haste and whose grace was immediate.
Having performed severe austerities, he indeed became enraged; on the seventh day,
having immediately severed his head and placed it before the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva),
he brought about his own destruction by offering that exceedingly small and fierce head as a tribute.
Who that possesses a virtuous mind would turn their face away from Jagannātha? || 4 ||
"Asceticism"—having established and made manifest—[is] extremely trivial and essence-less; [it is] fierce and cruel. This occurs regarding Viṣṇu. || 4 ||
Then, like a lord of deer fleeing from a hunter, he ran toward Rudra, the deliverer;
out of fear of the Daitya, the god turned in every direction, casting glances behind him.
While all the worlds remained silent, O Śarva, they gazed upon you as you were about to step upon his foot.
From afar, you stood before the Dānava in the form of a clever young brahmin boy. || 5 ||

"O Liberator! Thus [thinking], that Daitya rushed toward Rudra himself, just as a lion, the lord of beasts, freed from its bonds, rushes toward its captor. Your abode is Vaikuṇṭha; you remained there, having revealed yourself to the Dānava Vṛkāsura. ||5||

"May it be well with you, O son of Śakuni! Why do you now wander about? If your heart is filled with doubt by the words of a Piśāca, why, my dear, do you not place your finger upon my word on your head?
Thus, bewildered by his speech, he placed his hand upon his head and fell down with a crashing sound.
For even the downfall of one who worships another, as well as the ultimate goal of Śiva himself, is you alone.

"May it be well! [Thus saying,] he fell with a crashing sound, like a tree cut at its roots; even for one who serves another, such a downfall caused by you occurs. Yet, even for Śiva, you—being Viṣṇu alone—are his goal and his refuge. ||6||
It is said that the ascetics dwelling near the Sarasvatī river appointed Bhṛgu among the three forms [of Brahmā] to ascertain who possessed the greatest degree of goodness (sattva). However,
when Brahmā became angry at his being treated with disrespect and Viṣṇu was intent on killing him, he came to you while Pārvatī held him back.

Regarding the word *bhṛgum*: it refers to his superior strength and greatness. This Bhṛgu, a son of Brahmā, rose up without having offered salutation due to his disregard for him; while Rudra was thus provoked by that anger and yet restrained by brotherly affection, when he [Brahmā] began to embrace him and Rudra, desiring to strike him out of the wrath born of that disregard, wished to kill him, he was held back and stopped by Girijā (Pārvatī), and so he went to Vaikuṇṭha. || 7 ||
When you, the lotus-eyed one, were struck with a foot by a brahmin on the earth marked by the number seven (the Saptarṣi region), you rose up in joy;
O best of sages, forgive all this, and may it ever be so for me.
"You have declared that the mark of your foot is here an ornament. ||8||
Regarding the word "suptam" (asleep): it refers to the mark upon your foot known as Śrīvatsa. || 8 ||
Having reached this firm certainty, those excellent sages of the Sarasvatī, their hearts bound to you with steadfast devotion, have attained liberation;
for you, O Acyuta, are thus free from the defect of falling away again.
We worship only that single body which is the accumulation of all sentient beings. || 9 ||
"Having ascertained" means those whose fixed disposition is devotion; "Sārasvatas" refers to those dwelling on the banks of the Sarasvatī. || 9 ||
O Viṣṇu! At the beginning of the creation of the world, you—whose body is non-dual existence, consciousness, and supreme bliss—are praised by multitudes of Vedas as if by bards; O Infinite One!
You are the Supreme Self, the mass of good fortune for the wives of the individual souls.
O dweller of the city of wind! I resort to you for the sake of dispelling my feverish exhaustion. || 10 ||

"Jagat" (the world): at the beginning of the creation of the universe, He was praised as possessing attributes (*saguṇa*) by the multitudes of *Nigamas* (the Vedas) personified as the *Upaniṣads*. "Saccit" (Being-Consciousness): the sense is that He was also praised in the form of the Supreme Self, which is non-dual Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccidānanda*). "Paśupavanitānāṃ bhāgyaṃ": it is so called because it intensely bears—that is, brings about—the fortune of the wives of the *paśus* (individual souls); or alternatively, because it is the multitude of fortunes itself, having transformed into the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

And thus, it should also be understood that it has been stated that regarding this matter—that among the three forms (trimūrti) Viṣṇu alone possesses greatness—the eminent sages of the Sarasvata school and the collections of scriptural conclusions (nigama) are the authoritative evidence. || 10 ||
Thus ends the eighty-ninth decade, containing the description of the slaying of the demon Vṛka and the description of the preeminence of the Blessed One within the triad of forms.
Now, raising the objection that the greatness among the three forms belongs to Śrī Śaṅkara alone— as is frequently heard in the Skanda Purāṇa and other texts— the author refutes it as follows:
In the accounts of Vṛka, Bhṛgu, the sage Māhinya, Ambarīṣa, and others, Your greatness indeed stands triumphant over all, including Śarva and the rest;
O Supreme Self! that which appears here as something indistinguishable from the partless [Brahman] is truly Your very form. || 1 ||

Regarding the word *vṛka*: *Mohinī* is the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu. Your greatness as Viṣṇu is victorious over all the gods, beginning with Śarva, yet it brings about their inferiority. In that regard, within the accounts of the four starting with Vṛka, your greatness as Śiva consists in being victorious over them; and in [the episodes of] the abduction of Indrāṇī during the sacrifice, the carrying off of the child, the drinking of the fire, and the theft of the calf, your greatness as Viṣṇu consists in being victorious over Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Anala, Brahmā, and the others—this is established and further confirmed right here. The reason for this is stated: "O Supreme Self" (*paramātman*).

He establishes that very state of being the unconditioned Supreme Self with the words "niṣkala" (partless): "In the partless Supreme Self, and likewise in those below it—the conditioned ones such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Giriśa, and so forth—whatever undivided form of the Supreme Reality appears, that alone is Your form, O Viṣṇu; and that form belongs to You alone, not to them. For since Giriśa and the others are merely different states of Viṣṇu, the meaning is that among the three forms (trimūrti), greatness is attributed to Viṣṇu alone. This is stated in the Śrī Bhāgavata:

"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities of Prakṛti; joined with these, the one Supreme Puruṣa here assumes the names of Hari, Viriñca, and Hara for the sake of the world's maintenance and so forth. Among these, indeed, the auspicious states of men belong to Him whose body is Sattva. || 1 ||
But is it not said: "In this way, the one Great God appears as if divided through his illusory power consisting of the qualities (guṇas), by means of the distinctions of name, form, and action"?

Having raised the doubt that, according to this statement, there is merely a distinction of states and a predominance of the three forms belonging to Śiva alone, he resolves it by stating that this is only a difference in designation, not a difference in the essential nature of the designated reality:
"That which consists of the triad of forms and the pentad of Īśvara and Sadāśiva..."
They say that Sadāśiva is indeed the very body of the Supreme Self in this [universe];
therein, you alone are the Lord of the realm of Vikuṇṭha, yet you assume a threefold nature within the three divisions of the realm of Satya.

Regarding the phrase "mūrtitraya" (the three forms): Śaivas assert that Śiva is fivefold by way of the distinct forms known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Giriśa, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. In that system of the Śaivas, he who is denoted by the term "Sadāśiva," in this present system—where it is said, "I bow to Viṣṇu, the fivefold one"—is, according to the Bhāgavata school, none other than You, Viṣṇu, whose body is the Supreme Self (*parātmavapuḥ*), meaning Your very nature is that of the Supreme Lord (*paramātmasvarūpa*). Likewise, You alone, dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha (*vikuṇṭhapadaḥ*), are the one denoted by the word "Īśvara."

The term *tribhāgam* refers to that which consists of three parts—the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. Within that *satyapada*, the realm of truth (*satyaloka*), there are the three: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Giriśa (Śiva). Their state (*bhāva*) is their triadic nature; the meaning is that You alone assume even the form of the Trinity within the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva situated in Satyaloka. As it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"I am You, O omnipresent God! You alone am I, O Janārdana!
There is no difference between us, O Lord of the World, whether in words or in their meanings."
Thus [ends the second section].

Now, if there is non-difference between Viṣṇu and Śiva, then how is the preeminence of Viṣṇu asserted? True. Although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*) there is no difference, nevertheless, a secondary distinction consisting of superiority and inferiority does indeed exist between these two; thus he says: "In that regard as well, they call Viṣṇu your *sāttvika* form, while the Creator (Brahmā) is full of *rajas* alone, with *sattva* being sparse.
Furthermore, even in your form named Śaṅkara, there is an abundance of *sattva*, yet also the activity of the transformations of *tamas*. (3)
Regarding the phrase "there too": among those three forms, they call your *sāttvikī*—that is, your body composed of pure *sattva*, denoted by the word Viṣṇu alone—"Viṣṇu. As it has been said:
"The Lord Brahmā is *rājasa*; Viṣṇu is called *sāttvika*; and Rudra possesses a slight degree of *tamas*. The Unborn One creates, protects, and destroys."
Thus [ends section] 3.
But is it not said: "In that regard, the Lord is you yourself, whose abode is Vikuṇṭha"? That is incorrect, for [it is stated]:
"The Lord of Ambikā, the Ruler (Īśāna), is to be worshipped through his forms of the qualities (guṇamūrti).
The one Supreme Self is the Lord (Īśvara); he exists in three ways through Māyā."
If it is argued that this is because of such a statement, he says "no":
for indeed, even as Śarva, you— who have transcended the three forms (trimūrti) and are the Supreme Person (parapūruṣa)—
are [the object of worship] because of the reason that you consist of all things.
Although they praise that [form] in the injunction for worship, there is abundant and very firm evidence for us that it is, by its own nature, Your very form. || 4 ||

"And Him" means: the Purāṇic sages praise You—who have transcended the three forms (Trimūrti), who are beyond the triad of forms, who are the Supreme Brahman denoted by the word *Īśvara* for the Śaivas, who stand outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), yet having entered the city—the cosmic egg—with a single portion, remain there with many cosmic eggs contained within; indeed, they praise You toward the Śaivas in the ritual of worship as being of the nature of Śarva, that is, in the form of Śiva, because You consist of everything.

The meaning is that because You are the substratum of the three forms (trimūrti), even that [objection] is not entirely improper. Furthermore, even so, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that [form] is indeed Your own form and not that of Brahmā or Śiva; there are many proofs for this. The meaning is that there are numerous authorities, such as the words of the Śrutis and Purāṇas, as well as perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for the Śruti, it is found in the *Puruṣasūkta* and other texts. The Purāṇic statements begin with "O Lord of immeasurable power" (*keśigvidhāvigalita*) and so forth. Since Arjuna and others have seen You in such a form, perception is also an authority. Enough said. || 4 ||
Even the Lord Śrī Śaṅkara honors you alone among all beings, for he is indeed free from partiality;
for his *Sahasranāma* and other works are centered solely upon you.
He gave an exposition, intent on your praise, and at the end, he attained the supreme goal. ||5||

Regarding "Śrī Śaṅkara": furthermore, Śrī Śaṅkara is the venerable teacher Bhagavatpādācārya. Regarding the phrase "the *Sahasranāma* and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," the *Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā* and other texts are included. Although both of those [the *Gītā* and the *Sahasranāma*] could have been interpreted as being devoted to Śiva, he interpreted them precisely as being devoted to Viṣṇu. Moreover, at the end, while intent on praising you and offering praise to the feet and hair of the venerable one (Viṣṇu), he attained his goal—liberation—but not by being intent on praising Śiva. || 5 ||
Regarding what was stated—that you alone are honored among all [deities]—he says that very thing:
"And at the beginning of the Mantra-śāstra, he spoke of you, the Lord of the Sakala [aspect], who transcends the three forms and is as beautiful as a kalāya [bean];
and having indeed described the meditation on the Niṣkala [aspect] within the Praṇava."
There he described you alone in their entirety, and no one else.

Regarding the phrase "mūrtitraya" (the three forms): he spoke of you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who are beyond the three forms, who are the fourth Supreme Lord, and who are as beautiful as a kalāya pea—as being within the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) by virtue of being its meaning. Therein, as an ancillary to the meditation on the partless (*niṣkala*), he declared that you alone are the one with parts (*sakala*), and not any other Śiva; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
He states that the Purāṇas have as their primary subject the greatness of Viṣṇu, clearly so in the *Purāṇasaṃgraha*:
"In the *Purāṇasaṃgraha*, which is the essence of all [scriptures], your own greatness alone is described without doubt;
the supreme state beyond the three parts of the true station associated with the three forms has not been described as belonging to the wielder of the trident. (7)

Regarding the word "samasta" (all): Now, one might object that the world of Vaikuṇṭha is included within Satyaloka, for there is no world situated outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). To this he says, "not so," with the words "trimūrti. That state or world which is beyond the three worlds of Satyaloka associated with the three forms (*mūrti*), and which lies outside the cosmic egg—that is indeed your world of Vaikuṇṭha; thus it is stated in the *Purāṇasaṃgraha*. (7)

O Lord! That unconditioned form which was described here in the second book of the *Bhāgavata* as belonging to the Brahma-kalpa, its very name—Hari-Śarva-mukha—was proclaimed by the illustrious Mādhava in the *Purāṇasāra*, even though he is devoted to Śiva. (8)

Regarding the word *yat*: in that *brāhma* kalpa—the kalpa in which [the Lord] became Brahman—that form (*vapuḥ*) which was directly perceived by the Blessed Creator (Brahmā), Śrī Mādhavācārya designated that very form as "Hari-Śarvamukha" in the *Purāṇasāra*. Although this [text] is devoted to Śiva, nevertheless, in the *Purāṇasāra*, he did not state that the form shown to Brahmā was a form of Śiva; rather, the meaning is that he stated, "You alone are all-pervading," and thus spoke of You alone. || 8 ||
Is it not said:
"Viṣṇu is the protector, the embodiment of darkness (tamas), yet by his activity he is characterized by goodness (sattva)";
and "Hari is directly dependent upon him"?

Fearing that statements such as, "Viṣṇu and Viriñca bear his lotus-feet upon their heads," might suggest the inferiority of Hari, Vyāsa states— through the two verses beginning with "Those who, according to their own nature"— that such passages are merely *arthavādas* (laudatory statements) and not intended to convey literal truth: "Those who worship Giriśa in accordance with their own nature,
their fruit indeed arises from their firm devotion to Him."
For Vyāsa, indeed, for the sake of those who possess the qualification [to hear it], has composed in the Skanda Purāṇa and others the statements regarding its inferiority by means of arthavādas.

Regarding the word "yaḥ": according to the principle that "one should take refuge in whichever deity the desire for arises toward," [the devotee approaches] in accordance with their own nature and following the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births. Since the fruit will surely come about through their firm devotion to Him alone, for that reason Vyāsa—out of consideration for the qualified aspirant (*adhikārin*), specifically one qualified for the worship of Giriśa—uttered words of depreciation and statements of deficiency regarding you by means of *arthavādas*. And these *arthavādas* are intended to generate a taste for the worship of Giriśa. (9)
If it is argued that [the scripture] should praise Giriśa alone for the sake of generating devotion, and not employ speech that disparages others, the author replies:
