"The proclamation of actual facts (*bhūtārthakīrti*), restatement (*anuvāda*), and contradictory discourse (*viruddhavāda*)—these three modes of *arthavāda* indeed serve the purpose of generating devotion.
In the *Skānda* and other such texts, there are many contradictory discourses here, such as those concerning your being *tāmasa*, your humiliation, and so forth. (10)

Regarding the phrase "bhūtārtha" (the true meaning): the proclamation of the true meaning (*bhūtārthakīrti*) is the description of things as they actually exist; this is *anuvāda* (restatement). The attribution of non-contradictory qualities is [also *anuvāda*]. The statement of a meaning contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is *viruddhavāda* (contradictory discourse). These are the three ways or paths of *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). All three serve the purpose of creating interest (*rocanārtha*). Among those, the statements such as "you are *tāmasa*" and so forth are *viruddhavāda*, as they are words contradicted by other means of valid cognition; yet they too serve the purpose of creating interest. Even Viṣṇu requires his grace—oh, the mountain!... [text continues]...

The excellence of these [scriptures] lies solely in their capacity to generate a taste for the worship of Giriśa; they are not authoritative means for establishing such matters as Viṣṇu’s tamasic nature or his defeat. || 10 ||

To ward off any suspicion that the matter he has stated is merely his own fabrication, the poet inspires faith in the listener: "O All-pervasive Lord! Whatever I have said, even though I am unlearned, is indeed in accordance with the words of the mantra scriptures."
O Supreme Self, who are praised in the Bhāgavata which contains the essence of Vyāsa’s teachings! Cast off all afflictions and cultivate an abundance of devotion! 11.

"Whatever [has been said]" refers to the Purāṇas spoken by Vyāsa; among them, the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam consists of their very essence, for it brings about the fulfillment of the purpose of the venerable Vedavyāsa himself. Therefore, [O Lord], you are praised by that [text] and are its subject matter. || 11 || 559 ||
Thus ends the ninety-first decade, which establishes that the ultimate purport of the Āgamas and other scriptures lies solely in the Blessed One.
Thus concludes the commentary on the *Nārāyaṇīya-stotra* titled *Bhaktapriyā*.
The Tenth Chapter:
The pastimes characterized by worldly engagement have been proclaimed by the ancient verses; now, the pastimes of Hari characterized by renunciation are being described.

Now, beginning to describe the qualities of the Blessed One in order to show the path of liberation to devotees, [the author] first demonstrates the greatness of the worship of the Blessed One, which is the crown jewel among the means to liberation:

"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! I consider the worship of Your feet to be the most secure from fear for a distressed mortal whose vision of reality is bound by falsehood; for by that alone, fear departs as if by the very Self of all.
This is because one who abides here in the rules of devotion ordained by You remains on the path of delusion."
O God of gods, Soul of all! Even while running with eyes closed, one does not stumble anywhere. || 1 ||

"O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! [Thus: I consider the worship of Your feet to be the supreme source of fearlessness for a mortal—one whose vision is fixed on false objects such as the body and who possesses the egoistic conceit of "I" and "mine"—and consequently for one who is distressed, being afflicted by the sufferings of the internal self and so forth; for from that worship, there is no fear, and thus it is "fearless" (abhaya), and being exceedingly fearless, it is "supremely fearless" (abhayatama), removing the fear of worldly existence. He states its state of being supremely fearless with the words beginning "by which": By which [worship], O Lord, even those who have committed great sins, having abandoned all other duties, attain the eternal state through Your grace. (18.65) By which worship of Yours, O Lord, even those who have committed great sins—those who have performed heinous crimes—attain the eternal state through Your grace, having abandoned all other duties. Therefore, this alone is the supreme means for the removal of fear. (18.66) Even those who, having committed great sins, are devoted to You with single-minded intent, are purified of all sins and attain the eternal state. (18.67) Even those who are of low birth, women, vaiśyas, and śūdras, having attained You, attain the supreme goal. (18.68) Even those who are of low birth, women, vaiśyas, and śūdras—those excluded from the Vedic path—having attained You, attain the supreme goal. (18.69) Therefore, O Arjuna, fix your mind on Me alone; surrender your intellect to Me. Thus, with your mind established in Me, you shall come to Me without doubt. (18.65) Therefore, O Arjuna, fix your mind on Me alone; surrender your intellect to Me. Thus, with your mind established in Me, you shall come to Me without doubt. (18.66) If, however, you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, then seek to reach Me by the yoga of constant practice (abhyāsa-yoga). (18.53) If, however, you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, then seek to reach Me by the yoga of constant practice (abhyāsa-yoga). (18.54) If even by the yoga of practice you are unable to attain steady concentration, then perform actions for My sake, having renounced attachment, and you shall attain perfection. (18.55) If even by the yoga of practice you are unable to attain steady concentration, then perform actions for My sake, having renounced attachment, and you shall attain perfection. (18.56) If you are unable to do even this, then, resorting to the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga), perform all your actions while surrendering them to Me alone. (18.57) If you are unable to do even this, then, resorting to the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga), perform all your actions while surrendering them to Me alone. (18.58) Even if you perform actions merely for My sake, you will attain perfection. With your mind fixed on Me, you shall overcome all difficulties. (18.59) Even if you perform actions merely for My sake, you will attain perfection. With your mind fixed on Me, you shall overcome all difficulties. (18.60) The wise man, knowing this secret of wisdom and renunciation, and being liberated from the bonds of action, attains the blissful state of the Supreme Being. (18.61) The wise man, knowing this secret of wisdom and renunciation, and being liberated from the bonds of action, attains the blissful state of the Supreme Being. (18.62) Having taken refuge in this wisdom, and having become free from delusion, the sons of Pṛthā have cast off all doubts born of ignorance and are established in their own nature. (18.63) Having taken refuge in this wisdom, and having become free from delusion, the sons of Pṛthā have cast off all doubts born of ignorance and are established in their own nature. (18.64) Thus ends the Eighteenth Chapter, titled "Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga," in the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, in the Science of the Yoga of Liberation,

By that service to Your feet, fear departs and vanishes entirely, leaving nothing behind, for You are the Self of all. And regarding the means of worship, he says "yat" (that which), indicating that the dharma of the Lord is free from fear from any quarter.

Here, among the paths of worshiping the Lord, one who has gradually taken recourse to—through the medium of the company of the virtuous—the religious duties known as the *Bhāgavata* ordinances, which were proclaimed by the Lord Himself with His own mouth for the sake of favoring His devotees; and who, while running along the path of delusion—in places such as streets, marketplaces, brothels, and assembly halls that serve as gateways to ignorance—having bypassed this and that, proceeds with extreme haste, and moreover, whose eyes are covered.
"With the pair of eyes known as the Śruti and Smṛti closed" means even without knowing them. As they say:
"The Śruti and Smṛti are proclaimed to be the two eyes of the Brahmins;
one devoid of one is called one-eyed, and one devoid of both is proclaimed blind."

Thus: "In any place whatsoever" means that one does not stumble—by failing in performance or the like—and thus shall not incur sin (*pratyavāya*). Nor, because the fruit were transitory, shall one become a transmigrator once again; such is the meaning. The connection with the preceding is: "I consider that which is thus described to be the most fearless. || 1 ||
He speaks of the teachings of the Blessed One:
"O Infinite One! Whatever I do with body, speech, or even mind, my self being impelled by Your power—I offer all that here unto You, the Supreme."

In this world, even a dog-cooker (outcaste) purifies the entire universe if his mind, actions, speech, senses, objects, and life-breath are fixed upon You; but not so a preeminent brahmin whose mind is turned away from Your feet. ||2||

"O Infinite One!"—by means of the body, that is, the head, hands, and so forth; by speech, that is, the organ of speech; and by the mind, the internal organ. By the word "api" (also), the meaning is "by all the senses. O Antaryāmin, he whose self—that is, the mind—is impelled by Your power in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [says]: "Whatever I do, again and again."

The meaning is this: it is not only prescribed action that is so restricted by rule; rather, even worldly action performed according to one's own nature, if offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, certainly becomes the dharma of the Lord. Therefore, I offer all of that to You, the Supreme Self, the most transcendent Śrī Kṛṣṇa—offering it with the thought, "This is for Śrī Kṛṣṇa."

And this is the intention: "Just as the work of a king's servant, when impelled by the king, results in the king's pleasure, so may all my actions, being impelled by the Lord who is the Self of all, lead to the pleasure of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Or rather, it means: "I offer [this] preceded by the mantra of dedication. Thus, he describes the greatness of one who performs the duties of the Lord with the verse beginning with *jātyā*. The mental action consists of the mind characterized by resolve and doubt; *karman* refers to physical action; and *vāk* refers to verbal action.

The senses are characterized by cognition and action; their objects are the *arthas*; the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are five; and all action, characterized by injunction and prohibition, is primarily of body, speech, and mind, while the actions of the other senses are subordinate to them—thus these three are mentioned separately. One who has surrendered the mind, the organs of action, the objects of the senses, and the vital breaths unto You, the Lord—even if he is by birth a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), he purifies the entire universe. What need is there to mention that he purifies his own self?

One whose mind is turned away from your feet and devoid of remembrance and other such practices is described as such; the meaning is that even though he may be the best of brahmins, being in such a state, he is incapable of purifying either the Supreme or himself. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: "How can the surrender of mental, physical, and verbal actions to the Lord be possible for those whose minds are distracted by sense objects? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says—with the intention that there is no such thing as an "object" in reality, but that it is merely a play of the mind; therefore, one should surrender everything preceded by the restraint of the mind:
"Fear indeed arises from a second [entity], and the second is surely imagined by the mind.
Therefore, I shall restrain the heart here with my intellect according to my ability, through the practice of identifying with That (the One)."
But when that [world] is pierced by Māyā, it no longer appears as such; therefore, O Lord, by constantly worshipping You, the Sovereign of Māyā, with great devotion, may I abandon all fear. || 3 ||

"Fear" refers to [fear] of the body and so forth, which are conceived as "self" and "belonging to the self" starting from the second [ignorance]. The word "namely" (*nāma*) is used in the sense of well-known fact. It is well known even to others who maintain that the body is the self that birth and other states belong only to the body and not to the self, because the self is eternal. "Mentally constructed" means imagined or superimposed by the mind—that is, by the function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of resolve and deliberation.

One who is habituated to the practice of unity—thinking that just as a pot or other objects produced from clay have the nature of clay itself, so too, because everything has arisen from Brahman, all this is indeed Brahman and nothing exists apart from it—should, by means of the heart, that is, through a mental modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ characterized by certainty, restrain and fix [the mind] upon this contemplated object according to his ability, that is, to the full extent of his intellectual power.

When that heart is pierced by *māyā* and colored by the effects of *māyā*, such as desire, anger, and the like—even if the heart is subsequently restrained—it does not shine forth in that manner; the knowledge of oneness does not remain. Therefore, by constantly worshipping You, the Lord of *māyā* and Master of *māyā*, with great and unfailing devotion characterized by love, and serving You at every opportunity, may I utterly abandon fear—the dread of *saṃsāra*. || 3 ||
When it is said, "One should worship constantly with devotion," and there arises an expectation for the cause of the birth of that devotion, he says:

"The birth and growth of devotion come only through association with those men who resort to Your feet—just as in this world, the prosperity of the fortunate comes through association with the prosperous among the meritorious.
O Lord! May I indeed have constant association with them; for through the various modes of Your majesty emerging from their mouths, devotion becomes firm and one's sins are shaken off. (4)

Regarding the word "bhakteḥ" (of devotion): "utpatti-vṛddhī" means origination and growth; those who serve or resort to the feet of You, the Lord, are called "caraṇajuṣaḥ," meaning devotees. By their very association—that is, by contact with them—it is attainable or obtainable for embodied beings (puṃsām); the meaning is that there is no other means here. This is because of the scriptural statement: "Without service to the virtuous (sat), how can devotion to Viṣṇu arise in anyone? If one asks, "In that case, how might association with the virtuous occur?", he says: "of those possessing merit" (puṇyabhājām).

The sense is that association with the virtuous occurs only for those who have accumulated a store of merit earned over many lifetimes. To provide a corresponding illustration here, he says: "like prosperity" (*śriya iva*). The meaning is: just as the arising and increase of prosperity—such as wealth, grain, and so forth—are produced only through association with the prosperous, so it is here. O Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa! May I indeed have constant association—that is, contact and fellowship—with them, the devotees.

From their mouths—that is, from the mouths of those who resort to Your feet—[the stories arise] through discourses on Your deeds that emerge spontaneously among themselves, and not through those instructed by others. By this, it is suggested that they possess the natural disposition of describing the deeds of the Blessed One.

"By the various modes of Your majesty"—that is, by the different paths consisting of hearing, chanting, remembering, and so forth, which are based upon Your majesty as Viṣṇu—"may there arise in me toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa a very firm and imperishable devotion characterized by love. This is the ellipsis to be supplied: "just as the sun rises having driven away the mass of darkness from afar, so may that devotion, having cast far away the multitude of my sins, exist in me constantly. (4)

Then, perceiving how the realization of the goal— devotion (sādhya-bhakti)— arises through the means of devotion (sādhana-bhakti) by the mere association with the virtuous, he first describes his own attainment of qualification for the path of devotion:
"Having a very great regard for devotion among the paths to the highest good, repeatedly singing my birth-activities and my auspicious names, my soul ran forth toward both of them."
Sometimes bursting into laughter, sometimes weeping somewhere, roaring elsewhere, singing, and dancing like one mad—O Lord, show mercy so that I may become an outcast from the world!

Regarding the phrase "in the paths to the highest good": among the paths to the highest good (*śreyas*), that is, among the means of attainment such as ritual action, knowledge, austerity, self-restraint, and vows, one who possesses *adhika-bahumati*—meaning one whose great regard and faith are preeminent—is one who is qualified for the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*). This is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"But for that man in whom faith has arisen by chance in my stories and the like, who is neither despondent nor excessively attached, the yoga of devotion bestows perfection."

Thus [it is said]. "Births and deeds" refers to the descents and their respective activities, as well as the names based upon them; the meaning is that these are auspicious, consisting of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), and serving as the means to attain them. This is a qualification of the triad beginning with "birth. "Singing again and again" (*bhūyaḥ*) means repeatedly proclaiming; this also serves as an elliptical indication for remembering and so forth. Having thus described the goal which transcends the attributes of *saṃsāra*—attained through the devotion characterized by love that arises from the practice of instrumental devotion—he says: "From both of those."

The meaning is: "by reason of proclaiming his birth and deeds, and by reason of chanting his name. One whose self—that is, the mind—is *pradruta*, meaning extremely swift or melted with emotion (*dravībhūta*), is called *pradrutātmā*. At times he laughs aloud; having perceived the Lord, who is "conquered by his devotees," he laughs while clapping his hands. In some instances he even weeps, crying out, "I have been neglected for so long! or else from the exhaustion of his mind’s lack of one-pointedness toward the Lord.

Or rather, it means shedding tears of joy from the direct realization of that [divine] form; sometimes roaring—that is, making a loud sound out of extreme eagerness; singing aloud out of excessive joy; and in some places dancing with the cry "Victory! Victory!", performing a dance characterized by clapping of hands and shaking of the head. If it is argued that this is merely to manifest to others that "this man is a devotee," the author says "no," for he adds: "like one who is mad. The meaning is: like one possessed by a spirit.
O Blessed One! Have compassion for me, so that I may wander thus outside the world, having become one who transcends the worldly. || 5 ||

All these beings, though composed of the elements, as well as birds, fish, wild animals, mortals, friends, and even enemies—I, whose mind is restrained, perceive them all as consisting of You and as being bowed before You.
O Lord of the World! By Your grace, may firm devotion, dispassion, and the realization of Your true nature be accomplished for me through service to You, without any effort or distinction.

Regarding the term "beings" (*bhūtāni*): furthermore, these five elements, beginning with earth; and everything composed of the elements (*bhūtātmaka*), consisting of the five elements, including all that is moving and unmoving—birds, fish, wild animals, and others depending on water or land—as well as mortals, friends, and even enemies, including relatives, foes, and neutrals; with a disciplined mind, realizing that "all these are composed of You, they are Your very form," and contemplating that "all these are forms of Śrī Hari," I shall offer salutations (*ānamāni*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Devotion, as previously defined, is something to be accomplished by yogis even over many lifetimes; how then could it be attained through mere worship in a single lifetime? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For [devotion] would be perfected through service to You. This refers to the dedication of all actions.

The chanting of Your names, birth-rites, and deeds, as well as prostration everywhere with the vision of the Lord, is here called "service to You" (*tvatsevā*). When that service exists, Your grace is inevitable. Through that grace, the firmness and stability of my devotion and love for the Lord will arise; from that, dispassion—that is, detachment from sense objects; and from that, the realization—that is, the perfect experience—of Your true nature, the reality of the Lord. All three of these shall be accomplished without any distinction of effort.
I must exert effort solely through your grace; the meaning is that once that [grace] has arisen, these three will be accomplished simultaneously. || 6 ||
Furthermore, he says that through the grace of the Lord, once devotion, detachment, and knowledge have arisen, he may attain the status of a crest-jewel among the devotees:

"May I not be deluded by hunger, thirst, and other afflictions born of the path of worldly existence, for my heart is absorbed in You; may I possess constant mindfulness and remain unshakable from Your feet even for the duration of a moment.

Free from both satisfaction and distress regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant due to the realization of their illusory nature, may I move about with a self cooled even more than by the moonbeams of the moonlight of Your toenails. (7)

"May he not be deluded" means: may he not become deluded, that is, may he not fall into a state of dependence on others due to hunger, thirst, fear, longing, distress, and so forth—conditions arising from the path of beginningless saṃsāra and belonging to the stream of worldly existence. This is because his inner disposition is absorbed in You; that is, because the fluctuations of his mind are firmly established in You, the Lord. Furthermore, it refers to one who possesses "constancy in contemplation," meaning one whose practice of meditation is continuous and uninterrupted.

For even a moment, for even half the duration of a blink of an eye, may he remain unshakable—free from negligence—by worshipping your feet, the divine lotus-feet; free from both satisfaction and distress amidst the desirable and the undesirable; free from satisfaction upon the occurrence of desired events such as the birth of a son, and free from distress upon the occurrence of undesired events such as the death of a son; through the realization of their illusory nature by contemplating that all objects of enjoyment, such as the body and so forth, are fashioned by Māyā; [all this] by means of cool, moon-like radiances.
Characterized by a mind (ātman) marked by an excessive coolness—due to the absence of torment and the resulting intense joy—arising from the moon of your toenails, may I move about and live. || 7 ||
If you have no further authority now regarding the realization of your oneness with these living beings,
then let there be love for you, friendship toward you, compassion for those of dull intellect, and indifference toward your enemies;
or else, let my eagerness for worshiping your image increase through ever-greater faith.
Nevertheless, one who serves you quickly attains the state of being the most excellent among devotees. || 8 ||

Regarding the phrase "among beings": since You, the Lord whose sovereignty is never diminished, abide in the form of the individual soul (jīva) within all these beings—whether superior or inferior, even down to mosquitoes and the like—the realization of that oneness is its recollection and constant contemplation. The attainment of that [realization], which consists of the vision of the Blessed One as being fully pervasive both internally and externally within all beings, is the supreme duty of a devotee. If I do not now possess the qualification for its attainment, it is because I lack love for You, the Lord, and for those who belong to You, Your own servants.

"Towards devotees"—that is to say—let there be friendliness (*maitrī*) and fellowship; towards those of dull intellect, the deluded, let there be compassion (*kṛpā*); and towards enemies, let there be equanimity (*upekṣā*). Here, because the perception of difference (*bhedadṛṣṭi*) still exists even toward the Lord and others, these are the duties of a *madhyama-bhāgavata*. Even in that case, if one lacks the qualification [for the former], then let there be curiosity and earnest application toward the worship (*samarcā*) performed upon the *arcā*, the image; and let there be such through faith (*śraddhā*) and conviction regarding the Lord, the Guru, and the scriptures, which are of the highest degree. Likewise, one who serves you is the *adhama-bhakta* (lowest devotee).

He too, even if he is inferior, quickly perceives—that is, attains—[the goal] in this very life. The sense is that since even an inferior person will gradually become a supreme devotee, even the state of being inferior is to be sought. || 8 ||
Regarding the statement "pierced by māyā," in response to the desire to know the true nature of māyā, he says:

"Having veiled Your essential nature, she scatters [the world] through the forms of earth, water, air, and so forth; casting living beings—whose movements are rendered helpless by the multitude of their accumulated karmas—into the snare of suffering."

"O Mother, O Lord of the World! May I not be overcome by Your Māyā! For its pacification, nothing is as effective as devotion at Your feet"—thus did the awakened Siddhayogin declare, O All-pervading Lord! (9)

"Having veiled" (*āvṛtya*): having veiled Your own nature—Your very form, which is Brahman—by means of the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). By the word "beginning with earth, water, air, etc. (*kṣiti-jala-marud-ādi*), the five elements in their gross and subtle forms, the four types of gross bodies, and the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) are included.

"Projecting" (*vikṣipantī*) by means of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*), [She] manifests individual souls (*jīva*s), the embodied ones, whose movements are rendered helpless by the mass of their manifold karmas—the multitude (*āvali*) of those various actions of many kinds, distinguished as desirable (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*niṣiddha*), along with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced thereby.
"Thus, training in the Bhāgavata duties with devotion arising therefrom,
one who is intent on Nārāyaṇa easily crosses over the insurmountable Māyā"— this is the statement of the enlightened.

The sense is: "by these two. Those whose course—meaning the attainment of various high and low bodies—is helpless and lacking self-mastery, are thus described. May Your Māyā—that which casts and causes one to fall into the ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra), a web of suffering—which is dependent on You, not overcome even me, Your servant; that is to say, may it not seize my intellect and cause me to lose the remembrance of You. O Lord of the World, Śrī Kṛṣṇa! The sense is: "Please ward it off."

He said that devotion to Your feet alone is the means (*upāya*) capable of pacifying that *māyā*—that is, for its abandonment—and that there is no other means. A *siddhayogī* is one who is perfected, liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), and a yogi; he is one among the nine types of yogis. Among yogis, he is designated as *prabuddha* (awakened) because he is devoid of the knower, the known, and the knowledge. Indeed, to King Videha, he spoke only of devotion as the means of crossing over *māyā*, saying: "Therefore, the wise man should resort with singular devotion to Him, the Lord, from whom this *māyā* proceeds. (9)
Now, by means of dispassion and discernment, through the combination of devotion and knowledge obtained by approaching a Guru, he describes the method for conquering *māyā*:

"Having thoroughly observed the sufferings among living beings, I have developed discernment; having received from the best of teachers the reality of Your nature, and possessing an abundance of devotion arising from the stories of Your qualities and deeds, I shall cross over this *māyā* and rejoice in Your state, which consists of supreme bliss."
O Lord of the City of Wind, may this preliminary rite destroy all diseases. (10)

Regarding the word "sufferings" (*duḥkhāni*): while embodied beings are always striving among living creatures to avoid suffering and attain happiness, one who has developed an extraordinary degree of discernment (*viveka*) upon observing that sufferings arise from those very efforts—just as sons, friends, wealth, and so forth, though considered here to be means for attaining happiness, produce only suffering because they are fashioned by karma; and realizing through the arising of discriminative knowledge that it is the same even in heaven—one who is preeminent among teachers, endowed with both theoretical and practical knowledge (*jñāna-vijñāna*), and skilled in instructing others [speaks thus].

Therefore, having obtained—that is, attained—the *tattva*, the perfect knowledge, of your form, which is the very nature of the Lord; and [having attained] the discourse (*kathā*) concerning the qualities (*guṇa*)—such as the Lord’s affection for His devotees—and His deeds (*carita*); by the word "discourse" (*ārda*), chanting (*kīrtana*) and so forth are included; he is one in whom there is an abundance (*bhūmā*), a profusion, and an unfailing state of devotion (*bhakti*) arising from such discourse on qualities and deeds. The use of the word "this" (*enām*) refers to the experience of passion and other effects of *māyā*;
this, however, is the statement of the Siddha-yogin named Kavi.

Because of its being a state of honor (*mānatvāt*). Having crossed over and transcended, one "falls" (*padyate*) into Your station (*pada*); thus, *pada* means Brahman—Your own nature, that is to say, Brahman. Alternatively, the sense is: "I shall rejoice in Your lotus-feet, which consist of supreme bliss and generate unsurpassed joy; I shall become gracious, and together with the devotees, I shall serve through the practice of the duties of the Bhāgavatas."

This victory over Māyā is the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary rite) for that joy (*moda*), which must be performed first as its cause. As Bopadeva said: "Victory over Māyā is the lower devotion (*aparā bhakti*), arising from the combination of knowledge and action. Alternatively, this destruction of my disease—which is being repeatedly prayed for by me—is the *pūrvaraṅga* for that purpose of crossing over Māyā and so forth, which I am about to perform; it is something that must necessarily be accomplished first, just like the *nāndī* and other rites at the commencement of a dramatic performance.
And with the intention that "he [the Lord] is dependent solely upon your compassion, therefore I pray to you alone," he prays: "O Lord of the City of Wind! (10).
Thus ends the ninety-first decade, which describes how the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is caused by devotion alone, as well as the description of the nature and effects of devotion.

Now, an objection is raised: "It was stated that all actions should be performed by dedicating them to the Lord without any pursuit of results, in order to ensure they become the dharma of the Lord. That is untenable, because sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* are prescribed solely for the sake of heaven and the like, and only one who desires a fruit has the qualification (*adhikāra*) for them. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the intention that the purport of the Veda is difficult to discern due to its use of indirect speech (*parokṣavāda*).

O Lord! Having understood that all ritual actions described in the Vedas are intended to be performed without regard for their fruits, I indeed follow them only after offering them unto You, thereby attaining freedom from action (naiṣkarmya).

Let there be no engagement of mind, deed, or speech in anything forbidden by the Vedas; yet, if such an engagement occurs despite being difficult to avoid, I surely offer even that into the light of consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "by the Vedas": by the Vedas—that is, by the injunctive statements—all rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others are described as being without a focus on results; they are not enjoined as means for attaining results, but are rather enjoined for the sake of *naiṣkarmya* (the state of actionlessness). The mention of results, however, is for the purpose of encouragement (*rocanārthā*). Just as a mother, while giving medicine to a child, entices him with jaggery, sugar, and the like, making him drink it and then gives him that jaggery and sugar.

The purpose of drinking that medicine is not merely its acquisition, but rather the cessation of the disease; likewise, one should understand that the Veda also prescribes action solely for the sake of liberation from action, even while enticing with intermediate results. By the word "only" (eva), the intention for results is excluded, even though those [actions] are heard in scripture as being directed toward such results.

Now, one might object: "If freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*) is the fruit of actions, then why not abandon action at the very outset? Anticipating this doubt, the author says "samanucaran" with the intention that [otherwise] one falls through unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is characterized by improper action (*vikarma*). The meaning is: "so that I may attain *naiṣkarmya*—that is, knowledge accomplished through the cessation of action. The mention of "the Vedas" is also an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Smṛtis and other such authorities.

May there be no engagement of mind, action, or speech in prohibited acts such as eating forbidden food, nor even in any slight misdeeds whatsoever. If, however, that prohibited act which is difficult to avoid and impossible to renounce has been obtained—that is, performed—then I offer even that into Brahman, which is eternally manifest; the meaning is: "I surrender it," preceded by the sacred mantra. || 1 ||
Having explained the Vedic path of action (*karmayoga*), he now describes the Tantric one:

"As for that other path of action consisting of your worship, there, O Lord of the Eightfold Form, having meditated upon Your heart-pleasing form— which is of a single essence— whether on stone, in the heart, in clay, or anywhere else,"

O Lord of the Compassionate Heart! By constantly performing excellent worship with flowers, incense, and offerings prepared according to my ability and filled with devotion, may I receive Your gracious favor. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "But he who": another is a Vaidika, while another is a Tantrika; your worshipful one consists of your adoration—taking the form of your worship—and quickly generates your grace. [He worships] the desired form, such as Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, and so forth, which is heart-pleasing, distinguished by an exceedingly captivating appearance, and consisting solely of *sattva* (pure goodness). This may be in stone (*dṛṣad*), meaning made of rock; in clay (*mṛd*), meaning modeled; in the heart, meaning mental; or in some image made of bell-metal, silver, gold, and so on. As it has been said: "An image is traditionally held to be of eight kinds: made of stone, wood, metal, clay, paint, sand, mind, or gem."

Thus, having meditated upon Your form and having prepared [offerings] fashioned according to one's capacity—as prescribed by such scriptural injunctions as "leaves, flowers, fruits," and so forth—one should constantly and regularly, at the three times of day, perform the most excellent worship (*saparyā*) unto the Lord with flowers and other offerings purified by devotion. This is because it has been stated: "The wife is the abode of the husband; she is his worship. In this manner, one performs the worship characterized by the dissolution of one’s own body—consisting of causes and effects—into *prakṛti*, which is the Supreme Lord. || 2 ||
Now, in order to strengthen devotion, he describes the undesirable destiny of non-devotees in two verses beginning with "strīśūdrāḥ":

"Let women and Śūdras remain as they are, for they are worthy of your compassion, being deprived of hearing your stories and the like; but alas, I mourn for those born of the twice-born lineage who have come near your feet yet are unpeaceful, consuming the very essence of their own kin. Sacrificing for the sake of a livelihood, they do not listen to you even though you are described at great length; arrogant because of their learning and noble birth, what will they not do? Do not make me such a person. (3)

Regarding the phrase "women and Śūdras": by the word "etcetera" (ādi), names and so forth are included. This is also an elliptical expression for hearing, chanting, and other such acts. The meaning is that they are devoid of hearing Your stories, chanting Your name, remembering You, and so on. And this is due to ignorance, not because of a lack of qualification; for there is the scriptural statement: "If there is devotion, even among Śūdras and women. Therefore, they are worthy of compassion; they should be made happy through awakening by the virtuous out of mercy. The sense is that they remain in that state [of ignorance] for the time being.

Alas, I grieve for those born into the families of the twice-born—the three castes—who, having approached Your feet and attained the qualification for worshipping them through the sacraments beginning with the *upanayana* and through study culminating in the comprehension of meaning, remain unpeaceful and devoted to sense-objects; the sense is that I am distressed because these people cannot be awakened due to their being puffed up by a mere fragment of knowledge (*jñānalava*).

Sacrificing for the sake of livelihood—that is, for the sake of filling their bellies—and performing the slaughter of animals, they do not listen to You, the Lord, even though You have been described extensively in the Vedas and other scriptures as being distinguished by the categories of *saguṇa* (with attributes) and *nirguṇa* (without attributes); or even if they hear, they fail to obtain the fruit of hearing due to a lack of faith. He states the reason for this here: "Arrogant because of learning and noble birth. As it is said, "The pride of learning, the pride of wealth, and thirdly, the pride of noble birth"—those possessed of these three types of pride, what indeed do they not do? What is there that they will not perform?
The meaning is that they indeed perform even malevolent magic, the slandering of the virtuous, and so forth. Do not make me such a self-destroyer. || 3 ||
He elaborates upon this very censure:
"O Kṛṣṇa! This wicked man calls out 'Rāma' in order to seize his own evil conduct; by the words of this shameless one, my many younger brothers have been held captive."
"My brother, it is said, always worships Viṣṇu with a barren disposition"; thus do the wise censure you and laugh aloud at you for placing your love in such a person—do not make me like that!

"He is a sinner! [The thief says: "This man is a sinner, a thief of another's property. How is this known, O Kṛṣṇa? Because he calls out, 'Rāma! And that is so that he may conceal his own committed misconduct, such as the theft and so forth, by informing us that this good man does not do such things."

"This shameless man has nothing other than devotion to Hari as his essence"—speaking such things in my presence, having overcome all sense of shame, he has caused many matters that ought to have been told by me and many tasks to be examined by my kinsmen to be obstructed. If it is asked, "Why indeed is my brother not appointed to those duties?", he replies: "My brother is of barren character. He whose character (*śīla*) is barren (*vandhya*), meaning fruitless; the sense is that there is no benefit for me from him.

"He indeed always worships Viṣṇu; he performs offerings of flower-petals, prostrations, and the chanting of His names—that is surely his worship of Viṣṇu. What does that matter to him or to me? Thus, being restless, they revile the wise devotees—those by whom devotion characterized by love has been firmly established and fixed upon You, the Lord. They laugh loudly at them and mock their prayers for service to You and other such virtues along with others.
Since there is no possibility of these people ever attaining liberation from the cycle of worldly existence, do not make me like them. (4)
He describes the manner of service appropriate to each age:

In the Kṛta age, they please You, who possess the form of the best of sages and have a white luster, through austerities; in the Tretā age, they worship You in the form of sacrifice, marked by the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and having a reddish hue;
in the Dvāpara age, those of dark complexion serve You, who destroy the poison of enemies, according to the paths of Tantra.
In this age of Kali, human beings worship you here through the practice of congregational chanting (saṅkīrtana). || 5 ||

"Having a white radiance" means having a white complexion during the Kṛta age (the Kṛtayuga). "Possessing the body of an excellent sage" (*munivaravapuṣam*): here, by the word "sage" (*muni*), a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) is intended; the meaning is that he bears matted hair, bark garments, a black antelope skin, a sacred thread, a rosary, a staff, a water-pot, and so forth. "They please you"—that is, they propitiate you, who have four arms—by means of austerities, which are paths of meditation. The word "human beings" (*mānuṣāḥ*) is to be supplied everywhere [in each clause].

In the Tretā age, during the Tretā Yuga, they worship—meaning they perform Vedic rites—as characterized by the marks of the *sruc*, *sruva*, and other implements held at the tips of their hands. In the Dvāpara age, they serve and worship by means of the *tantra* paths, that is, the methods of ritual worship. [The phrase] "shining conch and mace" refers to the two [objects] shining...

"Whose [weapon] is the discus"—this is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for his other weapons as well. "Śyāmalāṅga" means having a dark-blue body, with the luster of an *atasī* flower; here, in this Kali age, "blue" refers to the black color (*kṛṣṇavarṇa*). By those for whom "saṅkīrtana"—the utterance of the Name—is "ādya," meaning primary or foremost, they worship and serve Him. || 5 ||
Regarding that, he describes the ease of service during the Kali age with five verses:

"O Enemy of Mura! Victorious is this very time of Kali, O Giver of All! For in this age, by means of paths such as congregational chanting (*saṅkīrtana*), which require no external materials, people attain Your grace before long.
Indeed, even those born in the Tretā, Kṛta, and other ages desire to be born in the Kali age."
O Lord, do not deceive us—who by fate were born right there—with the poisonous juices of sense-objects. 6.

"So 'yam iti" (Thus, this...). That aforementioned "this," the present Kali age—this Kāleya time—is victorious; it excels over the other ages. In this Kali age, even those who are devoid of effort attain Your grace quickly, without delay, through means such as *saṅkīrtana* (chanting) and the like. Now, one might object: "Are there not also those born in the Kṛta and other ages who speak thus? To which he replies: "jātāḥ" (born). The word *kila*, accompanied by the particle *hi*, indicates that this matter is well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources.

By fate, through the ripening of past merit, you have caused us—who were born in this very age of Kali—to be deceived by the poisonous juices of sense objects; for sense objects themselves are like poisonous juices, since by their consumption one falls into delusion. Do not deceive us with them. 6.
In the Kali age, let there be devotees first in the land of Draviḍa; then, let them be numerous there along the Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī, and indeed the holy Kṛtamālā flowing toward the west.

O Lord! Alas, even though my birth is within this [land], do not, O All-pervading One, bind me with the snares of hope for some flickering taste [of worldly pleasure] and cause me to wander! O Blessed One, fulfill my service unto You.

Regarding the word *bhaktāḥ*: first of all, in the Kali age, there will be many devotees in great numbers here and there; then, even in that Kali age, they will be in great numbers in the land of the Dramilas (Tamil country). And within that Dramila region, along the banks of rivers such as the Pūrṇā and Kāverī, they will be even more numerous than that. The sense is that those who drink the water of the Kāverī and other such rivers become exceedingly devoted. Furthermore, do not delude me—who am included within this [group], residing within the Dramila region, and whose heart has slightly turned toward You, having begun a modicum of devotion—with any error. 7.

Having seen that Kālika, who was devoid of compassion, King Parīkṣit—though he had drawn his sword to slay him—did not strike him, for as a knower of essence, he recognized a fraction of virtue within him.

Service to you is quickly accomplished here; it is not so with others. Alas! Since this timid man will surely be carried off by disease and other ailments even before then, instruct him in this matter.

"Having seen"—this means that in former times, King Parīkṣit, having seen that Kali who was a violator of dharma in the form of a bull, striking at dharma with his staff, drew his bow to kill him; yet, because of the presence of even a fraction of virtue (*guṇāṃśāt*), he did not strike him down. To the question, "Even if there were a fraction of virtue, why did he not kill the one who violates dharma?", he replies: "Knowing the essence" (*sāravedī*). This means he knew that even in its smallness, virtue constitutes the essential core. He explains this very point by saying: "Out of devotion to him" (*tad-bhakti-vātsalyāt*).

Worship, chanting of names, and so forth, would quickly succeed even in this very life and, through devotion, produce liberation; however, in this Kali age, evil and wicked karma do not perish so swiftly. Furthermore, this Kali is afraid of those devoted to You and Your devotees—the sense being that Kali prevails only over those who are averse to the Lord. Moreover, that which seizes one with disease and other afflictions even before the commencement of Your service, turning one away from Your worship—that very thing has befallen me, alas!
Therefore, punish this Kali for his theft; the intention is that you should act in such a way that Kali flees far away from one who is devoted to your service. ||8||
The Gaṅgā, the Gītā, the Gāyatrī, Tulasī, the Gopikā-candana,
the worship of the Sālagrāma, O Supreme Person, and likewise the Ekādaśī and the syllables of Your name—
these eight, even in the Kali age, become effortless through the increase of Your grace.
The sages have declared that these [paths] bestow liberation swiftly; you should apply yourself to them.

Regarding the word "Gaṅgā": he states that these [places] bestow liberation by means of her, through the increase of grace from you, thereby citing the authority of the Smṛti: "The sages declared... (verse 9).
Now, one might ask: "Since one who is born is bound by three debts, how can there be liberation if they are not discharged? To this, he says:
O Infinite One! He who has sought refuge in You with his whole being, having abandoned all duties, is neither a debtor nor a servant to the gods, the sages, or even the ancestors.

O Lord of the City of Wind! Just as the rising wind dispels every cloud, you who abide in the heart dispel even all the evil deeds that have arisen; therefore, grant me devotion to ward off the torments of worldly existence. 10.

Regarding the phrase "of the divine sages" (*devarṣīṇām*): this refers to the gods, the sages, and even the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Just as one who does not offer oblations becomes a debtor, an indigent person, and thus remains a servant (*kiṅkara*) to them, being required to perform sacrifices, Vedic study, procreation of sons, and so forth, in order to discharge that debt; so it is stated in the *Smṛti*: "One should compel a person of low caste who is destitute to perform labor for the sake of the debt. However, he who is a devotee (*bhakta*) is no longer a debtor or a servant. He states the reason for this: "He who is that... (*yo'sau*).

That person who has approached you for refuge with his whole self and entire being, having abandoned all duties—that is, all prescribed actions—is indeed free from them. Now, one might object: "In that case, since prohibited actions cannot be avoided by one's whole self, must not penance and other such rites be performed? To this he says: "Of him" (tasya). For one who has gone to you for refuge, the fruit of *vikarman*—that is, prohibited action—is not possible. Even if it should occur through negligence or the like, the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that even that [fruit] does not exist for him.

"Akhilam" means entirely and without remainder; "apanudasva" means you destroy. Now, one might object that the worship of the Blessed One is not for the sake of the destruction of sins; therefore, he says: "You who abide in the mind. For the power of a reality does not depend upon a desire for its effect to arise; rather, just as a medicine produces health and so forth without distinction for those seeking its fruit and those not seeking it, such is the sense here.

Therefore, since You, abiding in the mind, dispel sin, ward off (*rundhi*) the afflictions (*tāpān*) arising from sin—that is, the misfortunes produced by sinful deeds. Grant (*praṇīyāḥ*) me unfailing devotion (*bhaktim*); may You perform this for me. || 10 ||
Thus ends the ninety-second decade, which is a description of the nature of devotion mixed with action (*karma-miśra-bhakti*).

Having thus defined devotion mixed with action in twenty verses, the author, intending next to define devotion mixed with knowledge (*jñāna-miśra*), first describes the attainment of the qualification for it:
"Indeed, by Your compassion, I shall abandon affection for my kin, having surrendered my soul to You."

Having abandoned everything and beheld the entire world as a mere play of illusion, how could there be either injunction or prohibition for one whose mind is fixed upon You— whose intellect is free from partiality and who truly understands that the perception of diversity arises from delusion, wherein virtue and vice are but appearances? || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "affection for kinsmen" (*bandhusneham*): since affection for kinsmen—such as sons, friends, wives, and so forth—is produced by Your *māyā*, may I abandon it through Your grace. The word "hi" (indeed) indicates that there is no other means for its abandonment. Then, having fixed my soul in You alone through Your grace, with a concentrated mind, and having perceived and understood the world as a play of *māyā* fashioned by Your *māyā*, may I conduct myself having abandoned everything else—including all actions distinguished by injunctions and prohibitions—other than Your worship. This illuminates the lack of dependence on home and other worldly concerns.

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to neglect an enjoined action? Furthermore, if sin arises, a penance must certainly be performed. Anticipating this doubt, he states "due to diversity" (*nānātvāt*) to show that there is no fault for the knower in failing to perform such actions, since they fall within the domain of the ignorant. The delusion of identifying with the body as "I am a man" is the misconception of the self; the "diversity" born thereof consists of the distinctions of caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth.

Only upon the acceptance of that [world] as real do virtues and faults arise; for instance, regular and occasional ritual acts (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) are a virtue because they purify the *sattva*, while violence and the like are a fault; likewise, penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* are a virtue because they are means for the destruction of sin—it is only when there is such an understanding of virtue and fault that there can be an injunction (*vidhi*) or a prohibition (*niṣedha*).

For me, whose mind is fixed upon You and whose intellect has reached the certainty that "all this is indeed Brahman," and who for that very reason has abandoned all notions of inequality and discarded the delusion of manifoldness—how could those two, injunction and prohibition, apply? Therefore, the meaning is: since I have no authority regarding injunctions and prohibitions, I shall move about having renounced everything. In this way, it is also shown that one who has transcended injunctions and prohibitions is qualified for devotion mixed with knowledge (*jñāna-miśrā bhakti*). As it is said in the *Muktāphala*: "That which is mixed with knowledge is for mendicants (*bhikṣus*). (1)
To state that all this must be accomplished by means of a human body alone, he praises the state of being human (*puruṣatva*) as superior to the bodies of animals and other beings:

"There are infinite living beings whose minds are constantly fixed on the mere removal of hunger and thirst; among them, the human is the best here because of his possession of discernment (*vijñāna*), yet even his birth is difficult to obtain.

Even there, one may become a friend or even an enemy to oneself: he who has entrusted his mind to You remembers the means for the cessation of sleep and exhaustion—he indeed is a friend; any other than him is an enemy to his own self. (2)

Regarding "hunger and thirst": there are endless, numerous creatures such as beasts whose intellects are constantly fixed—meaning their minds are determined—only upon the cessation of hunger and thirst (aśanāyā-pipāsā), that is, merely on the chewing of grass and the drinking of water. Compared to them, because of his possession of discernment (*vijñāna*), the human being (*puruṣa*) on this earth is superior (*vara*) by virtue of his capacity for self-realization; indeed, human birth is the most excellent. Furthermore, even among humans, the self alone is one's own friend, providing benefit, and the self alone is one's enemy, causing harm.

He states the distinction: he whose mind is fixed upon You, and for that very reason remembers—meaning knows—the means (sādhana) for the cessation of suffering, which is liberation; if such a person exists, he alone would be the friend and kinsman of his own self. Other than him, no one else is such; he is an enemy of the self and a destroyer of the self. ||2||

One might object that it is inconsistent to say "the Self alone is the teacher of the Self," for this would imply that one cannot learn from others. Anticipating this, [the author] offers a rebuttal: since the intended meaning here is that whoever is the cause of destroying another's ignorance is their teacher, then because all things—both moving and stationary—are causes of such destruction, they must be accepted as teachers; how much more so, then, is the Self? Thus, while seeking from the Self those qualities such as forbearance which are to be learned from teachers like the Earth, he prays:

"O Infinite One! When Your compassion is active, who indeed is not a teacher even in worldly conduct? For the earth, though trodden upon by all, does not waver; therefore, may I learn true forbearance from her."

O Lord! May I attain non-attachment even while experiencing various sense objects, may my self possess pervasiveness like the wind, and may stainlessness shine forth within me by the grace of the Guru of the Sky (the Great Space). || 3 ||

"Through Your compassion"—for who indeed is not a teacher? The sense is that it is not only the Self alone, but even the categories of existence such as earth and the rest are indeed teachers. What is there to be learned from them? To this He says: "In the conduct of the world. "The worlds" refers to the moving and unmoving beings; their "conduct" consists of their inherent nature, such as forbearance, detachment, and non-attachment. The meaning is that in this regard, these very things are the teachers. O All-pervading One, O Viṣṇu! For the earth does not waver, even though it is trodden upon by all manner of wicked people.

From the earth, I would learn—understand as my duty—to possess true forbearance (*sat-kṣamā*), which consists in not deviating from one's own path; and even when there is acquaintance with or contact with various objects, whether excellent or flawed, I would acquire non-attachment (*aprasakti*) or freedom from clinging (*asaṅgatva*) from the wind. From the sky, I would acquire for myself all-pervasiveness (*vyāptatva*)—the state of pervading the interior and exterior of all bodies—despite appearing limited by the body, by virtue of its being the teacher of the sky.

For the sky, although perceived as delimited by objects such as jars, pervades both the exterior and the interior. Furthermore, "stainlessness" (*nirlepatā*) means being free from contact with that [body] even while residing within the body; its state is stainlessness. And may that shine forth for me solely through the grace of the Guru of the Sky. Just as the sky is not touched by clouds and the like, so too [may I remain untouched]. (3)
He states what is to be learned from water, fire, and the moon:
"May I be clear and purifying; may I be sweet like water; like fire, may I not grasp at faults even when consuming all things; and like the moon, may I pervade all beings."
By your grace, may I know that increase and decrease belong to the body alone—like the phases of the moon—and not to the Self;
and likewise, through your favor, may I realize the oneness of the Self within all bodies, just as the sun remains one even when reflected in various waters. || 4 ||

"Transparent": may I be as transparent, stainless, and purifying as water, cleansing sin by mere sight; and may I be sweet and sweet-spoken. "Eating all food": even though consuming everything, may I not incur fault like fire; may I not take on sin. He states another quality to be adopted from fire: "In trees," etc.

Just as that fire within logs and trees is perceived in forms identical to the wood—appearing short, long, thick, or thin according to the shape of the wood—so too may I perceive, may I understand, myself, the Self, as being identical in form to each respective [body] among all beings, such as gods, humans, and animals, due to the influence of those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Regarding what is to be learned from the moon, it should be noted that "ādadīya" is the correct form in place of "ādayām."

Regarding "nourishment" (*puṣṭi*): beginning from the first day of the waxing fortnight, fifteen successive portions of the solar disc situated at a distance are seen reflected in the water-like lunar disc. These reflections are called the digits (*kalā*) of the moon.

Just as one should know the nourishment and decay of those [waters] alone, and not of the moon, so too one should know that the six modifications of existence—birth, existence, transformation, growth, decline, and destruction—belong to the body alone, and not to the Self. This is the meaning. He states that this is to be understood through the analogy of the sun: "In water, etc.

Just as the single sun, though distributed among many vessels of water and so forth, appears as many, so too, although the Self appears divided within all bodies due to the differences in its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), one should know its oneness as well. The phrase "by your grace" is to be applied everywhere.
Out of affection, may I not become like the dead pigeon who, out of love for his offspring, was devoured by hunters;
may I endure even hunger like a lion when he has found his prey, and remain as unfathomable as the ocean.
May I not fall like a moth into a flame or like a bee into a woman and the like, but rather partake of the essence.
May I become great, O Lord, but may I not perish through the power of amassing wealth like that [Vaiśravaṇa]. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "out of affection" (*snehāt*): he explains that one should learn from the pigeon that affection is a cause of suffering, saying "out of affection. Acting like that pigeon who died out of love for his sons when they were captured and struck down by a hunter (*vyādha*), [the sage] says "acting like him. A certain forest-dweller, having spread a net near the nest, waited in ambush for the birds as they moved about. There, the young pigeons, unaware at first, became entangled in the net. Seeing them, the female pigeon fell into a state of grief.

And the pigeon, his intellect blinded by the grief and affection born from witnessing the lamentations and frantic gestures of his son and wife, himself began to wail and met his end. The sense is: "May I not become like him. He states what should be learned from the python (ajagara): "prāptam" and so forth. Like the *śayu*—that is, the python—one should endure hunger (*kṣudhaṃ saheya*), meaning one should be capable of enduring it by consuming only what is obtained, performing merely the maintenance of the body with whatever is found; [the form *saheya* is derived from the root *sah* with the potential suffix *liṅ*, and *aṅ* due to its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group].

According to the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*, "there is *etva* (the substitution of *e*) for the *liṭ* [affix] after the roots *naś* and *man*"—thus there is *etva*. However, according to the *Vṛtti*, the mention of the Vedic language (*chandograhaṇa*) is connected only with the roots *ami* and *pac* through a split in the sentence, in accordance with the attested forms such as "aneśat menakām. This is [the view] following that *Vṛtti*.

[May I] become [thus]. By this, it is also shown that since the fruit of commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*) must necessarily be experienced, even the effort aimed at attaining pleasure or avoiding pain results only in the fruit of wasting time in vain. It is "bottomless" (*agādha*), meaning deep; being such, it is impossible to fathom. He says, "Do not fall," implying that one who is deluded by the charms of form perishes—this is something to be learned from the moth.

Regarding a woman—that is, a young lady—through her gestures (*hāva*), expressions (*bhāva*), and so forth; by the word "and so forth," it includes such exceedingly captivating objects as bracelets, waist-bands, necklaces, and fine silken garments, which in reality are causes of suffering. May I not fall [into them] with the thought that they are objects of enjoyment, just as a moth, enticed by their color, falls into a fire. Furthermore, just as a bee resorts to the nectar—the essence—within flowers, so too may I resort only to the essential meaning found in all scriptures, which consists of the remembrance of Śrī Nārāyaṇa.

He states another point for instruction with the words "But" (*kintu*). However, there is a distinction. "Like that" means like a bee. Just as a bee, dwelling upon a single lotus out of greed for its particular fragrance, becomes trapped when it closes at sunset, so too I—by being attached to one place through my obsession with acquiring wealth and the like—might not go to my destruction; such is the meaning. || 5 ||

May I not be bound by a young woman, like an elephant by a female in heat; may I not fail to acquire a flood of wealth; for I would be a thief of what belongs to others, like a honey-stealer; and like a deer, may I not be deluded by vulgar songs.
May I not be excessively attached to food, like a fish at a hook; and like Piṅgalā, may I be free from worldly hope.
O Lord! Like a kurara bird with meat in its beak, I would sleep soundly, protected by my dependents, so that I might not be slain by others.

"May I not be bound"—thus one should learn from the elephant that contact with the bodies of women is a cause of bondage. For an elephant is shown a female elephant (kariṇī) and, having been lured into a pit covered over with earth, is captured; or else, he is bound by a man hidden within the belly of a female elephant whose skin has been sewn shut. "May I not acquire"—thus one should learn from the honey-thief that one should not accumulate wealth devoid of both renunciation and enjoyment. For another thief or the like will seize that mass of wealth.

For just as a honey-thief takes away the honey accumulated by bees within tree hollows and the like, so too attachment to sounds such as singing is a cause of destruction; thus one should learn from the deer. He says "like a deer": for a deer, being deluded by the song of a hunter, is captured by him; it is just like that. By the phrase "by vulgar songs," the intention is that attachment should be directed toward the songs of the Blessed One alone. Attachment to flavors is a cause of destruction; thus one should learn from the fish. He says "not too... [referring to the verse beginning with *nātyaśitaḥ*].

A fish (*jhaṣa*) is a fish caught on a hook—a metal barb covered with bait. "Hope is the cause of suffering; freedom from hope is the cause of happiness"—this is what one should learn from Piṅgalā. Thus he says: "Like Piṅgalā. Piṅgalā was by name a wanton woman who, out of desire for wealth, [fell into misery].

Disregarding the men who had first arrived and given her but little, her mind was tormented by the evil hope that perhaps another would come to her and give much; thus remaining awake even at midnight, she again severed the bonds of her wicked hopes for wealth and other things with the sword of world-weariness (*nirveda*) and slept peacefully. Having thus become hopeless, the phrase "I shall sleep" is intended to mean "may I obtain happiness."

The bird named *kurara* states that the acceptance of anything as "mine" (*mamatva*) is a cause of suffering: "By being supported... and so forth. Other birds struck a *kurara* as it was swooping down with its prey; likewise, by being connected to those who must be supported—that is, by the attachment of "mine" toward things to be protected—I should not be struck by others who are powerful. (6)

O Lord, having abandoned pride, may I live happily like a very young child; remaining alone like a single bracelet left from a pair of a maiden's bangles, may I move about without the noise of mutual conversation.
With my mind fixed on You, may I not perceive another, just as an arrow-maker does not notice the sound of a mountain approaching.
I dwell in houses built by others, like a snake in the burrows of a mouse.

Regarding the phrase "I shall conduct myself": he says "I shall conduct myself" to teach even a child that the renunciation of honor and dishonor is the cause of happiness. He says "without a companion" to instruct a young girl that if she moves about with many people, negligence may arise regarding the remembrance and glorification of Śrī Hari due to social gatherings, quarrels, and the like.

A certain maiden, while personally threshing rice to feed the men who had come for her hand in marriage, reduced herself to having only a single conch-bracelet remaining on her forearm out of loathing for the sound of the others. In that same manner, [the mind] should be freed from mutual noise and abandoned useless chatter with one another. He says, "In your own mind," implying: "I shall learn the practice of concentration upon the Lord from the arrow-maker."

Just as an arrow-maker, through his focused attention on straightening the arrow, did not perceive the sound of kettledrums and other noises when approaching the king, so too, with my mind fixed upon You, I do not perceive anything else. The sense is that the mind should neither be distracted by the latent impressions of sense-objects, nor should it dissolve entirely as in deep sleep. Thinking, "I shall learn from the serpent that the building of a house leads to misfortune," he says: "In houses... Just as a snake dwells in the holes and burrows of a mouse's dwelling, even so shall I dwell. 7.
"I understand from the spider that the world you have created is dissolved within you alone;

I am firmly instructed by the weaver that meditation upon you brings about your own true nature. Furthermore, the excellent teacher who possesses discernment and detachment becomes one whose body consists of excrement and ashes."
But when it is reflected upon by me, it brings only the affliction of many diseases, especially so. ||8||

Regarding the phrase "in you": he says "in you" to show that the Lord's status as the cause of the universe is to be learned from the spider (*ūrṇanābha*). Created by you—that is, brought forth by you acting as both the efficient and material cause—you dissolve [it] back into yourself; you withdraw it. The spider (*ūrṇanābha*) is a silkworm; for it itself withdraws the web of threads created by its own self as both efficient and material cause back into itself. Since meditation on the Blessed One brings about conformity with His nature, he says "your thought" to indicate that this is to be learned from the weaver (*peśakāra*).

"Your own nature" means identity with you. "Firmly" means with certainty. A *peśas* is a small hut; one who makes such a hut is a *peśakāra*, a specific type of bee. A worm that has entered and been confined within that small hut by it, meditating upon that very [bee] out of fear, attains identity with it. He speaks of what is to be learned from one's own body, saying "excrement," etc.: "The body becomes my excellent teacher. Why? Because when properly contemplated, it produces and brings about detachment and discrimination (*viveka*).

The sense is that when its rarity and its helpfulness are contemplated, it becomes the cause for the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self; and when its impermanence, vulnerability, and the resulting nature of suffering are contemplated, it becomes the cause for dispassion (*virakti*). He states its role as the cause for dispassion and discrimination: "Itself [becoming] feces or ashes. If it is devoured by dogs and the like, it becomes the essence of feces; if it is consumed by fire, it becomes the essence of ashes. Therefore, this body belongs to another and is impermanent.

The meaning is that the Self, however, is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is distinct from that [body]. Furthermore, this body of mine is afflicted by many diseases; being rendered helpless by various pains, it especially fosters discrimination and detachment—thus it connects with what precedes. || 8 ||

Now, one might wonder: "How could delusion not arise toward the body, which is beneficial as a cause for discrimination? Anticipating this doubt, [the author], revealing the fault in delusion regarding the body, prays to the Lord: "Alas!

Alas! O Lord of the City of Wind (Kāśī), abandon my delusion regarding the body! For the sake of love for it, people become helpless regarding their home, wealth, wife, and so forth, and thus forget Your feet.

These very eyes, ears, skin, tongue, and other senses—whether they belong to a dog or a fire—now and hereafter drag the helpless person away from this world; yet none of them lead anyone to Your lotus feet. (9)

"Hī hī!"—this "Hī hī" expresses the wonder: "Even though my body has become such as this, I still possess great delusion. Abandon that delusion regarding the body—the illusion that it is a means for attaining pleasure within the realm of the body. He states the defect therein: "On account of which [body] love..."—meaning, because of the cause of affection for that body, people are rendered helpless regarding their homes and other possessions, with their minds solely intent on its acquisition and preservation (*yoga-kṣema*). Furthermore, this very body, at the end among all living beings, serves only for the burning by fire or for being devoured by dogs.

And even now, while he still lives, the sun and other deities—who are the presiding lords of the eyes, ears, skin, tongue, and so forth—are understood here by the words "eyes, ears, skin, tongue, etc.," because the activity of the eyes and other organs is dependent upon them. By the word "etc.," the voice, hands, and so on are included. These [deities] draw him hither and thither toward their respective objects, such as forms and the like; yet none among them draws him toward the lotus of your feet, the lotus-feet of the Blessed One. (9)

If it is argued that since the fruit of *prārabdha* karma must necessarily be experienced, and since such experience depends on attachment to the body and home, its renunciation is impossible—then [the author] entreats him to make his birth fruitful by another means:

"O Lotus-eyed One! If the delusion regarding the body is now difficult to ward off, then, having seen all diseases completely destroyed, establish a firmest devotion toward the lotus-feet of Your Honor."
Surely, at the end of many births, this Brahmin body that grants liberation has been attained;
alas, do not, do not cast me into the taste of base sensual objects! O Māruteśa, protect me! 10.

Regarding the phrase "durvāra" (difficult to ward off): if, moreover, the delusion regarding the body is difficult to ward off, then [the author] says—through the words beginning with "nūnam"—"Protect me by making fruitful this most rare human body through the complete eradication of all external diseases such as wind-disorders (*vāta*) and so forth, and internal diseases such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, in this very life, and by establishing in me a firm conviction that is never-failing. || 10 ||
Thus ends the ninety-third decad, the description of that which is to be learned from the twenty-five teachers.
In this way, he shows the manner in which the knowledge of reality arises for one who has developed discriminative wisdom through the twenty-five teachers:
"By means of the stainless duties free from desire and by the words of the preeminent teacher, that supreme nature of yours [is revealed]."
They declare that [the Self] is pure, entirely devoid of the body, senses, and so forth, and all-pervading;

whereas qualities such as plurality, grossness, and thinness are superimposed upon it through contact with the body composed of the gunas, just as the states of flaming, smallness, and extinction are attributed to fire when it is in different types of wood. ||1||

"Purified" means those who have become pure through the duties of their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) performed according to the law of desirelessness—that is, without longing for fruits—and are thus free from defects such as passion; in other words, they are endowed with the fourfold means beginning with tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*). By the speech—which consists of instruction—of the preeminent Guru, who is excellent due to his mastery of the Vedas and their meaning and is adept at obstructing ignorance, they cause that partless nature of Yours, the Lord, to be known; that is, they understand it.

Of what nature is it? It is distinct and separate from the body, senses, and so forth; therefore, it is pure (*śuddha*), free from the coloring (*uparāga*) of *māyā* and its effects. It is supreme (*para*), known as the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*), all-pervasive (*akhila*), omnipresent (*vyāpta*), the support of all, and the thread that runs through everything. Now, one might object: "But isn't its being all-pervasive contradicted by such perceptions as 'I am thin' or 'I am fat'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As for multiplicity, etc. Multiplicity and the like attributed to your Self are superimposed and imagined due to association with the body born of the *guṇas*; they are projected by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the body composed of *māyā*.

Therefore, the meaning is that multiplicity and other such qualities, being adventitious (*aupādhika*), are not attributes of the Self (*ātman*). To this, he provides a corresponding illustration: "of fire" (*vahneḥ*). Just as there are [qualities] such as largeness and minuteness in the fire residing within various pieces of wood—namely, largeness, minuteness, brilliance, arising, subsiding, and destruction—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes multiplicity and the rest.

The meaning is this: just as these properties of wood are perceived as being the properties of fire because they are not distinct from the firewood, so too, due to the absence of knowledge that discriminates the self from the body, qualities such as multiplicity, as well as old age and death, are perceived as if they were properties of the self, though they are not so in ultimate reality. || 1 ||
And to clarify that this very knowledge, once obtained from the teacher, is alone capable of dispelling ignorance and its effects, he describes the arising of wisdom through a metaphor:

"When the dense forest of the delusion of the body, worlds, and the series of karmas along with their latent impressions (vāsanās)— which constitute a vast wilderness— is being consumed by the fire of perfectly clear awakening, kindled by the friction between the lower fire-drill known as the teacher and the upper fire-drill in the form of the disciple who seeks him out..."
When the fire of knowledge has ceased due to the absence of anything to be burned, that state is indeed identical with You.

Regarding the phrase "called the teacher" (*ācāryākhyeti*): the lower fire-drill (*avarāraṇi*) is that which is designated as the teacher; the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) is the disciple who, by means of initiation (*upanayana*), has come into the presence of the teacher. The friction (*āvedha*) between these two is their contact by means of the churning-stick (*mathanadaṇḍa*) in the form of instruction. By the fire manifested—that is, revealed—by that friction, there arises a most clear awakening, which is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). By means of that fire, the latencies of the series of actions (*karmālīvāsanāḥ*)—the impressions (*saṃskārāḥ*) that produce similar future actions—and those produced by them [are consumed].

The delusion of the body and the world is ignorance regarding the manifold expansion of the body and so forth. When that forest-thicket in the form of [ignorance] is being consumed—that is, when the fuel is destroyed due to the absence of anything further to be burned—then knowledge, which is the realization of Brahman, perishes by its own nature as it is included within that [destruction], owing to its similarity with fire. When that flame, the fire, has ceased because there is no longer any distinction between cause and effect, the state consisting of you indeed remains as your very form;
the sense is that one becomes of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda). || 2 ||

Thus, by these two verses, it has been stated that for one who is entirely dispassionate, there is the eradication of the suffering of saṃsāra and the attainment of supreme bliss through the knowledge of reality. To further solidify this, he refutes other doctrines:
"Indeed, there is no means other than attaining You for the destruction of all afflictions;
neither agriculture, nor medicine, nor the six political expedients, nor the six types of ritual action, nor yoga can provide that which is both certain and final."
