Even those who are unwell due to various deficiencies, though they have attained the fruits of the paths of the Vedas, are considered to forget You; thus, becoming attached to worldly existence, they fall into infinite despair. || 3 ||

Thus it is said. Now, one might raise this objection: since the removal of all afflictions for embodied beings is possible through various applications of gems, mantras, herbs, and elixirs; through the six policies and the four means; through rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma which accomplish desired ends like heaven; and through activities such as teaching—why then resort to the path of renunciation, which is so exceedingly difficult? To address this doubt, he says: "Not absolute," and so forth.

Agadas are medicinal herbs prescribed in the Āyurveda as means for health; ṣāḍguṇya refers to the six measures of statecraft—peace, war, and so forth—as taught in the science of polity (daṇḍanīti), which are means for acquiring wealth; and the six duties are study, teaching, and so on. Those methods taught in the Vedas are not absolute, meaning they do not bring about the cessation of all suffering, because they are causes of pleasure mixed with pain; nor are they final, meaning they do not prevent the recurrence of suffering, because their fruits are impermanent, like agriculture.

But surely, there exist Vedic rites here which result in the removal of obstacles such as sons, friends, wealth, grain, and health, and which are also means for attaining heaven and other goals in the hereafter; to this he replies: "by unavoidable defects. The paths of the Nigamas—the Vedic ways—are *akalyāḥ*, meaning incapable of being performed due to unavoidable deficiencies (*durvaikalyaiḥ*) consisting of defects in the substance, the ritual action, the time, and the agent. The sense of the word "also" (*api*) is that they are not merely non-conclusive and non-absolute. Furthermore, even if they are somehow free from defects, their fruits [are likewise].

Having attained the fruits such as heaven, they become intoxicated; sporting with women in celestial chariots in the Nandana groves and other places, they become heedless. When their karma is exhausted and the fall—the downward plunge—occurs, they undergo endless despondencies and sufferings. || 3 ||

Now, in response to the doubt that those who have reached Satyaloka through rituals such as the meditations taught in the Vedas rejoice with Brahmā, free from all afflictions, [the Lord] says: "O Padmanābha! Where indeed is there another world besides Your own that is free from fear, since even in Satyaloka, at the end of two *parārdhas*, the Lotus-born Brahmā dwells in happiness only out of fear of You?"
But what need is there to speak of the hell-beings who possess the densest darkness acquired through unrighteousness?
O Giver of Boons! O Kinsman of the Wretched! O Ocean of the Flood of Compassion! Cut asunder my bonds for me! || 4 ||

"From Your world" means: from Vaikuṇṭha, Your world, there is no other world—such as Satyaloka and so forth—that is free from fear, meaning free from the fear of destruction, anywhere at all. The reason for this is as follows: even the Lotus-born Brahmā is afraid of You, the Lord whose nature is Time, in that Satyaloka which has a limit of two *parārdhas*. Therefore, there is no "pleasant abode"—that is, a dwelling characterized by happiness and free from the fear of destruction—for anyone there.

The term "Padmabhū" (Lotus-born) illustrates the birth and destruction of Brahmā. Such being the case—meaning, this being so—even for the marvelous Brahmā, there is an absence of the absolute cessation of suffering through knowledge and action; what then can be said regarding the removal of affliction for those transmigrating beings who have fallen into hell, whose sins are many and acquired through unrighteousness? Therefore, "cut off bondage"—the meaning is: sever the identification of "I" and "mine" with the body and so forth, and grant me liberation. || 4 ||

Now, one might object: "The individual soul (jīva) is not other than the Lord; how, then, can it have bondage and liberation? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it: "O All-pervading One! Since I am indeed identical with You in reality, there is in truth neither bondage nor liberation for me.
Rather, those two—bondage and liberation—are fashioned by You through the bodies of Māyā and Vidya, and are comparable to dreaming and waking."

As long as one is bound and has not attained liberation while living, there remains such a distinction: one person, dwelling in the tree of the body, enjoys the flavorful fruits of sense-objects, while the other, whose self is free from suffering, does not.

Regarding the phrase "because of reality": in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), for me—the individual soul (*jīva*) who consists of you and is non-different from the Lord—there is in fact neither bondage nor liberation. Nevertheless, those two, bondage and liberation, are fashioned by you, the Lord, through your two powers in the form of knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā*), namely, through your *māyā* and *avidyā* bodies. The intended meaning is that bondage arises from ignorance and liberation arises from knowledge.

And these two are comparable to sleep and waking: just as for a dreamer there is bondage by means of a body seen in a dream, and upon awakening there is liberation from it, so too for the ignorant there is bondage of the body and for the wise there is liberation. Thus, although bondage is illusory like a dream, because it is a cause of suffering, its severance through knowledge is to be sought; this is the sense. He states that very distinction between the bound and the liberated with the words "the bound," etc.

While the bound one remains in saṃsāra and the one liberated while living has attained liberation while alive, there exists for each of them the state described hereafter. One is bound; his very body is a tree, because it possesses qualities such as impermanence like a tree. Abiding in that [body], being non-different from it, he enjoys the fruit of the essence of objects—that is, the fruit of karma consisting of the experience of sense-objects. The other, the one liberated while living, does not enjoy the fruit of the essence of objects. Nevertheless, by the power of knowledge, he is a soul free from affliction, devoid of pain. (5)

Now, one might object: "In that case, let liberation while living (jīvanmukti) itself be sought. Anticipating this and considering the lack of qualification for it, he prays for devotion with the words: "What is the fruit of [seeking] liberation while living? For one of impure intellect, the name of that state is not even within reach; nor is there any purification of the mind easier than through devotion."

O Viṣṇu! May You fulfill for me that burden of devotion, offered with a firm resolve upon You, by which I may quickly become one whose self is You, possessing an awakening to the reality that accords with even a small portion of the words of my Guru.

Regarding the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*): what is the fruit of mere words? That attainment will not occur. For one of impure intellect—whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is defiled by passion and other afflictions—that state of liberation while living is, indeed, far off. Anticipating the objection that one must therefore seek a means for the purification of the internal organ, he says "not so" (*na ca*), meaning: there is no purifier of the mind, nor any means for its purification, other than devotion (*bhakti*). Compared to other methods such as bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha-snāna*) and the like, devotion is the lighter, swifter, and effortless means.

Therefore, may you cultivate an unfailing devotion—a burden of devotion—toward me. This refers to that burden of devotion in which the offering of all things—the body and its relations—is performed and dedicated with the accompaniment of mantras. By the phrase "even by a slight word of the Guru," he demonstrates that when such devotion exists, knowledge arises spontaneously. The meaning is: "By means of the awakening to You—that is, the realization of Brahman—which quickly arises through the mere cause of the Guru's word, may Your Self become liberated. (6)
He says that for those who lack devotion, even the labor of the scriptures results only in mere scholarship:
"In this world, some whose minds have exerted themselves even toward the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman) do not know You;
alas, their labor is fruitless, and they carry the ox [of worldly existence] here for a very long time."

I shall not bear that speech in which your form—dense with being and consciousness, wherein all divine playful incarnations appear, enchanting the entire world and removing every stain—is not described. || 7 ||

Regarding the phrase "in the Śabdabrahman": even those who have applied their minds with effort to the Veda—augmented by its auxiliary limbs such as Mīmāṃsā—some here do not know You, the Supreme Brahman, who are the primary subject to be realized therein, nor do they perform meditation and the like. How tragic! Their labor is barren; their exertion is in vain. For a very long time, they merely maintain a cow of speech called frivolous talk and cavil, which is devoid of the production of the fruits of devotion and knowledge.

Alternatively, one might maintain—that is, nourish—a cow that is barren and yields no milk because it has ceased to give birth. But as for me, I shall not maintain—that is, I shall not employ—that speech which fails to describe the divine incarnations such as Śrī Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who delight all people (viśvābhirāmāḥ) and who are the removers of all impurities, misfortunes, and passions; nor shall I employ that speech which does not proclaim or establish the Supreme Brahman, whose form is the dense essence of existence and consciousness (saccitsāndra). Such speech, being devoid of any exposition of the Lord as both with and without attributes, I shall not utter. || 7 ||
Then, by means of three verses, he prays for devotion through the company of the virtuous:
"O Infinite One, O Enemy of Caidya! I do not understand at all who you are, how much you are, or what you are like; nevertheless, with undivided intent, I honor only the service of you.

May there be for me the sight and touch of your emblems, and of the assemblies of those dear to your feet; may there also be my zeal for your worship, prostration, praise, and the chanting of your qualities and deeds. (8)

"Who" means: I do not understand at all who You are—what Your essential nature is, what Your extent is, what Your majesty is, what Your kind is, or what Your attributes are. O Infinite One! O Lord! This being so, being of undivided devotion—that is, with my mind fixed solely on You—I honor only Your worship, Your service. To the question, "How can there be my worship without knowing [You]? He says: "O Enemy of Caidya. O Foe of Śiśupāla! The sense is that because You were heard of as the son of a cowherd, this much I do understand.

May I also have devotion for those devotees who are dear to Your feet—those who possess Your *liṅgas* (emblems) and Your images—and for their assemblies (*sadasām*). By "seeing, touching, and so forth," acts such as salutation are included; alternatively, the masculine gender is used because it qualifies "association with the virtuous" (*satsaṅga*). May I also have respect for *prapūjā* (excellent worship endowed with all ritual services), *nati* (prostration), *nuti* (praise), and the proclamation of the deeds of creation and so on performed through Your qualities such as *sattva*. ||8||

Whatever may be obtained, O Lord, let each of those be offered unto you; I am your servant, and let my constant task be the sweeping of your abode and other such duties performed with a mind free from artifice.
I worship you, whose four arms shine forth as the sun, fire, the Brahmanas, and the Supreme Self.
May my yoga of devotion, characterized by being moistened with love for you, flow forth constantly. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "whatever...": "offered" (*samupahṛtam*) means presented. May my action—which has as its primary element the sweeping away of dust (*unmārjanam*) from your dwellings, such as fields and so forth, along with watering, offerings of flowers, and the like—be performed repeatedly without hypocrisy (*nirmāyam*), that is, free from deceit. He states the bases for worship: "the Sun," etc. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), cows and other such objects are included. Upon these bases, may I worship the resplendent Four-Armed One; I honor Him with Saura hymns, oblations, hospitality, objects of enjoyment, fodder for cattle, and so forth.

"Moistened by love for you," meaning one whose heart is melted; "the state of that" means its essential nature; "may that form of the yoga of devotion constantly overflow"—that is to say, may it proceed toward you in the form of a continuous stream. || 9 ||

Oneness with You—which is difficult to attain through charity, fire-offerings, vows, observances, austerity, Sāṅkhya, or Yoga—has indeed been obtained by the cowherd women (gopīs) solely through association with You; they are truly the most virtuous of all.
Although there are many other devotees, You hold them in high regard, yet You cherish their devotion above all.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Vātālaya, strengthen my devotion to You alone and remove my afflictions! 10.

"Unity"—this oneness with You, which is difficult even for yogis to attain through charity and other means, the gopīs have indeed obtained solely through association with You; therefore, they are the most virtuous of all. [You are] "thick with bliss," whose sole essence is bliss. Although there are many other devotees such as Uddhava and others, You hold the devotion of these gopīs in the highest esteem. Therefore, please strengthen my own devotion to You, characterized by love, making it steadfast and imperishable. || 10 ||

Thus ends the ninety-fourth decade, which contains a description of the manner in which the knowledge of reality arises, a description of the nature of bondage and liberation, and a description of the prayer for devotion preceded by a censure of those lacking it.

Now, an objection is raised: "It was stated that when the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is attained through devotion, there is the cessation of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). This is untenable; for if the two are distinct, their identity is impossible, and if they are non-distinct, the transmigratory existence of the *jīva* would be inexplicable. Anticipating this, he refutes it by explaining that the state of being a transmigrator belongs to the Lord himself due to his connection with a body composed of *māyā*, and that upon the removal of that [connection], he abides in his own true nature: "O Source of the Universe! At first, you assumed the body of Hiraṇyagarbha, which consists of the undivided *jīvātman*;
having attained the state of a *jīva*, you exist adorned by the multitude of qualities of *māyā*."

There, having severed the pair of qualities with my heightened being and having entered into a state of devotion, I shall abandon even that sattva and exist once more as one who is unconditioned—indeed, as you alone are. || 1 ||

"At the beginning" means at the outset, at the conclusion of the dissolution of Brahmā, when your desire to create arises, you assumed that body belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha—that is, you became its presiding deity. Of what nature was it? It was "consisting of the undivided individual soul. Here, by the word *jīva*, the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) is meant; the sense is that it was in the form of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of subtle bodies. To answer the question "For what purpose?", he addresses him as the cause thereof: "O Source of the Universe! (*viśvayone*).

He is the source, that is, the cause, of the universe—the Virāṭ body, the manifested world. For from the subtle body, indeed, the gross body arises. Thus, the sense is that Hiraṇyagarbha became Brahmā for the purpose of creating the world.

Being thus, you alone, having attained the state of a living soul (*jīvatva*) which is the very form of reality, exist as one inlaid with—meaning bound by—the multitude of *māyā*-qualities and the products of *māyā*, namely the principles (*tattvas*) consisting of the great principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the elements, the senses, and the five vital breaths; that is to say, through the body composed of their aggregate. By means of identifying with the body, you alone become a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). Therefore, since I am of your nature, my identity with you is logical; this is the intended meaning.

Thus, for the transmigrating individual soul (jīva), when rajas and tamas increase, there is no cessation of saṃsāra. Regarding the specific case when sattva increases, he says: "But therein... The meaning is that among the qualities of Māyā, there is indeed a distinction when sattva increases. By means of service to Sāttvika objects, [the mind] becomes uplifted; therefore, it attains the state of devotion—that is, it transforms into the form of devotion.

The sense is this: having severed the pair of qualities—*rajas* and *tamas*—as well as their effects such as the body and so forth, by generating the knowledge that they consist of *māyā* and thereby casting them aside; and having abandoned even *sattva*, which serves as a means because its purpose has been fulfilled; then, being unconditioned due to the absence of any intervention between cause and effect, you alone, who are perfectly full, shall remain—I, that is, I shall experience union with You. Now, one might object: "In that case, let only the increase of *sattva* be sought; what is the use of devotion (*bhakti*)? To this doubt, he says:
"O Infinite One! Even when, through the awakening of *sattva*, there occasionally arises an awareness of the defects in the taste for sense-objects..."
Furthermore, when the darkness of ignorance and the rajas have surged forth, activity within these [guṇas] is difficult to restrain;

for as long as the mind and the senses remain bound together here, the sole refuge to block them all is single-minded devotion to You alone in Your fourth state (turya)—thus did You, in the form of a swan, declare. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to the unfolding of *sattva*": the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of *sattva* is its increase. Consequently, even when the perception of faults in the flavor of objects—that is, in the tasting of sensory objects—is present, engagement with those very objects becomes difficult to restrain. The reason for this is stated as: "when *rajas* is rampant in the darkness of *tamas*. The sense is that this occurs because *sattva* has been overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*. As long as this is the case, the qualities (*guṇas*), the objects, and the mind remain mutually entangled. For the mind enters into objects under the influence of attachment and other such passions.

Those experienced objects enter the mind in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, they become mutually intertwined—this is the meaning. To restrain or abandon all those qualities of the mind (*guṇacitta*), namely *rajas* and *tamas*, devotion alone is the refuge in You, the Lord, who are the Witness beyond the three states (*avasthātraya*) and situated in the fourth (*turya*). Regarding the term "in the form of a swan" (*haṃsarūpī*): a swan is one skilled in discriminating milk from water; likewise, a *paramahaṃsa* mendicant is one skilled in discriminating the Self from the non-Self. Having assumed that form, You taught and instructed Sanaka and the others before Brahmā.
Now, is there indeed any means for attaining the highest good equal to devotion? He says, "No":

"O Kṛṣṇa! There are many other means for the highest good fashioned for ritualists according to their diverse inclinations; they result in various states that are limited in scope and end in meager bliss. From those [means], may [I] arise [in You]."
And you, O friend, have indeed declared devotion to the Most Worshipful One to be the sole and most honored among all spiritual excellences;
for what joy could ever equal the bliss of devotion to You for those who indulge in sense objects? || 3 ||

Regarding the word "santi" (they exist): there are various means to the highest good (*śreyas*)—the practices for those engaged in action (*karmin*), who are qualified for ritual due to passion and other such factors—which have been formulated according to differences in inclination and differences in qualification by teachers such as Bṛhaspati, Vyāsa, Patañjali, and others. From those means to the highest good, there would arise various destinies (*gati*) in the form of heaven and so forth as their fruits; however, they are limited pleasures, consisting of little happiness because they are mixed with suffering, and they are finite (*sānta*).

And these [pleasures] are impermanent. You, however, have declared to your friend Uddhava that among all things conducive to the highest good, singular, exclusive, and unfailing devotion is most venerable—that is, it is to be honored beyond measure. What joy or happiness could possibly equal the bliss derived from devotion to You for those who indulge their senses with worldly objects? The meaning is: none at all. || 3 ||
He says that very thing:

"But for one whose mind is satisfied by devotion to You, who moves about here in happiness with all desires fallen away, all directions shall consist of bliss, just as for one dwelling within a watery cavern, all directions consist solely of water."
Indeed, he does not desire the world of Indra, the abode of Brahmā, nor the heart-pleasing perfections of yoga;
let that be, for he is even without longing for the bliss of liberation when it comes to him of its own accord. || 4 ||

"By devotion to You": by devotion to You, characterized by love, the intellect becomes satisfied; thus, having developed the sense of sufficiency—thinking "devotion alone is enough, what need for anything else"—one's desires fall away, becoming free from thirst for sense objects. Consequently, for one who moves about happily everywhere in this world, all directions (āśāḥ) become filled with bliss. The intended meaning is that everything being experienced is of the very nature of happiness.

Just as for a great lake that is a hollow of water, all directions become composed solely of water for a fish or other creature dwelling therein, so too for a devotee immersed in the bliss of devotion to You, all directions consist solely of happiness; this is the meaning.

Furthermore, let it suffice to say that this devotee does not desire the world of Indra and other gods, nor the heart-pleasing and enchanting yogic perfections (*yogasiddhis*)—which are the fruits of worship, such as entering another's body, the eight superhuman powers (*aṣṭaiśvarya*), hearing from afar, seeing from afar, and so forth; he is even indifferent and free from attachment toward the bliss of liberation (*mokṣa*). Why is that? Not because he perceives them as difficult to attain, but because they have appeared of their own accord through the majesty of devotion, having come forward spontaneously. || 4 ||
Let alone the discussion of supreme devotees; for even ordinary devotees have achieved their life's purpose—thus he says:

"Even when oppressed by the pleasures of the senses, which cause the lack of tranquility in the faculties, a devotee of yours cannot be conquered again by those very same weak things as they are overcome by devotion alone.
Just as a fire with seven flames, its radiance kindled, consumes a vast mass of wood."
In the same way, the flood of devotion to you burns away the wickedness of those whose senses are unrestrained. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "your devotee": although he is oppressed and drawn away by the tastes of sense-objects due to the lack of tranquility in his senses—that is, because his senses have not been mastered—he cannot be conquered by them; he cannot be brought under their control. The reason for this is given as: "by the weak ones."

The reason for this is: "being assailed," that is, being overwhelmed by powerful devotion. The meaning is: when devotion has once again arisen. Just as the seven-flamed fire consumes a vast expansion of wood—a great heap of timber—so too, while the flood or stream of devotion to You burns away sin, where is the intoxicating pride of the senses before such devotion? By this, it is shown that because the senses lack the power to oppose devotion, the very root of sin is severed.
He says that in the absence of devotion, any other means of accomplishment is futile:
"Abandoning the melting of the heart, the bristling of the body's hair, and tears of joy—
how indeed could the mind be purified by mere austerity or by knowledge for one devoid of devotion?"

This self, constantly anointed with the accomplished collyrium that is the taste of your verses, perceives the subtle reality as clearly as with the eyes; it does not do so through ten million syllogisms, however much they may have been practiced.

Regarding the phrase "the moistening of the mind": the meaning is that without devotion—which is understood through the clearly manifesting rays of consciousness—how could the mind be purified, once one has abandoned the very state of being moistened by the mind? Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the cessation of saṃsāra, which is imagined through ignorance, and the attainment of one's true nature result from the knowledge of Brahman alone, what does devotion accomplish here? In response to this doubt, he says: "Your song."

The tasting, hearing, or reciting of the verses of Your glory is itself the *siddhāñjana* (the magical ointment). By this, the self—the mind, the reality, the subtle object free from superimposition, that supreme truth—is constantly rubbed and purified again and again, and thus it attains and makes manifest that [truth]. It does not attain it in such a way through a multitude of arguments (*tarkakoṭi*) or through repeated intellectual reasoning. Knowledge is merely an intermediate function of devotion;
therefore, the effort toward it is entirely in vain—this is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
Thus, he describes the fitness for meditation of one whose mind is purified:

"You should practice meditation, having bound your posture in equanimity and bliss, with your gaze fixed on the tip of the nose; having conquered the path of the breath through inhalation and the other [breath-controls], you should turn the lotus of the mind downward, and having made its tip point upward, you should contemplate the Sun, Moon, and Fire above it."
I meditate upon you situated there, with limbs as tender as a fresh water-laden cloud and dark as a rain-bearing monsoon cloud.

Regarding "meditation": one whose body, head, and neck are aligned in evenness, having assumed a comfortable posture—there is no fixed rule such as the *svastika* and so forth. If the eyes are closed, the mind dissolves; if they are opened, the mind is distracted. To avoid both of these, the eyes should be half-closed, and the gaze naturally comes to rest upon the tip of the nose.

He is one by whom the pathways of the vital breath (*pavanapatha*)—the channels (*nāḍī*) that serve as the locus for the movement of air—have been conquered through various types of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), such as inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), and purified by the removal of defects such as phlegm (*kapha*). Having visualized the lotus of the mind (*cittapadma*), the heart-lotus, as being turned downward with its tip facing upward, he should contemplate, within its pericarp, the sun, moon, and fire situated one above the other; [he meditates on] the Fire situated therein, in the midst of those. || 7 ||

I shall meditate upon You, whose hair is dark-blue and smooth, who wears blazing makara-shaped earrings, who is moist with the radiance of a gentle smile, who is beautiful with a forest garland and a high necklace adorned by the splendor of the Kaustubha gem;
You who possess the Śrīvatsa mark, lovely arms, a soft and radiant belly, garments with the luster of gold, and charming, smooth thighs—You whose foot-posture is as graceful as a lotus. 8.

"Ānīla" means one whose hair is exceedingly dark, smooth, and well-knit; one whose earrings are shaped like blazing sea-monsters (makara); one who is moist and glossy with the fluid of his gentle smile; one who is beautiful with a forest garland (vanamālā) pervaded by the splendor of the Kaustubha gem and with clusters of large necklaces; one who has a mark named Śrīvatsa on the right side of his chest; one whose arms are handsome, long, and thick; and one whose belly is soft and radiant.
I meditate upon you, who are clothed in garments with a golden luster and wear yellow robes, and whose thighs are beautiful, smooth, and fleshy. (8)
Now, he describes the manner of ascending the stages of meditative absorption (samādhi) in succession:
"O Lord! Owing to the ever-arising curiosity in all my limbs, I repeatedly fix my mind there;
yet even there, I join it to the single point in Your beautiful lotus-face with its gentle smile."

There, my mind, having dissolved into the form of supreme bliss and non-dual consciousness, expanding without another [object] to think of, may I repeatedly contemplate thus; in this way, may I become one whose yoga has fully ascended. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "in all limbs": holding my mind—which has attained curiosity and is vibrating with wonder—repeatedly and again and again upon all the limbs, I join it to one specific limb among those very parts. Where is that? In the lotus of the face. "Gentle smile" is an epithet of the lotus of the face.

May my mind, steady and firmly fixed upon that glorious face where the smile is gentle, expand into the form of Brahman—which is of the nature of non-dual consciousness and supreme bliss, and whose essence is existence, consciousness, and bliss—and thus, making it take the form of Brahman, may I not think of anything else, such as the distinction between the meditator and the object of meditation. In this manner, throughout my life, may I repeatedly attain oneness with Brahman; thus, may I become one whose yoga is fully ascended and who is habituated to the worship of the Lord. 9.
O Murāri! When your meditative yoga is thus established, the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*, as well as distant hearing and the rest, shall surely descend in a competitive rush;
yet, since all this brings delay in attaining you, I disregard it—I desire only you.
O Ānandapūrṇa, Lord of the City of Wind! Protect me alone from all suffering. || 10 ||

"In this manner": in the way thus described, meditation upon You alone is *yoga*, the means to the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). When that exists, those eight perfections born of the excellence of *sattva*—the eight sovereign powers (*aiśvaryas*) as well as minor accomplishments such as hearing and seeing from afar and knowledge of the three periods of time—would descend with a competitive spirit of "I first, I first. However, I do not value all this, as it causes delay in attaining You; rather, I desire only You, who are full of bliss and the very nature of liberation.

Protect me from all the torments of saṃsāra; furthermore, do not cast me back into the ocean of saṃsāra through the eight supernatural powers and so forth, and do not cause me to wander—this is the intended meaning. || 10 ||
Thus ends the ninety-fifth decade, which describes the fitness for meditation on the true nature of the Lord belonging only to one whose mind is purified by devotion.

Now, in order to establish the fitness for the aforementioned meditation and for the worship of the Lord of the Universal Form (*viśvamūrtīśa*), he sets forth the divine manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the Lord:

For you, O Lord of supreme greatness, are indeed Brahman manifest; among the imperishable syllables you are the letter 'A', and among mantras you are the *Tāra* (Om); among kings you are Manu, and among sages you are both Bhṛgu and Nārada;

among the Dānavas you are Prahlāda, and among cattle you are Surabhi; among birds you are Vainateya, and among serpents you are Ananta; and among flowing streams, O Universal Form, you are the celestial river Ganges. || 1 ||

"Thou indeed... O Thou of vast majesty! O Universal Form! Thou art indeed the Supreme Brahman itself. In all instances, the genitive and locative cases are used for the purpose of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). Among syllables, [thou art] the letter 'A'; among mantras, [thou art] the Tāra, the Praṇava; thus "Thou" is to be joined [to each]. Regarding "among sages": among the Brahman-sages, [thou art] Bhṛgu; among the divine sages, [thou art] Nārada. (1)
Among those devoted to Brahman you are Bali; among sacrifices you are the silent recitation (japayajña); among heroes you are Pārtha;
among devotees you are Uddhava; among the strong you are strength; among the radiant you are the abode of splendor.
There is no end to the extent of your manifestations; every expanding and supreme object is you alone.
If you are the individual soul (jīva) and you are primordial matter (pradhāna), then whatever I am here in this world of manifestation (prapañca) is nothing at all.

"Of those devoted to Brahman" (*brahmaṇyānām*) means of those who are devoted to the Brāhmaṇas. "Of the strong and the radiant" (*balināṃ tejasvinām*) is a genitive used in connection [with the preceding]. Since there is no end to Your manifestation (*vibhūti*), I conclude this: whatever object possesses expanding excellence—that is, whatever object is endowed with manifestly perceived excellence—all that is You alone. Furthermore, You are the individual soul (*jīva*); You are primordial matter (*pradhāna*); You alone are both nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
Therefore, in this phenomenal world consisting of nature (prakṛti) and spirit (puruṣa), there is nothing whatsoever that is perceived apart from you; the meaning is that you alone are all this. ||2||

He states that for those who lack the qualification for the aforementioned forms of worship, liberation is attained through the practice of their own duties by offering them to the Lord, via the gateway of dispassion:
"By performing with devotion and dedication to You the duties of the castes and stages of life as ordained by the path of the Vedas,
they gradually attain [liberation] while renouncing them once inner dispassion has blossomed."

Pure is Your awakening—the realization that "I am the Supreme," which consists of the manifestation of existence, which is non-differentiated within all distinct objects, rootless yet the root of the universe. || 3 ||

Regarding the word "dharma": performing the duties prescribed for each of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) according to the path of the Vedas—whether they be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or otherwise—with devotion, being intent upon You, and as offerings to the Lord; then, when inner dispassion gradually blossoms and becomes manifest, renouncing those prescribed actions, abandoning them according to the injunctions, and becoming *paramahaṃsas*, one realizes the pure awakening that is Your own nature—free from the forms of sense objects—as the Supreme Brahman, thinking:
"I am the Supreme Brahman alone."

In this manner, they obtain or attain [it]. He states the *taṭasthalakṣaṇa* (indirect definition) of Brahman: "the root of the universe. This means it is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world. He establishes this by saying: "in all objects. In all created effects—objects that are distinct and separate by their very nature—it remains non-different, existing as a unity in the form of the cause, just as gold exists in bracelets, earrings, and the like.

If it is objected that Brahman—being existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda)—is not perceived within its own created effects, [the author] replies that it is indeed perceived, stating: "Existence" (sattā). That uniform existence which is perceived in diverse objects such as jars and cloths, in the form "the jar exists," "the cloth exists"; that uniform manifestation and cognition which is perceived as non-different amidst differences, in the form "this is a jar," "this is a cloth"; and that non-different quality of endearment, agreeableness, or bliss which is perceived in diverse things such as garlands and sandalwood—these [are Brahman].

The meaning is that Brahman is that whose very nature (*svarūpa*) consists of existence (*sattā*), manifestation (*sphūrti*), and bliss (*priyatva*). Here, by the phrase "undifferentiated within the differentiated," the non-duality (*advitīyatva*) is also stated through the declaration of the non-difference between cause and effect. Therefore, by the description "consisting of existence, manifestation, and bliss," the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman as non-dual *saccidānanda* is also shown. It is "rootless" (*nirmūla*), meaning without cause, and thus eternal (*nitya*); hence it is also indicated that for those who have attained it, there is no returning again. || 3 ||

Now, one might object: was it not already stated previously, in the passage beginning with "There are [other] higher goals," that people achieve their purpose through devotion alone? Why, then, is the employment of action (karma) and knowledge (jñāna) now introduced? Anticipating this doubt, he says that it is due to the difference in the qualifications (adhikāra) of the aspirants: "Knowledge, action, and devotion—this triad here leads to You; among these, first, those who are weary of all worldly objects possess the qualification for the yoga of knowledge."

For those who are attached, the yoga of action (karmayoga) is indeed prescribed in you; but for those who are neither excessively attached nor excessively detached, yet whose essence is fixed upon you, the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga) is intended.

"Jñāna" means that which leads to You, the means for liberation. Among those three, the qualification for the yoga of knowledge belongs to those who are disenchanted with—and detached from—all objects, whether in this world or the next, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, nectar, and so forth, as well as from this very body. For those who are attached and not disenchanted, the yoga of action (karmayoga) is prescribed, being dedicated to You, the Lord. But for those who are neutral—meaning those whose interest is fixed on You, the Lord, and who have developed faith through Your stories and the like by chance—for them, there is the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga). || 4 ||
And since these three are to be accomplished within a human body, one should not waste time in order to attain it; with this intention, he says:
"By the power of their past merits, those in the mortal world quickly obtain either knowledge or devotion to You;
therefore, O Blessed One, whether they be denizens of heaven or hell, they long for birth in that very place."

But since I have been possessed by destiny within this mortal body—which acts as a boat upon the ocean of worldly existence—may you, having made the Guru your helmsman, carry me across by acting as a favorable wind. (5)

"Knowledge," it is said. Or rather, by means of devotion to You, easily and without effort—by destiny or through past merit—when I have entered [the ocean] like a boat, yet am deprived of the means to cross, may You, the Lord of the Abode of Winds (Vātālayeśa), acting Yourself like a favorable wind, make me Your teacher, the instructor, the helmsman, and the navigator, and thus carry me across to the further shore. || 5 ||
Regarding this, he states that among the means of attainment, devotion alone is the easy path:
"Those who, longing for absolute knowledge, seek the Unmanifest through scriptures and logical systems, suffer excessively; they attain perfection only at the end of many more births."

Even though the yoga of action is remote from the supreme fruit, may this yoga of devotion—which is rooted in You and draws You near—swiftly increase within me, O Ārya, so that it may lead me to Your attainment.

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): those greedy for absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), or those solely desiring knowledge, while seeking and investigating the unmanifest Brahman through the *śrutis* (Upaniṣads) and through the *nyāyas* (logical arguments) set forth in the Mīmāṃsā, undergo extreme suffering. They attain success—the fruit—only at the end of many births. Furthermore, even the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is remote from the supreme fruit, the supreme human goal of liberation; it yields its fruit only after a long period of time and is of the nature of hardship.

But the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), by virtue of its intermediate fruits such as the attainment of the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka) and the world of truth (satyaloka), remains distant; yet from its very commencement through the sequence of hearing, chanting, and so forth, it is delightful from beginning to end and swiftly brings about Your attainment. O Blessed One! May that alone increase within me. || 6 ||
He confirms the stated meaning by means of the authority of the conduct of the virtuous:

"The sage censures excessive effort for the sake of knowledge alone; however, for one who listens to the reality of Brahman and takes firm refuge in devotion to Your feet, liberation is at the very tip of his hand."

Even here, in the meditation upon You, the difficulty is equal due to the fickleness of the mind; yet, through Your grace and the beauty of Your charm, even that can be quickly brought under control by means of practice.

"Only for the sake of knowledge" means that the sage Vedavyāsa censures—that is, prohibits in various places throughout the Purāṇas—excessive effort, which is the study of many books, solely for the purpose of attaining mere intellectual knowledge. Rather, for one who listens to the essence of the established doctrine regarding the reality of Brahman, reflects upon it through reasoning, and takes refuge with intense devotion at Your feet, liberation is at the very tip of his hand; the sense is that he is liberated even while living.

In this world, even in meditation upon You accompanied by [the observances of] Yama and the rest, the difficulty—meaning the state of being hard to practice—due to the fickleness of the mind, is equal [to that of other difficult tasks]. Nevertheless, the meaning is that even such a difficult meditation can be quickly mastered and brought under control through Your grace and through the beauty of the Śrīmūrti’s loveliness, by means of repeated practice. || 7 ||

O Lord of the World! Though I am weary of the path of ritual action which is indeed most treacherous, and though I have developed a deep faith in Your teachings and the like, I am simply unable to abandon my desires.
Therefore, with my mind firmly fixed upon You through resolute conviction, I shall pursue those [desires] while regarding them with the perception of their inherent defects.
I shall nourish only devotion toward you who have entered my heart; all attachments will quickly perish.

"Disgusted": furthermore, although one may become disgusted with—that is, detached from—the path of ritual action characterized by extreme inequality and abounding in suffering, such as the pursuit of heaven and the like, and may have developed faith in Your teachings and so forth, yet one is still unable to abandon desires, namely those things desired such as sons, friends, wealth, and so on. Therefore, having repeatedly and resolutely fixed my mind upon You, while experiencing those very desires through the perception of their defects, I shall nourish devotion alone.
Thus, when you have entered the heart through devotion and worship, attachments and desires for sense objects will quickly and gently perish—that is, they will go to destruction. || 8 ||

Since the restraint of the mind is essential for the worship of the Blessed One, he prays for peace of mind through two verses by means of the examples of the mendicant and Purūravas: "A certain Brahmin, whose intellect was purified by the loss of wealth acquired through afflictions and who was being driven away by crowds of people, spoke thus beforehand: 'Truly, neither people, nor time, nor karma, nor the planets have power over me.'"

"O Lord, my mind is the cause of my suffering; therefore, by cultivating a multitude of virtues here, may you become all-accomplishing. Having said this, he departed in peace. O All-pervading One, grant such tranquility of mind to me as well!

"Someone": long ago, a certain Brahmin, distressed by the loss—meaning the destruction caused by thieves and others—of wealth acquired with great hardship, became despondent. Having resolved to renounce the world, he possessed a pure mind; yet, being once again impelled and afflicted, he spoke thus: "I appear to be oppressed by people, but truly people are not the cause of my suffering, because there is oneness between this [world] and my own self."

Nor is Time [the cause], because it is of the nature of God (Īśvara), and because my own Self is a portion of God; furthermore, it is impossible for there to be suffering in that which is one's own part. Nor is Karma the cause of suffering, because action is incompatible with both the insentient body and the Self, whose essential nature is consciousness. Nor are the planets the cause of suffering, since—considering the time of birth—the affliction caused by planets situated in the twelfth, eighth, or other houses affects only the body of the person born, not my Self. Rather, it is the mind alone, which I mistakenly identify as the Self, that is the cause of my suffering.

That mind, while here in the self, cultivating and superimposing upon it a multitude of qualities consisting of agency, enjoyership, and so forth—being thus called "the maker of all" because it performs everything such as the bodies of gods, humans, and denizens of hell, as well as the objects of enjoyment and the places of enjoyment—it has become peaceful and has gone to You; that is, it has become liberated. Grant me, too, such peace of mind.
"For the Supreme, there is no transmigration, because He is pure consciousness and not the mind;
nor does it belong to the mind that identifies with the ego, because that mind is both conscious and unconscious, whereas the Supreme is only consciousness."
Thus is the established conclusion. 9.
In the past, Aila, having long served Urvaśī with a mind utterly overwhelmed by passion, eventually became deeply disillusioned;
singing that this pleasure of youth is indeed trivial, he attained devotion to You and, becoming fulfilled, lived most happily. In the same way, one should cast off attachment.
O Lord of the City of Wind! May my ritual action [of devotion] toward You, the crest-jewel of devotees, indeed ward off my diseases. 10.

Regarding "Aila": the passage beginning with "Aila [formerly] served Urvaśī" and so forth is clear. According to the well-known accounts of the Vedas and Purāṇas, Purūravas, having previously enjoyed Urvaśī who had come to him of her own accord, lost her again to the heavenly realm due to a breach of their agreement; however, having regained her through sacrifices and enjoyed her company for a long time, he eventually became weary of worldly pleasures and attained a tranquil mind. || 10 ||

Thus ends the ninety-sixth decade, which contains a description of the Lord’s manifestations, a description of those qualified for the paths of action, knowledge, and devotion, and a description of the prayer for the pacification of the mind.
Now, in order to bring about the cessation of dualities through mastery over the functions of the three qualities (*guṇas*), he speaks of the classification of the three qualities:

In this world, due to the three *guṇas*, everything indeed becomes differentiated in form—whether it be knowledge, faith, the agent, the dwelling place, happiness, action, or various types of food—as inferior, middling, or superior. However, that which consists of service to Your sacred field and so forth, and whatever else is dedicated to You, they declare all that to be established in the state beyond the *guṇas* (*nirguṇya*). By worshipping that, may I swiftly become perfected. || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "due to the three qualities" (*traiguṇyāt*): here in this world, whatever entity exists, such as knowledge and so forth, all of that consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and is therefore of diverse forms; for this very reason, it becomes inferior, middling, or superior. Among these, the knowledge of the oneness of the Self in all beings is *sāttvika*; knowledge [of them] as separate is *rājasa*; and knowledge similar to that of children and the like is *tāmasa*. Faith (*śraddhā*) is also threefold, according to its objects being spiritual merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), or neither. And the agent (*kartṛ*) is likewise threefold, through the distinctions of dispassion (*vairāgya*), passion (*rāga*), and ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Dwelling is also threefold, distinguished by forest, village, and the abode of a hunter. That [experience] is likewise threefold: the bliss of self-realization, the bliss of sense objects, and the bliss arising from sleep and so forth. Action is also threefold, distinguished by being offered to the Lord, optional, or prohibited. The substance of food is also threefold: pure, dear to the senses, and impure. He says "tvatkṣetra" (Your field) to show that all this becomes free from qualities (nirguṇa) through its orientation toward the Lord.

Furthermore, in this case, because you are my field (*kṣetra*), whatever service and so forth I perform toward you—if it is directed toward you alone and not toward [worldly] fruits—then they say that all of it culminates in the state beyond the qualities (*nirguṇa*). By worshipping you in that manner, may I quickly, instantly, become liberated. || 1 ||
Now, with two verses, he concludes the *bhāgavata* dharma introduced [in the previous verse] as "O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! the service of Your feet":
With my mind fixed on You alone, wandering happily, performing all activities for Your sake, and visiting holy places frequented by Your devotees even while being served by them;
with an equal mind toward a thief, a sage, a deer, and others, and being constantly freed from defects such as pride, humiliation, rivalry, and envy, may I worship You in all beings. (2)

"In you alone" means: performing all enjoined and unenjoined activities (*ceṣṭā*) and actions (*karmaṇi*) for your sake—this is the ellipsis. "Those already traversed by your devotees" refers to those previously served by them; or alternatively, it may be construed by dividing it as: regions currently being inhabited by your devotees, and holy places (*puṇya*) previously frequented by them. Regarding "in a bandit," "in a lowly person," "in a Brahmin," and "in the highest"—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), outcastes (*caṇḍāla*) and so forth are included.

Being one whose mind is equal even toward those beginning with enemies (lādiṣu), he states the means for this here: "mucyamāna... etc. Being one for whom faults such as contempt, rivalry, and envy—which are produced by the conceit of identifying with the body—are being liberated through the power of the knowledge of the single Self (aikātmyajñāna), may you worship me constantly among all beings. Alternatively, he states the intermediate fruit of having an equal mind: "mucyamāna... etc.; the destruction of faults such as contempt and so forth is indeed the intermediate fruit. || 2 ||
Thus, he states the limit for worship performed with equal vision:

"As long as the state of being You does not shine forth clearly within these [elements], so long one should perform such worship; then, when the realization of non-duality suddenly blossoms, one may move about as one who is identical with You."
O Blessed One! There is no destruction whatsoever of this dharma of yours that has been set forth; therefore, O Lord, with your whole soul, instruct me in the delightful path of devotion.

Regarding the phrase "your presence" (*tvadbhāva*): as long as this presence of yours—that is, your abiding within all living beings, including these outcasts, Brahmins, and others—in the form of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*) does not manifest clearly, nor does it enter the path of perfect experience, for that duration one should perform worship in the manner previously described. Furthermore, casting aside shame, one should offer salutations and so forth with the vision that "the Lord exists here even in Caṇḍālas and others in the form of the Inner Ruler. This is the meaning.

And then, when the realization of oneness suddenly blossoms—the experiential knowledge that there is but one Self in all beings—I shall move about as being composed of You. O Blessed One! Regarding this very Bhāgavata-dharma, the dharma of Your devotees, which has been introduced and commenced, may there be not even the slightest destruction or deficiency from its beginning until its completion, as is the case with sacrifices and other such rites.

Therefore, because it is easy to perform and so forth, please grant me the pleasing and correct path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*)—the means characterized by love (*prema*) consisting of the attributes of the Lord, together with all its required qualifications, limbs, and so on; that is to say, make me eligible for it. || 3 ||

Since one devoid of health has no qualification for any action whatsoever, he prays for that very thing: "O Lord! May I have the health and longevity required to accomplish this yoga of devotion; and even therein, alas, may Your feet be served as my medicine, like milk.
For Mārkaṇḍeya, in the past, was told by an astrologer that his life would last only twelve years."
Having served you for a year, he caused even Death himself to flee from your soldiers. || 4 ||

"And this" (taṃ cainam): In order to strengthen that aforementioned and summarized path of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), which consists of both the goal and the means, and to make what has begun firm, [the sage says]: "O Blessed One! Health—freedom from external and internal diseases—and longevity are my goals. For the sake of that longevity and health as well, Your feet must be served by me. Oh, by good fortune, since even the means itself is of the nature of bliss, I have become one who has achieved his purpose."

The meaning is: "just as milk is to be drunk for the sake of medicine, such as to cure a fever caused by the combination of humors (sannipāta), so [is this]. Now, one might object: since the lifespan is determined by the force of commenced karma (*prārabdha-karma*), the attainment of anything beyond that is not possible even through prayer. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the example of Mārkaṇḍeya, saying: "Mārkaṇḍeya. If it is argued that his long life was predetermined from before and not obtained through service to the Lord, he says "no," providing the word "gaṇaka" (the calculator).

The astrologer, an expert in the science of birth-horoscopes, declared that his life span was twelve years. However, according to the maxim that "one experiences the fruit of extremely intense merits and sins right here and now," he served You for one year with an exceedingly lofty and rigorous yoga of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). At the end of those twelve years, he caused Death—the Ender (*Antaka*)—who had arrived to take him away with noose and staff in hand—to flee, driving him away along with the hosts of Your soldiers, the messengers of Viṣṇu, who appeared at that very moment. (4) 64.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Bhaktapriyā*, a commentary on the *Nārāyaṇīya-stotra*.
The abiding state of the liberated as the nature of Brahman— being, consciousness, and bliss—
is now set forth as the twelfth stage of Hari’s divine play.

Now, in connection with the story of Mārkaṇḍeya, by means of the pretext of narrating his life—beginning with his penance and the vision of Viṣṇu, Māyā, and Śiva—the state of one who has attained Brahman through the threefold yoga and remains established as Brahman alone is described:
"That long-lived Mārkaṇḍeya, ever devoted to You, spent six Manvantaras performing penance on the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā, delighting in incomparable bliss;
while the seventh Indra, seeking to delude him with celestial nymphs, gods, and the god of love..."
Who indeed would not be able to conquer your people, even by means of yogic heat and human efforts? || 5 ||

Regarding Mārkaṇḍeya: although he had indeed attained long life, he remained devoted to you and intent upon the worship of the Blessed One. The reason for this is stated as: "possessing incomparable devotion to the Lord."

He who possesses devotion and faith toward the worship of You, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, spent six *manvantaras*—characterized by seventy-one sets of four ages—performing austerities on the bank of that river named Puṣpabhadrā, on the northern side of the Himavat. On its bank stands a rock named Citraśilā and a banyan tree named Bhadravaṭa; it was there, on the shore of the river Puṣpabhadrā, that he passed his time. By mentioning "the seventh Devendra," he indicates the rotation of Indra and the other gods throughout the various *manvantaras*.

In the seventh Manvantara, the one who was the seventh Lord of the Gods (Indra) desired to seize his own position through ascetic penance. Fearing this, the gods sought to delude Mārkaṇḍeya with celestial maidens, Apsarases, the spring breeze, the god of the wind, and the god of love. However, being scorched and consumed by the heat of his yoga and austerity, those celestial maidens and others were unable to delude him; they failed. Who could conquer one who is devoted to You? No one at all.
The sense is: "Oh, how great is the delusion even of the Lord of the Gods! || 5 ||
Then, out of love and joy, you who are named Nārāyaṇa approached the side of this [child] as his companion; though tempted by various boons, he did not consent,
for with his inner self satisfied by devotion, he desired only to behold your illusory power once more.
Unaware that this is suffering born of illusion, he surely pursues it for the sake of a teacher.

"Out of affection" (*prītyā*): through the grace born of that austerity, you, who are the friend of men and known as Nārāyaṇa, approached his side. Thereafter, being praised with satisfaction—offering praise repeatedly or with great intensity—he was enticed by you with various boons, yet he did not consent; he did not choose those boons. The reason for this is: "one whose inner self is satiated by devotion. One whose inner self—that is, the mind—is satisfied and fulfilled solely by devotion to you, that is, by your worship.

Furthermore, he even chose to witness your illusory power (māyā). For who indeed would choose an illusory power that bestows suffering? Thus, the meaning of the word "kila" (indeed) is that this is truly inconceivable in his case. Alternatively, from birth onwards, he has been ignorant of the suffering caused by *māyā*. Therefore, because of this cause for wonder—for wonder arises at the sight of what has never been experienced—I surmise that he surely seeks out, that is, desires to experience, even that suffering born of *māyā*. (6)

Once you had departed swiftly, and the world was submerged in the seven oceans which were overflowing with water gushing from clouds tossed by the wind, that [person] wandered in distress for ten million years amidst the waters;
then, in his misery, he beheld from afar you alone—a wondrous child with dark limbs, lying upon a bed of *vaṭa* leaves, with the toes of his feet resting upon your lotus-like face.

"Having gone": when you, known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, had departed—that is, having gone toward Badarikāśrama—immediately after his prayer for a vision of your illusory power (māyā); while the world was submerged by the seven oceans which were overflowing with water trickling from clouds agitated by the wind and tossed hither and thither, and which were therefore violently surging and spreading upward one over another; that Mārkaṇḍeya, wandering distressed in the waters for ten million years, beheld from afar a certain wondrous child lying upon a banyan leaf. || 7 ||

Upon seeing you, the Lord of Sages, his hair standing on end with joy, hastened toward you, desiring to touch you; yet, entering within by your breath, he beheld once more the entire multitude of worlds.

Again, emerging through the winds of your breath, he was gazed upon by your sidelong glances; and though longing to embrace you out of delight, he remained in his own hermitage as before, while your body remained hidden from him.
"Having seen"—having entered within by means of his breath, he beheld the multitude of worlds, the universe consisting of the fourteen realms;

and then, having emerged outside again while you had covered your body and remained invisible, he stood as before in his own hermitage on the banks of the Puṣpabhadrā, each in his proper place. And here, since it is impossible to demonstrate the true nature of Māyā directly, it should be understood that she was shown by the Blessed One through the medium of her effects. || 8 ||
Now, he describes the manner of the grace bestowed by Śiva, who was satisfied by devotion to Viṣṇu:
"Then Purandara (Indra), desiring to see your beloved, went before him together with Gaurī;
having granted him his desired boons, he himself attained freedom from old age, death, and other such states."

Thus, it became perfectly clear that even the enemy of Smara (Śiva) is pleased by service to you alone; therefore, you are indeed the controller of all, being the essence of the threefold form. || 9 ||

"Gaurī" and so forth: In the presence of that Mārkaṇḍeya, Śiva departed after granting him boons—such as freedom from old age and death, which were self-acquired through the power of his own penance (the word "ādi" including devotion to Viṣṇu, fame, spiritual knowledge, worldly wisdom, and being a teacher of the Purāṇas). By this, the fact that Viṣṇu is the Lord of all is established; thus he says: "In this way," etc. It became clearly certain that you, O Viṣṇu, are the controller of all and the Lord of all.

The reason for this is stated: "Are you not indeed composed of the three forms? The triad of forms consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva (Girīśa); "composed of that" means having that as one's essential nature. The reason for this is given: "by your service. Since even that enemy of Smara (Śiva) is pleased by your service alone, the intention is that the triad of forms is merely a distinction of states of Viṣṇu himself, occurring for the sake of his various functions. || 9 ||

Anticipating the objection, "Could this not be a difference in states of Śiva?", he states that even in the case of identity, a distinction from them on the part of Viṣṇu is possible by way of a difference in location:

"In this three-part Satyaloka, there are the palaces of Brahmā, Hari, and Purabhida, each higher than the last; but above even those shines the world of Vaikuṇṭha, which is devoid of the transformations of Māyā."
There, even within the waters of the causal ocean and among the multitude of animals, you exist as the singular form of pure being;
O Lord of the City of Wind, whose self is the non-dual Brahman of Existence-Consciousness, protect me from all disease! 10.

Regarding the term *tryaṃśa*: that which possesses three parts—namely the three worlds consisting of the realms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—is the *tryaṃśa*. Within that Satyaloka, "higher and higher" refers as follows: first, in the world of Brahmā, is the temple of Brahmā; above that, in the world of Viṣṇu, is the temple of Viṣṇu; and above that, in the world of Śiva, is the temple of Śiva. Residing there are the three forms (*trimūrti*) who are the agents of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Furthermore, "above even those" means outside of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

For this very reason, the transformations of *māyā*—the sixteen evolutes beginning with *mahat* and *ahaṅkāra*—are absent there; thus the realm of Vaikuṇṭha shines forth, composed of pure *sattva*. In that realm of Vaikuṇṭha, within the causal waters, the waters of the covering, in the herd of cattle, and even in the house of Nanda, you exist as the singular form of pure *sattva*; because of its purity, there is an absence of covering, and you are the non-dual Self of Being-Consciousness (*saccidbrahmādvayātman*), whose very body is the non-dual Brahman of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānandādvayabrahmavapuḥ*). Therefore, protect me from all diseases—that is, liberate me. ||10||

Thus ends the ninety-seventh decade, containing the description of Mārkaṇḍeya’s prayer of supreme devotion, the description of his witnessing the dissolution of the world, and the description of the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus established the partless nature (*niṣkalatva*) of Viṣṇu, who is the object of praise, he now praises Him in that very form:
In whom this shines forth; from whom this arose; by whom this exists;
who is indeed of a form transcending all this that is illumined by his own light;
he who is far, far beyond words, and yet again beyond the reach of minds—even for the gods and the lords of sages.
O Kṛṣṇa! even the lightning does not know Your true nature, so what need be said of others? Salutations to You! || 1 ||

Regarding the phrase "yasmin" (in whom): O Kṛṣṇa! Salutations to You, whose essential nature is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*). Now, one might ask: "Let Him be praised; what is the use of mere salutation? To this he replies with the words "yasya" (of whom). Even the gods and the lords of sages do not know that *tattva*—the word *tat* being a pronoun—nor its state (*bhāva*), which is its true nature (*tattva*), namely Brahmanhood (*brahmatva*). The sense is: "Who then am I here to know or to praise Him? He further describes His inscrutability with the words "yo vācām" (who [is beyond] words).

It is far, far beyond the words of both the worldly and the Vedic, because of the absence of a relationship between the signifier and the signified; furthermore, it is far, far beyond even the minds. The reason for this is as follows: by whose light—that is, by whose power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)—this entire universe is illumined and made manifest. Since the mind and other faculties have acquired their very existence through its illumination, it is impossible for them to illuminate that [consciousness] itself. If one then asks, "In that case, since it cannot be known, is this not simply non-existent? he says: "In whom... [etc.].

In that substratum upon which this world shines and abides; from which, as its efficient and material cause, this world arose; and by which this world—by the word "and" (ca), meaning it attains unity with and dissolves into it—exists; therefore, because He is the cause of the world, this world shines as the very form of that Lord alone, appearing in the form of the world. Thus, the sense is that once the reality of the Lord as perceived through the form of the world is established, there is no need for any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: if the Lord has the world as His nature, does it not follow that He is subject to modification (*vikāritva*)?
If this is argued, he says "no"—"he who [is distinct] from this. This refers to one whose form transcends and is distinct from this world imagined through ignorance within the self. || 1 ||
Having thus established that Īśvara is the cause of the world, he next describes his role as the benefactor of the world:
"Birth, death, action, name, and clearly the virtues and defects found here—none of these belong to him; yet for the sake of the worlds, he himself, following his own *māyā*, undergoes them."

O Viṣṇu! Though formless, You manifest in manifold forms while bearing Your sovereign powers; though Your essence is undecaying, You appear as the infinite Self—to You, the abode of liberation, who are perfectly full of the Supreme Reality, I bow. 2.

Regarding the word "birth" (*janma*): birth refers to the incarnations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others; thereafter, "action" (*karman*) refers to deeds such as the slaying of Kaṃsa; "name" refers to names based on those births and actions; "qualities and defects" (*guṇadoṣāḥ*) refer to acts of restraint, grace, and so forth; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), sons, friends, and others are included.

In whom these [births, actions, and so forth] do not clearly exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), yet for the welfare of the world—that is, for the sake of favoring the universe—he, following *māyā*, personally assumes and accepts those births, actions, and so on, being himself independent of any other nature; moreover, while bearing powers characterized by knowledge, ignorance, wisdom, sovereignty, and so forth, he, though himself formless and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), appears in manifold forms distinguished as stationary and moving, and as gods, humans, animals, and so on; therefore, he is of a wondrous nature (*adbhutātman*), a marvelous essence.

To him who bestows grace upon the world, who is filled with the supreme flavor of ultimate bliss, and who, for that very reason, is the abode of absolute liberation and the giver of emancipation. || 2 ||
Now, raising the objection that if there are many forms, how can it be formless, he establishes its true nature as the limit for the negation of all duality:
"They say Your form is neither horizontal nor mortal, nor divine or demonic; neither woman nor man, nor substance, action, genus, or quality; neither being nor non-being."

Salutations to You, who, when negated by hundreds of scriptural citations, remains as that which is to be indicated through figurative function (lakṣaṇā); though difficult to be made known, You shine forth as consisting of supreme bliss. || 3 ||

"Not an animal," they say: the scriptures or those who know them declare that Your form, the Supreme Brahman, is not an animal such as a beast or a bird; nor is it a mortal, a human, a god (*sura*), an asura, or a woman. Body is said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of female, male, and neuter. *Dravya* refers to objects of the senses; *karman* refers to the organs of action; *jāti* refers to [caste] such as Brahminhood; *guṇa* refers to the organs of perception; *sat* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); and *asat* refers to the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Because gods and others are limited and because bodies and such are insentient, these [scriptures] do not declare them to be His essential nature; rather, when such negations have been made through the Nigama (the Veda), that which remains as the ultimate limit must be [His nature]. For this very reason, it shines forth as consisting of supreme bliss and having the form of supreme joy, being made known and established by hundreds of Nigamas and Upaniṣads through the function of indication (lakṣaṇā-vṛtti) without the relationship of the denoted and the denoter (vācyavācaka-sambandha), albeit with great difficulty.

In this context, since the primary meaning of the prohibitive statement is sublated by its own negation, the function [of the word] toward that object which serves as its limit is the function of indication (lakṣaṇā). Thus, the meaning is that the Supreme Brahman—which is being presented as "I am Brahman" and which constitutes your very nature as being devoid of action—shines forth. || 3 ||
Now, he establishes that the remainder of what was negated is "without remainder" by virtue of being the witness of all:

Reflected in Māyā, you create the entire universe—consisting of the divisions of Mahat, Ahaṅkāra, and the Tanmātras, as well as the collection of elements and the senses—which is like a dream or a mental construction.
Having again withdrawn everything through your own power of Time, like a tortoise its limbs, you shine, free from darkness, while profound obscurity arises; salutations to You!

Regarding the phrase "in Māyā": when Māyā exists as distinct from yourself, you—reflected by the power of consciousness (cicchakti)—create the entire universe through the principle of Mahat, the various forms of ego (ahaṅkāra) consisting of the rājasa, tāmasa, and sāttvika types, the five subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, the gross elements (bhūtas), the eleven organs, and by the word "etcetera," even the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth. The phrase "like a dream or a mental construction" means that this waking world is false, because it is subject to appearance and disappearance, just like a dream or a mental fabrication.

Furthermore, just as a tortoise, after sporting for a long time, withdraws its limbs back into itself and becomes silent, so too, having withdrawn everything through the power of Time (*kāla-śakti*), You shine by Yourself in Your own essential nature. Thus, because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-existent in the beginning and at the end, its falsity (*mithyātva*) has been stated even with respect to the middle. Because the Lord exists in the beginning, middle, and end as the illuminator of the phenomenal world, His status as the Witness (*sākṣitva*) and His eternity have been stated. Now, [an objection]:

To the objection, "In the event of universal destruction, why should even the Lord not perish?", he says: "profound" (*gambhīre*). This means [the Lord] is born within the profound, inconceivable darkness of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The intention is this: when deep sleep occurs as the dissolution of everything, the ignorance denoted by the word "darkness," which is the cause of the entire world, does not undergo dissolution; otherwise, there would be no further arising of the world, and the reflection of one who has awakened—"I slept happily, I knew nothing"—would be untenable.

And thus, even then, you shine as free from darkness, as the witness of ignorance by virtue of being a light that is eternally risen and never-setting; for the meaning is that without a seer, the object of sight cannot be established. To You who are such, I bow. ||4||

Now, one might raise the objection that the Lord’s status as the cause of the universe is unestablished due to disagreements among disputants; in response to this, he states that the disagreement concerns only the terminology, not the referent itself: "O Blessed One! They address You—the single cause of the universe who is conceived in every way as being identical with all things—as 'Śabdabrahman', as 'Karma', as the 'Aṇu', and as 'Time'."

O Kṛṣṇa! That reality which is sung in the Vedāntas as the Supreme Person, whose nature is consciousness, and who by mere glance brings about the transformations of primordial nature—to You, that [reality], obeisance. ||5||

Regarding the term *śabdabrahman*: proponents declare You alone, the cause of the universe and the source of the world, by means of such words as "the Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*). Some declare that the Word-Brahman is the cause of the world; some say it is karma, namely the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings; others say it is the atom (*paramāṇu*); and still others say it is Time (*kāla*). The sense is that You alone are the referent of all these terms. The reason for this is stated: "by virtue of Your being the self of all," that is, because You consist of everything (*sakalamayatayā*).

The meaning is that, in every way, according to those respective philosophical systems (*darśana*), [the world] is imagined as being of the nature of *Śabdabrahman* and so forth, and thus it is you alone who are being conceptualized. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "by the Vedāntas. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "But that reality which is designated by the Vedāntas as the Supreme Person, the conscious Self (*paracidātmā*), is declared to be the creator of both primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*) merely by its presence. Here, "Person" (*puruṣa*) refers to what was previously stated: "You are reflected in Māyā"; "Supreme" (*para*) means devoid of connection to Māyā; "conscious" (*cit*) means pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*); and "Self" (*ātman*) means that which pervades all.

That whose designation is by words such as "Puruṣa" and so forth is thus described. That indeed is that very reality, the Supreme Brahman. By mere observation—that is, by the mere impelling of Māyā—it acts; Māyā is the root-prakṛti, and its modification is the effect, the world. It is so called because it creates that [world]. Now, one might ask: how can Brahman create the effect of Prakṛti? It is said in reply:

Just as a king performs his work through a female doorkeeper who has come into his presence merely by his glance, so too, without possessing the primary agency characterized by being the locus of an action and its fruit inherent in itself, the Lord’s authorship of the world occurs through the medium of *prakṛti*. This is the sense. O Kṛṣṇa! salutations be to You who are such. || 5 ||

Now, raising the doubt as to what this *mūlaprakṛti* (root-nature) is, he states that it is the power (*śakti*) of the Lord, consisting of both knowledge and ignorance, which is indefinable in terms of being or non-being:

"That which is called ignorance (*avidyā*)— which, like the notion of a snake in place of a rope, manifests the appearance of the entire visible world— is indeed not definable as being, nor as non-being, nor as both being and non-being."

Salutations to You, by the mere fragments of whose words regarding the Vedas even the state of "knowledge" (vidyātva) is attained; for upon obtaining the sight of Your compassionate face, that knowledge becomes an axe capable of felling the vast forest of saṃsāra. || 6 ||

Regarding the phrase "as being existent" (*sattvena*): that ignorance whose existence ceases upon the arising of knowledge cannot be said to be "existent," because its existence and manifestation are untenable. Nor is it "non-existent," for it is utterly untenable to claim that the very same thing is both existent and non-existent due to contradiction. Therefore, ignorance is not definable in terms of existence, non-existence, or both; it is that whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) is "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*), meaning it cannot be precisely articulated. If one then asks, "In that case, does it not exist? he says, "No—it exists. (*asau*).

The meaning is that since it is established by universal experience that "I am ignorant," it is impossible not to admit this [ignorance]. This ignorance—which, like the notion of a snake in a rope or the delusion of a serpent in a rope—brings about the manifestation of the entire visible world, the whole universe; and which produces for the individual soul (jīva) the state of worldly existence consisting of dwelling in suffering, in the form of egoism and possessiveness (*ahaṃ-mama-abhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth. This is the sense.
