Obeisance to that Lord, the flow and stream of whose grace—upon its attainment—causes even that very ignorance, through mere hearing of the fragments of Vedic declarations (the slight portions of Vedāntic statements), to attain the nature of knowledge; having become the form of knowledge, it serves as an axe for the immediate and swift cutting and splitting of the forest of saṃsāra. To Him, obeisance! || 1 ||
Thus, the causality of Brahman, which is established by its very nature, has been stated. Now, its identity with the world is declared through its non-difference from it:
"When the reality is contemplated—just as gold is in ornaments, or clay in objects such as pots and bowls—your non-dual form flashes forth even now."
O Kṛṣṇa, salutations to You, who—just as the dreamer awakens, as darkness vanishes, or as a worn-out rope is seen [to be a snake]—clearly unfolds upon the attainment of true knowledge. || 7 ||

Regarding the phrase "in ornaments": that body, known as the Supreme Brahman, which is the non-dual cause of the universe, even now—at this very time of the world's maintenance—manifests within the world, with respect to the world. To the objection that no one has the experience "this is Brahman," he says: "when the reality is contemplated. That is, when the ultimate reality is being reflected upon and investigated.

The meaning is that for one who reflects upon the fact that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*), the world is its effect (*kārya*), and the non-difference between cause and effect is established in the scriptures, the realization that "all this is indeed Brahman" certainly arises. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as in the case of ornaments," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: just as gold shines through its transformations such as bracelets and earrings, or as clay persists in objects like jars and bowls, so too, when effects such as bracelets are fashioned from gold and the like, there arises a cognition in the form of direct experience that "this is indeed gold. Furthermore, upon the attainment of knowledge—that is, the realization of Brahman—the cessation of ignorance causes [Brahman] to blossom clearly; it shines forth as the undivided Brahman, having abandoned the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Herein lies the illustration: "as in a dream."

The meaning is as follows: just as when a dreamer awakens, there is the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) imagined through ignorance; and just as when darkness is dispelled by a lamp or similar light, there is the dissolution of a snake imagined through that ignorance by means of the knowledge of the old dust; so it is exactly thus. O Kṛṣṇa! "Salutation to You" is the construction [of the verse] for Him whose body expands in the manner described. || 7 ||
Having thus praised its essential nature through the distinction between the manifold (saprapañca) and the non-manifold (niṣprapañca), he praises it as the controller of all:
Out of fear of whom the sun rises, the fire burns, and the wind blows; likewise, out of fear of whom the lotus-born Brahmā and others, at their appointed times, again gather their due offerings.
O Kṛṣṇa! To You, the Controller of the universe—who first established us in our own positions and later even displaced us from them—we too offer our salutation. || 8 ||

"Out of fear of whom... means: out of fear of whom the sun rises; whom the lotus-born Brahmā and others—who offer the customary oblations and perform worship according to their respective offices—first elevated to their own abodes such as Satyaloka, and who later, at the end of the two *parārdhas*, will cause them to fall from those positions; to Him, the Controller of the universe, the Regulator even of Brahmā and the rest, the Lord of All—to You, O Kṛṣṇa! we too offer our salutation. || 8 ||
Furthermore,

he meditates upon the three worlds as consisting of the three *guṇas*, as the single referent of the three syllables, as the unified form of the three lords, and as having a nature praised by all three Vedas.

I constantly worship you with three distinct modes of yoga— you who know the three states, who are served by those born in the three ages, who have traversed the universe in three strides, and who are devoid of differentiation throughout the three periods of time.

Regarding the phrase "the three worlds": this refers to Him who contemplates and, by necessity, creates the three worlds—which consist of the three *guṇas* (*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*) and are distinct from one another according to the varying proportions of these qualities—as the primary signification (*vācya*), that is, the denoted meaning, of the imperishable *praṇava*; He whose essential nature is the unity of the three lords (*trīśānāṃ aikyaṃ*), namely the three forms (*trimūrti*). This is in accordance with the scriptural statement: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are indeed the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the Supreme. Furthermore, He is He whose form is sung of and expounded by the three Vedas (*tribhir nigamaiḥ*).

He is the knower (*vidan*), one who knows the three states—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—and is thus the witness of the three states. He "enjoys birth" (*juṣata janima*) in the other three ages—the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas—because there was no need for an incarnation during the Kṛta Yuga as all beings had already accomplished their purpose. He is he by whom the universe has been traversed (*krāntam viśvam*) through the three steps (*tribhiḥ kramaiḥ*).

I worship You—who are devoid of division and non-dual throughout the three periods of time (past, future, and present), or who are free from the six modifications of existence such as "being born" and "existing"—constantly with the three distinct paths of yoga: karma, jñāna, and bhakti. 9.
Moreover:

Victorious is Your body—truthful, pure, awakened, eternally liberated, desireless, free from dualities, changeless, and the foundational substratum that manifests the entire multitude of auspicious qualities;
it is rootless, stainless, resplendent with boundless majesty, and an incomparable, intense radiance of supreme bliss for the unattached sages who are dissolved within it. (10)

"Truth. Your form—that is, your essential nature—is victorious; it shines forth with manifest, unsurpassed excellence. "Truth" and the other terms are qualifiers of that form. It is *satya* (truth), because it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*) that bestows existence upon that which is unreal. It is *vibuddha* (awakened), established through its own self-luminosity. It is *nityamukta* (eternally liberated), for if liberation were something produced, it would follow that it is not ultimately real. It is *nirīha* (inactive).

It is devoid of agency, enjoyership, and so forth; it is free from dualities and non-dual; it is changeless, being devoid of transformations such as modification and the like; it is the manifestation—that is, the source—of all the multitudes of qualities such as forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, and sovereignty, for it is upon that which these great qualities arise; it is rootless and causeless; it is stainless, being free from defects such as passion, and because it is the light of consciousness, it has dispelled ignorance.

It shines with boundless majesty, endowed with a glory that is not limited by time or space; it is firmly established, deeply absorbed in the internal meditative absorption of detached sages; and within it resides incomparable supreme bliss, as well as intense light and dense awakening.

Now, with the intention that there is no further cycle of rebirth for those who have attained the Supreme Brahman of the nature previously described, he prays for the cessation of the fear of wandering in the wheel of time: "The wheel of time, difficult to resist, with twelve spokes, encircled by three hundred and sixty joints,
revolving with a cruel velocity, which seizes and hurls the world about in an instant— "

O Viṣṇu! O ocean of compassion! O Lord of the City of Wind! May Your discus, which takes the form of Time, afflict him [the enemy], but not me, who relies solely upon Your feet; protect me from the flood of all diseases. 11.

"Difficult to ward off," it says: O Viṣṇu! let that wheel of yours—the wheel consisting of the year, and not [the wheel of time]—not afflict me; let it not cause the suffering of saṃsāra. Of what nature is it? Difficult to ward off (durvāram), unpreventable by anyone. It possesses twelve spokes, corresponding to the twelve months of the year. It is surrounded (abhivītam) and pervaded by three hundred and sixty joints (parvan), which are the days (dinaiḥ) and the transitions between the quarters (dhārā-sandhibhiḥ). It is whirling (saṃbhrāmyat), revolving incessantly.
[He saw him] running with great speed, moment after moment, snatching away the world and carrying it off to lead it out of sight.
Thus ends the ninety-first decad (consisting of ninety-one verses), which describes the origination of the universe and so forth from Brahman, whose nature consists of truth, knowledge, and the rest.
Now, the majesty of the Blessed One is described in nine verses:
Who indeed can recount the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu? And who can measure the particles of dust of the earth, by whose three strides alone the three worlds are measured and rejoice in full prosperity?
To that Lord who sustains all universes, the supreme abode, I shall proceed with devotion.
Where its devotees rejoice, and where there is a flowing stream of the nectar-essence of its sap. || 1 ||

Regarding the words "of Viṣṇu": who indeed could describe or count His heroic deeds and majesty? No one at all. And who measures the particles of dust of the earth? Even that, no one can do. Yet by the three strides—the placement of three steps—of that Viṣṇu, the triple world, the three realms, was encompassed and measured. Therefore, having taken [the kingdom] from Bali, He rejoices in full prosperity through the protection of His own arms, while remaining satisfied with all people.

Furthermore, may I go to—that is, attain—the beloved abode of that Viṣṇu who sustains and upholds all the worlds by his yogic sovereignty; [an abode] where his devotees revel. There, in Vaikuṇṭha, flows a stream of nectar—the essence of liberation—which is like honey dripping from every side. || 1 ||

He who, with a devoted soul, offers oblations and other gifts in the worship of sacrifices and the like to Viṣṇu— the primordial creator of all, who becomes ever-new at every moment, and the Lord of prosperity— or he who here describes the great birth of Kṛṣṇa and others; to him, being pleased and filled with glory, He shall swiftly grant that goal which is to be attained at the end.

"To the Primordial One" (ādyāya): to Him who exists from the beginning, and for that very reason, to the Maker of All, the Cause of Everything, who is ever-new at every moment—ever-fresh to His worshippers—and to the Lord of Vibhūti, that is, Śrī. "One whose self—that is, the mind—is endowed with devotion characterized by love."

He who, being such as described, offers oblations and other gifts to Viṣṇu in the form mentioned above during sacrifices, worship, and the like; or he who describes the great, worshipful birth or incarnation of the Great Viṣṇu, such as that of Kṛṣṇa—he alone is a true devotee here, delighted by the experience of desired happiness and filled with glory. At the fall of the body, he shall swiftly attain—that is, reach—that state, the world of Vaikuṇṭha, without delay for another birth; no one else.
Since this is so, he says, "Therefore, praise Him alone":
O praisers, O lords among poets! Just as you indeed perceive Him here, even so proclaim clearly the essence of the Veda through the accounts of the divine play assumed for the sake of living beings.
Knowing that his names bring all happiness, you should proclaim them:
"O Viṣṇu! Through the chanting and other acts of praise unto You, may I indeed attain realization of the Great Reality."

"O you who are praisers"—those here who are lords among poets, skilled in poetic art, and for that very reason devoted to the praise of kings and others: indeed, you, just as you perceive and understand, so too should you offer hymns of praise to that Viṣṇu through his incarnations and the divine sports (*līlā*) he has undertaken and accepted. [Praise him] as the manifest essence of the Veda, established by valid means of knowledge, and its primary subject matter.

O you who know! O knowers of the supreme truth! Since the names of this Viṣṇu bestow all happiness and grant liberation, therefore, chant them aloud. O Viṣṇu! Through the chanting and other acts of devotion toward You, the Great One, may I indeed attain the awakening to reality, the knowledge of the truth.
(3) Furthermore, always contemplate in your mind the deeds of Viṣṇu, by which He established the laws of righteousness.
He who, acting as Indra’s servant and like his dear friend, has spread security for all;
whom those perfected in yoga constantly behold as the manifestation of the supreme state; and whom the foremost of Brahmins, ever vigilant and having offered many hymns of praise, illuminate. (4)

Regarding the phrase "of Viṣṇu": you should always behold—that is, contemplate—in your minds the deeds, the actions, of Viṣṇu. Those deeds consist of the subduing of the wicked, the establishment of the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and the gathering of the world; through these acts, Viṣṇu bound together the *dharmas*—meaning those things conducive to worldly prosperity and the supreme good—with their respective qualified practitioners. This is the meaning of "behold those deeds."

This Viṣṇu is like a servant to Indra—who, having been appointed by his own self to protect the three worlds—because Indra, being unable to effect the protection of the world himself, performs it through him. For this very reason, the Blessed One has performed those deeds as if he were his dear friend, owing to this great service rendered to him; the meaning is that he is a bringer of security (*kṣemakārī*), whose nature is thus to protect the world.

Furthermore, the sages who have attained perfection in yoga—having conquered all qualities such as sovereignty through meditative absorption—constantly behold that supreme state, the place of attainment which is free from the connection with *māyā*. That supreme state is qualified as "the perfect light for all. The lords of birds (Garuḍas), being vigilant, intent, and having offered many hymns of praise, illuminate—that is, they manifest—that supreme state by means of praises distinguished as both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*). || 8 ||
O Lord Viṣṇu! Neither one already born nor one currently being born has ever reached the limit of Your greatness; therefore, knowing this, I repeatedly praise Your auspicious names.
I extol You with various hymns of praise—You who dwell in that realm of Vaikuṇṭha, shining resplendently even above these three worlds.

"No one has reached this limit. O Lord! No person, whether already born or currently being born, has ever attained or reached the end of Your greatness. Therefore, knowing what is truly beneficial and having determined that this alone is the highest good, I praise and glorify Your name repeatedly and incessantly. O Viṣṇu! I extol You, whose greatness is unlimited, with various words of hymn; the meaning is that since the mind cannot penetrate Your formless (nirguṇa) nature, I praise You through Your qualified (saguṇa) aspect.
He whose dwelling—his residence—is fashioned in that world of Vaikuṇṭha, which shines brilliantly above this triple-world cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 5 ||
Now he praises the form of Śrī Nārāyaṇa:
"O All-pervading Lord! At the beginning, the waters produced by the creation and so forth placed You within the womb;
there, O Hari who reclines upon the water, all living beings merged into You alone and attained oneness."

O Lord! That single lotus which was placed upon the navel of that Unborn One—whom they call the form of the world, with its petals as the cardinal directions and its pericarp as the golden mountain supporting the earth—was indeed established there.

"Āpaḥ" (the waters). According to the scriptural statement, "In the beginning, He created the waters alone," the waters produced at the time of creation and so forth first placed You within the womb. While You were situated in the midst of those waters, all living beings (jīvas) came together, attained union with You, and became reclined upon You; for at the end of the kalpa, all living beings recline together with Brahmā upon Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who lies upon the waters.

In the navel of that Viṣṇu, who is unborn and reclines upon the waters, there arose a single lotus situated and established. They say that this lotus is the very form of the world. He explains it thus: its petals and leaves are the directions, and its pericarp is the great Meru, the bearer of the golden earth. The meaning is that Śrī Viṣṇu himself, becoming the lotus-born Brahmā, produced the universe through that navel-lotus. || 6 ||
Lamenting those who do not know Viṣṇu in the form described above, he says: "O people, Viṣṇu brought forth this world, yet you do not know him;
for there exists within you something else entirely, which is the very form of Viṣṇu."
Those whose minds are shrouded by illusion, which resembles a mist, and who are deluded by name and form;
who are satisfied with the singular pleasure of vital breath, and are devoted to horses, chariots, and sacrifices—alas, they have no desire for Mukunda.

"O people! O worldlings! Do you not know that Viṣṇu who generated this manifest world? Furthermore, there exists within you another form of Viṣṇu, distinct from that [first one], which is situated inside your bodies and is characterized by the qualities of worldly existence. Alas, you do not even know that! Why do you not know? To this, he says: "By mist (nīhāra...)."

Those whose minds are enveloped and pervaded by Māyā, which is like frost in its power of obscuration, and who are thus deluded by names and forms—identifying with false things such as the body through the notions of "I" and "mine"—wander about devoted to sacrifices, intent on rites for desired fruits, being satisfied solely by the pleasure of the vital breaths (the senses) and desiring the happiness of heaven and the like. Alas! Oh, what a tragedy that there is no desire for Mukunda, Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation! 7.
Then he contemplates the formless [reality] as the embodied form of the universe:
"O You who possess a thousand heads, eyes, and feet, You indeed carry the complete universe; even while remaining beyond it, You shine within the limited space of the heart."

O Supreme Person! You are all that has been and all that is to be; moreover, having entered into the body, senses, and so forth, you alone experience the essence of immortal bliss due to your transcendence.

Regarding the phrase "of the heads": You, the presiding deity of Virāj, bear thousands of heads, eyes, and feet. Because there are many cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), there is a multiplicity of heads and other limbs belonging to the Satyaloka and other realms situated within them. Thus, having completely filled and pervaded the entire universe—the totality of cosmic eggs—and even while standing beyond that cosmic egg, You shine within the limited aperture, the extremely contracted interior of the mind, the space of the heart. O Supreme Person! You are the past, the future, and indeed all that exists.

Furthermore, you who, having entered into the body, senses, and so forth, experience the flavors of sense objects—you, being risen above those very things, likewise experience the flavor of the bliss of immortality, which is supreme bliss. (8)
Although you assume the form of the three worlds, you nevertheless exist as the essence of infinite pure knowledge that has emerged from them; such is indeed your greatness—what more need be said?

Only a small portion of you is perceived as the entirety of the universe, appearing as a mere third part; yet above that, you shine forth as the vast, dense, and blissful essence—to you, we offer our salutation.

"O Infinite One! That you, though assuming a form consisting of the three worlds, remain outside it as the pure self of consciousness—that indeed is Your majesty. What else? Nothing at all. Furthermore, only a small portion of You—merely a quarter—is seen in the form of the entire universe, that is, as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). Whereas Your form, which consists of intense bliss and is the nature of supreme joy, shines beyond that cosmic egg in the external region, being for the most part three-quarters, that is, generally fit for the designation of 'three-quarters'."
To him, whose self is undivided. ||9||

Thus, beginning with the verse "In whom... and continuing for twenty verses, [the author], while pursuing his meditation upon the Blessed One through the distinction between His qualified (saguṇa) and unqualified (nirguṇa) aspects under the guise of praise, begins to direct his mind toward His desired form, apprehending his own lack of qualification therein:
"Your true nature is unmanifest and most difficult to attain; yet that very same nature is pure, consisting solely of *sattva*.
And this manifest form is also clearly like the waves of an ocean of the nectar of immortality."

O Lord of the City of Wind (Kāśī)! I take refuge in Your form, which is most excellent and beloved, and which captivates the heart here by the very essence of its virtues; O Kṛṣṇa, protect me from disease! 10.

Regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*): that unmanifest is called *avyakta* because it is not manifested by anything else; it is the nature of Brahman, which is most difficult to comprehend, being exceedingly hard to grasp or to attain with ease, as the Lord has said: "The suffering of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater. However, that very nature of yours, consisting of pure *sattva*, is manifest and can be known.

Moreover, this very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others is like a wave in the ocean of the nectar of immortality; it is comparable to a wave in the ocean of the nectar of Brahman-bliss and is to be cherished by the mouth. Since it is thus, therefore, I take refuge in that most excellent and beloved form—the one that captivates the mind through those very "flavors" (rasas), such as affection for devotees, which belong to the Blessed Lord because they are worthy of being tasted—and I begin to praise or meditate upon it.
O Lord of the City of Wind (Pavana-pura-pati)! O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Protect me from disease, characterized here as worldly existence. ||10||
Thus ends the ninety-ninth decade, the description of the majesty of the Blessed One.

Having thus beheld the Lord—as if before his very eyes—with His specific limbs, dress, and other attributes clearly manifest, having descended into the space of his heart through the ripening of devotion characterized by love, which has been nourished by the remembrance, chanting, and other practices concerning the deeds of the Lord’s incarnations, he praises Him according to his experience:
"Before me I see a splendor, free from the allure of any partiality..."

Thereafter, I was bathed in nectar by that [Nārada] as he manifested the divine form of Kṛṣṇa, charming at the onset of youth and enveloping my limbs with horripilation through the relish of the essence of supreme bliss; and I was surrounded by Nārada and others, along with the circles of beautiful maidens who were the radiant Upaniṣads. || 1 ||

"Agra" means the circle of light (*tejaḥ-prabhā-maṇḍala*). Following that, I behold a divine, sattvic, and brilliantly radiant splendor; a certain form sixteen years of age, beautiful at the onset of youth, in which is the attire associated with that [age] from childhood up to the sixteenth year. It is "surrounded by" (*parivārita*) its own retinue. By the phrase "by the circles of the beautiful Upaniṣad-maidens," this is understood: Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman, the Gopīs are the Upaniṣads that expound Him, Śrī Nārada and others are His instructors, and the qualified observer is the seeker. ||1||
He describes that very thing called "the divine adolescent attire":

[a crown] with a dark-blue luster, its tips curled, joined by a thick and long creeper-like band with beautiful curves, delightful with jeweled crest-ornaments, and adorned with networks of peacock feathers tossed by the wind.

I behold your broad mass of hair adorned with a garland of Mandāra flowers, and also your exquisitely beautiful brow, which bears a smooth, white vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) like the path of the crescent moon. || 2 ||

"Blue-hued" means dense and thick. "With rising moons" refers to those possessing variegated colors on their shining upper portions. "Adorned with a garland of Mandāra flowers" means encircled by a fresh wreath fashioned from celestial blossoms. || 2 ||
He praises the pair of lotus-eyes as they were experienced:
"O Lord! May this pair of Your eyes—delightful with the playful movements of gentle waves from the ocean of full compassion; shimmering with a row of dark and glossy eyelashes;

possessing a dense luster, shaped like the petals of a large, reddish lotus, and with pupils so charmingly beautiful; and which cools the world with the play of its light of mercy—be cast upon me, who am without a protector. (3)
"Dear" means: in one who is helpless and without refuge. || 3 ||
May his face shine upon me—his nose lofty and radiant; his cheeks gleaming like mirrors of sapphire; illuminated by a pair of beautiful makara-shaped earrings swinging from his dangling ear-lobes;
its interior of bimba-like lips glowing with the redder luster of his emerging rows of teeth; and rendered most cool by a gentle smile that overflows with affection. 4.

"Uttaṅga" means: shining upon the cheeks—the regions of the temples—which gleam like mirrors made of emerald or sapphire; and radiant—that which has the nature of illuminating—by means of the pair of jeweled earrings shaped like crocodiles, which swing back and forth due to the dual forms of the original and reflected images [of the earrings] moving to and fro. || 4 ||

Taking up the bamboo flute held by Your arm—resplendent with jeweled bracelets and possessing a coral-like hand—with its surface variegated by the contact of fingers whose nails emit spreading rays of light, and manifesting a most sweet and blossoming passion within Your lotus-face, drench the pathways of my ears with the nectar of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahma), which cools the entire world. 5.

"With his two arms" means: variegated in color (*śārāṃ*) due to the contact of fingers whose rays of light from the nails are spread out; this is an adverbial modifier meaning "in which there is a very sweet, blossoming, and manifest passion (*rāga*), that is, a particular mode of singing. [He sang] with the nectar of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahmāmṛtaiḥ*), that is, with the nectars of sound (*nādāmṛtaiḥ*), which were being manifested or made manifest. || 5 ||

I meditate upon that jeweled necklace hanging upon your chest, which reddens your tender throat with the radiance of the Kaustubha gem rising upward; which is as beautiful as the Śrīvatsa mark on your breast, spreading out with the impact of its most tremulous rays; and which, like a wild garland of blossoming sprouts in various colors, has hovering bees clinging to it as it hangs from your heart.
"Rising up... [I] contemplate the expansion of laughter as a network of pearl garlands, and likewise a jeweled necklace upon the breasts of the swaying *lolambā* bees. (6)

On his limbs, with five-fold unguents whose exceedingly blooming fragrance attracts all people, he bears a slender waist-line that holds within it the vast expanse of the three worlds as if they were merged therein;
he wears yellow garments resembling blazing gold heated upon a diamond-stone.
We meditate upon you, adorned with a girdle of radiant gems and tinkling bells.

"O limb! [This refers to: he by whom people were attracted by an exceeding fragrance that blossomed and pervaded him through the five-fold unguents such as yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*) and cow-gall (*gorocanā*). "Though slender, containing many worlds"—that is, though it contained many *brahmāṇḍas* within it. The meaning is this: although this very *brahmāṇḍa* resides within the belly of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, nevertheless, the manifestation of those who were present at that time within this *brahmāṇḍa* as having their own physical forms in the manner of "this-ness" (*idantayā*) is due to the sovereign power of the Lord’s yogic mastery.

And thus, the reduction of the middle row to thinness is not a burden for him at all. Regarding the term "Śakrāśma" (diamond): the sense is that because the Lord’s form is dark like sapphire and his yellow garment resembles gold, it has attained a state of secondary radiance (*parabhāga*). [The face is] made manifest by brilliant rays—that is, by the luster of the jewels. || 7 ||

I worship your two thighs, O fair-limbed one, which possess a thick and smooth luster, which steal the heart of Lakṣmī, and whose forms are surely perpetually veiled by yellow garments out of fear of disturbing the universe;

and I worship your two knees, which cast a shadow like the ocean that holds the entire collection of objects for those who bow before you, and your two shanks, which are beautiful and gradually broad.

Regarding the thighs: fearing that they might cause universal agitation by bringing the beholder under their spell through their world-transcending loveliness; they possess a splendor like the radiance of a casket (*samudga*)—a container—holding the entire collection of all objects of human pursuit (*puruṣārtha*). || 8 ||

[The feet] which speak of the auspiciousness of serving at their lotus-feet as if through the sweet sounds of anklets; which act like the tortoise supporting Mount Mandara for the minds of prostrate devotees sinking in delusion;
and which, by the moonlight of their high, copper-red, shining toenails, [bring relief] to those who have taken refuge.
I offer my salutation to that row of auspicious fingers which destroys the darkness of suffering. || 9 ||

"Mañjīra" refers to the one who acts as a tortoise for the uprooting of Mount Mandara—the mind—of those supplicants who, seeking nectar, are sinking in the ocean of delusion; she is the destroyer of the darkness of affliction and the darkness of ignorance. ||9||

O Lord! Your foot-base is exceedingly sweet to the senses of those who possess liberation, it is the abode of devotees, and it is a sprout on the wish-fulfilling tree that rains down all desires. O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Pāṭaliputra, ocean of compassion, may it dwell eternally within my heart.
Having taken away all sufferings without remainder, may it bestow the splendor of the mass of supreme bliss. || 10 ||

"Of the lords of yogis" means: among the limbs of You, who are meditated upon by the lords of yogis, [this limb] is the most exceedingly sweet. For those who possess liberation, it is the "abode," meaning the refuge; and it is "mokṣa," the splendor consisting of a mass of supreme bliss. || 10 ||

Having thus concluded the praise, and having raised the doubt that defects or other flaws might have occurred therein, he offers it to the Lord for the sake of ensuring its perfection, and prays for the fruit of reading and hearing for both the speaker and the listener:
"O Lord of the Universe! If this has been recited here without knowing Your greatness, please forgive it.
And may this hymn, consisting of more than a thousand verses, lead to Your grace."

May this Nārāyaṇīya, which is twofold—abounding both in the Vedic scriptures and in descriptions of its praiseworthiness from birth, as well as in its divine play-incarnations—here bestow long life, health, and happiness. (11)

Regarding the phrase "not having known": the *Nārāyaṇīya* is twofold, because it was composed concerning Nārāyaṇa and because it was proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa. If it is argued that this hymn—whether enjoined or unenjoined—is being offered so that it may lead to grace from You, [the author] says "in the Śrutis" to show that it is indeed enjoined by the Vedas.

There exists a formal description (*vidhi*) of the Lord as being worthy of praise through His births and incarnations; by that, this hymn is "expanded" or pervaded. Alternatively, this hymn is expanded by describing through other words—such as "O you who praise"—that quality of being praiseworthy which belongs to Him by birth in the Vedas, as well as by His playful incarnations (*līlā-avatāras*). May this [hymn] bestow long life and health upon the speaker and the listeners here, and finally grant them happiness and liberation. || 11 || 38 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and first decad, the description of the feet beginning with the hair.
These verses, which describe the eightfold miseries as found in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*,
have been composed by me in the form of a commentary on the hymn.
This work was not composed by me; rather, it has been brought forth by those two who reside within my heart, by whose names this hymn is esteemed among the people from time to time.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the commentary on the Nārāyaṇīya-stotra titled Bhaktimīmāṃsā.
And the noble treatise is completed.
